docs.title: General Debug Checklist
docs.text:
Step 1: Check status_code
    → 2xx? Continue
    → 4xx? Your request is wrong
    → 5xx? The server is broken, retry

Step 2: Check Content-Type
    → application/json? You can call response.json()
    → text/html? The server returned an HTML error page

Step 3: Look at the first 300 characters of the body
    → response.text[:300]

Step 4: Check what Python sent
    → response.request.url
    → response.request.headers
    → response.request.body

Step 5: Bypass Python
    → curl -v "https://..." in a terminal
    → ping domain.com
    → telnet host port

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Term Definition HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol — a text-based L7 protocol Stateless Every request is isolated; the server does not remember previous ones TCP Handshake 3-way (SYN-SYN/ACK-ACK) connection establishment TLS Transport Layer Security — HTTPS encryption DNS Domain Name System — converting a domain into an IP PreparedRequest An internal requests object: a ready HTTP byte string Blocking I/O recv() stops the Python process until the response arrives Serialization Python dict → JSON string → bytes Deserialization bytes → JSON string → Python dict Timeout tuple (connect_timeout, read_timeout) in seconds raise_for_status() Raises HTTPError if status_code >= 400 Session An object that keeps headers/cookies/auth between requests Retry / Backoff Repeated attempts with a growing pause between them Rate Limiting The server limits the number of requests (429 Too Many Requests) Thundering Herd All retries fire at the same time → server overload Circuit Breaker A pattern: after N errors — fail immediately, do not retry

Documentation for Lesson 31 · Module 4 · Python Networking Course

docs.title: Lesson: Network Foundation — From the Wire to Python
docs.text: Before learning Django, you need to understand where your code lives. Django is just one layer in a large stack. This document describes all the layers below it.

docs.title: Why learn this?
docs.text: When you run python manage.py runserver and open the browser, dozens of operations take place: a DNS query, a TCP connection, HTTP negotiation, request parsing. Most developers do not know what happens before the request reaches their Python code. That is the cause of most production bugs.

docs.title: 1. What is a network?
docs.text: A network is a system in which two or more computers can exchange data. Physically, it is wires, optical fiber, a Wi-Fi signal. Logically, it is a set of protocols (agreements about a language).

docs.title: Levels of abstraction (the OSI model — simplified)
docs.text:
Layer What it does Example Physical Transmits bits Cable, Wi-Fi Data link Addressing within a local network MAC address Network Routing between networks IP Transport Reliable transmission TCP, UDP Application Protocols for programs HTTP, DNS, SSH

Key idea: Each layer solves one task and does not know the details of the other layers.

docs.title: 2. IP address — where a computer lives
docs.text: An IP address (Internet Protocol Address) is a unique numeric identifier of every device on a network.

docs.title: IPv4
docs.text:
192.168.1.105

Four numbers (0–255) separated by dots. About 4 billion addresses in total. Almost exhausted.

docs.title: IPv6
docs.text:
2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334

A 128-bit address. A practically unlimited space.

docs.title: Public vs Private IP
docs.text:
Type Example Visible from the Internet Public 104.21.14.55 Yes Private 192.168.1.x, 10.0.0.x No (only within the local network)

When you open localhost:8000, you are addressing 127.0.0.1, the address of the machine itself (loopback).

docs.title: 3. DNS — the phone book of the Internet
docs.text:
Computers communicate through IP addresses. But people remember google.com, not 142.250.74.46.

DNS (Domain Name System) is a distributed system that translates domains into IP addresses.

docs.title: How DNS resolution happens
docs.text:
1. You type github.com into the browser
  2. The browser checks its local cache (does it already know this address?)
  3. If not, it asks a DNS Resolver (usually your ISP's or 8.8.8.8)
  4. The resolver asks a Root DNS Server (which only knows the TLD servers)
  5. The root server points to the TLD server (for .com — Verisign)
  6. The TLD server points to the Authoritative DNS (where the real github.com records are stored)
  7. The Authoritative DNS returns the IP: 140.82.121.4
  8. The browser caches the answer and connects to the server

docs.title: DNS records
docs.text:
Type What it does Example A Domain → IPv4 github.com → 140.82.121.4 AAAA Domain → IPv6 CNAME Alias to another domain www.example.com → example.com MX Where the email server is TXT Arbitrary text (SPF, verification)

Real backend: When deploying a Django project, you buy a domain and add an A record pointing to the IP of your cloud VM.

Why does a site load faster the second time? — The DNS answer is cached for the TTL (Time To Live). The repeated query is served straight from the cache.

docs.title: 4. Ports — apartments in a building
docs.text:
An IP address delivers a packet to the right computer. But one computer may run dozens of programs. A port specifies which program the traffic is meant for.

192.168.1.100:80   ← web server (Nginx)
192.168.1.100:5432 ← PostgreSQL
192.168.1.100:22   ← SSH
192.168.1.100:8000 ← Django runserver

docs.title: Well-known ports
docs.text:
Port Protocol Usage 80 HTTP Web (unencrypted) 443 HTTPS Web (with TLS) 22 SSH Secure access to a server 5432 PostgreSQL Database 6379 Redis Cache / broker 25 SMTP Email 53 DNS DNS queries

Real backend: If you start two Django projects at the same time on port 8000, the second one will print Address already in use. The OS cannot bind one port to two processes.

docs.title: 5. TCP — reliable delivery
docs.text: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides guaranteed and ordered delivery of data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Data is split into packets (chunks). Each packet: - has a sequence number - may travel along different routes across the Internet - may arrive out of order

TCP on the receiving side: - checks the sequence numbers - requests retransmission of lost packets - reassembles the packets in the correct order

docs.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
docs.text:
Before sending any data, TCP establishes a connection:

Client → Server: SYN         (Hi, can we talk?)
Server → Client: SYN-ACK     (Yes, I'm ready)
Client → Server: ACK         (Great, let's begin)
         [Connection established]
Client → Server: HTTP GET /  (Now we send the data)

Analogy: Imagine you are mailing a 300-page book one page at a time. The postal service (IP) may send the pages along different routes. Your friend (TCP) looks at the page numbers, puts the book together in order and asks you to resend page 47 if it got lost.

docs.title: UDP — a fast, unreliable alternative
docs.text: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends packets without acknowledgment. It is used where losing a packet is better than a delay: video calls, online games, DNS.

docs.title: 6. HTTP — the language of the web
docs.text: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a text-based application-layer protocol. It describes the format of requests and responses between the browser and the server.

docs.title: Structure of an HTTP request
docs.text:
PATCH /api/users/42/ HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGc...
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Alice"}
Part What it is PATCH Method (action) /api/users/42/ Path (resource) HTTP/1.1 Protocol version Host, Accept... Headers (metadata) {"name": "Alice"} Body (only for POST/PUT/PATCH)

docs.title: HTTP methods
docs.text: Method Purpose Idempotent GET Retrieve a resource Yes POST Create a resource No PUT Replace completely Yes PATCH Partially update No DELETE Delete Yes

docs.title: Structure of an HTTP response
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 48
Set-Cookie: sessionid=abc123; HttpOnly

{"id": 42, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@mail.com"}

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text: Range Meaning Examples 2xx Success 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content 3xx Redirect 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found 4xx Client error 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found 5xx Server error 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable

docs.title: 7. HTTPS and TLS
docs.text: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS (Transport Layer Security). TLS encrypts the data between the client and the server.

docs.title: Why is it needed?
docs.text: Without HTTPS, any node between the client and the server (a router in a café, your ISP) can read your request — including passwords and tokens.

docs.title: TLS Handshake (simplified)
docs.text:
1. Client: "I support TLS 1.3, here is my random key"
  2. Server: "OK, here is my SSL certificate and public key"
  3. Client: "I've verified the certificate (signed by a trusted CA). Generating a session key."
  4. Both sides: "From now on we encrypt everything with the session key"

SSL certificates are issued by trusted organizations (Certificate Authorities): Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, etc. Nginx stores the certificate and performs the TLS handshake before the request reaches Python.

docs.title: 8. Sockets — the foundation of network programming
docs.text: A socket is a bidirectional connection endpoint between two programs. It is a low-level API provided by the operating system.

docs.title: How Python opens a network connection (low level)
docs.text:
import socket

# Server
server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
server.bind(('0.0.0.0', 8080))   # Bind to a port
server.listen(5)                  # Wait for connections
conn, addr = server.accept()      # Blocks until a client connects
data = conn.recv(1024)            # Read the data
conn.send(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\nHello")
conn.close()

# Client
client = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
client.connect(('127.0.0.1', 8080))
client.send(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
response = client.recv(4096)

Django, Flask, FastAPI — all of them ultimately use exactly this mechanism, just with lots of abstractions on top.

docs.title: Unix Domain Sockets
docs.text: In production, Nginx and uWSGI often communicate through a Unix socket (a file in the file system, e.g. /run/django.sock) instead of a network socket. This is faster because it does not go through the network stack.

docs.title: 9. A stateless protocol and session state
docs.text: HTTP is stateless by nature — it has no memory. Every request is completely independent. The server does not remember that you already made a request a second ago.

docs.title: Then how does a site know you are logged in?
docs.text:
Through cookies and sessions:

The flow: 1. You send POST /login/ with your username/password 2. The server checks the data and creates a session in the database with a unique ID 3. The server sends a response with the header Set-Cookie: sessionid=abc123 4. The browser stores the cookie and automatically adds it to every subsequent request: Cookie: sessionid=abc123 5. The server reads sessionid, finds the session in the DB and knows who you are

docs.title: Cookie attributes
docs.text: Attribute What it does HttpOnly JavaScript cannot read it (protection against XSS) Secure Sent only over HTTPS SameSite Protection against CSRF Expires When the cookie becomes invalid

docs.title: 10. Client/Server architecture
docs.text:
In the classic architecture there are two roles:

Role Who What it does Client Browser, mobile app Initiates the request, displays the result Server Nginx, Django, PostgreSQL Passively waits, processes, responds

docs.title: The full request lifecycle (from URL to HTML)
docs.text:
1. The user enters https://shop.example.com/products/
2. DNS: shop.example.com → 203.0.113.10
3. TCP Handshake with the server 203.0.113.10:443
4. TLS Handshake (encryption)
5. HTTP GET /products/ is sent
6. Nginx receives the request
7. Nginx forwards it to uWSGI over a Unix socket
8. uWSGI turns HTTP into a Python dict (WSGI environ)
9. Middleware: SecurityMiddleware → SessionMiddleware → AuthMiddleware
10. Django URL Dispatcher: /products/ → ProductListView
11. View: Product.objects.all() → SQL SELECT → Python objects
12. Template: rendering HTML with the data
13. HttpResponse 200 OK with HTML
14. Nginx sends the response to the client
15. The browser parses the HTML, loads CSS/JS

docs.title: 11. REST API architecture
docs.text: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing APIs.

docs.title: REST principles
docs.text: Principle Explanation Stateless Every request contains all the information it needs Resource-based The URL describes a resource (/users/, /products/42/) HTTP Verbs The action is expressed by the method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) Uniform Interface Standard behavior for all resources

docs.title: REST URL conventions
docs.text:
GET    /api/products/         → list all products
POST   /api/products/         → create a product
GET    /api/products/42/      → get product #42
PUT    /api/products/42/      → fully update product #42
PATCH  /api/products/42/      → partially update product #42
DELETE /api/products/42/      → delete product #42

docs.title: 12. How the backend receives a request — under the hood
docs.text:
What happens at the OS level when an HTTP request arrives:

1. The NIC (network card) receives an electrical signal → turns it into bytes
2. OS: the TCP/IP stack processes the packets → assembles the HTTP request
3. OS: looks at which program is listening on port 80 → it's Nginx
4. OS: copies the data into Nginx's buffer via the recv() system call
5. Nginx: parses the HTTP headers
6. Nginx: looks at the location rules in nginx.conf
7. Nginx: proxy_pass → sends it to unix:/run/django.sock
8. uWSGI: reads from the socket → parses HTTP → builds the WSGI environ dict
9. uWSGI: calls the Django application(environ, start_response)
10. Django: the rest is Python

Key insight: The whole path is a series of byte transformations between different programs via OS buffers. The Python code is the last link in the chain.

docs.title: 1. Blocking requests in synchronous code
docs.text:
# BAD: blocks the whole process for the duration of the HTTP request
import requests

def my_view(request):
    response = requests.get("https://slow-api.example.com/data")  # waits 5 sec
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

# GOOD: async view (Django 3.1+)
import httpx

async def my_view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get("https://slow-api.example.com/data")
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

docs.title: 2. Misunderstanding statelessness
docs.text: Do not keep state in Python global variables — with several workers, each one has its own memory. State must live in the DB or Redis.

docs.title: 3. No HTTPS
docs.text: Never deploy to production without TLS. Session cookies, passwords, tokens — everything travels as plain text.

docs.title: Self-check questions
docs.text:
1. What happens if the DNS server is unavailable? Will the request reach the site?
  2. Why is a TCP handshake needed if you could just send the data right away?
  3. Why are 127.0.0.1 and localhost the same thing?
  4. How does the server know you are logged in if HTTP is stateless?
  5. Why is python manage.py runserver not suitable for production?

sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant Cache as Local OS cache
    participant Resolver as DNS Resolver<br>(ISP / 8.8.8.8)
    participant Root as Root DNS Server
    participant TLD as TLD Server (.com)
    participant Auth as Authoritative DNS<br>(github.com)

    Browser->>Cache: github.com → IP?
    Cache-->>Browser: None (cache is empty)
    Browser->>Resolver: github.com → IP?
    Resolver->>Root: github.com → IP?
    Root-->>Resolver: Ask the TLD for .com
    Resolver->>TLD: github.com → IP?
    TLD-->>Resolver: Ask ns1.p16.dynect.net
    Resolver->>Auth: github.com → IP?
    Auth-->>Resolver: 140.82.121.4 (TTL=60s)
    Resolver-->>Browser: 140.82.121.4
    Note over Browser,Cache: The browser caches the result for TTL seconds
    Browser->>Browser: Connect to 140.82.121.4:443

docs.title: 4. TCP — Three-Way Handshake + HTTP + Teardown
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (Browser)
    participant S as Server (Nginx)

    Note over C,S: Phase 1 — TCP Three-Way Handshake
    C->>S: SYN (seq=100)
    S-->>C: SYN-ACK (seq=200, ack=101)
    C->>S: ACK (ack=201)
    Note over C,S: Connection established ✓

    Note over C,S: Phase 2 — HTTP exchange
    C->>S: HTTP GET /products/ (headers + body)
    Note over S: Nginx processes it, Django generates the response
    S-->>C: HTTP 200 OK + HTML (Content-Length: 4200)

    Note over C,S: Phase 3 — Closing the connection
    C->>S: FIN
    S-->>C: ACK
    S->>C: FIN
    C-->>S: ACK
    Note over C,S: Connection closed

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as 👤 User
    participant B as Browser
    participant DNS as DNS
    participant S as Server

    U->>B: Enters https://shop.com/cart/
    B->>DNS: shop.com → IP?
    DNS-->>B: 93.184.216.34
    B->>S: TCP + TLS Handshake
    Note over B,S: Encrypted channel established
    B->>S: GET /cart/ HTTP/1.1<br>Host: shop.com · Cookie: sessionid=abc
    Note over S: Server logic: reads sessionid, finds the user,<br>queries the DB, renders HTML
    S-->>B: HTTP/1.1 200 OK · Content-Type: text/html<br>#lt;html#gt;...#lt;/html#gt;
    B->>U: Displays the cart page

docs.title: 6. HTTPS / TLS Handshake
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (Browser)
    participant S as Server (Nginx + SSL cert)
    participant CA as Local store of<br>trusted CAs (OS/browser)

    Note over C,S: The TCP connection is already established (TLS 1.2 with RSA key exchange)
    C->>S: ClientHello (TLS version, cipher suites, random_C)
    S-->>C: ServerHello + SSL Certificate (signed by a CA)
    C->>CA: Verifying the certificate chain (locally, no request to the CA)
    CA-->>C: Certificate is valid ✓
    C->>S: Pre-master secret (encrypted with the server's public key)
    Note over C,S: Both sides generate the session key
    C->>S: Finished (the first encrypted packet)
    S-->>C: Finished (confirmation)
    Note over C,S: All subsequent data is encrypted with the session key
    C->>S: HTTP GET / (now encrypted)
    S-->>C: HTTP 200 OK + HTML (encrypted)

docs.title: Python Web Servers, the Kernel and Production Networking
The main idea
docs.text:
Most beginners think that:

from fastapi import FastAPI

or:

from flask import Flask

is already a:

web server

But that is NOT the case.

docs.title: Framework ≠ Server
docs.text:
FastAPI, Flask, Django — are:

application frameworks

They: - describe routes, - business logic, - request handlers, - middleware.

But they do NOT: - open TCP sockets directly, - do NOT call accept(), - do NOT manage epoll/select, - do NOT work with the kernel networking stack directly.

docs.title: Who actually works with the network?
docs.text:
The real networking is done by:

  • Gunicorn
  • Uvicorn
  • Hypercorn
  • uWSGI
  • Daphne

They are the ones that: - open sockets, - bind() to a port, - listen(), - accept(), - recv(), - send().

docs.title: Architecturally
docs.text:
Python App
    ↓
WSGI / ASGI
    ↓
Python Server
    ↓
OS Kernel
    ↓
TCP/IP Stack
    ↓
Network

docs.title: What is WSGI?
docs.text:
WSGI = 

Web Server Gateway Interface

The old synchronous standard for Python web.

docs.title: The WSGI model
docs.text:
HTTP Request
↓
1 worker/thread/process
↓
Framework handles request
↓
HTTP Response

docs.title: Frameworks that work through WSGI
docs.text: Framework Type Flask minimal WSGI Django (classic) full-stack WSGI

docs.title: What is ASGI?
docs.text:
ASGI = 

Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface

The new async Python standard.

docs.title: ASGI supports
docs.text:
• asyncio
  • WebSocket
  • long connections
  • streaming
  • async I/O
  • event loops

docs.title: Frameworks that work through ASGI
docs.text: Framework Type FastAPI modern ASGI Starlette lightweight ASGI Quart async Flask aiohttp async HTTP modern Django async hybrid

docs.title: The most important systems-thinking point
docs.text:
The framework: 

defines the application logic

The server: 

defines the networking model

docs.title: What does Gunicorn actually do?
docs.text: Gunicorn: - socket() - bind() - listen() - fork workers - accept() - recv() - passes the request to the Flask/Django app

docs.title: What does Uvicorn actually do?
docs.text:
Uvicorn is an async ASGI server.

It: - uses an event loop, - epoll/select, - non-blocking sockets, - asyncio tasks.

docs.title: Production Architecture
docs.text:
A typical production setup for FastAPI:

                 INTERNET
                      │
══════════════════════╪══════════════════════
                      ▼
               ┌────────────┐
               │   Nginx    │
               │ :80 / :443 │
               └─────┬──────┘
                     │ reverse proxy
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │     Uvicorn         │
          │   ASGI Server       │
          └─────┬──────┬────────┘
                │      │
         Worker 1   Worker 2
                │      │
                ▼      ▼
             FastAPI App

docs.title: For Django
docs.text:
Browser
↓
Nginx
↓
Gunicorn
↓
Django

docs.title: What does Nginx do?
docs.text: Nginx: - listens on 80/443, - TLS/HTTPS, - reverse proxy, - buffering, - static files, - load balancing, - keep-alive connections.

docs.title: Why NOT run FastAPI/Flask directly?
docs.text:
Because:

app.run()

is a:

development server

docs.title: A development server does NOT properly handle
docs.text:
• multiprocessing
  • worker management
  • graceful shutdown
  • production buffering
  • efficient concurrency
  • load balancing
  • advanced socket handling

docs.title: The full Mental Model
docs.text:
USER SPACE
═══════════════════════════════════

 FastAPI / Django / Flask
            │
            ▼
    Uvicorn / Gunicorn
            │
            ▼
════════ syscall boundary ════════

         OS KERNEL
═══════════════════════════════════

 TCP Stack
 Socket Buffers
 Scheduler
 epoll/select
 File Descriptors

═══════════════════════════════════

        NETWORK LAYER
═══════════════════════════════════

 TCP/IP
 Ethernet
 Wi-Fi
 Routers
 Internet

docs.title: What does recv() mean in a production server?
docs.text:
When Uvicorn or Gunicorn does:

sock.recv(1024)

it means:

crossing the syscall boundary into the kernel

docs.title: Then the kernel:
docs.text:
• checks the receive buffer,
  • if there are bytes → returns the data,
  • if there are no bytes → blocks the thread/process.

docs.title: The most important conclusion
docs.text:
A Python framework is only the application layer.

The real networking: - sockets, - TCP, - buffers, - event loops, - epoll/select, - scheduler, - kernel wakeups

is done by: - Gunicorn, - Uvicorn, - the kernel networking stack.

docs.title: Part II. Django Core
docs.text:
Django is a pipeline: an HTTP request passes through middleware → URL dispatcher → view → response. This part builds a mental model of that pipeline.

Prerequisites: Part I (HTTP). Level: Beginner.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Document What we will learn Django Architecture MTV pattern, settings, INSTALLED_APPS, lifecycle overview URL Routing urlpatterns, path(), include(), name=, reverse(), namespace Views FBV vs CBV, request object, HttpResponse, render(), redirect() Request Lifecycle middleware pipeline, exception handling, response lifecycle WSGI vs ASGI sync vs async entrypoint, Daphne, ProtocolTypeRouter Project Structure where things live, settings split, manage.py Management Commands runserver, migrate, shell, createsuperuser, custom commands Diagrams Mermaid diagrams of MTV, middleware, URL routing

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
MTV (Model-Template-View):

URL → View → Model (ORM)
           → Template (HTML render)
           → HttpResponse

Request lifecycle through middleware:

# settings.py MIDDLEWARE (order matters)
[
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",   # HTTPS redirect, HSTS
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",  # session → request.session
    "django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",       # CSRF token check
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",  # session → request.user
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
]

URL routing:

# notes_project/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('accounts/', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')),
    path('', include('notes_app.urls')),    # all notes_app routes
]

# notes_app/urls.py
path('notes/', views.note_list, name='note_list'),
path('notes/<int:pk>/edit/', views.note_edit, name='note_edit'),

View:

# FBV — explicit GET/POST
@login_required
def note_create(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user)
        if form.is_valid():
            note = services.create_note(user=request.user, **form.cleaned_data)
            return redirect('note_detail', pk=note.pk)  # PRG
    else:
        form = NoteForm(user=request.user)
    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_form.html', {'form': form})

docs.title: 1. What Django is and why it is a framework
docs.text:
A framework is not a library. A library gives you tools that you call. A framework calls your code according to established rules (Inversion of Control).

Django provides: - ready-made HTTP request handling - an ORM for working with the database - an authentication system - an admin panel out of the box - protection against XSS, CSRF, SQL injection - a migration system

You write: models (DB schema), views (HTTP orchestration), templates (HTML), services (business logic), selectors (reading data). Django does everything else itself.

docs.title: Django vs Flask vs FastAPI
docs.text: Parameter Django Flask FastAPI Size Large Micro Medium Batteries Included (ORM, auth, admin) Minimal Dependencies Async Django 3.1+ (partial) Quart Native Development speed High Medium High Best suited for Full-featured web applications Microservices API services

docs.title: 2. MVT architecture
docs.text:
Django uses MVT (Model-View-Template) — a variant of classic MVC.

Component Role MVC equivalent Model DB schema, relationships, ORM — no business logic Model View HTTP orchestrator: validates the request, delegates to a service/selector, returns a Response Controller Template HTML template for rendering View

In a production architecture, business logic lives in services.py and reads live in selectors.py. MVT describes standard Django; for an API backend, Templates are usually replaced with DRF Serializers.

Key idea: a View is not a "visual interface". A View is a Python function or class that handles a request.

docs.title: Why not MVC?
docs.text: In Django, the "View" is responsible for logic (like the Controller in MVC), and the "Template" is responsible for presentation (like the View in MVC). The names are different, but the essence is the same.

docs.title: 3. Django project structure
docs.text:
myproject/                    ← project root
├── manage.py                 ← CLI tool
├── myproject/                ← configuration package
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py           ← all settings
│   ├── urls.py               ← root URL router
│   ├── wsgi.py               ← WSGI entry point
│   └── asgi.py               ← ASGI entry point
└── myapp/                    ← Django application (bounded context)
    ├── models.py             ← DB schema (structure only, no business logic)
    ├── services.py           ← Business logic (mutations, transactions, side effects)
    ├── selectors.py          ← Reading data (named queries, ORM optimizations)
    ├── serializers.py        ← Transport layer (InputSerializer, OutputSerializer)
    ├── views.py              ← HTTP orchestrator (thin, delegates to services/selectors)
    ├── urls.py               ← application URL routes
    ├── tasks.py              ← Celery tasks (transport, not logic)
    ├── filters.py            ← django-filter
    ├── permissions.py        ← DRF permissions
    ├── admin.py              ← registering models in the admin
    ├── apps.py               ← application config
    ├── templates/            ← HTML templates (for SSR)
    ├── static/               ← CSS, JS, images
    ├── tests/                ← tests
    └── migrations/           ← DB migration files

docs.title: 4. Django Request Lifecycle — step by step
docs.text: Here is what happens when the request GET /books/42/ reaches Django:

docs.title: Step 1: WSGI/ASGI receives the request
docs.text:
Nginx passes the HTTP bytes to uWSGI or Gunicorn. The server turns them into a Python dictionary:

# WSGI environ — what Django receives
{
    'REQUEST_METHOD': 'GET',
    'PATH_INFO': '/books/42/',
    'HTTP_HOST': 'example.com',
    'HTTP_COOKIE': 'sessionid=abc123',
    'wsgi.input': <BytesIO>,  # request body
    ...
}

docs.title: Step 2: Middleware (inbound path — top to bottom)
docs.text:
Imagine that middleware is a series of checkpoints (or layers) that every user request passes through, one after another, before it reaches your main program.

The order of these checkpoints is critical, because one checkpoint usually depends on the results of the previous one.

Here is how it works: 1. SessionMiddleware is like a security guard who checks the visitor and pulls out their "ID ticket" (the session data). 2. AuthenticationMiddleware is like an administrator who takes that ticket, looks it up in the database, and determines exactly who has arrived (authenticates the user).

If the administrator (AuthenticationMiddleware) tries to recognize the user before the guard (SessionMiddleware) has handed out the ticket, they simply won't know whom to look for. That is why session handling must always come higher in the list.

This is configured in your project's main configuration file — settings.py. That file contains a special list called MIDDLEWARE. To add, remove, or reorder middleware, you simply edit this list, placing the dotted paths to them in the required order from top to bottom.

# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',      # HTTPS redirect, HSTS
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware', # reads the session cookie
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',           # normalizes the URL
    'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',           # CSRF protection
    'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware',  # request.user
    'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware',
]

Each middleware receives the request, can modify it, or can return an HttpResponse immediately (breaking the chain). The order is critical: AuthenticationMiddleware must come AFTER SessionMiddleware, because it reads the session data.

docs.title: Step 3: URL Dispatcher
docs.text:
Imagine that the URL Dispatcher (router) is the main mail sorting office.

When a user enters an address (for example, /books/42/), this "letter" (the request) goes through the following sorting stages:

  1. The main hub (include): First, the request arrives at your main myproject/urls.py file. The "sorter" sees the books/ part and says: "Aha, this goes to the books department!", forwarding the request to the books.urls file for further processing.
  2. The books department (<int:pk>): The books.urls file looks at the rest of the address — 42/. The <int:pk> expression works like a smart scanner: it understands that 42 is a numeric value (the primary key, or ID, of a book), "captures" it, and passes it directly to the class-based view BookDetailView (wired up via .as_view()) so that it can fetch exactly book No. 42 from the database.

Why is the order so important? The router reads your urlpatterns list strictly from top to bottom and stops searching at the very first match that fits the rule. If it reaches the end of the list and no line matches, it returns a 404 Not Found response (page not found).

# myproject/urls.py
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('api/', include('api.urls')),
    path('books/', include('books.urls')),
]

# books/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from .views import BookListView, BookDetailView

urlpatterns = [
    path('', BookListView.as_view(), name='book-list'),
    path('<int:pk>/', BookDetailView.as_view(), name='book-detail'),  # ← pk=42
]

Django goes through urlpatterns from top to bottom. The first match calls the corresponding View. If there are no matches — 404 Not Found.

Note: Django does not look for the "best" match — it takes the first one.

docs.title: Step 4: View — the heart of the logic
docs.text:
Imagine that the View is the head chef in a restaurant who has received your order from the dispatcher.

Here is what happens in this code, step by step:

  1. Receiving the order (request, pk): The "chef" receives the request object and the specific number of the requested book (for example, 42), which the router has just "captured" and passed on.
  2. Querying the database (get_object_or_404): The function asks the ORM to find book No. 42 in the database. If no such book exists, the function immediately returns a 404 Not Found error (page not found) instead of crashing the program because of missing data.
  3. Building the response (render): The chef takes the book that was found and the information about the current user (which the AuthenticationMiddleware carefully added at the first stage). He packs them into a dictionary and passes it to the HTML template (detail.html) for the final presentation of the page.
# books/views.py
from django.shortcuts import render, get_object_or_404
from .models import Book

def book_detail(request, pk):  # function-based equivalent of BookDetailView
    # ORM: SELECT * FROM books_book WHERE id=42
    book = get_object_or_404(Book, pk=pk)

    # Template rendering
    return render(request, 'books/detail.html', {
        'book': book,
        'user': request.user,  # added by AuthenticationMiddleware
    })

docs.title: Step 5: ORM → Database
docs.text:
Imagine that the ORM is your personal translator-assistant.

You give it an instruction in plain Python (Book.objects.get(pk=42)), and it instantly translates it into the database's language — SQL.

Here is how it works under the hood: 1. Book.objects — you are addressing the database, specifically the table of books. 2. get(...) — you give the command to find strictly only one specific record. 3. pk=42 — pk means "primary key". The ORM understands that it needs to find the book whose unique identifier (id) equals 42.

The database finds the required row and returns it. The ORM then automatically wraps that row in a convenient Python object, book. Now your View has all the data about the book and can pass it on to be displayed on the page.

book = Book.objects.get(pk=42)
# Generates: SELECT "books_book"."id", "books_book"."title", ... 
#           FROM "books_book" WHERE "books_book"."id" = 42 LIMIT 1

docs.title: Step 6: Template rendering
docs.text:
Imagine that the Template is the beautiful plating of a dish before it is served to the customer.

The View (the head chef) has passed the "raw" data here (the book and user objects), and the template engine simply inserts them into the HTML skeleton.

Here is exactly what happens:

  1. {{ book.title }} (Variables): Double curly braces mean "output data here". Django automatically replaces this with the book's actual title.
  2. {{ book.author.name }} and the "N+1" trap: This line accesses a related object (the author). If your View did not "pull" the author from the database together with the book earlier (using the select_related optimization), this tiny line will make Django quietly run one more separate database query to find out the author's name. If you display a list of 100 books, Django will make 100 extra queries (this is the well-known "N+1" problem).
  3. {% if user.is_authenticated %} (Logic tags): This is the template's built-in logic. It checks the user's status (yes, the very user our administrator AuthenticationMiddleware recognized at the first step).
  4. {% url 'add-to-cart' book.pk %}: Instead of hardcoding a link (for example, /cart/add/42), this tag generates the correct path itself, based on the route name from your urls.py. This protects the site: if you ever change the URL structure in your settings, all links in the templates will update automatically.

After this step, the fully generated HTML is packed into a response and sent back to the user's browser.

<!-- books/templates/books/detail.html -->
<h1>{{ book.title }}</h1>
<p>Author: {{ book.author.name }}</p>  {# WARNING: this may be an N+1 query! #}
{% if user.is_authenticated %}
    <a href="{% url 'add-to-cart' book.pk %}">Buy</a>
{% endif %}

The Django Template Engine substitutes the values and automatically escapes HTML (protection against XSS).

docs.title: Step 7: Middleware (outbound path — bottom to top)
docs.text:
Imagine that our finished dish (the web page) is now going back to the customer. It has to pass through the same checkpoints (middleware), but now in reverse order.

At this stage, the middleware acts as a "packing service" before the final dispatch:

  1. Vacuum-packing (GZip): They compress the finished page so it travels across the internet much faster.
  2. Attaching labels (Content-Length): They calculate the exact size of the page and add this header so the user's browser knows exactly how much data it needs to download.
  3. Stamping the seal (Cookies/Session): If something changed while the request was being processed (for example, the user logged in), the middleware commits these changes and asks the browser to save the updated session data or cookies.

After passing through the last middleware (the one highest in the list), the fully formed and packed response is handed to the web server, which delivers it to the browser.

And that's the entire request lifecycle in Django!

docs.title: 5. Models and the ORM
docs.text:
Imagine that a Model is the blueprint of a database table, and the ORM is your personal translator that turns Python code into SQL queries. One class equals one table.

Here is what actually happens under the hood of your code:

1. Field types (Fields) Each class attribute is a column in the database table. * CharField and EmailField: Create text columns. EmailField additionally checks whether the text is a valid email address, and unique=True guarantees that the database will never contain two authors with the same email. * DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True): Django automatically records the exact date and time when the record is created; you don't need to pass this value manually. * DecimalField: A special field for financial data (prices) that preserves the precision of arithmetic operations, unlike ordinary floating-point numbers.

2. Relationships between tables (ForeignKey) The line author = models.ForeignKey(...) creates a "one-to-many" relationship — one author can have many books. * on_delete=models.CASCADE: Protects the integrity of the database. If you delete an author, Django automatically (in a cascade) deletes all of their books so that they are not left "hanging" without an owner. * related_name='books': This is the magic of reverse lookup. Thanks to it, you can take an author object and write author.books.all() to instantly get a list of all their works.

3. Metadata (the Meta class) The Meta class contains model settings that are not table fields. * ordering = ['name']: Tells the database to always return the list of authors sorted alphabetically by default. * db_table = 'library_authors': By default, Django would name the table appname_author. This parameter lets you set your own table name in the DBMS explicitly.

4. The __str__ method Instead of showing the system-generated and unhelpful <Author object (1)> in the admin panel, this method tells Django to display the object in a human-friendly way — simply by printing the author's name.

docs.title: Defining a model
docs.text:
from django.db import models

class Author(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    email = models.EmailField(unique=True)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    class Meta:
        ordering = ['name']
        db_table = 'library_authors'  # explicit table name

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

class Book(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=300)
    author = models.ForeignKey(Author, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='books')
    published = models.DateField()
    price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    is_active = models.BooleanField(default=True)

docs.title: ORM QuerySet API
docs.text:
Imagine that a QuerySet is a smart list of instructions for the database that Django assembles but does not execute until the very last moment.

Here is an in-depth breakdown of each stage of your code:

1. CREATE The create() method is a convenient shortcut. Instead of creating an object in memory and then calling save() on it separately, create() does it in one step, immediately executing an SQL INSERT command.

2. READ and Lazy Evaluation When you write Book.objects.filter(...), Django does not touch the database at all. QuerySets are "lazy": they only accumulate your filters and conditions. The translation to SQL and the actual database access (SELECT) happen only when you start iterating over the results, for example in a for book in books: loop.

3. Optimization and select_related By default, if you call book.author.name in a loop over 100 books, Django will make 100 additional queries to find the author of each book (this is the well-known N+1 problem). The select_related('author') method solves this by using an SQL JOIN. It fetches both the book and its author in a single, more complex query, significantly improving performance. This method is ideal for foreign key (ForeignKey) relationships.

4. UPDATE (Bulk update) The update() method translates directly into an SQL UPDATE command and is applied immediately to all filtered records. This is a very efficient approach, because Django updates the data directly in the database and does not load these objects into Python's memory.

5. DELETE Calling delete() immediately executes an SQL DELETE query. An important architectural nuance: if you delete an object (for example, an Author), Django uses CASCADE behavior by default and automatically deletes all objects related to it (their Books), so that no "orphaned" data is left in the database.

6. AGGREGATE Instead of loading all the books into Python and calculating the average price manually with a loop, aggregate() makes the database itself (which is optimized for this) do the math. Unlike filter(), which returns a QuerySet, aggregate() is a final (terminal) operation that immediately returns a regular Python dictionary with the computed results.

# CREATE
author = Author.objects.create(name="Frank Herbert", email="frank@dune.com")

# READ — lazy! The database has not been queried yet
books = Book.objects.filter(is_active=True)  
books = books.select_related('author')  # JOIN — avoids N+1

# The database is queried here (iteration)
for book in books:
    print(f"{book.title} by {book.author.name}")  # author is already loaded!

# UPDATE
Book.objects.filter(author=author).update(is_active=False)

# DELETE
Book.objects.get(pk=42).delete()

# AGGREGATE
from django.db.models import Avg, Count
stats = Book.objects.aggregate(avg_price=Avg('price'), total=Count('id'))

docs.title: The N+1 problem — the most common ORM mistake
docs.text:
# BAD: N+1 queries — 1 query for books + N queries for authors
books = Book.objects.all()
for book in books:
    print(book.author.name)  # an SQL query every time!

# GOOD: 2 queries (JOIN or IN)
books = Book.objects.select_related('author').all()  # for ForeignKey
books = Book.objects.prefetch_related('tags').all()  # for ManyToMany

docs.title: How to write your own middleware
docs.text:
class LoggingMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        # --- BEFORE the View ---
        print(f"→ {request.method} {request.path}")

        response = self.get_response(request)  # all of Django is inside

        # --- AFTER the View ---
        print(f"← {response.status_code}")
        response['X-Processing-Time'] = '42ms'

        return response

docs.title: Where middleware is useful
docs.text: Task Middleware Rate limiting (DDoS protection) Custom or django-ratelimit JWT authentication Custom + djangorestframework-simplejwt Request logging Custom or django-request CORS headers django-cors-headers GZip compression GZipMiddleware (built-in)

docs.title: How Django stores a session
docs.text:
1. After login, Django creates a record in the django_session table: 
    session_key: "abc123xyz"
session_data: {base64-encoded: {"_auth_user_id": "42", "_auth_user_backend": "..."}}
expire_date: 2025-06-01 10:00:00
  2. It sends the client a cookie: Set-Cookie: sessionid=abc123xyz; HttpOnly; Secure
  3. On subsequent requests, SessionMiddleware reads sessionid from the cookie
  4. AuthenticationMiddleware loads the user: request.user = User.objects.get(id=42)

docs.title: Login/Logout
docs.text:
from django.contrib.auth import authenticate, login, logout

def login_view(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        user = authenticate(
            request,
            username=request.POST['username'],
            password=request.POST['password']
        )
        if user:
            login(request, user)           # creates the session
            return redirect('dashboard')
        return render(request, 'login.html', {'error': 'Invalid credentials'})
    return render(request, 'login.html')

def logout_view(request):
    logout(request)                        # deletes the session from the DB
    return redirect('home')

docs.title: Protecting a view from anonymous users
docs.text:
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin

@login_required                    # → redirects to /accounts/login/
def my_profile(request):
    return render(request, 'profile.html')

class DashboardView(LoginRequiredMixin, View):
    login_url = '/login/'
    def get(self, request):
        return render(request, 'dashboard.html')

docs.title: WSGI (synchronous, traditional)
docs.text:
Browser → Nginx → Gunicorn (8 workers) → Django WSGI App
  • Each worker is a separate Python process
  • A worker handles 1 request at a time
  • If a view does time.sleep(5), the worker is blocked for 5 seconds
  • 8 workers = at most 8 concurrent requests
# wsgi.py
import os
from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')
application = get_wsgi_application()

docs.title: ASGI (asynchronous, modern)
docs.text:
Browser → Nginx → Uvicorn (8 workers with an event loop) → Django ASGI App
  • Each worker is an event loop (asyncio)
  • A worker can handle thousands of concurrent connections
  • While await db.query() is running, the worker handles other requests
  • Support for WebSockets and Server-Sent Events
# asgi.py
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')
application = get_asgi_application()

# Async view (Django 3.1+)
from django.http import JsonResponse
import asyncio

async def async_view(request):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)         # does not block the server!
    return JsonResponse({'status': 'ok'})

docs.title: When to use what
docs.text: Scenario Recommendation Traditional website WSGI + Gunicorn REST API (lots of requests) ASGI + Uvicorn WebSockets (chat, real-time) ASGI + Django Channels Mixed (both) Gunicorn + Uvicorn workers

docs.title: 9. Migrations — evolving the DB schema
docs.text:
Imagine that Migrations are a version control system (like Git), but for your database.

Django does not require you to write SQL queries by hand to create or change tables. Instead, you change Python classes (models), and Django takes care of all the database work.

Here is what the full workflow looks like:

1. Changing the code (models.py) You add, remove, or change fields in your models.

2. Recording the changes (makemigrations) The python manage.py makemigrations command scans your models, finds the changes, and creates a new migration file (for example, 0002_book_add_isbn.py). This file is just a "blueprint" or record of exactly what changed. The database itself has not been touched yet at this stage.

3. Applying the changes (migrate) The python manage.py migrate command reads these blueprints and executes real SQL commands to change the database structure (create a new column, table, and so on). Django keeps a special internal table (django_migrations) to remember which migrations have already been applied and which have not.

Additional useful commands:

  • python manage.py showmigrations: Shows a list of all existing migrations in your project. Those that have already been successfully applied to the database are marked with an [X].
  • python manage.py sqlmigrate app_name migration_number: Shows the "raw" SQL that Django plans to execute. This command changes nothing in the database, but it is very useful when you want to check exactly what will happen under the hood.
# After changing models.py — generates a migration file
python manage.py makemigrations

# Applies the migrations to the DB
python manage.py migrate

# View the SQL that will be executed
python manage.py sqlmigrate myapp 0002

A migration file is Python code that describes schema changes:

# migrations/0002_book_add_isbn.py
from django.db import migrations, models

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [('books', '0001_initial')]

    operations = [
        migrations.AddField(
            model_name='book',
            name='isbn',
            field=models.CharField(max_length=13, blank=True),
        ),
    ]

Never edit migration files by hand if they have already been applied to a production DB.

Why can't you edit migration files that have already been applied? Because Django tracks the history precisely, manually tampering with old files will cause the real database structure to fall out of sync with your Python code, and later attempts to update the database will produce errors.

docs.title: Nginx configuration
docs.text:
upstream django {
    server unix:/run/django.sock;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name example.com;

    ssl_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/example.com.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/example.com.key;

    # Static files — Django is not involved
    location /static/ {
        alias /app/staticfiles/;
        expires 30d;
    }

    # Dynamic requests → Gunicorn → Django
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://django;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

docs.title: 12. Celery — background tasks
docs.text:
# tasks.py — the task only transports the call to a service
from celery import shared_task

@shared_task
def send_welcome_email_task(user_id: int) -> None:
    from .selectors import user_get_by_id
    from .services import user_send_welcome_email

    user = user_get_by_id(user_id=user_id)
    user_send_welcome_email(user=user)   # the logic lives in the service


# services.py — the logic is here, not in the task
from django.db import transaction

@transaction.atomic
def user_register(*, email: str, password: str):
    user = User(email=email)
    user.set_password(password)
    user.full_clean()
    user.save()
    # the task is launched AFTER the commit — safe
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_welcome_email_task.delay(user.id))
    return user


# views.py — thin, delegates to the service
def register_view(request):
    serializer = UserRegisterInputSerializer(data=request.data)
    serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
    user = user_register(**serializer.validated_data)
    return Response({'id': user.id}, status=201)

docs.title: Blocking calls in a view
docs.text:
# BAD: blocks the entire WSGI worker
import time
def slow_view(request):
    time.sleep(10)  # 10 seconds — the worker is unavailable
    return HttpResponse("done")

# GOOD: async view
async def slow_view(request):
    await asyncio.sleep(10)  # the event loop is free for other requests
    return HttpResponse("done")

docs.title: Django — The Command System
docs.text: python manage.py is Django's command line. Every command is a Python class with access to all of Django (ORM, settings, signals).

docs.title: Why commands
docs.text:
Django commands are scripts for tasks outside HTTP: migrations, loading data, cleaning up old records, sending newsletters.

# A plain Python script has no access to the Django ORM without setup:
python scripts/seed_data.py     # ← ImportError or AppRegistryNotReady

# Django command — ORM, settings, all apps are ready automatically:
python manage.py seed_demo_data

docs.title: Cheat sheet — command table
docs.text: Command Syntax When Start the server python manage.py runserver Development Generate migrations python manage.py makemigrations After changing models.py Apply migrations python manage.py migrate After makemigrations View SQL python manage.py sqlmigrate notes_app 0004 Debug Migration status python manage.py showmigrations DB audit Roll back a migration python manage.py migrate notes_app 0003 Rollback Create a superuser python manage.py createsuperuser After the first migration Collect static files python manage.py collectstatic Before deployment Python shell python manage.py shell Debug ORM SQL shell python manage.py dbshell Raw SQL Run tests python manage.py test CI/CD Check the project python manage.py check Configuration check Security audit python manage.py check --deploy Before deployment Custom command python manage.py seed_demo_data Automation

docs.title: Anatomy of manage.py
docs.text:
# manage.py — in the root of every Django project
import os
import sys

def main():
    os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')
    from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
    execute_from_command_line(sys.argv)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

When you run python manage.py migrate: 1. os.environ sets which settings.py to use 2. Django initializes (all INSTALLED_APPS, DATABASES, etc.) 3. execute_from_command_line(['manage.py', 'migrate']) looks for the migrate command among all management/commands/ directories

docs.title: Where Django looks for commands
docs.text:
every INSTALLED_APP/
└── management/
    └── commands/
        └── *.py   ← each file = one command

notes_app has:

notes_app/
└── management/
    └── commands/
        └── seed_demo_data.py   ← python manage.py seed_demo_data

docs.title: makemigrations — recording schema changes
docs.text:
Scans models.py, compares it with the saved state and generates a Python script:

python manage.py makemigrations
python manage.py makemigrations notes_app         # for a specific app
python manage.py makemigrations --name add_tags   # with a descriptive name

Important: The command does not change the database — it only creates a plan.

# Example of a generated file migrations/0005_note_is_archived.py
class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [('notes_app', '0004_chatmessage')]
    operations = [
        migrations.AddField(
            model_name='note',
            name='is_archived',
            field=models.BooleanField(default=False),
        ),
    ]

docs.title: migrate — applying migrations
docs.text:
python manage.py migrate           # all apps
python manage.py migrate notes_app # only one app
python manage.py migrate notes_app 0003  # roll back to a specific version

How it is tracked: Django stores applied migrations in the django_migrations table.

# View the SQL before applying
python manage.py sqlmigrate notes_app 0004
# BEGIN;
# CREATE TABLE "notes_app_chatmessage" (...)
# CREATE INDEX chat_group_ts_idx ON ...
# COMMIT;

docs.title: runserver — the dev server
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver           # localhost:8000
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8001  # reachable on the network

Development only

runserver is a dev server: it is multithreaded by default (--nothreading turns that off), but it has no SSL, no buffering, and no security or performance hardening. In production use only Uvicorn or Gunicorn + nginx.

docs.title: check --deploy — security audit
docs.text:
python manage.py check --deploy

It checks: DEBUG=False, a non-default SECRET_KEY, ALLOWED_HOSTS, HTTPS headers, cookie security.

docs.title: collectstatic — preparing static files

python manage.py collectstatic

Collects all static files into STATIC_ROOT. In production, nginx serves them from there without Django.

docs.title: Custom command — seed_demo_data
docs.text:
Full implementation from notes_app/management/commands/seed_demo_data.py:

from django.core.management.base import BaseCommand
from django.contrib.auth.models import User, Group
from notes_app.models import Note, Tag, Notebook

class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = 'Seed demo data (users, groups, notes, todos, chats)'

    def add_arguments(self, parser):
        parser.add_argument(
            '--reset',
            action='store_true',
            help='Delete existing demo data before seeding',
        )

    def handle(self, *args, **options):
        if options['reset']:
            self.stdout.write('Resetting demo data...')
            User.objects.filter(username__startswith='demo_').delete()

        # get_or_create → safe to run repeatedly
        alice, created = User.objects.get_or_create(
            username='demo_alice',
            defaults={'email': 'alice@demo.com'}
        )
        if created:
            alice.set_password('demo1234')
            alice.save()
            self.stdout.write(self.style.SUCCESS('✓ Created user: demo_alice'))
        else:
            self.stdout.write('  User demo_alice already exists, skipping')

        # Demo notes
        notebook, _ = Notebook.objects.get_or_create(
            user=alice, title='Мої нотатки', defaults={'is_default': True}
        )
        Note.objects.get_or_create(
            user=alice, title='Перша нотатка',
            defaults={
                'content': 'Привіт! Це демо-нотатка.',
                'notebook': notebook,
                'priority': Note.PRIORITY_MEDIUM,
            }
        )

        self.stdout.write(self.style.SUCCESS('Seeding complete!'))

Key parts: - BaseCommand — the base class; provides stdout, style, add_arguments, handle - add_arguments — command-line arguments (--reset) - handle — all of the command's logic runs here - self.style.SUCCESS(...) — green text in the output - get_or_create — an idempotent operation (safe to run repeatedly)

docs.title: HTTP request lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Nginx as Nginx
    participant Web as wsgi.py / asgi.py
    participant Route as urls.py
    participant View as views.py
    participant DB as models.py (ORM)
    participant HTML as templates/

    Nginx->>Web: Incoming HTTP request
    Web->>Route: Handing off to the dispatcher
    Route->>View: Calling the matching function
    View->>DB: Book.objects.all()
    DB-->>View: QuerySet (data)
    View->>HTML: render(request, 'books.html', data)
    HTML-->>View: Compiled HTML string
    View-->>Web: HttpResponse
    Web-->>Nginx: Response bytes

docs.title: manage.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Command-line orchestrator for the whole project Internal role Sets DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and runs Django commands In the request lifecycle No part at all — does not handle live web traffic In CI/CD Runs tests, collects static files, applies migrations

Mental model: A foreman on a construction site — you give him orders, he delegates to the framework.

Mistake: Thinking that manage.py runs the production server. In production this file is ignored when handling traffic.

docs.title: settings.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Central configuration hub Internal role A Python module with global variables (DB, installed apps, security keys) In the request lifecycle Loaded into memory once when the server starts External services PostgreSQL, Redis, AWS S3, Celery — all connected here

Mental model: The main electrical panel and control board for the whole building.

# Critical settings
INSTALLED_APPS = ['django.contrib.auth', 'myapp']
DATABASES = {'default': {'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql', ...}}
MIDDLEWARE = ['django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware', ...]

Mistake: Trying to change settings.py dynamically for different users at runtime. Settings are global and static.

docs.title: wsgi.py and asgi.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Entry points for application servers (Gunicorn, Uvicorn) Internal role Provides the standard application object for talking to Django In the request lifecycle The first line of Django code when an HTTP request arrives wsgi.py Synchronous protocol — traditional HTTP requests asgi.py Asynchronous protocol — WebSockets, Server-Sent Events

Mental model: An interpreter's desk — turns "raw" network HTTP bytes into Python dictionaries.

Mistake: Thinking that Django listens to the Internet on its own. Traffic always goes through a WSGI/ASGI server first.

docs.title: urls.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose URL dispatcher Internal role The urlpatterns list — maps URL strings to Python functions Algorithm Searches top to bottom, stops at the first match For APIs Defines the endpoint contract

Mental model: A mail sorter — reads the address and hands the envelope to the right courier.

Mistake: Expecting Django to find the "best" match. It takes the first one — static routes must come before dynamic ones.

docs.title: views.py
apps.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Configuration of a specific app Internal role An AppConfig subclass — initialization when Django starts (for example, connecting Signals) In the request lifecycle No part at all — runs only once when the framework starts

Mistake: Writing business logic or DB queries here — it will cause a failure at startup.

docs.title: models.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Defining the database schema Internal role Python classes (subclasses of models.Model) → SQL tables Single source of truth The data structure is described here — not in SQL scripts In the request lifecycle Used by views.py for reading/writing

Mental model: The architectural blueprints of the database.

Mistake: Adding a field and thinking the DB will update itself. You need makemigrations + migrate.

docs.title: migrations/
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Version control for the database schema Internal role Automatically generated Python scripts of schema changes In the request lifecycle No part at all In CI/CD The foundation of safe deployment — guarantees an identical schema on all servers

Mental model: Git commits for DB tables — every schema change is recorded as a version.

Dangerous mistake: Deleting migration files "to keep things clean" after they have been applied — this breaks the dependency graph and synchronization with the DB.

docs.title: admin.py
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Configuration of the built-in admin interface Internal role Registers models on admin.site → CRUD via /admin/ In the request lifecycle Handles only requests to /admin/ paths Saves Hundreds of hours of developing internal dashboards

Mental model: A store's back office — for trusted staff only.

Mistake: Using the admin panel as the frontend for regular customers.

docs.title: templates/
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose HTML structure with dynamic data Internal role DTL (Django Template Language) — {{ variables }}, {% tags %} In the request lifecycle Called at the end of a view to generate an HTML string In modern SPAs Replaced by a JSON response if the frontend is React/Vue

Mental model: A document form with blank fields to fill in.

Mistake: Writing full-blown Python code in templates. DTL is intentionally limited — business logic belongs in views.py.

docs.title: static/
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Unchanging assets (CSS, JS, fonts, images) Internal role Sent to the client "as is", without Python processing In the request lifecycle In production it bypasses Django completely — Nginx serves it directly collectstatic Collects all static files from apps into STATIC_ROOT

Mental model: The paint, furniture and decorations of the building.

Mistake: Expecting Django to serve static files automatically on a real server without Nginx.

docs.title: How files interact during a request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Nginx
    participant Gateway as wsgi.py
    participant Route as urls.py
    participant View as views.py
    participant DB as models.py (ORM)
    participant HTML as templates/

    Nginx->>Gateway: Incoming HTTP request
    Gateway->>Route: Handing off to the dispatcher (Router)
    Route->>View: Calling the matching View function
    View->>DB: Book.objects.all()
    DB-->>View: Returns a QuerySet (Data)
    View->>HTML: render(request, 'books.html', data)
    HTML-->>View: Returns the compiled HTML string
    View-->>Gateway: HttpResponse(HTML)
    Gateway-->>Nginx: Sends the bytes to the browser

docs.title: Modern production architecture of a Django project
docs.text: The standard my_project/my_app/ structure is fine for learning and small apps. Medium and large systems use a different approach — a bounded context structure.

docs.title: Production project structure
docs.text:
project/
│
├── config/                      ← Configuration (instead of my_project/)
│   ├── settings/                ← Split settings: base.py, local.py, prod.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   ├── asgi.py
│   └── wsgi.py
│
├── apps/                        ← All business domains
│   │
│   ├── users/                   ← One bounded context = one app
│   │   ├── models.py
│   │   ├── views.py
│   │   ├── urls.py
│   │   ├── services.py          ← Business logic (mutations)
│   │   ├── selectors.py         ← Reading data (SELECT)
│   │   ├── serializers.py       ← HTTP validation + serialization
│   │   ├── permissions.py       ← DRF permissions
│   │   ├── tasks.py             ← Celery tasks (transport, not logic)
│   │   ├── validators.py        ← Complex domain validation
│   │   ├── filters.py           ← django-filter
│   │   ├── admin.py
│   │   ├── tests/
│   │   └── migrations/
│   │
│   ├── flood/                   ← A separate business domain
│   ├── dem/
│   ├── ml/
│   └── papers/
│
├── shared/                      ← Shared abstractions between apps
│   ├── exceptions/              ← Custom DRF exception handler
│   ├── middleware/
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── utils/
│   └── logging/
│
├── infrastructure/              ← Integrations with the outside world
│   ├── redis/
│   ├── s3/
│   ├── email/
│   ├── celery/
│   └── external_apis/
│
├── requirements/
├── docker/
├── scripts/
└── manage.py

docs.title: The main rule: app = bounded context
docs.text:
An app is not a technical module but a separate business domain.

✅ Correct            ❌ Wrong
apps/users/           models/          ← global for everything
apps/payments/        views/           ← global for everything
apps/flood/           utils/           ← global for everything
apps/papers/

Each app encapsulates the whole stack for its domain: models, logic, queries, serializers, tasks.

docs.title: New files inside an app
docs.text:
Compared with the standard my_app/, new files appear in the production architecture:

File Role Detailed documentation services.py Business logic: mutations, transactions, side effects DJANGO_SERVICES.md selectors.py Reading data: named queries, ORM optimizations DJANGO_SELECTORS.md serializers.py HTTP ↔ domain: InputSerializer, OutputSerializer DJANGO_SERIALIZERS.md tasks.py Celery tasks — a transport layer, delegating to services — validators.py Complex domain validation (validate_dem_resolution()) — permissions.py DRF permissions (IsOwner, IsAdminOrReadOnly) — filters.py django-filter FilterSet for dynamic filtering —

docs.title: services.py
docs.text:
# BAD — business logic in the model
class FloodEvent(models.Model):
    def run_ml_pipeline(self):
        ...

# GOOD — business logic in a service
# services.py
def flood_event_process(*, event: FloodEvent) -> FloodEvent:
    ...

More details: DJANGO_SERVICES.md

docs.title: selectors.py
docs.text:
# BAD — ORM right in the view, duplicated across the whole project
FloodEvent.objects.filter(is_active=True, region_id=region_id)

# GOOD — a named query in a selector
# selectors.py
def flood_events_get_for_region(*, region_id: int) -> QuerySet:
    return FloodEvent.objects.filter(is_active=True, region_id=region_id)

More details: DJANGO_SELECTORS.md

docs.title: tasks.py
docs.text:
# BAD — business logic in a Celery task
@shared_task
def calculate_everything(event_id):
    event = FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    event.status = 'done'
    event.save()
    send_email(event.user.email, ...)

# GOOD — the task only transports the call into a service
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id: int):
    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_process(event=event)

docs.title: views.py in the production architecture
docs.text:
A view should be as thin as possible:

# A view must NOT:         A view MUST:
# ❌ contain SQL           ✅ validate via a serializer
# ❌ contain ML            ✅ call a service
# ❌ orchestrate logic     ✅ return a Response
# ❌ compute metrics

class FloodEventCreateAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = FloodEventInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
        event = flood_event_create(**serializer.validated_data, created_by=request.user)
        return Response(FloodEventOutputSerializer(event).data, status=201)

docs.title: shared/ — shared abstractions
docs.text:
shared/ contains code used by several apps that does not belong to any specific domain.

Folder What's inside shared/exceptions/ Custom DRF exception handler (mapping DjangoValidationError → HTTP 400) shared/middleware/ Middleware for logging, correlation ID, rate limiting shared/auth/ Shared authentication logic between apps shared/utils/ Small utilities with no business domain shared/logging/ Structured logging configuration 
# shared/exceptions/handlers.py — registered once in settings.py
# and automatically catches errors in all apps
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'shared.exceptions.handlers.custom_exception_handler',
}

docs.title: infrastructure/ — integrations with the outside world
docs.text:
infrastructure/ contains adapters to external services. The key idea:

Business Layer     →   WHAT the system does
Infrastructure     →   HOW the system talks to the outside world
Folder What's inside infrastructure/redis/ Redis client, cache configuration infrastructure/s3/ AWS S3 / MinIO client for file storage infrastructure/email/ Email backend (SendGrid, SES) infrastructure/celery/ Celery configuration, task routing infrastructure/external_apis/ Clients for external APIs (SlideRule NASA, OpenWeather, etc.) 
# infrastructure/s3/client.py
# S3 is neither the flood domain nor the dem domain.
# It is an external storage service, isolated in infrastructure/.
class S3Client:
    def upload_file(self, file_path: str, bucket: str) -> str:
        ...

Apps import from infrastructure, but infrastructure does not know about the apps.

docs.title: Comparison: learning vs production structure
docs.text:
Aspect Learning (standard) Production Configuration my_project/settings.py config/settings/base.py + local.py + prod.py Apps my_app/ in the root apps/users/, apps/flood/ Business logic In views.py In services.py ORM queries In views.py or models.py In selectors.py Serialization ModelSerializer InputSerializer + OutputSerializer External services Directly in views.py infrastructure/ Shared code utils.py in the root shared/

The learning structure is the right one for studying Django. The production structure is right when the project grows and a team works on it.

docs.title: Django Request Lifecycle
docs.text: When an HTTP request reaches Django, it passes through several layers before coming back as a response. Understanding these layers means understanding where to look for bugs and how to organize your code.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Request([HTTP Request]) --> MW[Middleware stack]
    MW --> URLConf[URL Routing]
    URLConf --> View[View function]
    View --> Selector["selectors.py<br>read-only queries"]
    View --> Service["services.py<br>mutating ops"]
    View --> Form["Forms<br>validation"]
    Selector --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
    Service --> DB
    View --> Template["Template<br>rendering"]
    Template --> Response([HTTP Response])
    MW -.->|exits in reverse order| Response

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class Request,MW,URLConf,Selector,Service,Form,DB,Template step;
    class View warning;
    class Response success;

docs.title: 1. Middleware stack — inbound
docs.text:
Every request passes through the MIDDLEWARE list from top to bottom:

# notes_project/settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'whitenoise.middleware.WhiteNoiseMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',    # ← reads the session cookie
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',               # ← /notes → /notes/
    'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',              # ← checks the CSRF token
    'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware', # ← sets request.user
    'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware',
]

What each middleware does:

Middleware Input What it adds to the request SecurityMiddleware request HTTP→HTTPS redirect (prod) SessionMiddleware request request.session dict CsrfViewMiddleware POST request checks csrftoken cookie == POST param AuthenticationMiddleware request + session request.user (User or AnonymousUser) MessageMiddleware request request._messages storage

Order matters: AuthenticationMiddleware must come AFTER SessionMiddleware, because it reads request.session['_auth_user_id'].

docs.title: 2. URL Routing
docs.text:
The middleware hands the request to the URLconf:

# notes_project/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('accounts/', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')),
    path('', include('notes_app.urls', namespace='notes_app')),
]

Django iterates over urlpatterns from top to bottom, comparing request.path with each pattern. The first match wins.

# notes_app/urls.py
app_name = 'notes_app'

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.home, name='home'),                              # GET /
    path('notes/', views.note_list, name='note_list'),              # GET /notes/
    path('notes/new/', views.note_create, name='note_create'),      # GET/POST /notes/new/
    path('notes/<int:pk>/', views.note_detail, name='note_detail'), # GET /notes/42/
    path('notes/<int:pk>/edit/', views.note_update, name='note_update'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/delete/', views.note_delete, name='note_delete'),
    ...
]

If no pattern matches → 404 Not Found.

docs.title: 3. View function
docs.text:
URL routing calls the view with two kinds of arguments: request and the URL parameters:

# notes_app/views.py

@login_required  # ← a middleware-like decorator: if AnonymousUser → redirect /login/
def note_detail(request, pk):   # pk from the URL pattern <int:pk>
    # 1. Get the data (via a selector)
    note = selectors.get_note_for_user(pk=pk, user=request.user)
    if note is None:
        raise Http404   # → 404 response

    # 2. Process the form (if POST)
    if request.method == 'POST':
        # handling a comment or another action
        ...
        return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=pk)   # PRG pattern

    # 3. Render the template
    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_detail.html', {
        'note': note,
    })

A view has THREE responsibilities — and only three: 1. Take data from the request 2. Coordinate selectors/services/forms 3. Return a response (render or redirect)

docs.title: 4. Selector — reading from the DB
docs.text:
# notes_app/selectors.py

def get_note_for_user(pk: int, user) -> Note | None:
    """Returns the note if the user has access. None if not, or if it does not exist."""
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    return Note.objects.filter(
        Q(pk=pk) &
        (Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups))
    ).select_related('user', 'notebook').prefetch_related('tags').first()

A selector is read-only. Never save(), never delete(), never create().

docs.title: 5. Service — mutations
docs.text:
# notes_app/services.py

def update_note(*, note: Note, title: str, content: str, priority: int, ...) -> Note:
    """Updates the note and returns it."""
    note.title = title
    note.content = content
    note.priority = priority
    note.save()
    return note

A service does mutations only. It is called after form validation.

docs.title: 6. Template rendering
docs.text:
return render(request, 'notes_app/note_detail.html', {
    'note': note,
    'tags': note.tags.all(),
})

Django finds the template in TEMPLATES[0]['DIRS'] and, with APP_DIRS = True, also looks in notes_app/templates/.

docs.title: 7. Middleware stack — outbound (reverse order)
docs.text:
The response passes through the middleware in reverse order:

Response ← XFrameOptions ← Messages ← Auth ← Csrf ← Common ← Session ← Whitenoise ← Security

SecurityMiddleware adds the HSTS header, XFrameOptionsMiddleware adds X-Frame-Options: DENY.

docs.title: Where things break
docs.text: Symptom Where to look 403 Forbidden on POST CsrfViewMiddleware — a form without {% csrf_token %} 403 Forbidden on login SessionMiddleware — the cookie is blocked (HTTPS only?) 404 for a valid URL URL order in urlpatterns — check for conflicting patterns redirect loop /login/ → /login/ @login_required + LOGIN_URL points to itself The view returns another user's data The selector does not filter by user 500 SynchronousOnlyOperation ORM in an async view without sync_to_async

docs.title: 403 CSRF: the most common form error
docs.text:
Forbidden (403): CSRF verification failed. Request aborted.

Cause: CsrfViewMiddleware checks that the POST contains a token matching the cookie. If the form has no {% csrf_token %}:

<!-- WRONG — you will get a 403 -->
<form method="post">
  <input type="text" name="title">
  <button type="submit">Зберегти</button>
</form>

<!-- CORRECT -->
<form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}   ← generates <input type="hidden" name="csrfmiddlewaretoken" value="...">
  <input type="text" name="title">
  <button type="submit">Зберегти</button>
</form>
