docs.title: Django URL Routing
docs.text:
When an HTTP request reaches your backend, Django does not just call some random function. It uses the URL Dispatcher — a strict system of rules for determining exactly which Python code should respond to this particular request.

Here is an architectural breakdown of how this system works.

docs.title: 1. The core mechanism and execution flow
docs.text:
Routing follows a clear algorithm:

  1. Initialization: ROOT_URLCONF. Django reads the ROOT_URLCONF setting to find the main routes file (usually the project-level urls.py).

  2. Loading patterns: urlpatterns. It looks for the urlpatterns variable — a plain list (sequence) of path() or re_path() objects.

  3. Top-down search: Top-down matching. Django reads this list strictly from top to bottom and compares the requested URL with each pattern. It stops at the very first match.

  4. Calling the view: HttpRequest. As soon as a match is found, Django imports the corresponding view function, passes it the HttpRequest object and any variables "captured" from the URL.

  5. 404 error: Resolver404. If no route matches, a Resolver404 exception is raised and the error handler is called (404 Page Not Found).

Mental model: Imagine a mail carrier walking down a long street (your urlpatterns list) and comparing the address on the envelope with the house numbers. As soon as they see a house whose number matches the address on the letter, they drop the letter there (calling the view) and stop searching. They do not walk to the end of the street to check whether there is a "better" house.

docs.title: 2. Modular backend architecture and include()
docs.text:
To scale the backend, Django uses the include() function. It lets you split one giant list of routes into isolated modules for each app.

When Django encounters include(), it cuts off the part of the URL that has already matched and passes the rest of the string to the nested urls.py file for further searching.

Architectural significance: This makes apps "plug-and-play" (independent modules). The polls app has no idea whether it lives at /polls/ or /api/v1/polls/. It only handles its own segment of the path.

docs.title: Example of the main urls.py (project level)
docs.text:
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    # All requests starting with /users/ are passed to the users_app app
    path('users/', include('users_app.urls')), 
    # API versioning
    path('api/v1/', include('api_v1.urls')),
]

docs.title: 3. Two kinds of dynamic parameters
docs.text: Django lets you pass data to a view in two different ways: through the structure of the path itself (Path Converters) and through request parameters (Query Strings).

docs.title: Type A: extracting parameters from the path (Path Converters)
docs.text:
Dynamic URLs use path converters to automatically turn parts of the URL text into Python variables. When the dispatcher finds a match (for example <int:id>), it "captures" that value, converts it to the specified type and passes it to the function.

  • <int:id>: captures an integer and passes it to the view as id=5.
  • <slug:post_slug>: captures text (letters, digits, hyphens).
  • <str:username>: captures any string up to the next slash /.

urls.py (app level):

from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    # Matches /users/42/
    path('<int:id>/', views.user_profile, name='profile'),

    # Matches /users/johndoe-99/
    path('<slug:username_slug>/', views.user_by_slug, name='profile_slug'),
]

views.py:

from django.shortcuts import render, get_object_or_404
from .models import User

def user_profile(request, id):
    # Behind the scenes Django executed: user_profile(request, id=42)
    user = get_object_or_404(User, pk=id)
    return render(request, 'profile.html', {'user': user})

docs.title: Type B: GET parameters (Query Strings)
docs.text:
Unlike converters, the URL dispatcher completely ignores everything in the address after the question mark ?. The router treats /users/ and /users/?id=42&sort=asc as one and the same route.

This data is automatically collected into the request.GET dictionary. It is convenient for filtering, sorting or pagination. This is a safe approach: if the parameters are missing, you simply use a default value via the .get() method.

views.py:

def users_list(request):
    # Look for the 'id' parameter (e.g. ?id=42). Returns None if it is missing.
    user_id = request.GET.get('id')

    # Look for 'sort'. If it is missing, default to 'asc'
    sort_by = request.GET.get('sort', 'asc')

    # Processing logic...
    return render(request, 'users_list.html', {'sort_by': sort_by})

docs.title: 4. Common misconceptions and edge cases
docs.text:
• The "best match" trap: Students often think Django looks for the most precise match. It does not — it takes the first one. If you put the <str:name>/ route above about/, a request to /about/ will be intercepted by the first route, and the view will receive the string "about" in the name variable. Always put static routes above dynamic ones.
  • Debugging intuition: When you see a 404 error in development mode (DEBUG = True), Django shows you the exact list of regular expressions and routes it checked, in exactly the order in which it checked them. This is your main tool for understanding where the system "took a wrong turn".

Here is a learning section that explains the architectural difference between handling GET and POST requests and shows how to safely pass data from the user to the database.

docs.title: Handling user data: GET filtering and POST forms
docs.text: In web application architecture, the GET and POST methods play fundamentally different roles. GET is used exclusively for reading and filtering data (it does not change server state). POST is used for writing or modifying data (it changes server state).

docs.title: Part 1: Filtering the database via GET parameters
docs.text:
When a user applies filters on a site (for example, picks a category or a sort order), the URL looks like this: /books/?category=fiction&sort=-price. Django collects these parameters into the request.GET dictionary.

Your task is to extract these parameters and safely pass them into ORM methods (.filter(), .order_by()).

docs.title: Architectural pattern: query chaining
docs.text: A Django QuerySet is "lazy". This means you can apply filters one after another, and Django will not hit the database until you pass the final result to the template.

docs.title: Code example: dynamic filtering and sorting
docs.text:
from django.shortcuts import render
from .models import Book

def book_list(request):
    # 1. Start with a base query (the DB is not called yet)
    queryset = Book.objects.all()

    # 2. Extract the GET parameters
    # Returns None if the parameter is missing
    category_query = request.GET.get('category') 
    # If the parameter is missing, sort by title by default
    sort_query = request.GET.get('sort', 'title') 

    # 3. Apply filtering if the parameter exists
    if category_query:
        # Translates to SQL: WHERE category = 'fiction'
        queryset = queryset.filter(category=category_query)

    # 4. Safe sorting
    # IMPORTANT: Always check the allowed sort fields!
    # If the user enters ?sort=invalid_column, the DB will raise a 500 error.
    allowed_sort_fields = ['title', '-title', 'price', '-price']
    if sort_query in allowed_sort_fields:
        # Translates to SQL: ORDER BY price DESC
        queryset = queryset.order_by(sort_query)

    # 5. Pass the finished QuerySet to the template (this is where the SQL query happens)
    return render(request, 'books/list.html', {'books': queryset})

Mental model: A GET request is like talking to a librarian. You ask: "Show me the fiction books, sorted by price" (?category=fiction&sort=price). The librarian (the view) applies these filters to the catalog (the QuerySet) and hands you a list. The state of the library does not change.

docs.title: Part 2: Handling POST requests from HTML forms
docs.text: When a user fills in a form (for example, registration or adding a product), the data is sent with the POST method. This data ends up in the request.POST dictionary.

docs.title: Form handling lifecycle (the PRG pattern)
docs.text:
Correct handling of a POST request requires following the PRG (Post/Redirect/Get) pattern. You should never return an HTML template directly after a successful POST request, because refreshing the page in the browser (F5) will resubmit the form (a double charge or a duplicate record).

  1. GET request (displaying the form): The user navigates to the page. The server sees that the method is GET and returns an empty HTML form.

  2. Submitting the data: The user fills in the fields and clicks "Submit". The browser builds a POST request.

  3. POST request (processing the logic): The server receives request.POST, extracts the data, checks it for errors and saves it to the database.

  4. Redirect: Instead of rendering a template, the server returns a 302 Redirect status. This forces the browser to make a new, clean GET request to another page (for example, a success page).

docs.title: Code example: handling "raw" POST data
docs.text:
The HTML form (note the mandatory {% csrf_token %}, which protects against cross-site request forgery):

<!-- create_book.html -->
<form method="POST" action="{% url 'create_book' %}">
    {% csrf_token %}
    <input type="text" name="title" placeholder="Book title">
    <input type="number" name="price" placeholder="Price">
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

The handler in views.py:

from django.shortcuts import render, redirect
from .models import Book

def create_book(request):
    # If the request came with the POST method (the form was submitted)
    if request.method == 'POST':
        # 1. Extract the data by the 'name' attribute from the HTML form
        book_title = request.POST.get('title')
        book_price = request.POST.get('price')

        # 2. Raw validation (are the fields non-empty?)
        if book_title and book_price:
            # 3. Save to the database
            Book.objects.create(title=book_title, price=book_price)

            # 4. Mandatory redirect (protection against double submission)
            return redirect('book_list') 
        else:
            # If there are errors, you can return the form with a message
            error_message = "Please fill in all fields."
            return render(request, 'create_book.html', {'error': error_message})

    # If the method is GET, just show an empty form
    return render(request, 'create_book.html')

docs.title: Why is "raw" request.POST rarely used?
docs.text:
Extracting data via request.POST.get() and writing checks by hand (is the price a number, is the title too long, is the email unique) takes a very long time and leads to bugs.

In real-world engineering, the Django Forms or ModelForms system is used for this. They automatically generate HTML, check data types on their own and guarantee safety.

Handling "raw" data via request.POST.get() quickly becomes unmanageable when a form has 10 fields, checkboxes, dates and files. You have to check manually whether a string is a number, whether it exceeds the character limit, and what to do if the user entered malicious code.

Django Forms (specifically ModelForm) is a mechanism that takes your database model and automatically builds a validation and HTML generation system for it.

docs.title: 1. Mental model: "The smart secretary"
docs.text: Imagine that a ModelForm is a smart secretary at the front desk. When a client comes for the first time (a GET request), the secretary hands them a blank form. When the client returns the completed form (a POST request), the secretary picks up a pen, checks every line against the rules (is this really a date? is the password too short?), and only if everything is perfect passes the document on to the director (the database). If there are errors, the secretary returns the form to the client, underlining in red marker exactly what needs to be fixed.

docs.title: 2. Step by step: dropping manual processing
Step 1: Creating the forms.py file
docs.text:
Instead of describing the rules in views.py, you create a separate file where you link the form to your model.

# forms.py
from django import forms
from .models import Book

class BookForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Book
        fields = ['title', 'price', 'category'] # Specify which fields may be edited

Architectural benefit: The form will automatically read your Book model. It will know that title is text (with a length limit) and price is a number, and will generate the corresponding checks and HTML tags (<input type="text">, <input type="number">).

docs.title: Step 2: Optimizing views.py
docs.text:
Now we remove all the manual code that parses the request.POST dictionary.

# views.py
from django.shortcuts import render, redirect
from .forms import BookForm

def create_book(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        # Pass all the user's data into the form (Bound Form)
        form = BookForm(request.POST)

        # The magic happens here: automatic checking of all the rules
        if form.is_valid():
            # If the data is clean and correct, save it to the database
            form.save()
            return redirect('book_list')
    else:
        # GET request: create an empty form (Unbound Form)
        form = BookForm()

    # If the form is invalid (has errors), or this is a GET request,
    # we simply pass the form object to the template.
    return render(request, 'create_book.html', {'form': form})

docs.title: Step 3: Simplifying the HTML template
docs.text:
Previously you had to write every <input> by hand. Now Django renders the form itself.

<!-- create_book.html -->
<form method="POST">
    {% csrf_token %}

    <!-- Outputs all fields, labels and error messages -->
    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">Save book</button>
</form>

If the user types text into the price field, form.is_valid() will return False, and Django will automatically render the page again, adding a red "Enter a number" message next to the price field. You do not need to write a single line of logic for this.

docs.title: 3. What happens under the hood of .is_valid()?
docs.text:
Calling form.is_valid() starts a deep data-cleaning pipeline:

  1. To Python (type conversion): All data from the web arrives as text (strings). Django tries to turn the string "15.99" into a Python Decimal object and "2026-05-19" into a datetime object.
  2. Checking model constraints: max_length, unique=True and whether a field with null=False is empty are checked.
  3. Creating cleaned_data: If all checks pass, Django creates the protected form.cleaned_data dictionary. After calling is_valid() you should never work with the "raw" request.POST — use only cleaned_data.
  4. Calling save(): The .save() method takes the safe cleaned_data dictionary and generates an INSERT query to the database.

docs.title: 4. Maximum optimization: Class-Based Views (CreateView)
docs.text:
We have already seen how ModelForm takes over validation and HTML generation. But views.py still contains boilerplate code: checking if request.method == 'POST', calling form.is_valid(), saving and redirecting.

Django has a built-in tool, CreateView, which encapsulates this whole lifecycle (GET, POST, validation, saving and redirecting) in a few lines of code.

docs.title: Code example: switching to classes
docs.text:
Instead of the create_book function, we create a class:

# views.py
from django.urls import reverse_lazy
from django.views.generic.edit import CreateView
from .models import Book
from .forms import BookForm

class BookCreateView(CreateView):
    model = Book
    form_class = BookForm
    template_name = 'create_book.html'

    # Where to redirect the user after the form is saved successfully
    success_url = reverse_lazy('book_list')

docs.title: How does it work under the hood?
docs.text:
The CreateView class contains all the standard logic you used to write by hand. When a request arrives, this class runs the following algorithm:

  1. If it is a GET request: The class automatically creates an empty BookForm instance and passes it to the create_book.html template as the form variable.
  2. If it is a POST request: The class automatically binds the data from request.POST to the BookForm form.
  3. Validation: .is_valid() is called.
  4. If there are errors, the class automatically returns the HTML page with the errors highlighted (you do not need to write an else block).
  5. If the data is clean, the class calls form.save(), writes the data to the database and performs an HTTP 302 Redirect to the address given in success_url.

docs.title: Wiring it up in urls.py
docs.text:
For the URL dispatcher to understand this class, you need to call it via the .as_view() method:

# urls.py
from django.urls import path
from .views import BookCreateView, book_list

urlpatterns = [
    path('books/', book_list, name='book_list'),
    path('books/new/', BookCreateView.as_view(), name='create_book'),
]

Architectural summary: Using CBVs (CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView) turns standard CRUD operations into configuration instead of imperative code. This minimizes the number of bugs and makes the backend architecture much cleaner.

docs.title: 5. Prediction exercise
docs.text:
Analyze the following URL dispatcher code:

# urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('api/users/', views.all_users),               # 1
    path('api/<str:username>/', views.user_profile),   # 2
    path('api/users/active/', views.active_users),     # 3
]

Question to think about: What happens if the user sends a request to /api/users/active/? Which view runs, and why?

Answer: Route #3 (active_users) runs. Route #1 (api/users/) does not match, because the path is longer. Route #2 does not match either: the <str:username> converter captures any characters except /, so the string users/active (which contains a slash) cannot become the value of username. So Django gets to route #3.

The top-down ordering trap here is a different one: route #2 captures any single-segment path. For example, /api/users/ matches both #1 and #2, but #1 runs because it comes first. If a static route such as path('api/active/', ...) were placed after #2, it would never be reached: active would be treated as a username. That is why static routes go above routes with parameters.

docs.title: Main router (notes_project/urls.py)
docs.text:

from django.urls import path, include

    path('accounts/', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')),  # login, logout, password

docs.title: Named URLs — reverse() and {% url %}
docs.text:

return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)

# reverse() — get the URL string
from django.urls import reverse
url = reverse('notes_app:note_detail', kwargs={'pk': 42})
# url == '/notes/42/'

docs.title: Django Views — FBV and CBV
docs.text:
Where you are in the knowledge map: RELATIONAL_DB_FOUNDATIONS → DJANGO_ORM_DEEP → DJANGO_FORMS → DJANGO_VIEWS ← you are here

A view is the point where an HTTP request meets your business logic. Django receives a request and returns a response. Everything else is implementation detail.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Section What's inside 1. The view contract HttpRequest → callable → HttpResponse 2. Request lifecycle URL dispatch → View → Response 3. FBV — function-based views def view, GET/POST, forms, decorators 4. CBV — class-based views dispatch(), as_view(), class attributes 5. Generic Views ListView, DetailView, CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView 6. Mixins LoginRequiredMixin, UserPassesTestMixin, custom ones 7. Forms in views FBV + Form, FormView, CreateView 8. Decorating CBVs method_decorator, LoginRequiredMixin vs @decorator 9. Choosing FBV vs CBV When to use which 10. Anti-patterns Fat View, ORM in the view, logic in the template

docs.title: 1. The view contract
docs.text:
A Django view is a Python callable (a function or a class method) that follows a single contract:

HttpRequest  →  [ callable ]  →  HttpResponse

That is the whole contract. Django requires nothing more.

from django.http import HttpRequest, HttpResponse

# The smallest possible view — a function:
def hello(request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse:
    return HttpResponse("Hello!")

# The class equivalent:
from django.views import View

class HelloView(View):
    def get(self, request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse:
        return HttpResponse("Hello!")

Key idea: A view knows nothing about SQL, knows nothing about business logic and holds no state. A view only: (1) receives the request, (2) delegates the work to a selector/service, (3) returns a response.

graph LR
    A["HttpRequest<br>(request)"] --> B["View<br>(callable)"]
    B --> C["HttpResponse<br>(HTML / JSON / redirect)"]
    B -.->|delegate| D["selectors.py<br>(READ)"]
    B -.->|delegate| E["services.py<br>(WRITE)"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

    class A,B,C step;
    class D,E success;

docs.title: The full path from the browser to the response
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant Middleware as Middleware Stack
    participant URLconf as urls.py
    participant View as views.py
    participant Service as services / selectors
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    Browser->>Middleware: HTTP Request
    Middleware->>Middleware: CSRF / Session / Auth checks
    Middleware->>URLconf: request (checked)
    URLconf->>View: view(request, **url_kwargs)

    alt GET request
        View->>Service: selectors.get_user_notes(user)
        Service->>DB: SELECT ...
        DB-->>Service: rows
        Service-->>View: QuerySet
        View->>Browser: render(template, context) → 200 HTML
    else POST request
        View->>View: form = NoteForm(request.POST)
        View->>View: form.is_valid()
        alt valid
            View->>Service: services.create_note(...)
            Service->>DB: INSERT ...
            DB-->>Service: created object
            Service-->>View: Note
            View->>Browser: redirect('note_detail', pk) → 302
        else invalid
            View->>Browser: render(form with errors) → 200
        end
    end

docs.title: URL dispatch — how Django finds the view
docs.text:
# notes_project/urls.py  — the main router
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', include('notes_app.urls', namespace='notes_app')),
]

# notes_app/urls.py  — the app-level router
from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = 'notes_app'

urlpatterns = [
    path('notes/',                 views.note_list,   name='note_list'),
    path('notes/new/',             views.note_create, name='note_create'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/',        views.note_detail, name='note_detail'),

docs.title: 3. FBV — Function-Based Views
docs.text: An FBV is a plain Python function. It accepts a request and returns an HttpResponse.

docs.title: 3.1 Basic anatomy of an FBV
docs.text:
# notes_app/views.py
from django.shortcuts import render, redirect, get_object_or_404
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.contrib import messages

from .models import Note
from .forms import NoteForm
from . import selectors, services


@login_required                             # ← decorator: checks authentication
def note_list(request):
    """
    GET /notes/  → list of notes with filters.

    The view does exactly three things:
    1. Reads parameters from the request
    2. Delegates to a selector
    3. Renders the template
    """
    # 1. Parameters from the URL query string: /notes/?q=python&tag=5
    search = request.GET.get('q', '').strip()
    tag_id = request.GET.get('tag')

    # 2. Reading via a selector — not raw ORM in the view!
    notes     = selectors.get_user_notes(request.user, search=search or None)
    notebooks = selectors.get_user_notebooks(request.user)
    tags      = selectors.get_user_tags(request.user)

    # 3. Render: the QuerySet is still lazy — the SQL runs here during rendering
    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_list.html', {
        'notes':     notes,
        'notebooks': notebooks,
        'tags':      tags,
        'search':    search,
    })

@login_required
def note_create(request):
    """
    GET  /notes/new/ → show an empty form
    POST /notes/new/ → process and save

    PRG (Post / Redirect / Get) is the standard pattern for forms.
    """
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user)

        if form.is_valid():
            note = services.create_note(
                user=request.user,
                title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
                content=form.cleaned_data.get('content', ''),
                priority=form.cleaned_data.get('priority', 1),
                tag_ids=[t.id for t in form.cleaned_data.get('tags', [])],
            )
            messages.success(request, f'Нотатку "{note.title}" створено!')
            return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)  # ← PRG!
        # is_valid=False → fall through to render below (form with errors)

    else:
        form = NoteForm(user=request.user)    # GET: empty form

    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_form.html', {
        'form':   form,
        'action': 'Створити',
        'title':  'Нова нотатка',
    })

docs.title: 3.3 get_object_or_404 and permission checks
docs.text:
@login_required
def note_edit(request, pk):
    # get_object_or_404:
    #   if not found → 404 Not Found (not 500 Internal Server Error)
    #   user=request.user → we check that this is OUR note (not someone else's!)
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, instance=note, user=request.user)
        if form.is_valid():
            services.update_note(
                note,
                title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
                content=form.cleaned_data.get('content', ''),
            )
            return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)
    else:
        # instance=note → the form is pre-filled with the current data
        form = NoteForm(instance=note, user=request.user)

    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_form.html', {
        'form':   form,
        'note':   note,
        'action': 'Зберегти',
        'title':  f'Редагувати: {note.title}',
    })


@login_required
def note_delete(request, pk):
    """
    GET  /notes/42/delete/ → confirmation page
    POST /notes/42/delete/ → deletion → redirect

    Why only POST for deletion?
    Browsers, bots and search engines follow GET links automatically.
    GET /notes/42/delete/ on clicking a link → the note disappears without confirmation!
    """
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        title = note.title
        services.delete_note(note)
        messages.warning(request, f'Нотатку "{title}" видалено.')
        return redirect('notes_app:note_list')

    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_confirm_delete.html', {'note': note})

docs.title: 4.1 Why CBVs exist
docs.text:
FBVs have a problem: boilerplate logic gets repeated. Every CRUD view has the same structure:

# FBV for List — always the same:
def note_list(request):
    qs = Note.objects.filter(user=request.user)
    return render(request, 'note_list.html', {'notes': qs})

# FBV for Detail — almost the same:
def note_detail(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

# FBV for Delete — the same structure again...
def note_delete(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
    if request.method == 'POST':
        note.delete()
        return redirect('note_list')
    return render(request, 'confirm_delete.html', {'note': note})

CBVs solve this with OOP: inheritance, method overriding, mixins.

docs.title: 4.2 dispatch() — the heart of a CBV
docs.text:
When a request reaches a CBV, Django calls dispatch(). It is an HTTP method router:

HTTP Request → as_view() → dispatch() → get() / post() / put() / delete()

# Simplified internal implementation of View.dispatch():
class View:
    http_method_names = ['get', 'post', 'put', 'patch', 'delete', 'head', 'options']

    @classmethod
    def as_view(cls, **initkwargs):
        """Returns a wrapper function for urls.py."""
        def view(request, *args, **kwargs):
            self = cls(**initkwargs)         # ← a new instance for every request!
            self.setup(request, *args, **kwargs)
            return self.dispatch(request, *args, **kwargs)
        return view

    def dispatch(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        """Routes to the matching class method based on the HTTP method."""
        method_name = request.method.lower()
        if method_name in self.http_method_names:
            handler = getattr(self, method_name, self.http_method_not_allowed)
        else:
            handler = self.http_method_not_allowed
        return handler(request, *args, **kwargs)

    A["HTTP POST /notes/new/"] --> B["URLconf: NoteCreateView.as_view()"]
    B --> C["View.__init__() — new instance"]
    C --> D["View.setup(request, *args, **kwargs)"]
    D --> E["View.dispatch(request)"]
    E --> F{request.method.lower?}
    F -->|get| G["View.get(request)"]
    F -->|post| H["View.post(request)"]
    F -->|delete| I["View.delete(request)"]
    F -->|Not defined| J["405 Method Not Allowed"]
    G --> K["HttpResponse"]
    H --> K

# ─── FBV ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def note_list(request):
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:
        return redirect('/login/')
    if request.method == 'GET':
        notes = selectors.get_user_notes(request.user)
        return render(request, 'note_list.html', {'notes': notes})
    return HttpResponseNotAllowed(['GET'])


# ─── CBV (base View) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
from django.views import View
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin

class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, View):
    template_name = 'note_list.html'     # ← class attribute

    def get(self, request):              # ← a separate method for GET
        notes = selectors.get_user_notes(request.user)
        return render(request, self.template_name, {'notes': notes})
    # POST → 405 automatically (there is no post() method)
    # auth → LoginRequiredMixin (no if is_authenticated)

docs.title: 4.5 Overriding class attributes
docs.text:
# Inheritance lets you change behavior without editing the parent class:

class BaseUserView(LoginRequiredMixin, View):
    """Base class for all views that need filtering by user."""
    model = None

    def get_queryset(self):
        return self.model.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)


class NoteListView(BaseUserView):
    model = Note
    template_name = 'note_list.html'

    def get_queryset(self):
        # Extend the parent — + optimization
        return super().get_queryset().select_related('notebook').prefetch_related('tags')

    def get(self, request):
        return render(request, self.template_name, {'notes': self.get_queryset()})


class NotebookListView(BaseUserView):
    model = Notebook
    template_name = 'notebook_list.html'

    def get(self, request):
        return render(request, self.template_name, {'notebooks': self.get_queryset()})

docs.title: 5.1 ListView
docs.text:
from django.views.generic import ListView
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin

class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    model = Note
    template_name = 'notes_app/note_list.html'
    context_object_name = 'notes'           # ← name in the template (default: object_list)
    paginate_by = 20                         # ← pagination automatically!
    ordering = ['-is_pinned', '-updated_at']

    def get_queryset(self):
        """
        Override the default queryset (Model.objects.all())
        to filter by user and add optimization.
        """
        qs = Note.objects.filter(
            user=self.request.user,
            is_archived=False,
        ).select_related('notebook').prefetch_related('tags')

        search = self.request.GET.get('q')
        if search:
            qs = qs.filter(title__icontains=search)

        return qs

    def get_context_data(self, **kwargs):
        """Add extra data to the context."""
        context = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)   # ← 'notes' is already here!
        context['notebooks'] = selectors.get_user_notebooks(self.request.user)
        context['tags']      = selectors.get_user_tags(self.request.user)
        context['search']    = self.request.GET.get('q', '')
        return context

# ListView automatically:
# 1. Calls get_queryset()
# 2. Puts the result into context[context_object_name]
# 3. Handles paginate_by → adds page_obj to the context
# 4. Renders template_name

docs.title: 5.2 DetailView
docs.text:
from django.views.generic import DetailView

class NoteDetailView(LoginRequiredMixin, DetailView):
    model = Note
    template_name = 'notes_app/note_detail.html'
    context_object_name = 'note'

    def get_queryset(self):
        """Filter by user → automatic 404 for other people's notes."""
        return Note.objects.filter(
            user=self.request.user
        ).select_related('notebook', 'user').prefetch_related('tags', 'reminders')

# DetailView automatically:
# 1. Takes pk or slug from the URL kwargs
# 2. Calls get_queryset().get(pk=pk) → either the object or 404
# 3. Puts the object into context[context_object_name]
# 4. Renders template_name

docs.title: 5.3 CreateView
docs.text:
from django.views.generic.edit import CreateView
from django.urls import reverse_lazy

class NoteCreateView(LoginRequiredMixin, CreateView):
    model = Note
    form_class = NoteForm                              # ← our form
    template_name = 'notes_app/note_form.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('notes_app:note_list') # ← after success

    def get_form_kwargs(self):
        """Pass user into the form (to filter the queryset in fields)."""
        kwargs = super().get_form_kwargs()
        kwargs['user'] = self.request.user
        return kwargs

    def form_valid(self, form):
        """Called when form.is_valid() == True."""
        # Use a Service instead of form.save():
        note = services.create_note(
            user=self.request.user,
            title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
            content=form.cleaned_data.get('content', ''),
            priority=form.cleaned_data.get('priority', 1),
            tag_ids=[t.id for t in form.cleaned_data.get('tags', [])],
        )
        messages.success(self.request, f'Нотатку "{note.title}" створено!')
        return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)

    def form_invalid(self, form):
        """Called when form.is_valid() == False."""
        messages.error(self.request, 'Виправ помилки у формі.')
        return super().form_invalid(form)

    def get_context_data(self, **kwargs):
        context = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)
        context['action'] = 'Створити'
        context['title'] = 'Нова нотатка'
        return context

# CreateView automatically:
# GET  → get_form() → render with an empty form
# POST → get_form(request.POST) → is_valid():
#          True  → form_valid(form)  → success_url redirect
#          False → form_invalid(form) → render with errors

docs.title: 5.4 UpdateView
docs.text:
from django.views.generic.edit import UpdateView

class NoteUpdateView(LoginRequiredMixin, UpdateView):
    model = Note
    form_class = NoteForm
    template_name = 'notes_app/note_form.html'

    def get_queryset(self):
        # Only your own notes — other people's → 404
        return Note.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)

    def get_form_kwargs(self):
        kwargs = super().get_form_kwargs()
        kwargs['user'] = self.request.user
        return kwargs

    def form_valid(self, form):
        services.update_note(
            self.object,
            title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
            content=form.cleaned_data.get('content', ''),
        )
        return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=self.object.pk)

    def get_context_data(self, **kwargs):
        context = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)
        context['action'] = 'Зберегти'
        context['title'] = f'Редагувати: {self.object.title}'
        return context

# UpdateView ≈ CreateView, but:
# - get_queryset().get(pk=pk) to find the object
# - GET → the form is pre-filled with instance=self.object

docs.title: 5.5 DeleteView
docs.text:
from django.views.generic.edit import DeleteView

class NoteDeleteView(LoginRequiredMixin, DeleteView):
    model = Note
    template_name = 'notes_app/note_confirm_delete.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('notes_app:note_list')

    def get_queryset(self):
        return Note.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)

    def form_valid(self, form):
        """Override to use a Service and a message."""
        title = self.object.title
        services.delete_note(self.object)
        messages.warning(self.request, f'Нотатку "{title}" видалено.')
        return redirect(self.success_url)

# DeleteView automatically:
# GET  → renders the confirmation page
# POST → self.object.delete() → redirect success_url

docs.title: What Generic Views do automatically
docs.text: Generic View Automatically Usually overridden ListView all(), paginate, render get_queryset() — filtering by user DetailView get(pk=pk) → 404, render get_queryset() — access permissions CreateView GET form, POST validation, form.save() form_valid() if a Service is needed UpdateView GET pre-filled form, POST update get_queryset() + form_valid() DeleteView GET confirmation, POST deletion get_queryset() + form_valid()

docs.title: 6. Mixins
docs.text: A mixin is a class that provides one specific behavior and is not a standalone view. It is combined through multiple inheritance.

docs.title: 6.1 Built-in auth mixins
docs.text:
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import (
    LoginRequiredMixin,
    PermissionRequiredMixin,
    UserPassesTestMixin,
)

# LoginRequiredMixin: if not logged in → redirect to login
class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    login_url = '/accounts/login/'       # ← where to redirect (default: settings.LOGIN_URL)
    redirect_field_name = 'next'         # ← ?next=/notes/ to come back after login
    model = Note
    ...


# PermissionRequiredMixin: checks a specific permission
class AdminNoteView(PermissionRequiredMixin, ListView):
    permission_required = 'notes_app.can_moderate'
    model = Note


# UserPassesTestMixin: arbitrary check logic
class OwnerOnlyNoteView(UserPassesTestMixin, DetailView):
    model = Note

    def test_func(self):
        """Returns True → access allowed, False → 403 Forbidden."""
        note = self.get_object()
        return self.request.user == note.user

docs.title: 6.2 Correct MRO order
docs.text:
# ✅ CORRECT: Mixin FIRST, Generic View LAST
class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    ...

# ❌ WRONG: putting the Generic View first breaks the MRO
class NoteListView(ListView, LoginRequiredMixin):
    ...

graph LR
    A["NoteListView"] -->|MRO order| B["LoginRequiredMixin"]
    B --> C["ListView"]
    C --> D["View"]
    D --> E["object"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;

    class A,D,E step;
    class C success;
    class B warning;

Why: Python's MRO (C3 linearization) goes from left to right. dispatch() from LoginRequiredMixin must run BEFORE dispatch() from View. That is why the mixin always comes first.

docs.title: 6.3 A custom mixin
docs.text:
class UserQuerySetMixin:
    """
    Automatically filters the queryset by the current user.
    Plugs into any Generic View that has get_queryset().
    """
    def get_queryset(self):
        return super().get_queryset().filter(user=self.request.user)


# Usage — one line instead of get_queryset() in every view:
class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, UserQuerySetMixin, ListView):
    model = Note        # get_queryset() filters by user automatically!

class NoteDetailView(LoginRequiredMixin, UserQuerySetMixin, DetailView):
    model = Note

class NoteDeleteView(LoginRequiredMixin, UserQuerySetMixin, DeleteView):
    model = Note
    success_url = reverse_lazy('notes_app:note_list')

docs.title: 6.4 Limitation: one Generic View parent
docs.text:
# ❌ WILL NOT WORK: two Generic Views in one class
class BadView(ListView, CreateView):
    # The get() and post() methods conflict between ListView and CreateView
    # The MRO will not resolve it — behavior is unpredictable
    ...

# ✅ Solution 1: separate classes
class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView): ...
class NoteCreateView(LoginRequiredMixin, CreateView): ...

# ✅ Solution 2: an FBV for complex combinations (list + form on one page)
@login_required
def note_list_and_create(request):
    notes = selectors.get_user_notes(request.user)
    form = NoteForm(request.POST or None, user=request.user)
    if request.method == 'POST' and form.is_valid():
        services.create_note(user=request.user, **form.cleaned_data)
        return redirect('notes_app:note_list')
    return render(request, 'note_list_create.html', {'notes': notes, 'form': form})

docs.title: 7.1 FBV + Form — the standard pattern
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant FBV as FBV (note_create)
    participant Form as NoteForm
    participant Service as services.create_note

    Browser->>FBV: GET /notes/new/
    FBV->>Form: NoteForm(user=request.user)
    Form-->>FBV: empty form
    FBV->>Browser: render(form) → 200 HTML

    Browser->>FBV: POST /notes/new/ (form data)
    FBV->>Form: NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user)
    FBV->>Form: form.is_valid()

    alt valid
        Form-->>FBV: True + cleaned_data
        FBV->>Service: create_note(user, title, ...)
        Service-->>FBV: Note object
        FBV->>Browser: redirect(note_detail, pk) → 302
    else invalid
        Form-->>FBV: False + form.errors
        FBV->>Browser: render(form with errors) → 200
    end
# The standard structure of an FBV with a form — memorize it for good:
@login_required
def note_create(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user)    # ← bound form
        if form.is_valid():
            note = services.create_note(user=request.user, ...)
            return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)  # ← PRG
    else:
        form = NoteForm(user=request.user)                  # ← unbound form

    return render(request, 'template.html', {'form': form})

docs.title: 7.2 FormView — a CBV for any form
docs.text:
from django.views.generic.edit import FormView
from django.urls import reverse_lazy

class NoteCreateFormView(LoginRequiredMixin, FormView):
    template_name = 'notes_app/note_form.html'
    form_class = NoteForm
    success_url = reverse_lazy('notes_app:note_list')

    def get_form_kwargs(self):
        """Add user to the form kwargs."""
        kwargs = super().get_form_kwargs()
        kwargs['user'] = self.request.user
        return kwargs

    def form_valid(self, form):
        """Called automatically when form.is_valid() == True."""
        services.create_note(
            user=self.request.user,
            title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
        )
        return super().form_valid(form)  # ← redirect to success_url

docs.title: 8. Decorating CBVs
docs.text: FBVs are decorated with @decorator. CBVs are trickier, because they are classes, not functions.

docs.title: Option 1: via the URLconf (a single instance)
docs.text:
# urls.py
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.views.generic import TemplateView

urlpatterns = [
    # The decorator applies only to this URL:
    path('secret/', login_required(TemplateView.as_view(template_name='secret.html'))),
]
# ⚠️ Does not decorate the whole class — only this specific URL

docs.title: Option 2: method_decorator on dispatch (the whole class)
docs.text:
from django.utils.decorators import method_decorator
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.views.decorators.cache import never_cache
from django.views.generic import TemplateView

# One decorator — on the class:
@method_decorator(login_required, name='dispatch')
class ProtectedView(TemplateView):
    template_name = 'secret.html'

# Several decorators — a list:
decorators = [never_cache, login_required]

@method_decorator(decorators, name='dispatch')
class ProtectedView(TemplateView):
    template_name = 'secret.html'
# Execution order: never_cache → login_required (left to right)

# Or decorate a specific method (not dispatch):
class NoteDetailView(DetailView):
    @method_decorator(login_required)
    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        return super().get(request, *args, **kwargs)

docs.title: Option 3: LoginRequiredMixin (recommended for auth)
docs.text:
# The cleanest way for auth:
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin

class NoteListView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    model = Note
    # LoginRequiredMixin overrides dispatch() automatically — cleaner than a decorator

docs.text: Approach Code When to use URLconf decorator login_required(View.as_view()) Quick, for a single URL @method_decorator @method_decorator(dec, name='dispatch') Non-standard decorators (cache, vary_on) Mixin LoginRequiredMixin Auth/permissions — always better

docs.text: Anti-pattern What's wrong Fix ORM directly in the view Note.objects.filter(...) in views.py Move it to selectors.py Business logic in the view if note.priority > 3: note.is_pinned = True Move it to services.py Logic in the template {% if note.user.profile.settings.allow_pin %} Logic → View / Service Fat View 200+ lines in a view function Split into Selector + Service + forms .get() without 404 Note.objects.get(pk=pk) → 500 if missing get_object_or_404() DELETE via GET GET /notes/delete/?pk=5 Only POST for destructive operations print() in production print(request.POST) Django logging + Debug Toolbar request.POST[key] in the ORM Directly in Note.objects.create(title=request.POST['title']) Through a form → cleaned_data

docs.title: Quick cheat sheet
docs.text:
# === FBV template ===
@login_required
def my_view(request, pk):
    obj = get_object_or_404(MyModel, pk=pk, user=request.user)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = MyForm(request.POST, instance=obj)
        if form.is_valid():
            services.update_my_object(obj, **form.cleaned_data)
            return redirect('my_app:detail', pk=obj.pk)
    else:
        form = MyForm(instance=obj)

    return render(request, 'template.html', {'form': form, 'obj': obj})


# === CBV (ListView) ===
class MyListView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    model = MyModel
    template_name = 'my_list.html'
    context_object_name = 'objects'
    paginate_by = 20

    def get_queryset(self):
        return MyModel.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)

    def get_context_data(self, **kwargs):
        ctx = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)
        ctx['extra'] = 'data'
        return ctx


# === URL registration ===
urlpatterns = [
    # FBV:
    path('',       views.my_view,            name='my_view'),
    # CBV:
    path('list/',  views.MyListView.as_view(), name='my_list'),
]

docs.title: WSGI vs ASGI — a practical breakdown
docs.text: WSGI is enough for sync HTTP Django. ASGI is needed for WebSocket and an async runtime. In notes_chat_app both protocols coexist in a single Uvicorn process.

docs.title: The short difference
docs.text: WSGI ASGI Standard PEP 3333 (2010) A separate ASGI specification (not a PEP; version 3.0 in 2019) Protocols HTTP only HTTP + WebSocket + HTTP/2 Execution Synchronous (blocking I/O) Asynchronous (asyncio event loop) File in the project notes_project/wsgi.py notes_project/asgi.py Server Gunicorn, uWSGI Uvicorn, Daphne Suitable for CRUD, forms, authentication + WebSocket, real-time, streaming

docs.title: Where to find it in the project
notes_project/wsgi.py
docs.text:
# notes_project/wsgi.py
import os
from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')

application = get_wsgi_application()
# ↑ The standard Django WSGI callable
# Used if you run the app through Gunicorn:
#   gunicorn notes_project.wsgi:application
#
# In notes_chat_app this file is NOT used in production —
# we use asgi.py and Uvicorn.
# The file is kept for compatibility (some platforms look for wsgi.py)

What's in it: one line of real code — application = get_wsgi_application(). It is a callable that accepts an environ dict and a start_response function. Never touch it without a reason.

docs.title: notes_project/asgi.py
docs.text:
# notes_project/asgi.py
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
from channels.routing import ProtocolTypeRouter, URLRouter
from channels.auth import AuthMiddlewareStack

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')

# CRITICAL: the FIRST line before any imports from notes_app
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()

# After get_asgi_application() it is safe to import models, consumers
from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns

application = ProtocolTypeRouter({
    "http": django_asgi_app,          # HTTP → regular Django
    "websocket": AuthMiddlewareStack(
        URLRouter(websocket_urlpatterns)  # WebSocket → Consumer
    ),
})

What to change here: - Add a new protocol (for example, "lifespan") — very rarely - Replace AuthMiddlewareStack with your own middleware — if you need custom WS authentication

What NOT to change: - The order: get_asgi_application() always comes first - ProtocolTypeRouter — this structure is mandatory for Channels

docs.title: notes_project/routing.py
docs.text:
# notes_project/routing.py
from django.urls import re_path
from notes_app import consumers

websocket_urlpatterns = [
    re_path(
        r'^ws/groups/(?P<group_pk>\d+)/chat/$',
        consumers.GroupChatConsumer.as_asgi(),
    ),
]

What to change here: - Add a new WebSocket URL → a new line in websocket_urlpatterns - Change a URL pattern → edit the regex - Hook up a new Consumer → consumers.NewConsumer.as_asgi()

Do not confuse it with notes_app/urls.py — that one is for HTTP URLs, this one is for WebSocket URLs.

docs.text:
entrypoint.sh:
  exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8001

Uvicorn:
  → loads notes_project/asgi.py
  → gets application = ProtocolTypeRouter({...})

On an HTTP request from nginx:

On a WebSocket from nginx (Upgrade: websocket):

  → AuthMiddlewareStack → URLRouter → GroupChatConsumer

docs.title: Part III. Models, Database and ORM
docs.text:
Models are a Python description of the domain. The ORM turns Python calls into SQL. This part covers the whole stack: relational DBs → Django models → migrations → QuerySet API → PostgreSQL specifics → optimization.

Prerequisites: Part II (Django Core). Level: Beginner → Intermediate.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Document What we will learn Relational DBs tables, keys, JOIN, ACID, SQL basics Django Models models.Model, fields, relationships, Meta, __str__, constraints ORM in depth Q, F, annotate, values(), only(), defer(), N+1 Migrations makemigrations, migrate, squash, data migrations PostgreSQL data types, jsonb, full-text search, EXPLAIN ANALYZE Indexes B-tree, partial index, composite index, db_index=True Transactions atomic(), isolation levels, select_for_update(), race conditions ORM Diagrams Mermaid ER diagrams, QuerySet pipeline

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Models — a Python description of tables:

class Note(models.Model):
    PRIORITY_LOW     = 1
    PRIORITY_MEDIUM  = 2
    PRIORITY_HIGH    = 3
    PRIORITY_URGENT  = 4
    PRIORITY_CHOICES = [(1,'🟢 Низький'),(2,'🟡 Середній'),(3,'🟠 Високий'),(4,'🔴 Терміново')]

    user      = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    group     = models.ForeignKey(Group, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True)
    notebook  = models.ForeignKey(Notebook, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True)
    tags      = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True)
    title     = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    priority  = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=1, validators=[MaxValueValidator(4)])
    is_pinned = models.BooleanField(default=False)

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.CheckConstraint(check=Q(priority__gte=1) & Q(priority__lte=4), name='...')
        ]

QuerySet API (lazy queries):

# A QuerySet is not SQL yet:
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user).select_related('notebook').prefetch_related('tags')

# SQL runs only on materialization:
for note in notes:          # evaluate
    print(note.title)

list(notes)                 # evaluate
notes.count()               # SELECT COUNT(*)
notes.exists()              # SELECT 1 FROM ... LIMIT 1

The N+1 problem and optimization:

# ❌ N+1: for 50 notes → 51 SQL queries
notes = Note.objects.all()
for note in notes:
    print(note.notebook.title)   # a separate SELECT for every note

# ✅ select_related: 1 JOIN
notes = Note.objects.select_related('notebook').all()

# ✅ prefetch_related: 2 queries (for M2M and reverse FK)
notes = Note.objects.prefetch_related('tags').all()

Q objects and complex conditions:

from django.db.models import Q

# Your own notes OR the group's notes:
Note.objects.filter(Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user.groups.all()))

# Pinned notes that are NOT archived:
Note.objects.filter(Q(is_pinned=True) & ~Q(is_archived=True))

on_delete — what happens when the parent record is deleted:

on_delete Behavior CASCADE deletes the dependent records along with it SET_NULL sets the FK to NULL (requires null=True) PROTECT blocks deletion if there are dependent records DO_NOTHING nothing (dangerous — can break the FK constraint)

docs.title: Lazy evaluation — a step-by-step breakdown
docs.text:
A QuerySet is a query object, not a result. filter() only adds a condition; SQL is sent to the DB only on materialization.

Step 1: filter() — no SQL yet

notes = Note.objects.filter(user=request.user)
# A Python QuerySet object. Nothing has been sent to the DB yet.
print(type(notes))  # <class 'django.db.models.query.QuerySet'>

Step 2: conditions accumulate without SQL

qs = Note.objects.filter(user=request.user)  # lazy
qs = qs.filter(is_pinned=True)               # lazy, a condition is added
qs = qs.order_by('-updated_at')              # lazy
qs = qs.select_related('notebook')           # lazy

notes = list(qs)  # ← only here: ONE SELECT with all conditions and the JOIN

When materialization happens:

Action SQL for note in notes: SELECT * list(notes) SELECT * notes[0] SELECT * LIMIT 1 notes.count() SELECT COUNT(*) notes.exists() SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1 len(notes) SELECT * (loads everything)

docs.title: N+1 — a hidden problem in the template
docs.text:
Precisely because a QuerySet is lazy, N+1 quietly appears when a template is rendered:

# views.py — looks fine: a single filter()
def notes_list(request):
    notes = Note.objects.filter(user=request.user)   # 1 query
    return render(request, 'notes_list.html', {'notes': notes})

{# notes_list.html #}
{% for note in notes %}
    {{ note.user.username }}     {# ← Django materializes a separate QuerySet for every note.user! #}
    {{ note.notebook.title }}    {# ← another SELECT for every note.notebook! #}
{% endfor %}

100 notes → 201 SQL queries instead of the expected one. Django does not know in advance that note.user will be needed for every note — it fetches the data "on demand".

Solution: select_related and prefetch_related

# select_related — for ForeignKey and OneToOne (does a JOIN, still 1 query)
notes = (
    Note.objects.filter(user=request.user)
    .select_related('user', 'notebook')      # FK → JOIN
    .prefetch_related('tags', 'reminders')   # M:N, reverse FK → 2 extra queries
)
# Total: 1 + 2 = 3 queries instead of 1 + 100 + 100

All optimizations live in selectors.py — views stay thin:

# notes_app/selectors.py
def get_user_notes(user):
    return (
        Note.objects.filter(Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user.groups.all()))
        .select_related('user', 'notebook')
        .prefetch_related('tags', 'reminders')
        .order_by('-updated_at')
    )

The real implementation: notes_app/selectors.py — 13 functions, each with optimized queries.

docs.title: Django Project Architecture and Database Evolution
docs.text: This guide reveals the deep internals of how Django works, focusing on how Django manages database evolution through migrations.

docs.title: Part 1: Orchestrating Database Evolution (Migrations and the ORM)
1. The Core Mechanism: Why Migrations Exist
docs.text: Databases require raw SQL (for example, CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE) to change their structure. At the same time, Django models are written in Python. Migrations serve as the bridge between them, acting as a version control system for your database schema. They ensure that as your Python code evolves, the database structure safely evolves along with it without losing user data.

docs.title: 2. The Execution Flow: makemigrations vs migrate
docs.text:
• makemigrations: Django reads your models.py files and compares them with an in-memory representation of the historical database schema. It then generates a new Python file on your hard drive (for example, 0001_initial.py). This file contains a declarative list of operations (what changed) and dependencies (what must happen first). This command makes no changes to the database itself.
  • migrate: Django connects to the database and checks a special internal table called django_migrations to find out which files have already been applied. For any unapplied files, Django converts the Python operations into database-specific SQL and executes them, irreversibly changing the database structure.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model: The Architect and the Builders
docs.text: Imagine that makemigrations is the architect who draws the blueprint of a new floor plan. And migrate is the construction crew that reads the blueprint and actually knocks down walls and pours concrete.

docs.title: 4. Migration Dependencies
docs.text: Migrations are not executed in alphabetical order; they are executed based on a dependency graph. If your books app adds a ForeignKey field pointing to the authors app, the migration file for books will automatically add a dependency on the authors migration. This guarantees that the authors table is created before the database tries to create a constraint that references it.

docs.title: Visualization: Schema Evolution Timeline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Py as models.py
    participant Make as makemigrations
    participant Mig as migrate
    participant DB as Database (django_migrations)

    Dev->>Py: 1. Adds the 'isbn' field to the Book class
    Dev->>Make: 2. python manage.py makemigrations
    Make->>Make: Compares models.py with past migrations
    Make-->>Dev: 3. Creates 0002_book_isbn.py
    Dev->>Mig: 4. python manage.py migrate
    Mig->>DB: 5. Checks the 'django_migrations' table
    Mig->>DB: 6. Executes: ALTER TABLE book ADD COLUMN isbn;
    Mig->>DB: 7. Records 0002_book_isbn as [X] applied

docs.text:
graph TD
    A[authors/0001_initial.py] -->|Creates the Author table| B(books/0001_initial.py)
    B -->|Creates the Book table| C(books/0002_book_isbn.py)
    A -->|ForeignKey dependency| D(publishers/0001_initial.py)

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

    class A,B,D step;
    class C success;

docs.title: 5. Common Beginner Problems with Migrations
docs.text:
• The Non-Nullable Field: If you add a new field to an existing model (for example, age = models.IntegerField()) without providing a default value, the database panics because it does not know what to write into the already existing rows. Django will intercept makemigrations and ask you in the terminal to provide a one-off default value.
  • Inconsistent History: Deleting a migration file from the hard drive after it has already been applied via migrate breaks the dependency graph. Django will refuse to run future migrations until the history is fixed manually.

docs.title: 6. Debugging Intuition
docs.text: If you want to know exactly what changes Django plans to make to the system right now, run python manage.py sqlmigrate <app_name> <migration_number>. This command does not change the database; it simply prints the exact "raw" SQL statements (for example, CREATE INDEX or ALTER TABLE) that Django plans to execute to the terminal.

docs.title: 7. Relevance for Production Deployment
docs.text: Migration files are committed to your Git repository along with the Python code. When your code is deployed to a production server, the CI/CD pipeline automatically runs python manage.py migrate. Because the dependency graph is clearly defined in the files, the production database updates its schema in exactly the same sequence you used on your local machine.

docs.title: Django Models
docs.text: A model is both a Python class and a database table. Each class attribute → a column in the table. The Django ORM turns Python into SQL.

docs.title: Why models
docs.text:
Without an ORM you would write SQL by hand:

# Without ORM — SQL by hand
cursor.execute(
    "INSERT INTO notes (title, content, user_id, priority) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)",
    [title, content, user.id, priority]
)

With the Django ORM:

# With ORM — a Python class
note = Note.objects.create(
    title=title, content=content, user=user, priority=Note.PRIORITY_MEDIUM
)

The ORM: - generates SQL automatically (and efficiently) - protects against SQL injection - makes refactoring possible (rename a field → an ALTER TABLE is generated) - supports PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL without code changes

docs.title: Anatomy of a Model class
docs.text:
# notes_app/models.py

class Note(models.Model):
    # ── Constants for choices ─────────────────────────────────────────
    PRIORITY_LOW    = 1
    PRIORITY_MEDIUM = 2
    PRIORITY_HIGH   = 3
    PRIORITY_URGENT = 4

    PRIORITY_CHOICES = [
        (PRIORITY_LOW,    '🟢 Низький'),
        (PRIORITY_MEDIUM, '🟡 Середній'),
        (PRIORITY_HIGH,   '🟠 Високий'),
        (PRIORITY_URGENT, '🔴 Терміново'),
    ]

    # ── Fields (Field types) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    user     = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='notes')
    group    = models.ForeignKey(Group, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True, related_name='notes')
    notebook = models.ForeignKey(Notebook, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True, related_name='notes')
    tags     = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True, related_name='notes')

    title      = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    content    = models.TextField(blank=True)
    priority   = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(choices=PRIORITY_CHOICES, default=PRIORITY_LOW)
    is_pinned  = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    is_archived= models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)   # ← set once on CREATE
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)        # ← updated on every save()

    # ── Special methods ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    def __str__(self):
        pin = "📌 " if self.is_pinned else ""
        return f"{pin}{self.title}"

    # ── Meta class ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    class Meta:
        ordering = ['-is_pinned', '-priority', '-updated_at']  # default ORDER BY
        verbose_name = 'Нотатка'
        verbose_name_plural = 'Нотатки'
        indexes = [
            models.Index(fields=['user', '-updated_at'], name='cnote_user_updated_idx'),
            models.Index(fields=['user', 'is_pinned'],   name='cnote_user_pinned_idx'),
        ]
        constraints = [
            models.CheckConstraint(
                check=models.Q(priority__gte=1) & models.Q(priority__lte=4),
                name='cnote_priority_valid_range'
            ),
        ]

docs.title: Django ORM — From the Basics to the Deep Mechanics
docs.text: ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) is a translator between Python and SQL. You write Note.objects.filter(user=user) — Django generates SELECT ... WHERE user_id = ?. But the ORM is smart: it runs SQL only when needed, caches results, and protects against SQL injection.

docs.title: Why the ORM and Not Raw SQL
docs.text:
# Without the ORM — dangerous and hard:
cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM notes WHERE user_id = {user.id}")
# ↑ SQL injection! a title with ' OR 1=1-- will break the system

# With the ORM — safe and clear:
Note.objects.filter(user=user)
# ↑ automatically: WHERE user_id = %s, [user.id]
# ↑ the same on SQLite and PostgreSQL
# ↑ the result is Python objects, not raw rows

Note.objects.filter(is_archived=False)
     ← this is a RECIPE, not SQL

.select_related('user')
     ← we add an ingredient to the recipe

.order_by('-created_at')
     ← one more refinement

list(qs)  ← HERE Django cooks the dish — runs ONE SQL query

SQL execution triggers:

for note in qs:          ← iteration
list(qs)                 ← explicit conversion
qs.first()               ← LIMIT 1
qs[0]                    ← LIMIT 1 OFFSET 0
qs.count()               ← SELECT COUNT(*)
bool(qs)                 ← EXISTS()
len(qs)                  ← executes and caches

# A basic model with a Custom Manager

class ActiveNoteManager(models.Manager):
    """Custom Manager — returns only non-archived notes."""
    def get_queryset(self):
        return super().get_queryset().filter(is_archived=False)

    def recent(self):
        """The last 10 non-archived notes."""
        return self.get_queryset().order_by('-updated_at')[:10]

docs.title: 3. The N+1 Problem and select_related / prefetch_related
docs.text:
N+1 is the most common performance mistake in Django.

# ❌ PROBLEM — N+1
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user)
for note in notes:
    print(note.notebook.title)  # ← a separate SQL query for every note!
# 1 query for the notes + N queries for the notebooks = N+1

# ✅ SOLUTION for ForeignKey — select_related (SQL JOIN)
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user).select_related('notebook', 'group')
# 1 SQL query with a JOIN:
# SELECT notes.*, notebooks.*, groups.*
# FROM notes_app_note notes
# LEFT JOIN notes_app_notebook notebooks ON notes.notebook_id = notebooks.id
# LEFT JOIN auth_group groups ON notes.group_id = groups.id

# ✅ SOLUTION for ManyToMany — prefetch_related (a separate IN query)
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user).prefetch_related('tags')
# Query 1: SELECT * FROM notes_app_note WHERE user_id = 1
# Query 2: SELECT * FROM notes_app_tag
#          INNER JOIN notes_app_note_tags ON ... WHERE note_id IN (1,2,...,50)
# Result: 2 queries regardless of the number of notes

docs.title: 4. F() Expressions — Atomic Operations
docs.text:
F() is a reference to a column's value inside the DB itself. It solves race conditions.

from django.db.models import F

# An illustrative example: suppose Note has a views_count counter
# (the project's model has no such field)

# ❌ DANGEROUS — race condition under concurrent requests
note = Note.objects.get(id=1)
note.views_count += 1  # we read 100, 1000 processes do the same thing at once
note.save()            # all of them write 101, though it should be 1100

# ✅ SAFE — an atomic operation at the DB level
Note.objects.filter(id=1).update(views_count=F('views_count') + 1)
# SQL: UPDATE notes SET views_count = views_count + 1 WHERE id=1
# PostgreSQL executes this atomically, without a race condition

# F() for a toggle (used in notes_chat_app services.py!)
Note.objects.filter(pk=note.pk).update(is_pinned=~F('is_pinned'))
note.refresh_from_db(fields=['is_pinned'])  # ← the Python object does not know about the change in the DB

# F() for comparing two columns
Note.objects.filter(priority__gt=F('is_pinned'))  # a hypothetical example

# F() with arithmetic
Note.objects.update(views_count=F('views_count') * 2)

docs.title: 5. annotate() and aggregate()
docs.text:
from django.db.models import Count, Sum, Avg, Max, Q

# aggregate() — one value for the whole QuerySet
result = Note.objects.filter(user=user).aggregate(
    total=Count('id'),
    avg_priority=Avg('priority'),
    max_priority=Max('priority'),
)
# result = {'total': 42, 'avg_priority': 2.1, 'max_priority': 4}

# annotate() — a computed column for EACH object
# Used in notes_chat_app selectors.py!
notebooks = Notebook.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
    note_count=Count('notes', filter=Q(notes__is_archived=False))
).order_by('-is_default', 'title')
# SQL: SELECT notebooks.*, COUNT(notes.id) AS note_count
#      FROM notebooks LEFT JOIN notes ON ... WHERE notes.is_archived = false
#      GROUP BY notebooks.id
# Usage: notebook.note_count → without a single extra SQL query!

# Two annotations together
TodoList.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
    total_items=Count('items'),
    done_items=Count('items', filter=Q(items__is_done=True))
)
# todo.total_items, todo.done_items — available in the template without SQL

# alias() — compute for filtering, but do not include in SELECT
Note.objects.alias(
    tag_count=Count('tags')
).filter(tag_count__gt=3)
# WHERE COUNT(tags) > 3, but tag_count is NOT in SELECT

docs.title: 6. transaction.atomic()
docs.text:
atomic() is "all or nothing" for a group of operations.

from django.db import transaction

# ✅ CORRECT — related operations in a single transaction
def create_note(*, user, title, content='', tag_ids=None):
    with transaction.atomic():
        note = Note.objects.create(user=user, title=title, content=content)
        if tag_ids:
            valid_tags = Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids, user=user)
            note.tags.set(valid_tags)   # ← M:N inside the transaction
    return note
# If tags.set() fails → create() is rolled back too. No orphaned notes.

# ❌ CRITICAL MISTAKE — try/except inside atomic!
with transaction.atomic():
    try:
        note = Note.objects.create(...)
    except Exception:
        pass  # ← the TRANSACTION IS "BROKEN", TransactionManagementError!

# ✅ CORRECT — catch the exception OUTSIDE
try:
    with transaction.atomic():
        note = Note.objects.create(...)
        note.tags.set(tags)
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Failed: {e}")
    return None

# on_commit — run AFTER a successful COMMIT
def create_note_and_notify(user, title):
    with transaction.atomic():
        note = Note.objects.create(user=user, title=title)
        # The Celery task will not start if the transaction is rolled back
        transaction.on_commit(
            lambda: send_reminder_email.delay(note.id)
        )

docs.title: Nested atomic → Savepoints
docs.text:
with transaction.atomic():         # BEGIN
    note = Note.objects.create(...)
    with transaction.atomic():     # SAVEPOINT sp_1
        note.tags.set(tags)        # if it fails → ROLLBACK TO sp_1
    # The Note is kept even if tags failed

docs.text:
# get_or_create — CREATE if it does not exist (an idempotent operation)
notebook, created = Notebook.objects.get_or_create(
    user=user, is_default=True,
    defaults={'title': 'Основний', 'color': '#4A90E2'}
)
# Returns (object, bool) — bool=True if it was JUST CREATED

# update_or_create — UPDATE if it exists, CREATE if not
profile, _ = UserProfile.objects.update_or_create(
    user=user,
    defaults={'bio': new_bio, 'timezone': timezone_str}
)

# bulk_create — bulk creation (1 SQL query instead of N)
tags = [Tag(name=name, user=user) for name in ['python', 'django', 'orm']]
Tag.objects.bulk_create(tags, ignore_conflicts=True)

# bulk_update — bulk update (1 SQL query)
notes_to_archive = list(Note.objects.filter(user=user, is_archived=False))
for note in notes_to_archive:
    note.is_archived = True
Note.objects.bulk_update(notes_to_archive, ['is_archived'])

# values() and values_list() — dict/tuple instead of Model objects
Note.objects.filter(user=user).values('id', 'title', 'priority')
# → [{'id': 1, 'title': '...', 'priority': 2}, ...]

Note.objects.filter(user=user).values_list('id', flat=True)
# → QuerySet([1, 2, 3, ...])

# Used in selectors.py for a JSON response:
return list(
    Reminder.objects.filter(...).values('id', 'message', 'remind_at', 'note__title')
)

# only() / defer() — deferred field loading
Note.objects.only('id', 'title')    # only these fields (a smaller SELECT)
Note.objects.defer('content')       # everything EXCEPT content

# iterator() — streaming for large QuerySets (does not load everything into RAM)
for note in Note.objects.filter(user=user).iterator(chunk_size=1000):
    process(note)

docs.title: 8. An Architecture Question: Why the Price Is Fixed in the Order
docs.text:
A classic interview question. It reveals an understanding of the immutability of transactional data.

Scenario: Order → Product via a ForeignKey, and the price is taken from Product.current_price.

May 1: A student bought a book for $20. Order → Product (current_price=20)
May 10: The price was raised to $25
May 15: The student views the order → order.product.current_price = $25 (WRONG!)

The solution is denormalization: store the price directly in the order:

class OrderItem(models.Model):
    order   = models.ForeignKey(Order, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='items')
    product = models.ForeignKey(Product, on_delete=models.RESTRICT)
    quantity = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=1)
    # A snapshot of the price at the moment of purchase — never changes
    purchase_price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)

    def get_cost(self):
        return self.purchase_price * self.quantity

# When placing an order:
OrderItem.objects.create(
    order=order,
    product=product,
    purchase_price=product.current_price,  # ← copy the current price
    quantity=1
)

Principle: The catalog (Product) is mutable. The transaction (OrderItem) is an immutable fact. Financial integrity matters more than normalization.

docs.title: 9. MVCC — How PostgreSQL Provides Concurrency
docs.text:
MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) — PostgreSQL keeps several versions of a row at the same time.

Architectural rule: "Readers do not block writers, writers do not block readers."

Transaction A reads Notes:     [row_v1: id=1, title='Django', xmin=100]
Transaction B updates:         [row_v2: id=1, title='Django ORM', xmin=101]
Transaction A (still active):  ← sees row_v1, does not see row_v2
Transaction A finishes COMMIT:
Transaction B finishes COMMIT:
New reader: ← sees row_v2

Isolation levels: - Read Committed (the default in PostgreSQL and Django): protects against dirty reads, but allows non-repeatable reads - Repeatable Read: freezes the snapshot for the whole transaction - Serializable: maximum isolation, lowers throughput

select_for_update() — explicit row locking:

with transaction.atomic():
    note = Note.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=pk)
    # SQL: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    # Locks the row until the end of the transaction
    note.title = new_title
    note.save()
    # Other transactions trying to change this row wait
