docs.title: PostgreSQL Indexes — The Deep Mechanics
docs.text:
Indexes exist to avoid reading every row on disk. This document explains WHY indexes are so effective (B-Tree, GIN), when to add them, when not to, and how to check their effectiveness with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

🔬 See EXPLAIN ANALYZE in action: docs/reference/legacy_source/orm_laboratory_reference.md

⚠️ The notebook itself is not part of this repository: the linked file only explains that. The section names in the table below point to the notebook's original structure, they are not anchors. You can run the same queries yourself in python manage.py shell or in the ORM lab.

Concept Notebook section queryset.explain(analyze=True) — Index Scan vs Seq Scan ## 11. 🔬 SQL Inspection .query — viewing the generated SQL ## 11. 🔬 SQL Inspection connection.queries — all SQL queries of the session ## 11. 🔬 SQL Inspection N+1 → indexes solve part of the problem ## 8. ⚡ N+1 Problem

🧠 Mental model: A database WITHOUT an index is like a library without a catalog. To find the book "Django ORM", you have to look through every shelf in order. With an index, you walk up to the card catalog, find "Django ORM" → "rack 7, row 3, spot 42". Seconds instead of hours.

📚 Why indexes are not "free": An index = a separate data structure on disk. On every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE → PostgreSQL updates both the table and all the indexes on it. 10 indexes on a table = every write costs 11 write operations (1 table + 10 indexes). Too many indexes → slow writes.

🌐 How PostgreSQL decides to use an index: The Query Planner computes the cost: sequential scan (read the whole table) vs index scan (B-Tree traversal + heap fetch). If a SELECT returns >5-10% of the table's rows → a sequential scan may be cheaper! The Planner knows the table statistics and picks the optimal plan.

❌ A typical beginner mistake: "I'll add an index on every field — it'll be faster." In reality, an unnecessary index slows down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, takes up disk space, and may not be used by the Planner if the condition is not selective. Indexes are a strategic decision, not "more is always better".

docs.title: 1. Sequential Scan vs Index Scan — The Physics
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: Sequential Scan = reading a book from the first page to the last to find one paragraph. Index Scan = first you look at the table of contents → find the page number → open it right away. The difference: O(N) vs O(log N).

📚 The physical level: A PostgreSQL table is stored in 8KB "pages". Sequential Scan = read all the pages in a row. 1 million rows (≈10 rows per page → 100,000 pages × 8KB) = ~800MB to read. With an index: B-Tree traversal (3-4 disk I/Os) → get the heap tuple pointer → 1 heap read. In total: 4-5 I/O operations instead of a million.

🌐 When the Planner chooses a Sequential Scan instead of an index: If the WHERE clause returns >10-15% of the rows, a sequential scan will be more efficient (one pass over the disk vs many random I/Os through the index). The Planner takes this into account.

❌ A typical mistake: Adding an index and wondering why it is not used. WHERE status = 'published' on a table where 80% of rows = 'published' → the Planner correctly chooses a Sequential Scan. An index is useful when the condition is selective (returns a small % of rows).

Sequential Scan (O(N)):
Table notes_note: 1,000,000 rows

Disk: [ Page 1 ][ Page 2 ][ Page 3 ] ... [ Page 100,000 ]
          ↑──────────────────────────────────────────────────
          We read EVERYTHING to find WHERE user_id=5

Operations: 100,000 page reads (800MB!)
Time: ~500ms - 2s depending on the disk and cache

Index Scan (O(log N)):
B-Tree index on user_id:

                    [Root: 500]
                   /            \
          [250]                    [750]
         /     \                  /     \
    [125]      [375]          [625]      [875]
     / \        / \            / \        / \
  [100][150] [300][400]    [600][650] [800][900]
   ↑
   Leaf: [5] → pointer to heap page 42, slot 7

Operations: log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 comparisons → 3-4 disk I/O
Time: ~0.05ms - 1ms

docs.title: 2. B-Tree Index — The Internal Structure
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: A B-Tree (Balanced Tree) is an ordered tree-like structure where search, insertion and deletion are O(log N). "Balanced" means all leaves are at the same depth. For a table with 1 billion rows, a binary tree would be ≈ log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30 levels deep. But a B-Tree node is a whole page holding hundreds of keys, so the real B-Tree depth is only 3–5 levels: a few page reads and ~30 comparisons instead of a billion!

📚 How a B-Tree is stored on disk: Each node = one page (8KB). Each page holds ~200-400 entries. Root → Branch nodes → Leaf nodes. Leaf nodes store the values + TID (tuple identifier = pointer to a heap page + offset). Sequential reads across leaf nodes = an efficient range scan.

🌐 B-Tree for Django: db_index=True, unique=True, and a standard models.Index(fields=[...]) all create a B-Tree. Efficient for: =, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, LIKE 'prefix%'. NOT efficient for: LIKE '%suffix', LOWER(), UPPER() (unless there is a functional index).

❌ A typical mistake: Using LIKE '%python%' and expecting the index to work. A B-Tree index cannot efficiently search for "contains a substring" (only "starts with"). For icontains → you need a trigram index (GIN with pg_trgm).

B-Tree structure for index on notes_note(user_id):

                        ┌──────────────┐
                        │  Root Node   │
                        │   [250,500]  │
                        └──────────────┘
                        /       │       \
              ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐
              │ Branch │   │ Branch │   │ Branch │
              │ [5,50] │   │[251,350]│  │[501,750]│
              └────────┘   └────────┘   └────────┘
              /       \         ...         ...
      ┌──────┐   ┌──────┐
      │ Leaf │ ↔ │ Leaf │   ← leaves are DOUBLY linked!
      │ [1,2,│   │[6,7, │   (efficient for range scans: ORDER BY)
      │  3,4]│   │ 8,9] │
      │  TIDs│   │ TIDs │   TID = (page_number, slot_number) → pointer into the heap
      └──────┘   └──────┘

Searching for user_id=5:
  Root: 5 < 250 → go left
  Branch: 5 ≤ 50 → go to the first leaf
  Leaf: we find 5 → TID = (42, 7)
  Heap: read page 42, slot 7 → return the row

In total: 3-4 I/O operations for a billion rows.

docs.title: 3. Composite Index — The "Leading Column" Rule
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: A composite index is like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. Searching by the last name "Shevchenko" → efficient. Searching by the first name "Taras" → you'll have to read the whole book (the last name isn't given → no idea where to look).

📚 The leading column rule: A composite index (A, B, C) is efficient for: WHERE A=, WHERE A= AND B=, WHERE A= AND B= AND C=, ORDER BY A, B. NOT efficient for: WHERE B= (A not given), WHERE C= (A and B not given). Always start with the most selective or most frequently used field.

🌐 How this looks in Django: models.Index(fields=['user', '-updated_at']) → CREATE INDEX ON notes_note (user_id, updated_at DESC). Efficient for filter(user=X).order_by('-updated_at') — a typical query for a list of notes.

❌ A typical mistake: Relying on a composite index where the leading column is not used. Index(fields=['status', 'user']) → WHERE user=5 without WHERE status= → the index is NOT used (not the leading column!). You need a separate Index(fields=['user']).

class Note(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, ...)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, ...)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)
    views_count = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            # ✅ Index for a typical query: a user's notes sorted by date
            # Efficient for: filter(user=X).order_by('-updated_at')
            models.Index(
                fields=['user', '-updated_at'],
                name='note_user_updated_idx'
            ),

            # ✅ For: filter(user=X, status='published')
            models.Index(
                fields=['user', 'status'],
                name='note_user_status_idx'
            ),

            # ✅ For analytics: top by views
            models.Index(
                fields=['-views_count'],
                name='note_views_desc_idx'
            ),
        ]

Composite index (user_id, updated_at) usage table:

Query                                    | Index?
─────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────
filter(user=X).order_by('-updated_at')   | ✅ Yes
filter(user=X)                           | ✅ Yes (leading column)
filter(user=X, status='pub')             | ✅ Partially (only the user_id part)
filter(status='pub').order_by('-updated_at') | ❌ No (status is not leading!)
order_by('-updated_at')                  | ❌ No (user_id not given)

docs.title: 4. Covering Index — Index-Only Scan
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: A covering index is a catalog that contains not only the "rack" number but also the information itself. Instead of: catalog → "rack 42, spot 7" → walk to the rack → read the book. Now: catalog → all the needed information is already there → no need to go anywhere.

📚 Index-Only Scan: If all the fields in SELECT and WHERE are in the index, PostgreSQL reads only the index, without the heap (the table's main data). This is Index Only Scan in EXPLAIN — very efficient for aggregations and analytics.

🌐 The include parameter in Django: Index(fields=['user', 'status'], include=['title', 'updated_at']) → PostgreSQL INCLUDE syntax. Fields in include are stored in the index leaves but are not part of the sort key. SELECT title, updated_at WHERE user=X AND status='pub' → Index Only Scan.

❌ A typical mistake: Covering too many fields. A wide covering index takes more space and slows down writes. Cover only the fields that are DEFINITELY needed for a specific "hot" query.

# Covering index: include fields that are often SELECTed but are not in WHERE
class Note(models.Model):
    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            # index (user_id, status) INCLUDE (title, updated_at)
            # SELECT title, updated_at WHERE user_id=X AND status='published'
            # → Index Only Scan (does not read the heap!)
            models.Index(
                fields=['user', 'status'],
                include=['title', 'updated_at'],  # PostgreSQL 11+ syntax
                name='note_user_status_cover_idx'
            ),
        ]

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE will show the difference:

-- WITHOUT a covering index:
Seq Scan / Index Scan on notes_note
  + Heap Fetch (reading data pages)
  → 2 I/O operations: index + heap

-- WITH a covering index:
Index Only Scan using note_user_status_cover_idx
  → 1 I/O operation: index only
  (the heap is still visited for the "visibility check", but much less often)

docs.title: 5. GIN Index — For JSON and Arrays
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: A B-Tree is efficient for comparing one value with another (user_id = 5). GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) is efficient for "contains" (tags @> ['python'], metadata ? 'word_count'). GIN is like the index at the back of a book: "python → pages 5, 42, 100". One index entry can point to THOUSANDS of rows.

📚 How GIN works: GIN breaks each value into "elements" (JSON keys, array elements, words of text) and for each element stores a list of TIDs (pointers to the rows containing that element). Searching WHERE tags @> ['python'] → find 'python' in the GIN → get the list of TIDs → return the rows.

🌐 GIN in Django: GinIndex(fields=['tags']) for an ArrayField, GinIndex(fields=['metadata']) for a JSONField. For full-text search: GinIndex(fields=['content'], opclasses=['gin_trgm_ops']) requires the pg_trgm extension.

❌ A typical mistake: Not adding a GIN index for a JSONField and filtering by JSON fields. Note.objects.filter(metadata__language='uk') without GIN → a sequential scan over billions of rows. With GIN → milliseconds.

from django.contrib.postgres.fields import ArrayField
from django.contrib.postgres.indexes import GinIndex

class Note(models.Model):
    tags = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True)
    metadata = models.JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)
    quick_labels = ArrayField(
        models.CharField(max_length=50), blank=True, default=list
    )

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            # GIN for an ArrayField — searching by array elements
            GinIndex(
                fields=['quick_labels'],
                name='note_labels_gin_idx'
            ),
            # GIN for a JSONField — searching by JSON keys and values
            GinIndex(
                fields=['metadata'],
                name='note_metadata_gin_idx'
            ),
        ]

# Efficient queries with a GIN index:
Note.objects.filter(quick_labels__contains=['python'])
# WHERE quick_labels @> ARRAY['python']  → GIN O(log N)

Note.objects.filter(metadata__language='uk')
# WHERE metadata @> '{"language": "uk"}'  → GIN O(log N)

Note.objects.filter(metadata__has_key='word_count')
# WHERE metadata ? 'word_count'  → GIN O(log N)

docs.title: 6. Trigram Index — Fuzzy Search
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: A trigram is a split of text into groups of 3 characters. "Django" → ["Dja", "jan", "ang", "ngo"]. A trigram GIN index stores each trigram → the list of rows that contain it. LIKE '%django%' → find all rows that have the trigrams "dja", "jan", "ang", "ngo" → intersect the lists → result. Without trigrams: a sequential scan.

📚 Enabling pg_trgm: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm; — or via a Django migration: TrigramExtension() (BtreeGinExtension() enables a different extension, btree_gin, not pg_trgm).

🌐 icontains with trigrams: Note.objects.filter(title__icontains='python') without trigrams → LIKE '%python%' → a sequential scan. With a trigram GIN → an O(log N) search over trigrams.

❌ A typical mistake: Expecting db_index=True + icontains = fast search. A regular B-Tree does NOT help with %contains%. Only a trigram GIN does.

# First you need to activate the pg_trgm extension:

# migrations/0010_trigram_extension.py
from django.contrib.postgres.operations import TrigramExtension

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    operations = [
        TrigramExtension(),  # CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm
    ]


# Then we add a trigram index:
from django.contrib.postgres.indexes import GinIndex

class Note(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    content = models.TextField(blank=True)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            # GIN trigram for title — fast LIKE '%...%'
            GinIndex(
                fields=['title'],
                opclasses=['gin_trgm_ops'],  # trigram operator class
                name='note_title_trgm_idx'
            ),
            # GIN trigram for content (large text — useful)
            GinIndex(
                fields=['content'],
                opclasses=['gin_trgm_ops'],
                name='note_content_trgm_idx'
            ),
        ]

# Now these queries will use the trigram GIN:
Note.objects.filter(title__icontains='python')
# WHERE title ILIKE '%python%' → trigram GIN O(log N)

Note.objects.filter(
    Q(title__icontains='django') | Q(content__icontains='django')
)

docs.title: 7. AddIndexConcurrently — No Downtime in Production
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: A regular CREATE INDEX locks the table for the whole time the index is being built. On a table with 50 million rows, that is 10-30 minutes without being able to insert or update data. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds the index without locking the table — at the cost of two passes and a somewhat slower build.

📚 How CONCURRENTLY works: Two table scans: the first collects a snapshot, the second catches the changes that happened during the first. Between the scans, the table remains available for reads and writes. Build time: a bit longer. Locking: minimal (only a few Share Update Exclusive Locks for milliseconds).

🌐 In Django: migrations.AddIndexConcurrently (in django.contrib.postgres.operations). It requires atomic = False in the migration (CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction).

❌ A typical mistake: Adding a large index through a regular migrations.AddIndex on a production table with millions of rows. 10-30 minutes of downtime. Always use AddIndexConcurrently in production.

# notes_app/migrations/0015_add_concurrent_index.py
from django.contrib.postgres.operations import AddIndexConcurrently
from django.db import migrations, models

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    # REQUIRED: atomic=False — CONCURRENTLY is not allowed inside a transaction!
    atomic = False

    dependencies = [
        ('notes_app', '0014_previous_migration'),
    ]

    operations = [
        AddIndexConcurrently(
            model_name='note',
            index=models.Index(
                fields=['user', '-updated_at'],
                name='note_user_updated_concurrent_idx'
            ),
        ),
    ]

# The SQL that gets executed:
# CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY note_user_updated_concurrent_idx
# ON notes_app_note (user_id, updated_at DESC)
# (without locking the table!)

docs.title: 8. When to Add an Index (and When Not To)
docs.text:
✅ ADD AN INDEX:

  1. Fields in the WHERE clause (filtering)
     filter(user=X) → index on user_id

  2. Fields in ORDER BY (sorting without a sort operation)
     order_by('-updated_at') → index on updated_at DESC

  3. Foreign Key fields
     Django automatically creates an index on an FK (ForeignKey has db_index=True by default).
     Don't turn it off (db_index=False) without a reason; for composite conditions use Meta.indexes

  4. Fields in JOIN conditions
     JOIN ... ON note.user_id = user.id → index on user_id

  5. Fields in UNIQUE constraints
     Django adds it automatically with unique=True

  6. JSON/Array fields that are filtered on
     GinIndex(fields=['metadata'])

❌ DO NOT ADD AN INDEX:

  1. Fields with low selectivity
     Boolean (only 2 values)
     Status with 2-3 values where 80% = one value
     The Planner will choose a Sequential Scan (correctly!)

  2. Small tables (< 1000 rows)
     A Sequential Scan is more efficient (everything is in cache)

  3. Fields that are rarely used in WHERE/ORDER BY
     It only takes up space and slows down writes

  4. Fields that are updated very often
     UPDATE → rewrite the index → overhead

  5. "Just in case" fields
     Every unnecessary index = slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE

docs.title: 9. REINDEX and Index Maintenance
docs.text:
-- Check index sizes
SELECT indexname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

-- Bloat: how many dead entries are in the index (after bulk DELETE/UPDATE)
-- PostgreSQL VACUUM cleans them up automatically

-- REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL 12+): rebuild an index without locking
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY note_user_updated_idx;

-- Or via Django:
# python manage.py shell
# from django.db import connection
# connection.cursor().execute('REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY note_user_updated_idx')

docs.title: Exercise 1: Selectivity
docs.text:
class Order(models.Model):
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20)  # 'pending', 'completed', 'cancelled'
    # Distribution: 5% pending, 90% completed, 5% cancelled

Question: Is it worth adding db_index=True on status?

Answer: It depends on the query. filter(status='pending') → 5% of rows → the index is useful. filter(status='completed') → 90% of rows → the Planner will correctly choose a Sequential Scan. Solution: partial indexes or leave it without an index.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Composite index
docs.text:
Index(fields=['user', 'status', 'updated_at'])

Question: For which WHERE conditions will this index be effective?

Answer: filter(user=X), filter(user=X, status='pub'), filter(user=X, status='pub', updated_at__gte=date). NOT for: filter(status='pub'), filter(updated_at__gte=date), filter(status='pub', updated_at__gte=date) — the leading column user is missing.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: A migration is a versioned file of database schema changes. Instead of a manual ALTER TABLE, Django generates and applies migrations automatically.

docs.title: Why migrations
docs.text:
Without migrations, every time you changed a model you would write the SQL yourself:

-- Added an is_archived field to Note?
ALTER TABLE notes_app_note ADD COLUMN is_archived BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;
-- And on the production server? And on a colleague's machine? And how do you roll it back?

Django migration: 

python manage.py makemigrations   # generates the change file
python manage.py migrate          # applies the SQL to the DB

Advantages: - Version control of the schema (git history) - Automatic application in new environments - A rollback mechanism (migrate app 0003)

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: models.py (change) → makemigrations → 0005_add_is_archived.py → migrate → DB

docs.title: Step 1: Change the model
docs.text:
# notes_app/models.py
class Note(models.Model):
    ...
    is_archived = models.BooleanField(default=False)  # ← new field

docs.title: Step 2: Generate the migration
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py makemigrations

Migrations for 'notes_app':
  notes_app/migrations/0005_note_is_archived.py
    - Add field is_archived to note

docs.title: Step 3: Inspect the SQL (optional)
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py sqlmigrate notes_app 0005

BEGIN;
--
-- Add field is_archived to note
--
ALTER TABLE "notes_app_note" ADD COLUMN "is_archived" boolean DEFAULT false NOT NULL;
COMMIT;

docs.title: Step 4: Apply the migration
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate

Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, auth, contenttypes, notes_app, sessions
Running migrations:
  Applying notes_app.0005_note_is_archived... OK

docs.title: Anatomy of a migration file
docs.text:
# notes_app/migrations/0004_chatmessage.py

from django.db import migrations, models
import django.db.models.deletion

class Migration(migrations.Migration):

    dependencies = [
        ('notes_app', '0003_note_group'),  # ← previous migration
        ('auth', '0012_alter_user_first_name_max_length'),  # ← dependency on auth
    ]

    operations = [
        migrations.CreateModel(
            name='ChatMessage',
            fields=[
                ('id', models.BigAutoField(auto_created=True, primary_key=True)),
                ('content', models.TextField(verbose_name='Повідомлення')),
                ('timestamp', models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)),
                ('author', models.ForeignKey(
                    on_delete=django.db.models.deletion.CASCADE,
                    to='auth.user',
                )),
                ('group', models.ForeignKey(
                    on_delete=django.db.models.deletion.CASCADE,
                    to='auth.group',
                )),
            ],
        ),
        migrations.AddIndex(
            model_name='chatmessage',
            index=models.Index(fields=['group', 'timestamp'], name='chat_group_ts_idx'),
        ),
    ]

Key parts: - dependencies — the list of migrations that must be applied before this one - operations — the list of changes: CreateModel, AddField, AlterField, DeleteModel, AddIndex

[X] — applied, [ ] — not applied.

docs.title: How migrations are tracked
docs.text:
Django stores the list of applied migrations in the django_migrations table:

SELECT app, name, applied
FROM django_migrations
WHERE app = 'notes_app';

notes_app | 0001_initial     | 2024-01-15 12:00:00
notes_app | 0002_...         | 2024-01-20 09:30:00
notes_app | 0003_...         | 2024-02-01 11:00:00
notes_app | 0004_chatmessage | 2024-02-10 15:00:00

migrate compares the list of files with the table and applies only the new ones.

docs.title: Data migrations — changing data
docs.text:
Besides schema changes you can write data migrations — Python code that changes data during deployment:

# notes_app/migrations/0005_set_default_notebook.py

from django.db import migrations

def set_default_notebook(apps, schema_editor):
    Note = apps.get_model('notes_app', 'Note')
    Notebook = apps.get_model('notes_app', 'Notebook')
    User = apps.get_model('auth', 'User')

    for user in User.objects.all():
        notebook, _ = Notebook.objects.get_or_create(
            user=user, is_default=True,
            defaults={'title': 'Основний'}
        )
        Note.objects.filter(user=user, notebook=None).update(notebook=notebook)

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [('notes_app', '0004_chatmessage')]
    operations = [
        migrations.RunPython(set_default_notebook, migrations.RunPython.noop),
    ]

Always use apps.get_model() in data migrations

Do not import the model directly (from notes_app.models import Note). apps.get_model() returns the version of the model as of this migration, not the current one — which protects against conflicts if fields were renamed later.

docs.title: Rolling back a migration
docs.text:
# Return to the state AFTER 0003 (roll back 0004)
docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate notes_app 0003

Django runs Migration.operations in reverse order if the operation supports it.

A rollback that drops a table is a destructive operation

CreateModel → rollback = DROP TABLE. All data in that table WILL BE DELETED. Always make a backup before rolling back in production.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Error Cause Solution InconsistentMigrationHistory the migrations in the DB do not match the files showmigrations, find the conflict django.db.utils.ProgrammingError: relation does not exist migrate was not run docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate MigrationSyntaxError a migration file was edited incorrectly fix it, or delete it and regenerate No changes detected the model was not changed or the app is not in INSTALLED_APPS check INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py ValueError: Field 'X' expected a number but got 'abc' a data migration changed the type of a field that already has data a two-stage migration is needed

docs.title: entrypoint.sh — migrations on container startup
docs.text:
In notes_chat_app, migrations run automatically:

# entrypoint.sh
python manage.py migrate --noinput
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

Every docker compose up automatically applies new migrations.

docs.title: 5. N+1 Problem vs select_related
docs.text:
What it shows: The difference in the number of SQL queries between N+1 and select_related. Without optimization: 1 + N queries. With select_related: 1 query.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Django View
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    Note over App,DB: ❌ N+1 PROBLEM (100 notes)
    App->>DB: SELECT * FROM notes WHERE status='published' LIMIT 100
    DB-->>App: 100 rows (user_id=5,3,7,8,...)
    App->>DB: SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE id=5
    App->>DB: SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE id=3
    App->>DB: SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE id=7
    Note over App,DB: ... 97 more queries ...
    Note over App,DB: TOTAL: 101 SQL queries!

    Note over App,DB: ✅ select_related (ALWAYS 1 query)
    App->>DB: SELECT n.*, u.*, nb.* FROM notes n LEFT JOIN users u ON n.user_id=u.id LEFT JOIN notebooks nb ON n.notebook_id=nb.id WHERE status='published' LIMIT 100
    DB-->>App: 100 rows (already with user + notebook data!)
    Note over App,DB: note.user.username → from cache, 0 SQL!

docs.title: 6. select_related vs prefetch_related — Architecture
docs.text:
What it shows: The mechanism of each method at the SQL level. select_related = SQL JOIN. prefetch_related = a separate query + a Python join.

graph TD
    subgraph "select_related → SQL JOIN"
        A1["Note.objects.select_related('user', 'notebook')"] --> B1[1 SQL query with JOIN]
        B1 --> C1["SELECT n.*, u.*, nb.*<br>FROM notes n"]
        C1 --> C1b["LEFT JOIN users u ON n.user_id=u.id<br>LEFT JOIN notebooks nb ON n.notebook_id=nb.id"]
        C1b --> D1["All the data in one result row"]
        D1 --> E1["✅ For FK and OneToOne"]
    end

    subgraph "prefetch_related → Python JOIN"
        A2["Note.objects.prefetch_related('tags')"] --> B2[SQL #1: Fetch Notes]
        B2 --> C2["SELECT * FROM notes"]
        A2 --> B3[SQL #2: Fetch Tags]
        B3 --> C3["SELECT t.*, nt.note_id<br>FROM tags t INNER JOIN note_tags nt"]
        C3 --> C3b["WHERE nt.note_id IN (1,2,3,...,100)"]
        C2 --> D2["Python: obj._prefetched_objects_cache<br>is filled with a dict note_id → [tags]"]
        C3b --> D2
        D2 --> E2["✅ For ManyToMany and reverse FK"]
    end

docs.title: 9. Query Execution Lifecycle — 8 Phases
docs.text:
What it shows: What happens to an SQL query inside PostgreSQL, from parsing to the result.

graph TD
    A["SQL: SELECT * FROM notes<br>WHERE user_id=5 ORDER BY updated_at DESC"] --> B

    B["1. PARSING: Lexer + Parser<br>Tokenize SQL → Build AST"] --> C

    C["2. SEMANTIC ANALYSIS<br>Check tables, permissions, system catalog lookup"] --> D

    D["3. REWRITER<br>View expansion, rule system application"] --> E

    E["4. PLANNER: Enumerate plans<br>Seq Scan / Index Scan user_id / Index Scan updated_at"] --> F

    F["5. OPTIMIZER: Choose cheapest<br>(based on table statistics)"] --> F2

    F2["cost(Seq Scan)=5000 ← rejected<br>cost(Index Scan)=23 ← chosen!"] --> G

    G["6. EXECUTION PLAN<br>Index Scan on note_user_updated_idx → Heap fetch"] --> H

    H["7. EXECUTION ENGINE<br>Read index pages → fetch heap tuples → apply remaining filters"] --> I

    I["8. RESULT<br>Rows → psycopg2 cursor → Django ModelIterable → List[Note]"]

docs.text:
What it shows: How a B-Tree index finds a record in O(log N) instead of O(N). Each level = one disk I/O. Depth: log₂(N) levels.

graph TD

    Root --> B2["Branch<br>[260, 300, 400]"]
    Root --> B3["Branch<br>[510, 600, 700]"]
    Root --> B4["Branch<br>[760, 800, 900]"]

    B1 --> L1["Leaf [1,2,3,4,5]<br>TID→heap"]
    B1 --> L2["Leaf [6,7,8,9]<br>TID→heap"]
    B1 --> L3["Leaf [11,12,15]<br>TID→heap"]

    L2 -.->|"doubly linked list<br>(for range scans)"| L3

    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

docs.title: 11. transaction.atomic() — SQL Lifecycle
docs.text:
What it shows: What happens in SQL with transaction.atomic() and when an exception occurs.

sequenceDiagram
    participant PY as Python (atomic block)
    participant PG as PostgreSQL

    PY->>PG: BEGIN (on entering atomic())
    PY->>PG: INSERT INTO notes (title, ...) VALUES ('Django', ...)
    PG-->>PY: id=42
    PY->>PG: SAVEPOINT sp_1 (nested atomic)
    PY->>PG: INSERT INTO reminders (...) VALUES (...)
    PG-->>PY: id=5

    alt Success (no exception):
        PY->>PG: RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp_1
        PY->>PG: COMMIT
        PG-->>PY: OK
        Note over PY,PG: on_commit() callbacks run here
    else Exception in the nested atomic:
        PY->>PG: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp_1
        Note over PY,PG: only the reminder was rolled back, the note is kept
        PY->>PG: COMMIT (the outer one succeeds)
    else Exception in the outer atomic:
        PY->>PG: ROLLBACK
        Note over PY,PG: EVERYTHING was rolled back, on_commit does NOT run
    end

docs.title: 12. select_for_update() — Row Locking Timeline
docs.text:
What it shows: How select_for_update() prevents a race condition under concurrent access.

sequenceDiagram
    participant T1 as Transaction 1 (Alice)
    participant T2 as Transaction 2 (Bob)
    participant PG as PostgreSQL

    T1->>PG: BEGIN
    T1->>PG: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE
    PG-->>T1: event(seats=1) ← lock acquired!

    T2->>PG: BEGIN
    T2->>PG: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE
    Note over T2,PG: T2 WAITS (the row is locked by T1)

    T1->>PG: UPDATE events SET seats=0 WHERE id=1
    T1->>PG: INSERT INTO bookings (event_id, user_id) VALUES (1, alice)
    T1->>PG: COMMIT ← the lock is released

    PG-->>T2: event(seats=0) ← T2 gets the lock, sees seats=0
    T2->>T2: seats=0 → raise ValueError("No seats left")
    T2->>PG: ROLLBACK

docs.title: 13. Deadlock — Mutual Locking
docs.text:
What it shows: How a deadlock arises when locks are taken in a different order. Solution: always lock in a stable order (by id ASC).

graph LR
    subgraph "Deadlock situation"
        T1A["T1: lock(note_id=1)"] -->|"waits"| T1B["T1: lock(note_id=2)"]
        T2B["T2: lock(note_id=2)"] -->|"waits"| T2A["T2: lock(note_id=1)"]
        T1A -.->|"blocked by T2"| T2B
        T2B -.->|"blocked by T1"| T1A
    end

    subgraph "Solution: a stable order"
        S1["T1 and T2: always lock<br>order_by('id') ASC"] --> S2["T1: lock(1) → lock(2)<br>T2: lock(1) ← waits for T1"]
        S2 --> S2b["T2 does NOT take lock(2) first!"]
        S2b --> S3["T1 finishes → T2 continues<br>A deadlock is impossible!"]
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;

    class S2 step;
    class S3 success;
    class T1A,T1B,T2A,T2B error;
    class S1,S2b warning;

docs.title: 14. MVCC — Tuple Versioning
docs.text:
What it shows: How PostgreSQL keeps several versions of a row for MVCC. xmin = the transaction that created it, xmax = the transaction that deleted/replaced it.

graph TD
    subgraph "The notes table (internally)"
        T1["Tuple v1: id=42, title='Django'<br>xmin=100, xmax=NULL · visible: txid >= 100"]
        T2["Tuple v2: id=42, title='Django ORM'<br>xmin=200, xmax=NULL · visible: txid >= 200"]
        T3["Tuple v1 (dead): id=42, title='Django'<br>xmin=100, xmax=200 · visible: 100 <= txid < 200"]
    end

    TX150["Transaction txid=150<br>(started before the UPDATE)"] -->|"sees"| T3
    TX250["Transaction txid=250<br>(started after the UPDATE)"] -->|"sees"| T2
    VACUUM["VACUUM<br>(cleans up dead tuples)"] -->|"removes"| T3

    end

        R4 --> R6["Python join in memory"]

docs.title: 16. PostgreSQL System Architecture
docs.text:
What it shows: How PostgreSQL handles a Django query at the system level. Shared Buffers = cache. WAL = the fault-tolerance log.

graph TD
    Client["Django + psycopg2<br>TCP connection"] --> PM["Postmaster :5432<br>accepts connections"]
    PM -->|"fork()"| BP["Backend Process<br>(an isolated process for each connection)"]
    BP --> QP["Parser → AST → Planner → Optimizer<br>→ Execution Plan"]
    QP --> EE["Execution Engine"]
    EE <-->|"read/write"| SB["Shared Buffers<br>(25% of RAM as cache, shared by all processes)"]
    SB -->|"dirty pages"| WW["WAL Writer<br>(WRITE-AHEAD LOG)"]
    WW -->|"fsync"| WAL["WAL Files /pg_wal/<br>(the log comes first!)"]
    WAL -.->|"checkpoint (async)"| DF["Data Files /base/<br>(actual tables)"]

docs.title: 20. F() Expression — Race Condition Prevention
docs.text:
What it shows: The difference between an unsafe Python read-modify-write and an atomic F().

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Process A
    participant B as Process B
    participant PG as PostgreSQL

    Note over A,PG: ❌ UNSAFE (Python RMW)
    A->>PG: SELECT views_count FROM notes WHERE id=42
    PG-->>A: views=100
    B->>PG: SELECT views_count FROM notes WHERE id=42
    PG-->>B: views=100
    A->>PG: UPDATE notes SET views_count=101 WHERE id=42
    B->>PG: UPDATE notes SET views_count=101 WHERE id=42
    Note over A,PG: Result: views=101 instead of 102 (one view lost!)

    Note over A,PG: ✅ SAFE: F() Expression
    A->>PG: UPDATE notes SET views_count=views_count+1 WHERE id=42
    B->>PG: UPDATE notes SET views_count=views_count+1 WHERE id=42
    Note over A,PG: PostgreSQL serializes them: first A, then B
    Note over A,PG: Result: views=102 (correct!)

docs.title: PostgreSQL Advanced — Architecture, Docker, and Production Patterns
docs.text:
A continuation after django_orm_full.md. Here: the internal mechanics of PostgreSQL, why it is so fast, how to connect to it via Docker, PostgreSQL-specific fields, and production optimization.

🔬 SQL inspection in the notebook: docs/reference/legacy_source/orm_laboratory_reference.md

⚠️ The notebook itself is not part of this repository: the linked file only explains that. The section names in the table below point to the notebook's original structure, they are not anchors. You can run the same queries yourself in python manage.py shell or in the ORM lab.

Concept Notebook section queryset.explain(analyze=True) — query plan ## 11. 🔬 SQL Inspection connection.queries — SQL logging ## 11. 🔬 SQL Inspection Raw SQL via cursor.execute() ## 14. 🧪 Raw SQL

🧠 Mental model: PostgreSQL is not just "a place to store things". It is a complex client-server system with a multi-process architecture, its own memory manager (Shared Buffers), an isolation mechanism (MVCC), and a fault-tolerance log (WAL). Understanding this = understanding why some queries are fast and others are not.

📚 Why this matters for a Django developer: When you write Note.objects.filter(user=user), Django sends SQL to PostgreSQL, PostgreSQL decides where to look for the data (disk or memory, index or sequential scan), executes the query, and returns the result. If you understand this process, you know where the bottleneck is and how to remove it.

🌐 Practical value: Sooner or later every Django developer runs into "why does my page take 5 seconds to load?" The answer is always in PostgreSQL: a missing index, N+1 queries, a sequential scan on a large table. EXPLAIN ANALYZE + knowledge of the architecture = a diagnosis in 5 minutes.

❌ A typical mistake: Thinking that PostgreSQL = "just storage". In reality, PostgreSQL is a powerful server with a query planner, a cache, and a transaction manager. The right configuration can give a 10-100x performance boost without changing any code.

docs.title: 1. PostgreSQL vs SQLite — Why We Switch in Production
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: SQLite is a "file database". All access goes through a single file descriptor. Only ONE process can write at any given moment. PostgreSQL is a separate server process. Hundreds of clients at once → each one gets its own backend process → MVCC provides isolation.

📚 A real scenario: Gunicorn with 4 workers → 4 parallel Django requests → 4 simultaneous INSERTs. In SQLite: the first one writes, three wait. In PostgreSQL: all 4 write independently without locking (thanks to MVCC).

❌ A typical mistake: Deploying to production with SQLite. Django even documents: "SQLite is not suitable for production". For real traffic (50+ concurrent users), SQLite = a bottleneck.

SQLite (Serverless):
  Django Process A ─────────────────┐
  Django Process B ─────────────────┤ → [db.sqlite3 file] ← ONE file
  Django Process C ─────────────────┘   (write lock on the whole file)

  Problem: Process A writes → B and C WAIT

PostgreSQL (Client-Server):
  Django + psycopg2 ──TCP──► [postmaster :5432]
                                 │  ─ fork()  ─► [backend process 1] ─► [Shared Buffers]
                                 │  ─ fork()  ─► [backend process 2] ─► [Shared Buffers]
                                 │  ─ fork()  ─► [backend process 3] ─► [Shared Buffers]

  All three backend processes run in parallel, each with its own transaction (MVCC).
Characteristic SQLite PostgreSQL Architecture Serverless, a single file Client-server, a separate daemon Concurrent writes Database-level lock MVCC: thousands in parallel DB size Up to ~1 TB in practice Unlimited (even petabytes) JSON/Arrays Basic Full support + GIN indexes Full-text search Limited GIN + tsvector, trigram DDL transactions Limited Full support Connection Direct file TCP socket (or Unix socket) For production ❌ Never ✅ Always

docs.title: 2. PostgreSQL Process Model — How the Server Handles Queries
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: When Django connects to PostgreSQL, the postmaster daemon fork()s a new process specifically for that connection. This backend process serves ONE connection while it is active. Shared Buffers is memory shared among all the backend processes: the data cache.

📚 Why fork() and not threads: PostgreSQL uses processes (not threads) for isolation. If a backend process crashes, it does not kill the whole server. Shared Buffers is shared memory (not copies): all processes see one and the same cache.

🌐 CONN_MAX_AGE in Django: Every new Python process → a new connection to PostgreSQL → a fork() on the PostgreSQL side. That is expensive (10-100ms). CONN_MAX_AGE=60 → keep the connection between HTTP requests → no fork() every time → 5-10x less overhead on DB connections.

❌ A typical mistake: CONN_MAX_AGE=None (persistent) without PgBouncer. With 100 Gunicorn workers = 100 permanent connections to PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL keeps 100 backend processes. With max_connections=100 → the 101st client gets a "too many connections" error.

                ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │                 PostgreSQL Server                        │
                │                                                           │
  Django ────► │ Postmaster (port 5432)                                   │
  psycopg2     │   │                                                        │
               │   ├─ fork() ──► Backend Process 1 (your query)           │
               │   │              │  ← Query Parser                        │
               │   │              │  ← Query Planner & Optimizer            │
               │   │              │  ← Execution Engine                    │
               │   │              │                                         │
               │   │              └──► Shared Buffers (8GB RAM cache)     │
               │   │                     │                                  │
               │   │              WAL Writer ──► WAL Log (disk)           │
               │   │              Checkpointer ──► Data Files (disk)      │
               │   │                                                        │
               │   ├─ fork() ──► Backend Process 2 (another client)       │
               │   └─ fork() ──► Backend Process 3 (one more)             │
               └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 3. MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: Imagine that every row in a table has "versions". When you start a transaction, you see a snapshot of the DB state at the moment it began. Other transactions may change the same rows in parallel — you do not see those changes until they commit, and they do not see yours. It is like Google Docs: several people edit at the same time without conflicts.

📚 How PostgreSQL implements this: Each row stores xmin (which transaction created it) and xmax (which transaction deleted or replaced it). On SELECT, PostgreSQL sees only rows where xmin <= current_transaction and xmax is either NULL (not deleted) or xmax > current_transaction (deleted later than your transaction started).

🌐 What this gives Django: READ COMMITTED (the default) — every query in a transaction sees fresh committed data. No "dirty reads" (reading uncommitted changes). Parallel transactions do not block each other when reading.

❌ A typical mistake: Thinking that PostgreSQL "locks the table" on every SELECT. No. Readers do not block writers, writers do not block readers (MVCC). Locking happens only with SELECT FOR UPDATE or with concurrent writes to one and the same row.

MVCC — tuple versioning:

the notes_note table (internal representation):
┌─────┬───────────┬──────────┬───────────┬──────────────┐
│ id  │ title     │ xmin     │ xmax      │ Visible to   │
├─────┼───────────┼──────────┼───────────┼──────────────┤
│  42 │ "Django"  │ txid=100 │ NULL      │ all ≥ 100    │ ← active version
│  42 │ "Django!" │ txid=200 │ NULL      │ all ≥ 200    │ ← new version (UPDATE)
│  42 │ "Django"  │ txid=100 │ txid=200  │ transactions │ ← old (xmax=200: deleted)
│     │           │          │           │  < 200       │
└─────┴───────────┴──────────┴───────────┴──────────────┘

Transaction txid=150 (started between 100 and 200):
  → sees the row with xmin=100, xmax=NULL (the old version)
  → does NOT see the row with xmin=200 (it did not exist yet when 150 started)

Transaction txid=250 (started after 200):
  → sees the row with xmin=200 (the new version)
  → the old version (xmax=200) is "deleted" for it

VACUUM cleans up "dead" tuples (xmax != NULL and not visible to any active transaction)

docs.title: 4. WAL — Write-Ahead Logging
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: WAL is the database's "flight data recorder". Before making any change to the data, PostgreSQL writes the intent to the WAL log. If the server crashes, on restart PostgreSQL reads the WAL and restores all confirmed transactions. No data loss after COMMIT.

📚 Why "Write-Ahead": "Write-Ahead" = "write the log BEFORE changing the data". If the question is what is more important to keep — the log or the data? The log! With the log → the data can be restored. Data without a log → we don't know which state to restore to.

🌐 WAL and performance: PostgreSQL first writes changes to Shared Buffers (RAM) → then the WAL to disk. The Checkpointer syncs dirty pages to disk. synchronous_commit=on (the default) → COMMIT waits for the WAL to be written to disk. synchronous_commit=off → faster, but there is a risk of losing the latest transactions on a crash. For non-critical data (logs, analytics), off may be acceptable.

❌ A typical mistake: Running PostgreSQL with fsync=off "to speed up development". That is OK for local development, but in production = guaranteed data corruption on a crash. Never in production.

The path of data from COMMIT to disk:

1. Django: leaving transaction.atomic() (or autocommit)
           │
2. SQL: COMMIT
           │
3. PostgreSQL WAL Writer:
   ┌─ WAL Buffer (in RAM) ────────────────────────────────┐
   │  LSN 0/1234ABC: BEGIN txid=200                        │
   │  LSN 0/1234DEF: INSERT notes_note (id=42, title=...)  │
   │  LSN 0/1235000: COMMIT txid=200                       │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
           │ fsync() — flush to disk
           ▼
   WAL file: pg_wal/000000010000000000000001
   (Now even after a crash, the transaction can be recovered!)
           │
4. COMMIT returns to the client (Django gets OK)
           │
5. Later: the Checkpointer writes dirty pages from Shared Buffers to the Data Files
   (asynchronously, without delaying the client)

docs.title: 5. Connecting Django to PostgreSQL via Docker
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: Docker for PostgreSQL is a "virtual server" that starts in 5 seconds. A PostgreSQL container = a separate network namespace → Django connects over TCP to localhost:5432 as if it were a real server.

📚 Why Docker instead of installing PostgreSQL: Versioning (easy to switch to postgres:15 or postgres:16), isolation (does not clutter your system), the same environment for the whole team, easy to clean up (docker-compose down -v).

🌐 docker-compose.yml for development: volumes: postgres_data keeps the data between container restarts. Without a volume, a restart = a new empty DB. healthcheck — Django does not connect until PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.

❌ A typical mistake: Setting empty passwords or POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust in docker-compose. For local development, that is OK. But if port 5432 is exposed to the outside (for example, port forwarding in the cloud), someone can connect without a password.

docs.title: A Complete docker-compose.yml for Development:
docs.text:
# docker-compose.yml

version: '3.9'

services:

  # ── PostgreSQL ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine          # alpine = a minimal image (~25MB)
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: notes_db            # database name
      POSTGRES_USER: notes_user        # user name
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: notes_pass    # password (in an .env file in production!)
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data  # data is kept between restarts
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"                    # host:container
    healthcheck:
      # Django (app) will not start until PostgreSQL is ready
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U notes_user -d notes_db"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

  # ── Django App (optional) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://notes_user:notes_pass@db:5432/notes_db
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy    # wait until the db healthcheck = healthy
    command: >
      sh -c "python manage.py migrate &&
             python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000"

volumes:
  postgres_data:     # named volume — the data is kept outside the container

# Commands for working with it:

# Start only PostgreSQL (for local development)
docker-compose up -d db

# Start the whole stack
docker-compose up -d

# Check that PostgreSQL is running
docker-compose ps
docker-compose logs db

# Connect to the psql console
docker-compose exec db psql -U notes_user -d notes_db

# Show all tables
docker-compose exec db psql -U notes_user -d notes_db -c "\dt notes_app*"

# Stop and keep the data
docker-compose stop

# Stop and DELETE the data (a full cleanup!)
docker-compose down -v

docs.title: 6. psycopg2 and PgBouncer
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: psycopg2 is the "phone line" between Python and PostgreSQL. PgBouncer is the "telephone exchange": instead of each Django worker holding a direct line to PostgreSQL, they connect through an exchange that switches between a limited number of real lines.

📚 The problem without PgBouncer: Gunicorn with 10 workers + 5 threads = 50 parallel connections. PostgreSQL fork()s 50 backend processes. With 100 workers → 100 backend processes → max_connections=100 → the 101st gets an error. PgBouncer → 1000 Django connections → 20 real connections to PostgreSQL.

🌐 PgBouncer modes: Session pooling (1 PostgreSQL connection per Django session), Transaction pooling (1 real PostgreSQL connection per transaction — the best balance for Django), Statement pooling (the most aggressive connection reuse, but does not support multi-statement transactions).

❌ A typical mistake: Transaction pooling + CONN_MAX_AGE in Django. With Transaction pooling, each transaction may go through a different physical connection. Persistent connections to PostgreSQL then make no sense. With PgBouncer: CONN_MAX_AGE=0.

Without PgBouncer:
  Django w1 ──────────────────────────── TCP ──► PostgreSQL :5432
  Django w2 ──────────────────────────── TCP ──► PostgreSQL :5432
  Django w3 ──────────────────────────── TCP ──► PostgreSQL :5432
  ... (100 workers = 100 postgres backend processes)

With PgBouncer:
  Django w1 ──┐
  Django w2 ──┤── PgBouncer :6432 ──[ pool: 20 conns ]──► PostgreSQL :5432
  Django w3 ──┘  (100 Django connections → 20 real ones)

# settings.py with PgBouncer:
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'NAME': 'notes_db',
        'USER': 'notes_user',
        'PASSWORD': 'notes_pass',
        'HOST': 'pgbouncer',  # the PgBouncer host, not PostgreSQL!
        'PORT': '6432',       # the PgBouncer port
        'CONN_MAX_AGE': 0,    # with PgBouncer, persistent connections are not needed
    }
}

docs.title: 7. PostgreSQL-Specific Django Fields
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: PostgreSQL supports data types that SQLite or MySQL do not have: arrays, JSONB, UUID, hstore, range types. Django provides fields for working with them. These fields are for the PostgreSQL backend only!

📚 JSONField vs a separate table: A JSONField stores an arbitrary structure in a single column. When to use it: configuration, metadata, data whose structure changes often. When NOT to use it: data that needs complex JOINs, frequent updates of individual fields, a strict schema.

🌐 GIN index for JSON and arrays: A regular B-Tree index cannot index JSON or an array (many values in one column). GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes each array element or each JSON key. GinIndex(fields=['metadata']) → fast search by JSON keys.

❌ A typical mistake: Using a JSONField as a "fallback" for a poorly thought-out schema. A JSONField without a GIN index + filtering with filter(metadata__key=val) → a sequential scan (a full table scan). Always add a GIN index if you filter on JSON.

docs.title: JSONField — Structured Data in a Column:
docs.text:
from django.db import models

class Note(models.Model):
    # JSONField stores a Python dict/list in a PostgreSQL JSONB column
    # JSONB = binary JSON → faster than TEXT JSON
    metadata = models.JSONField(
        default=dict,
        blank=True,
        help_text='Arbitrary metadata: word_count, reading_time, language, etc.'
    )

# Filling it in:
note.metadata = {
    'word_count': 450,
    'reading_time_minutes': 3,
    'language': 'uk',
    'ai_tags': ['python', 'orm', 'database'],
    'last_spell_check': '2024-01-15'
}
note.save()

# Filtering by JSON fields:
Note.objects.filter(metadata__language='uk')
# WHERE metadata->>'language' = 'uk'

Note.objects.filter(metadata__word_count__gte=100)
# WHERE (metadata->>'word_count')::int >= 100

Note.objects.filter(metadata__ai_tags__contains=['python'])
# WHERE metadata->'ai_tags' @> '["python"]'

# Annotation with a JSON field:
from django.db.models import F
Note.objects.annotate(
    word_count=F('metadata__word_count')
).order_by('-word_count')

docs.title: ArrayField — Arrays in PostgreSQL:
docs.text:
from django.contrib.postgres.fields import ArrayField

class Note(models.Model):
    # An array of strings — an alternative to M:N for simple tags
    quick_labels = ArrayField(
        base_field=models.CharField(max_length=50),
        blank=True,
        default=list,
        help_text='Quick labels (no FK, no junction table)'
    )

    # An array of IntegerField
    related_note_ids = ArrayField(
        base_field=models.IntegerField(),
        blank=True,
        default=list,
    )

# SQL: quick_labels TEXT[] DEFAULT '{}'

# Filtering:
Note.objects.filter(quick_labels__contains=['python'])
# WHERE quick_labels @> ARRAY['python']  (the array contains 'python')

Note.objects.filter(quick_labels__overlap=['python', 'django'])
# WHERE quick_labels && ARRAY['python', 'django']  (at least one match)

Note.objects.filter(quick_labels__len=3)
# WHERE array_length(quick_labels, 1) = 3  (an array of 3 elements)

docs.title: UniqueConstraint and CheckConstraint:
docs.text:
class Note(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    slug = models.SlugField(max_length=200)
    views_count = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)
    priority = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=1)

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            # COMPOSITE UNIQUE: slug is unique within a single user
            # (alice can have /notes/python/, bob can too, but alice cannot have it twice)
            models.UniqueConstraint(
                fields=['user', 'slug'],
                name='unique_note_slug_per_user'
            ),

            # CHECK: views_count >= 0 (cannot be negative)
            # Checked even on a direct SQL INSERT (not only through Django)
            models.CheckConstraint(
                check=models.Q(views_count__gte=0),
                name='note_views_count_non_negative'
            ),

            # CHECK: priority from 1 to 4
            models.CheckConstraint(
                check=models.Q(priority__gte=1) & models.Q(priority__lte=4),
                name='note_priority_valid_range'
            ),
        ]

-- What gets generated in SQL:
ALTER TABLE notes_note
  ADD CONSTRAINT unique_note_slug_per_user UNIQUE (user_id, slug),
  ADD CONSTRAINT note_views_count_non_negative CHECK (views_count >= 0),
  ADD CONSTRAINT note_priority_valid_range CHECK (priority >= 1 AND priority <= 4);

docs.title: 8. EXPLAIN ANALYZE — Diagnosing Queries
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: EXPLAIN ANALYZE is an MRI scan for your SQL query. It shows which plan the Planner chose, how long each step took, and how many rows were processed. With it, you see where the bottleneck is: a missing index, a JOIN that is too wide, suboptimal sorting.

📚 EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE: EXPLAIN shows the plan without executing it (fast). EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows real metrics (slow, but accurate). For production, always test on a copy — EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the query!

🌐 How to read a plan: Seq Scan = reads the whole table, O(N). Index Scan = uses a B-Tree, O(log N). Index Only Scan = a covering index (does not read the heap). Hash Join = an efficient JOIN for large tables. Nested Loop Join = efficient for small tables with an index.

❌ A typical mistake: Ignoring a Seq Scan on large tables. Seq Scan on notes_note (cost=0.00..5000.00 rows=100000) = reading all ~100,000 rows. You need an index on the field in the WHERE clause.

# Django: qs.explain(analyze=True) — sends EXPLAIN ANALYZE to PostgreSQL
from notes_app.models import Note

qs = Note.objects.filter(user_id=5, is_archived=False).order_by('-updated_at')
print(qs.explain(analyze=True))

-- Typical EXPLAIN ANALYZE output:

-- A GOOD query (there is an index):
Index Scan using note_user_updated_idx on notes_note  (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=100)
                                                       (actual time=0.023..0.025 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((user_id = 5) AND (is_archived = false))
Planning Time: 0.150 ms
Execution Time: 0.045 ms   ← milliseconds!

-- A BAD query (Seq Scan without an index):
Seq Scan on notes_note  (cost=0.00..25000.00 rows=500000 width=100)
                         (actual time=0.050..1500.000 rows=150 loops=1)
  Filter: ((user_id = 5) AND (is_archived = false))
  Rows Removed by Filter: 499850    ← 500K rows scanned to find 150!
Planning Time: 0.250 ms
Execution Time: 1500.000 ms   ← 1.5 seconds!

-- Reading the plan:
-- cost=0.00..8.31      → cost: estimated start..total cost (in PostgreSQL units)
-- rows=1               → estimated number of rows
-- actual time=0.023..0.025 → real time: first row..last row (ms)
-- rows=1 loops=1       → rows actually returned, number of iterations

-- Operations:
-- Seq Scan            → ❌ full table scan O(N)
-- Index Scan          → ✅ B-Tree index O(log N)
-- Index Only Scan     → ✅✅ covering index (no heap reads)
-- Bitmap Index Scan   → ✅ for a large number of rows via an index
-- Hash Join           → JOIN via a hash table (efficient for large tables)
-- Nested Loop         → JOIN via a loop (efficient when there is an index on the inner table)
-- Sort                → ORDER BY without an index (can be slow)

docs.title: 9. CONN_MAX_AGE and Connection Pooling
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: Connecting to PostgreSQL is an expensive operation: TCP handshake, authentication, fork() of a backend process — 5-50ms. CONN_MAX_AGE tells Django: "keep the connection between HTTP requests instead of opening/closing it every time".

📚 How CONN_MAX_AGE works with Gunicorn: Each Gunicorn worker = a separate process = a separate connection. With CONN_MAX_AGE=60, a worker keeps the connection for 60 seconds after the last request. On the next HTTP request to that worker, the connection is already ready.

🌐 A rule for production: Gunicorn + CONN_MAX_AGE=60 + no PgBouncer: number of connections = number of workers * threads. 10 workers * 2 threads = 20 connections max. If max_connections=100, that is safe. If there are more workers, either reduce CONN_MAX_AGE or add PgBouncer.

❌ A typical mistake: CONN_MAX_AGE=None (infinite). The connection is never closed. When a new version is deployed, the old connections remain. Over time, PostgreSQL accumulates "hanging" connections. Better to use CONN_MAX_AGE=60 or 300.

Connections without CONN_MAX_AGE (CONN_MAX_AGE=0):

HTTP Request 1 → [open connection] → [SQL] → [close connection]   +50ms overhead
HTTP Request 2 → [open connection] → [SQL] → [close connection]   +50ms overhead
HTTP Request 3 → [open connection] → [SQL] → [close connection]   +50ms overhead

Connections with CONN_MAX_AGE=60:

HTTP Request 1 → [open connection] → [SQL] → [keep open]   +50ms (the first time)
HTTP Request 2 → [reuse connection] → [SQL] → [keep open]  +0ms!
HTTP Request 3 → [reuse connection] → [SQL] → [keep open]  +0ms!
... (after 60 seconds without requests → it is closed)

docs.title: 10. The Production Stack
docs.text:
Internet
    │
    ▼
[nginx] (port 443, SSL termination, static files)
    │
    ▼
[Gunicorn] (4-8 workers, Unix socket)
    │
    │  Django WSGI app
    │  CONN_MAX_AGE=60
    ▼
[PgBouncer] (port 6432, transaction pooling)
    │
    │  pool_size=20
    ▼
[PostgreSQL 16] (port 5432)
    │
    ├── Shared Buffers: 25% RAM
    ├── WAL: pg_wal/
    └── Data Files: /var/lib/postgresql/data/

# settings/production.py

DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'NAME': config('DB_NAME'),
        'USER': config('DB_USER'),
        'PASSWORD': config('DB_PASSWORD'),
        'HOST': config('DB_HOST', default='pgbouncer'),  # pgbouncer host
        'PORT': config('DB_PORT', default='6432'),        # pgbouncer port
        'CONN_MAX_AGE': 0,        # with PgBouncer, a persistent conn is not needed
        'OPTIONS': {
            'connect_timeout': 10,
            'options': '-c lock_timeout=3s',   # timeout for locks
        },
    }
}

# SQL query logging: django.db.backends emits it only when DEBUG=True,
# so in production this block shows nothing — keep it in dev settings
LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'handlers': {
        'console': {'class': 'logging.StreamHandler'},
    },
    'loggers': {
        'django.db.backends': {
            'handlers': ['console'],
            'level': 'DEBUG',    # shows all SQL queries
        },
    },
}

docs.title: Exercise 1: Connections
docs.text:
# settings.py:
DATABASES = {'default': {'CONN_MAX_AGE': 0, ...}}
# Gunicorn: 4 workers, each handles 100 requests per minute

Question: How many connections to PostgreSQL are opened per minute?

Answer: 400 connections (100 req/minute × 4 workers). Each request = open + close. With CONN_MAX_AGE=60 → 4 connections (one per worker, kept for 60 seconds).

docs.title: Exercise 2: MVCC
docs.text:
Transaction T1 starts at 10:00:00
Transaction T2 inserts a new row and COMMITs at 10:00:01
T1 runs a SELECT at 10:00:02

Question: Does T1 see T2's new row?

Answer (depends on the isolation level): - READ COMMITTED (the default in PostgreSQL) → YES, it sees it. Each query in T1 sees fresh committed data. - REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE → does NOT see it. T1's snapshot is taken at the first query in the transaction (not at BEGIN/START TRANSACTION). So T1 does not see the row if it already ran at least one query before T2's COMMIT at 10:00:01; if the SELECT at 10:00:02 is its first query, it will see it.

docs.title: Self-Check Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does PostgreSQL not lock the table on every SELECT (MVCC)?
  2. What is WAL, and why is it needed?
  3. What is CONN_MAX_AGE, and which values are recommended?
  4. When should you use a JSONField, and when a separate table?
  5. Why does a JSONField need a GIN index?
  6. What does Seq Scan in EXPLAIN ANALYZE show, and when is it a problem?
  7. Why PgBouncer, and when is it needed?
  8. What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
  9. What do xmin and xmax mean in PostgreSQL's internal representation?
  10. Why is POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust dangerous in production?

docs.title: QuerySet Optimization
docs.text: A Django QuerySet is lazy: SQL runs only when you ask for the data. The N+1 problem is the most common performance mistake in Django.

docs.title: QuerySet — lazy by nature
docs.text:
# This line does NOT run any SQL:
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user)

# SQL runs here — on iteration or len():
for note in notes:         # ← SQL runs
    print(note.title)

count = notes.count()      # ← SQL: SELECT COUNT(*)
first = notes.first()      # ← SQL: SELECT ... LIMIT 1
list(notes)                # ← SQL: SELECT * FROM ...

Chaining — every .filter(), .order_by(), .exclude() returns a new QuerySet without SQL:

qs = Note.objects.all()
qs = qs.filter(user=user)
qs = qs.filter(is_archived=False)
qs = qs.order_by('-priority')
# No SQL has run yet!

result = list(qs)          # ← only here: one SQL query with all conditions

docs.title: N+1 Problem
docs.text:
The most common performance mistake in Django.

Imagine: you display a list of 50 notes and show the notebook name for each one.

docs.title: The problem (N+1 queries)
docs.text:
# view
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user)

# template
{% for note in notes %}
  {{ note.title }} — {{ note.notebook.title }}
{% endfor %}

SQL: 

SELECT * FROM notes_app_note WHERE user_id = 1;          -- 1 query
SELECT * FROM notes_app_notebook WHERE id = 5;           -- for note 1
SELECT * FROM notes_app_notebook WHERE id = 5;           -- for note 2
SELECT * FROM notes_app_notebook WHERE id = 7;           -- for note 3
... (50 separate queries for notebooks!)

Total: 1 + 50 = 51 queries for a single list.

docs.title: Solution: select_related
docs.text:
# ForeignKey and OneToOne — a JOIN in a single SQL query
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user).select_related('notebook', 'group')

SQL: 

SELECT notes.*, notebooks.*, groups.*
FROM notes_app_note notes
LEFT JOIN notes_app_notebook notebooks ON notes.notebook_id = notebooks.id
LEFT JOIN auth_group groups ON notes.group_id = groups.id
WHERE notes.user_id = 1;

Total: 1 query. Django caches the JOIN results in memory.

docs.title: Solution: prefetch_related
docs.text:
# ManyToMany and reverse FK — a separate SELECT with an IN lookup
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user).prefetch_related('tags')

SQL: 

SELECT * FROM notes_app_note WHERE user_id = 1;         -- query 1
SELECT * FROM notes_app_tag
  INNER JOIN notes_app_note_tags ON tag_id = notes_app_tag.id
  WHERE note_id IN (1, 2, 3, ..., 50);                  -- query 2

Total: 2 queries regardless of the number of notes.

docs.title: When to use what
docs.text: Relationship type Method Number of SQL queries ForeignKey (1 level) select_related('notebook') 1 JOIN ForeignKey (2 levels) select_related('notebook__user') 1 JOIN ManyToMany prefetch_related('tags') 2 queries Reverse FK prefetch_related('reminders') 2 queries Complex prefetch Prefetch('reminders', queryset=...) 2 queries with filters

docs.title: get_user_notes — an optimized list
docs.text:
# notes_app/selectors.py

def get_user_notes(user, *, archived=False, notebook=None, tag=None, search=None):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    qs = Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups), is_archived=archived
    ).select_related('notebook', 'group').prefetch_related('tags')
    # ↑ select_related: FK → JOIN (notebook, group)
    # ↑ prefetch_related: M:N → separate SELECT IN (tags)

    if notebook is not None:
        qs = qs.filter(notebook=notebook)
    if search:
        qs = qs.filter(Q(title__icontains=search) | Q(content__icontains=search))

    return qs.order_by('-is_pinned', '-priority', '-updated_at')

docs.title: get_note_detail — with Prefetch filtering
docs.text:
def get_note_detail(user, note_id):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    return Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups)
    ).select_related(
        'notebook', 'user'
    ).prefetch_related(
        'tags',
        Prefetch(
            'reminders',
            queryset=Reminder.objects.filter(
                remind_at__gte=timezone.now()   # ← only upcoming reminders
            ).order_by('remind_at'),
            to_attr='upcoming_reminders'        # ← note.upcoming_reminders instead of note.reminders.all()
        )
    ).get(id=note_id)

docs.title: get_user_notebooks — annotate Count
docs.text:
def get_user_notebooks(user):
    return Notebook.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
        note_count=Count('notes', filter=Q(notes__is_archived=False))
    ).order_by('-is_default', 'title')

SQL: 

SELECT notebooks.*, COUNT(notes.id) FILTER (WHERE notes.is_archived = false) AS note_count
FROM notes_app_notebook notebooks
LEFT JOIN notes_app_note notes ON notes.notebook_id = notebooks.id
WHERE notebooks.user_id = 1
GROUP BY notebooks.id
ORDER BY notebooks.is_default DESC, notebooks.title;

Result: notebook.note_count is available as an attribute — with no extra queries in the template.

docs.title: get_user_todo_lists — two annotates
docs.text:
def get_user_todo_lists(user):
    return TodoList.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
        total_items=Count('items'),
        done_items=Count('items', filter=Q(items__is_done=True))
    ).order_by('is_completed', '-created_at')

This lets you write in the template: 

{{ todo.done_items }} / {{ todo.total_items }} виконано
— without a single extra SQL query.

docs.title: values() and values_list() — lighter queries
docs.text:
If you only need individual fields, do not load the whole Model:

# Full model — unnecessary data
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user)   # SELECT * (all columns)

# Only the fields you need
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user).values('id', 'title', 'priority')
# → [{'id': 1, 'title': 'Note', 'priority': 2}, ...]

# For a JSON response or simple processing
ids = Note.objects.filter(user=user).values_list('id', flat=True)
# → [1, 2, 3, ...]

In selectors.py it is used for browser notifications: 

return list(
    Reminder.objects.filter(...).values('id', 'message', 'remind_at', 'note__title')
)
