docs.title: How to read this file
docs.text:
This reference is built from simple to complex:

Level What's here For whom 🟢 Start Installation + your first form in 5 minutes Complete beginners 🟡 Practice FormHelper, Layout, all components You already know the basics 🔵 Reference Formsets, Dynamic API, template packs Full control

Recommendation: if this is your first time seeing crispy-forms, read from top to bottom without skipping ahead. If you are looking for a specific component, use the Layout objects table.

docs.title: 🟢 Start: Your First Crispy Form in 5 Minutes
The problem: why does "HTML spaghetti" happen?
docs.text:
Imagine you need to display a form with Bootstrap 5. Without crispy you write:

<!-- ❌ Without crispy: 18 lines of HTML for ONE field -->
<div class="mb-3">
  <label for="id_title" class="form-label fw-semibold">
    Заголовок
    <span class="text-danger">*</span>
  </label>
  <input type="text"
         name="title"
         id="id_title"
         class="form-control {% if form.title.errors %}is-invalid{% endif %}"
         required>
  {% if form.title.errors %}
    {% for error in form.title.errors %}
    <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ error }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
  {% endif %}
</div>
<!-- repeat for EVERY field... -->

And so on for every field. 5 fields = ~90 lines of HTML. When the form changes, you edit the HTML in the template. When Bootstrap changes, you edit every template.

With crispy: 

<!-- ✅ With crispy: 1 line — Bootstrap, validation and structure all included -->
{% crispy form %}

🧠 Mental model: crispy-forms moves the Bootstrap markup from the template into Python code. The template becomes thin ({% crispy form %}), and the form describes itself (FormHelper + Layout).

docs.title: Step 1: Installation
docs.text:
pip install django-crispy-forms crispy-bootstrap5

# settings.py — add TWO packages to INSTALLED_APPS
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'crispy_forms',       # ← 1. the core package
    'crispy_bootstrap5',  # ← 2. the template pack for Bootstrap 5
]

# Specify which CSS framework you use
CRISPY_ALLOWED_TEMPLATE_PACKS = "bootstrap5"
CRISPY_TEMPLATE_PACK = "bootstrap5"

Why two packages? Since version 2.0, crispy has been split: crispy_forms is the core, and the Bootstrap templates are a separate crispy_bootstrap5. This lets you plug in another framework (Tailwind, Bulma) without changing the core.

docs.title: Step 2: Load it in the template
docs.text:
<!-- At the top of the template — once per file -->
{% load crispy_forms_tags %}

<!-- And wherever you need to show the form -->
{% crispy form %}

That's it! The form is rendered with Bootstrap 5: form-control, form-label, invalid-feedback — all automatic.

docs.title: Step 3: FormHelper — describing the form from Python
docs.text:
Without FormHelper, crispy just adds Bootstrap classes. With FormHelper, you describe: - the form method (POST/GET) - the order and structure of the fields (Layout) - the Submit button

# forms.py
from django import forms
from crispy_forms.helper import FormHelper
from crispy_forms.layout import Layout, Submit

class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    name    = forms.CharField(label='Your name')
    email   = forms.EmailField(label='Email')
    message = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea, label='Message')

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

        # FormHelper — attached to the form via self.helper
        self.helper = FormHelper()
        self.helper.form_method = 'post'          # <form method="post">
        self.helper.layout = Layout(
            'name',                               # a field by name
            'email',
            'message',
            Submit('submit', 'Send'),              # submit button
        )

# views.py — nothing special
def contact(request):
    form = ContactForm()
    return render(request, 'contact.html', {'form': form})

<!-- contact.html -->
{% load crispy_forms_tags %}
{% crispy form %}

🧠 What happens: {% crispy form %} finds form.helper, looks at form.helper.layout, and renders every Layout object through Bootstrap 5 templates. That's all the "magic" there is.

docs.title: Step 4: Check that everything works
docs.text: After the first run, make sure that: - The form looks like Bootstrap (label + input + button) - Red validation errors appear automatically on an empty submit - There is no ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'crispy_forms'

docs.title: FormHelper — what it controls
docs.text:
self.helper = FormHelper()

# Attributes of the <form> tag
self.helper.form_method = 'post'          # POST or GET
self.helper.form_id = 'my-form'           # id="my-form"
self.helper.form_class = 'my-class'       # class="my-class"
self.helper.form_action = '/submit/'      # action="/submit/"

# Behavior
self.helper.form_tag = True               # True = renders <form>...</form>
                                          # False = fields only (useful for AJAX)
self.helper.disable_csrf = False          # True = remove CSRF (rarely needed)
self.helper.include_media = True          # Insert form.media automatically
self.helper.form_show_errors = True       # Show errors
self.helper.form_show_labels = True       # Show labels

💡 Most commonly used: form_method, form_tag, form_id. The rest — as needed.

docs.title: FormHelper with a bound form
docs.text:
If the form is large and you don't want to list all the fields manually, pass self to FormHelper:

def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
    super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
    self.helper = FormHelper(self)   # ← crispy finds all the fields itself
    # Now you can skip Layout() — crispy builds a default one automatically

docs.title: Layout — how to describe the form structure
docs.text:
Layout is a tree of objects that describes the order and structure of the fields.

from crispy_forms.layout import Layout, Fieldset, Row, Column, Field, Submit, HTML, Div

self.helper.layout = Layout(
    'simple_field',                              # just a field name — a string
    Field('title', placeholder='Hint'),          # a field with attributes
    Row(                                         # a horizontal row (Bootstrap row)
        Column('first_name', css_class='col-md-6'),
        Column('last_name',  css_class='col-md-6'),
    ),
    Fieldset('Section title',                    # <fieldset><legend>
        'field_1',
        'field_2',
    ),
    HTML('<hr>'),                                # arbitrary HTML
    Submit('submit', 'Save'),                    # button
)

🧠 Rule: you specify fields as strings ('title') or via Field('title', ...). Field lets you set additional HTML attributes.

Field('title', placeholder='Hint')           # placeholder="Hint"
Field('title', autofocus=True)               # autofocus
Field('title', rows=8)                       # rows="8" (textarea)
Field('title', type='hidden')                # type="hidden"

💡 Underscore → hyphen: in Python kwargs, an underscore _ becomes - in HTML. data_name="val" → data-name="val". Exceptions: css_class, css_id, wrapper_class.

docs.title: Template Tags and Filters
docs.text:
{% load crispy_forms_tags %}

{# The main tag — full rendering with FormHelper #}
{% crispy form %}

{# With an explicit helper (if the helper is not attached to the form) #}
{% crispy form my_helper %}

{# The filter — quick Bootstrap styling without FormHelper #}
{{ form|crispy }}

{# Formset — pass the helper explicitly #}

{# A single field on its own #}

When to use {% crispy %} vs |crispy:

{% crispy form %} {{ form\|crispy }} FormHelper + Layout Yes — full control No — Bootstrap classes only <form> tag + CSRF Yes (by default) No Submit button Via Layout Not included When Production A quick preview

💡 Rule: for any real form — always {% crispy form %} with FormHelper. |crispy — only for a quick preview during development.

<!-- {% crispy form %} -->

docs.title: DJANGO FORMS — From Raw Data to the Database
docs.text:
Where you are in the knowledge map: RELATIONAL_DB_FOUNDATIONS → DJANGO_ORM_DEEP → DJANGO_FORMS ← you are here

Forms are the bridge between the browser and the ORM. They turn unsafe HTTP strings into typed Python objects that are ready to be written to the database.

🔬 QuerySets in forms — in the notebook: docs/reference/legacy_source/orm_laboratory_reference.md

⚠️ The notebook itself is not part of this repository: the linked file only explains that. The section names in the table below point to the notebook's original structure, they are not anchors. You can run the same queries yourself in python manage.py shell or in the ORM lab.

Forms concept Notebook section ModelForm + FK choices (queryset for the choices) ## 2. 🔍 Lazy Methods → filter() form.cleaned_data → ORM (Trust Boundary) ## 14. 🧪 Raw SQL — safe parameters PRG pattern after POST README.md → section 03 · WRITE flow

docs.title: 1. Core Mechanism — What Is a Django Form on the Inside?
🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Picture a customs checkpoint on the border between two countries:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                           TRUST BOUNDARY                                │
│                                                                         │
│  🌐 Browser (unsafe zone)         ║     🔒 Django + DB (safe zone)      │
│  ─────────────────────────────    ║    ──────────────────────────────   │
│  request.POST["title"] = "..."    ║    form.cleaned_data["title"]       │
│  request.POST["price"] = "abc"    ║    (typed str, int, Decimal)        │
│  (THESE ARE JUST STRINGS, nothing ║    (validated, safe objects)        │
│   more)                           ║                                     │
│                           [  FORM  ]                                    │
│                      customs at the border                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A Django form is a Python class that defines: - Which fields are expected (structure) - How to validate each field (validation) - How to convert an HTTP string into a Python type (coercion) - How to render HTML for the browser (widget)

docs.title: 📚 Why does this exist?
docs.text:
HTTP is a text protocol. The browser sends everything as strings: 

POST /notes/create/ HTTP/1.1

title=My+Note&priority=2&price=abc

Without a form you would have to: 1. Manually get request.POST.get("priority") 2. Manually check whether it is a number: try: int(value) except ... 3. Manually check the range: if 1 <= priority <= 4 4. Manually escape it against XSS before displaying it 5. Manually protect against SQL injection

A form does all of this automatically and safely.

docs.title: ❌ Common mistake
docs.text:
# ❌ UNSAFE: straight from POST into the ORM — never do this!
Note.objects.create(
    title=request.POST["title"],   # may contain "<script>alert(1)</script>"
    priority=request.POST["priority"],  # may be "abc", None, "-999"
)

# ✅ CORRECT: through a form
form = NoteForm(request.POST)
if form.is_valid():
    Note.objects.create(**form.cleaned_data)

docs.title: 2. Form Lifecycle — The Sequence of Form States
📚 Step 0: Browser Submission → request.POST (QueryDict)
docs.text:
Before a Django form receives the data, it passes through the HTTP layer:

Browser → URL encode → HTTP POST body → Django parses → QueryDict

HTML:  <input name="title" value="Моя нотатка">
       <input name="priority" value="2">
       <input name="csrfmiddlewaretoken" value="abc123...">

HTTP body: title=My+Note&priority=2&csrfmiddlewaretoken=abc123...

Django:
request.POST = QueryDict({
    'title': ['Моя нотатка'],       # ← always a list of strings!
    'priority': ['2'],              # ← the string "2", not the int 2!
    'csrfmiddlewaretoken': ['abc123...'],
})

request.POST['title']     → 'Моя нотатка'   (a single string)
request.POST.getlist('tags') → ['1', '3', '5']  # M:N: multiple values

Key fact: QueryDict is immutable, and all values are strings. The form converts these strings into typed Python objects.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
A form goes through 7 clear states. Like an assembly line in a factory:

Browser                    Django View                      Database
   │                            │                               │
   │──── HTTP POST ─────────────►│                               │
   │                            │                               │
   │              form = NoteForm(request.POST)                  │
   │                    │ STATE: bound                          │
   │                            │                               │
   │              form.is_valid()                               │
   │                    │ → runs the validation pipeline        │
   │                            │                               │
   │              ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐               │
   │              │ is_valid=True               │ is_valid=False │
   │              │                             │               │
   │              ▼                             ▼               │
   │     form.cleaned_data             form.errors              │
   │     (typed objects)               (dict of errors)         │
   │              │                             │               │
   │              ▼                             ▼               │
   │     services.create_note(...)      render(request,         │
   │              │                     template, {'form':form}) │
   │              ▼                             │               │
   │     return redirect(...)           HTTP 200 with the form ◄┘
   │◄─── HTTP 302 ──────────────         (fields with errors)

docs.title: 📚 Why exactly this sequence?
docs.text:
Why redirect after success (the PRG pattern)?

WITHOUT A REDIRECT:
  POST /notes/create/ → 200 OK (HTML page)
  User presses F5 → browser asks "Resubmit POST?" → duplicate note!

WITH A REDIRECT:
  POST /notes/create/ → 302 Redirect → GET /notes/42/ → 200 OK
  User presses F5 → browser repeats the GET → safe, no duplicate

Why is the form shown again with errors?

So the user does not lose the data they entered! A bound form keeps the values already entered in form.data (that is, request.POST) and puts them back into the HTML when it re-renders.

docs.title: 🌐 Sequence Diagram: both paths (success + validation failure)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant View
    participant Form

    Browser->>View: POST /notes/create/
    View->>Form: form = NoteForm(request.POST)
    Form->>Form: is_valid() → validation pipeline

    alt Validation Passes
        Form-->>View: True + form.cleaned_data
        View->>View: services.create_note(...)
        View->>Browser: HTTP 302 Redirect → GET /notes/42/
        Browser->>View: GET /notes/42/
        View->>Browser: HTTP 200 Note Detail Page
    else Validation Fails
        Form-->>View: False + form.errors
        View->>Browser: HTTP 200 re-render form
        Note over Browser: Fields pre-filled with submitted data
        Note over Browser: Error messages shown next to fields
    end

Why HTTP 200 on errors (not 400)? Django returns 200 so the browser can display the form with errors normally. HTTP 400 (Bad Request) would be more semantically correct, but in practice most Django applications use 200 to re-render a form.

docs.title: ❌ Common mistake
docs.text:
# ❌ Wrong: no redirect after POST
def note_create(request):
    form = NoteForm(request.POST)
    if form.is_valid():
        note = Note.objects.create(...)
        return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})
        # F5 = repeated POST = duplicate!

# ✅ Correct: PRG (Post/Redirect/Get)
def note_create(request):
    form = NoteForm(request.POST)
    if form.is_valid():
        note = services.create_note(...)
        return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)  # ← 302!

docs.title: 3. Mental Models — Three Ways to Think About Forms
🧠 Mental model 1: Trust Boundary
docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph Untrusted["❌ Unsafe zone (Client / Network)"]
        A[Browser Submission] -->|HTTP POST| B["request.POST<br>Raw Strings"]
    end

    subgraph Boundary["⚠️ Trust boundary (Django Form Pipeline)"]
        B --> C{is_valid?}
        C -- Fails --> D[form.errors]
    end

    subgraph Trusted["✅ Safe zone (Backend / ORM)"]
        C -- Passes --> E["form.cleaned_data<br>Typed Python Objects"]
        E --> F[Database Save]
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A step;
    class C decision;
    class E,F success;
    class D error;
    class B warning;

Everything to the left of is_valid() is unsafe strings. Everything to the right is safe objects.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model 2: Validation Pipeline (a chain of filters)
docs.text:
A form is not just HTML, it is a chain of filters:

Raw string
    │
    ▼
[to_python()]     → "2" → int(2)     "abc" → ValidationError!
    │
    ▼
[validate()]      → int(2), min=1, max=4 → OK   int(99) → Error!
    │
    ▼
[run_validators()] → custom functions → OK or Error
    │
    ▼
[clean_<field>()]  → your business logic → OK or Error
    │
    ▼
[clean()]          → cross-field validation
    │
    ▼
cleaned_data["priority"] = 2    ← Python int, guaranteed 1–4

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model 3: HTML ↔ Python Bridge (a two-way bridge)
docs.text:
GET request (displaying the form):
  Model / initial data
        │
        ▼
    Form Field ──► Widget ──► HTML <input value="...">
    (Python)                  (Text for the browser)

POST request (processing the response):
  HTML <input value="...">
        │
        ▼
    Form Field ──► cleaned_data ──► ORM save()
    (Text→Python)  (Python object)  (SQL INSERT/UPDATE)

docs.title: 📚 Why is server-side validation mandatory?
docs.text:
HTML5 attributes such as required, maxlength, type="email" are convenient UX, but not protection. Anyone can bypass the browser check:

# An attacker bypasses HTML5 validation with curl:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/notes/create/ \
  -d "title=&priority=999&content=<script>alert(1)</script>"

# Browser required="required" → has no effect with curl
# priority=999 → outside the allowed range
# <script> → XSS attack

Django's server-side validation catches all of this:

form = NoteForm(request.POST)  # POST: priority=999, title=""
form.is_valid()  # → False
form.errors
# {
#   'title': ['Це поле обов'язкове.'],
#   'priority': ['Значення 999 не є допустимим вибором.']
# }
# content with <script> is safely escaped by the Django template engine

docs.title: 🌐 How does Django handle it?
docs.text: HTML5 attribute Django equivalent Where it is checked required blank=False (model) or required=True (field) Server maxlength="200" max_length=200 on a CharField Server type="email" EmailField() Server min="1" max="4" MinValueValidator(1) Server No equivalent clean_<field>() (business logic) Server only

docs.title: 5. Django Forms Internals — The Architecture on the Inside
🧠 Mental model: Field vs Widget
docs.text:
These are two independent components with different responsibilities:

CharField (field)                   TextInput (widget)
───────────────────────────         ──────────────────────────────
Responsible for:                    Responsible for:
  • Data type (str)                   • HTML rendering
  • max_length validation             • attrs (class, placeholder)
  • the required check                • <input type="text">
  • to_python() conversion            • reading the value from POST

One field → several different widgets:

# A CharField can be rendered as:
CharField(widget=TextInput)    # → <input type="text">
CharField(widget=Textarea)     # → <textarea>
CharField(widget=HiddenInput)  # → <input type="hidden">
CharField(widget=PasswordInput)# → <input type="password">

# One field — the same data type, but different HTML!

docs.title: 📚 Why are Field and Widget separated?
docs.text:
The Single Responsibility principle: the field knows about data, the widget knows about HTML. This lets you change the presentation without changing the validation logic:

class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ['title', 'content']
        widgets = {
            # We change the widget — the CharField validation stays the same!
            'content': forms.Textarea(attrs={
                'class': 'form-control',
                'rows': 8,
                'placeholder': 'Текст нотатки...',
            }),
        }

docs.title: 🌐 Error Collection — How errors are collected
docs.text:
# After form.is_valid() == False:
form.errors
# {
#   'title': ['Це поле обов'язкове.'],
#   'priority': ['Значення 5 не є допустимим вибором.'],
#   '__all__': ['Помилка між полями']  # non_field_errors
# }

# In the template:
# {{ form.title.errors }}   → errors for a specific field
# {{ form.non_field_errors }} → cross-validation errors
# {{ form.errors }}          → all errors together

docs.title: 6. ModelForms Internals — Auto-generation from the Model
🧠 Mental model: Model introspection
docs.text:
ModelForm reads the model through Meta.model and generates fields automatically:

Model Field                    →    Form Field
─────────────────────────────       ─────────────────
CharField(max_length=200)      →    CharField(max_length=200)
TextField(blank=True)          →    CharField(widget=Textarea, required=False)
PositiveSmallIntegerField(     →    TypedChoiceField(choices=...,
    choices=PRIORITY_CHOICES)           coerce=int)
ForeignKey(Notebook)           →    ModelChoiceField(queryset=Notebook.objects.all())
ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=T)  →    ModelMultipleChoiceField(queryset=Tag.objects.all())
BooleanField(default=False)    →    BooleanField(widget=CheckboxInput)

docs.title: 📚 Why does save(commit=False) exist?
docs.text:
The classic scenario: a note requires a user, but user is not in the form:

class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ['title', 'content']  # user is NOT in the form (security!)
        # If user were in the form, anyone could substitute someone else's user.id

def note_create(request):
    form = NoteForm(request.POST)
    if form.is_valid():
        # commit=False → creates the Note object in memory but does NOT write it to the DB
        note = form.save(commit=False)
        note.user = request.user  # ← add the user from the session (safe!)
        note.save()               # ← now save it to the DB
        note.tags.set(form.cleaned_data['tags'])  # M:N after save()!

docs.title: 🌐 Sequence Diagram: the full cycle POST → ModelForm → DB
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant View
    participant Form
    participant ORM

    Browser->>View: POST /notes/create/
    View->>Form: form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user)
    Form->>Form: is_valid() → validation pipeline
    Form-->>View: True — generates cleaned_data

    View->>Form: note = form.save(commit=False)
    Form-->>View: Note instance (memory only, no SQL yet)
    View->>View: note.user = request.user
    View->>ORM: note.save() → SQL INSERT
    View->>ORM: note.tags.set(...)→ INSERT into junction table
    View->>Browser: HTTP 302 Redirect → GET /notes/42/

save(commit=False) stops after the Python object has been created. The SQL INSERT happens only when you call note.save() yourself. This lets you safely add user or any other server-side data before saving.

docs.title: ❌ Common mistake
docs.text:
# ❌ M:N fields after commit=False require a separate save!
note = form.save(commit=False)
note.user = request.user
note.save()
# form.save_m2m() ← FORGOTTEN! The tags were not saved!

# ✅ Correct: always call save_m2m() after commit=False when there are M:N fields
note = form.save(commit=False)
note.user = request.user
note.save()
form.save_m2m()  # ← saves the ManyToMany fields

# Or better: through Services (as in our notes_chat_app)
note = services.create_note(
    user=request.user,
    title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
    tag_ids=[t.id for t in form.cleaned_data['tags']],
)

docs.title: 📚 The enterprise approach: django-crispy-forms
docs.text:
In large projects, crispy-forms is used instead of manual attrs:

# Without crispy: manually adding a class to every widget
# With crispy: an automatic Bootstrap layout
from crispy_forms.helper import FormHelper
from crispy_forms.layout import Layout, Row, Column, Submit

class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.helper = FormHelper()
        self.helper.form_method = 'POST'          # ← <form method="post">
        self.helper.layout = Layout(
            Row(Column('title', css_class='col-md-8'),
                Column('priority', css_class='col-md-4')),
            'content',
            Row(Column('notebook'), Column('tags')),
            Submit('submit', 'Зберегти', css_class='btn btn-primary'),
        )
        # In the template, simply: {% load crispy_forms_tags %}  {% crispy form %}
        # crispy-forms renders the whole Bootstrap grid automatically!

🧠 Mental model: 5 levels of checks
docs.text:
for field in form.fields:
    │
    ├─ 1. to_python()
    │      "2026-05-24" → datetime.date(2026, 5, 24)
    │      "abc"        → raises ValidationError("Введіть коректну дату")
    │
    ├─ 2. validate()
    │      datetime.date(2026, 5, 24) → emptiness check, BaseValidator
    │
    ├─ 3. run_validators()
    │      MinValueValidator(1)(value)
    │      MaxValueValidator(4)(value)
    │      EmailValidator()(value)    ← for EmailField
    │
    ├─ 4. clean_<fieldname>()         ← your method, if defined
    │      def clean_title(self):
    │          value = self.cleaned_data['title']
    │          if 'spam' in value.lower():
    │              raise forms.ValidationError("Спам заборонено!")
    │          return value.strip()   # ← always return the value!
    │
    └─ FIELD SUCCEEDED → cleaned_data['fieldname'] = typed_value

after all fields:
    └─ 5. clean()                     ← cross-validation between fields
           def clean(self):
               title = self.cleaned_data.get('title')
               priority = self.cleaned_data.get('priority')
               # 'is_pinned' may be missing if that field failed!
               # → always .get(), never ['key']!
               ...
               return self.cleaned_data

docs.title:
🌐 Practical example: clean_ 
class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ['title', 'content', 'priority', 'notebook', 'tags', 'is_pinned']

    def clean_title(self):
        """
        Runs after to_python() and validate().
        self.cleaned_data['title'] is already a str (not the raw string from POST).
        """
        title = self.cleaned_data['title']

        # Business rule: do not allow titles that are empty after strip()
        title = title.strip()
        if not title:
            raise forms.ValidationError("Заголовок не може бути порожнім або пробілами.")

        # Business rule: minimum length
        if len(title) < 3:
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Заголовок надто короткий (мінімум %(min)s символів).",
                code='min_length',
                params={'min': 3},
            )

        return title  # ← ALWAYS return the value!

    def clean(self):
        """
        Cross-validation: runs after clean_<field> for all fields.
        Fields that failed validation → are missing from cleaned_data!
        So always use .get(), never []
        """
        cleaned = super().clean()  # ← runs the parent clean()

        priority = cleaned.get('priority')
        is_pinned = cleaned.get('is_pinned')

        # Only high-priority notes can be pinned
        if is_pinned and priority and priority < Note.PRIORITY_HIGH:
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Закріплювати можна лише нотатки з пріоритетом 'Високий' або 'Терміново'.",
                code='pin_priority_mismatch',
            )

        return cleaned

❌ Common mistake in clean() 
def clean(self):
    # ❌ UNSAFE: KeyError if the field failed validation!
    priority = self.cleaned_data['priority']    # → KeyError if priority is invalid!
    is_pinned = self.cleaned_data['is_pinned']  # → KeyError!

    # ✅ CORRECT: always .get()
    priority = self.cleaned_data.get('priority')   # → None if missing
    is_pinned = self.cleaned_data.get('is_pinned') # → None if missing
    if priority is None or is_pinned is None:
        return self.cleaned_data  # one of the fields already has an error, skip

🧠 Mental model: a map of unsafe zones 
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ UNSAFE ZONE — never trust this data                              │
│                                                                  │
│   request.POST                  request.GET                      │
│   request.FILES                 request.META                     │
│   request.COOKIES               URL kwargs (pk=... can be too!) │
│   (everything from the network is strings)                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                    [Django Form]
                    is_valid() = True
                          │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SAFE ZONE — cleaned, typed Python objects                        │
│                                                                  │
│   form.cleaned_data['title']    → str (stripped, validated)     │
│   form.cleaned_data['priority'] → int (1–4, guaranteed)         │
│   form.cleaned_data['tags']     → QuerySet[Tag] (valid objects) │
│   form.cleaned_data['notebook'] → Notebook | None               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📚 add_error() — adding errors programmatically 
def clean(self):
    cleaned = super().clean()
    title = cleaned.get('title', '')

    # Check the DB: does this user already have a note with this title?
    # IMPORTANT: self.instance.pk — for edit forms we skip the current object
    if Note.objects.filter(
        user=self.user,
        title__iexact=title
    ).exclude(pk=getattr(self.instance, 'pk', None)).exists():
        # Add the error to a specific field (not non_field_errors)
        self.add_error('title', 'У вас вже є нотатка з таким заголовком.')

    return cleaned

🧠 Mental model: two rendering directions 
GET request (empty form or an instance):
    NoteForm(instance=note) → initial values → HTML with the current data

POST request with errors:
    NoteForm(request.POST) → form.errors → HTML with errors + the entered data
    (Django restores the entered values automatically!)

🧠 Mental model: a CSRF attack 
Attack scenario without CSRF protection:

  1. Alice is logged in to bank.com (she has a session cookie)
  2. Alice visits evil.com
  3. evil.com contains:
     <form action="http://bank.com/transfer" method="post">
       <input type="hidden" name="to" value="hacker">
       <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="10000">
     </form>
     <script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
  4. Alice's browser automatically sends a POST request to bank.com
     (with cookies! — the browser always attaches the domain's cookies)
  5. bank.com thinks this is Alice and transfers the money!

Django protection:
  1. When {% csrf_token %} is rendered, Django issues a secret in the csrftoken cookie
     (by default it lives in a cookie; in the session only with CSRF_USE_SESSIONS = True)
  2. The same secret (in masked form) goes into the form as a hidden field
  3. On POST Django checks: does the token from POST match the secret from the cookie?
  4. evil.com does not know the token (Same-Origin Policy) → 403 Forbidden!

  ⚠️ CsrfViewMiddleware checks only "unsafe" methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
     It won't stop a GET attack like <img src="http://bank.com/transfer?...">,
     so a GET must never change data.

❌ Myth 1: "request.POST is safe" 
# ❌ CHANGE THIS: request.POST is NEVER safe!
Note.objects.create(
    title=request.POST["title"],     # what if title = "DROP TABLE notes;"?
    priority=request.POST["priority"] # what if priority = "hacked"?
)

# ✅ RULE: always through a form → cleaned_data
form = NoteForm(request.POST)
if form.is_valid():
    # Now cleaned_data['title'] = str (max 200 chars, validated)
    # cleaned_data['priority'] = int (1-4, guaranteed by choices)
    services.create_note(user=request.user, **form.cleaned_data)

❌ Myth 2: "Client-side validation is enough" 
Client-side (browser):  required, maxlength, type=email  → easy to bypass
Server-side (Django):   ValidationError, clean(), is_valid() → mandatory!

Rule: client-side validation = a UX improvement.
      Server-side validation = security and data integrity.

❌ Myth 4: "cleaned_data always exists" 
# ❌ cleaned_data does not exist before is_valid() is called!
form = NoteForm(request.POST)
title = form.cleaned_data['title']  # AttributeError: 'NoteForm' has no attribute 'cleaned_data'

# ✅ Always check is_valid() before cleaned_data
form = NoteForm(request.POST)
if form.is_valid():
    title = form.cleaned_data['title']  # OK!

🌐 Empty POST (a missing field) 
# POST: {'content': 'Текст'}  # title is missing entirely!
form = NoteForm({'content': 'Текст'})
form.is_valid()  # → False
form.errors
# {'title': ['Це поле обов'язкове.']}
# A missing field = the same as an empty one for required=True fields
14. Debugging Intuition — How to Debug Forms

HTML ↔ Django ↔ ORM (a two-way bridge)

    subgraph Frontend["Browser Domain"]
        HTML_Form["HTML Form<br>Raw Text Input"]
    end

    subgraph Backend["Django Form Domain — Trust Boundary"]
        Widget["Widget<br>HTML generation"]
        Field["Form Field<br>Type coercion & Validation"]
        CleanedData["cleaned_data<br>Safe Python Objects"]
    end

    subgraph Database["ORM Domain"]
        Model["Django Model<br>DB Table mapping"]
    end

    HTML_Form -- POST Data --> Field
    Field --> CleanedData
    CleanedData -- "form.save() / services.create()" --> Model
    Model -- Initial Data --> Field
    Field --> Widget
    Widget -- Render HTML --> HTML_Form

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;

📚 Where forms are used in production    Area Example Why forms are critical     CMS A WordPress-like article editor Complex content + media files + M:N tags   Auth Login/Registration Password hashing, unique email check   E-commerce Checkout Cross-validation: address + payment + coupon   API DRF Serializer (= a Form for JSON) Validating incoming JSON data   Admin panel Django Admin A ModelForm for every model   Import CSV/Excel import Batch validation without HTTP

🌐 ModelForm + transaction.atomic() + M:N

The most complex real-world scenario is a form with Many-to-Many inside a transaction:

# services.py (our approach in notes_chat_app)
def create_note(*, user, title, content='', notebook=None, priority=1, tag_ids=None):
    """
    An atomic operation: note + M:N tags in a single transaction.
    If note.tags.set() fails → note.objects.create() is rolled back too!
    """
    with transaction.atomic():
        note = Note.objects.create(
            user=user, title=title, content=content,
            notebook=notebook, priority=priority
        )
        if tag_ids:
            # Check that the tags belong to this particular user!
            valid_tags = Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids, user=user)
            note.tags.set(valid_tags)  # INSERT into the junction table
    return note

# views.py — the view is thin, HTTP only
def note_create(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user)
        if form.is_valid():
            tags = form.cleaned_data.get('tags', [])
            note = services.create_note(
                user=request.user,
                title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
                content=form.cleaned_data.get('content', ''),
                priority=form.cleaned_data.get('priority', 1),
                notebook=form.cleaned_data.get('notebook'),
                tag_ids=[t.id for t in tags],
            )
            messages.success(request, f'Нотатку "{note.title}" створено!')
            return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)
    else:
        form = NoteForm(user=request.user)
    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_form.html', {'form': form})
Self-check
docs.text:
Predict the result before running it:

# 1. What will form.is_valid() return?
form = NoteForm({'title': '', 'priority': '999'})
# → ___?

# 2. Where will the error be?
form.errors
# → ___?

# 3. What will this code print?
form2 = NoteForm({'title': 'Нотатка', 'priority': '2'}, user=some_user)
if form2.is_valid():
    print(type(form2.cleaned_data['priority']))
# → ___?

# 4. What will happen?
form3 = NoteForm({'title': 'Test'})
print(form3.cleaned_data)  # before is_valid()!
# → ___?
Answers 1. `False` — title is empty (required), priority=999 is not in the choices 2. `{'title': ['Це поле обов\'язкове.'], 'priority': ['Значення 999 не є допустимим вибором.']}` 3. `` — cleaned_data['priority'] is a Python int, not a str! 4. `AttributeError` — cleaned_data does not exist before is_valid() is called

Key takeaway: A Django form is not just HTML markup. It is an architectural boundary between the unsafe HTTP space and the safe ORM space. Every byte that passes through is_valid() → cleaned_data is typed, validated, and safe to write to the database.

docs.text:
Three-level template inheritance in Notes Chat App:

templates/base.html
  ← templates/layouts/dashboard.html
      ← notes_app/templates/notes_app/note_list.html

# base.html: DOCTYPE, head, navbar, messages, {% block content %}
# dashboard.html: {% extends 'base.html' %} + sidebar, content block
# note_list.html: {% extends 'layouts/dashboard.html' %} + the specific content

DTL syntax:

{# Variable #}
{{ note.title }}
{{ note.title|truncatechars:50 }}
{{ note.created_at|date:"d M Y" }}

{# Control flow #}
{% if note.is_pinned %}📌{% endif %}
{% for note in notes %}{{ note.title }}{% empty %}Нотаток немає{% endfor %}

{# Template inheritance #}
{% extends 'layouts/dashboard.html' %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ note.title }}</h1>
{% endblock %}

{# Include partial #}
{% include 'notes_app/_note_card.html' with note=note %}

{# URL reverse #}
<a href="{% url 'notes_app:note_edit' note.pk %}">Редагувати</a>

Static files:

{% load static %}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'notes_app/css/style.css' %}">
<script src="{% static 'notes_app/js/group_chat.js' %}"></script>

STATIC_URL  = '/static/'

STATICFILES_DIRS = [BASE_DIR / 'notes_app' / 'static']  # dev

  • 8. Self-check questions
  • 🧠 Mental model: Context Processors are "global variables" for templates. Imagine there is data that EVERY template in your project needs — the site name, the number of notifications, the current user. Without context processors you have to pass this data manually in every view. Context processors automatically "inject" this data into every template, as if it had always been there.
  • 📚 Why it exists: Django deliberately separates logic (views) from presentation (templates). Context processors are the official mechanism for passing "ambient" data (data from the surrounding environment) into templates without wiring up every view manually.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: On every call to render(request, template, context) Django collects all registered context processors, calls each of them with request, gets a dict from each one, and then MERGES all of these dicts together with the context you passed from the view. Only after that is the template rendered with the combined context.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Forgetting to register a custom context processor in settings.py → the variable in the template is simply empty, with no errors. Even worse — running a heavy DB query in a context processor without caching. It runs on EVERY HTTP request.

docs.title: §1. Context Processors — Global Context
docs.text:
Context processors solve the classic DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) problem in Django views. First, let's look at what happens WITHOUT them — and why that is bad.

Imagine that every view has to manually collect the data that every template needs:

# ❌ Without context processors: every view has to do this:
def notes_view(request):
    return render(request, 'notes.html', {
        'user': request.user,
        'site_name': settings.SITE_NAME,
        'notifications_count': Notification.objects.filter(user=request.user).count(),
        # ... every view has to repeat this
    })

def dashboard_view(request):
    return render(request, 'dashboard.html', {
        'user': request.user,           # ← a copy
        'site_name': settings.SITE_NAME, # ← a copy
        'notifications_count': ...,      # ← a copy
    })

Context processors solve this: they run ONCE per request and automatically add the data to EVERY template. Here is what the call chain looks like:

Request arrives
     ↓
Django calls each context processor in CONTEXT_PROCESSORS list
     ↓
Each processor returns a dict
     ↓
All dicts are MERGED into the template context
     ↓
Template renders with merged context

Notice: the built-in django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth adds {{ user }} and {{ perms }} to EVERY template — that is exactly why you can use {{ user.username }} in any template without adding it in every view.

docs.title: The problem without Context Processors
docs.text:
Below is a concrete demonstration of the problem: two ordinary views that are forced to repeat the same context-collecting code:

# ❌ Repeating ourselves in every view
def notes_list(request):
    return render(request, 'notes/list.html', {
        'user': request.user,
        'site_name': 'MyApp',
        'unread_count': Notification.objects.filter(user=request.user, read=False).count(),
    })

def notes_detail(request, pk):
    return render(request, 'notes/detail.html', {
        'user': request.user,           # ← again
        'site_name': 'MyApp',           # ← again
        'unread_count': ...,            # ← again
    })

docs.title: Built-in Context Processors
docs.text:
Django ships with a set of built-in context processors. These lines in settings.py define which of them are active. Each processor is a Python function that takes request and returns a dict:

# settings.py — TEMPLATES → OPTIONS → context_processors
'context_processors': [
    'django.template.context_processors.debug',      # {{ debug }}
    'django.template.context_processors.request',    # {{ request }}
    'django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth',   # {{ user }}, {{ perms }}
    'django.contrib.messages.context_processors.messages',  # {{ messages }}
],
Processor What it adds to the context When to use it debug {{ debug }} — True/False Conditionally showing debug blocks request {{ request.user }}, {{ request.path }} A navbar with the current URL, breadcrumbs auth {{ user }}, {{ perms.app.permission }} Auth checks in templates messages {% for msg in messages %} Django Messages → Bootstrap Alert

docs.title: A custom Context Processor
docs.text:
Here we write our own context processor. Notice its structure: it is an ordinary Python function that takes request and returns a dict. Django itself takes care of calling this function and merging the result into the template context:

# notes_app/context_processors.py

from .models import Notification

def global_context(request):
    """Data for all of the app's templates."""
    context = {
        'site_name': 'Bootstrap Notes',
        'site_version': '2.0',
    }

    # Only for authenticated users
    if request.user.is_authenticated:
        context['unread_notifications'] = (
            Notification.objects
            .filter(user=request.user, read=False)
            .count()
        )

    return context

After writing the function, you have to register it in settings.py. Django does not "find" context processors automatically — each one must be added manually:

# settings.py — registration
'context_processors': [
    ...
    'notes_app.context_processors.global_context',  # ← add this
],

After registration, the unread_notifications variable becomes available in ANY template of the project — without a single line of code in the view:

{# base.html — now available everywhere without passing it from the view #}
<span class="badge bg-danger">{{ unread_notifications }}</span>

docs.title: The Context Processor call chain
docs.text:
This diagram shows the exact order in which Django assembles the context before rendering a template. Important: the view context OVERRIDES identical keys from context processors — the view always takes priority:

RequestFactory
    ↓ request
    ↓
Context Processors (all are called for every render())
    ↓ merged dict
    ↓
View context (overrides identical keys)
    ↓
Template Engine

Rule: A Context Processor must not run heavy queries without caching. It runs for every HTTP request.

docs.title: Caching in a Context Processor
docs.text:
This is a critically important pattern for production. Because a context processor runs on EVERY request, a DB query in it without caching can cause hundreds of unnecessary queries per second. Here is the correct approach with a Redis/Memcached cache via the Django cache framework:

from django.core.cache import cache

def global_context(request):
    if request.user.is_authenticated:
        cache_key = f'unread_count_{request.user.pk}'
        count = cache.get(cache_key)
        if count is None:
            count = Notification.objects.filter(
                user=request.user, read=False
            ).count()
            cache.set(cache_key, count, timeout=60)  # 1 minute
        return {'unread_notifications': count}
    return {}
  • 🧠 Mental model: Custom Template Tags are Python functions you can call DIRECTLY FROM TEMPLATES. The Django Template Language (DTL) is deliberately limited: you cannot call arbitrary Python functions in a template. Custom tags are the official "safe bridge" between a template and Python logic.
  • 📚 Why it exists: Separation of concerns: templates are responsible for display, Python for logic. But sometimes you need "light logic" right at render time (formatting a Badge, checking permissions, counting). Custom tags provide this safely, without breaking the architecture.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: {% load hello_tags %} makes Django find the hello_tags.py module in any templatetags/ folder of the installed apps. Django AUTO-DISCOVERS templatetags/ folders — if an app is in INSTALLED_APPS, Django scans its templatetags/. register = template.Library() registers functions as tags. During rendering Django calls the registered Python function and substitutes the result into the HTML.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Forgetting {% load hello_tags %} at the top of the template — the tag simply will not work. Or running a DB query in a simple_tag that is called in a loop over 100 items — a classic source of N+1.

docs.title: Why Custom Tags?
docs.text:
DTL is deliberately limited — no function calls, no complex logic. Custom Tags let you extend DTL safely: logic in Python, presentation in the template.

The Django Template Language does not allow {{ Note.objects.count() }} — it is a syntax error. But what if you need to show the number of notes in the sidebar? Custom tags are the answer.

There are three types of custom tags, each for its own job:

simple_tag   → Python function → returns a VALUE (number, string)
inclusion_tag → Python function → returns a CONTEXT → renders a TEMPLATE
filter       → Python function → transforms a VALUE → returns the transformed VALUE

The templatetags/ folder name is mandatory. Django automatically finds templatetags/ folders in all installed apps. __init__.py makes the folder a Python package:

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
notes_app/
├── templatetags/          ← mandatory directory name
│   ├── __init__.py        ← empty file
│   └── hello_tags.py      ← your tags

register = template.Library() is the tag registry. The decorators @register.simple_tag, @register.inclusion_tag, @register.filter register Python functions as DTL tags:

# notes_app/templatetags/hello_tags.py
from django import template
from django.utils.html import format_html
from notes_app.models import Note

register = template.Library()
  • 🧠 Mental model: simple_tag = function → value. Think of it as {{ variable }}, except the value is computed by a Python function at render time instead of being passed from the view.
  • 📚 Why it exists: Sometimes a value depends on template parameters or needs a light computation. For example: {% multiply price quantity %} is clearer and safer than passing precomputed data from every view.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: When it meets {% multiply 6 7 %}, Django parses the arguments, finds the registered multiply function, calls multiply(6, 7) and substitutes the returned value into the HTML. takes_context=True passes the whole current template context as the first argument — that is how you can get request, user and everything else.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Running a DB query in a simple_tag that is called inside a loop {% for note in notes %}{% notes_count request.user %}{% endfor %} — that is 100+ DB queries instead of one. Always count how many times a tag is called.

docs.title: simple_tag — returns a value
docs.text:
simple_tag is the simplest type. The function takes arguments and returns a value that is substituted into the HTML. takes_context=True gives access to the whole template context, including request:

@register.simple_tag
def multiply(a, b):
    return a * b

@register.simple_tag(takes_context=True)
def current_user_name(context):
    user = context['request'].user
    return user.get_full_name() or user.username

@register.simple_tag
def notes_count(user=None):
    qs = Note.objects.all()
    if user:
        qs = qs.filter(author=user)
    return qs.count()

Note the call syntax: {% tag_name arg1 arg2 %}. The as my_count construct stores the result in a context variable instead of outputting it — that way you can use the value several times:

{% load hello_tags %}

{# Basic call #}
{% multiply 6 7 %}           {# → 42 #}

{# Store in a variable #}
{% notes_count request.user as my_count %}
<span>Твоїх нотаток: {{ my_count }}</span>

{# With context #}
{% current_user_name %}      {# → "Victor Nikoriak" #}
  • 🧠 Mental model: inclusion_tag = a mini-view inside a template. The function returns a CONTEXT (dict), and Django renders a separate HTML template with that context and inserts the result into the current template. This is the closest thing to a "component system" in DTL.
  • 📚 Why it exists: For reusable UI components that have their own logic. For example: a notification badge is needed in the navbar of every page, but it has its own logic (counting, checking authentication). Moving this logic into every view breaks DRY.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: @register.inclusion_tag('partial.html', takes_context=True) tells Django: "call this function, get a dict, render partial.html with that dict as the context, and insert the resulting HTML into the parent template".
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Passing the parent template's full context (return context) instead of a minimal context for the sub-template. This can lead to unexpected variables and hard debugging.

docs.title: inclusion_tag — renders a sub-template
docs.text:
inclusion_tag returns a dict that becomes the context for a separate HTML template. It is a powerful mechanism for reusable components: badge, avatar, breadcrumbs, navigation. Real use cases: a notification badge in the navbar, a user avatar with a name, breadcrumb navigation:

@register.inclusion_tag('notes_app/partials/notification_badge.html',
                         takes_context=True)
def notification_badge(context):
    request = context['request']
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:
        return {'count': 0}

    count = Notification.objects.filter(
        user=request.user, read=False
    ).count()
    return {'count': count, 'user': request.user}

This template is rendered SEPARATELY from the parent one, with its own context. It knows nothing about the parent template — only about what the function returned:

{# notes_app/partials/notification_badge.html #}
{% if count %}
<a href="{% url 'notifications' %}" class="btn position-relative">
    <i class="bi bi-bell"></i>
    <span class="position-absolute top-0 start-100 translate-middle
                 badge rounded-pill bg-danger">
        {{ count }}
    </span>
</a>
{% endif %}

Calling the tag in a template looks like any other tag. Django itself finds the Python function, calls it, renders the sub-template and puts the result in place of the tag:

{# base.html — usage #}
{% load hello_tags %}
<nav class="navbar navbar-dark bg-dark">
    ...
    {% notification_badge %}   {# ← inserts notification_badge.html #}
</nav>
  • 🧠 Mental model: filter = transforming a value in a pipeline. {{ value|my_filter:arg }} reads as "take value, pass it through my_filter with the argument arg, output the result". It is a Unix pipe for template values.
  • 📚 Why it exists: For transformations closely tied to presentation (formatting a date, shortening text, converting a status into a color). Filters are the "vocabulary" of your templates.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: Django auto-escapes all template output to protect against XSS. format_html() is the CORRECT way to build HTML strings in Python: it escapes the variables (XSS protection) but preserves your HTML structure. NEVER use string concatenation or mark_safe for user-provided content — that is an XSS vulnerability.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Writing return f'<span class="badge bg-{color}">{status}</span>' instead of format_html(...). If status contains <script>alert('XSS')</script>, the first version will execute the script in the browser. format_html automatically escapes all variables.

docs.title: filter — transforming a value
docs.text:
Django automatically escapes all template output to protect against XSS. format_html is the CORRECT way to build HTML strings in Python: it escapes variables but preserves your HTML structure. NEVER use string concatenation or mark_safe for user-provided content — that is an XSS vulnerability.

The first filter, truncate_words, is safe: it returns plain text without HTML. The second, status_badge, returns HTML, so format_html is mandatory:

@register.filter(name='truncate_words')
def truncate_words(value, num_words):
    words = str(value).split()
    if len(words) <= num_words:
        return value
    return ' '.join(words[:num_words]) + '...'

@register.filter
def status_badge(status):
    """Note status → Bootstrap badge HTML."""
    colors = {
        'draft': 'secondary',
        'published': 'success',
        'archived': 'warning',
    }
    color = colors.get(status, 'primary')
    return format_html(
        '<span class="badge bg-{}">{}</span>',
        color,
        status.capitalize()
    )

Filter syntax in a template: {{ value|filter_name:argument }}. Filters can be chained: {{ value|filter1|filter2:arg }}:

{% load hello_tags %}

{{ note.body|truncate_words:20 }}
{{ note.status|status_badge }}

docs.title: Comparing Template Tag types
docs.text:
Type Syntax in the template Returns When to use it simple_tag {% my_tag arg %} A value Computations, DB queries inclusion_tag {% my_tag %} Renders HTML Reusable components (badge, card) filter {{ value\|my_filter }} A transformed value Formatting strings, colors block tag {% my_tag %}...{% end_my_tag %} An HTML block Complex wrappers (permission check, cache)
  • 🧠 Mental model: crispy-forms = Django forms + Bootstrap/Tailwind styling, through a Pythonic Layout API instead of HTML templates. Think of it this way: instead of writing Bootstrap HTML by hand for every form field, you describe the form's STRUCTURE in Python, and crispy-forms generates the Bootstrap HTML automatically.
  • 📚 Why it exists: Django forms generate minimal HTML (<input>, <label>) without Bootstrap classes. For every Bootstrap field you would have to write <div class="mb-3"><label class="form-label">...</label><input class="form-control">.... crispy-forms automates this boilerplate and lets you describe the form layout in Python.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: FormHelper does not change the form's validation — it ONLY changes how it is rendered to HTML. Layout is a tree of Python objects describing the structure: Row(Column('field1'), Column('field2')) = a Bootstrap 2-column layout. During rendering crispy-forms walks this tree and generates the matching Bootstrap HTML for each node.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Thinking that crispy-forms affects the form's validation or behavior. It ONLY affects how the HTML looks. Also: using {{ form.as_p }} and {{ form|crispy }} at the same time — pick one approach.

docs.title: §3. crispy-forms — Python Form Layouts
docs.text: Here is a concrete demonstration of the problem: the HTML you have to write BY HAND for every Bootstrap form without crispy-forms. Notice how many lines it takes for just a few fields:

docs.title: The problem with plain Django forms
docs.text:
{# ❌ The template is overloaded with form HTML logic #}
<form method="post">
    {% csrf_token %}
    {% for field in form %}
        <div class="mb-3">
            <label for="{{ field.id_for_label }}" class="form-label">
                {{ field.label }}
                {% if field.field.required %}<span class="text-danger">*</span>{% endif %}
            </label>
            {{ field }}
            {% if field.errors %}
                {% for error in field.errors %}
                    <div class="invalid-feedback d-block">{{ error }}</div>
                {% endfor %}
            {% endif %}
        </div>
    {% endfor %}
    <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Зберегти</button>
</form>

docs.title: crispy-forms + crispy-bootstrap5
docs.text:
Installing two packages: django-crispy-forms is the main package, crispy-bootstrap5 is the template pack for Bootstrap 5. They are separate so that different CSS frameworks can be supported (Tailwind, Bootstrap 4/5):

pip install django-crispy-forms crispy-bootstrap5

CRISPY_TEMPLATE_PACK tells crispy-forms which HTML to generate. For Bootstrap 5 it knows the right classes, structure and attributes:

# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'crispy_forms',
    'crispy_bootstrap5',
]

CRISPY_ALLOWED_TEMPLATE_PACKS = "bootstrap5"
CRISPY_TEMPLATE_PACK = "bootstrap5"

docs.title: Option 1 — quick (template tag)
docs.text:
The simplest option: the |crispy filter turns an ordinary Django form into Bootstrap-styled HTML automatically. This is the "quick start mode" — zero configuration:

{% load crispy_forms_tags %}

<form method="post">
    {% csrf_token %}
    {{ form|crispy }}
    <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Зберегти</button>
</form>

docs.title: Option 2 — FormHelper (a Python layout)
docs.text:
FormHelper is defined right inside the form class — this matters. The layout logic lives in the same place as the form instead of being scattered across templates. Layout is a Python tree that describes the structure: Fieldset → Row → Column → fields. {% crispy form %} renders the whole <form> tag, including action, method and id from the FormHelper:

# notes_app/forms.py
from django import forms
from crispy_forms.helper import FormHelper
from crispy_forms.layout import (
    Layout, Submit, Row, Column, Fieldset, HTML, Div
)
from .models import Note

class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ['title', 'body', 'category', 'tags', 'is_public']

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.helper = FormHelper()
        self.helper.form_method = 'post'
        self.helper.form_id = 'note-form'

        self.helper.layout = Layout(
            Fieldset(
                'Основна інформація',
                'title',
                Row(
                    Column('category', css_class='col-md-6'),
                    Column('tags', css_class='col-md-6'),
                ),
            ),
            Fieldset(
                'Зміст',
                'body',
            ),
            Div(
                'is_public',
                css_class='form-check mb-3',
            ),
            HTML("""
                <hr>
                <p class="text-muted">
                    <i class="bi bi-info-circle"></i>
                    Публічні нотатки видні всім користувачам.
                </p>
            """),
            Submit('submit', 'Зберегти нотатку', css_class='btn btn-primary'),
        )

{% crispy form %} is all you need in the template. All the Bootstrap HTML is generated automatically from the FormHelper and Layout defined in the form class:

{% load crispy_forms_tags %}

{% crispy form %}   {# ← renders the whole form from the helper, including the <form> tag #}

docs.title: FormHelper attributes
docs.text:
A complete reference of FormHelper attributes. form_tag = False is useful when you need to wrap the form in your own <form> tag (for example, for HTMX or multi-step forms). error_text_inline = True shows errors next to the field rather than at the top of the form:

helper = FormHelper()

helper.form_method = 'post'           # GET or POST
helper.form_action = '/notes/create/' # action=""
helper.form_id = 'my-form'
helper.form_class = 'needs-validation' # Bootstrap validation class
helper.attrs = {'novalidate': ''}     # HTML attributes

helper.form_tag = False               # Do not render the <form> tag
helper.include_media = True           # Include {{ form.media }}
helper.error_text_inline = True       # Errors next to the field
helper.label_class = 'fw-bold'        # CSS for all labels
helper.field_class = 'col-lg-10'      # CSS for all fields

docs.title: Layout elements
docs.text:
These classes are the building blocks of a Layout. Row/Column generate a Bootstrap grid. Field lets you add HTML attributes to a specific field. HTML inserts arbitrary HTML unchanged — useful for separators, hints, icons:

from crispy_forms.layout import (
    Layout,      # Root container
    Div,         # <div css_class="">
    Row,         # Bootstrap Row
    Column,      # Bootstrap Column
    Fieldset,    # <fieldset><legend>title</legend>...</fieldset>
    HTML,        # An arbitrary HTML string
    Field,       # A field with custom attributes
    Submit,      # <button type="submit">
    Reset,       # <button type="reset">
    Hidden,      # <input type="hidden">
    MultiField,  # Several fields on one line
)

# Field with attributes
Layout(
    Field('title', placeholder='Введіть назву', autofocus=True),
    Field('body', rows=5, css_class='font-monospace'),
)
  • 🧠 Mental model: Vite is a "build system" for frontend assets. It takes your SOURCE files (TypeScript, SCSS, ES modules) and produces OPTIMIZED output files for production. Think of it as python manage.py collectstatic, but for JavaScript and CSS — only far more powerful.
  • 📚 Why it exists: A modern frontend cannot simply be "wired together" with <script> tags. SCSS has to be compiled to CSS. TypeScript to JavaScript. ES modules have to be bundled. Files have to be minified and "content-hashed" for cache busting. Vite solves all of these tasks together.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: Development: Vite runs a dev server on port 5173 with Hot Module Replacement (HMR) — a CSS change updates the browser WITHOUT a reload. Production: npm run build generates a dist/ folder with manifest.json. The manifest contains a mapping: {"src/main.js": {"file": "assets/main-a4b3c2.js"}}. Django reads this manifest, and {% vite_asset 'src/main.js' %} turns it into the correct URL with the hash.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Running npm run build in development instead of npm run dev. Or forgetting to add static_dist/ to STATICFILES_DIRS in settings.py — Django will not know where to look for the Vite output.

docs.title: §4. Vite + ManifestStaticFilesStorage — A Modern Asset Pipeline
docs.text:
Why not just {% load static %} and link the files directly? Here is why: - Modern CSS: Sass/SCSS has to be compiled into plain CSS - Modern JS: TypeScript has to be compiled, ES modules have to be bundled - Production optimization: minification, code splitting, content hashing (cache busting)

The asset pipeline looks like this:

Development:
  Vite dev server on port 5173
  Hot Module Replacement (HMR): CSS change → browser updates instantly (no reload!)
  Django templates → {% vite_asset 'main.js' %} → URL of the Vite dev server

Production:
  npm run build → generates the dist/ folder
  dist/manifest.json: { "main.js": "assets/main-a4b3c2.js" }
  python manage.py collectstatic → copies dist/ into STATIC_ROOT
  Django templates → {% vite_asset 'main.js' %} → /static/assets/main-a4b3c2.js

Content hashing = cache busting: main-a4b3c2.js contains a hash of the file's contents. If you change the file, the hash changes and the browser downloads a fresh copy. If the file has not changed, the browser uses the cached version.

docs.title: Why Vite instead of webpack?
docs.text: webpack Vite Cold start ~30-60 sec <1 sec (ESM native) HMR Full recompilation Targeted update Production build Good Good (Rollup) Django integration django-webpack-loader django-vite

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
Note the separation: frontend/ contains all the JavaScript/CSS source code and npm dependencies. static_dist/ is the Vite output; it ends up in Git only if there is no CI/CD. In production this folder is generated by a Docker build stage:

django_bootstrap_project/
├── frontend/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── vite.config.js
│   └── src/
│       ├── main.js           ← entry point
│       ├── main.scss         ← Bootstrap + custom CSS
│       └── components/       ← JS components
├── notes_app/
│   └── static/               ← Django static (legacy)
├── static_dist/              ← Vite output (collectstatic source)
└── manage.py

docs.title: vite.config.js
docs.text:
base: '/static/' is critical! Vite uses this path to generate URLs in the HTML. It must match Django's STATIC_URL. manifest: true generates manifest.json; without it Django will not know the real names of the hashed files:

// frontend/vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { resolve } from 'path'

export default defineConfig({
    base: '/static/',          // Django STATIC_URL

    build: {
        outDir: '../static_dist',
        manifest: true,        // ← generates manifest.json (needed by Django)
        rollupOptions: {
            input: {
                main: resolve(__dirname, 'src/main.js'),
            }
        }
    },

    server: {
        origin: 'http://localhost:5173',  // Vite dev server
        port: 5173,
    }
})

docs.title: main.js — Bootstrap via npm
docs.text:
Instead of a Bootstrap CDN, we now use npm. The benefit: tree-shaking — we import only the Bootstrap components we actually use, not the whole of Bootstrap. This reduces the size of the final bundle:

// frontend/src/main.js

// Bootstrap JS (selectively — only what is needed)
import { Modal, Toast, Tooltip } from 'bootstrap'

// Bootstrap CSS via SCSS
import './main.scss'

// Your components
import './components/search'
import './components/delete-confirm'

// Initialize Tooltips
document.querySelectorAll('[data-bs-toggle="tooltip"]').forEach(el => {
    new Tooltip(el)
})

:root CSS variables defined BEFORE @import 'bootstrap' override the Bootstrap defaults — this is the official way to brand Bootstrap without forking it:

// frontend/src/main.scss

// Custom CSS variables BEFORE Bootstrap
:root {
    --bs-primary: #2563eb;      // Overriding a Bootstrap color
    --bs-border-radius: 0.5rem;
}

// You can include Bootstrap modules selectively
@import 'bootstrap/scss/bootstrap';

// Your styles
.note-card {
    transition: transform .2s ease;
    &:hover {
        transform: translateY(-4px);
    }
}

docs.title: settings.py — ManifestStaticFilesStorage
docs.text:
ManifestStaticFilesStorage reads staticfiles.json (the equivalent of Vite's manifest.json, but for Django) and automatically turns {% static 'main.js' %} → /static/main.abc123.js. This happens during collectstatic:

# settings.py

STATIC_URL = '/static/'
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles'  # collectstatic destination

# Vite build output — Django looks here
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / 'static_dist',
]

# Production: files with a hash (main.abc123.js)
# Django 4.2+: the STORAGES setting (STATICFILES_STORAGE was removed in Django 5.1)
STORAGES = {
    'default': {'BACKEND': 'django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage'},
    'staticfiles': {'BACKEND': 'django.contrib.staticfiles.storage.ManifestStaticFilesStorage'},
}
# → generates staticfiles.json with the mapping main.js → main.abc123.js
# → {% static 'main.js' %} → /static/main.abc123.js

docs.title: django-vite integration (dev mode)
docs.text:
django-vite provides seamless switching between dev and production modes. In dev it connects to the Vite HMR server (live updates). In production it reads manifest.json and generates the correct hashed URLs. DJANGO_VITE_DEV_MODE = DEBUG switches automatically:

pip install django-vite

# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = ['django_vite', ...]

DJANGO_VITE_ASSETS_PATH = BASE_DIR / 'static_dist'
DJANGO_VITE_DEV_MODE = DEBUG  # True in dev, False in prod
DJANGO_VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL = 'http://localhost:5173'

{% vite_hmr_client %} inserts the Vite HMR client script — it enables Hot Module Replacement. {% vite_asset 'src/main.js' %} generates a URL to the Vite server in dev, and a hashed URL to the built file in prod:

{# base.html #}
{% load django_vite %}

<head>
    {% if debug %}
        {# Dev: connect via the Vite dev server with HMR #}
        {% vite_hmr_client %}
        {% vite_asset 'src/main.js' %}
    {% else %}
        {# Production: Vite manifest → hashed files #}
        {% vite_asset 'src/main.js' %}
    {% endif %}
</head>

docs.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile with Vite
docs.text:
A multi-stage build is a key pattern for production. Stage 1 (Node.js) builds the frontend assets. Stage 2 (Python) builds Django. COPY --from=frontend-builder copies only the Vite output between stages — the Node.js modules (hundreds of MB) do not end up in the final image:

# Dockerfile

# Stage 1: Build frontend assets
FROM node:20-alpine AS frontend-builder
WORKDIR /frontend
COPY frontend/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY frontend/ .
RUN npm run build   # → ../static_dist/

# Stage 2: Django production image
FROM python:3.12-slim AS django
WORKDIR /app

# Python dependencies
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Django project
COPY . .

# Copy Vite output from frontend-builder
COPY --from=frontend-builder /static_dist/ ./static_dist/

# collectstatic
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "notes_chat_app.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

docs.title: Production asset pipeline
docs.text:
This diagram shows the full path from source code to the browser: dev mode (directly via Vite HMR) and production mode (via hashed files on nginx):

Frontend Dev                    Production
─────────────                   ─────────────
npm run dev                     npm run build
    ↓                               ↓
Vite HMR server             static_dist/
(port 5173)                     ├── main.abc123.js
    ↓                           ├── main.def456.css
Browser JS modules              └── manifest.json
(no bundling)                       ↓
                            python manage.py collectstatic
                                    ↓
                            staticfiles/
                                    ↓
                            nginx /static/ → hash files
  • 🧠 Mental model: The SaaS Dashboard architecture is a 3-level template inheritance tree. base.html (the HTML skeleton) → layouts/dashboard.html (sidebar + topbar) → notes/list.html (the page content). Each level adds its own layer without repeating the parent.
  • 📚 Why it exists: So that changing ONE line propagates to ALL pages. Changing the sidebar: you edit layouts/dashboard.html once — every dashboard page is updated. Changing the HTML skeleton: you edit base.html — the whole site is updated.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: Django template inheritance is a compile-time operation. On the first render Django compiles the template into a tree of nodes, where each {% block %} is an extension point. The child template "inserts" its content into the parent's blocks.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Duplicating the navbar or sidebar in every template instead of moving it into layouts/. Or making the hierarchy too flat (all templates directly extend base.html) — then the sidebar has to be copied into every layout.

docs.title: §5. SaaS Dashboard Architecture
docs.text:
Three levels of template hierarchy work like an inheritance tree. The root level defines the skeleton, intermediate levels define the sections, and leaf templates define the content.

Why this architecture scales: - Add a new page: just create a new leaf template that extends layouts/dashboard.html - Change the sidebar: edit layouts/dashboard.html once — ALL pages are updated - Change the HTML skeleton: edit base.html once — EVERY page is updated

The component philosophy: sidebar, topbar, pagination, empty_state, confirm_modal are COMPONENTS moved out into include files. Each has a single responsibility.

docs.title: A typical SaaS template hierarchy
docs.text:
templates/
├── base.html                   ← HTML5 shell, Bootstrap CDN/Vite
├── layouts/
│   ├── dashboard.html          ← base + sidebar + topbar
│   ├── auth.html               ← base + centered card (login/register)
│   └── landing.html            ← base + marketing nav
├── components/
│   ├── sidebar.html            ← inclusion_tag component
│   ├── topbar.html             ← with notification_badge
│   ├── breadcrumb.html         ← dynamic breadcrumb
│   ├── pagination.html         ← Bootstrap pagination
│   ├── empty_state.html        ← "No items yet" placeholder
│   └── confirm_modal.html      ← Delete confirmation modal
└── notes/
    ├── list.html               ← extends layouts/dashboard.html
    ├── detail.html
    ├── create.html
    └── edit.html

docs.title: base.html — HTML shell
docs.text:
base.html is an HTML5 skeleton with no content at all. Every {% block %} is an extension point for child templates. data-bs-theme is Bootstrap 5.3+ dark mode support through a CSS variable controlled by the child template:

{# templates/base.html #}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="uk" data-bs-theme="{% block theme %}light{% endblock %}">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <meta name="description" content="{% block meta_description %}Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %}">
    <title>{% block title %}Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %} — {{ site_name }}</title>

    {# Bootstrap CSS via CDN or Vite #}
    {% block css %}
    <link rel="stylesheet"
          href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css">
    <link rel="stylesheet"
          href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/font/bootstrap-icons.css">
    {% endblock %}

    {% block extra_css %}{% endblock %}
</head>
<body class="{% block body_class %}{% endblock %}">

    {% block body %}{% endblock %}

    {# Bootstrap JS #}
    {% block js %}
    <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"
            defer></script>
    {% endblock %}

    {% block extra_js %}{% endblock %}
</body>
</html>

docs.title: layouts/dashboard.html — sidebar layout
docs.text:
layouts/dashboard.html extends base.html and adds a sidebar + topbar layout. Note request.resolver_match.url_name — this is dynamic highlighting of the active menu item. resolver_match is available thanks to the built-in context_processors.request:

{# templates/layouts/dashboard.html #}
{% extends 'base.html' %}
{% load hello_tags static %}

{% block body_class %}bg-light{% endblock %}

{% block body %}
<div class="d-flex" style="min-height: 100vh;">

    {# ===== SIDEBAR ===== #}
    <nav id="sidebar"
         class="d-flex flex-column flex-shrink-0 bg-dark text-white"
         style="width: 260px;">

        {# Brand #}
        <a href="{% url 'notes_app:dashboard' %}"
           class="d-flex align-items-center p-3 text-white text-decoration-none border-bottom border-secondary">
            <i class="bi bi-journal-text fs-4 me-2"></i>
            <span class="fs-5 fw-bold">{{ site_name }}</span>
        </a>

        {# Navigation links #}
        <ul class="nav nav-pills flex-column mb-auto p-3">
            <li class="nav-item mb-1">
                <a href="{% url 'notes_app:note_list' %}"
                   class="nav-link text-white {% if request.resolver_match.url_name == 'note_list' %}active{% endif %}">
                    <i class="bi bi-file-text me-2"></i>Мої нотатки
                </a>
            </li>
            <li class="nav-item mb-1">
                <a href="{% url 'notes_app:note_create' %}"
                   class="nav-link text-white {% if request.resolver_match.url_name == 'note_create' %}active{% endif %}">
                    <i class="bi bi-plus-circle me-2"></i>Нова нотатка
                </a>
            </li>
            <li class="nav-item mb-1">
                <a href="{% url 'notes_app:category_list' %}"
                   class="nav-link text-white">
                    <i class="bi bi-tags me-2"></i>Категорії
                </a>
            </li>
        </ul>

        {# User section #}
        <div class="p-3 border-top border-secondary">
            <div class="d-flex align-items-center">
                <div class="flex-shrink-0">
                    <div class="rounded-circle bg-primary d-flex align-items-center
                                justify-content-center text-white"
                         style="width:36px; height:36px;">
                        {{ user.username|first|upper }}
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="flex-grow-1 ms-2 overflow-hidden">
                    <div class="fw-semibold text-truncate">{{ user.get_full_name|default:user.username }}</div>
                    <small class="text-muted">{{ user.email|truncatechars:20 }}</small>
                </div>
                <a href="{% url 'logout' %}" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary ms-1"
                   title="Вийти">
                    <i class="bi bi-box-arrow-right"></i>
                </a>
            </div>
        </div>
    </nav>

    {# ===== MAIN CONTENT ===== #}
    <div class="flex-grow-1 d-flex flex-column">

        {# Top bar #}
        <header class="navbar navbar-light bg-white border-bottom shadow-sm px-4 py-2">
            <div class="d-flex align-items-center gap-3">
                {# Mobile sidebar toggle #}
                <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary d-lg-none"
                        data-bs-toggle="offcanvas" data-bs-target="#mobileSidebar">
                    <i class="bi bi-list"></i>
                </button>

                {# Breadcrumb #}
