Margin Collapse happens between:
  - adjacent block elements vertically
  - a parent and its first/last child (if there is no border/padding)

It does not happen:
  - in flex containers
  - in grid containers
  - between inline-block elements
  - if there is a border or padding between them

Solution:

/* Option 1: add padding instead of margin */
.parent { padding-top: 1px; }  /* breaks the collapse */

/* Option 2: make the parent a flex container */
.parent { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }

/* Option 3: overflow (a hack, avoid it) */
.parent { overflow: auto; }

docs.title: Stacking Context (z-index)
docs.text:
z-index is not global — it works inside its own stacking context.

<div style="position: relative; z-index: 1;">   <!-- Context A -->
    <div style="position: relative; z-index: 999;">
        <!-- z-index=999, but it is inside context A (z-index=1) -->
    </div>
</div>

<div style="position: relative; z-index: 2;">   <!-- Context B -->
    <div style="position: relative; z-index: 1;">
        <!-- z-index=1, but the whole context B (z-index=2) is above A -->
    </div>
</div>

Result: The element with z-index: 1 from context B will be on top of the element with z-index: 999 from context A, because context B (z-index: 2) is higher than context A (z-index: 1).

What creates a new stacking context: - position + z-index (not auto) - opacity < 1 - transform, filter, clip-path - will-change - isolation: isolate

/* Isolating a component from the global z-index */
.modal-wrapper {
    isolation: isolate;  /* ← explicitly create a context, protects against leaking */
}

🧠 Mental model: CSS performance is about how expensive the operations you force the browser to perform are. Some CSS changes cost 1 unit of work (opacity), some cost 1000 units (changing width recalculates the whole layout). Knowing the "cost", you can write animations and styles that don't "slow down" the browser.

📚 Why CSS performance matters for Django: If your CSS file is 500KB (unmodified Bootstrap + custom styles), the user sees a white screen for ALL of that download time, because CSS blocks rendering. Solution: minify (remove whitespace/comments), use only the Bootstrap components you need, include critical CSS inline and load the rest asynchronously.

🌐 GPU layers: Some CSS properties (transform, opacity, filter) run on the GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) instead of the CPU. The GPU is specialized in parallel pixel processing — GPU animations are much smoother (60fps vs 15fps). will-change: transform "asks" the browser to move the element to a GPU layer in advance.

❌ Common beginner mistake: Animating top/left/width/height instead of transform. top: 0 → top: 100px triggers Layout (the most expensive operation). transform: translateY(0) → translateY(100px) is handled by the GPU without Layout — dozens of times cheaper.

docs.title: 17. CSS Performance — what happens under the hood
Critical Rendering Path
docs.text:
Back to the Critical Rendering Path — this time with a focus on performance. CSS is a "render-blocking" resource. The browser won't paint anything until it has downloaded and processed all the CSS in <head>. Therefore: minimize the CSS size, use a CDN for Bootstrap (cached across sites), consider Critical CSS (inline the most important CSS right in the HTML).

HTML parsing → DOM
                 \
                  → Render Tree → Layout → Paint → Composite
                 /
CSS parsing → CSSOM

Render blocking: <link rel="stylesheet"> blocks rendering until the CSS is loaded. That is why the Bootstrap CDN is included in <head> — the browser doesn't paint anything until it knows the styles.

docs.title: Properties by cost
docs.text:
Knowing the "cost" of CSS properties helps you write efficient animations. The general rule: if a CSS change requires recalculating the positions of other elements (Layout/Reflow), it is expensive. If it only repaints pixels without changing positions, it is cheaper. If it is handled by the GPU without the CPU, it is the cheapest.

Cheap (doesn't trigger layout):
  opacity, transform, filter, color, background-color

Expensive (triggers Reflow — recalculation of positions):
  width, height, margin, padding, font-size, border,
  top, left, right, bottom

Most expensive (triggers a synchronous reflow in JS):
  el.offsetHeight, el.clientWidth, el.getBoundingClientRect()

Here is a concrete example of why transform is more efficient than left for animations. Both look the same to the user, but one loads the CPU and triggers Layout, while the other is lightweight GPU rendering.

/* ❌ An animation that triggers Layout → expensive */
@keyframes slide { from { left: 0; } to { left: 100px; } }

/* ✅ An animation only on the Composite layer → cheap */
@keyframes slide { from { transform: translateX(0); } to { transform: translateX(100px); } }

docs.title: will-change — a hint to the browser
docs.text:
will-change is a "warning" to the browser: "this element will change soon". The browser can move it to a GPU layer in advance, which makes the upcoming animation smoother. But don't overuse it: each GPU layer consumes video memory. Add will-change only to elements that WILL be animated, and remove it after the animation has finished.

/* Move the element to a GPU layer in advance */
.animated-card {
    will-change: transform;  /* the browser will promote it to a GPU layer */
}
/* Remove will-change once the animation has finished — it consumes GPU memory */

docs.title: 18. Self-check questions
docs.text:
1. The browser received HTML and CSS at the same time. What is built first — the DOM or the CSSOM?
  2. What is the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden? Which one triggers reflow?
  3. There are two rules: .card p { color: blue; } and #main .card p { color: red; }. Which one wins?
  4. Why does margin: 0 auto center a block horizontally but not vertically?
  5. An element with position: absolute and z-index: 999 hides behind an element with z-index: 1. Why?
  6. Why does width: 100% on a flex child sometimes not take up the whole row?
  7. @media (min-width: 768px) vs @media (max-width: 768px) — what is the difference in approach?
  8. There is a Bootstrap class col-12 col-md-6. On a 900px screen, what is the width?
  9. Why is transition: all 0.3s a bad practice for performance?
  10. Which three CSS properties can be animated without triggering reflow?

docs.title: Design Foundations for Django Projects
docs.text:
User interface architecture in Django applications

To build scalable, maintainable and user-friendly Django applications, a developer has to change their mindset: not "drawing pages" but designing systematic frontend architectures. A professional Django interface is based on a clear separation of structure, presentation and data — with active use of components and predictable information hierarchies.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• 1. Design Thinking and UX Principles
  • 2. Information Architecture (IA)
  • 3. Layout Systems and Examples
  • 4. Design Systems and the Bootstrap Philosophy
  • 5. Django Template Architecture
  • 6. Form Design and Data Presentation
  • 7. Dashboard Design
  • 8. Common Beginner Mistakes
  • 9. Organizing Large Django Projects
  • 10. Tailwind CSS vs Bootstrap in Django
  • 11. Static Files in Django
  • 12. Integrating React with Django
  • 13. Detailed Django Template Architecture
  • 14. Detailed Crispy Forms Architecture

docs.title: "Don't Make Me Think" (Steve Krug)
docs.text:
The main UX principle is "Don't make me think" (Steve Krug, the classic book on usability). Users don't read pages — they scan them, looking for visual landmarks. They "satisfice" — they choose the first acceptable option instead of analyzing all possible alternatives.

Your architecture should embody the key UX qualities: Useful, Usable, Findable, Credible, Desirable, Accessible, Valuable.

Practical consequences: - Every page should have one obvious action - Clickable elements should look clickable - Button labels: "Save note", not "OK" - If a logged-in user ends up on the login page, redirect them automatically

docs.title: CRAP design principles
docs.text:
CRAP is an acronym for four fundamental design principles described by Robin Williams in "The Non-Designer's Design Book":

Principle Description C — Contrast If two elements are not the same, make them very different to avoid confusion R — Repetition Visual elements repeat throughout the design — color, font, shape, buttons A — Alignment Every element is visually connected to others. Avoid placing things "by eye" P — Proximity Related elements are grouped together. More space between groups, less inside them

docs.title: Consistency and Conventions
docs.text: Standardized patterns (conventions) reduce cognitive load. If you use a standard shopping cart or profile icon, users instantly understand the function without any explanation.

docs.title: Error Prevention and Feedback
docs.text: A good interface is "error-tolerant". It limits the possibility of doing something wrong (for example, it allows only digits in a credit card field) and provides immediate, clear feedback after every action.

docs.title: Simplicity and Openness
docs.text: Always start designing with the core function, not with the surrounding shell. Establish a clear visual hierarchy — the most important elements should be the most noticeable, naturally guiding the user's eye.

docs.title: Visual Hierarchy and Weight
docs.text: Not every element can be "important". If everything shouts, nothing is heard. Build a hierarchy through: - Size: large → small - Color: bright → muted - Weight: Bold → Regular → Light - Position: the top left attracts attention first - Whitespace: an isolated element is perceived as more important

docs.title: Typography on Screen
docs.text:
• Body text: 16px minimum (less eye strain)
  • Line height: 1.5–1.6 for readability
  • Line length: 45–75 characters ideally (neither too narrow nor too wide)
  • A maximum of 2–3 fonts in one design
  • Bootstrap scale: .fs-1 (2.5rem) → .fs-6 (1rem)

docs.title: 2. Information Architecture (IA)
docs.text: Information architecture is the structural design of an application's shared information environments, balancing business goals, user needs and content.

docs.title: Page Hierarchy
docs.text: Applications use both a "top-down" architecture (the home page anticipates the main needs) and a "bottom-up" one (users arrive directly from deep links or search results).

docs.title: Persistent Navigation
docs.text: Global navigation should stay in the same place on every page — this creates a sense of "where am I". It should contain: - Logo (site identifier) - Main sections (primary links) - Utilities (Help, Login) - Search

docs.title: Breadcrumb Navigation
docs.text:
For deep applications, "breadcrumbs" show the path from the home page to the current location, providing an obvious way to go back up the hierarchy.

graph TD
    A[Global / Persistent Navigation] --> B[Home / Dashboard]
    A --> C[Utilities: Profile, Settings]
    A --> D[Search]
    B --> E[Sections: CRM, Reports, etc.]
    E --> F[Subsections / Details]
    F -.->|Breadcrumbs| E

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class B,C,D,E step;
    class F success;
    class A warning;

docs.title: 3. Layout Systems and Examples
docs.text: Professional web applications usually use a sectioned layout — like a control panel with separate functional frames.

docs.title: Admin Panels and Dashboards
docs.text: They usually use a fixed sidebar for primary navigation, a top header for utilities (search, profile) and a fluid content area.

docs.title: SaaS and CRM
docs.text: They rely on responsive grid systems, where complex data is presented in the main content area, switching to a single-column view on mobile devices.

docs.title: E-commerce and Blogs
docs.text:
They usually use top navigation, a hero section for the value proposition and a grid of cards for products or articles.

graph TD
    subgraph Layout Architecture
        H[Header: Logo, Search, Utilities]
        S[Sidebar: Main Navigation]
        C[Content Area: Dynamic Views]
        F[Footer: Secondary Links]
        H --- S
        S --- C
        C --- F
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class H,S,F step;
    class C success;

docs.title: 4. Design Systems and the Bootstrap Philosophy
docs.text: Frontend frameworks like Bootstrap exist as an abstraction layer for standardizing design, eliminating the chaos of custom CSS and speeding up interface creation.

docs.title: Constraining Choice
docs.text: A design system limits your options (for example, specific font sizes, a defined spacing scale and a color palette). This prevents "choice paralysis" and guarantees consistency. Instead of guessing between 120px and 125px, you use a predefined spacing scale based on 16px.

docs.title: Grid Systems
docs.text: Built on a 12-column mobile-first flexbox system: - Containers limit the width and center the content - Rows act as wrappers with negative margins - Columns (Col) define percentage widths

docs.title: Utility Classes
docs.text: Classes for margins (m-3), padding (p-4) and display (d-none, d-md-block) let you change rendering and responsive behavior right in the HTML without writing custom CSS.

docs.title: Ready-made Components
docs.text: Elements like buttons, cards and alerts are predefined abstractions. By combining these components, you quickly create a complex UI without duplication.

docs.title: 5. Django Template Architecture
docs.text:
Design systems map perfectly onto Django's template inheritance system. By breaking the UI into blocks, you follow the DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself).

  • base.html — the main shell: the <html> structure, <head> (CSS/JS), persistent navigation, footer.
  • Template inheritance: child templates {% extends 'base.html' %} insert specific UI into {% block content %}.
  • Partials/Components: small UI elements (a KPI card, a menu, alerts) are stored in components/ and included via {% include 'components/card.html' with title="Користувачі" %}.
graph TD
    A["base.html<br>Global Shell, Head, Footer"] --> B["layouts/dashboard.html<br>Sidebar + Topbar"]
    B --> C["notes_app/note_list.html<br>Notes grid"]
    B --> D["notes_app/note_form.html<br>Form"]
    C -.-> E["components/empty_state.html"]
    C -.-> F["components/pagination.html"]
    C -.-> G["components/confirm_modal.html"]
    D -.-> H["crispy_forms FormHelper + Layout"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class B,C,D step;
    class E,F,G,H success;
    class A warning;

docs.title: 3-Level Template Hierarchy (the SaaS Dashboard Pattern)
docs.text:
templates/
├── base.html                   ← HTML5 shell, Bootstrap CDN, {% block %} slots
├── layouts/
│   ├── dashboard.html          ← base + sidebar + topbar (extends base.html)
│   ├── auth.html               ← base + centered card (login/registration)
│   └── landing.html            ← base + marketing navigation
├── components/
│   ├── pagination.html         ← reusable Bootstrap pagination
│   ├── empty_state.html        ← "No items yet" with a CTA
│   └── confirm_modal.html      ← Delete confirmation dialog
└── notes_app/
    ├── note_list.html          ← extends layouts/dashboard.html
    ├── note_form.html          ← {% crispy form %} — ONE TAG!
    └── note_detail.html        ← extends layouts/dashboard.html

docs.title: Visual Hierarchy of Forms
docs.text: Forms should clearly communicate the relationships between elements. Avoid over-relying on semantic HTML headings (<h1>, <h2>) if they visually overpower the form's content. Separate the visual hierarchy from the document hierarchy.

docs.title: Labels and Feedback
docs.text:
Don't hide field labels and don't rely on placeholders alone — this harms accessibility. Forms should provide immediate feedback through colored states (green — success, red — error) and clear helper text.

Form errors in Bootstrap: Django automatically adds the is-invalid CSS class to fields with errors — crispy-forms wires this up automatically.

docs.title: Three Levels of Form Rendering in Django
docs.text: Approach Template code Lines Result Plain Django {{ form.as_p }} 1 No styles Manual Bootstrap <div class="mb-3">... for every field 60+ Bootstrap style django-bootstrap5 {% bootstrap_form form %} 1 Bootstrap style Crispy Forms {% crispy form %} 1 Bootstrap + custom layout

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: For presenting data, use .table-responsive to avoid horizontal scrolling on mobile. Improve readability with contextual classes (.table-striped, .table-hover).

docs.title: 7. Dashboard Design
docs.text: Dashboards should turn complex data into an easy-to-scan format.

docs.title: Organizing Information
docs.text: Dashboards often use a sectioned layout — navigation, filters and legends are placed in side panels.

docs.title: KPIs and Charts
docs.text: Key metrics are placed at the top (a card component). Choose the right chart type (pie, bar, line, scatter) depending on the comparison you need (time series, correlation, item).

docs.title: Empty States
docs.text:
Don't ignore empty states. When a user opens a CRM for the first time and there is no data, use an empty state with a clear Call to Action (CTA): "Add your first contact" instead of an empty or broken table.

graph LR
    A[User opens the application] --> B{Is there data?}
    B -->|no| C[Empty State<br>+ CTA Button]
    B -->|yes| D[Dashboard with<br>KPI cards + Table]
    C -->|Clicks the CTA| E[Creates the first item]
    E --> D

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,E step;
    class B decision;
    class D success;
    class C warning;

docs.title: Giant Templates
docs.text:
Putting thousands of lines of HTML into one file instead of using {% include %} components.

Solution: Move repeating UI blocks into a components/ or partials/ directory.

docs.title: Logic in Templates
docs.text:
Writing {% if note.priority == 4 and not note.is_archived and user.profile.timezone %} in templates.

Solution: Move it into a custom template filter or the service layer. Keep templates "dumb".

docs.title: Duplicated HTML
docs.text:
Copying the header/footer/navbar into every template file.

Solution: Mandatory template inheritance via {% extends 'base.html' %}.

docs.title: Too Much Stuff (Clutter/Noise)
docs.text:
Too many elements on one screen without a clear hierarchy. Three colors, five different font sizes, buttons everywhere.

Solution: A maximum of 3 hierarchy levels in one view. One primary action (.btn-primary), secondary ones — .btn-outline-secondary.

docs.title: Weak Contrast
docs.text:
Gray text on a white background, "soft" buttons that look like text.

Solution: Minimum WCAG contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text. Check it with the Colour Contrast Checker.

docs.title: Wrong Alignment and Centering
docs.text:
Placing elements "by eye", over-centering everything — a centered left navigation sidebar, a centered data table.

Solution: Bootstrap grid + Flexbox + text-start alignment for data, text-center only for headings/icons.

docs.title: Form Design Mistakes
docs.text:
• A placeholder instead of a label (hides the hint after the first character is typed)
  • A "Cancel" button in the same color as "Save"
  • No delete confirmation

Solution: 

{# BAD — label inside the input #}
<input placeholder="Enter email" type="email">

{# GOOD — a separate label #}
<label for="email" class="form-label">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" class="form-control" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: Relying on Color Alone
docs.text:
Using only color to indicate status (red/green) doesn't work for people with color vision deficiency.

Solution: 

{# BAD: color only #}
<span class="badge bg-success"></span>

{# GOOD: color + icon + text #}
<span class="badge bg-success"><i class="bi bi-check-circle me-1"></i>Active</span>

docs.title: Missing Empty States
docs.text:
Showing an empty table or page when there is no data.

Solution: Always render an empty_state.html component with a useful CTA.

docs.title: 9. Organizing Large Django Projects
docs.text:
To keep production Django applications scalable:

my_project/
├── templates/                  ← Global layouts (base.html, layouts/)
│   ├── base.html
│   ├── layouts/
│   │   ├── dashboard.html
│   │   └── auth.html
│   └── components/             ← Reusable UI elements
│       ├── pagination.html
│       ├── empty_state.html
│       └── confirm_modal.html
│
├── my_app/
│   ├── templates/my_app/       ← App-specific page templates
│   │   ├── note_list.html      ← extends layouts/dashboard.html
│   │   └── note_form.html      ← {% crispy form %}
│   ├── static/my_app/
│   │   ├── css/app.css         ← Custom overrides (minimal!)
│   │   └── js/app.js
│   ├── models.py
│   ├── services.py             ← Business logic (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)
│   ├── selectors.py            ← Read queries (SELECT)
│   ├── views.py                ← HTTP layer only
│   └── forms.py                ← FormHelper + Layout (crispy)
│
└── static/                     ← collectstatic output (production)

Rule: Avoid writing custom CSS for layout if the grid system (Bootstrap) already handles it. Custom CSS should override only branding (colors, fonts), not layout.

graph TD
    subgraph Template Responsibility
        A[base.html] -->|extends| B[layouts/dashboard.html]
        B -->|extends| C[app/page.html]
        C -->|includes| D[components/pagination.html]
        C -->|includes| E[components/empty_state.html]
    end

    subgraph Python Responsibility
        F[views.py] -->|delegates to| G[selectors.py]
        F -->|delegates to| H[services.py]
        F -->|passes the form to| I[forms.py FormHelper]
        I -->|renders via| J["{% crispy form %}"]
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,G,H,I step;
    class D,E,J success;
    class F warning;

docs.title: 10. Tailwind CSS vs Bootstrap in Django
Bootstrap in Django
docs.text:
Pros: - Ready-made components "out of the box" (cards, modals, navbar) - django-crispy-forms + crispy-bootstrap5 — excellent integration - Gentler learning curve - Easy to include via a CDN

Cons: - The "Bootstrap look" — sites look alike without customization - A larger CSS file (even with purge) - Less flexibility for unique designs

docs.title: Tailwind CSS in Django
docs.text:
Pros: - Unique design — there is no "Tailwind look" - Atomic CSS classes — a smaller final file (after purge) - Full control over styles without writing custom CSS

Cons: - Requires django-tailwind + Node.js for the build - crispy-tailwind is less mature than crispy-bootstrap5 - Steeper learning curve - No ready-made components (you need Flowbite, Headless UI, etc.)

docs.title: Integrating Tailwind with Django
docs.text:
# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'tailwind',
    'theme',  # generated by django-tailwind
]
TAILWIND_APP_NAME = 'theme'
NPM_BIN_PATH = '/usr/local/bin/npm'

# Running in development:
# python manage.py tailwind start

docs.title: When to choose which
docs.text: Situation Recommendation Educational project / prototype Bootstrap (CDN, no build) SaaS with unique branding Tailwind Admin panel / back office Bootstrap + django-unfold Public site with a designer-made design Tailwind The team knows Bootstrap well Bootstrap

docs.title: Configuring settings.py
docs.text:
# URL for accessing static files in development
STATIC_URL = '/static/'

# Directories with static files OUTSIDE the apps (project-level)
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / 'static',        # project/static/css/global.css
]

# Directory for production (collectstatic)
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles'

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
my_project/
├── static/                     ← project-level (STATICFILES_DIRS)
│   ├── css/
│   │   └── global.css
│   └── js/
│       └── global.js
│
└── my_app/
    └── static/
        └── my_app/             ← namespace (important!)
            ├── css/
            │   └── app.css
            └── js/
                └── app.js

Namespacing: Always put files in a subfolder named after the app (static/my_app/) to avoid conflicts between apps during collectstatic.

docs.title: Using Them in Templates
docs.text:
{% load static %}

{# Loading CSS #}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'my_app/css/app.css' %}">

{# Loading JS #}
<script src="{% static 'my_app/js/app.js' %}"></script>

{# Image #}
<img src="{% static 'my_app/images/logo.png' %}" alt="Logo">

docs.title: Production Commands
docs.text:
# Collects all static files into STATIC_ROOT
python manage.py collectstatic

# Checking the configuration
python manage.py findstatic css/global.css

docs.title: Serving in Production
docs.text:
Django does not serve static files in production (DEBUG=False). Use Nginx, WhiteNoise or a CDN:

# WhiteNoise (the simplest option for Heroku/Railway)
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'whitenoise.middleware.WhiteNoiseMiddleware',
    ...
]
# Django 4.2+ (STATICFILES_STORAGE was removed in Django 5.1):
STORAGES = {
    'default': {'BACKEND': 'django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage'},
    'staticfiles': {'BACKEND': 'whitenoise.storage.CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage'},
}

docs.title: Approach 1: Embedded Widget
docs.text:
One or more Django pages render HTML in which React is mounted into a specific <div>. The rest of the application consists of regular Django templates.

{# Django template #}
{% extends 'base.html' %}
{% block content %}
  <!-- React is mounted here -->
  <div id="react-root"
       data-notes="{{ notes_json|escapejs }}"
       data-user="{{ user.pk }}">
  </div>
{% endblock %}

{% block extra_js %}
  <script src="{% static 'notes_app/js/notes_widget.bundle.js' %}"></script>
{% endblock %}

When to use it: One complex component (for example, an interactive map or a text editor), while the rest of the site is Django SSR.

docs.title: Approach 2: SPA + API (Full Separation)
docs.text:
Django provides only a REST API (DRF or API Views), and React is a separate application built with Vite/CRA.

backend/   ← Django REST API (port 8000)
├── api/
│   ├── views.py     ← APIView or ViewSet
│   └── serializers.py
└── settings.py      ← CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS = ['http://localhost:5173']

frontend/  ← React + Vite (port 5173)
├── src/
│   ├── api/         ← axios/fetch clients
│   └── components/
└── vite.config.js

Configuring CORS for Django: 

# pip install django-cors-headers
INSTALLED_APPS = [..., 'corsheaders']
MIDDLEWARE = ['corsheaders.middleware.CorsMiddleware', ...]
CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS = ['http://localhost:5173', 'https://my-app.com']

docs.title: Comparing the Approaches
docs.text: Criterion Embedded Widget SPA + API Setup complexity Low High SEO Django SSR (excellent) Requires SSR/SSG Django authentication Built in (cookies/sessions) Requires JWT or a token API reuse Limited Yes (mobile, partners) Time to MVP Fast Slower When to choose One complex component A full-fledged SPA

docs.title: The SSR Concept and the Role of the Template
docs.text:
Django templates are a powerful Server-Side Rendering (SSR) system that strictly separates business logic from presentation. In a proper backend architecture:

  • The View acts as the controller: it fetches data from the ORM and prepares it
  • The Template Engine has a single job: take the data (the context) and insert it into HTML

Django deliberately restricts the Django Template Language (DTL) to prevent arbitrary Python code from being executed in templates. This architectural constraint forces you to keep complex business logic, database queries and mutations exclusively in the View or Model.

docs.title: The Template Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Browser Request] -->|URL Router| B[Django View]
    B -->|Query| C[(Database)]
    C -->|Model Instances| B
    B -->|Context Dictionary| D[Template Engine]
    D -->|Compilation and Rendering| E[Compiled HTML string]
    E -->|HTTP Response| A

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,D step;
    class E success;

Pipeline steps:

  1. Request — the browser initiates an HTTP request, which is routed to a Django View
  2. View Logic — the View processes the request, runs database queries and builds the context dictionary
  3. Template Compilation — the Template Engine parses the HTML file and compiles it into an AST (a tree of nodes) in the server's memory
  4. Context Interpolation — the engine walks the AST, substitutes template variables and executes tags
  5. Response Generation — the engine joins the results into the final HTML string and returns an HttpResponse

docs.title: Template Inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance is the architectural foundation of DRY UI systems in Django. Instead of copying <head>, the navigation and the footer into every file, you create a base "skeleton" template (base.html) with {% block %} tags. Child templates inherit the whole skeleton and override only the blocks they need.

graph TD
    A["base.html<br>HTML skeleton, Navbar, Footer, empty Blocks"]
    B["base_dashboard.html<br>Extends base.html, adds a Sidebar"]
    C["base_public.html<br>Extends base.html, adds a Hero section"]
    D["analytics.html<br>Extends base_dashboard.html, Charts"]
    E["settings.html<br>Extends base_dashboard.html, Forms"]
    F["home.html<br>Extends base_public.html"]

    B -->|"{% extends 'base.html' %}"| A
    C -->|"{% extends 'base.html' %}"| A
    D -->|"{% extends 'base_dashboard.html' %}"| B
    E -->|"{% extends 'base_dashboard.html' %}"| B
    F -->|"{% extends 'base_public.html' %}"| C

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class B,C step;
    class D,E,F success;
    class A warning;

docs.title: Template Composition ({% include %})
docs.text:
Inheritance builds pages top-down, composition builds them bottom-up. A complex UI is broken into isolated micro-templates (cards, pagination, forms) that are included via {% include %}.

graph LR
    A[article_list.html] -->|"{% include 'components/card.html' %}"| B[card.html]
    A -->|"{% include 'components/pagination.html' %}"| C[pagination.html]
    A -->|"{% include 'components/navbar.html' %}"| D[navbar.html]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class A step;
    class B,C,D success;

docs.title: Advanced DTL Tags
docs.text: Tag Purpose {% extends %} / {% block %} The core pair for inheritance trees {% include %} Inserting a sub-template {% with %} Caching a complex variable or passing isolated arguments to a component {% url %} Resolving named URL routes into absolute paths {% csrf_token %} Inserting a hidden input with the CSRF security token {% load %} Loading tag/filter libraries (for example, static, crispy_forms_tags)

docs.title: Template Filters
docs.text:
Filters transform context data right before rendering it into HTML, using the | syntax:

Filter Example Result default {{ value\|default:"Не вказано" }} Fallback if the value is False length {{ list\|length }} Size of a list or string truncatechars {{ text\|truncatechars:50 }} Truncates a string to N characters date {{ dt\|date:"d.m.Y" }} Formats a datetime safe {{ html\|safe }} ⚠️ Disables HTML escaping (only for trusted HTML!) lower / upper {{ name\|lower }} String case

docs.title: Architectural Mistakes in Templates
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Solution Business logic in templates (filtering QuerySets, database queries) Violates MVT, impossible to test All data preparation goes into the View or selectors.py Copying HTML (a navbar in every file) A design change = editing dozens of files {% extends 'base.html' %} Monolithic templates (2000+ lines of HTML) Impossible to maintain {% include %} components Abusing \|safe on untrusted input XSS vulnerabilities Never use \|safe for user data

docs.title: The Core Concept
docs.text:
Standard Django Forms are excellent at data validation and security, but they deliberately leave the HTML layout unstructured. The as_p() and as_table() methods generate raw HTML without Bootstrap classes.

Django Crispy Forms solves this by acting as a powerful UI abstraction layer. It intercepts Django's standard rendering and programmatically injects framework-specific styles directly from Python code, keeping the UI architecture DRY and drastically reducing boilerplate.

docs.title: The Form Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Django Model] -->|Meta introspection| B[ModelForm]
    B -->|Field instantiation| C[Form Fields]
    C -->|Type mapping| D[Widgets]
    D -->|Crispy interception| E[Crispy FormHelper]
    E -->|Template Pack injection| F[Styled HTML Output]
    F --> G[Browser]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,D step;
    class F,G success;
    class E warning;

Without Crispy Forms, the pipeline stops at Widgets — you get raw HTML without Bootstrap classes. With Crispy Forms, the FormHelper intercepts rendering and, via CRISPY_TEMPLATE_PACK, automatically adds all the required classes.

docs.title: Crispy Forms Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Django Form] --> B[FormHelper Instance]
    B --> C["form_method = 'POST'"]
    B --> D[Layout Object]
    D --> E[Row / Column]
    D --> F[Fieldset / Div]
    B --> G[Submit Button]
    B --> H["Template: {% crispy form %}"]
    H --> I[Fully Styled Bootstrap Form]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G step;
    class I success;
    class H warning;

docs.title: FormHelper Components
docs.text:
FormHelper is the orchestrator attached to the form; it defines: - The attributes of the <form> tag (method, id, class, action) - The HTTP method (GET/POST) - The overall Layout structure

FormHelper does NOT affect: - Validation (is_valid() works identically) - cleaned_data (unchanged) - Business logic

docs.title: Layout Components
docs.text: Component HTML rendering Purpose Fieldset('назва', ...) <fieldset><legend>назва</legend> Grouping related fields Row(...) <div class="row"> A Bootstrap grid row Column('поле', css_class='col-md-6') <div class="col-md-6"> A Bootstrap column Field('поле', placeholder='...') <input class="form-control" ...> A field with HTML attributes Div('поле', css_class='custom') <div class="custom"> An arbitrary container Submit('submit', 'Зберегти') <button type="submit" class="btn"> A submit button HTML('<hr>') An arbitrary HTML string Inserting any HTML ButtonHolder(...) <div class="form-group"> Grouping buttons

docs.title: Integration with Bootstrap 5
docs.text: With CRISPY_TEMPLATE_PACK = 'bootstrap5' set, Crispy Forms automatically: - Wraps inputs in the Bootstrap grid - Injects the required .form-control class into text fields - Dynamically applies .is-invalid together with Bootstrap validation error messages

docs.title: The Validation Pipeline
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Browser] -->|POST request| B[Django Form with request.POST]
    B --> C{is_valid?}
    C -->|yes| D[form.cleaned_data → Save]
    C -->|no| E[form.errors are generated]
    E --> F[Crispy Template Pack]
    F -->|Injects .is-invalid CSS| G[Re-render with Bootstrap validation states]
    G --> A

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,F step;
    class C decision;
    class D success;
    class E error;
    class G warning;

docs.title: The Advanced Layout System
docs.text:
# Example of a complex Layout — pure Python, no HTML in the template!
self.helper.layout = Layout(
    Fieldset(
        'Основна інформація',          # → <legend>
        Field('title', autofocus=True), # → <input class="form-control" autofocus>
        Row(
            Column('priority', css_class='col-md-4'),  # → <div class="col-md-4">
            Column('notebook', css_class='col-md-8'),  # → <div class="col-md-8">
        ),
    ),
    Fieldset(
        'Зміст',
        Field('content', rows=8),
    ),
    HTML('<hr class="my-4">'),
    Submit('submit', 'Зберегти', css_class='btn btn-primary me-2'),
    HTML('<a href="javascript:history.back()" class="btn btn-outline-secondary">Скасувати</a>'),
)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text: Misconception Truth Crispy Forms is validation No. Crispy affects only presentation. Validation is exclusively Django's job Crispy replaces Django Forms No. It is an enhancing wrapper. You still define fields and Meta as usual Crispy changes the data No. It only transforms the HTML output: <form> tags, CSRF tokens, CSS classes

docs.title: Comparison: Before vs After
docs.text:
BEFORE — manual Bootstrap (the earlier variant; the NoteForm docstring in notes_app/forms.py shows it): 

class NoteFormManual(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        widgets = {
            'title': forms.TextInput(attrs={'class': 'form-control', 'placeholder': '...'}),
            'content': forms.Textarea(attrs={'class': 'form-control', 'rows': 8}),
            'priority': forms.Select(attrs={'class': 'form-select'}),
            # ... repeat for EVERY field!
        }
# Template: 60+ lines of Bootstrap HTML

AFTER — Crispy Forms (the current notes_app/forms.py, simplified): 

class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.helper = FormHelper()
        self.helper.layout = Layout(
            Row(Column('title'), Column('priority')),
            'content',
            Submit('submit', 'Зберегти'),
        )
# Template: {% crispy form %} — 1 line!

docs.text:
File What it shows BOOTSTRAP_5.md Grid system, breakpoints, utility classes DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md Template inheritance, DTL syntax, SSR ADVANCED_TEMPLATES.md §3 crispy-forms FormHelper + Layout — theory ADVANCED_TEMPLATES.md §5 SaaS Dashboard architecture — 3-level hierarchy CRISPY_FORMS.md A short reference for django-crispy-forms notes_app/forms.py + notes_app/templates/notes_app/note_form.html A practical demonstration of all the concepts above in the project code

Learning path: Read this file → study ADVANCED_TEMPLATES.md §3 + §5 → open notes_app/forms.py (the NoteForm docstring compares BEFORE and AFTER) → look at notes_app/templates/notes_app/note_form.html

docs.title: DESIGN_README — Designing a Django Application from Scratch
docs.text:
This tutorial takes you from an empty <html> to a full-featured SaaS Dashboard with a dark theme, sidebar navigation and note cards — step by step.

Language: CrispyNotes (crispy_notes_chat_app) — the course's real project. Every code example is a live line from the project files.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. How to connect Bootstrap to Django
  2. Bootstrap 5 Dark Mode
  3. Django static files
  4. CSS Custom Properties — design tokens
  5. Layout: a SaaS Dashboard with Flexbox
  6. Sidebar: styles, hover, active state
  7. Cards and typography
  8. Bootstrap vs Custom CSS — what goes where
  9. Course documentation

docs.title: 1 · How to connect Bootstrap to Django
docs.text: Bootstrap is a library of ready-made CSS classes and JavaScript components. Instead of writing button { background: blue; padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 4px; ... } you simply write class="btn btn-primary" — and the style is already there.

docs.title: Two ways: CDN vs npm
docs.text:
CDN (for learning) npm/Vite (for production) Installation Copy two lines into the HTML npm install bootstrap + build Time to start Instant ~30 minutes of setup Customization Limited (CSS variables only) Full (Sass variables) Offline work ❌ Requires internet ✅ File size The CDN is cached by the browser Only the code you need (tree-shaking)

For learning projects — always CDN. The goal is to learn Django, not build tooling.

docs.title: What to copy into <head>
docs.text:
<!-- Bootstrap 5 CSS — REQUIRED in <head> -->
<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css"
      rel="stylesheet"
      integrity="sha384-QWTKZyjpPEjISv5WaRU9OFeRpok6YctnYmDr5pNlyT2bRjXh0JMhjY6hW+ALEwIH"
      crossorigin="anonymous">

<!-- Bootstrap Icons — a separate icon library (bi-journal-text, bi-trash...) -->
<link rel="stylesheet"
      href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/font/bootstrap-icons.min.css">

<!-- Bootstrap JS — BEFORE </body>, not in <head> -->
<!-- Needed for: Dropdown, Modal, Collapse, Carousel... -->
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script>

Why JS before </body> and not in <head>? HTML loads from top to bottom. JS in <head> blocks page rendering — the user sees a white screen while the JS loads. With JS before </body>, the HTML is displayed first, then interactivity is added.

docs.title: Where this is in our project
docs.text:
File: crispy_notes_chat_app/templates/base.html

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="uk" data-bs-theme="dark">   <!-- ← dark mode here -->
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>{% block title %}Notes{% endblock %} — CrispyNotes</title>

  <!-- 1. Bootstrap CSS -->
  <link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css"
        rel="stylesheet" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">

  <!-- 2. Bootstrap Icons -->
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/font/bootstrap-icons.min.css">

  <!-- 3. Our custom CSS (on top of Bootstrap) -->
  {% load static %}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'notes_app/css/app.css' %}">

  {% block extra_css %}{% endblock %}   <!-- ← slot for page-specific CSS -->
</head>
<body>
  {% block body %}{% endblock %}

  <!-- Bootstrap JS (before </body>) -->
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script>
  {% block extra_js %}{% endblock %}   <!-- ← slot for page-specific JS -->
</body>
</html>

CSS order matters: Bootstrap CSS → then our CSS. Our app.css overrides Bootstrap styles where needed. If you include them the other way around, Bootstrap will overwrite our styles.

docs.title: Bootstrap Icons — how to use them
docs.text:
<!-- An icon is added with an <i> tag with a bi-* class -->
<i class="bi bi-journal-text"></i>         <!-- notes -->
<i class="bi bi-trash me-1"></i>Видалити   <!-- + me-1 spacing on the right -->
<i class="bi bi-plus-lg fs-5"></i>          <!-- larger size fs-5 -->
<i class="bi bi-person-circle text-primary"></i>  <!-- with a Bootstrap color -->

Full list of icons: https://icons.getbootstrap.com/ — search by name.

docs.title: 2 · Bootstrap 5 Dark Mode
docs.text: Bootstrap 5.3+ has a built-in dark theme. You do not need to write any CSS — a single attribute on <html> turns on dark mode for ALL Bootstrap components.

docs.title: Turn on the dark theme
docs.text:
<!-- Instead of: -->
<html lang="uk">

<!-- We write: -->
<html lang="uk" data-bs-theme="dark">

What changes automatically:

Component Light theme Dark theme <body> white #fff dark gray #212529 .card white background gray #2b2d31 .form-control white input dark input .btn-outline-* colored border the same border + dark background .dropdown-menu white dark .nav-link dark text light text <hr> gray semi-transparent white

docs.title: Dark/light toggle (JavaScript)
docs.text:
<!-- Toggle button -->
<button id="themeToggle" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary">
  <i class="bi bi-moon-stars"></i>
</button>

<script>
  document.getElementById('themeToggle').addEventListener('click', () => {
    const html = document.documentElement;
    const current = html.getAttribute('data-bs-theme');
    html.setAttribute('data-bs-theme', current === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark');
  });
</script>

docs.title: Our project — the dark theme is fixed
docs.text: In CrispyNotes the theme is fixed to dark (base.html line 2). In addition, we override the Bootstrap colors with our own palette via app.css (section 4).

docs.title: 3 · Django static files
docs.text: Static files are CSS, JavaScript, images. Django does not "understand" them as templates — it simply serves them to the browser. But Django needs to know where to look for them.

docs.title: Two places for static files
docs.text:
crispy_notes_chat_app/
│
├── static/                          ← PROJECT-LEVEL static (STATICFILES_DIRS)
│   └── css/
│       └── project.css              ← global variables (--sidebar-width: 260px)
│
└── notes_app/
    └── static/
        └── notes_app/               ← APP-LEVEL static (APP_DIRS=True)
            └── css/
                └── app.css          ← the main CSS of our application ★

docs.title: settings.py — configuration
docs.text:
# settings.py

STATIC_URL = '/static/'

# Project-level static (in addition to app/static/)
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / 'static',   # ← the crispy_notes_chat_app/static/ folder
]

# With APP_DIRS=True Django automatically finds notes_app/static/
# No need to add each app separately

docs.title: In the template: {% load static %}
docs.text:
{% load static %}   <!-- ← REQUIRED at the top of the template (or in base.html) -->

<!-- Including CSS -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'notes_app/css/app.css' %}">
<!--                                   ↑ path relative to notes_app/static/ -->

<!-- Including an image -->
<img src="{% static 'notes_app/img/logo.png' %}" alt="Logo">

docs.title: collectstatic — for production
docs.text:
# Collects all static files into STATIC_ROOT for Nginx/Apache
python manage.py collectstatic

In development (DEBUG=True) Django serves static files itself. In production (DEBUG=False) static files should be served by Nginx, not Django.

Why two levels of static (project vs app)? App-level static — each app is responsible for its own files. When you move the app to another project, its static files go with it. Project-level — for shared files (favicon, fonts, the shared palette).

docs.title: 4 · CSS Custom Properties — design tokens
docs.text:
CSS Custom Properties (or CSS variables) are named values in CSS that can be reused throughout the code.

A design token is one "named color" instead of dozens of hex codes all over the CSS. Want to change the sidebar color? Edit one variable — it changes everywhere.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
/* Declaration — in :root{} (global scope) */
:root {
  --accent: #7c6efa;          /* the name starts with -- */
  --text-primary: #e2e8f0;
  --card-bg: #1e1e2e;
}

/* Usage — the var() function */
.card {
  background: var(--card-bg);      /* substitutes #1e1e2e */
  color: var(--text-primary);      /* substitutes #e2e8f0 */
}

.btn-accent {
  background: var(--accent);       /* #7c6efa */
}

/* Fallback (backup value) */
color: var(--text-primary, #ffffff);  /* if the variable is not declared → #ffffff */

docs.title: All tokens of our project
docs.text:
File: notes_app/static/notes_app/css/app.css

:root {
  /* ── SIDEBAR ───────────────────────────────── */
  --sidebar-bg:          #16161e;   /* sidebar background (the darkest) */
  --sidebar-hover:       rgba(255,255,255,0.06);  /* nav-link hover highlight */
  --sidebar-border:      rgba(255,255,255,0.07);  /* thin dividers */
  --sidebar-label:       #6060a0;   /* color of the NOTES / TASKS / TAGS headings */
  --sidebar-accent:      #7c6efa;   /* accent purple (not used directly) */
  --sidebar-active-bg:   rgba(124,110,250,0.15);  /* background of the active nav-link */

  /* ── LAYOUT ────────────────────────────────── */
  --topbar-bg:           #0f0f18;   /* topbar background (the darkest of all) */
  --main-bg:             #1a1a27;   /* main content background */
  --card-bg:             #1e1e2e;   /* note card background */

  /* ── BORDERS ───────────────────────────────── */
  --card-border:         rgba(255,255,255,0.08);  /* thin card border at rest */
  --card-hover-border:   rgba(124,110,250,0.55);  /* card border on hover */

  /* ── TEXT ──────────────────────────────────── */
  --text-primary:        #e2e8f0;   /* main text (headings, content) */
  --text-secondary:      #9a9ac0;   /* secondary text (date, hints) */
                                    /* WCAG 4.5:1 on #1e1e2e — accessible contrast */

  /* ── INTERACTIVITY ─────────────────────────── */
  --accent:              #7c6efa;   /* main accent color (buttons, links) */
  --focus-ring:          0 0 0 3px rgba(124,110,250,0.35);  /* outline on focus */
}

File: static/css/project.css (project-level)

:root {
  --sidebar-width:  260px;  /* sidebar width */
  --topbar-height:  56px;   /* topbar height */
}

docs.title: Why split into two files?
docs.text: project.css — structural values (sizes, spacing). They rarely change. app.css — color tokens. If you change the theme, you edit only app.css.

docs.title: Bootstrap uses CSS variables too
docs.text:
Bootstrap has its own --bs-* variables:

/* Bootstrap generates these on load */
:root {
  --bs-primary: #0d6efd;
  --bs-secondary: #6c757d;
  --bs-body-bg: #212529;    /* in dark mode */
  --bs-body-color: #dee2e6;
}

You can override Bootstrap variables in your own CSS:

:root {
  --bs-primary: #7c6efa;   /* now btn-primary will be purple */
}

docs.title: 5 · Layout: a SaaS Dashboard with Flexbox
docs.text: A SaaS Dashboard is a UI pattern: a fixed sidebar on the left + scrollable content on the right. Notion, Gmail, Linear, Figma — they are all built this way.

docs.title: HTML structure (3 levels)
docs.text:
base.html                  ← Bootstrap CDN, app.css
└── layouts/dashboard.html ← Sidebar + Topbar
    └── note_list.html      ← Page content

docs.title: The full HTML structure of the dashboard
docs.text:
File: templates/layouts/dashboard.html

<!-- Level 1: Outer wrapper — the whole viewport -->
<div class="d-flex vh-100 overflow-hidden">
  <!--
    d-flex        — display: flex (horizontal placement of sidebar + main)
    vh-100        — height: 100vh (takes the full screen height)
    overflow-hidden — so the scroll happens inside, not on body
  -->

  <!-- Level 2a: SIDEBAR — fixed width on the left -->
  <nav id="sidebar"
       class="sidebar d-flex flex-column p-3"
       style="width: 260px; min-height: 100vh;">
    <!--
      sidebar       — our CSS class (background, border-right)
      d-flex        — flex container for a vertical stack
      flex-column   — flex-direction: column (children stack from top to bottom)
      p-3           — padding: 1rem on all sides
      width:260px   — fixed width (the --sidebar-width token)
      min-height    — stretches to the full height even if the content is short
    -->

    <!-- Brand, navigation, tags... -->
  </nav>

  <!-- Level 2b: MAIN — takes the remaining width -->
  <div class="d-flex flex-column flex-grow-1 overflow-auto">
    <!--
      d-flex        — flex container for a vertical stack (topbar + content)
      flex-column   — topbar on top, content below
      flex-grow-1   — takes all available width (100% - 260px sidebar)
      overflow-auto — scrolling here, not on the whole page
    -->

    <!-- Level 3a: TOPBAR — fixed height at the top -->
    <header class="topbar d-flex align-items-center px-4 py-2">
      <!--
        topbar            — our CSS class (background, border-bottom)
        d-flex            — horizontal flex (title | search | user)
        align-items-center — vertical centering
        px-4              — horizontal padding 1.5rem
        py-2              — vertical padding 0.5rem
      -->

      <h6 class="mb-0 me-auto fw-semibold">
        <!--
          me-auto — margin-right: auto → pushes everything else to the right
          fw-semibold — font-weight: 600
        -->
        {% block topbar_title %}Нотатки{% endblock %}
      </h6>

      <!-- Search: me-3 = margin-right 1rem, spacing from the user dropdown -->
      <form class="d-flex me-3" method="get">...</form>

      <!-- User dropdown: the last element — sticks to the right edge -->
      <div class="dropdown">...</div>
    </header>

    <!-- Level 3b: PAGE CONTENT — scrolls -->
    <main class="flex-grow-1 p-4 overflow-auto">
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
      <!--
        flex-grow-1   — takes the full height (100% - topbar height)
        p-4           — padding 1.5rem (spacing from the edges)
        overflow-auto — scrolls if the content does not fit
      -->
    </main>

  </div>
</div>

docs.title: Why Flexbox and not Grid?
docs.text:
Flexbox CSS Grid One-dimensional (a row OR a column) Two-dimensional (rows AND columns) Sidebar + main → Flexbox A complex grid of cards → Grid d-flex, flex-grow-1 row, col-md-4

In Bootstrap d-flex = Flexbox, row/col-* = Grid.

docs.title: Sidebar CSS classes (from app.css)
docs.text:
/* Sidebar background and border */
.sidebar {
    background: var(--sidebar-bg) !important;  /* #16161e */
    border-right: 1px solid var(--sidebar-border);  /* thin line on the right */
    flex-shrink: 0;  /* does not shrink when the window gets smaller */
}

docs.title: Section labels (NOTES / TASKS / TAGS)
docs.text:
.sidebar-label {
    font-size: 0.7rem;       /* small — does not compete with the links */
    font-weight: 700;        /* bold */
    letter-spacing: 0.08em;  /* spaced-out letters — classic uppercase style */
    color: var(--sidebar-label) !important;  /* #6060a0 — muted purple */
}

In the HTML (dashboard.html): 

<p class="sidebar-label text-uppercase fw-semibold mb-1 px-2">Нотатки</p>
<!--
  sidebar-label  — our CSS class (font-size, letter-spacing, color)
  text-uppercase — Bootstrap: text-transform: uppercase
  fw-semibold    — Bootstrap: font-weight: 600
  mb-1           — Bootstrap: margin-bottom: 0.25rem
  px-2           — Bootstrap: padding-left/right: 0.5rem
-->

docs.title: Nav-links: hover and active
docs.text:
/* Resting state */
.sidebar .nav-link {
    color: #9898c8 !important;   /* muted purple-gray */
    padding: 0.42rem 1rem;
    border-radius: 5px;
    margin: 1px 6px;
    transition: background 0.12s, color 0.12s;  /* smooth hover */
    font-size: 0.875rem;  /* 14px — slightly smaller than the main text */
}

/* Hover */
.sidebar .nav-link:hover {
    background: var(--sidebar-hover);  /* rgba(255,255,255,0.06) — barely visible */
    color: #d8d8f8;  /* becomes lighter */
}

/* Active (current page) */
.sidebar .nav-link.active {
    background: var(--sidebar-active-bg) !important;  /* rgba(124,110,250,0.15) */
    color: var(--accent) !important;  /* #7c6efa — bright purple */
    border-left: 3px solid var(--accent);  /* accent stripe on the left ← */
    padding-left: calc(1rem - 3px);  /* compensate for the 3px border */
}

docs.title: Active state via Django
docs.text:
<!-- dashboard.html — the active item is determined by the URL -->
<a href="{% url 'notes_app:note_list' %}"
   class="nav-link {% if request.resolver_match.url_name == 'note_list' %}active{% endif %}">
  <i class="bi bi-journal-text me-2"></i>Всі нотатки
</a>

request.resolver_match.url_name — Django returns the name of the current URL: - On /notes/ → 'note_list' → the active class is added - On /notes/new/ → 'note_create' → the active class is NOT added for "Всі нотатки"

To check by part of the name (for example, all todo pages): 

class="nav-link {% if 'todo' in request.resolver_match.url_name %}active{% endif %}"
<!-- todo_list, todo_create, todo_detail — all of them will be highlighted -->

docs.title: Bootstrap nav-pills
docs.text:
<ul class="nav nav-pills flex-column mb-3">
<!--
  nav         — Bootstrap: base nav styles (removes bullet points)
  nav-pills   — Bootstrap: pills (pill shape for the active item)
  flex-column — Bootstrap: vertical flex (list from top to bottom)
  mb-3        — Bootstrap: margin-bottom: 1rem (spacing between sections)
-->
  <li class="nav-item">
    <a href="..." class="nav-link">...</a>
  </li>
</ul>

docs.title: Separator and dividers
docs.text:
<hr>
<!-- .sidebar hr in CSS: -->
/* border-color: var(--sidebar-border); margin: 0.4rem 0; */

docs.title: Note Cards — hover animation
docs.text:
/* Resting state */
.note-card {
    background: var(--card-bg) !important;         /* #1e1e2e */
    border: 1px solid var(--card-border) !important;  /* rgba(255,255,255,0.08) */
    border-radius: 10px;
    /* transition — what is animated and how fast */
    transition: transform 0.18s ease,
                border-color 0.18s ease,
                box-shadow 0.18s ease;
}

/* On hover */
.note-card:hover {
    transform: translateY(-2px);  /* lifts 2px up */
    border-color: var(--card-hover-border) !important;  /* purple border */
    box-shadow: 0 6px 24px rgba(124,110,250,0.15) !important;  /* shadow */
}

Why translateY(-2px)? A small lift without changing the size — the card "detaches" from the surface. transform does not affect layout (it does not shift neighboring elements).

docs.title: Typography — 3 levels of text
docs.text:
/* Page title (h5 in note_list.html) */
.page-title {
    font-size: 1.2rem;    /* 19.2px */
    font-weight: 600;
    color: var(--text-primary);  /* #e2e8f0 — bright */
}

/* Card title */
.note-card .card-title a {
    font-size: 0.95rem;      /* 15.2px */
    font-weight: 600;
    letter-spacing: -0.01em; /* slightly condensed — looks modern */
    color: var(--text-primary);
}
.note-card .card-title a:hover {
    color: var(--accent);    /* purple on hover */
}

/* Note text preview */
.note-card .card-text {
    color: var(--text-secondary) !important;  /* #9a9ac0 — muted */
    font-size: 0.85rem;   /* 13.6px */
    line-height: 1.55;
}

docs.title: WCAG — accessible contrast
docs.text:
--text-primary  #e2e8f0  on  --card-bg  #1e1e2e  → contrast 11.5:1  ✅ (norm 4.5:1)
--text-secondary #9a9ac0 on  --card-bg  #1e1e2e  → contrast ~4.5:1  ✅ (norm 4.5:1)

WCAG — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Minimum contrast of 4.5:1 between text and background. If the contrast is lower, people with visual impairments will not be able to read it. Check it: https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/

docs.title: Bootstrap Badges
docs.text:
<!-- In the sidebar (task counter) -->
<span class="badge bg-primary rounded-pill">{{ sidebar_todo_count }}</span>
<!--
  badge         — Bootstrap: base badge styles (padding, font-size)
  bg-primary    — Bootstrap: blue background (#0d6efd in light, an equivalent in dark)
  rounded-pill  — Bootstrap: border-radius: 50rem (pill)
-->

<!-- In note_list.html (number of notes) -->
<span class="badge rounded-pill bg-primary bg-opacity-10 text-primary"
      style="font-size: 0.72rem;">{{ notes|length }}</span>
<!--
  bg-opacity-10 — Bootstrap: opacity 10% → a very transparent background
  text-primary  — Bootstrap: blue text
  Together: a "ghost badge" — only color, no bright background
-->

docs.title: Crispy Forms — styling the fieldset
docs.text:
/* app.css — styling the <fieldset><legend> that crispy generates */
fieldset legend {
    font-size: 0.9rem;
    font-weight: 600;
    color: var(--text-secondary);
    text-transform: uppercase;
    letter-spacing: 0.03em;
    padding-bottom: 0.4rem;
    border-bottom: 1px solid var(--card-border);  /* thin line under the section */
    margin-bottom: 1rem;
}

Crispy generates <fieldset><legend>Основна інформація</legend> — our CSS automatically styles them as section dividers.

docs.title: Custom Scrollbar
docs.text:
/* A thin custom scrollbar for Webkit (Chrome, Edge, Safari) */
::-webkit-scrollbar       { width: 6px; }  /* thinner than the default */
::-webkit-scrollbar-track { background: transparent; }  /* transparent track */
::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
    background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12);  /* semi-transparent */
    border-radius: 3px;
}
::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
    background: rgba(255,255,255,0.2);  /* becomes more visible */
}

Firefox: scrollbar-width: thin; (without color customization).

docs.title: Focus Ring — accessibility
docs.text:
/* Instead of the browser's default blue outline */
:focus-visible {
    outline: none;
    box-shadow: var(--focus-ring);  /* 0 0 0 3px rgba(124,110,250,0.35) */
    border-radius: 4px;
}

:focus-visible — triggers only during keyboard navigation (Tab), not on a mouse click. Important for accessibility.

docs.title: 8 · Bootstrap vs Custom CSS — what goes where
docs.text: Bootstrap is the foundation, our CSS is the customization. Bootstrap provides structure and components; we add the brand and the details.

docs.title: Division of responsibility
docs.text: What Bootstrap provides What we write in app.css d-flex, vh-100, flex-grow-1 .sidebar, .topbar, .note-card data-bs-theme="dark" (base dark theme) CSS tokens (--sidebar-bg, --accent...) btn, btn-primary, btn-sm Hover animations .note-card:hover card, card-body, card-footer Active state border-left: 3px solid accent nav, nav-pills, nav-link .sidebar-label (section headers) badge, rounded-pill Custom scrollbar ::-webkit-scrollbar dropdown, dropdown-menu-dark fieldset legend styles for crispy p-4, me-3, px-2, mb-3 :focus-visible ring Bootstrap Icons (bi-*) --focus-ring, --card-hover-border form-control, form-select transition animations alert, alert-dismissible Typography .page-title, .card-text

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
To build the CrispyNotes Dashboard:

1. base.html
   └── Bootstrap CDN (CSS + Icons + JS)
   └── data-bs-theme="dark"
   └── {% static 'app.css' %}

2. app.css
   └── :root {} → CSS tokens (colors, spacing)
   └── .sidebar, .topbar, .note-card → custom components
   └── transitions, hover effects, scrollbar

3. dashboard.html
   └── d-flex vh-100            → full-screen layout
   └── nav.sidebar 260px        → fixed column
   └── flex-grow-1              → main takes the rest
   └── nav-pills flex-column    → vertical menu
   └── request.resolver_match   → active state without JS

4. Pages
   └── {% extends 'layouts/dashboard.html' %}
   └── Only {% block content %} — sidebar/topbar for free

Key idea: Bootstrap gives you ~80% ready-made — Grid, buttons, forms, dark mode. The remaining 20% — CSS tokens and a few custom classes — and the project looks like a product.

docs.title: Django Admin — Administration
docs.text: Django Admin is an automatically generated interface for managing the data in the database. It is available at: http://127.0.0.1:8001/admin/ (the port of the web service in Docker)

docs.title: 1. What is Django Admin?
docs.text:
Imagine you have an application with 1000 notes. You need to find and delete spam notes or grant moderator permissions to a particular user. Without the Admin you would have to write separate views for that.

Django Admin is a ready-made interface where you can: - View and edit any record in the database - Search and filter data - Manage users and their permissions - Perform bulk operations (for example, delete 50 spam notes with one click)

docs.title: 2. Who has access to the Admin?
docs.text:
# Two types of privileged users:

user.is_staff = True
# ↑ Can log in to /admin/
# ↑ But has NO permissions unless they are explicitly granted!

user.is_superuser = True  
# ↑ Automatically has ALL permissions in the system
# ↑ Even those that are not explicitly granted
# ↑ has_perm() always returns True

Critical rule:

Never use a superuser for everyday work!

Reason: if a superuser tests the functionality, has_perm() is always True. This masks authorization bugs. A real user without permissions may run into an error that you never saw while testing as a superuser.

docs.title: Differences:
docs.text: Attribute Access to /admin/ Permissions is_staff=True ✓ Only explicitly granted ones is_superuser=True ✓ All permissions automatically Regular user ✗ None

docs.title: 3. How to register a model in the Admin
docs.text:
# notes_app/admin.py — a teaching example.
# The real project currently uses only the simple way: admin.site.register(...)

from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Note

# Option 1. The simple way — basic registration:
admin.site.register(Note)

# Option 2. The extended way — with customization.
# Use it INSTEAD OF option 1: registering the same model twice
# raises admin.sites.AlreadyRegistered.
@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ('title', 'user', 'group', 'priority', 'created_at')
    # ↑ Which columns to show in the list

    list_filter = ('priority', 'group', 'is_pinned')
    # ↑ Filters in the right-hand panel (/admin/notes_app/note/?priority=4)

    search_fields = ('title', 'content', 'user__username')
    # ↑ Search across these fields
    # user__username → search through an FK (notes of the user named 'alice')

    raw_id_fields = ('user', 'notebook')
    # ↑ For an FK, shows an ID input field instead of a select (faster with 1000+ records)

What we get at /admin/: 

[ ] | Заголовок          | Юзер  | Група  | Пріоритет | Дата
[ ] | Зустріч з клієнтом | alice | Робота | Терміново | 2025-06-03
[ ] | Купити молоко      | alice | Сімя   | Низький   | 2025-06-02

docs.title: 4. Managing users and permissions through the Admin
docs.text:
/admin/auth/user/     ← list of all users
/admin/auth/group/    ← list of groups and their permissions

How to grant permissions to a user through the Admin: 1. /admin/auth/user/42/change/ 2. The "Permissions" section → tick ✓ next to the required permissions 3. Or add the user to a Group that already has the required permissions

docs.title: 5. Creating a superuser (command line)
docs.text:
# First run (the stack is already up via docker compose up -d):
docker compose exec web python manage.py createsuperuser

# Django will ask:
Username: admin
Email: admin@example.com
Password: (at least 8 characters)

# Open your browser:
# http://127.0.0.1:8001/admin/

docs.title: Django Admin + Unfold — Internal Tools Architecture
docs.text: Django Admin is the built-in admin interface for managing models. Unfold is a modern UI layer on top of it, built with Tailwind CSS. This file covers the standard Django admin and the complete Unfold system, from basic setup to enterprise architecture.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• 0. What Django Admin is and why Unfold
  • 1. AdminSite — the interface coordinator
  • 2. ModelAdmin — the CRUD generator
  • 3. Admin Request Lifecycle — from HTTP to the DB
  • 4. ChangeList — the list engine
  • 5. Query Architecture — query optimization
  • 6. Admin Rendering Pipeline — templates and TemplateResponse
  • 7. Unfold — installation and basic configuration
  • 8. Sidebar + Navigation Architecture
  • 9. Dashboard — layouts and DASHBOARD_CALLBACK
  • 10. Widget Systems — Card, Chart, Tracker, Cohort
  • 11. Information Hierarchy — Fieldset tabs, Conditional fields
  • 12. Enterprise Patterns — parallel UnfoldAdminSite, InfinitePaginator
  • 13. Admin Anti-Patterns
  • 14. Self-check questions
  • 15. Advanced Filtering — AutocompleteSelectFilter, RangeDateTimeFilter
  • 16. Bulk Actions and Dialog Actions — BaseDialogForm
  • 17. Component Classes — @register_component
  • 18. Custom Pages — UnfoldModelAdminViewMixin
  • 19. Advanced Widgets — WysiwygWidget, ArrayWidget
  • 20. Performance and Caching — cached.Loader, full-text search, Redis
  • 21. Datasets — related records in the ChangeForm
  • 22. Production Checklist
  • 🧠 Mental model: Django Admin is a LEGO kit for internal tools. Every model (Note, Category, User) is a set of bricks. Django automatically builds a complete CRUD interface from them: a list, an add form, an edit form, deletion. Unfold is a new set of "LEGO" on top of the old one: the same bricks, but a modern design and new components.
  • 📚 Why it exists: Before Django Admin, every project had to build its admin panel by itself: HTML forms, validation, access permissions, pagination. Django Admin solved this problem once and for all — automatic CRUD for any registered model, with permissions, auditing, and search out of the box. Unfold solved the problem of the standard admin's outdated look (Django's own CSS, not Bootstrap) — without changing business logic.
  • 🌐 What happens under the hood: When Django starts, the apps.py of every installed app is executed. admin.autodiscover() finds and loads admin.py in every app. Each admin.site.register(Model, ModelAdmin) registers the model in the global AdminSite singleton. On a request to /admin/, Django calls AdminSite.urls, which dynamically generates URL routes for all registered models.
  • ❌ Common beginner mistake: Thinking that Django Admin is for end users. The admin is intended EXCLUSIVELY for the internal team: administrators, editors, support. External users should get a separate interface built on regular Django Views + Bootstrap. Using the admin as a "frontend" is an anti-pattern.

docs.title: Orientation: How to Read This Document
docs.text:
Before diving into the sections, understand the overall architectural picture:

The whole Django Admin is three layers stacked on top of each other:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Your code                           │
│   ModelAdmin, actions, inlines, custom views        │
│   (§2, §4, §11, §16–18)                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Unfold Layer                          │
│   Tailwind UI, Dashboard, Sidebar, Components       │
│   (§7–12, §15–21)                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│           django.contrib.admin                      │
│   AdminSite, ModelAdmin base, ChangeList, ORM       │
│   (§1–6)                                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│           Django Core                               │
│   ORM, Template Engine, Middleware, Auth            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Reading order for beginners:

  1. §0 → the big picture, why Admin at all
  2. §3 → Request Lifecycle (you understand how Django handles an admin request)
  3. §2 → ModelAdmin (the main tool, 80% of your time is here)
