docs.text: Topic File Services (business logic, mutations, transactions) DJANGO_SERVICES.md Services + Selectors + Serializers (the full picture) DJANGO_SERVICES_SELECTORS.md ORM: QuerySet API, N+1, select_related DJANGO_ORM_DEEP.md Views: how to call a Selector from a View notes_chat_app/README.md — Step 8

docs.title: Django Serializers — Transport Layer
docs.text: serializers.py is the boundary between HTTP and the domain. A serializer knows no business logic. It only: accepts raw HTTP data → validates it → returns validated_data, or accepts a domain object → formats it → returns JSON.

docs.title: What a Serializer is architecturally
docs.text:
HTTP Request
    │  {"region_name": "Kyiv", "severity": "high"}
    ▼
InputSerializer.is_valid()
    │  validated_data = {"region_name": "Kyiv", "severity": "high"}
    ▼
Service
    │  FloodEvent object
    ▼
OutputSerializer(event)
    │  {"id": 1, "region_name": "Kyiv", ...}
    ▼
HTTP Response

A serializer is a guard at the entrance and a formatter at the exit.

Class Direction Role InputSerializer HTTP → Domain Validation of types, formats, cross-field rules OutputSerializer Domain → HTTP Response formatting, field selection

docs.title: The problem: the ModelSerializer anti-pattern
docs.text:
ModelSerializer is a convenient class that automatically generates fields from a model.

# BAD — ModelSerializer is tightly coupled to the DB schema
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = FloodEvent
        fields = '__all__'

What breaks: - A model change → an automatic API change (unexpected for clients) - One serializer for reading AND writing → an implicit contract - Business fields (for example, created_by as a ForeignKey) leak into the response as an ID - Logic in serializer.save() — business logic in the transport layer

docs.title: When ModelSerializer is acceptable
docs.text: ModelSerializer is fine for simple CRUD endpoints where the model and the API match. For complex workflows — explicit InputSerializer and OutputSerializer.

docs.title: The basis: serializers.Serializer
docs.text:
# apps/flood/serializers.py

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name    = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField()

The base Serializer (not ModelSerializer) gives an explicit contract: - Fields do not depend on the DB schema - A model change does not change the API automatically - It is immediately clear what is expected from the client

docs.title: Usage in a View
docs.text:
# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventCreateAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = FloodEventInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        # validated_data — guaranteed clean, checked data
        event = flood_event_create(**serializer.validated_data, created_by=request.user)

        output = FloodEventOutputSerializer(event)
        return Response(output.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)

raise_exception=True — if validation fails, DRF automatically returns HTTP 400 with a description of the errors. No extra if not serializer.is_valid(): return Response(...).

docs.title: OutputSerializer — formatting the response
docs.text:
class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id             = serializers.IntegerField()
    region_name    = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField()
    created_by     = serializers.EmailField(source='created_by.email')
    created_at     = serializers.DateTimeField()

source='created_by.email' — instead of returning created_by: 42 (an ID), we return the email. The client gets what it needs, not internal DB details.

docs.title: A list of objects
docs.text:
# many=True — serializing a QuerySet or a list
events = flood_events_get_list()
output = FloodEventOutputSerializer(events, many=True)
return Response(output.data)

docs.title: Nested objects
docs.text:
class RegionOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id           = serializers.IntegerField()
    display_name = serializers.CharField()


class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id             = serializers.IntegerField()
    region         = RegionOutputSerializer()   # nested object
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()

If nested serializers trigger N+1 queries, switch to a pure Python function (see the section below).

docs.title: Basic types
docs.text: Field Python type Example CharField str names, descriptions IntegerField int IDs, counts FloatField float coordinates, numbers BooleanField bool flags DateTimeField datetime timestamps DateField date dates without time EmailField str (with email validation) addresses URLField str (with URL validation) links UUIDField UUID unique identifiers

docs.title: Choosing from a list
docs.text:
severity = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])

# Or via constants from the model
severity = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=FloodEvent.SEVERITY_CHOICES)

docs.title: Optional and default fields
docs.text:
# The field is not required — if not provided, it will be None
description = serializers.CharField(required=False, allow_null=True)

# The field is not required — if not provided, it gets the default value
page_size = serializers.IntegerField(required=False, default=20)

docs.title: Read-only / write-only
docs.text:
# read_only — the field is in the response but is not accepted in the request
id         = serializers.IntegerField(read_only=True)
created_at = serializers.DateTimeField(read_only=True)

# write_only — the field is accepted in the request but not returned in the response
password   = serializers.CharField(write_only=True)

docs.title: SerializerMethodField — computed fields
docs.text:
class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id             = serializers.IntegerField()
    severity_label = serializers.SerializerMethodField()

    def get_severity_label(self, obj) -> str:
        labels = {'low': 'Низький', 'medium': 'Середній', 'high': 'Високий'}
        return labels.get(obj.severity_level, obj.severity_level)

docs.title: validate() — cross-field validation
docs.text:
validate(self, data) runs after all individual fields have been checked. It is the place for: - validating dependencies between fields - auto-generating values (slug, token) - transforming data before validated_data

class EventRangeInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    start_date = serializers.DateField()
    end_date   = serializers.DateField()

    def validate(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        if data['end_date'] < data['start_date']:
            raise serializers.ValidationError(
                "end_date не може бути раніше ніж start_date"
            )
        return data

docs.title: Auto-generating a field in validate()
docs.text:
class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name = serializers.CharField()
    slug        = serializers.SlugField(read_only=True)  # generated by the server

    def validate(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        data['slug'] = slugify(data['region_name'])
        return data

read_only=True is mandatory — otherwise DRF will require slug in the request and fail before validate() is called.

docs.title: validate_<field>() — validating a single field
docs.text:
class UserRegisterInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    email    = serializers.EmailField()
    password = serializers.CharField(write_only=True)

    def validate_email(self, value: str) -> str:
        if User.objects.filter(email=value).exists():
            raise serializers.ValidationError("Email вже зареєстрований")
        return value.lower()   # transformation — normalize to lowercase

    def validate_password(self, value: str) -> str:
        if len(value) < 8:
            raise serializers.ValidationError("Мінімум 8 символів")
        return value

docs.title: Validation execution order
docs.text:
1. Parsing the request body (JSON → Python dict)
        │
        ▼
2. Checking each field individually
   CharField(max_length=200)? → checks
   ChoiceField(choices=[...])? → checks
        │
        ▼
3. validate_<field>() for each field
   validate_email() → checks uniqueness
        │
        ▼
4. validate() → cross-field validation
   end_date > start_date?
        │
        ▼
5. validated_data — guaranteed clean data
        │
        ▼
6. The View passes validated_data to the Service

If any step raises ValidationError, the following steps are not executed and the client receives HTTP 400.

docs.title: Mapping domain errors to HTTP
docs.text:
The Service calls full_clean() and raises django.core.exceptions.ValidationError. DRF expects rest_framework.exceptions.ValidationError.

Without configuration, Django will return a 500 HTML page instead of a JSON 400.

# shared/exceptions/handlers.py

from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError as DjangoValidationError
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
from rest_framework.exceptions import ValidationError as DRFValidationError
from rest_framework.serializers import as_serializer_error


def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
    if isinstance(exc, DjangoValidationError):
        exc = DRFValidationError(detail=as_serializer_error(exc))

    return exception_handler(exc, context)

# settings.py
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'shared.exceptions.handlers.custom_exception_handler',
}

After this: full_clean() in any Service → automatically a JSON 400.

docs.title: Complex serialization — a pure Python function
docs.text:
When an OutputSerializer triggers N+1 or the response structure is too complex:

# apps/flood/serializers.py  (or selectors.py)

def flood_feed_serialize(events) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Instead of a nested OutputSerializer — a Python function
    after a single optimized SQL query.
    """
    region_cache: dict[int, str] = {}

    result = []
    for event in events:
        region_id = event.region_id
        if region_id not in region_cache:
            region_cache[region_id] = event.region.display_name  # already in select_related

        result.append({
            'id': event.id,
            'region': region_cache[region_id],
            'severity': event.severity_level,
            'detected_at': event.detected_at.isoformat(),
            'image_count': event.image_count,  # from annotate()
        })

    return result

# views.py
events = flood_events_get_list()   # selector: select_related + annotate
data   = flood_feed_serialize(events)
return Response(data)

Advantage: full control over the SQL footprint. The selector runs one optimized query, Python builds the structure — no hidden queries from nested serializers.

docs.title: Full example: a CRUD endpoint
docs.text:
# apps/flood/serializers.py

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name    = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField()

    def validate_region_name(self, value: str) -> str:
        return value.strip().title()


class FloodEventUpdateInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField(required=False)


class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id             = serializers.IntegerField()
    region_name    = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField()
    created_by     = serializers.EmailField(source='created_by.email')
    created_at     = serializers.DateTimeField()

# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventCreateAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = FloodEventInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        event = flood_event_create(
            **serializer.validated_data,
            created_by=request.user,
        )

        return Response(
            FloodEventOutputSerializer(event).data,
            status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
        )


class FloodEventDetailAPIView(APIView):

    def get(self, request, event_id: int):
        event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
        return Response(FloodEventOutputSerializer(event).data)

    def patch(self, request, event_id: int):
        event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)

        serializer = FloodEventUpdateInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        event = flood_event_update(event=event, **serializer.validated_data)

        return Response(FloodEventOutputSerializer(event).data)

docs.title: Logic in save()
docs.text:
# BAD — business logic in the transport layer
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    def save(self):
        instance = super().save()
        send_notification_email(instance)   # a side effect in the serializer
        return instance

# GOOD — logic in the Service
event = flood_event_create(**serializer.validated_data)
# The Service is responsible for the notification via on_commit + Celery

docs.title: A direct queryset in a serializer
docs.text:
# BAD — the serializer runs DB queries
class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    related_events = serializers.SerializerMethodField()

    def get_related_events(self, obj):
        return FloodEvent.objects.filter(region=obj.region).count()  # N+1

# GOOD — annotate in the Selector, pass it to the serializer
class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    related_count = serializers.IntegerField()  # from annotate() in the selector

docs.title: One serializer for writing and reading
docs.text:
# BAD — an unclear contract
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = FloodEvent
        fields = ['id', 'region_name', 'severity_level', 'created_by']
        # id is read-only, created_by is read-only,
        # but that is not obvious from the code

# GOOD — explicit separate classes
class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name    = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=[...])

class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id             = serializers.IntegerField()
    region_name    = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()
    created_by     = serializers.EmailField(source='created_by.email')

docs.title: Table: what a Serializer must not do
docs.text: Action Why not Save to the DB (save() with logic) That is the Service Run ORM queries in a SerializerMethodField N+1, that is the Selector Contain business rules That is the Service or full_clean() on the model Know about transaction.atomic That is the Service Know about Celery tasks That is the Service Return a Response That is the View

docs.title: Quick cheat sheet
docs.text:
# serializers.py — template

class <Model>InputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    """Input data contract. Independent of the model."""
    <field_1> = serializers.<FieldType>(...)
    <field_2> = serializers.<FieldType>(...)

    def validate_<field_1>(self, value):
        # Validation of a single field
        return value

    def validate(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        # Cross-field validation or transformation
        return data


class <Model>OutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    """Output data contract. What the client sees in the response."""
    id        = serializers.IntegerField()
    <field_1> = serializers.<FieldType>()
    <computed> = serializers.SerializerMethodField()

    def get_<computed>(self, obj):
        return ...

docs.title: Connection to the rest of the documentation
docs.text: Topic File Services (what to do with validated_data) DJANGO_SERVICES.md Selectors (how to prepare data for the OutputSerializer) DJANGO_SELECTORS.md Services + Selectors + Serializers (the full picture) DJANGO_SERVICES_SELECTORS.md Views: how to put it all together Django_Views.md

docs.title: Django Services — the business logic layer
docs.text: services.py is a separate file in every Django app where all the business logic lives. A service is a transport-agnostic function that describes what the system does.

docs.title: The problem without Services
docs.text:
In a typical Django project, business logic gradually settles into the View:

# views.py — the "Fat View" anti-pattern
class RegisterUserView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        # validation
        if User.objects.filter(email=request.data['email']).exists():
            return Response({'error': 'Email вже зайнятий'}, status=400)

        # password hashing
        password = make_password(request.data['password'])

        # saving
        user = User.objects.create(
            email=request.data['email'],
            password=password,
        )

        # sending an email
        send_welcome_email(user.email)

        # response
        return Response({'id': user.id}, status=201)

What breaks: - This logic cannot be reused from a Celery task - It cannot be called from a management command - It cannot be tested without an HTTP request - The logic is duplicated if registration is needed in two places

docs.title: The solution: a Service
docs.text:
# apps/users/services.py

def user_create(*, email: str, password: str) -> User:
    user = User(email=email)
    user.set_password(password)
    user.full_clean()
    user.save()
    send_welcome_email(user.email)
    return user

# views.py — thin, no logic
class RegisterUserView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = UserRegisterInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        user = user_create(**serializer.validated_data)

        return Response({'id': user.id}, status=201)

The same logic is now available from anywhere:

# From a Celery task
user_create(email='bot@example.com', password='secret')

# From a management command
user_create(email='admin@example.com', password='admin123')

# From a test
user = user_create(email='test@example.com', password='pass')
assert user.id is not None

docs.title: What a Service is architecturally
docs.text:
A service is the layer between the HTTP transport and the database that describes the business domain.

Transport Layer     views.py, tasks.py, management commands
        │
        │  validated_data / parameters
        ▼
Application Layer   services.py          ← THE LOGIC LIVES HERE
        │
        │  domain objects
        ▼
Data Layer          selectors.py, models.py, ORM
        │
        ▼
     PostgreSQL
Layer Answers the question View How did the request arrive? HTTP, WebSocket, CLI? Service What does the system do with this data? Selector How do we get the needed data from the DB? ORM How do we formulate the SQL?

docs.title: Basic rules
docs.text:
• Lives in <app_name>/services.py
  • A stateless Python function (not a class, unless there is complex state)
  • Keyword-only arguments (*) — protection against argument-order mistakes during refactoring
  • Strict type annotations
  • Knows nothing about HTTP — does not import request, does not return Response
  • Returns a domain object or None
# apps/flood/services.py

from django.db import transaction
from apps.flood.models import FloodEvent


def flood_event_create(
    *,
    region_name: str,
    severity_level: str,
    detected_at,
    created_by,
) -> FloodEvent:
    event = FloodEvent(
        region_name=region_name,
        severity_level=severity_level,
        detected_at=detected_at,
        created_by=created_by,
    )
    event.full_clean()   # Django validation at the domain level
    event.save()
    return event


def flood_event_update(
    *,
    event: FloodEvent,
    severity_level: str,
) -> FloodEvent:
    event.severity_level = severity_level
    event.full_clean()
    event.save(update_fields=['severity_level'])
    return event


def flood_event_delete(*, event: FloodEvent) -> None:
    event.delete()

The * before the arguments is Python syntax for keyword-only parameters. It can only be called like this: flood_event_create(region_name="Kyiv", ...). The order of arguments does not matter — there is no risk of mixing them up.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
The Service is responsible for transaction boundaries. If several operations must be atomic, the whole function is wrapped in @transaction.atomic.

def user_complete_onboarding(*, user: User) -> User:
    # Without atomic — if the second operation fails,
    # the first one has already run and will not be rolled back
    user.onboarding_completed = True
    user.save(update_fields=['onboarding_completed'])

    profile = UserProfile(user=user, bio='')
    profile.save()

    return user

@transaction.atomic
def user_complete_onboarding(*, user: User) -> User:
    # With atomic — either everything is saved, or nothing
    user.onboarding_completed = True
    user.save(update_fields=['onboarding_completed'])

    profile = UserProfile(user=user, bio='')
    profile.save()

    return user

docs.title: When you need @transaction.atomic
docs.text: Situation Atomic? A single save() No — Django is atomic on its own at the row level Two or more save() calls Yes save() + delete() Yes Any related operations that must all happen or none at all Yes

docs.title: Side Effects and on_commit
docs.text: A side effect is an action outside the main transaction: sending an email, a Celery task, a write to an external API.

docs.title: The problem without on_commit
docs.text:
@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_create(*, region_name: str, ...) -> FloodEvent:
    event = FloodEvent(...)
    event.save()

    # DANGEROUS — Celery will receive the task before
    # the transaction has closed and the record has appeared in the DB.
    # The worker will try to find the event — and won't find it.
    notify_emergency_task.delay(event.id)

    return event

docs.title: The solution: transaction.on_commit
docs.text:
@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_create(*, region_name: str, ...) -> FloodEvent:
    event = FloodEvent(...)
    event.save()

    # SAFE — the task starts ONLY after a successful commit.
    # If the transaction is rolled back, the task will not start at all.
    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: notify_emergency_task.delay(event.id)
    )

    return event

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
on_commit → a guarantee that the side effect
            happens only if the data was actually saved to the DB

docs.title: A Celery Task is also the Transport Layer
docs.text:
A Celery task is a delivery queue, not a place for logic. The task delegates to a Service.

# apps/flood/tasks.py

# BAD — logic directly in the task
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id: int):
    event = FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    event.status = 'processed'
    event.save()
    send_report_email(event.created_by.email)

# GOOD — the task only transports the call
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id: int):
    from apps.flood.selectors import flood_event_get_by_id
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_mark_processed

    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_mark_processed(event=event)

The same flood_event_mark_processed can be called from a View, a test or the CLI — without changing the logic.

docs.title: Mapping domain errors to HTTP
docs.text:
A Service knows nothing about HTTP. But if full_clean() raises django.core.exceptions.ValidationError, DRF does not know how to format it into a 400 response.

The solution is a custom exception handler (once, in settings.py):

# shared/exceptions/handlers.py

from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError as DjangoValidationError
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
from rest_framework.exceptions import ValidationError as DRFValidationError
from rest_framework.serializers import as_serializer_error


def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
    if isinstance(exc, DjangoValidationError):
        exc = DRFValidationError(detail=as_serializer_error(exc))

    return exception_handler(exc, context)

# settings.py
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'shared.exceptions.handlers.custom_exception_handler',
}

Now full_clean() in any Service automatically returns a nice JSON 400 to the client.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
# apps/flood/models.py

class FloodEvent(models.Model):
    SEVERITY_CHOICES = [('low', 'Low'), ('medium', 'Medium'), ('high', 'High')]

    region_name    = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    severity_level = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=SEVERITY_CHOICES)
    detected_at    = models.DateTimeField()
    created_by     = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    created_at     = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

docs.title: Serializer
docs.text:
# apps/flood/serializers.py

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name    = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField()


class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    id             = serializers.IntegerField()
    region_name    = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()
    detected_at    = serializers.DateTimeField()
    created_by     = serializers.EmailField(source='created_by.email')

docs.title: View
docs.text:
# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventCreateAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = FloodEventInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        event = flood_event_create(
            **serializer.validated_data,
            created_by=request.user,
        )

        output = FloodEventOutputSerializer(event)
        return Response(output.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)

View: 7 lines. All the logic is in the Service. The View does not know what happens inside.

docs.title: A Service does not know where it is called from
docs.text:
The same function:

# From a REST API View
event = flood_event_create(region_name="Kyiv", severity_level="high", ...)

# From a Celery task
event = flood_event_create(region_name="Lviv", severity_level="medium", ...)

# From a management command
event = flood_event_create(region_name="Odesa", severity_level="low", ...)

# From a test
event = flood_event_create(region_name="Test", severity_level="high", ...)

The logic runs the same way regardless of how the call arrived.

docs.title: Naming Convention
docs.text:
# Creation
user_create(*, email, password) -> User
flood_event_create(*, region_name, severity_level) -> FloodEvent

# Update
user_update(*, user, name) -> User
flood_event_update(*, event, severity_level) -> FloodEvent

# Deletion
user_delete(*, user) -> None
flood_event_delete(*, event) -> None

# Complex workflows
user_complete_onboarding(*, user) -> User
flood_event_mark_processed(*, event) -> FloodEvent
payment_process(*, order, card_token) -> Payment
pipeline_run_dem_validation(*, dem_file) -> ValidationResult

Name = action + what happens. Not process(), not handle(), not do_stuff().

docs.title: What a Service must NOT do
docs.text: Action Why not return Response(...) A Service does not know HTTP import request or self.request A Service does not know about Views Direct SELECTs without a Selector Reading is the Selector's responsibility Render templates That is the Template / View level Contain business logic in a Celery task A task is transport, not domain Raise HTTP status codes The domain raises ValidationError, not 400

docs.title: Quick cheat sheet
docs.text:
# services.py — template

from django.db import transaction
from apps.<app>.models import <Model>


def <model>_create(
    *,
    <field_1>: <type>,
    <field_2>: <type>,
) -> <Model>:
    obj = <Model>(
        <field_1>=<field_1>,
        <field_2>=<field_2>,
    )
    obj.full_clean()
    obj.save()
    return obj


@transaction.atomic
def <model>_create_with_side_effect(
    *,
    <field>: <type>,
) -> <Model>:
    obj = <Model>(<field>=<field>)
    obj.full_clean()
    obj.save()

    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: some_celery_task.delay(obj.id)
    )

    return obj


def <model>_update(
    *,
    obj: <Model>,
    <field>: <type>,
) -> <Model>:
    obj.<field> = <field>
    obj.full_clean()
    obj.save(update_fields=['<field>'])
    return obj


def <model>_delete(*, obj: <Model>) -> None:
    obj.delete()

docs.title: Django Services, Selectors & Serializers — The Business Logic Layer
docs.text: This document describes the production architecture of the Django business layer: where the logic lives, who reads data, who writes it, and how HTTP never gets into the domain.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Section What's inside Architecture map Where each layer lives Serializers InputSerializer, OutputSerializer, validate() Services Stateless functions, transactions, side effects Selectors CQRS-light, N+1, query abstraction Full data flow HTTP → View → Serializer → Service → Selector → DB Anti-patterns What not to do and why Responsibility table Who does / does not do what

docs.title: Architecture map
docs.text:
HTTP Request
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  View (views.py)            │  ← Thin HTTP orchestrator
│  Receives the request       │
│  Calls the serializer       │
│  Passes data to the Service │
│  Returns a Response         │
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  InputSerializer            │  ← Validation + transformation
│  (serializers.py)           │     of input data
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │ validated_data
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  Service (services.py)      │  ← Business logic + transaction
│  Orchestrates operations    │     + side effects
│  Knows nothing about HTTP   │
│  Calls the Selector         │
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
     ┌───────┴───────┐
     │               │
     ▼               ▼
┌──────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Selector │   │  Infrastructure      │
│(selectors│   │  (email, S3, Celery) │
│  .py)    │   └──────────────────────┘
│  Reading │
│  data    │
└────┬─────┘
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  ORM (models.py)            │  ← DB schema, relationships
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
         PostgreSQL
             │
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  OutputSerializer           │  ← Response formatting
│  (serializers.py)           │
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
         HTTP Response

docs.title: The core principle
docs.text: A serializer is the boundary between HTTP and the domain. It knows nothing about business logic. It only: - takes raw HTTP data → validates it → returns validated_data - takes domain objects → formats them → returns JSON

docs.title: Anti-pattern: ModelSerializer as the only entry point
docs.text:
# BAD — ModelSerializer tightly couples HTTP to the DB schema
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = FloodEvent
        fields = '__all__'

The problem: a change in the model → a change in the API. Business rules end up in save(). There is no explicit contract.

docs.title: The right way: InputSerializer + OutputSerializer
docs.text:
# serializers.py

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    """Input data contract — independent of the model."""
    region_name = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])
    detected_at = serializers.DateTimeField()


class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    """Output data contract — what the client sees in the response."""
    id = serializers.IntegerField()
    region_name = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()
    detected_at = serializers.DateTimeField()
    created_by_email = serializers.EmailField(source='created_by.email')

docs.title: The validate() method — Intercepting before validated_data
docs.text:
validate(self, data) is the place for cross-field validation and transformation.

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name = serializers.CharField()
    # slug is generated by the server — read_only so that DRF does not require it in the request
    slug = serializers.SlugField(read_only=True)

    def validate(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        # Auto-generate the field before validated_data
        data['slug'] = slugify(data['region_name'])
        return data

Important: server-generated fields must be read_only=True in Meta.read_only_fields, otherwise the serializer will fail validation before validate() is even called.

docs.title: Complex serialization — A pure Python function
docs.text:
When the response structure is too complex for an OutputSerializer:

# selectors.py or a separate module

def flood_feed_serialize(events: list) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Works around OutputSerializer limitations for complex joined structures.
    Builds the response in Python after an optimized SQL query.
    """
    region_cache = {}  # in-memory cache for repeated values

    result = []
    for event in events:
        region_id = event.region_id
        if region_id not in region_cache:
            region_cache[region_id] = event.region.display_name

        result.append({
            'id': event.id,
            'region': region_cache[region_id],
            'severity': event.severity_level,
            'detected_at': event.detected_at.isoformat(),
        })
    return result

The advantage: full control over the SQL footprint, no N+1 from nested serializers.

docs.title: Mapping domain errors → HTTP
docs.text:
Domain code raises django.core.exceptions.ValidationError. DRF expects rest_framework.exceptions.ValidationError.

The solution is a custom exception handler:

# shared/exceptions/handlers.py

from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError as DjangoValidationError
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
from rest_framework.exceptions import ValidationError as DRFValidationError
from rest_framework.serializers import as_serializer_error


def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
    if isinstance(exc, DjangoValidationError):
        exc = DRFValidationError(detail=as_serializer_error(exc))

    return exception_handler(exc, context)

# settings.py
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'shared.exceptions.handlers.custom_exception_handler',
}

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
A service is a transport-agnostic business function. It knows nothing about HTTP, does not return a Response and does not import DRF. The same service is called from:

  • a REST API View
  • a Celery Task
  • a Django Management Command
  • a WebSocket consumer
  • a Pytest test

docs.title: Anatomy of a stateless service
docs.text:
# apps/flood/services.py

from django.db import transaction
from apps.flood.models import FloodEvent
from apps.flood.tasks import notify_emergency_services_task


def flood_event_create(
    *,                              # keyword-only — protects against argument-order mistakes
    region_name: str,
    severity_level: str,
    detected_at,
    created_by,
) -> FloodEvent:
    """
    The single place where the FloodEvent creation logic lives.
    Does not return a Response — returns a domain object.
    """
    event = FloodEvent(
        region_name=region_name,
        severity_level=severity_level,
        detected_at=detected_at,
        created_by=created_by,
    )
    event.full_clean()   # Django validation at the domain level
    event.save()

    return event

The * before the arguments is Python syntax for keyword-only parameters. flood_event_create(region_name="Kyiv", severity_level="high", ...) — explicit and safe during refactoring.

docs.title: Transactions and Side Effects
docs.text:
The critical rule: side effects (email, a Celery task) run only after a successful commit.

# apps/flood/services.py

@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_complete_processing(*, event: FloodEvent) -> FloodEvent:
    # 1. DB mutation
    event.status = 'processed'
    event.save(update_fields=['status'])

    # 2. Side effect — runs ONLY if the transaction closed without an error
    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: notify_emergency_services_task.delay(event.id)
    )

    return event

If you write notify_emergency_services_task.delay(event.id) without on_commit, Celery may receive the task before the record appears in the DB.

docs.title: A Celery Task is a transport layer too
docs.text:
# apps/flood/tasks.py

@shared_task
def notify_emergency_services_task(event_id: int):
    """A task is a delivery queue, not a place for logic."""
    from apps.flood.selectors import flood_event_get_by_id
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_notify

    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_notify(event=event)   # the logic lives in the service

docs.title: Full View + Service example
docs.text:
# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventCreateAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = FloodEventInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        event = flood_event_create(
            **serializer.validated_data,
            created_by=request.user,
        )

        output = FloodEventOutputSerializer(event)
        return Response(output.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)

View: 6 lines. All the logic is in the service.

docs.title: The principle (CQRS-light)
docs.text:
The architecture distinguishes two fundamentally different operations:

Services Selectors What they do Mutate data, orchestrate business operations Read data Operation type CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, side effects SELECT Transactions @transaction.atomic No Parallel load Vertical scaling Horizontal (read replicas)

docs.title: Why not a model property?
docs.text:
# BAD — a hidden query in a Python loop → N+1
class FloodEvent(models.Model):
    @property
    def region_display(self):
        return self.region.display_name  # a SELECT on every loop iteration

# GOOD — an optimized query in a selector
def flood_events_get_list(*, user) -> QuerySet:
    return (
        FloodEvent.objects
        .filter(created_by=user)
        .select_related('region')      # one JOIN instead of N queries
        .prefetch_related('tags')      # batched prefetch for M2M
        .annotate(
            comment_count=Count('comments')
        )
        .order_by('-detected_at')
    )

docs.title: Anatomy of a selector
docs.text:
# apps/flood/selectors.py

def flood_event_get_by_id(*, event_id: int) -> FloodEvent:
    """A basic selector — returns the object or raises a 404."""
    try:
        return FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    except FloodEvent.DoesNotExist:
        raise FloodEvent.DoesNotExist(f"FloodEvent {event_id} не знайдено")


def flood_events_get_visible_for(*, user) -> QuerySet:
    """
    Hides SQL details behind a domain name.
    Returns a QuerySet — the View can add pagination or filtering.
    """
    return (
        FloodEvent.objects
        .filter(
            Q(created_by=user) | Q(is_public=True)
        )
        .select_related('region', 'created_by')
        .order_by('-detected_at')
    )

docs.title: QuerySet vs evaluated list
docs.text:
Selectors can return:

Returns When to use QuerySet The View can add .filter(), pagination, django_filters list[dict] When complex Python optimization is needed before returning 
# A selector that returns a QuerySet — the View adds pagination
def flood_events_get_list() -> QuerySet:
    return FloodEvent.objects.all().select_related('region')

# In the View:
queryset = flood_events_get_list()
page = self.paginate_queryset(queryset)   # DRF pagination — safe

docs.title: Selector + django-filter without leaking the ORM into the View
docs.text:
# apps/flood/filters.py

import django_filters
from apps.flood.models import FloodEvent

class FloodEventFilter(django_filters.FilterSet):
    severity = django_filters.ChoiceFilter(choices=FloodEvent.SEVERITY_CHOICES)
    after = django_filters.DateTimeFilter(field_name='detected_at', lookup_expr='gte')

    class Meta:
        model = FloodEvent
        fields = ['severity', 'after']

# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventListAPIView(ListAPIView):

    def get_queryset(self):
        qs = flood_events_get_visible_for(user=self.request.user)  # selector
        return FloodEventFilter(self.request.GET, queryset=qs).qs  # filtering

The View does not know SQL. The Selector does not know the request filters. The Filter does not know the business rules.

docs.title: Business logic in serializer.save()
docs.text:
# BAD
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    def save(self):
        self.instance.notify_emergency_services()  # business logic in the serializer
        super().save()

# GOOD
# View → Service → a separate notification call
event = flood_event_create(**validated_data)
flood_event_notify(event=event)

docs.title: HTTP objects in a service
docs.text:
# BAD
def process_flood(request):
    user = request.user       # the Service knows about the HTTP request
    data = request.data

# GOOD
def flood_event_create(*, region_name: str, created_by):
    pass   # the Service receives already-parsed data

docs.title: ORM in a View
docs.text:
# BAD
class FloodListView(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        events = FloodEvent.objects.filter(
            created_by=request.user
        ).select_related('region')   # ORM directly in the View

# GOOD
class FloodListView(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        events = flood_events_get_visible_for(user=request.user)  # Selector

docs.title: Business logic in a Celery task
docs.text:
# BAD
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id):
    event = FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    event.status = 'processed'
    event.save()
    send_email(event.created_by.email, ...)   # logic directly in the task

# GOOD
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id):
    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_complete_processing(event=event)   # delegation to the service

docs.title: Responsibility table
docs.text: Layer Should Should NOT View Handle HTTP, call the serializer and the service, return a Response Know SQL, contain business logic, make ORM queries InputSerializer Validate types and formats, transform data, return validated_data Save to the DB, contain business rules OutputSerializer Format a domain object into a JSON structure Query the DB, contain logic Service Orchestrate business operations, open transactions, trigger side effects Know HTTP, import DRF, return a Response Selector Read data from the DB, optimize queries (select_related, annotate) Mutate data, contain business logic ORM / Model Describe the DB schema and relationships Contain business orchestration, know HTTP Celery Task Transport the call into the queue, delegate to the service Contain business logic

docs.title: File structure in an app
docs.text:
apps/flood/
    ├── models.py          ← DB schema
    ├── selectors.py       ← Reading data (SELECT + optimization)
    ├── services.py        ← Business logic (CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE + side effects)
    ├── serializers.py     ← Input/Output contracts (HTTP ↔ domain)
    ├── views.py           ← Thin HTTP orchestrator
    ├── urls.py            ← URL routes
    ├── tasks.py           ← Celery tasks (transport, not logic)
    ├── filters.py         ← django-filter
    ├── permissions.py     ← DRF permissions
    ├── admin.py           ← Admin configuration
    ├── tests/
    └── migrations/

docs.title: Mental model: three boundaries
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TRANSPORT LAYER                                    │
│  views.py + serializers.py + tasks.py               │
│  "How data arrives and where it goes"               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  APPLICATION LAYER                                  │
│  services.py                                        │
│  "WHAT the system does"                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DATA LAYER                                         │
│  selectors.py + models.py + ORM                     │
│  "Where data comes from and how it is fetched"      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rule: each layer knows only about the layer directly beneath it. View → Service → Selector → ORM. No jumping across layers.

docs.title: Django Tasks — Celery and Asynchronous Tasks
docs.text: tasks.py is the transport layer for background operations. A task contains no business logic. It only queues the work and delegates execution to a Service.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Section What's inside Why Celery The problem of blocking operations Architecture Broker, Worker, Backend Anatomy of a Task Basic structure, rules Task = Transport Layer Why logic does not belong in a task on_commit A guarantee of consistency with the DB Retry and errors autoretry_for, max_retries, retry_backoff Idempotency Tasks that are safe to run again Common patterns Chains, Groups, Chords Configuration Configuring Celery in Django Anti-patterns What not to do and why Template A copy-paste template for a new task

docs.title: The problem of blocking operations
docs.text:
An HTTP request should complete within ~200–500 ms. Some operations take much longer:

Operation Time Problem Sending an email 1–3 s The client waits Processing a DEM file 30–120 s Nginx/client timeout ICESat-2 request to SlideRule 10–60 s The worker is blocked ML inference 5–30 s The client waits Generating a PDF report 3–10 s The client waits

docs.title: The solution: an asynchronous queue
docs.text:
HTTP Request
    │
    ▼
View → queues the task → immediately returns 202 Accepted
    │
    ▼ (independently, in the background)
Celery Worker → runs the task → stores the result

The client does not wait. The worker does not block HTTP requests.

docs.title: Celery + Django architecture
docs.text:
Django App
    │
    │  task.delay(args)   ← queues the task
    ▼
Redis (Broker)            ← message queue
    │
    │  receives the task
    ▼
Celery Worker             ← a separate process, runs the task
    │
    │  result (optional)
    ▼
Redis / PostgreSQL (Backend)   ← stores the result if needed
Component Role Broker Message queue (usually Redis or RabbitMQ) Worker A separate Python process that runs tasks Backend Result storage (Redis, PostgreSQL) — optional Beat Scheduler for periodic tasks (similar to cron)

docs.title: Basic structure
docs.text:
# apps/flood/tasks.py

from celery import shared_task


@shared_task
def notify_emergency_services_task(event_id: int) -> None:
    from apps.flood.selectors import flood_event_get_by_id
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_notify

    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_notify(event=event)

docs.title: Why the imports are inside the function
docs.text:
Module-level imports can cause circular dependencies when the Celery worker starts. Local imports inside the task function are a safe pattern.

# DANGEROUS — circular import when the worker starts
from apps.flood.services import flood_event_notify

@shared_task
def notify_task(event_id):
    ...

# SAFE — the import happens only when the task runs
@shared_task
def notify_task(event_id):
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_notify
    ...

docs.title: Passing arguments
docs.text:
# GOOD — pass simple types: int, str, list, dict
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id: int) -> None:
    ...

# Call
process_flood_task.delay(event_id=42)


# BAD — passing Python objects (they do not serialize reliably)
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event: FloodEvent) -> None:   # ❌
    ...

Celery serializes arguments via JSON. Pass IDs, strings, numbers — not ORM objects.

docs.title: Task = Transport Layer
docs.text: A task is a queue for delivering a call, not a place for logic.

docs.title: Anti-pattern: logic in the task
docs.text:
# BAD — all the logic in the task
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id: int):
    event = FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    event.status = 'processing'
    event.save()

    # ML pipeline
    result = run_ml_model(event.geometry)
    event.risk_level = result['risk']
    event.status = 'done'
    event.save()

    # Email
    send_mail(
        subject='Flood processed',
        message=f'Event {event_id} done',
        from_email='system@example.com',
        recipient_list=[event.created_by.email],
    )

Problems: - The logic cannot be called from a View or the CLI without Celery - It cannot be tested without starting a worker - On retry, the whole pipeline runs again

docs.title: Correct: the task delegates to a service
docs.text:
# GOOD — the task only transports the call
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id: int) -> None:
    from apps.flood.selectors import flood_event_get_by_id
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_process

    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_process(event=event)   # all the logic is in the service

# services.py — the logic is here, independent of Celery
@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_process(*, event: FloodEvent) -> FloodEvent:
    event.status = 'processing'
    event.save(update_fields=['status'])

    result = run_ml_model(event.geometry)
    event.risk_level = result['risk']
    event.status = 'done'
    event.save(update_fields=['risk_level', 'status'])

    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: send_flood_report_task.delay(event.id)
    )

    return event

The same flood_event_process can be called from a View, a management command, a test — without Celery.

docs.title: The problem without on_commit
docs.text:
@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_create(*, region_name: str, ...) -> FloodEvent:
    event = FloodEvent(...)
    event.save()

    # ❌ DANGEROUS:
    # The Celery worker may start BEFORE the transaction has closed.
    # The worker runs a SELECT — the record has not appeared in the DB yet.
    # The task fails with DoesNotExist.
    process_flood_task.delay(event.id)

    return event

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_create(*, region_name: str, ...) -> FloodEvent:
    event = FloodEvent(...)
    event.save()

    # ✅ SAFE:
    # The task is queued ONLY after a successful commit.
    # If the transaction is rolled back, the task will not start at all.
    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: process_flood_task.delay(event.id)
    )

    return event

Rule: any task.delay() inside @transaction.atomic must always go through on_commit.

docs.title: autoretry_for — automatic retry on exceptions
docs.text:
import httpx
from celery import shared_task


@shared_task(
    autoretry_for=(httpx.HTTPError, ConnectionError),  # which errors to retry on
    max_retries=3,                                      # maximum number of attempts
    retry_backoff=60,                                   # exponential delay: base of 60 s
    retry_jitter=False,                                 # no random spread of the delay
)
def fetch_sliderule_data_task(job_id: int) -> None:
    from apps.satellite.services import icesat2_job_fetch

    icesat2_job_fetch(job_id=job_id)

With retry_backoff=60 and retry_jitter=False the delays will be: 60s → 120s → 240s. (retry_backoff=True means a base of 1 s: 1s → 2s → 4s, and countdown is an argument of apply_async()/self.retry(), not an option of the @shared_task decorator.)

docs.title: Manual retry
docs.text:
@shared_task(bind=True, max_retries=5)
def process_dem_task(self, dem_id: int) -> None:
    from apps.dem.services import dem_process

    try:
        dem_process(dem_id=dem_id)
    except TemporaryProcessingError as exc:
        # Manual retry with a custom delay
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=30 * (self.request.retries + 1))

bind=True gives access to self — the current task instance with its metadata.

docs.title: Handling after all attempts
docs.text:
from celery.utils.log import get_task_logger

logger = get_task_logger(__name__)


@shared_task(
    autoretry_for=(Exception,),
    max_retries=3,
    default_retry_delay=60,
)
def critical_processing_task(job_id: int) -> None:
    from apps.flood.services import flood_job_process, flood_job_mark_failed

    try:
        flood_job_process(job_id=job_id)
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.error(f"Task failed for job_id={job_id}: {exc}")
        flood_job_mark_failed(job_id=job_id)
        raise   # lets Celery know the task failed → retry or FAILURE

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: A task may run several times (a network error, a retry, a duplicate message). Every task must be idempotent — running it again with the same arguments must not break the system.

docs.title: Non-idempotent (dangerous)
docs.text:
@shared_task
def send_welcome_email_task(user_id: int) -> None:
    user = User.objects.get(id=user_id)
    send_mail(subject='Ласкаво просимо!', ...)
    # On retry — the email will be sent a second time

docs.title: Idempotent (safe)
docs.text:
@shared_task
def send_welcome_email_task(user_id: int) -> None:
    user = User.objects.get(id=user_id)

    if user.welcome_email_sent:   # check before sending
        return

    send_mail(subject='Ласкаво просимо!', ...)

    User.objects.filter(id=user_id).update(welcome_email_sent=True)

docs.title: A simple delay — fire and forget
docs.text:
# Run the task in the background
process_flood_task.delay(event_id=42)

# With keyword arguments
process_flood_task.apply_async(kwargs={'event_id': 42})

docs.title: apply_async — extended options
docs.text:
from datetime import timedelta
from django.utils import timezone

# Delay execution by 10 minutes
process_flood_task.apply_async(
    kwargs={'event_id': 42},
    countdown=600,
)

# Run at a specific time
process_flood_task.apply_async(
    kwargs={'event_id': 42},
    eta=timezone.now() + timedelta(hours=1),
)

# Put it in a specific queue
process_flood_task.apply_async(
    kwargs={'event_id': 42},
    queue='high_priority',
)

pipeline = chain(
    fetch_sliderule_data_task.s(job_id=42),

    finalize_icesat2_job_task.s(job_id=42),

docs.title: Business logic in a task
docs.text:
# BAD
@shared_task
def process_task(event_id):
    event = FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    event.status = 'done'   # logic here
    event.save()

# GOOD
@shared_task
def process_task(event_id):
    from apps.flood.selectors import flood_event_get_by_id
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_complete
    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_complete(event=event)

docs.title: Passing an ORM object to a task
docs.text:
# BAD — an ORM object cannot be serialized to JSON (EncodeError), and with pickle it would carry stale state
process_task.delay(event=flood_event_object)

# GOOD — pass only the ID
process_task.delay(event_id=flood_event_object.id)

docs.title: task.delay() without on_commit inside a transaction
docs.text:
# BAD — a race condition with the DB
@transaction.atomic
def create_event():
    event = FloodEvent.objects.create(...)
    process_task.delay(event.id)   # the worker may not find the record

# GOOD
@transaction.atomic
def create_event():
    event = FloodEvent.objects.create(...)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: process_task.delay(event.id))

docs.title: Calling a task synchronously in a View
docs.text:
# BAD — blocks the HTTP response
result = process_task(event_id=42)   # runs synchronously

# GOOD — queues it and returns immediately
process_task.delay(event_id=42)
return Response({'status': 'queued'}, status=202)

docs.title: Table: what a task should and should not do
docs.text: Action Should it? Receive simple arguments (int, str) ✅ Run a SELECT to get an object ✅ (via a selector) Delegate to a service ✅ Log errors ✅ Be idempotent ✅ Contain business logic ❌ Receive ORM objects as arguments ❌ Open @transaction.atomic ❌ (that is the service's role) Return a Response ❌ Know about HTTP ❌

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
# apps/<app>/tasks.py

from celery import shared_task
from celery.utils.log import get_task_logger

logger = get_task_logger(__name__)


@shared_task(
    autoretry_for=(Exception,),
    max_retries=3,
    retry_backoff=60,
    retry_jitter=False,
)
def <model>_<action>_task(<model>_id: int) -> None:
    from apps.<app>.selectors import <model>_get_by_id
    from apps.<app>.services import <model>_<action>

    logger.info(f"Starting <action> for <model>_id={<model>_id}")

    obj = <model>_get_by_id(<model>_id=<model>_id)
    <model>_<action>(obj=obj)

    logger.info(f"Completed <action> for <model>_id={<model>_id}")

# Calling it from a service via on_commit
@transaction.atomic
def <model>_create(*, <field>: <type>) -> <Model>:
    obj = <Model>(<field>=<field>)
    obj.full_clean()
    obj.save()

    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: <model>_<action>_task.delay(<model>_id=obj.id)
    )

    return obj

docs.title: Django Services, Selectors & Serializers — The Business Logic Layer
docs.text: This document describes the production architecture of the Django business layer: where logic lives, who reads data, who writes it, and how HTTP never leaks into the domain.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Section What's inside Architecture map Where each layer lives Serializers InputSerializer, OutputSerializer, validate() Services Stateless functions, transactions, side effects Selectors CQRS-light, N+1, query abstraction Full data flow HTTP → View → Serializer → Service → Selector → DB Anti-patterns What not to do and why Responsibility table Who does / doesn't do what

docs.title: Architecture map
docs.text:
HTTP Request
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  View (views.py)            │  ← Thin HTTP orchestrator
│  Receives the request       │
│  Calls the serializer       │
│  Passes data to the Service │
│  Returns a Response         │
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  InputSerializer            │  ← Validation + transformation
│  (serializers.py)           │     of input data
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │ validated_data
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  Service (services.py)      │  ← Business logic + transaction
│  Orchestrates operations    │     + side effects
│  Knows nothing about HTTP   │
│  Calls the Selector         │
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
     ┌───────┴───────┐
     │               │
     ▼               ▼
┌──────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Selector │   │  Infrastructure      │
│(selectors│   │  (email, S3, Celery) │
│  .py)    │   └──────────────────────┘
│  Reading │
│  data    │
└────┬─────┘
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  ORM (models.py)            │  ← DB schema, relationships
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
         PostgreSQL
             │
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  OutputSerializer           │  ← Response formatting
│  (serializers.py)           │
└────────────┬────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
         HTTP Response

docs.title: The core principle
docs.text: A serializer is the boundary between HTTP and the domain. It knows nothing about business logic. It only: - takes raw HTTP data → validates it → returns validated_data - takes domain objects → formats them → returns JSON

docs.title: Anti-pattern: ModelSerializer as the single entry point
docs.text:
# BAD — ModelSerializer tightly couples HTTP to the DB schema
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = FloodEvent
        fields = '__all__'

The problem: a change in the model → a change in the API. Business rules end up in save(). There is no explicit contract.

docs.title: The right way: InputSerializer + OutputSerializer
docs.text:
# serializers.py

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    """Input data contract — independent of the model."""
    region_name = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
    severity_level = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['low', 'medium', 'high'])
    detected_at = serializers.DateTimeField()


class FloodEventOutputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    """Output data contract — what the client sees in the response."""
    id = serializers.IntegerField()
    region_name = serializers.CharField()
    severity_level = serializers.CharField()
    detected_at = serializers.DateTimeField()
    created_by_email = serializers.EmailField(source='created_by.email')

docs.title: The validate() method — Intercepting before validated_data
docs.text:
validate(self, data) is the hook for cross-field validation and transformation.

class FloodEventInputSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    region_name = serializers.CharField()
    # slug is generated by the server — read_only so DRF doesn't require it in the request
    slug = serializers.SlugField(read_only=True)

    def validate(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        # Auto-generate a field before validated_data
        data['slug'] = slugify(data['region_name'])
        return data

Important: server-generated fields must be declared with read_only=True (a plain Serializer has no Meta; Meta.read_only_fields is a ModelSerializer option), otherwise the serializer will fail validation before validate() is even called.

docs.title: Complex serialization — A pure Python function
docs.text:
When the response structure is too complex for an OutputSerializer:

# selectors.py or a separate module

def flood_feed_serialize(events: list) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Works around OutputSerializer limitations for complex joined structures.
    Builds the response in Python after an optimized SQL query.
    """
    region_cache = {}  # in-memory cache for repeated values

    result = []
    for event in events:
        region_id = event.region_id
        if region_id not in region_cache:
            region_cache[region_id] = event.region.display_name

        result.append({
            'id': event.id,
            'region': region_cache[region_id],
            'severity': event.severity_level,
            'detected_at': event.detected_at.isoformat(),
        })
    return result

The benefit: full control over the SQL footprint, no N+1 from nested serializers.

docs.title: Mapping domain errors → HTTP
docs.text:
Domain code raises django.core.exceptions.ValidationError. DRF expects rest_framework.exceptions.ValidationError.

The solution is a custom exception handler:

# shared/exceptions/handlers.py

from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError as DjangoValidationError
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
from rest_framework.exceptions import ValidationError as DRFValidationError
from rest_framework.serializers import as_serializer_error


def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
    if isinstance(exc, DjangoValidationError):
        exc = DRFValidationError(detail=as_serializer_error(exc))

    return exception_handler(exc, context)

# settings.py
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'shared.exceptions.handlers.custom_exception_handler',
}

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
A Service is a transport-agnostic business function. It knows nothing about HTTP, does not return a Response, and does not import DRF. The same Service is called from:

  • a REST API View
  • a Celery Task
  • a Django Management Command
  • a WebSocket consumer
  • a Pytest test

docs.title: Anatomy of a stateless service
docs.text:
# apps/flood/services.py

from django.db import transaction
from apps.flood.models import FloodEvent
from apps.flood.tasks import notify_emergency_services_task


@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_create(
    *,                              # keyword-only — protects against argument-order mistakes
    region_name: str,
    severity_level: str,
    detected_at,
    created_by,
) -> FloodEvent:
    """
    The single place where FloodEvent creation logic lives.
    Does not return a Response — returns a domain object.
    """
    event = FloodEvent(
        region_name=region_name,
        severity_level=severity_level,
        detected_at=detected_at,
        created_by=created_by,
    )
    event.full_clean()   # Django validation at the domain level
    event.save()

    # Side effect — only after a successful commit
    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: notify_emergency_services_task.delay(event.id)
    )

    return event

The * before the arguments is Python syntax for keyword-only parameters. flood_event_create(region_name="Kyiv", severity_level="high", ...) — explicit and safe during refactoring.

docs.title: Transactions and Side Effects
docs.text:
A critical rule: side effects (email, Celery task) run only after a successful commit.

# apps/flood/services.py

@transaction.atomic
def flood_event_complete_processing(*, event: FloodEvent) -> FloodEvent:
    # 1. DB mutation
    event.status = 'processed'
    event.save(update_fields=['status'])

    # 2. Side effect — runs ONLY if the transaction closed without an error
    transaction.on_commit(
        lambda: notify_emergency_services_task.delay(event.id)
    )

    return event

If you write notify_emergency_services_task.delay(event.id) without on_commit, Celery may receive the task before the record appears in the DB.

docs.title: A Celery Task is also a transport layer
docs.text:
# apps/flood/tasks.py

@shared_task
def notify_emergency_services_task(event_id: int):
    """A task is a delivery queue, not a place for logic."""
    from apps.flood.selectors import flood_event_get_by_id
    from apps.flood.services import flood_event_notify

    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_notify(event=event)   # the logic lives in the service

docs.title: Full example: View + Service
docs.text:
# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventCreateAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = FloodEventInputSerializer(data=request.data)
        serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)

        event = flood_event_create(
            **serializer.validated_data,
            created_by=request.user,
        )

        output = FloodEventOutputSerializer(event)
        return Response(output.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)

View: 6 lines. All the logic is in the service.

docs.title: The principle (CQRS-light)
docs.text:
The architecture distinguishes two fundamentally different operations:

Services Selectors What they do Mutate data, orchestrate business operations Read data Operation types CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, side effects SELECT Transactions @transaction.atomic No Scaling under load Vertical scaling Horizontal (read replicas)

docs.title: Why not a model property?
docs.text:
# BAD — a hidden query inside a Python loop → N+1
class FloodEvent(models.Model):
    @property
    def region_display(self):
        return self.region.display_name  # a SELECT every time in the loop

# GOOD — an optimized query in a selector
def flood_events_get_list(*, user) -> QuerySet:
    return (
        FloodEvent.objects
        .filter(created_by=user)
        .select_related('region')      # one JOIN instead of N queries
        .prefetch_related('tags')      # batched prefetch for M2M
        .annotate(
            comment_count=Count('comments')
        )
        .order_by('-detected_at')
    )

docs.title: Anatomy of a selector
docs.text:
# apps/flood/selectors.py

def flood_event_get_by_id(*, event_id: int) -> FloodEvent:
    """Basic selector — returns the object or raises FloodEvent.DoesNotExist (the View turns it into a 404)."""
    try:
        return FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    except FloodEvent.DoesNotExist:
        raise FloodEvent.DoesNotExist(f"FloodEvent {event_id} не знайдено")


def flood_events_get_visible_for(*, user) -> QuerySet:
    """
    Hides SQL details behind a domain name.
    Returns a QuerySet — the View can add pagination or filtering.
    """
    return (
        FloodEvent.objects
        .filter(
            Q(created_by=user) | Q(is_public=True)
        )
        .select_related('region', 'created_by')
        .order_by('-detected_at')
    )

docs.title: QuerySet vs evaluated list
docs.text:
Selectors can return:

Returns When to use QuerySet The View can add .filter(), pagination, django_filters list[dict] When complex Python optimization is needed before returning 
# A selector that returns a QuerySet — the View adds pagination
def flood_events_get_list() -> QuerySet:
    return FloodEvent.objects.all().select_related('region')

# In the View:
queryset = flood_events_get_list()
page = self.paginate_queryset(queryset)   # DRF pagination — safe

docs.title: Selector + django-filter without leaking the ORM into the View
docs.text:
# apps/flood/filters.py

import django_filters
from apps.flood.models import FloodEvent

class FloodEventFilter(django_filters.FilterSet):
    severity = django_filters.ChoiceFilter(choices=FloodEvent.SEVERITY_CHOICES)
    after = django_filters.DateTimeFilter(field_name='detected_at', lookup_expr='gte')

    class Meta:
        model = FloodEvent
        fields = ['severity', 'after']

# apps/flood/views.py

class FloodEventListAPIView(ListAPIView):

    def get_queryset(self):
        qs = flood_events_get_visible_for(user=self.request.user)  # selector
        return FloodEventFilter(self.request.GET, queryset=qs).qs  # filtering

The View doesn't know SQL. The Selector doesn't know the request filters. The Filter doesn't know the business rules.

docs.title: Business logic in serializer.save()
docs.text:
# BAD
class FloodEventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    def save(self):
        self.instance.notify_emergency_services()  # business logic in the serializer
        super().save()

# GOOD
# View → Service → a separate notification call
event = flood_event_create(**validated_data)
flood_event_notify(event=event)

docs.title: HTTP objects in a service
docs.text:
# BAD
def process_flood(request):
    user = request.user       # the Service knows about the HTTP request
    data = request.data

# GOOD
def flood_event_create(*, region_name: str, created_by):
    pass   # the Service receives already-parsed data

docs.title: ORM in the View
docs.text:
# BAD
class FloodListView(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        events = FloodEvent.objects.filter(
            created_by=request.user
        ).select_related('region')   # ORM directly in the View

# GOOD
class FloodListView(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        events = flood_events_get_visible_for(user=request.user)  # Selector

docs.title: Business logic in a Celery task
docs.text:
# BAD
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id):
    event = FloodEvent.objects.get(id=event_id)
    event.status = 'processed'
    event.save()
    send_email(event.created_by.email, ...)   # logic directly in the task

# GOOD
@shared_task
def process_flood_task(event_id):
    event = flood_event_get_by_id(event_id=event_id)
    flood_event_complete_processing(event=event)   # delegation to the service

docs.title: Responsibility table
docs.text: Layer Should Should NOT View Handle HTTP, call the serializer and the service, return a Response Know SQL, contain business logic, make ORM queries InputSerializer Validate types and formats, transform data, return validated_data Save to the DB, contain business rules OutputSerializer Format a domain object into a JSON structure Query the DB, contain logic Service Orchestrate business operations, open transactions, trigger side effects Know HTTP, import DRF, return a Response Selector Read data from the DB, optimize queries (select_related, annotate) Mutate data, contain business logic ORM / Model Describe the DB schema and relationships Contain business orchestration, know HTTP Celery Task Transport the call into the queue, delegate to the service Contain business logic

docs.title: File structure in an app
docs.text:
apps/flood/
    ├── models.py          ← DB schema
    ├── selectors.py       ← Reading data (SELECT + optimization)
    ├── services.py        ← Business logic (CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE + side effects)
    ├── serializers.py     ← Input/Output contracts (HTTP ↔ domain)
    ├── views.py           ← Thin HTTP orchestrator
    ├── urls.py            ← URL routes
    ├── tasks.py           ← Celery tasks (transport, not logic)
    ├── filters.py         ← django-filter
    ├── permissions.py     ← DRF permissions
    ├── admin.py           ← Admin configuration
    ├── tests/
    └── migrations/

docs.title: Mental model: three boundaries
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TRANSPORT LAYER                                    │
│  views.py + serializers.py + tasks.py               │
│  "How data arrives and where it goes"               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  APPLICATION LAYER                                  │
│  services.py                                        │
│  "WHAT the system does"                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DATA LAYER                                         │
│  selectors.py + models.py + ORM                     │
│  "Where data comes from and how it's fetched"       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The rule: each layer knows only about the layer directly beneath it. View → Service → Selector → ORM. No skipping layers.

docs.title: Part VII. Authentication and Security
docs.text:
Authentication (AuthN): who are you? → credential check → session. Authorization (AuthZ): what are you allowed to do? → object-level permissions.

@login_required is only AuthN. Without an object-level permission → an IDOR vulnerability.

Prerequisites: Parts II, VI. Level: Intermediate → Advanced.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Document What we'll learn Authentication authenticate(), login(), logout(), request.user, password hashing Sessions session engine, SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE, lifecycle Permissions @login_required, object-level permission, Q-scoped QuerySet, IDOR Django security architecture middleware order, CSRF, clickjacking, XSS, SQL injection Security foundations CIA triad, threat modeling, principle of least privilege Common mistakes @login_required ≠ permission, public pk, mass assignment OWASP Top 10 A01–A10: Injection, Broken Auth, XSS, IDOR, Misconfig, ... Zero Trust "never trust, always verify", network perimeter myth SIEM security event logging, incident analysis

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference):

# ❌ VULNERABLE: any logged-in user can read someone else's note
@login_required
def note_detail(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)  # pk=42 → someone else's note!
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

# ✅ SAFE: Q-scoped queryset
@login_required
def note_detail(request, pk):
    note = selectors.get_note_detail(user=request.user, note_id=pk)
    if not note:
        raise Http404
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

A Q-filter in the selector — protection against IDOR:

# selectors.py
def get_note_detail(user, note_id):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    return Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups),
        pk=note_id
    ).select_related('notebook', 'group').prefetch_related('tags').first()

def get_note_for_edit(user, pk):
    # edit/delete — owner only (not group members)
    return Note.objects.filter(user=user, pk=pk).first()

Session lifecycle:

POST /accounts/login/ (username, password)
  → authenticate() → User or None
  → login(request, user)
      → create session: {_auth_user_id: 42, ...} → DB/cache
      → Set-Cookie: sessionid=abc123; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
  → redirect /

GET /notes/ (Cookie: sessionid=abc123)
  → SessionMiddleware: session['_auth_user_id'] = 42
  → AuthenticationMiddleware: request.user = User(pk=42)
  → @login_required → OK

Notes Chat App permission matrix:

Object Read Edit/Delete Note owner OR group member owner only Notebook / Tag owner owner TodoList owner OR shared_with owner ShoppingList owner OR shared_with OR group owner ChatMessage group members (WS) —

Security settings in Notes Chat App:

# settings.py
SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True    # JS cannot read the cookie
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'  # CSRF protection via the cookie
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE      = True    # CSRF cookie over HTTPS only
X_FRAME_OPTIONS         = 'DENY'  # clickjacking protection
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT     = True    # HTTP → HTTPS redirect (prod)

WebSocket authentication:

# consumers.py
async def connect(self):
    user = self.scope['user']
    if not user.is_authenticated:
        await self.close()      # ← anonymous → rejected
        return
    group_pk = self.scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk']
    is_member = await database_sync_to_async(self.check_membership)(group_pk, user)
    if not is_member:
        await self.close()      # ← not a group member → rejected
        return
    await self.accept()

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
• What is the difference between AuthN and AuthZ? Which of them does @login_required check?
  • What is IDOR? Give an example of vulnerable code and of the fixed version.
  • Why does Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups) protect against IDOR when reading?
  • Why is only Q(user=user) used for editing/deleting, without Q(group...)?
  • What is HttpOnly on a cookie? Which attack does it protect against?
