docs.title: SIEM — Security Information and Event Management Systems
docs.text:
SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is a tool that collects logs from across your server, analyzes them in real time and alerts the administrator about suspicious activity.

Analogy: Imagine your house has 100 video cameras. A SIEM is the security guard who watches all the screens at once and presses the alarm button when they notice something suspicious.

docs.title: What is a SIEM and why do you need it?
docs.text:
Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems are designed for: - Collecting logs from various sources (Django, nginx, PostgreSQL, system logs) - Storing and indexing large volumes of data - Analysis and correlation — searching for suspicious patterns - Threat detection in real time

Popular SIEM platforms: - Splunk — the most popular commercial SIEM - ELK Stack (Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana) — free and open-source - IBM QRadar — enterprise level - LogRhythm — for SOC teams (Security Operations Center)

docs.title: Why isn't simply storing logs locally enough?
docs.text:
Problem 1: An attacker breached the server → deleted the log files → no evidence
Problem 2: A 10 GB log file → impossible to read by hand
Problem 3: A Docker container restarted → all the logs are gone
Problem 4: You need to compare Django + nginx + PostgreSQL logs → different files

Solution: A SIEM collects everything in one place and analyzes it automatically

docs.title: Log shipping architecture: Django → SIEM
docs.text:
[Django App]
    ↓ (Python logging → SysLogHandler)
[Syslog Daemon (rsyslog)] ← /dev/log socket
    ↓ (stunnel: SSL/TLS encryption)
[SIEM Server (Splunk/ELK)]
    ↓
[Dashboards + Alerts]

docs.title: Step 1: Configuring Django logging (settings.py)
docs.text:
Instead of writing to a local file, we send logs to the system syslog:

# settings.py

import logging

LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'disable_existing_loggers': False,

    'formatters': {
        'security': {
            # Format: [level] [time] [module] message
            'format': '[%(levelname)s] %(asctime)s %(name)s: %(message)s',
        },
    },

    'handlers': {
        # Send to the system syslog (/dev/log)
        'syslog': {
            'class': 'logging.handlers.SysLogHandler',
            'address': '/dev/log',           # Linux syslog socket
            'facility': 'local7',            # category for SIEM filtering
            'formatter': 'security',
        },
        # Additionally — to the console during development
        'console': {
            'class': 'logging.StreamHandler',
            'formatter': 'security',
        },
    },

    'loggers': {
        # Django's built-in security logger
        'django.security': {
            'handlers': ['syslog', 'console'],
            'level': 'WARNING',
            'propagate': False,
        },
        # Our custom security logger
        'security': {
            'handlers': ['syslog', 'console'],
            'level': 'INFO',
            'propagate': False,
        },
    },
}

docs.title: Step 2: Which events should you log?
2.1. Failed login attempts (Brute-Force Detection)
docs.text:
# views.py
import logging
security_log = logging.getLogger('security')

def login_view(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = AuthenticationForm(request, data=request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            user = form.get_user()
            login(request, user)
            security_log.info(
                f"LOGIN_SUCCESS user_id={user.pk} username={user.username} "
                f"ip={request.META.get('REMOTE_ADDR')}"
            )
        else:
            security_log.warning(
                f"LOGIN_FAILED username={request.POST.get('username', 'unknown')} "
                f"ip={request.META.get('REMOTE_ADDR')}"
            )

A SIEM rule: If LOGIN_FAILED occurs > 5 times within 1 minute from one IP → alert!

docs.title: 2.2. Unauthorized access attempts (IDOR Detection)
docs.text:
from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied

@login_required
def note_edit(request, pk):
    try:
        note = Note.objects.get(pk=pk)
    except Note.DoesNotExist:
        raise Http404

    # Record the attempt to access someone else's resource
    if note.user != request.user:
        security_log.warning(
            f"UNAUTHORIZED_ACCESS user_id={request.user.pk} "
            f"tried to access note_id={pk} owned_by={note.user_id} "
            f"ip={request.META.get('REMOTE_ADDR')}"
        )
        raise PermissionDenied

    # ... rest of the view

docs.title: 2.3. Privileged actions (Audit Trail)
docs.text:
# We log deletions, permission changes, group operations
@login_required
def note_delete(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)
    if request.method == 'POST':
        security_log.info(
            f"NOTE_DELETED user_id={request.user.pk} note_id={pk} "
            f"note_title={note.title[:50]!r}"
        )
        note.delete()

docs.title: Step 3: Configuring the Syslog Daemon
docs.text:
rsyslog is a system daemon that collects logs from applications.

# /etc/rsyslog.conf or /etc/rsyslog.d/django.conf

# Receive logs from Django (via /dev/log)
local7.*    /var/log/django-security.log

# Forward to the SIEM server (`@` = UDP, port 514, unencrypted)
local7.*    @log.mycompany.com:514

# Variant for stunnel from step 4: `@@` = TCP, to the local tunnel entry
# local7.*    @@127.0.0.1:514

# Restart rsyslog after changes:
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog

docs.title: Step 4: Encrypting log transport (stunnel)
docs.text:
Without encryption, logs travel across the network in plain text! An attacker inside the network can intercept them.

stunnel creates an SSL/TLS tunnel for any TCP connection:

# Installation:
sudo apt install stunnel4

# /etc/stunnel/siem.conf:
[siem-forward]
client = yes
accept = 127.0.0.1:514    # local TCP port (rsyslog writes here via @@)
connect = siem.company.com:6514  # SIEM server (TLS port)
cert = /etc/ssl/certs/client.pem

Without stunnel:  Django → rsyslog → [open network] → SIEM  ← DANGEROUS
With stunnel:     Django → rsyslog → stunnel (SSL) → [encrypted] → SIEM

docs.title: Step 5: Rules and Alerts in the SIEM
docs.text:
Once the logs arrive in the SIEM, we configure automatic rules:

Rule Condition Action Brute-Force LOGIN_FAILED > 5 within 60 sec from one IP Email to the administrator IDOR Attack UNAUTHORIZED_ACCESS > 3 within 5 min Block the IP (via SOAR) Privilege Escalation GROUP_ADDED for a new admin Immediate alert After-Hours Access Login between 2:00-6:00 Suspicious activity Mass Deletion NOTE_DELETED > 10 within 1 min Possible data leak

SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) — automated incident response: 

The SIEM detected brute force
    ↓
SOAR automatically:
    1. Blocks the IP at the nginx level
    2. Sends an SMS to the administrator
    3. Opens a ticket in Jira
    4. Saves the IP to a blacklist

docs.title: ELK Stack — a free alternative for learning
docs.text:
ELK = Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana

Django → rsyslog → Logstash (parsing) → Elasticsearch (storage) → Kibana (dashboards)

Kibana lets you build dashboards: - A chart of login attempts over time - A map of attackers' IP addresses - The top 10 most frequent authorization errors

docs.title: Where is this in our project?
docs.text:
In crispy_notes_chat_app a SIEM isn't connected yet. For a learning project this is enough:

# settings.py — minimal security logging:
LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'handlers': {
        'console': {'class': 'logging.StreamHandler'},
    },
    'loggers': {
        'django.security': {
            'handlers': ['console'],
            'level': 'WARNING',
        },
    },
}

For production, connect ELK or Splunk following the scheme above.

docs.title: Zero Trust Architecture
docs.text:
"Never trust, always verify" — no user, device or network should be considered safe just because it is "inside" the system.

Analogy: Even if an employee passes through the office turnstile every day, every time they open the door to the server room the system checks their card again. That's Zero Trust.

docs.title: What is Zero Trust?
docs.text:
Zero Trust Architecture is a security philosophy and design pattern that rejects the notion of "implicit trust" based on: - A user or device being inside the internal network - A previous successful authentication

The principle: "never trust, always verify" — explicit confirmation of identity and permissions for every request to the system.

Important: Zero Trust Architecture isn't a product you can "buy and install". It's an approach to system design where every component distrusts the others by default.

docs.title: 6 key principles of Zero Trust
docs.text:
1. Continuous Verification

Simply having a token or having logged in doesn't mean the user can be trusted permanently. Every privileged action must go through a check. Blind trust in a token is a serious vulnerability.

2. Least Privilege

Every user, device or script gets access only to what they absolutely need. If a manager needs access to the cafeteria menu, they shouldn't see the company's customer database.

3. Strict identity management (IAM)

The system must clearly know EVERYONE: people, devices, programs. Tactics: - MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication): password + smartphone + biometrics - SSO (Single Sign-On): one trusted authentication provider

4. Micro-segmentation

Instead of general access to the whole environment — strict rules for each department, user and device. If an attacker gains access to one resource, they can't automatically reach the others.

5. Continuous Monitoring

Log and inspect all network traffic. Watch all entities to see whether they exceed their authority.

6. Framework-level protection

Correct use of built-in security mechanisms (CSRF protection in Django, parameterized ORM queries) is part of the Zero Trust approach.

docs.title: 1. Continuous authorization (Continuous Verification)
docs.text:
Zero Trust requires checking every call to a privileged function, not just a one-time login.

Having a valid token doesn't mean unconditional trust — the user's status may have changed.

Django implementation: 

# NOT enough — checking only at login:
@login_required
def edit_note(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)  # IDOR vulnerability!

# Zero Trust — checking on every request:
@login_required
@permission_required('notes_app.change_note')
def edit_note(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)  # ← explicit check

docs.title: 2. Object-Level Permissions
docs.text:
Global permissions aren't enough for Zero Trust. You need to check ownership of the specific object.

The IDOR problem: 

# Alice knows the URL: /notes/42/edit/
# Note 42 belongs to Bob. Without a check:
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=42)   # Alice gets access!

# Zero Trust — checking the owner:
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=42, user=request.user)  # 404 for Alice

For group access: 

from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from django.db.models import Q

def check_note_access(note, user):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    has_access = (
        note.user == user or                          # owner
        (note.group and note.group in user_groups)    # group member
    )
    if not has_access:
        raise PermissionDenied

Recommendation: Use a UUID instead of an auto-incrementing integer PK for important objects — the next ID can't be guessed.

docs.title: 3. Strict data validation (Zero Trust Input)
docs.text:
No client-side input can be trusted implicitly.

# NOT enough — frontend validation only:
# <input type="number" min="1" max="100">  ← an attacker bypasses it

# Zero Trust — server-side validation in the model:
class Note(models.Model):
    priority = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(
        validators=[MinValueValidator(1), MaxValueValidator(4)]
    )

    def clean(self):
        if self.priority not in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
            raise ValidationError("Invalid priority")

# or in the form:
class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def clean_title(self):
        title = self.cleaned_data['title'].strip()
        if len(title) < 3:
            raise forms.ValidationError("The title is too short.")
        return title

docs.title: 4. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
docs.text:
Zero Trust relies heavily on MFA — ordinary passwords are easily compromised.

# Installation:
pip install django-two-factor-auth

# settings.py:
INSTALLED_APPS += ['two_factor']
LOGIN_URL = 'two_factor:login'
TWO_FACTOR_PATCH_ADMIN = True

# urls.py:
from two_factor.urls import urlpatterns as tf_urls
urlpatterns = [path('', include(tf_urls)), ...]

Factors: - Knowledge — a password - Possession — an OTP code (Google Authenticator, SMS) - Inherence — biometrics (FaceID, fingerprint)

docs.title: 5. Micro-segmentation and Monitoring
docs.text:
Zero Trust uses continuous monitoring to detect anomalies.

# settings.py — extended security logging:
LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'disable_existing_loggers': False,
    'handlers': {
        'security_file': {
            'class': 'logging.FileHandler',
            'filename': 'logs/security.log',
        },
        'console': {'class': 'logging.StreamHandler'},
    },
    'loggers': {
        'django.security': {
            'handlers': ['security_file', 'console'],
            'level': 'WARNING',
            'propagate': False,
        },
    },
}

# views.py — logging privileged actions:
import logging
security_log = logging.getLogger('django.security')

@login_required
def note_delete(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)
    if request.method == 'POST':
        security_log.warning(
            f"User {request.user.pk} deleted note {pk}",
            extra={'request': request}
        )
        note.delete()

docs.title: 6. Continuous Verification (In detail)
docs.text: Continuous Verification is a key component of Zero Trust. The mere fact of a previous authentication isn't enough. The system must check every call to a privileged function.

docs.title: 6.1 Centralized access checks
docs.text:
To avoid adding checks by hand in every function, centralize the logic:

# DRF: a custom permission class
from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

class IsOwner(BasePermission):
    def has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj):
        return obj.user == request.user

# Globally in settings.py:
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': ['notes_app.permissions.IsOwner'],
}

# For regular views — use mixins:
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin, PermissionRequiredMixin

class NoteUpdateView(LoginRequiredMixin, PermissionRequiredMixin, UpdateView):
    permission_required = 'notes_app.change_note'
    # Authorization runs BEFORE the business logic

docs.title: 6.2 Middleware as a global shield
docs.text:
A custom Middleware that blocks all unprotected endpoints:

# notes_app/middleware.py
class RequireAuthMiddleware:
    PUBLIC_URLS = ['/accounts/login/', '/accounts/register/', '/']

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        if request.path not in self.PUBLIC_URLS:
            if not request.user.is_authenticated:
                from django.shortcuts import redirect
                return redirect('login')
        return self.get_response(request)

docs.title: 6.3 Validating JWT token state (for APIs)
docs.text:
The JWT problem: a token stays valid until it expires, even if the user has been blocked.

# Solution: a blacklist of revoked refresh tokens in the DB (token_blacklist tables, requires migrate)
# pip install djangorestframework-simplejwt[crypto]

# settings.py:
INSTALLED_APPS += ['rest_framework_simplejwt.token_blacklist']

# On logout — add the token to the blacklist:
from rest_framework_simplejwt.tokens import RefreshToken

def logout_api(request):
    refresh_token = request.data.get('refresh')
    token = RefreshToken(refresh_token)
    token.blacklist()   # DB: a row in the BlacklistedToken table

docs.title: 6.4 Object-level checks (IDOR Prevention)
docs.text:
# BAD — we only check "whether there's a role":
@login_required
def edit_note(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)   # IDOR! Alice edits Bob's note

# GOOD — we check the permission for the specific object:
@login_required
def edit_note(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
    if note.user != request.user:
        raise PermissionDenied   # Continuous verification!
    # ...

docs.title: 6.5 Protection against Mass Assignment
docs.text:
# Attack: POST {'is_admin': True} → a role change

# NOT safe:
class UserForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = User
        fields = '__all__'  # ← an attacker can send is_superuser=True!

# SAFE — an explicit whitelist of fields:
class UserProfileForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = UserProfile
        fields = ['display_name', 'bio', 'timezone']  # ← only the allowed ones

docs.title: Zero Trust in our project
docs.text: ZT principle Implementation in crispy_notes_chat_app Continuous Verification @login_required on every view Object-Level Permissions get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user) Input Validation NoteForm.clean_*(), MinValueValidator in models Least Privilege user.groups.all() filtering for Group sharing Audit Logging (for extension) django.security logger MFA (for extension) django-two-factor-auth

docs.title: Part VIII. Testing and Quality
docs.text:
Tests turn a learning project into a system you can change without fear. Notes Chat App has ~205 tests in 6 files — from unit tests to Selenium E2E.

Prerequisites: Parts II–VII. Level: Intermediate → Advanced.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Document What we will learn Testing foundations AAA pattern, the test pyramid, what to test, what to mock unittest TestCase, setUp, assert*, subTest, test isolation pytest fixtures, parametrize, plugins, pytest-django Django Testing Client, force_login, RequestFactory, TestCase vs TransactionTestCase Mocking unittest.mock, patch, MagicMock, spy, when to mock Test Data setUp, factories, fixtures, seed_demo_data Selenium StaticLiveServerTestCase, WebDriver, find_element, wait strategies CI/CD GitHub Actions, jobs, matrix, artifact upload, secrets Testing in practice an end-to-end example of a test suite for a Django project

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
The Notes Chat App test pyramid:

         E2E (Selenium)         ← 10 tests, slow, brittle
        Consumer Tests           ← 30 tests, TransactionTestCase!
       View Tests (Client)       ← 70 tests, status codes, redirects
      Service/Form Tests         ← 65 tests, no HTTP
    Model Tests                  ← 30 tests, constraints, __str__

Test file structure:

notes_app/tests/
├── test_models.py      ← TestCase: constraints, __str__, CASCADE
├── test_services.py    ← TestCase: return value + persistence
├── test_forms.py       ← TestCase: is_valid, invalid data, clean_*
├── test_views.py       ← TestCase: Client.force_login, status codes, IDOR
├── test_consumers.py   ← TransactionTestCase: WebsocketCommunicator
└── test_selenium.py    ← StaticLiveServerTestCase: real browser

A typical service test (AAA):

class CreateNoteTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass')

    def test_create_note_returns_note_instance(self):
        # Arrange
        title, content = 'Test', 'Body'
        # Act
        note = services.create_note(user=self.user, title=title, content=content)
        # Assert
        self.assertIsInstance(note, Note)
        self.assertEqual(note.title, title)

    def test_create_note_persists_to_db(self):
        services.create_note(user=self.user, title='Test', content='')
        self.assertEqual(Note.objects.filter(user=self.user).count(), 1)

An IDOR test in test_views.py:

def test_alice_cannot_read_bobs_note(self):
    bob  = User.objects.create_user('bob', password='pass')
    note = Note.objects.create(user=bob, title='Secret')

    self.client.force_login(self.user)  # alice logged in
    response = self.client.get(reverse('note_detail', args=[note.pk]))

    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)   # not 200!

CRITICAL: TransactionTestCase for consumer tests:

# ❌ TestCase for a consumer → setUp objects "disappear"
# Reason: TestCase wraps each test in a transaction → rollback afterwards.
# The async consumer reads the DB from a separate worker thread —
# that thread cannot see TestCase's uncommitted transaction.

# ✅ ALWAYS use TransactionTestCase for WebSocket tests
class GroupChatConsumerTest(TransactionTestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user  = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass')
        self.group = Group.objects.create(name='Chat')
        self.group.user_set.add(self.user)

    async def test_member_can_connect(self):
        comm = _make_communicator(self.group.pk, self.user)
        connected, _ = await comm.connect()
        self.assertTrue(connected)
        await comm.disconnect()

Running the tests:

# unit + integration + consumer
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test \
  notes_app.tests.test_models notes_app.tests.test_services \
  notes_app.tests.test_forms notes_app.tests.test_views \
  notes_app.tests.test_consumers -v 2

# Selenium (requires a running stack)
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2

GitHub Actions CI:

# .github/workflows/django-tests.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      db:    # PostgreSQL
      redis: # Redis channel layer
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test ...

docs.title: CI/CD and GitHub Actions: automated testing of a Django project
docs.text: This file is a self-contained reference on CI/CD in the context of Django Testing. It explains: what CI/CD is, how GitHub Actions works, how to read the existing django-tests.yml in our project, and how all of this relates to the tests you are already writing.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Concepts - 1. The problem CI/CD solves - 2. What CI/CD is - 3. Continuous Integration vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment

GitHub Actions - 4. GitHub Actions components - 5. How to read a YAML workflow - 6. Our django-tests.yml — line by line - 7. Events — when to run - 8. Jobs and Steps — what runs and how - 9. Actions — ready-made building blocks - 10. Runners — where the code runs

Practice - 11. How to view results on GitHub - 12. CI/CD and the testing pyramid - 13. GitHub Pages — publishing a static site - 14. Common errors and how to read them - 15. Self-check questions

docs.title: 1. The problem CI/CD solves
docs.text:
Imagine this situation. You wrote a function create_note_for_user. It passed the local tests. You did git push. Two hours later it turns out that the form on the registration page no longer saves data.

How does that happen? You didn't touch the form. But somewhere a change in the service layer pulled in a dependency you didn't see.

Without automation, this chain looks like this:

Developer A         Developer B         Deploy to production
writes feature ─┐   writes feature ─┐
                │                   │
                └── manual merge ───┴── manual tests ── manual deploy
                   (merge conflicts!)  (someone forgot)  (2+ hrs of rituals)

And then there's a bug in production. And nobody knows exactly whose change caused it.

This is exactly what CI/CD solves: every git push automatically runs the full test suite on a clean server. If the tests pass, the code is safe to merge. If they fail, the developer sees it before the code ever reaches main.

docs.title: 2. What CI/CD is
docs.text:
CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Deployment).

It is not a single tool or a single button. It is a way of organizing a team's work so that testing and deployment happen automatically after every change.

In short:

Abbreviation Name What it does CI Continuous Integration Automatically builds and tests the code after every push CD Continuous Delivery Automatically prepares a build for production — but a human deploys it CD Continuous Deployment Automatically deploys to production without human involvement

The difference between Delivery and Deployment comes down to one word: human. In Delivery, a human clicks the confirm button. In Deployment, nobody does.

An important idea:

CI/CD is not about tools. It is about tests running automatically and feedback arriving quickly.

docs.title: 3. Continuous Integration vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
docs.text:
A detailed diagram:

flowchart LR
    subgraph CI["Continuous Integration"]
        direction LR
        A[git push] --> B["Build<br>Install deps"]
        B --> C["Lint<br>Type check"]
        C --> D["Unit Tests<br>Integration Tests"]
        D --> E{Passed?}
        E -- yes --> F[Notify: OK]
        E -- no --> G["Block PR<br>Notify: Failed"]
    end

    subgraph DELIVERY["Continuous Delivery"]
        direction LR
        H[Artifact ready] --> I[Deploy: Staging]
        I --> J[Smoke Tests]
        J --> K{OK?}
        K -- yes --> L[Human approves]
        L --> M[Deploy: Production]
        K -- no --> N[Rollback Staging]
    end

    subgraph DEPLOYMENT["Continuous Deployment"]
        direction LR
        O[Artifact ready] --> P[Deploy: Staging]
        P --> Q[Automated Tests]
        Q --> R{OK?}
        R -- yes --> S[Auto Deploy: Production]
        R -- no --> T[Auto Rollback]
    end

    CI --> DELIVERY
    CI --> DEPLOYMENT

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,D,H,I,J,O,P,Q step;
    class E,K,R decision;
    class F,M,S success;
    class G,N,T error;
    class L warning;

Where is our notes_chat_app right now? At the CI level: every push to main runs the tests. Deployment is not automated yet — but this is the first and most important step.

docs.title: 4. GitHub Actions components
docs.text:
GitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform built right into GitHub. No third-party services are needed.

The component hierarchy:

Repository
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── django-tests.yml     ← Workflow
            │
            ├── on: push         ← Event (trigger)
            │
            └── jobs:
                ├── unit-and-integration:  ← Job 1
                │   ├── step 1   ← Step: checkout
                │   ├── step 2   ← Step: setup-python
                │   └── step 3   ← Step: manage.py test
                │
                └── selenium-e2e:  ← Job 2 (needs: unit-and-integration)
                    ├── step 1
                    └── step 2
Component What it is Analogy Workflow The whole scenario in a YAML file The script of a play Event The trigger that starts the workflow The curtain rises Job A set of steps on one runner An act of the play Step One command or action A single scene Action A ready-made reusable step A prop from a store Runner The server where the code runs The stage

docs.title: 5. How to read a YAML workflow
docs.text:
A workflow is a YAML file. Here is a minimal example with explanations:

name: Django Tests          # Name (shown in GitHub → Actions)

on:                         # When to run
  push:
    branches: [main]        # On push to main

jobs:                       # What to do
  test:                     # Job name
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest  # On which OS

    steps:                  # Steps in order
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4       # Clone the repository
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5   # Install Python
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt   # Shell command
      - run: python manage.py test             # Run the tests

Reading rules: - uses: — use a ready-made action (from the marketplace) - run: — run a shell command - with: — parameters for an action - needs: — this job waits for another one - env: — environment variables

docs.title: 6. Our django-tests.yml — line by line
docs.text:
Our project already has a workflow:

.github/workflows/django-tests.yml

Note: the Django project (manage.py, requirements.txt) sits right in the repository root, so the workflow lives in the root .github/workflows/ too, and GitHub runs it automatically. GitHub ignores a workflow placed in any other folder (for example, inside docs/). There is only one correct place:

<repo-root>/.github/workflows/django-tests.yml

Let's go through it piece by piece.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]   # push to main or master
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]   # PR to main or master
  workflow_dispatch:             # manual run via a button in the UI

In the real file, push and pull_request also have a paths: filter (notes_app/**, notes_project/**, templates/**, static/**, requirements.txt and the workflow itself): changes that touch only the documentation do not run the tests.

What happens: if someone opens a Pull Request to main → GitHub sees on: pull_request → runs the workflow → the result (green/red) appears right in the PR.

docs.title: Job 1: Unit + Integration tests
docs.text:
jobs:
  unit-and-integration:
    name: Unit, Integration & Consumer Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      db:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_DB: notes_db
          POSTGRES_USER: notes_user
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: notes_pass
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        # ... health-check options (pg_isready)

    env:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://notes_user:notes_pass@localhost:5432/notes_db

ubuntu-latest is a fresh VM on Azure that is destroyed after every run. There is no state between runs.

services.db is a PostgreSQL container next to the runner: the project works only with PostgreSQL, so the tests get their database through DATABASE_URL.

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

The first step is always the same: clone the repository onto the VM. Without this step, the runner doesn't have your code at all.

      - name: Cache pip dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-pip-

A cache of pip dependencies. If requirements.txt hasn't changed, pip packages are loaded from the cache instead of the internet. This speeds up the pipeline from 3 minutes to 1 minute.

      - name: Django system check
        run: python manage.py check

manage.py check is a built-in Django command. It checks the configuration, models, and middleware without starting the server. If you have an error in settings.py, you'll find out before the tests even run.

      - name: Run unit, integration and consumer tests
        run: |
          python manage.py test \
            notes_app.tests.test_models \
            notes_app.tests.test_services \
            notes_app.tests.test_forms \
            notes_app.tests.test_views \
            notes_app.tests.test_consumers \
            -v 2

Runs all tests except Selenium (those are in a separate job), including the WebSocket tests in test_consumers. The -v 2 parameter means verbose — it shows the name of every test.

      - name: Generate coverage report
        run: |
          coverage run manage.py test ...
          coverage report --show-missing
          coverage xml -o coverage.xml

Coverage: runs the tests via coverage run to track which lines of code were executed. coverage xml generates a file for integration with services such as Codecov.

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-xml
          path: coverage.xml

Saves coverage.xml as an artifact — a file you can download through the GitHub UI after the workflow finishes.

docs.title: Job 2: Selenium E2E
docs.text:
selenium-e2e:
    name: Selenium E2E Tests
    needs: unit-and-integration   # Run AFTER the "unit-and-integration" job succeeds
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      db:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        # ... the same as in Job 1

      selenium:
        image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
        ports:
          - 4444:4444
        options: >-
          --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway
          --shm-size=2gb
        # ... health-check options

    env:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://notes_user:notes_pass@localhost:5432/notes_db
      SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL: http://localhost:4444/wd/hub
      WEB_HOST: host.docker.internal

services are Docker containers that start alongside the runner. Selenium/standalone-chrome runs Chrome in headless mode. Our test connects to it via http://localhost:4444. --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway together with WEB_HOST=host.docker.internal lets Chrome inside the container open the Django test server running on the runner.

    steps:
      # ... checkout, setup-python, cache, pip install
      - name: Run Selenium E2E tests
        run: python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2

SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL is an environment variable read by _make_headless_driver() in notes_app/tests/test_selenium.py. WEB_HOST is read by _DockerLiveServerMixin: it binds the test server to 0.0.0.0 and puts host.docker.internal into live_server_url. If it is set, Selenium connects to a Remote WebDriver instead of a local browser.

docs.title: 7. Events — when to run
docs.text:
The most commonly used triggers:

on:
  # On push to specific branches
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
    paths: ['notes_app/**', 'tests/**']  # Only if these files changed

  # When a PR is opened or updated
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

  # On a schedule (cron syntax)
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * 1'   # Every Monday at 6:00 UTC

  # Manual run via the GitHub UI
  workflow_dispatch:

  # When a release is published
  release:
    types: [published]

Practical tip: for a learning project, push and pull_request are enough. schedule is useful for nightly full test runs, and release for deploying when a version is published.

docs.title: 8. Jobs and Steps — what runs and how
Parallelism and dependencies
docs.text:
By default, jobs run in parallel. needs changes that:

jobs:
  lint:          # Starts immediately
    ...
  test:          # Starts immediately (in parallel with lint)
    ...
  test-selenium:
    needs: test  # Waits for test
    ...
  deploy:
    needs: [lint, test]   # Waits for BOTH
    ...

What it looks like over time:

Time:   0s          30s         60s         90s
        │           │           │           │
lint    ├───────────┤
test    ├───────────────────────┤
selenium                        ├───────────┤
deploy              (won't start until lint and test pass)

docs.title: Conditional execution
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: Deploy (only on success)
    if: success()
    run: ./deploy.sh

  - name: Notify about a failure (any failure)
    if: failure()
    run: ./notify.sh

  - name: Clean up temp files (always)
    if: always()
    run: rm -rf /tmp/test_*

  - name: Deploy only from main
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    run: ./deploy.sh

docs.title: 9. Actions — ready-made building blocks
docs.text: Actions are reusable steps from the GitHub Marketplace.

docs.title: The most commonly used ones in Django projects
docs.text:
# Clone the repository (always the first step)
- uses: actions/checkout@v4

# Install Python with a pip cache
- uses: actions/setup-python@v5
  with:
    python-version: '3.12'
    cache: 'pip'            # Caches pip automatically

# Manual cache (more control)
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/pip
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}

# Save a file as an artifact
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: test-results
    path: coverage.xml
    retention-days: 7       # Keep for 7 days

# Download an artifact in another job
- uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: test-results

docs.title: Passing data between Jobs
docs.text:
Jobs do not share a file system. To pass data, use artifacts or outputs:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.ver.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - id: ver
        run: echo "version=$(cat VERSION)" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}"

docs.title: GitHub-hosted runners
docs.text:
Runner OS CPU RAM ubuntu-latest Ubuntu 22.04 2-core 7 GB windows-latest Windows Server 2022 2-core 7 GB macos-latest macOS 13 3-core 14 GB

For Django projects, always use ubuntu-latest — the fastest and cheapest.

docs.title: What happens when you do git push
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant DEV as Developer
    participant GH as GitHub
    participant VM as Runner VM (Azure)

    DEV->>GH: git push main
    GH->>GH: Detect workflow trigger

    GH->>VM: Provision fresh Ubuntu VM
    VM->>VM: actions/checkout → clone repo
    VM->>VM: pip install -r requirements.txt
    VM->>VM: python manage.py check
    VM->>VM: python manage.py test -v 2
    VM-->>GH: Test results

    GH-->>DEV: ✅ All tests passed (or ❌ Failed)
    GH->>VM: Terminate VM (ephemeral!)

    Note over VM: The VM is destroyed. Next push gets a new clean VM.

An important detail: the VM is ephemeral — it is destroyed after every run. There is no "state" whatsoever between runs. If tests pass on the runner, they pass on a clean machine without your local settings.

docs.title: 11. How to view results on GitHub
docs.text:
1. Open the repository on GitHub
  2. The Actions tab — a list of all workflow runs
  3. Click a specific run — you'll see the jobs graph
  4. Click a job — you'll see the list of steps
  5. Click a step — you'll see live logs

docs.title: What the colors mean
docs.text: Color Meaning Green ✅ The Step/Job finished successfully Yellow 🟡 The Step/Job is running right now Red ❌ The Step/Job failed Gray ⏭ The Step/Job was skipped (because of if: or needs:)

docs.title: Live logs — your best debugging tool
docs.text:
Each step expands into a full log with: - A timestamp for every line - The process's stdout and stderr - A "Download log archive" button

If a test fails, expand the test step and read the output the same way you read it locally.

docs.title: 12. CI/CD and the testing pyramid
docs.text:
Remember the pyramid from the "Testing pyramid" section?

        E2E / Selenium
      integration tests
    unit tests (foundation)

In CI/CD, each level has its own role:

flowchart TD
    PUSH([git push]) --> CI

    subgraph CI["CI Pipeline"]
        direction LR
        L["Lint · ~30s<br>black, flake8"] --> U["Unit Tests · ~60s<br>test_models, test_services"]
        U --> I["Integration Tests · ~90s<br>test_forms, test_views"]
        I --> E["E2E Selenium · ~120s<br>test_selenium"]
    end

    CI --> STATUS{Status?}
    STATUS -- ✅ All green --> MERGE[Safe to merge PR]
    STATUS -- ❌ Lint failed --> FIX_LINT[Fix formatting]
    STATUS -- ❌ Unit failed --> FIX_LOGIC[Fix business logic]
    STATUS -- ❌ Integration failed --> FIX_VIEWS[Fix views/forms]
    STATUS -- ❌ E2E failed --> FIX_E2E[Fix user flow]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class PUSH,L,U,I,E step;
    class STATUS decision;
    class MERGE success;
    class FIX_LINT,FIX_LOGIC,FIX_VIEWS,FIX_E2E error;

Why does the order matter? Lint fails within 30 seconds. If there's a formatting problem, you'll find out before you spend 5 minutes on a full run. "Fail fast" is a principle of good CI.

docs.title: 13. GitHub Pages — publishing a static site
docs.text: GitHub Pages is a built-in way to publish a static site directly from a repository. Useful for Django documentation or a landing page.

docs.title: Option 1: Publishing from a branch (simple)
docs.text:
Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from a branch
    └── Branch: main, /docs

Put HTML/CSS into the docs/ folder → push → the site is available at username.github.io/repo.

docs.title: Option 2: Via GitHub Actions (flexible)
docs.text:
name: Deploy Documentation

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - name: Build MkDocs site
        run: |
          pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material
          mkdocs build

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: ./site

  deploy:
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
        id: deployment

docs.title: Important limitations
docs.text:
⚠️  The site is PUBLICLY available on the internet — even if the repository is private.

⚠️  A CNAME file in the repository does NOT configure a custom domain.
    The domain is changed only via Settings → Pages.

ℹ️  A push via GITHUB_TOKEN does not trigger a Pages rebuild
    (protection against infinite recursion).

docs.title: 14. Common errors and how to read them
The workflow does not start
docs.text:
Symptom:  the push was made, but there is no new run in the Actions tab

Causes:
  - The YAML file is not in <repo-root>/.github/workflows/ (for example, it sits in docs/)
  - A syntax error in the YAML (check the indentation)
  - The branch does not match the filter in on.push.branches

Diagnosis:  GitHub → Actions → "Check workflows", or look for the red icon
            next to the commit in the commit list

docs.title: Process completed with exit code 1
docs.text:
Symptom:  The "Run unit tests" step is red, and the log shows:
          FAIL: test_login_required (notes_app.tests.test_views.NoteListViewTest.test_login_required)

Cause:    A test failed. That's normal — this is what CI is for.

Action:   Expand the step → read the traceback → fix the code or the test

docs.title: Permission denied / Resource not accessible
docs.text:
Symptom:  The "Upload artifact" or "Deploy Pages" step is red

Cause:    The workflow lacks the required permissions

Solution: Add at the top level of the YAML:
          permissions:
            contents: read
            pages: write
            id-token: write

docs.title: Cache miss every time
docs.text:
Symptom:  pip install takes 3 minutes on every run

Cause:    the cache key keeps changing — maybe hashFiles picks the wrong file

Solution: Check the path:
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements.txt') }}
                                       ↑ the glob looks for requirements.txt
                                         in any subfolder

docs.title: A secret is not passed into the environment
docs.text:
Symptom:  The step fails with "API key not found" or "env var is None"

Cause:    The secret exists in Settings but is not passed into the workflow

Solution:
    - name: Deploy
      env:
        API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MY_API_KEY }}  ← pass it explicitly
      run: ./deploy.sh

docs.title: 15. Self-check questions
docs.text:
1. How does CI differ from Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
  2. Why is the runner VM destroyed after every run — is it an advantage or a limitation?
  3. Why must actions/checkout@v4 be the first step?
  4. Why is needs: unit-and-integration in selenium-e2e important?
  5. What happens if on: push is specified without branches: [main]?
  6. Why cache pip dependencies if you could simply install them every time?
  7. Where is our django-tests.yml located, and why does GitHub run it automatically?
  8. What role does SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL play in Job 2, and where does the test code read this variable?
  9. Why does lint run first in the pipeline and Selenium last?
  10. If a test fails in CI but passes locally — what should you check first?

docs.title: Testing a Django application: the complete reference
docs.text: After this file you will be able to write Django tests with TestCase, understand the test database, check models/forms/views/URLs, test authorization, mock external services, write Selenium E2E tests, and read the results of python manage.py test.

docs.title: 1. Why testing exists
docs.text:
In backend development, bugs are inevitable — an application is a complex abstract model of the real world. Every time you make a change, you create risk. Changing one field in a model can break views, serializers, and templates across the whole project.

Testing exists as a confidence mechanism. By writing tests, you teach the application to check itself.

How experienced developers think about tests:

Mental model What it means Insurance policy Tests raise the alarm before a bug reaches production Contract A test pins down exactly what a function or endpoint promises to do Experiment You form a hypothesis ("invalid data → 400") and run the code to prove it Regression protection A bug fixed once never comes back

Limitation: tests only check the scenarios you have explicitly described. They do not magically protect the application and do not catch unknown edge cases.

Django provides a test runner:

python manage.py test

It:

  1. finds the tests;
  2. creates a separate test database;
  3. runs the checks;
  4. cleans up the data;
  5. shows the result.

docs.title: 2. Mental model: the test database
docs.text:
Django tests are a training copy of your application.

A real project has a production database. Tests must not touch it.

Django creates a separate test database:

real database      -> do not touch
test database      -> create, populate, clean up

That's why in a test you can freely do:

Note.objects.create(...)

This data exists only during the test and is fully isolated.

docs.title: 3. Types of tests
docs.text:
graph TD
    A["End-to-End Tests<br>Browser / Selenium / Slow"] --> B
    B["Integration Tests<br>Django Client / API / Medium speed"] --> C
    C["Unit Tests<br>Isolated logic / Fast / Large volume"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A warning;
    class B step;
    class C success;
Type What it checks Speed Share Unit One function or method in isolation Very fast ~70% of tests Integration Interaction of components (view + DB + form) Medium ~20% of tests Functional API endpoint behavior: HTTP codes, JSON payload Medium — E2E The whole path from the browser to the DB Slow ~10% of tests Regression Reproduces a specific bug so it does not come back Depends —

docs.title: 4. Django Testing Architecture
docs.text:
Django extends Python's unittest for web-specific scenarios.

flowchart TD

    Q{"What are we testing?"}

    Q -->|"Pure Python logic"| S["SimpleTestCase"]

    Q -->|"ORM / Models"| T["TestCase"]

    Q -->|"Transaction checks"| TT["TransactionTestCase"]

    Q -->|"Selenium / Browser"| LS["LiveServerTestCase"]

    Q -->|"Selenium + CSS/JS"| SLS["StaticLiveServerTestCase"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    class Q decision;
    class S,T,TT,LS,SLS step;
Class Database What for SimpleTestCase No access URL tests, simple views without a DB TestCase Test database, rollback between tests The most common choice (90% of cases) TransactionTestCase Real transaction behavior commit, rollback, select_for_update() LiveServerTestCase Test DB + live HTTP server Selenium StaticLiveServerTestCase Live server + static files Selenium with CSS/JS

docs.title: 5. A minimal notes example
docs.text:
Let's imagine a notes app.

notes/models.py:

from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models


class Note(models.Model):
    owner = models.ForeignKey(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name="notes",
    )
    title = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    content = models.TextField()
    is_archived = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

    def archive(self):
        self.is_archived = True
        self.save(update_fields=["is_archived"])

What is worth testing here:

Part Test it? Why CharField stores a string No That tests Django itself __str__ returns the title Yes This is our behavior archive() changes is_archived Yes This is our business logic owner is a ForeignKey Usually not It is a model declaration

docs.title: 6. Model tests
docs.text:
Structure:

notes/
└── tests/
    └── test_models.py

# notes/tests/test_models.py
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.test import TestCase

from notes.models import Note


User = get_user_model()


class NoteModelTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(username="student", password="pw")

    def test_note_str_returns_title(self):
        note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="First note",
            content="Hello",
        )

        self.assertEqual(str(note), "First note")

    def test_archive_marks_note_as_archived(self):
        note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="First note",
            content="Hello",
        )

        note.archive()
        note.refresh_from_db()  # re-read from the DB, not from memory

        self.assertTrue(note.is_archived)

    def test_note_creation_and_ownership(self):
        note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="My note",
            content="Testing models"
        )

        self.assertEqual(note.owner, self.user)
        self.assertFalse(note.is_archived)

Why refresh_from_db()?

The archive() method saves the changes to the database. refresh_from_db() re-reads the object from the DB and verifies that the change was really saved, not just made in Python's memory.

docs.title: 7. Form tests
docs.text:
notes/forms.py:

from django import forms

from notes.models import Note


class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ["title", "content"]

    def clean_title(self):
        title = self.cleaned_data["title"].strip()

        if title.lower() == "admin":
            raise forms.ValidationError("Title cannot be admin.")

        return title

Tests:

# notes/tests/test_forms.py
from django.test import TestCase

from notes.forms import NoteForm


class NoteFormTest(TestCase):
    def test_form_is_valid_with_title_and_content(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={"title": "My note", "content": "Hello"})
        self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())

    def test_form_is_invalid_without_title(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={"title": "", "content": "Hello"})
        self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())
        self.assertIn("title", form.errors)

    def test_form_strips_title_spaces(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={"title": "  My note  ", "content": "Hello"})
        self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())
        self.assertEqual(form.cleaned_data["title"], "My note")

    def test_form_rejects_reserved_title(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={"title": "admin", "content": "Hello"})
        self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())
        self.assertIn("title", form.errors)

What matters:

  • in a form test we pass "raw" data, as if from an HTML form (a dictionary);
  • then we call form.is_valid();
  • after a valid form you can inspect cleaned_data;
  • after an invalid form we inspect form.errors.

docs.title: 9. View tests with the Django Client
docs.text:
Django's self.client is not a real browser. It is a fast test HTTP client.

graph LR
    A["Test Code<br>self.client.get()"] --> B["Django Middleware"]
    B --> C["View Logic"]
    C --> D[("Test Database")]
    C --> E["Response Object"]
    E --> F["Test Assertions"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,D,E step;
    class F success;

It can:

  • make a GET/POST request;
  • go through URL routing, middleware, and the view;
  • return a response with a status code, template, and context.

It cannot:

  • execute JavaScript;
  • check the real CSS layout;
  • click a button like a browser does.

View:

# notes/views.py
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.shortcuts import render

from notes.models import Note


@login_required
def note_list(request):
    notes = Note.objects.filter(owner=request.user, is_archived=False)
    return render(request, "notes/note_list.html", {"notes": notes})

Test:

# notes/tests/test_views.py
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse

from notes.models import Note


User = get_user_model()


class NoteListViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(username="student", password="pw")

    def test_anonymous_user_is_redirected_to_login(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_logged_user_can_open_note_list(self):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertTemplateUsed(response, "notes/note_list.html")

    def test_note_list_shows_only_current_user_notes(self):
        other_user = User.objects.create_user(username="other", password="pw")
        own_note = Note.objects.create(owner=self.user, title="Mine", content="Hello")
        Note.objects.create(owner=other_user, title="Not mine", content="Secret")

        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

        notes = list(response.context["notes"])
        self.assertIn(own_note, notes)
        self.assertEqual(len(notes), 1)

The last test is important: it checks ownership — User A cannot see User B's notes.

docs.title: 10. POST tests: creating a note
docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_views.py
class NoteCreateViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            username="student",
            email="student@example.com",
            password="pw",
        )

    def test_logged_user_can_create_note(self):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "Created from test",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)
        self.assertTrue(Note.objects.filter(title="Created from test").exists())

    def test_created_note_belongs_to_current_user(self):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "Owner test",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        note = Note.objects.get(title="Owner test")
        self.assertEqual(note.owner, self.user)

    def test_invalid_form_does_not_create_note(self):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)  # the form again — no redirect
        self.assertFalse(Note.objects.exists())

What we checked:

  • a POST request with valid data → the note is saved + redirect;
  • the owner is taken from request.user, not from the form;
  • an invalid POST → the form is returned back (no redirect).

docs.title: 11. Testing authorization and ownership
docs.text:
The most important class of tests for a notes app — we check that User A cannot read/modify User B's data.

graph TD
    A["Test: Access Private Note"] --> B{"Logged in?"}
    B -->|no| C["Assert 302 → login"]
    B -->|yes| D{"Note owner?"}
    D -->|no| E["Assert 403 Forbidden or 404"]
    D -->|yes| F["Assert 200 OK + data"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A step;
    class B,D decision;
    class C warning;
    class E error;
    class F success;
# notes/tests/test_views.py
class NoteAuthorizationTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user(username="alice", password="pw")
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user(username="bob",   password="pw")
        self.alice_note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.alice,
            title="Alice's Secret",
            content="Private",
        )

    def test_anonymous_access_redirects_to_login(self):
        response = self.client.get(f"/notes/{self.alice_note.id}/edit/")
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)
        self.assertIn("/accounts/login/", response["Location"])

    def test_alice_can_edit_her_own_note(self):
        self.client.login(username="alice", password="pw")
        response = self.client.post(
            f"/notes/{self.alice_note.id}/edit/",
            {"title": "Updated", "content": "Changed"},
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_bob_cannot_edit_alice_note(self):
        self.client.login(username="bob", password="pw")
        response = self.client.post(
            f"/notes/{self.alice_note.id}/edit/",
            {"title": "Hacked", "content": "By bob"},
        )
        # 403 Forbidden or 404 depending on the view implementation
        self.assertIn(response.status_code, [403, 404])
        # The note has NOT changed
        self.alice_note.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertEqual(self.alice_note.title, "Alice's Secret")

force_login() vs login():

Method How it works When to use self.client.login(username=, password=) Checks the password via the auth backend When you test the login process itself self.client.force_login(user) Sets up the session immediately In 95% of tests — faster

docs.title: 12. Django Test Client: useful assertions
docs.text:
Assertion What it checks Example assertEqual(a, b) Equality self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200) assertTrue(x) Truth self.assertTrue(form.is_valid()) assertFalse(x) Falsity self.assertFalse(form.is_valid()) assertIn(a, b) Membership self.assertIn("title", form.errors) assertTemplateUsed Template self.assertTemplateUsed(response, "notes/list.html") assertRedirects Redirect self.assertRedirects(response, reverse("note_list")) assertContains Text in the HTML self.assertContains(response, "Alice's Note") assertNotContains Text is absent self.assertNotContains(response, "Bob's Secret") assertNumQueries Number of SQL queries with self.assertNumQueries(2): ...

An assertRedirects example:

def test_create_note_redirects_to_list(self):
    self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

    response = self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
        "title": "Redirect test",
        "content": "Hello",
    })

    self.assertRedirects(response, reverse("note_list"))

docs.title: 13. Checking for N+1 with assertNumQueries
docs.text:
The N+1 problem: a page makes one query for the list and then one more for each object.

For 10 notes — 11 queries. For 1000 — 1001 queries. This kills performance.

def test_note_list_query_count_is_stable(self):
    for index in range(10):
        Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title=f"Note {index}",
            content="Hello",
        )

    self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

    with self.assertNumQueries(3):
        self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

The number 3 must be determined after an actual run. The goal is for the number of queries not to grow as the number of notes grows.

docs.title: 14. Mocking external services
docs.text:
A mock replaces a real object or function with a fake for the duration of a single test.

Why: if the application sends emails, charges credit cards, or calls an external API, during tests we do not want to actually contact those services. It is slow, expensive, and makes tests unreliable.

graph LR
    subgraph "Testing Environment"
        A["Unit Test"] --> B["Django View: Checkout"]
        B --> C["Mocked Payment Service"]
        C -.->|"Returns Fake 200 OK"| B
    end

    subgraph "Real World"
        D["Real Payment Service"]
    end

    C -.-x|"Network Call Prevented"| D

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,D step;
    class C warning;

notes/services.py:

from django.core.mail import send_mail


def send_note_created_email(email, title):
    send_mail(
        subject="Note created",
        message=f"Your note '{title}' was created.",
        from_email="noreply@example.com",
        recipient_list=[email],
    )

A test with @patch:

# notes/tests/test_services.py
from unittest.mock import patch
from django.test import SimpleTestCase

from notes.services import send_note_created_email


class NoteEmailServiceTest(SimpleTestCase):
    @patch("notes.services.send_mail")
    def test_send_note_created_email_calls_send_mail(self, mock_send_mail):
        send_note_created_email("student@example.com", "My note")

        mock_send_mail.assert_called_once_with(
            subject="Note created",
            message="Your note 'My note' was created.",
            from_email="noreply@example.com",
            recipient_list=["student@example.com"],
        )

A view test + mock:

# notes/tests/test_views.py
from unittest.mock import patch

class NoteCreateViewTest(TestCase):
    ...

    @patch("notes.views.send_note_created_email")  # mock it where it is used
    def test_logged_user_can_create_note(self, mock_send_email):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "Created from test",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertRedirects(response, reverse("note_list"))
        mock_send_email.assert_called_once_with(
            "student@example.com",
            "Created from test",
        )

    @patch("notes.views.send_note_created_email")
    def test_invalid_form_does_not_send_email(self, mock_send_email):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        mock_send_email.assert_not_called()

Why patch("notes.views.send_note_created_email") and not patch("notes.services.send_note_created_email")?

Because the view imports and uses this name in the file notes/views.py. We mock the place where it is used, not where it is defined.

docs.title: 16. Coverage
docs.text:
Installation:

pip install coverage

Running:

coverage run manage.py test
coverage report
coverage html

How to read it:

Name                    Stmts   Miss  Cover
-------------------------------------------
notes/models.py            18      0   100%
notes/forms.py             20      2    90%
notes/views.py             45      8    82%

What coverage shows:

  • which lines were executed during the tests;
  • which files are barely touched;
  • where the "dark zones" are.

What coverage does not show:

  • whether the assertions are correct;
  • whether important business scenarios are tested;
  • whether you are accidentally testing nonsense.

80% meaningful coverage is better than 100% from tests that check nothing important.

docs.title: 17. pytest for Django
docs.text:
Python's unittest (on which TestCase is built) is a proven system. But modern backends often use pytest.

Aspect unittest (Django TestCase) pytest Style OOP: class MyTest(TestCase), self.assertEqual() Functional: def test_..., plain assert Fixtures setUp() / tearDown() — run before every test @pytest.fixture — injected only into the tests that need it The same test with different data A separate method for each scenario @pytest.mark.parametrize Failure messages Standard Assertion rewriting — shows the exact values Django integration Built in The pytest-django plugin

An @pytest.mark.parametrize example:

import pytest
from notes.forms import NoteForm


@pytest.mark.parametrize("title,valid", [
    ("My note", True),
    ("", False),
    ("admin", False),
    ("  ", False),
])
def test_note_form_title_validation(title, valid):
    form = NoteForm(data={"title": title, "content": "Hello"})
    assert form.is_valid() == valid

Instead of 4 separate test functions — one parametrized function.

Fixtures for a DRY setUp:

# conftest.py
import pytest
from django.contrib.auth.models import User


@pytest.fixture
def alice(db):
    return User.objects.create_user(username="alice", password="pw")


@pytest.fixture
def alice_note(alice):
    from notes.models import Note
    return Note.objects.create(owner=alice, title="Alice's Note", content="Hello")

# test_views.py
def test_note_owner_can_view(client, alice, alice_note):
    client.force_login(alice)
    response = client.get(f"/notes/{alice_note.id}/")
    assert response.status_code == 200

docs.title: 18. E2E tests: Selenium
docs.text:
While unit and integration tests prove that isolated backend components work with mathematical precision, E2E tests prove that the whole system works as a single product.

E2E tests open a real browser, click buttons, fill in forms, and check that the final HTML is exactly what a real user would see.

graph LR
    A["Python TestCase"] -->|"Commands"| B["WebDriver<br>chromedriver / geckodriver"]
    B -->|"Controls"| C["Real Browser<br>Chrome / Firefox"]
    C -->|"HTTP Requests"| D["Django LiveServerTestCase"]
    D -->|"Queries"| E[("Test Database")]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,E step;
    class D success;

Selenium vs the Django Test Client:

Django Test Client Selenium Browser No (Python HTTP) Yes (real Chrome/Firefox) JavaScript Not executed Executed CSS rendering Not checked Checked Speed Very fast Slow (~3–15s per test) Access to response.context Yes No When to use 95% of view tests Critical user flows

docs.title: Basic structure
docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_e2e.py
import unittest
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.contrib.staticfiles.testing import StaticLiveServerTestCase

try:
    from selenium import webdriver
    from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
    from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options as ChromeOptions
    from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
    from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
    SELENIUM_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
    SELENIUM_AVAILABLE = False


User = get_user_model()


def _make_headless_driver():
    options = ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument("--headless=new")
    options.add_argument("--no-sandbox")
    options.add_argument("--disable-dev-shm-usage")
    return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)  # Selenium Manager auto-downloads chromedriver


@unittest.skipUnless(SELENIUM_AVAILABLE, "selenium not installed — pip install selenium")
class NoteAppE2ETest(StaticLiveServerTestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        if SELENIUM_AVAILABLE:
            cls.driver = _make_headless_driver()
            cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        if SELENIUM_AVAILABLE:
            cls.driver.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            username="student",
            email="student@example.com",
            password="password123",
        )

    def test_login_and_create_note(self):
        login_url = f"{self.live_server_url}/accounts/login/"
        self.driver.get(login_url)

        self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, "username").send_keys("student")
        self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, "password").send_keys("password123")
        self.driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "[type='submit']").click()

        # Wait for the redirect — click() is asynchronous
        WebDriverWait(self.driver, 5).until(EC.url_changes(login_url))

        self.assertIn("/notes/", self.driver.current_url)

docs.title: Waiting strategies
docs.text:
Pages load dynamically. Selenium may click an element before it appears in the DOM.

Strategy How When Implicit wait driver.implicitly_wait(5) Globally for all find_element calls Explicit wait WebDriverWait(driver, 5).until(condition) For a specific condition (URL change, element clickable) time.sleep() DO NOT use it Needlessly slow or unreliable 
# Explicit wait: wait until the button becomes clickable
confirm_btn = WebDriverWait(self.driver, 5).until(
    EC.element_to_be_clickable((By.ID, "confirm-delete"))
)
confirm_btn.click()

# Explicit wait: wait for the URL to change after login
WebDriverWait(self.driver, 5).until(
    EC.url_changes(f"{self.live_server_url}/accounts/login/")
)

docs.title: The session cookie trick
docs.text:
Instead of filling in the login form in the browser (slow and dependent on the form's state), use the session cookie:

def _login_via_cookie(self, user):
    # 1. Log in via the Django Test Client
    self.client.force_login(user)
    session_cookie = self.client.cookies["sessionid"]

    # 2. Open any page of the domain (the browser needs an open page)
    self.driver.get(f"{self.live_server_url}/")

    # 3. Pass the session cookie to Selenium
    self.driver.add_cookie({
        "name":  "sessionid",
        "value": session_cookie.value,
        "path":  "/",
    })

docs.title: Selecting elements
Common Selenium mistakes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix NoSuchElementException Wrong selector or the page hasn't loaded yet Check the selector + implicit wait StaleElementReferenceException The DOM was updated after the element was found Re-find the element after the DOM update The test fails intermittently (flaky) Animation or AJAX WebDriverWait instead of time.sleep() ChromeDriver mismatch chromedriver version != Chrome Selenium Manager resolves it automatically

import os

SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL = os.environ.get("SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL")

def _make_driver():
    if SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL:
        return webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL,
            options=webdriver.ChromeOptions(),
        )
    options = ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument("--headless=new")
    return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

docs.title: 20. Real-world engineering: strategy by domain
docs.text:
The testing strategy depends on the business domain:

Domain Test focus Notes / Blog Ownership: User A cannot see User B's data. An alice vs bob test for all views. Ecommerce E2E checkout flow. Unit tests for price calculation. Mock the external payment gateway (Stripe). Dashboard / Analytics assertNumQueries — N+1 is not allowed. Performance is critical. API JSON payload contracts. HTTP status codes (201 vs 403). Token auth. Auth/Permissions A test for each access level: anonymous, user, staff, superuser.

Rules for a notes app in particular:

  1. Most tests should have alice and bob — we test tenant isolation.
  2. Every view should have an anonymous redirect test.
  3. An ownership test: User B cannot edit/delete/view someone else's note.

docs.title: 21. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens How to fix it Testing the Django ORM instead of their own logic They want to cover the model Test __str__, methods, constraints, ownership Checking only status_code == 200 It's the easiest thing Add template, context, and content assertions Not testing the anonymous user Locally they are always logged in Add a redirect test for every protected URL Not testing another user They think only about the happy path Create User A and User B Mocking the form or model They want isolation Test forms/models for real through the test DB Starting straight with Selenium It looks "complete" First model → form → view tests Not adding stable selectors HTML is for eyes, not tests Add id or data-test-id for E2E Using time.sleep() An easy way to wait Use WebDriverWait There's coverage, but the assertions are weak They look at the number Check the substance of the tests, not the percentage Hardcoding /notes/ in tests Laziness Use reverse("note_list")

docs.title: 22. The main diagram: testing architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["python manage.py test"] --> B["Django creates the test database"]
    B --> C["Runs the TestCase"]
    C --> D["setUp: user/note/form data"]
    D --> E["Client makes a GET or POST"]
    E --> F["View returns a response"]
    F --> G["Assertions check the behavior"]
    G --> H["Rollback: Django cleans up the data"]
    H --> I["Next test"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G step;
    class H warning;
    class I success;
