docs.title: Mock and patch: how to substitute email, APIs, and payments in tests
docs.text: After this file you will understand what a mock is, when you need one, how patch works, why it matters to mock the right path, and how not to turn your tests into a fake show.

docs.title: 1. Why you need this
docs.text:
In a real Django project, code often interacts with the outside world:

  • sends email;
  • calls a payment gateway;
  • makes HTTP requests to an API;
  • writes a file;
  • reads the current time;
  • calls a slow service.

In tests we don't want to:

  • send real emails;
  • charge real money;
  • wait on a slow network;
  • depend on someone else's server;
  • have a test break because of an unstable internet connection.

A mock lets you replace a real dependency with a controlled object.

docs.title: 2. Mental model
docs.text:
A mock is a stunt double for an actor at a rehearsal.

In the real movie, the actor jumps off a roof. At a rehearsal that is dangerous, so a stunt double is used.

The same goes for a test:

  • we don't call the real email service;
  • we don't touch the payment gateway;
  • but we check that our code correctly called the "stunt double."

docs.title: 3. The simplest example
docs.text:
app/services.py:

def send_email(email):
    print(f"Sending email to {email}")


def register_user(email):
    # the user creation logic could be here
    send_email(email)

Test:

from unittest.mock import patch

from app.services import register_user


@patch("app.services.send_email")
def test_registration_sends_email(mock_send_email):
    register_user("student@example.com")

    mock_send_email.assert_called_once_with("student@example.com")

What happens:

Line Explanation @patch("app.services.send_email") Temporarily replaces send_email mock_send_email A fake function instead of the real one register_user(...) We run the code that should trigger the email assert_called_once_with(...) We check that the call happened exactly once and with the right argument

docs.title: 4. The most important rule: patch where used
docs.text:
This is where beginners trip up most often.

You must mock not where the function is defined, but where it is used.

Example:

app/email.py:

def send_email(email):
    ...

app/services.py:

from app.email import send_email


def register_user(email):
    send_email(email)

Here register_user uses the name send_email inside app.services.

The correct patch:

@patch("app.services.send_email")
def test_registration_sends_email(mock_send_email):
    ...

Not this one:

@patch("app.email.send_email")
def test_registration_sends_email(mock_send_email):
    ...

Why? Because app.services has already imported the function into its namespace. The code under test looks at app.services.send_email.

docs.title: 5. Mock return value
docs.text:
A payment gateway example:

shop/services.py:

class PaymentGateway:
    def charge(self, amount):
        # a real request to the payment system
        ...


def checkout(amount):
    gateway = PaymentGateway()
    success = gateway.charge(amount)

    if not success:
        return "payment_failed"

    return "paid"

Test:

from unittest.mock import patch

from shop.services import checkout


@patch("shop.services.PaymentGateway.charge")
def test_checkout_success(mock_charge):
    mock_charge.return_value = True

    result = checkout(50)

    assert result == "paid"
    mock_charge.assert_called_once_with(50)


@patch("shop.services.PaymentGateway.charge")
def test_checkout_payment_failed(mock_charge):
    mock_charge.return_value = False

    result = checkout(50)

    assert result == "payment_failed"

Here we don't call the real payment service. We check how our code reacts to success and failure.

docs.title: 6. Mock side effect: simulating an error
docs.text:
Sometimes an external service fails.

from unittest.mock import patch

import pytest

from shop.services import checkout


@patch("shop.services.PaymentGateway.charge")
def test_checkout_gateway_error(mock_charge):
    mock_charge.side_effect = TimeoutError("gateway timeout")

    with pytest.raises(TimeoutError):
        checkout(50)

Or, if your code is supposed to handle the error:

def checkout(amount):
    gateway = PaymentGateway()

    try:
        success = gateway.charge(amount)
    except TimeoutError:
        return "payment_unavailable"

    if not success:
        return "payment_failed"

    return "paid"

Test:

@patch("shop.services.PaymentGateway.charge")
def test_checkout_handles_gateway_timeout(mock_charge):
    mock_charge.side_effect = TimeoutError("gateway timeout")

    result = checkout(50)

    assert result == "payment_unavailable"

docs.title: 7. Mocking Django email
docs.text:
Django has a test email backend, but sometimes you want to check the call to your own service.

notes/services.py:

from django.core.mail import send_mail


def send_note_created_email(email, title):
    send_mail(
        subject="Note created",
        message=f"Your note '{title}' was created.",
        from_email="noreply@example.com",
        recipient_list=[email],
    )

Test:

from unittest.mock import patch

from notes.services import send_note_created_email


@patch("notes.services.send_mail")
def test_send_note_created_email_calls_django_send_mail(mock_send_mail):
    send_note_created_email("student@example.com", "My note")

    mock_send_mail.assert_called_once_with(
        subject="Note created",
        message="Your note 'My note' was created.",
        from_email="noreply@example.com",
        recipient_list=["student@example.com"],
    )

docs.title: 8. When a mock is useful and when it is harmful
9. Mermaid diagram
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Code calls an external service"] --> B{"Is it an email/API/payment/slow dependency?"}
    B -->|yes| C["Replace it with a mock"]
    B -->|no| D["Call the real logic in the test database"]
    C --> E["Set return_value or side_effect"]
    E --> F["Check the result and the call arguments"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,D,E step;
    class B decision;
    class C warning;
    class F success;

docs.title: 10. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens How to fix it Mocking the wrong path They didn't understand the import namespace Patch where used Mocking everything in sight They want to "isolate" Mock only the external boundaries Not checking the arguments They look only at called Use assert_called_once_with A mock makes the test green but meaningless All the logic has been replaced Keep the real model/form/view where possible Not testing API errors They only checked success Add a side_effect

docs.title: pytest: short tests, fixtures, and pytest-django
docs.text: After this file you will be able to write tests with pytest, run them, use fixtures and parametrization, and hook pytest up to a Django project.

docs.title: 1. Why you need this
docs.text:
pytest is often chosen because it lets you write tests more simply:

def test_add_two_numbers():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5

No class, no self.assertEqual, no extra boilerplate.

But simpler syntax does not mean "less thinking." A good pytest test still needs a clear expectation, an understandable name, and sensible test data.

Installation:

pip install pytest

Running:

pytest

docs.title: 2. Mental model
docs.text:
pytest is a test runner that is very good at finding tests and supplying them with the data they need.

Imagine a test says:

def test_user_has_email(user_data):
    ...

pytest sees the user_data parameter and asks:

"Do I have a fixture with that name?"

If it does, it runs the fixture and passes the result into the test.

docs.title: 3. A first example from scratch
docs.text:
Structure:

testing_playground/
├── math_utils.py
└── test_math_utils.py

math_utils.py:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def is_even(number):
    return number % 2 == 0

test_math_utils.py:

from math_utils import add, is_even


def test_add_two_numbers():
    result = add(2, 3)

    assert result == 5


def test_four_is_even():
    assert is_even(4)


def test_five_is_not_even():
    assert not is_even(5)

Running:

pytest

Result:

3 passed in 0.03s

docs.title: 4. How pytest finds tests
docs.text:
The usual rules:

What Rule Example File test_*.py or *_test.py test_math_utils.py Function test_* test_add_two_numbers Class Test* without __init__ class TestCart:

pytest can also run unittest tests, but while learning it's better not to mix styles in one file without a reason.

docs.title: 5. A plain assert
docs.text:
pytest uses the ordinary Python assert.

def test_add_two_numbers():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5

If a test fails, pytest shows the details.

Example:

E       assert -1 == 5

This is convenient: you can see the actual result and the expected value.

Comparison:

unittest pytest self.assertEqual(result, 5) assert result == 5 self.assertTrue(user.is_active) assert user.is_active self.assertFalse(form.is_valid()) assert not form.is_valid() self.assertIn("title", errors) assert "title" in errors

docs.title: 6. Fixtures: test data without duplication
docs.text:
The problem:

def test_user_has_email():
    user = {"username": "student", "email": "student@example.com"}

    assert user["email"] == "student@example.com"


def test_user_has_username():
    user = {"username": "student", "email": "student@example.com"}

    assert user["username"] == "student"

The data is duplicated.

The solution:

import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def user_data():
    return {
        "username": "student",
        "email": "student@example.com",
    }


def test_user_has_email(user_data):
    assert user_data["email"] == "student@example.com"


def test_user_has_username(user_data):
    assert user_data["username"] == "student"

What happens:

  1. pytest sees the user_data parameter;
  2. looks for a fixture named user_data;
  3. runs the fixture;
  4. passes the result into the test.

docs.title: 7. conftest.py: shared fixtures
docs.text:
If a fixture is needed by many files, it is often placed in conftest.py.

tests/
├── conftest.py
├── test_users.py
└── test_notes.py

conftest.py:

import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def note_data():
    return {
        "title": "Test note",
        "content": "Hello",
    }

test_notes.py:

def test_note_has_title(note_data):
    assert note_data["title"] == "Test note"

You don't need to import note_data. pytest finds the fixture by itself.

docs.title: 8. Parametrization: many scenarios without copy-paste
docs.text:
Bad:

def test_empty_title_is_invalid():
    ...


def test_empty_content_is_invalid():
    ...


def test_long_title_is_invalid():
    ...

Better:

import pytest


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "title, content",
    [
        ("", "Text"),
        ("Valid title", ""),
        ("x" * 256, "Text"),
    ],
)
def test_note_form_invalid_data(title, content):
    form = NoteForm(data={"title": title, "content": content})

    assert not form.is_valid()

pytest will run this test three times with different data.

When parametrization is useful:

Situation Example Several invalid inputs "", None, a very long string Several expected results slug generation Checking edge cases 0, -1, max value

docs.title: 9. pytest-django
docs.text:
For Django you need a plugin:

pip install pytest-django

Usually a pytest.ini file is added:

[pytest]
DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE = notes_project.settings
python_files = tests.py test_*.py *_tests.py

A test with the database:

import pytest

from notes_app.models import Note


@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_note_str_returns_title(django_user_model):
    user = django_user_model.objects.create_user(username="student", password="pw")
    note = Note.objects.create(user=user, title="Pytest note", content="Hello")

    assert str(note) == "Pytest note"

Without @pytest.mark.django_db, pytest won't allow access to the database. This isn't a whim. It's a safeguard: a test must state explicitly that it needs the database.

docs.title: 10. pytest or unittest
docs.text:
Question unittest pytest Needs installing? No Yes Style Classes and methods Functions, fixtures Assertions self.assertEqual assert Django by default Yes Via pytest-django Convenient for Django built-in style Quick tests, fixtures, parametrization

Conclusion:

  • if the course or team uses the Django default — learn unittest/TestCase;
  • if you want shorter syntax and flexible fixtures — learn pytest;
  • in real projects you can come across both styles.

docs.title: 11. Mermaid diagram
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["pytest"] --> B["Finds test_*.py"]
    B --> C["Finds test_* functions"]
    C --> D{"Does the test have parameters?"}
    D -->|yes| E["Looks up fixtures"]
    D -->|no| F["Runs the test"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Executes assert"]
    G --> H{"Did the expectation match?"}
    H -->|yes| I["passed"]
    H -->|no| J["failed with an explanation"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class A,B,C,E,F,G step;
    class D,H decision;
    class I success;
    class J error;

docs.title: 12. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens How to fix it The fixture is named differently from the parameter pytest looks up fixtures by name Make the names match Forgot @pytest.mark.django_db The test reaches into the DB without permission Add the marker A parametrized test has become unreadable Too much data in one place Split it up or give it clear ids A fixture does everything at once You want a "ready-made world" Make small fixtures Mixing unittest and pytest without a reason Copied from different sources Pick one style per file

docs.title: 13. Practice
docs.text:
1. Create math_utils.py with a function is_even(number).
  2. Write pytest tests for 2, 3, 0, -4.
  3. Rewrite these tests using @pytest.mark.parametrize.
  4. Create a note_data fixture.
  5. If you have a Django project, install pytest-django and write a test for Note.__str__.

A parametrization example:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "number, expected",
    [
        (2, True),
        (3, False),
        (0, True),
        (-4, True),
    ],
)
def test_is_even(number, expected):
    assert is_even(number) is expected

docs.text:
1. How does pytest differ from unittest in writing style?
  2. How does pytest find fixtures?
  3. What is conftest.py for?
  4. When is parametrization better than several separate tests?
  5. Why do you need @pytest.mark.django_db?

docs.title: Selenium WebDriver: browser automation from your first script to Django E2E
docs.text:
This file is a self-contained reference on Selenium for Python. From installation and your first driver.get() to Django's StaticLiveServerTestCase, the session cookie trick, and Remote WebDriver on GitHub Actions. All the code is tied to the real test_selenium.py in our project.

📖 Official documentation: https://selenium.dev/selenium/docs/api/py 📖 API Reference: https://selenium.dev/selenium/docs/api/py/api.html 📖 GitHub: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/Selenium

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Concepts - 1. Why Selenium — what it does that the Test Client can't - 2. Mental model — WebDriver, Driver, Browser - 3. Selenium Manager — automatic driver management

First steps - 4. Installation - 5. Your first script — 8 basic components - 6. Browsers and headless mode

Finding and interacting - 7. Finding elements — By strategies - 8. Interacting with elements - 9. Waits — implicitly_wait and WebDriverWait

Selenium in tests - 10. Selenium + unittest - 11. Selenium + pytest - 12. Django + Selenium — StaticLiveServerTestCase - 13. Session Cookie Trick — logging in without a form - 14. Remote WebDriver and Selenium Grid

Our project - 15. _make_headless_driver() — how it works in our project - 16. Walking through test_selenium.py class by class

Reference - 17. Common errors and how to read them - 18. Anti-patterns - 19. Self-check questions

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
The Django Test Client checks HTTP. But between HTTP and what the user sees, there is one more layer.

The Django Test Client checks:

  Python ──► Django middleware ──► view ──► HTTP response (bytes)
             ↑ everything is automated here, no browser


Selenium checks:

  Python ──► chromedriver ──► Chrome ──► HTTP ──► Django server ──► HTML
                                 ↑
                              HTML + CSS rendering
                              JavaScript execution
                              clicks, forms, navigation
                              everything the user sees in the browser

docs.title: What the Test Client cannot check
docs.text: Situation Test Client Selenium @login_required protects a URL ✓ ✓ Redirect after POST ✓ ✓ Text in the HTML response ✓ ✓ JavaScript shows/hides an element ✗ ✓ CSS breaks how a form is displayed ✗ ✓ A button can actually be clicked ✗ ✓ A field has the correct placeholder ✗ ✓ The real redirect chain in the browser ✗ ✓ A form isn't submitted without a required field ✗ ✓

docs.title: When Selenium is needed and when it is overkill
docs.text:
Selenium is needed for: - A critical user flow (login → create → see result) - Forms with JavaScript validation - Single Page Applications (React, Vue) - Checking that CSS doesn't break the layout

Selenium is overkill for: - Checking business logic (that's for unit tests) - Checking status_code and redirect (that's for integration tests) - Anything that can be checked without a browser

The rule: if a test can be written with self.client, write it with self.client. Selenium is only for what requires a real browser.

docs.title: Three components
docs.text:
your Python code
      │
      │  selenium package (pip install selenium)
      │  sends commands via the WebDriver Protocol (HTTP/JSON)
      ▼
chromedriver / geckodriver        ← driver: translates WebDriver commands
      │                              into native browser commands
      │
      ▼
Chrome / Firefox                  ← a real browser,
                                     opens pages, runs JS

Your Python code never "controls" the browser directly. It sends JSON commands to the driver (using the W3C WebDriver protocol). The driver translates them into the browser's native API.

docs.title: WebDriver Protocol
docs.text:
Every command is an HTTP request to the local driver:

Python: driver.find_element(By.ID, "username")
            │
            ▼
POST http://localhost:9515/session/abc123/element
{"using": "id", "value": "username"}
            │
            ▼
chromedriver: CDP command to Chrome → find the element
            │
            ▼
Chrome: returns an element reference → id=XYZ

That is exactly why Selenium is slower than the Test Client — every action is a real HTTP round-trip to the driver.

docs.title: 3. Selenium Manager
docs.text:
In older versions of Selenium (before 4.6), you had to manually: 1. Download chromedriver.exe / geckodriver 2. Put it on the PATH or specify the path in the code 3. Keep track of versions — Chrome version ≠ chromedriver version → error

Starting with Selenium 4.6, there is Selenium Manager — a built-in driver manager:

# OLD WAY (before Selenium 4.6):
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.service import Service
driver = webdriver.Chrome(service=Service('/usr/local/bin/chromedriver'))

# NEW WAY (Selenium 4.6+):
driver = webdriver.Chrome()   # Selenium Manager finds and downloads chromedriver by itself

Selenium Manager: 1. Detects the installed Chrome version 2. Finds the matching chromedriver in the cache or downloads it 3. Starts chromedriver automatically

This is especially convenient for GitHub Actions: ubuntu-latest includes Chrome, and Selenium Manager downloads the matching chromedriver without any extra steps in the workflow.

📖 Selenium Manager documentation

docs.title: 4. Installation
docs.text:
# Latest stable version
pip install -U selenium

# Check the installed version
python -c "import selenium; print(selenium.__version__)"

Supported Python versions: 3.10+

Supported browsers: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, WebKitGTK, WPEWebKit

After installation, you don't need to download chromedriver separately — Selenium Manager does it automatically on the first run.

For our project, selenium is already in requirements.txt:

# requirements.txt
selenium>=4.6.0

docs.title: 5. Your first script — 8 basic components
docs.text:
Every Selenium interaction consists of 8 basic operations. Here they are all together:

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

# 1. Start the session — open the browser
driver = webdriver.Chrome()

# 2. Act on the browser — open a URL
driver.get("https://www.selenium.dev/selenium/web/web-form.html")

# 3. Request information about the browser
title = driver.title   # → "Web form"

# 4. Waiting strategy
driver.implicitly_wait(0.5)   # wait up to 0.5 seconds for an element to appear

# 5. Find elements
text_box     = driver.find_element(by=By.NAME,         value="my-text")
submit_button = driver.find_element(by=By.CSS_SELECTOR, value="button")

# 6. Interact with elements
text_box.send_keys("Selenium")
submit_button.click()

# 7. Request information about an element
message = driver.find_element(by=By.ID, value="message")
text = message.text   # → "Received!"

# 8. End the session — close the browser
driver.quit()

docs.title: What happens at each step
docs.text: Step Method What it does 1 webdriver.Chrome() Starts Chrome and chromedriver, opens an empty window 2 driver.get(url) Navigates to the URL, waits until the page loads 3 driver.title Returns the <title> of the current page 4 driver.implicitly_wait(n) A global wait for find_element (once per session) 5 driver.find_element(By.X, "val") Finds the first matching element in the DOM 6 .send_keys() / .click() Types text / clicks 7 .text Returns the element's visible text 8 driver.quit() Stops the driver process, closes the browser

docs.title: The difference between quit() and close()
docs.text:
driver.close()  # Closes the current tab. The driver process keeps running.
driver.quit()   # Stops the driver process and closes all tabs. ALWAYS call it in tearDown.

If you don't call driver.quit(), the chromedriver process stays in memory. After several tests, several zombie processes pile up.

docs.title: Launching different browsers
docs.text:
from selenium import webdriver

driver = webdriver.Chrome()    # Chrome (the most popular in CI)
driver = webdriver.Firefox()   # Firefox (geckodriver)
driver = webdriver.Edge()      # Microsoft Edge
driver = webdriver.Safari()    # Safari (macOS only)

docs.title: Headless mode — no GUI window
docs.text:
Headless = the browser performs all actions without a graphical interface. It is needed for: - CI/CD servers (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) — there is no display there - Speed — no resources spent on rendering pixels - Docker containers — there is usually no display server

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options

options = Options()
options.add_argument('--headless=new')          # headless mode (Chrome 112+)
options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')            # needed in Docker / CI
options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage') # avoid shared memory problems in Docker

driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
# the driver opens pages in memory, with no window on the screen

docs.title: Useful options for Chrome
docs.text:
options = Options()
options.add_argument('--window-size=1920,1080')     # window size
options.add_argument('--disable-extensions')         # disable extensions
options.add_argument('--disable-gpu')               # needed in some environments
options.add_argument('--lang=uk')                   # browser language
options.add_experimental_option('prefs', {
    'profile.default_content_setting_values.notifications': 2  # disable notifications
})

docs.title: 7. Finding elements — By strategies
docs.text: find_element() returns the first element found. find_elements() returns a list of all elements found (an empty list if nothing is found).

docs.title: All By strategies
docs.text:
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

# By the HTML attribute id="username"
elem = driver.find_element(By.ID, "username")

# By the HTML attribute name="password"
elem = driver.find_element(By.NAME, "password")

# By CSS selector
elem = driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "input[type='submit']")
elem = driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, ".btn-primary")
elem = driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "#note-form button")

# By XPath
elem = driver.find_element(By.XPATH, "//button[@type='submit']")
elem = driver.find_element(By.XPATH, "//h1[contains(text(), 'Нотатки')]")

# By HTML tag name
elems = driver.find_elements(By.TAG_NAME, "input")

# By CSS class
elem = driver.find_element(By.CLASS_NAME, "btn")

# By the text of an <a> link
elem = driver.find_element(By.LINK_TEXT, "Увійти")

# By partial link text
elem = driver.find_element(By.PARTIAL_LINK_TEXT, "Вий")

docs.title: Which strategy to choose
docs.text:
Strategy When to choose Pros Cons By.ID There is a unique id The fastest, stable There isn't always an id By.NAME Forms — fields have a name Convenient for inputs May not be unique By.CSS_SELECTOR Flexible selection Readable, powerful Requires knowing CSS By.XPATH Complex DOM structure The most powerful Fragile when the HTML is refactored By.CLASS_NAME A CSS class Simple Unreliable (a class can repeat) By.TAG_NAME All elements with a tag For find_elements Unreliable as the only criterion

Recommended order: By.ID → By.NAME → By.CSS_SELECTOR → By.XPATH.

docs.text:

submit = form.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]')
# Searches for submit only inside form, not across the whole page

from selenium.common.exceptions import NoSuchElementException

try:

except NoSuchElementException:

If find_element doesn't find the element, it raises NoSuchElementException; it doesn't return None.

docs.title: The problem without waits
docs.text:
driver.get("http://localhost:8000/notes/new/")
driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'title')  # ← MAY FAIL!
# If the page hasn't fully loaded yet, the element isn't in the DOM

The browser is asynchronous. driver.get() returns when it has received the response, but the DOM may not be fully built yet.

docs.title: implicitly_wait — a global wait
docs.text:
driver.implicitly_wait(5)
# Now every find_element waits up to 5 seconds before raising NoSuchElementException

It is set once per session (usually in setUpClass). On every find_element: - If the element is there, it returns immediately - If not, it waits and checks again, up to the timeout - If it still hasn't found it within 5 seconds — NoSuchElementException

# Our project: test_selenium.py
@classmethod
def setUpClass(cls):
    super().setUpClass()
    cls.driver = _make_headless_driver()
    cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)   # ← set once for the whole class

docs.title: WebDriverWait — an explicit wait for a specific condition
docs.text:
implicitly_wait only waits for an element to appear. But sometimes you need to wait for a different condition: a URL change, text, visibility.

from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC

wait = WebDriverWait(driver, timeout=5)

# Wait until the URL changes
wait.until(EC.url_changes("http://localhost:8000/accounts/login/"))

# Wait until the element becomes clickable
wait.until(EC.element_to_be_clickable((By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]')))

# Wait until the element becomes visible
wait.until(EC.visibility_of_element_located((By.ID, "message")))

# Wait until text appears in the element
wait.until(EC.text_to_be_present_in_element((By.ID, "status"), "Saved"))

# Wait until the element disappears
wait.until(EC.invisibility_of_element_located((By.CLASS_NAME, "loading")))

docs.title: Common expected_conditions
docs.text: Condition What it checks url_changes(url) The current URL differs from the given one url_contains("path") The URL contains a substring title_contains("text") The <title> contains the text element_to_be_clickable(locator) The element exists and is clickable visibility_of_element_located(locator) The element exists and is visible invisibility_of_element_located(locator) The element is invisible or absent text_to_be_present_in_element(locator, text) The text is in the element staleness_of(element) The old element has left the DOM (after a reload)

docs.title: When to choose which
docs.text:
implicitly_wait(n):
  + Simple, set once
  + Automatic for every find_element
  - Only waits for the element to appear in the DOM
  - Doesn't check visibility or clickability

WebDriverWait + EC:
  + Flexible — any condition
  + You can set different timeouts for different situations
  - More code

In our project: implicitly_wait(5) for general lookups, and WebDriverWait(driver, 5).until(EC.url_changes(...)) after clicking Submit (because we need to wait for a redirect, not for an element to appear).

docs.title: 10. Selenium + unittest
docs.text:
The classic way — with unittest.TestCase:

import unittest
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options


class SeleniumTestCase(unittest.TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        """Runs before every test — opens a new browser."""
        options = Options()
        options.add_argument('--headless=new')
        self.driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
        self.addCleanup(self.driver.quit)  # ← quit() even if the test failed

    def test_page_title(self):
        self.driver.get("https://selenium.dev")
        self.assertIn("Selenium", self.driver.title)

    def test_find_element(self):
        self.driver.get("https://www.selenium.dev/selenium/web/web-form.html")
        field = self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, "my-text")
        self.assertIsNotNone(field)

self.addCleanup(self.driver.quit) guarantees that quit() is called even if the test raises an exception. This is better than tearDown, because tearDown is not called when there are exceptions in setUp.

docs.title: setUpClass — one driver for all the tests in a class (faster)
docs.text:
class SeleniumTestCase(unittest.TestCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        """Runs once before all tests in the class."""
        super().setUpClass()
        options = Options()
        options.add_argument('--headless=new')
        cls.driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
        cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        """Runs once after all tests in the class."""
        cls.driver.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def test_page_one(self):
        self.driver.get("https://selenium.dev")
        # ...

    def test_page_two(self):
        self.driver.get("https://selenium.dev/documentation")
        # ...

Important: with setUpClass, all tests in the class share one driver. If a test leaves the browser in an unexpected state (cookies, open dialogs), the next test may fail. In our project we work around this with the session cookie trick (we log in every time via setUp).

docs.title: 11. Selenium + pytest
docs.text:
import pytest
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options


@pytest.fixture
def driver():
    """Fixture — opens the driver before the test, closes it afterwards."""
    options = Options()
    options.add_argument('--headless=new')
    d = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
    d.implicitly_wait(5)
    yield d        # ← the test runs here
    d.quit()       # ← always called after the test (even on error)


def test_page_title(driver):
    driver.get("https://selenium.dev")
    assert "Selenium" in driver.title


def test_form(driver):
    from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
    driver.get("https://www.selenium.dev/selenium/web/web-form.html")
    driver.find_element(By.NAME, "my-text").send_keys("pytest test")
    driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "button").click()
    message = driver.find_element(By.ID, "message")
    assert message.text == "Received!"

docs.title: scope="session" — one driver for all tests
docs.text:
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def driver():
    """One driver for the whole pytest test session."""
    options = Options()
    options.add_argument('--headless=new')
    d = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
    yield d
    d.quit()

scope="session" runs the fixture once. It's faster, but the tests share the browser state.

For Django it's better to use django.test.TestCase + StaticLiveServerTestCase rather than pytest fixtures — they integrate with Django's test database.

docs.title: The problem with a regular TestCase
docs.text: Selenium opens a real browser that makes HTTP requests. A regular Django TestCase does not start an HTTP server — it simulates requests inside the process. Selenium cannot connect.

docs.title: StaticLiveServerTestCase — a real HTTP server
docs.text:
from django.contrib.staticfiles.testing import StaticLiveServerTestCase

StaticLiveServerTestCase: 1. Starts a real Django HTTP server in a separate thread 2. The server runs on a random port: http://127.0.0.1:XXXXX 3. self.live_server_url contains this address 4. Each test has an isolated test DB (with rollback — like in TestCase) 5. Additionally: it serves static files (CSS, JS) — hence "Static" in the name

from django.contrib.staticfiles.testing import StaticLiveServerTestCase
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By


class MyDjangoSeleniumTest(StaticLiveServerTestCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        # Start headless Chrome once for all tests in the class
        options = ChromeOptions()
        options.add_argument('--headless=new')
        cls.driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
        cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        cls.driver.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def setUp(self):
        # Create a test user in the test DB
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass')

    def test_login_flow(self):
        # self.live_server_url → "http://127.0.0.1:38471" (random port)
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/accounts/login/')
        self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'username').send_keys('alice')
        self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'password').send_keys('pass')
        self.driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]').click()
        self.assertIn('/notes/', self.driver.current_url)

docs.title: LiveServerTestCase vs StaticLiveServerTestCase
docs.text:
from django.test import LiveServerTestCase              # does not serve static files
from django.contrib.staticfiles.testing import StaticLiveServerTestCase  # ← use this one

Most tests need StaticLiveServerTestCase — because if the Bootstrap CSS doesn't load, some elements may be hidden and Selenium won't click them.

docs.title: 13. Session Cookie Trick — logging in without a form
The problem with logging in via the form in E2E tests
docs.text:
The most obvious way to authenticate in a Selenium test:

# AN UNSTABLE WAY — via the form
def login_via_form(driver, url, username, password):
    driver.get(f'{url}/accounts/login/')
    driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'username').send_keys(username)
    driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'password').send_keys(password)
    driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]').click()

Problems: - If the form has a CSRF check involving JavaScript, the test may depend on the loading order - If the form layout changes (renamed CSS classes), the test fails for reasons unrelated to the logic - If you add reCAPTCHA, the test breaks completely - It's slow: every test does a full round-trip through the form

docs.title: The solution: a session cookie
docs.text:
def _login_via_cookie(self):
    """
    The standard E2E login technique via a session cookie:
    1. The Django Test Client logs in (no browser, instantly)
    2. We get the session cookie
    3. We pass the cookie to the Selenium driver
    4. The driver is authenticated — without filling in the form
    """
    # Step 1: the Test Client logs in
    self.client.force_login(self.user)

    # Step 2: Get the session cookie
    session_cookie = self.client.cookies['sessionid']

    # Step 3: Open any page on the same domain
    # (the browser doesn't allow setting cookies without an active domain)
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/')

    # Step 4: Add the cookie to the driver
    self.driver.add_cookie({
        'name':  'sessionid',
        'value': session_cookie.value,
        'path':  '/',
    })

    # Now the driver is authenticated. The next get() goes out as a logged-in user.

docs.title: Why force_login and not login
docs.text:
# force_login — sets up the session without authentication (for tests only)
self.client.force_login(self.user)   # ← fast, no password check

# login — full authentication with a password check
self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass')  # ← slower, for login tests

In the session cookie trick we are not testing login — we are testing functionality after login. That's why force_login is the right choice.

docs.title: The full pattern with a session cookie in a test
docs.text:
class SeleniumNoteFlowTest(StaticLiveServerTestCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.driver = _make_headless_driver()
        cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        cls.driver.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def setUp(self):
        # The test DB is clean (rollback between tests)
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass')
        self._login_via_cookie()   # ← log in via cookie before EVERY test

    def _login_via_cookie(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.user)
        session_cookie = self.client.cookies['sessionid']
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/')
        self.driver.add_cookie({'name': 'sessionid', 'value': session_cookie.value, 'path': '/'})

    def test_create_note(self):
        # Here the driver is already authenticated as alice
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/notes/new/')
        self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'title').send_keys('My Note')
        self.driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]').click()
        # ...

docs.title: When you need Remote WebDriver
docs.text:
Local WebDriver: the driver and the browser are on the same machine.

Remote WebDriver: the driver is on one machine, the browser on another (in Docker, in the cloud).

Uses: - Selenium Grid — run tests in parallel on several browsers - Docker — run Chrome in a container - BrowserStack, Sauce Labs — cloud testing on real devices

docs.title: Selenium Grid + Docker
docs.text:
# Start Selenium standalone-chrome in Docker
docker run -d -p 4444:4444 selenium/standalone-chrome:latest

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options

options = Options()
driver = webdriver.Remote(
    command_executor="http://localhost:4444/wd/hub",  # Grid address
    options=options,
)
driver.get("https://selenium.dev")

docs.title: Our _make_headless_driver() — dynamic selection
docs.text:
test_selenium.py has an environment variable SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL. If it is set — Remote WebDriver; if not — local Chrome:

SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL = os.environ.get("SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL")

def _make_headless_driver():
    options = ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
    options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage')

    if SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL:
        # CI with a separate Selenium container
        return webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL,
            options=options,
        )

    # Locally or on GitHub Actions without a container
    options.add_argument('--headless=new')
    return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

This lets you run ONE test file in both environments.

📖 Remote WebDriver documentation

docs.title: 15. _make_headless_driver() — how it works in our project
docs.text:
Let's look at the full _make_headless_driver() from our project and go through each argument:

def _make_headless_driver():
    options = ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
    options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage')

    if SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL:
        return webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL,
            options=options,
        )

    options.add_argument('--headless=new')
    return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
Argument Explanation --no-sandbox The Chrome sandbox isolates processes. In Docker and on the GitHub Actions runner this conflicts with the container's namespace isolation. We disable it. --disable-dev-shm-usage By default Chrome writes to /dev/shm (shared memory). In Docker this is limited to 64MB → Chrome crashes. This flag makes Chrome write to /tmp. --headless=new The new headless mode (Chrome 112+). The old --headless is kept for compatibility.

docs.title: Why GitHub Actions doesn't use a service container
docs.text:
The template crispy_notes_chat_app/.github/.../django-tests.yml has services: selenium: image: selenium/standalone-chrome. But the real workflow in .github/workflows/django-tests.yml doesn't use it.

Problem:
  The Selenium container opens http://localhost:PORT
  BUT its localhost ≠ the runner's localhost
  → Chrome in the container cannot connect to the Django server on the runner

Solution:
  Chrome and the Django server on the same machine (the runner)
  → localhost is shared
  → everything works

That's why in the real workflow the Selenium tests run without a service container — Chrome is already on ubuntu-latest, and Selenium Manager downloads the matching chromedriver.

docs.title: 16. Walking through test_selenium.py class by class
The _DockerLiveServerMixin mixin
docs.text:
Every live-server class in the file inherits _DockerLiveServerMixin. It solves a networking problem: a Remote Selenium in a separate container cannot see 127.0.0.1 of the web container.

Variable:   WEB_HOST (from the environment)
Locally:    WEB_HOST is empty → host = '127.0.0.1' → live_server_url = 'http://127.0.0.1:PORT'
In Docker:  WEB_HOST=web → host = '0.0.0.0' (bind to all interfaces),
            after setUpClass() the host name goes into the URL → 'http://web:PORT'
In CI:      WEB_HOST=host.docker.internal → Chrome in the selenium container can reach the runner

ChannelsLiveServerTestCase computes live_server_url in advance and stores the string in cls.__dict__, so the mixin also replaces 0.0.0.0 with WEB_HOST in it.

docs.title: The SeleniumLoginFlowTest class
docs.text:
Tests:    The login flow through a real browser
Method:   Filling in the form (not the session cookie)
Tests:
  test_login_page_renders         — the form is in the DOM
  test_valid_login_redirects_to_notes — correct password → redirect
  test_invalid_login_shows_error  — wrong password → we stay on login

The key point: test_valid_login_redirects_to_notes uses WebDriverWait(driver, 5).until(EC.url_changes(login_url)) — it waits until Chrome finishes the redirect after the POST.

def test_valid_login_redirects_to_notes(self):
    login_url = f'{self.live_server_url}/accounts/login/'
    self.driver.get(login_url)

    self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'username').send_keys('seleniumuser')
    self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'password').send_keys('testpass123')
    self.driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]').click()

    # Without this wait, current_url is checked before the redirect
    WebDriverWait(self.driver, 5).until(EC.url_changes(login_url))

    self.assertIn('/notes/', self.driver.current_url)

docs.title: The SeleniumNoteFlowTest class
docs.text:
Tests:    Note workflow: viewing and creating
Method:   Session cookie trick for login
Tests:
  test_note_list_page_loads   — the /notes/ page loaded
  test_create_note_via_form   — the note creation form works
  test_created_note_appears_in_list — the note is visible in the list

test_created_note_appears_in_list doesn't fill in the form — it creates a note via the ORM and checks that page_source contains its title:

def test_created_note_appears_in_list(self):
    Note.objects.create(user=self.user, title='Visible Note', content='Test')
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/notes/')
    self.assertIn('Visible Note', self.driver.page_source)

This checks not the business logic (which is covered by unit tests), but that the template renders the data correctly — {% for note in notes %} displays note.title.

docs.title: The SeleniumGroupChatPageTest class
docs.text:
Tests:    The group chat page /groups/<pk>/chat/
Server:   StaticLiveServerTestCase (no ASGI → the WebSocket does NOT connect)
Tests:
  test_chat_page_loads_for_member      — a group member opens the chat
  test_chat_page_shows_group_name      — the group name is visible
  test_chat_input_element_present      — #chat-input exists
  test_chat_send_button_present        — #chat-send-btn exists
  test_chat_messages_feed_present      — #chat-messages exists
  test_non_member_redirected_from_chat — a non-member gets a redirect
  test_group_detail_has_chat_link      — group_detail contains a link to the chat

docs.title: The SeleniumWebSocketChatTest class
docs.text:
Tests:    The real WebSocket chat in a browser
Server:   ChannelsLiveServerTestCase (Daphne ASGI in a child process)
Tests:
  test_websocket_connects_and_enables_input         — after onopen, #chat-input becomes enabled
  test_send_message_appears_in_chat_feed            — the message appears in #chat-messages
  test_status_shows_connected_after_websocket_opens — #status-text shows 'Підключено' ("Connected")

The full path: browser → WebSocket → GroupChatConsumer → DB → group_send → DOM. The class replaces ProtocolServerProcess with _FreshConnectionDaphneProcess, which closes the DB connections inherited through fork and sets TEST["NAME"], so the Daphne child process works with the same test database.

Besides these classes, the file also has SeleniumReminderToastTest (reminder toasts from reminders.js) and SeleniumDockerStackSmokeTest (smoke tests against an already running Docker stack; they run only when SELENIUM_EXTERNAL_BASE_URL is set).

docs.title: 17. Common errors and how to read them
NoSuchElementException — element not found
docs.text:
selenium.common.exceptions.NoSuchElementException:
Message: no such element: Unable to locate element: {"method":"css selector","selector":"[type='submit']"}

Causes:
  1. The element isn't in the DOM yet (the page hasn't loaded)
     → Increase implicitly_wait or add a WebDriverWait
  2. Wrong selector
     → Open the browser DevTools (F12), check the selector in the console: document.querySelector('[type="submit"]')
  3. The element is in a different iframe
     → driver.switch_to.frame("frame_name") before find_element

docs.title: StaleElementReferenceException — a stale element
docs.text:
selenium.common.exceptions.StaleElementReferenceException:
Message: stale element reference: stale element not found in the current frame

Cause:
  You found an element, then the page reloaded (or JS rebuilt the DOM),
  and that element reference is no longer valid.

Solution:
  # WRONG:
  button = driver.find_element(By.ID, "submit")
  do_something_that_reloads_page()
  button.click()   # ← StaleElementReferenceException!

  # RIGHT:
  do_something_that_reloads_page()
  driver.find_element(By.ID, "submit").click()  # ← find it again

docs.title: TimeoutException — WebDriverWait ran out of time
docs.text:
selenium.common.exceptions.TimeoutException

Cause:
  WebDriverWait(driver, 5).until(EC.url_changes(...)) didn't get its condition within 5 seconds.

Actions:
  1. Increase the timeout: WebDriverWait(driver, 10)
  2. Check that the condition can actually be met
  3. Add a screenshot for diagnosis:
     driver.save_screenshot('/tmp/debug.png')
     # See what is displayed at the moment of the timeout

docs.title: ElementNotInteractableException — cannot interact
docs.text:
selenium.common.exceptions.ElementNotInteractableException:
Message: element not interactable

Cause:
  The element is in the DOM, but hidden (display:none) or covered by another element.

Solution:
  # Check visibility
  if elem.is_displayed():
      elem.click()
  else:
      # Scroll to the element
      driver.execute_script("arguments[0].scrollIntoView(true);", elem)
      elem.click()

docs.title: WebDriverException — the driver didn't start
docs.text:
selenium.common.exceptions.WebDriverException:
Message: 'chromedriver' executable needs to be in PATH

Cause (old Selenium version < 4.6):
  chromedriver is not on the PATH and was not found by Selenium Manager.

For newer versions (4.6+):
  Selenium Manager should download chromedriver automatically.
  If it didn't work: check that Chrome is installed on the system.
  chrome --version  (or google-chrome --version)

docs.title: Anti-pattern 1: time.sleep instead of a wait
docs.text:
# BAD — unstable and slow
driver.find_element(By.ID, "submit").click()
time.sleep(3)   # wait 3 seconds "to be sure it loaded"
assert "Success" in driver.page_source

# GOOD — wait for a specific condition
driver.find_element(By.ID, "submit").click()
WebDriverWait(driver, 5).until(
    EC.text_to_be_present_in_element((By.ID, "message"), "Success")
)
assert "Success" in driver.page_source

time.sleep(3) always waits 3 seconds, even if the page loaded in 0.1s. WebDriverWait waits at most 5 seconds and returns as soon as the condition is met.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 2: Selenium for what the Test Client does better
docs.text:
# BAD — Selenium for checking an HTTP status
def test_unauthenticated_redirect(self):
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/notes/')
    self.assertIn('/accounts/login/', self.driver.current_url)

# GOOD — that's what an integration test is for
def test_unauthenticated_redirect(self):
    response = self.client.get('/notes/')
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)
    self.assertIn('/accounts/login/', response['Location'])

Checking @login_required is an integration test. Selenium is needed only if you must check that the redirect happens in a real browser with navigation.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 3: opening a new driver in every test
docs.text:
# BAD — 100 tests × 3 seconds of Chrome startup = 5 minutes of wasted time
class BadTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.driver = webdriver.Chrome()   # every test launches a new Chrome

    def tearDown(self):
        self.driver.quit()

# GOOD — one driver per class
class GoodTest(TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        cls.driver = webdriver.Chrome()

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        cls.driver.quit()

docs.title: Anti-pattern 4: fragile XPath
docs.text:
# BAD — breaks on any change to the HTML structure
elem = driver.find_element(By.XPATH, "/html/body/div[2]/main/div[1]/form/div[3]/button")

# GOOD — a stable CSS selector or data attribute
elem = driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type="submit"]')
# or add data-testid to the HTML:
# <button data-testid="submit-note" type="submit">
elem = driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[data-testid="submit-note"]')

docs.title: Anti-pattern 5: Selenium tests for every little thing
docs.text:
Unit test: 0.01s  × 100 = 1 second
Selenium:  10s    × 100 = 16 minutes

+ Selenium tests are brittle (a CSS change breaks the test)
+ They require a browser driver, versions, configuration

Rule: Selenium only for critical user flows.
      Anything that can be checked with the Test Client — check it with the Test Client.

docs.title: 19. Self-check questions
docs.text:
1. How does Selenium differ from the Django Test Client? What does each of them check?
  2. What is the WebDriver Protocol, and why is Selenium slower than the Test Client?
  3. What problem does Selenium Manager solve, and in which version did it appear?
  4. What is the difference between driver.close() and driver.quit()?
  5. Which lookup strategy should you choose if the element has an id? If it only has a CSS class?
  6. How does implicitly_wait differ from WebDriverWait? When should you use each?
  7. Why do you need WebDriverWait(...).until(EC.url_changes(...)) after submit_button.click()?
  8. What is StaticLiveServerTestCase, and why is it needed for Django Selenium tests?
  9. Explain the session cookie trick: what are the 4 steps, and why is it better than filling in the login form?
  10. Why is there one driver for the whole class in setUpClass, while _login_via_cookie() is called every time in setUp?
  11. What is StaleElementReferenceException, and how do you avoid it?
  12. When is Remote WebDriver necessary, and when can you make do with a local one?
  13. Why doesn't the real workflow use selenium/standalone-chrome as a service container?
  14. Why use --no-sandbox and --disable-dev-shm-usage in GitHub Actions / Docker?
  15. In which cases is it better to write an integration test rather than a Selenium test?

docs.title: Test data and fixtures: how to prepare state for tests
docs.text: After this file, you will understand how to create data for tests, and when to use an object right inside the test, setUp(), setUpTestData(), pytest fixtures, and factories.

docs.title: 1. Why you need this
docs.text:
A test almost never lives in a vacuum.

To check a list of notes, you need a note. To check permissions, you need two users. To check a form, you need data that looks like a POST request.

A bad approach:

“I already have a user student in my local database, so let the test use it.”

Such a test will break:

  • on another computer;
  • in CI;
  • after the database is cleared;
  • if someone changes the local data.

The right approach:

Each test creates the minimal data it needs by itself.

docs.title: 2. Mental model
docs.text:
Test data is a prop for a scene.

If a scene needs a chair, the director does not hope that a chair just happens to already be on stage. It is placed there before the scene and removed afterwards.

The same goes for tests:

  • before the test, we created a user/note/category;
  • the test checked the behavior;
  • Django cleaned up the test database.

docs.title: 3. The simplest way: create data right in the test
docs.text:
def test_note_str_returns_title(self):
    user = User.objects.create_user(username="student", password="pw")
    note = Note.objects.create(
        owner=user,
        title="First note",
        content="Hello",
    )

    self.assertEqual(str(note), "First note")

This is fine if:

  • there is little data;
  • there is only one test;
  • everything important is visible right in the test.

Pro: the test is easy to read.

Con: if there are 20 such tests, copy-paste begins.

docs.title: 4. setUp(): data before each test
docs.text:
class NoteModelTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(username="student", password="pw")
        self.note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="First note",
            content="Hello",
        )

    def test_note_str_returns_title(self):
        self.assertEqual(str(self.note), "First note")

    def test_note_belongs_to_user(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.note.owner, self.user)

setUp() runs before each test method.

This is good when each test should get clean, new objects.

But do not put everything into setUp(). If a test does not need a category, do not create it just “in case”.

docs.title: 5. setUpTestData(): data once per class
docs.text:
Django has an optimization:

class NoteModelTest(TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpTestData(cls):
        cls.user = User.objects.create_user(username="student", password="pw")
        cls.note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=cls.user,
            title="First note",
            content="Hello",
        )

    def test_note_str_returns_title(self):
        self.assertEqual(str(self.note), "First note")

setUpTestData() creates the data once for the whole class, not before each test.

When to use which:

Approach When setUp() The test changes the data or needs a clean object setUpTestData() The data is the same and must not change

If a test changes shared data from setUpTestData(), be careful. Do not let one test affect another.

docs.title: 6. A helper factory without extra libraries
docs.text:
You can create a simple helper function:

def make_user(username="student"):
    return User.objects.create_user(username=username, password="pw")


def make_note(owner=None, title="Test note", content="Hello"):
    if owner is None:
        owner = make_user()

    return Note.objects.create(
        owner=owner,
        title=title,
        content=content,
    )

Then the test:

def test_note_str_returns_title(self):
    note = make_note(title="Readable note")

    self.assertEqual(str(note), "Readable note")

Advantage: less duplication.

Danger: a helper can hide important details. If the owner matters for the test, it is better to show it explicitly in the test.

docs.title: 7. pytest fixtures for Django
docs.text:
import pytest

from notes.models import Note


@pytest.fixture
def user(db, django_user_model):
    return django_user_model.objects.create_user(
        username="student",
        password="pw",
    )


@pytest.fixture
def note(user):
    return Note.objects.create(
        owner=user,
        title="Fixture note",
        content="Hello",
    )


def test_note_str_returns_title(note):
    assert str(note) == "Fixture note"

What matters:

  • db allows the fixture to work with the database;
  • django_user_model gives you the correct User model;
  • the note fixture can depend on the user fixture.

docs.title: 8. Factory libraries
docs.text:
Large projects often use factory_boy.

Example:

import factory

from notes.models import Note


class UserFactory(factory.django.DjangoModelFactory):
    class Meta:
        model = "auth.User"

    username = factory.Sequence(lambda n: f"user{n}")


class NoteFactory(factory.django.DjangoModelFactory):
    class Meta:
        model = Note

    owner = factory.SubFactory(UserFactory)
    title = factory.Sequence(lambda n: f"Note {n}")
    content = "Hello"

Test:

def test_note_str_returns_title():
    note = NoteFactory(title="Factory note")

    assert str(note) == "Factory note"

For a beginner, a factory library is not required. First learn to create objects by hand and through helpers.

docs.title: 9. Comparing the approaches
docs.text: Method When to use Pro Con Object right in the test One simple test Everything is visible Copy-paste setUp() Several tests in a class Clean state for each test Can grow bloated setUpTestData() Shared immutable data Faster You must not corrupt shared state Helper factory Repeated creation Simple and flexible Can hide important fields pytest fixture pytest projects Composition of fixtures You need to understand the mechanics factory_boy Many models and relations Powerful An extra library

docs.title: 11. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens How to fix it The test depends on the local DB “But I have that data” Create the data in the test setUp() creates a whole world You want everything ready Create the minimum A helper factory hides important fields Too many defaults Pass what matters explicitly One test changes another test's data Shared state Do not rely on test order Using a factory library too early You want it “like in production” Start with simple helpers

docs.title: 12. Practice
docs.text:
1. Write make_user() and make_note().
  2. Rewrite two model tests using make_note().
  3. Write an ownership test:
  4. User A has their own note;
  5. User B has their own note;
  6. User A's list does not contain User B's note.
  7. Rewrite the same scenario using setUp().
  8. If you use pytest, create user and note fixtures.
