docs.text:
1. Why should a test not depend on the real database?
  2. When is it better to create an object right in the test?
  3. How does setUp() differ from setUpTestData()?
  4. How does a helper factory differ from a pytest fixture?
  5. Why can overly “clever” factories make a test harder to read?

docs.title: Testing foundations: a complete study guide
docs.text:
This file is a self-contained reference on the philosophy, tools, and practice of testing. From the first assert to Selenium → it is all here.

Covers: why tests exist, mental models, unittest, pytest, Django TestCase, Selenium, TDD, misconceptions, debugging, architecture diagrams.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Philosophy and mindset - 1. Why testing exists - 2. Fear of change and technical debt - 3. The core philosophy: confidence, not proof - 4. Mental models - 5. What an invariant is

Structure and methodology - 6. The AAA pattern and scientific thinking - 7. Types of tests - 8. The testing pyramid - 9. The nature of bugs

Tools - 10. unittest.TestCase — Python's base framework - 11. pytest — the modern approach - 12. Django TestCase — testing with a DB - 13. Selenium — testing through a browser

Deep understanding - 14. Misconceptions about testing - 15. Debugging failing tests - 16. Testing and architecture - 17. Developer psychology - 18. Real-world context: risk and cost - 19. Manual check vs automated test

Practice - 20. Common beginner mistakes - 21. Architecture diagrams - 22. A basic example for practice - 23. Questions for deep reflection

docs.title: The problem testing solves
docs.text:
Bugs in code are an unavoidable reality. Not because programmers are bad. But because people naturally make mistakes, and in software systems the number of interactions between components grows faster than a human can comprehend.

When there is one function, it is easy to check in your head. When there are thousands of functions and they are connected to each other, it is not.

Every time you change code, add a feature, or fix a bug, you risk breaking something else. Even if you do not intend to. Even if you read the code carefully.

What does testing solve? It is a systematic, repeatable mechanism for checking that the system behaves correctly, regardless of what you changed.

docs.title: Four reasons to write tests
docs.text:
1. Preventing regressions

A regression is when a new feature or a bug fix breaks existing functionality. Tests leave a "trail" of verified behavior. If a regression appears, a test will immediately show where.

2. Reducing the fear of change

Changes break things. Without tests, developers are naturally afraid to touch legacy code. A full test suite lets you refactor and optimize without fear: if something breaks, the tests will tell you.

3. Living documentation

Tests are executable documentation. They do not go stale the way written text does. The test name test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default explains a business rule better than any comment.

4. Improving design

Writing tests, especially before the implementation (TDD), forces you to think about the interface and write more modular, loosely coupled code.

docs.title: A down-to-earth example
docs.text:
def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity

You can check it by hand: print(calculate_total(10, 2)) → you see 20 — "looks good".

But you also need to check: quantity=0, a negative value, rounding, a discount, large numbers. And running print() every time is inconvenient. Plus print() will not automatically tell you that the result is wrong.

A test does this for you, automatically, on every git push:

def test_calculate_total_two_items():
    assert calculate_total(10, 2) == 20

def test_calculate_total_zero_quantity():
    assert calculate_total(10, 0) == 0

def test_calculate_total_rejects_negative_quantity():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        calculate_total(10, -1)

docs.title: 2. Fear of change and technical debt
docs.text: This is probably the most important section. This is where we explain why large projects without tests slowly die.

docs.title: Why developers are afraid of change
docs.text:
In a system without tests, every change is a leap into the unknown:

You change the discount calculation function...
  → Does the orders API suddenly break?
  → Could it affect invoicing?
  → What about the mobile app?
  → What if there are users in the system with old data?

Nobody knows. So nobody changes anything. Or they change things very carefully, very slowly.

docs.title: Technical debt born of fear
docs.text:
When confidence is lacking, developers:

  • refuse to refactor — "it somehow works, better not to touch it"
  • copy code instead of extracting it into a shared function — "extracted it → broke something else"
  • work around old code instead of fixing it — "I'll write a new function next to it"
  • postpone deploys — "we'll check it manually once more after the weekend"

Over time, the codebase becomes a maze of warning notes: # DO NOT TOUCH, # MAGIC, NO IDEA HOW IT WORKS, # TODO for three years already.

This is architectural degradation — not because of bad intentions, but because there is no safety net.

docs.title: What tests change
docs.text:
WITHOUT TESTS                           WITH TESTS
─────────────────────────────────────── ───────────────────────────────────────
"Don't touch it, it somehow works"      "Refactor freely, tests will show if it broke"
Deploy once a month (scary)             Deploy several times a day (confidently)
Customers find the bug a week later     A test finds the bug in 30 seconds
Refactoring is a risky operation        Refactoring is ordinary work
1 year: "we need to rewrite everything" 1 year: "we keep growing calmly"

docs.title: 3. The core philosophy: confidence, not proof
docs.text: "Testing is a process of accumulating confidence, not proving perfection."

docs.title: Why it is impossible to prove the absence of bugs
docs.text:
This has been proven mathematically. In any non-trivial program, the number of possible execution paths approaches infinity.

Edsger W. Dijkstra put it concisely:

"Testing can demonstrate the presence of bugs, but never their absence." ("Testing can prove that bugs are present, but never that they are absent.")

Imagine a simple function with one if:

def process(x):
    if x > 0:
        return x * 2
    return -x

There are 2³² input values of type int. We test five of them. The remaining 4 billion are unchecked.

Real systems have thousands of such conditions. Database states come in countless combinations.

docs.title: So what do tests give us?
docs.text:
Test passed → we could not prove the code is broken in this scenario → confidence grew
Test failed → we proved there is a bug in this scenario → we fix it

Tests collect empirical evidence that the system correctly handles specific, anticipated scenarios. Each additional test reduces uncertainty.

docs.title: The safety net
docs.text:
[Developer]
            | changes code at height
            |
    ════════════════════════  ← test suite
            |
         (ground)

With tests, you can perform complex operations confidently: a large refactoring, replacing a library, changing the DB schema.

docs.title: A scientific experiment
docs.text: Science Testing Hypothesis "The function should return 20" Setting up conditions price = 10, quantity = 2 Running the experiment result = calculate_total(price, quantity) Observation result = 20 Conclusion Hypothesis confirmed / refuted

docs.title: Living documentation
docs.text:
Ordinary documentation goes stale. A test is documentation that cannot be ignored: if the behavior changed but the test was not updated, it will fail.

def test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default(self):
    # This name = a living document of the business rule:
    # "each user can have only one default notebook"

docs.title: A contract between components
docs.text:
A test pins down the agreement between parts of the system:

def test_create_note_returns_note_with_correct_user(self):
    note = services.create_note(user=alice, title='Test')
    self.assertEqual(note.user, alice)

def test_create_note_saves_to_database(self):
    services.create_note(user=alice, title='Test')
    self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)

If someone changes services.create_note() and breaks the contract, the test will show it immediately.

docs.title: A regression prevention system
docs.text:
Bug found → Write a test that reproduces the bug (it fails)
          → Fix the bug (the test turns green)
          → The test stays in the suite forever
          → A year later: refactoring → the same bug → test fails → fixed immediately

docs.title: 5. What an invariant is
docs.text:
An invariant is a property of the system that must remain true no matter how the internal state changes.

Invariant Where it breaks without a test 1 is_default notebook per user create_notebook(is_default=True) without resetting the old one A user sees only their own notes A wrong ORM filter quantity cannot be negative Removing a CheckConstraint Tag labels are unique per user Removing unique_together Deleting a group does not delete notes Changing on_delete=SET_NULL to CASCADE 
# A test of the invariant (not of the implementation):
def test_only_one_default_notebook_per_user(self):
    services.create_notebook(user=alice, title='Old', is_default=True)
    services.create_notebook(user=alice, title='New', is_default=True)
    defaults = Notebook.objects.filter(user=alice, is_default=True)
    self.assertEqual(defaults.count(), 1)  # ← the rule, not the way it is done

docs.title: 6. The AAA pattern and scientific thinking
docs.text:
Every test = three clear steps. This is the standard across all languages and frameworks.

Arrange → Act → Assert
Step What it means Ask yourself Arrange Prepare the system state "What does this test need?" Act Perform what we are testing "Which single action is being examined?" Assert Check the expected result "What must be true afterwards?"

docs.title: A simple example
docs.text:
def test_calculate_total_for_two_items():
    # Arrange
    price    = 10
    quantity = 2

    # Act
    result = calculate_total(price, quantity)

    # Assert
    assert result == 20

docs.title: A Django example
docs.text:
def test_note_list_page_returns_200(self):
    # Arrange: create a user, log in
    user = User.objects.create_user(username='student', password='pw')
    self.client.login(username='student', password='pw')

    # Act: perform one action — a GET request
    response = self.client.get(reverse('note_list'))

    # Assert: check the result
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

docs.title: A service example with two asserts
docs.text:
def test_create_note_assigns_tags(self):
    # Arrange
    tag1 = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='work')
    tag2 = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='python')

    # Act
    note = services.create_note(
        user=self.alice, title='Tagged', tag_ids=[tag1.id, tag2.id]
    )

    # Assert
    note_tags = list(note.tags.all())
    self.assertIn(tag1, note_tags)
    self.assertIn(tag2, note_tags)

docs.title: 7. Types of tests
docs.text: Type What it checks Example When to write it Unit One function / method / class in isolation calculate_tax() Constantly during development Integration Several components together Form + Model + DB When the interaction matters Functional One feature / business function A user creates a note For business requirements E2E The whole path through a browser Selenium: login → create note For critical user flows Regression A specific old bug "An empty title must not be saved" After fixing a bug Smoke Whether the app is alive after a deploy Home page → 200 Before a deploy Acceptance Whether the product meets business requirements Checkout flow Sign-off with the product owner

docs.title: 8. The testing pyramid
docs.text:
╱╲
             ╱E2E╲          Selenium / Cypress
            ╱──────╲        Slow, brittle, expensive
           ╱Integration╲    Django Client, API tests
          ╱──────────────╲  Medium complexity and speed
         ╱     Unit        ╲ pytest, TestCase
        ╱────────────────────╲ Fast, reliable, cheap

     ~70% Unit | ~20% Integration | ~10% E2E

graph TD
    A["End-to-End Tests (Selenium, real browser)<br>Slow · Fragile · Expensive"]
    B["Integration Tests (Test Client, DB, APIs)<br>Medium Speed"]
    C["Unit Tests (logic, models, utils)<br>Blazing Fast · Reliable · Cheap"]

    A --- B
    B --- C

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A warning;
    class B step;
    class C success;

docs.title: Why not do everything through E2E?
docs.text:
E2E test: 15 seconds per test × 100 tests = 25 minutes per run
Unit test: 0.05 seconds × 100 tests = 5 seconds per run

E2E: if it breaks — where exactly? view? service? template? JS? CSS?
Unit: if it breaks — we know exactly where, because we test in isolation

docs.title: Types of bugs
docs.text: Type What it looks like Which test helps Logic error + instead of -, >= instead of > A unit test with concrete values Boundary error Breaks on 0, "", None Parametrized tests Integration failure The parts work separately but not together Integration test Permission bug User B sees user A's data A security test with two users Requirement bug The code correctly implements a wrong requirement A test derived from business requirements Heisenbug Disappears as soon as you start debugging Deterministic tests, atomic()

docs.title: Cognitive traps
docs.text:
• Confirmation bias — you see what you meant to write, not what is written
  • The author's blind spot — your own mistakes are harder to see
  • Happy path testing — we test what "should work" and avoid unpleasant scenarios

A test is free of these traps. It checks exactly what is written. Without fatigue, without bias.

docs.title: 10. unittest.TestCase
docs.text: Python has a built-in unittest — an object-oriented framework based on Java's JUnit.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
import unittest


class TestMathOperations(unittest.TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        """Runs BEFORE each test. We prepare the state."""
        self.x = 10

    def test_divide_normal(self):
        """Happy path — the normal case."""
        self.assertEqual(divide(self.x, 2), 5.0)

    def test_divide_edge_case(self):
        """Edge case — a boundary case."""
        self.assertTrue(divide(self.x, self.x) == 1.0)

    def test_divide_by_zero(self):
        """Wrong input — we expect an exception."""
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            divide(self.x, 0)

    def test_divide_not_equal(self):
        """assertFalse — we make sure the result is NOT equal."""
        self.assertFalse(divide(self.x, 5) == 99.0)

    def tearDown(self):
        """Runs AFTER each test. We clean up the state."""
        self.x = None

docs.title: Main rules
docs.text:
• Test discovery: the framework automatically finds test*.py files
  • Naming: every test method MUST start with test_
  • setUp / tearDown: setUp runs BEFORE each test, tearDown runs AFTER

docs.title: Table of assert methods
docs.text: Method Checks Example assertEqual(a, b) a == b assertEqual(result, 20) assertNotEqual(a, b) a != b assertNotEqual(result, 0) assertTrue(x) bool(x) is True assertTrue(note.is_active) assertFalse(x) bool(x) is False assertFalse(note.is_pinned) assertIsNone(x) x is None assertIsNone(note.group) assertIsNotNone(x) x is not None assertIsNotNone(note.created_at) assertIn(a, b) a in b assertIn(tag, note.tags.all()) assertNotIn(a, b) a not in b assertNotIn(bob_nb, queryset) assertRaises(exc) an exception of type exc assertRaises(ValueError) assertAlmostEqual(a, b) floating-point numbers assertAlmostEqual(1.1+2.2, 3.3) assertIsInstance(obj, cls) isinstance(obj, cls) assertIsInstance(note, Note) assertGreaterEqual(a, b) a >= b assertGreaterEqual(updated, old)

docs.title: setUpClass / tearDownClass
docs.text:
If setUp is expensive, use setUpClass (it runs once for the whole class):

class TestExpensiveSetup(unittest.TestCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        """Runs ONCE for the whole class. For example, a DB connection."""
        cls.db_connection = create_expensive_connection()

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        """Runs ONCE after the whole class."""
        cls.db_connection.close()

    def test_something(self):
        # cls.db_connection is available via self.db_connection
        ...

docs.title: A complete example: notes.py + test_notes.py
docs.text:
# notes.py
class ValidationError(Exception):
    pass

def create_note(title, content):
    if not title:
        raise ValidationError("Title cannot be empty")
    if len(content) > 500:
        raise ValidationError("Content exceeds maximum length of 500 characters")
    return {"title": title.upper(), "content": content, "status": "saved"}

# test_notes.py
import unittest
from notes import create_note, ValidationError


class TestNoteCreation(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_create_note_success(self):
        # Arrange
        title   = "Meeting"
        content = "Discuss project timeline."
        # Act
        result = create_note(title, content)
        # Assert — check the status and the title transformation
        self.assertEqual(result["status"], "saved")
        self.assertEqual(result["title"], "MEETING")

    def test_create_note_empty_title(self):
        # Empty title → ValidationError
        with self.assertRaises(ValidationError):
            create_note("", "Some content")

    def test_create_note_exceeds_length(self):
        # Content > 500 characters → ValidationError
        long_content = "A" * 501
        with self.assertRaises(ValidationError):
            create_note("Long Note", long_content)

docs.title: 11. pytest
docs.text: Although unittest is built into Python, most teams use pytest.

docs.title: Why pytest?
docs.text: Feature unittest pytest Syntax A class + self.assertEqual A plain function + assert Error messages Basic Detailed, colored diff Fixtures setUp/tearDown (rigid) @pytest.fixture (flexible) Parametrization Manual @pytest.mark.parametrize Plugins Limited A huge ecosystem

docs.title: A simple pytest test
docs.text:
# No class needed, no TestCase needed
def test_calculate_total():
    assert calculate_total(10, 2) == 20  # ← just assert, not self.assertEqual

docs.title: @pytest.fixture — flexible setup
docs.text:
Fixtures are state-preparation functions that are injected into tests through arguments:

import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def sample_user():
    """Returns a dictionary with user data."""
    return {"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}

@pytest.fixture
def empty_db():
    """A yield fixture: setup + cleanup in one function."""
    db = Database()
    db.connect()
    yield db          # ← the test runs here
    db.close()        # ← runs after the test (teardown)

def test_user_has_name(sample_user):           # ← pytest injects it automatically
    assert sample_user["name"] == "Alice"

def test_db_starts_empty(empty_db):
    assert empty_db.count() == 0

docs.title: scope='module' — one fixture for the whole module
docs.text:
@pytest.fixture(scope='module')
def db_connection():
    """Created ONCE for the whole module — for expensive resources."""
    conn = create_connection()
    yield conn
    conn.close()

docs.title: @pytest.mark.parametrize
docs.text:
@pytest.mark.parametrize("a, b, expected", [
    (10,  2,   20),
    (0,   5,    0),
    (3,   3,    9),
    (-1,  4,   -4),
])
def test_multiply(a, b, expected):
    assert calculate_total(a, b) == expected
# ↑ Automatically generates 4 separate tests

docs.title: How it differs from a regular TestCase
docs.text:
import unittest
from django.test import TestCase

class PureUnitTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_math(self):
        assert 2 + 2 == 4   # ← no DB, fast

class DjangoTest(TestCase):
    def test_with_db(self):
        user = User.objects.create_user('alice')   # ← needs the test DB
        self.assertEqual(user.username, 'alice')

docs.title: Lifecycle — what happens automatically
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Before ALL tests of the class:                                 │
│    → Creates the test DB (test_<db_name> or SQLite in-memory)   │
│    → Applies all migrations                                     │
│                                                                 │
│  Before EACH test:                                              │
│    → Opens a transaction                                        │
│    → Calls setUp()                                              │
│                                                                 │
│    ┌─── THE TEST RUNS ─────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│    │  User.objects.create(...)  ← rows in the test DB      │   │
│    │  Note.objects.create(...)  ← isolated from the real DB│   │
│    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                 │
│  After EACH test:                                               │
│    → ROLLBACK of the transaction (all rows disappear!)          │
│    → Calls tearDown()                                           │
│                                                                 │
│  After ALL tests:                                               │
│    → Deletes the test DB                                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Three levels of isolation
docs.text:
1. ISOLATION FROM THE REAL DB:
   db.sqlite3 (yours) ≠ test DB (separate, temporary)
   Tests cannot break real data.

2. ISOLATION BETWEEN TESTS:
   Each test has its own transaction → rollback.
   Test A does not see Test B's data.

3. ISOLATION FROM EXTERNAL SYSTEMS:
   EMAIL_BACKEND = console (nothing is actually sent)
   Files are not changed in production

docs.title: Testing views with the Django Test Client
docs.text:
from django.test import TestCase, Client
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from .models import Note


class NoteApplicationTests(TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        self.client = Client()
        self.user1 = User.objects.create_user(username='alice', password='pass123')
        self.user2 = User.objects.create_user(username='bob',   password='pass123')
        self.note  = Note.objects.create(
            user=self.user1, title="Alice's Note", content="Secret"
        )

    def test_anonymous_user_redirected_to_login(self):
        """Not logged in → redirect 302."""
        response = self.client.get('/notes/1/')
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_user_can_access_own_notes(self):
        """Alice sees her own note."""
        self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass123')
        response = self.client.get('/notes/1/')
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertContains(response, "Alice's Note")

    def test_user_cannot_edit_another_users_note(self):
        """Bob cannot edit Alice's note — 403 Forbidden."""
        self.client.login(username='bob', password='pass123')
        response = self.client.post('/notes/1/edit/', {'title': 'Hacked'})
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 403)

    def test_form_rejects_empty_title(self):
        """Empty title → a validation error in the form."""
        self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass123')
        response = self.client.post('/notes/new/', {'title': '', 'content': 'Body'})
        self.assertFormError(response.context['form'], 'title', 'This field is required.')

docs.title: What is Selenium?
docs.text:
Selenium is a framework for controlling a real browser from Python. Instead of an HTTP request (like the Django Test Client), Selenium:

  1. Opens Firefox / Chrome
  2. Navigates to a URL
  3. Finds HTML elements
  4. Clicks, types text, presses Enter
  5. Checks that the correct data appeared in the DOM

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.common.keys import Keys

driver = webdriver.Firefox()
driver.implicitly_wait(5)   # wait up to 5 sec for elements to appear

driver.get("http://localhost:8000/login")

# Finding elements
username_input = driver.find_element(By.NAME, "username")
password_input = driver.find_element(By.NAME, "password")
submit_button  = driver.find_element(By.ID, "login-btn")

# Interaction
username_input.send_keys("testuser")
password_input.send_keys("secret123")
submit_button.click()

# Check
assert "Welcome" in driver.page_source

driver.quit()

docs.title: A full test: login + creating a note
docs.text:
import unittest
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.common.keys import Keys


class TestNoteApplicationFlow(unittest.TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        self.driver = webdriver.Firefox()
        self.driver.implicitly_wait(5)

    def test_login_and_create_note(self):
        driver = self.driver

        # 1. Open the login page
        driver.get("http://localhost:8000/login")

        # 2. Fill in the form
        driver.find_element(By.NAME, "username").send_keys("testuser")
        driver.find_element(By.NAME, "password").send_keys("secret123")
        driver.find_element(By.ID,   "login-btn").click()

        # 3. Go to the note form
        driver.get("http://localhost:8000/notes/new")
        title_input = driver.find_element(By.NAME, "title")
        title_input.send_keys("My First Note")
        title_input.send_keys(Keys.RETURN)

        # 4. Check the result
        self.assertIn("My First Note", driver.page_source)

    def tearDown(self):
        self.driver.quit()

docs.title: Selenium vs Django Test Client
docs.text: Criterion Django Test Client Selenium What it tests Backend: views, permissions, API Frontend: DOM, UI, clicks Speed Milliseconds Seconds (waits for rendering) Brittleness Stable Breaks on CSS changes Closeness to the user Far Exactly like a real user When to use All the time Only for critical flows

docs.title: "Tests prove the program has no bugs"
docs.text: False. Tests prove that specific described scenarios behave correctly. All other scenarios remain unchecked.

docs.title: "Testing is only for big projects"
docs.text: False. Even a 50-line script can break when a dependency is updated or unexpected data arrives. If the code matters, it is worth a test.

docs.title: "Selenium replaces unit tests"
docs.text: False. Selenium tests the whole stack. If a test fails, where exactly? view? service? JS? CSS? Unknown. A unit test shows the exact place. Besides, 100 Selenium tests = 25 minutes. 100 unit tests = 5 seconds.

docs.title: "More tests = better quality"
docs.text:
False. Tests are code. Code needs maintenance. A test that: - checks trivial Django ORM behavior - tests implementation details instead of behavior - is written incorrectly (always green)

— raises the cost of maintenance, not the quality.

docs.title: "Testing slows down development"
docs.text:
False in the long run:

Month 1 without tests: +20% speed
Month 3: first regressions, fear of change
Month 6: deploy once a week, most of the time spent debugging
Month 12: "we need to rewrite it"

Month 1 with tests: a bit slower
Month 3: refactoring freely
Month 12: deploy daily, trust is high

docs.title: "Testing is QA's responsibility"
docs.text: False. Quality cannot be "bolted on from the outside". If a developer writes code without tests → the architecture naturally becomes untestable. The right way: the developer writes unit/integration tests, QA writes acceptance and E2E tests.

docs.title: "One big test is better than many small ones"
docs.text: False. If the first of 20 asserts fails, the test stops. You know nothing about the other 19. Small tests = precise diagnostics.

docs.title: 15. Debugging failing tests
docs.text: A failing test is not a punishment. It is a system that protects you from regressions.

docs.title: Reading pytest messages
docs.text:
pytest rewrites assert and shows a detailed diff:

FAILED test_services.py::test_create_note_assigns_tags
AssertionError: assert <Tag: #work> in []
E       assert <Tag: #work> in []
E         where [] = <built-in method all of ManyRelatedManager object at 0x...>()

→ The test says: expected the tag to be in note.tags.all(), but the list is empty
→ We look in services.create_note() for why the tags were not attached

docs.title: Isolating a failing test
docs.text:
# Don't run all 500 tests every time:
pytest tests/test_services.py::NoteServiceTest::test_create_note_assigns_tags

# Stop after the first failure:
pytest -x            # or --exitfirst

# Verbose — see every test:
pytest -v

docs.title: TDD for fixing bugs
docs.text:
1. A user reported a bug in production
2. We do NOT touch the application code right away
3. We write a test that reproduces the bug → it fails (RED)
4. We fix the code → the test turns green (GREEN)
5. The test stays in the suite — the bug will never come back

docs.title: When to fix the test rather than the code
docs.text:
Ask yourself: "Did the application logic break, or did the business requirements change?"

  • The logic broke → we fix the code
  • The requirements changed → we fix the test (it is outdated)

Never delete a test just to stop it from failing. A failing test is information, not an inconvenience.

docs.title: Testability as a design signal
docs.text:
If code is hard to test, it is a symptom of poor architecture:

# Hard to test (hidden dependencies):
def send_welcome_email():
    user = User.objects.get(id=settings.CURRENT_USER_ID)  # ← global state
    smtp.send(user.email, "Welcome!")                       # ← side effect

# Easy to test (dependencies are explicit):
def send_welcome_email(user, email_backend):
    email_backend.send(user.email, "Welcome!")
    # ← in the test: email_backend = MockEmailBackend()

If a test needs 10+ mocks, that is a signal that the function has too many responsibilities.

docs.title: TDD — design through tests
docs.text:
[Write a failing test] → RED
        ↓
[Write the minimal code that passes] → GREEN
        ↓
[Refactor without changing behavior] → REFACTOR
        ↓
[Write the next failing test] → RED

graph LR
    A[Write a Failing Test] -->|Red| B(Write Application Code)
    B -->|Green| C{Run Test Suite}
    C -->|Pass| D[Refactor and Clean Up]
    C -->|Fail| B
    D --> A

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class A error;
    class B success;
    class C decision;
    class D step;

docs.title: Layered architecture (CrispyNotes)
docs.text:
domain / services  ← pure logic, no I/O → unit tests directly
    ↑
infrastructure     ← DB, email, API → integration tests or mocks
    ↑
api / views        ← HTTP → integration tests via self.client

docs.title: Overconfidence bias
docs.text: After writing a complex algorithm, you want to see that it works, so you test the happy path. A test written with the intent to try to break the code is the opposite stance. That is the stance that finds real bugs.

docs.title: The team's collective memory
docs.text:
def test_create_note_ignores_other_users_tags(self):
    """
    Mass Assignment vulnerability: an attacker sends another user's tag_id.
    We filter by user before set() to block it.
    """

A new developer reads the name → understands the security rule → does not break the protection while refactoring.

docs.title: 18. Real-world context: risk and cost
docs.text:
System type Risk from a bug Testing focus Prototype, MVP Low Minimal or none SaaS web application Medium Unit + integration tests Note app with many users Authorization Security tests with alice + bob Financial system High — users' money Exhaustive testing + audit Medical / Aerospace Critical — people's lives Formal verification

The law of diminishing returns:

Test #1 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~    ← maximum value: catches the biggest risks
Test #10 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Test #100 ~~~           ← less value: rare edge cases
Test #1000 ~            ← marginal: cost > benefit

docs.title: 19. Manual check vs automated test
docs.text:
Criterion Manual check Automated test First run Instant (nothing to write) You need to write code Repeatability Slow, you can forget a step Instant, identical Regressions Easy to miss Catches them well Edge cases Limited by time Exhaustive UX research Irreplaceable Not suitable

Rule: A manual check is irreplaceable for new behavior and UX. But if you check the same thing manually more than twice, it is time to write a test.

docs.title: 20. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How to fix it A test without a clear expectation Phrase it: "should return X under condition Y" One huge test Split it: each test covers one behavior Testing implementation details Check behavior and invariants, not internal details Only the happy path Deliberately look for boundary + edge + error cases A test that is "always green" Make sure the test FAILS when the code is wrong Mocking everything Mock = an echo chamber. Mock only external I/O, not your own logic Testing Django internals Do not test .save() to the DB — Django has already done that A bad name test_1 → test_delete_group_sets_note_group_to_null

docs.title: Especially: a test that is "always green"
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS — always passes, guarantees nothing:
def test_create_note(self):
    try:
        note = services.create_note(user=self.user, title='Test')
    except Exception:
        pass   # ← we ignore errors!

# CORRECT:
def test_create_note(self):
    note = services.create_note(user=self.user, title='Test')
    self.assertIsNotNone(note)
    self.assertEqual(note.title, 'Test')

Rule: Temporarily "break" the code and make sure the test really fails.

docs.title: 22. A basic example for practice
docs.text:
Do it now — two files, 5 minutes:

cart.py:

def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    if quantity < 0:
        raise ValueError("quantity cannot be negative")
    return price * quantity

test_cart.py:

import pytest
from cart import calculate_total


def test_two_items():
    assert calculate_total(10, 2) == 20       # happy path

def test_zero_quantity():
    assert calculate_total(10, 0) == 0         # edge case

def test_negative_quantity_raises():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        calculate_total(10, -1)                # error case

def test_large_values():
    assert calculate_total(1_000_000, 1_000) == 1_000_000_000  # boundary

Steps:

# 1. Run it — all green
pytest test_cart.py -v

# 2. Break the function: return price + quantity
# 3. Run it — you will see a failing test (that's correct!)
# 4. Restore the function → green again

Seeing a test fail on wrong code is the best confirmation that the test is real.

docs.title: 23. Questions for deep reflection
docs.text:
On the limits of testing: 1. If all tests pass, what do we know with confidence? What remains unknown? 2. What can tests NOT check: UX, business value, performance under load?

On cost: 3. When does the cost of maintaining a test exceed its value? How do you determine that? 4. At what level of coverage does it become "confident enough" to deploy to production? 5. Why does 100% code coverage not guarantee the absence of bugs?

On architecture: 6. Why does hard-to-test code almost always mean poor architecture? 7. If you cannot write a unit test without 10 mocks, what does that say about the function's design?

On the real world: 8. Why do catastrophic bugs sometimes survive thousands of tests and careful code review? 9. How do you tell a "bug in the implementation" from a "bug in the requirements"? Which is more dangerous? 10. How will you decide which behavior to test when you have to choose among 100 possible scenarios?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Without tests:  "Seems like everything is fine"  ← emotional confidence
With tests:     "82/82 tests passed"             ← evidence-based confidence

Testing is an engineering discipline for managing uncertainty. It gives you:

What How A safety net Refactoring without fear Living documentation Test name = business rule Catching regressions Old bugs do not come back A security guard IDOR and Mass Assignment become impossible Architectural pressure Poor design is hard to test → you can see where the problem is

Next step: basics/01_first_test.py → your first test that runs.

docs.title: Practice project: testing notes_chat_app from model to Selenium
docs.text: After this file, you will assemble a complete learning scenario for testing a Django notes app: model, form, URL, view, permissions, a service with email, mock, Selenium E2E, Docker headless, and coverage.

docs.title: 1. Why you need this
docs.text:
Individual examples are useful, but in real learning a student needs a route.

Not just:

Here is a model test.
Here is a mock.
Here is Selenium.

But like this:

1. Here is a small notes app.
2. Here is the behavior we expect.
3. Here are the tests we write first.
4. Here is how to run them.
5. Here is what a failure looks like.
6. Here is when we add Selenium.

This file is the final practical lesson. It brings all the previous topics together into one project.

docs.title: 2. Mental model
docs.text:
Testing an application is like checking a delivery route.

First we check the small things:

  • whether the box has the right label;
  • whether the address is valid;
  • whether the courier does not take someone else's parcel.

Then we check the bigger route:

  • the user logs in;
  • creates a note;
  • sees it in the list;
  • does not see other people's notes.

And only one or two of the most important routes are checked through a real browser with Selenium.

docs.title: 3. What we are building
docs.text:
Project: notes_chat_app

App: notes

Functionality:

  1. a user can create a note;
  2. a note has title, content, owner, is_archived;
  3. the list shows only the current user's notes;
  4. the form strips spaces from the title;
  5. the title admin is forbidden;
  6. creating a note calls an email service;
  7. Selenium checks the main path: login -> create note -> note appears.

Structure:

notes_chat_app/
├── manage.py
├── notes_chat_app/
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── urls.py
└── notes/
    ├── models.py
    ├── forms.py
    ├── services.py
    ├── views.py
    ├── urls.py
    ├── templates/
    │   └── notes/
    │       ├── note_form.html
    │       └── note_list.html
    └── tests/
        ├── test_models.py
        ├── test_forms.py
        ├── test_urls.py
        ├── test_views.py
        ├── test_services.py
        └── test_e2e.py

docs.title: 4.1 Model
docs.text:
# notes/models.py
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models


class Note(models.Model):
    owner = models.ForeignKey(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name="notes",
    )
    title = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    content = models.TextField()
    is_archived = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

    def archive(self):
        self.is_archived = True
        self.save(update_fields=["is_archived"])

What is ours here:

  • __str__;
  • archive;
  • ownership via owner.

The mere fact that a CharField stores a string does not need testing. Django already tests that.

docs.title: 4.2 Form
docs.text:
# notes/forms.py
from django import forms

from notes.models import Note


class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ["title", "content"]

    def clean_title(self):
        title = self.cleaned_data["title"].strip()

        if title.lower() == "admin":
            raise forms.ValidationError("Title cannot be admin.")

        return title

What to test:

  • valid data;
  • missing title;
  • strip spaces;
  • reserved title.

docs.title: 4.3 Service
docs.text:
# notes/services.py
from django.core.mail import send_mail


def send_note_created_email(email, title):
    send_mail(
        subject="Note created",
        message=f"Your note '{title}' was created.",
        from_email="noreply@example.com",
        recipient_list=[email],
    )

We will mock email in the tests.

docs.text:

from notes import views


urlpatterns = [
    path("notes/", views.note_list, name="note_list"),

from django.urls import include, path


urlpatterns = [
    path("admin/", admin.site.urls),
    path("", include("django.contrib.auth.urls")),

]

docs.title: 5. Test plan
docs.text:
We write tests not chaotically, but in layers.

Step File What we check 1 test_models.py __str__, archive() 2 test_forms.py valid/invalid form, clean_title() 3 test_urls.py URL names lead to the right views 4 test_views.py GET/POST, redirects, templates, ownership 5 test_services.py the email service via mock 6 test_e2e.py the main path in a browser 7 coverage what actually ran

docs.title: 6. Model tests
docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_models.py
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.test import TestCase

from notes.models import Note


User = get_user_model()


class NoteModelTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            username="student",
            email="student@example.com",
            password="pw",
        )

    def test_note_str_returns_title(self):
        note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="First note",
            content="Hello",
        )

        self.assertEqual(str(note), "First note")

    def test_archive_marks_note_as_archived(self):
        note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="Archive me",
            content="Hello",
        )

        note.archive()
        note.refresh_from_db()

        self.assertTrue(note.is_archived)

Running:

python manage.py test notes.tests.test_models

docs.title: 7. Form tests
docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_forms.py
from django.test import TestCase

from notes.forms import NoteForm


class NoteFormTest(TestCase):
    def test_form_is_valid_with_title_and_content(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={
            "title": "My note",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())

    def test_form_is_invalid_without_title(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={
            "title": "",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())
        self.assertIn("title", form.errors)

    def test_form_strips_title_spaces(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={
            "title": "  My note  ",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())
        self.assertEqual(form.cleaned_data["title"], "My note")

    def test_form_rejects_reserved_admin_title(self):
        form = NoteForm(data={
            "title": "admin",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())
        self.assertIn("title", form.errors)

What the student should notice:

  • a form test does not need a browser;
  • a form test does not need to create a Note in the DB;
  • we check the validation logic directly.

docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_urls.py
from django.test import SimpleTestCase
from django.urls import resolve, reverse

from notes.views import note_create, note_list


class NoteUrlsTest(SimpleTestCase):
    def test_note_list_url_resolves_to_note_list_view(self):
        match = resolve(reverse("note_list"))

        self.assertEqual(match.func, note_list)

    def test_note_create_url_resolves_to_note_create_view(self):
        match = resolve(reverse("note_create"))

        self.assertEqual(match.func, note_create)

We use SimpleTestCase here because no database is needed.

docs.title: 9. View tests: list
docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_views.py
from unittest.mock import patch

from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse

from notes.models import Note


User = get_user_model()


class NoteListViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            username="student",
            email="student@example.com",
            password="pw",
        )

    def test_anonymous_user_redirects_to_login(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_logged_user_can_open_note_list(self):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertTemplateUsed(response, "notes/note_list.html")

    def test_note_list_shows_only_current_user_notes(self):
        other_user = User.objects.create_user(username="other", password="pw")
        own_note = Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="Mine",
            content="Hello",
        )
        Note.objects.create(
            owner=other_user,
            title="Other user note",
            content="Secret",
        )

        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

        notes = list(response.context["notes"])
        self.assertIn(own_note, notes)
        self.assertEqual(len(notes), 1)

    def test_archived_notes_are_hidden(self):
        Note.objects.create(
            owner=self.user,
            title="Archived",
            content="Hello",
            is_archived=True,
        )

        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_list"))

        self.assertEqual(list(response.context["notes"]), [])

These tests matter more than just status_code == 200, because they check business rules.

docs.title: 10. View tests: create + mock email
docs.text:
# notes/tests/test_views.py
class NoteCreateViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            username="student",
            email="student@example.com",
            password="pw",
        )

    def test_anonymous_user_cannot_open_create_page(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_create"))

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_logged_user_can_open_create_page(self):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.get(reverse("note_create"))

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertTemplateUsed(response, "notes/note_form.html")

    @patch("notes.views.send_note_created_email")
    def test_logged_user_can_create_note(self, mock_send_email):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "Created from test",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertRedirects(response, reverse("note_list"))
        note = Note.objects.get(title="Created from test")
        self.assertEqual(note.owner, self.user)
        mock_send_email.assert_called_once_with(
            "student@example.com",
            "Created from test",
        )

    @patch("notes.views.send_note_created_email")
    def test_invalid_form_does_not_create_note_or_send_email(self, mock_send_email):
        self.client.login(username="student", password="pw")

        response = self.client.post(reverse("note_create"), {
            "title": "",
            "content": "Hello",
        })

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertFalse(Note.objects.exists())
        mock_send_email.assert_not_called()

Why patch exactly notes.views.send_note_created_email?

Because the view imports and uses that name in the notes/views.py file. We mock the place where it is used.

docs.title: 11. Service test
docs.text:
You can test the email service separately:

# notes/tests/test_services.py
from unittest.mock import patch

from django.test import SimpleTestCase

from notes.services import send_note_created_email


class NoteEmailServiceTest(SimpleTestCase):
    @patch("notes.services.send_mail")
    def test_send_note_created_email_calls_send_mail(self, mock_send_mail):
        send_note_created_email("student@example.com", "My note")

        mock_send_mail.assert_called_once_with(
            subject="Note created",
            message="Your note 'My note' was created.",
            from_email="noreply@example.com",
            recipient_list=["student@example.com"],
        )

No database is needed here, so we use SimpleTestCase.

docs.title: 12. Selenium E2E smoke test
docs.text:
You do not need to write Selenium tests for every little thing. But one smoke test for the main route is useful.

Installation:

pip install selenium

Test:

# notes/tests/test_e2e.py
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.contrib.staticfiles.testing import StaticLiveServerTestCase
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait


User = get_user_model()


class NoteAppE2ETest(StaticLiveServerTestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.browser = webdriver.Firefox()
        cls.browser.implicitly_wait(3)

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        cls.browser.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def setUp(self):
        User.objects.create_user(
            username="student",
            email="student@example.com",
            password="password123",
        )

    def test_user_can_login_and_create_note(self):
        self.browser.get(f"{self.live_server_url}/login/")

        self.browser.find_element(By.NAME, "username").send_keys("student")
        self.browser.find_element(By.NAME, "password").send_keys("password123")
        self.browser.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "button[type='submit']").click()

        create_link = WebDriverWait(self.browser, 5).until(
            EC.element_to_be_clickable((By.ID, "create-note-link"))
        )
        create_link.click()

        self.browser.find_element(By.NAME, "title").send_keys("Selenium Note")
        self.browser.find_element(By.NAME, "content").send_keys("E2E works")
        self.browser.find_element(By.ID, "submit-note").click()

        note_title = WebDriverWait(self.browser, 5).until(
            EC.visibility_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, ".note-title"))
        )

        self.assertEqual(note_title.text, "Selenium Note")

What you need to add to the HTML:

<!-- notes/note_list.html -->
<a id="create-note-link" href="{% url 'note_create' %}">Create note</a>

{% for note in notes %}
  <h2 class="note-title">{{ note.title }}</h2>
{% endfor %}

<!-- notes/note_form.html -->
<form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form.as_p }}
  <button id="submit-note" type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

Stable selectors are part of UI testability.

docs.title: 13. Selenium in Docker/CI headless
docs.text: A CI server has no monitor. There are three strategies for running Selenium without a physical display.

docs.title: 13.1 Strategy A — install geckodriver/chromedriver in the Dockerfile
docs.text:
Firefox + geckodriver — download the binary from GitHub Releases:

ARG GECKODRIVER_VERSION=0.35.0

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y firefox-esr wget \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    && wget -q "https://github.com/mozilla/geckodriver/releases/download/v${GECKODRIVER_VERSION}/geckodriver-v${GECKODRIVER_VERSION}-linux64.tar.gz" \
    && tar -xzf geckodriver-v${GECKODRIVER_VERSION}-linux64.tar.gz \
    && mv geckodriver /usr/local/bin/ \
    && rm geckodriver-v${GECKODRIVER_VERSION}-linux64.tar.gz

Chrome + chromedriver — simpler via a package:

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    chromium \
    chromium-driver \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

In the tests, use headless mode:

# Firefox headless
from selenium.webdriver.firefox.options import Options as FirefoxOptions
options = FirefoxOptions()
options.add_argument("--headless")
driver = webdriver.Firefox(options=options)

# Chrome headless
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options as ChromeOptions
options = ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument("--headless=new")
options.add_argument("--no-sandbox")             # required in Docker
options.add_argument("--disable-dev-shm-usage")  # shared memory in the container
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
Argument Why --headless=new Run without a GUI window (the new headless implementation, Chrome 112+) --no-sandbox The Chrome sandbox conflicts with Docker namespaces --disable-dev-shm-usage /dev/shm is 64 MB by default in Docker → Chrome crashes

How to run it (if you have xvfb for old Firefox versions without --headless):

xvfb-run -s "-screen 0 1024x768x24" python manage.py test

docs.title: 13.2 Strategy B — official Selenium Docker images (recommended for CI)
docs.text:
selenium/standalone-chrome and selenium/standalone-firefox are ready-made images from the Selenium Project. They already contain: browser + driver + VNC server. Nothing to install or download.

docker-compose.yml — two services: web (Django tests) + selenium (browser):

version: "3.9"
services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: python manage.py test
    environment:
      - SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://selenium:4444/wd/hub
    depends_on:
      selenium:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - test-net

  selenium:
    image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
    shm_size: "2gb"   # Chrome needs shared memory for rendering
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:4444/status"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - test-net

networks:
  test-net:

In the tests, a function that switches between Local and Remote via an env var:

import os
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.firefox.options import Options as FirefoxOptions

SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL = os.environ.get("SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL")


def _make_driver():
    if SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL:
        # CI / docker-compose → Remote WebDriver to the Selenium container
        options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
        return webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL,
            options=options,
        )
    # Locally → headless Firefox (if geckodriver is installed)
    options = FirefoxOptions()
    options.add_argument("--headless")
    return webdriver.Firefox(options=options)

Running:

docker compose up --build --abort-on-container-exit

Bonus: VNC is available at http://localhost:7900 (password: secret) — you can watch what the browser is doing.

docs.title: 13.3 Strategy C — a ready-made GitHub Actions recipe
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/tests.yml
name: Django Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      selenium:
        image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
        options: --shm-size=2gb
        ports:
          - 4444:4444

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt selenium

      - name: Run tests
        env:
          SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL: http://localhost:4444/wd/hub
        run: python manage.py test

The same SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL env var is picked up by _make_driver() — the code is identical locally and in CI.

docs.title: 13.4 Which strategy to choose
docs.text:
Strategy Where geckodriver lives Complexity Recommended for xvfb + Firefox installed locally ⭐⭐ CI without Docker, Linux Dockerfile + wget geckodriver in the Dockerfile ⭐⭐ your own Docker image selenium/standalone-chrome + Remote in the Selenium image ⭐ docker-compose, GitHub Actions

For new projects: selenium/standalone-chrome + webdriver.Remote() — the simplest option; the browser is always the same in every environment.

docs.title: 14. Coverage
docs.text:
Running:

pip install coverage
coverage run manage.py test
coverage report
coverage html

How to read it:

Name                    Stmts   Miss  Cover
-------------------------------------------
notes/models.py            18      0   100%
notes/forms.py             20      2    90%
notes/views.py             45      8    82%

Do not blindly chase 100%. Ask:

  • are permissions checked?
  • are there invalid form tests?
  • are there edge cases?
  • is payment/email/API checked via mock?
  • is there at least one Selenium smoke test for the main route?

docs.title: 16. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens How to fix it Starting with Selenium It looks the “most complete” Model/form/view tests first Not testing ownership Thinking only about your own user Create User A and User B Mocking the form/model Wanting isolation Form/model are better tested for real via the test DB Not adding stable selectors HTML is written only for human eyes Add an id or data-test-id for E2E Using time.sleep() An easy way to wait Use WebDriverWait Coverage is there, but assertions are weak Looking only at the number Check what the tests actually contain

docs.title: 19.1 What CI is and why you need it
docs.text:
CI (Continuous Integration) is the practice of automatically running tests every time code lands in the repository.

Without CI: 

Developer writes code → push → tests are run manually (or not at all) → the bug lands in main

With CI: 

Developer writes code → push → GitHub runs the tests automatically → if a test fails → merge is blocked

GitHub Actions is the CI/CD built into GitHub. It is free for public repositories and for private ones within a quota.

docs.title: 19.2 Where the file must live — IMPORTANT
docs.text:
GitHub Actions reads .yml files only from the repository root folder:

<repo-root>/.github/workflows/*.yml   ← GitHub sees and runs these

A file anywhere else is ignored:

docs/08_testing_and_quality/.github/workflows/  ← DOES NOT WORK

The correct structure for our project (the notes_chat_app repository, with the Django project right in the root):

notes_chat_app/                        ← repository root
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── django-tests.yml           ← HERE, not inside docs/
├── manage.py
├── requirements.txt
├── notes_project/
├── notes_app/
└── docs/

Since manage.py sits in the repository root, our workflow does not need working-directory. If the Django project lives in a subfolder of the repository, you point to it with working-directory:

defaults:
  run:
    working-directory: path/to/django_project   # the folder that contains manage.py

YAML format — GitHub Actions uses YAML to describe the pipeline.

docs.title: 19.3 The full workflow file, explained
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/django-tests.yml

name: Django Tests       # pipeline name in the GitHub UI

# ── Triggers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]   # run on push to main
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]   # run on a PR to main
  workflow_dispatch:             # the "Run workflow" button in the GitHub UI

# ── Jobs ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
jobs:

  # ── Job 1: Unit + Integration (fast tests without a browser) ──────────────
  test:
    name: Unit & Integration Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest       # runner type (a VM from GitHub)

    steps:
      # Step 1: download the code
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Step 2: install Python
      - name: Set up Python 3.12
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      # Step 3: pip cache (speeds up repeated runs)
      - name: Cache pip
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}

      # Step 4: install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      # Step 5: check the Django configuration
      - name: Django system check
        run: python manage.py check

      # Step 6: run the tests without Selenium
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          python manage.py test \
            notes_app.tests.test_models \
            notes_app.tests.test_services \
            notes_app.tests.test_forms \
            notes_app.tests.test_views \
            -v 2

      # Step 7: coverage
      - name: Coverage report
        run: |
          coverage run manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_models \
            notes_app.tests.test_services \
            notes_app.tests.test_forms \
            notes_app.tests.test_views
          coverage report
          coverage xml

      # Step 8: save coverage as an artifact
      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-report
          path: coverage.xml


  # ── Job 2: Selenium E2E tests ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  test-selenium:
    name: Selenium E2E Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: test              # run only after Job 1 succeeds

    # Selenium as a separate Docker service
    services:
      selenium:
        image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
        options: --shm-size=2gb
        ports:
          - 4444:4444

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python 3.12
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      # SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL → _make_driver() will use Remote WebDriver
      - name: Run Selenium tests
        env:
          SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL: http://localhost:4444/wd/hub
        run: python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2

docs.title: 19.4 How GitHub runs the pipeline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant GH as GitHub
    participant Runner as Ubuntu Runner
    participant Selenium as Selenium Container

    Dev->>GH: git push main
    GH->>Runner: Start Job 1 (test)
    Runner->>Runner: checkout code
    Runner->>Runner: setup-python 3.12
    Runner->>Runner: pip install -r requirements.txt
    Runner->>Runner: manage.py test (123 tests)
    Runner-->>GH: ✅ Job 1 passed

    GH->>Runner: Start Job 2 (test-selenium)
    Runner->>Selenium: start selenium/standalone-chrome
    Runner->>Runner: pip install -r requirements.txt
    Runner->>Selenium: webdriver.Remote(SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL)
    Selenium-->>Runner: 6 E2E tests passed
    Runner-->>GH: ✅ Job 2 passed

    GH-->>Dev: ✅ All checks passed — PR can be merged

docs.title: 19.5 How to see the results on GitHub
docs.text:
1. Open the repository on GitHub
  2. Click the Actions tab
  3. On the left is the list of workflows, on the right is the run history
  4. Click a specific run → you see the jobs → click a job → you see the steps

If a test fails:

❌ Run tests
  FAILED: notes_app.tests.test_views.NoteAuthorizationTest.test_bob_cannot_edit_alice_note
  AssertionError: 200 != 403
  ...

The error text is visible right in the GitHub UI.

docs.title: 19.6 Status badge
docs.text:
Add this to README.md to show whether the tests pass:

![Django Tests](https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPO/actions/workflows/django-tests.yml/badge.svg)

It looks like this:

[passing] Django Tests

Colleagues and employers immediately see that the project has CI and the tests are green.

docs.title: 19.7 Branch Protection
docs.text:
In the repository settings:

Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule
  ☑ Require status checks to pass before merging
  ☑ Require branches to be up to date before merging
      Status checks: "Unit & Integration Tests"

After this, merging into main is blocked if the tests fail.

❌ Cannot merge — "Unit & Integration Tests" check failed

docs.title: 19.8 Diagram: what CI checks on every push
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["git push / PR"] --> B["GitHub Actions trigger"]
    B --> C["Job 1: Unit + Integration<br>123 tests, ~2-3 minutes"]
    C -->|pass| D["Job 2: Selenium E2E<br>6 tests, ~1-2 minutes"]
    C -->|fail| E["❌ Merge blocked<br>PR gets a red cross"]
    D -->|pass| F["✅ Merge allowed<br>PR gets a green check mark"]

docs.title: unittest: first tests with standard Python tools
docs.text: After this file, you will be able to create a test file, write a unittest.TestCase class, run tests with python -m unittest, and understand the basic assert methods.

docs.title: 1. Why you need this
docs.text:
unittest is Python's standard library for testing. You do not need to install it.

Why learn it if pytest exists?

  1. Django's TestCase is built on the ideas of unittest.
  2. Many older and larger projects use exactly this style.
  3. unittest shows the structure of a test well: class, method, assertion.
  4. Once you understand unittest, Django tests become much clearer.

docs.title: 2. Mental model
docs.text:
A unittest.TestCase is a separate lab room for a group of similar checks.

The class TestMathFunctions means:

“Checks for math functions live here.”

The method test_add_two_numbers means:

“Here is a specific experiment: adding two numbers.”

docs.title: 3. A first example from scratch
docs.text:
Folder structure:

testing_playground/
├── math_utils.py
└── test_math_utils.py

The file math_utils.py:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

The file test_math_utils.py:

import unittest

from math_utils import add, divide


class TestMathFunctions(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add_two_numbers(self):
        result = add(2, 3)

        self.assertEqual(result, 5)

    def test_divide_by_zero_raises_error(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ZeroDivisionError):
            divide(10, 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

Running all tests in the folder:

python -m unittest

Running a specific file:

python -m unittest test_math_utils.py

A possible result:

..
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 2 tests in 0.001s

OK

What the two dots mean:

Symbol Meaning . One test passed F Assertion failed E An error in the test code or in the code under test

docs.title: 4. How unittest finds tests
docs.text:
unittest looks for:

What Rule Example File Usually test_*.py test_math_utils.py Class Inherits from unittest.TestCase class TestMathFunctions(unittest.TestCase) Method Starts with test_ def test_add_two_numbers(self):

If you name a method like this:

def check_add_two_numbers(self):
    ...

unittest will not run it.

This is a common mistake: the test code exists, but the test runner does not see it.

docs.title: 5. Arrange -> Act -> Assert in unittest
docs.text:
A poor version:

def test_add_two_numbers(self):
    self.assertEqual(add(2, 3), 5)

It is short, but a beginner cannot see the steps.

Better for learning:

def test_add_two_numbers(self):
    a = 2
    b = 3

    result = add(a, b)

    self.assertEqual(result, 5)
Step Lines Arrange a = 2, b = 3 Act result = add(a, b) Assert self.assertEqual(result, 5)

docs.title: 6. The main assert methods
7. setUp(): preparing data before each test
docs.text:
If several tests use the same data, you can add setUp().

class TestCart(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.cart = []

    def test_cart_starts_empty(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.cart, [])

    def test_can_add_item_to_cart(self):
        self.cart.append("Book")

        self.assertIn("Book", self.cart)

setUp() runs before each test.

This matters: each test gets a clean state.

Bad:

cart = []


class TestCart(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add_book(self):
        cart.append("Book")

    def test_cart_is_empty(self):
        self.assertEqual(cart, [])

The second test may fail because the first one left data behind.

docs.title: 8. What a failing test looks like
docs.text:
Suppose the test is:

def test_add_two_numbers(self):
    result = add(2, 3)

    self.assertEqual(result, 5)

And the function is:

def add(a, b):
    return a - b

Result:

AssertionError: -1 != 5

How to read it:

Part Meaning -1 The actual result 5 The expected result AssertionError The expectation did not match

There is no need to panic after this. You need to answer:

  1. Is the code wrong?
  2. Is the test wrong?
  3. Did the expectation change because of a new requirement?

docs.title: Part IX. Async and Real-Time
docs.text:
HTTP polling for a chat means 100 requests/sec for 100 clients. WebSocket gives you one long-lived connection. Django Channels implements WebSocket on top of ASGI, and Redis handles broadcast between processes.

Prerequisites: Parts II, III, VIII. Level: Advanced.

docs.title: Conceptual bridge: asyncio → ASGI → Channels
docs.text:
Three concepts form a single stack. Each one answers a specific question:

asyncio          — How do you hold thousands of connections without thousands of threads?
    ↓               one event loop; await instead of blocking
ASGI             — How does Django receive async requests from the server?
    ↓               an async interface between Daphne/Uvicorn and Django; replaces WSGI
Django Channels  — How does Django route WebSocket alongside HTTP?
    ↓               ProtocolTypeRouter → "http" → views, "websocket" → Consumer
Redis            — How does Worker 1 send messages to Worker 2's clients?
                    channel layer: pub/sub between processes

Dependencies between the levels:

Without What becomes impossible asyncio ASGI is impossible — there is no event loop for async I/O ASGI Channels cannot be plugged into Django — there is no async entry point Channels No WebSocket routing and no Consumer API Redis WebSocket messages will not reach clients of another worker process

WSGI vs ASGI — why the transition is needed:

# WSGI — synchronous: one request = one thread, the thread blocks until the response
def application(environ, start_response):
    data = requests.get(url)   # blocks the thread — nobody else can use it
    ...

# ASGI — asynchronous: one thread = thousands of coroutines, await frees the thread
async def application(scope, receive, send):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        data = await client.get(url)   # the thread is free — it handles other connections
    ...

Django Channels is the Django implementation of ASGI that adds a WebSocket Consumer API on top of the standard. ProtocolTypeRouter is the first routing point: HTTP goes to Django views, WebSocket goes to a Consumer.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Coroutine and await:

import asyncio

async def fetch_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)   # does not block the event loop
    return "data"

async def main():
    result = await fetch_data()
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())

ASGI entrypoint:

# notes_project/asgi.py
# IMPORT ORDER IS CRITICAL!
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
from django.contrib.staticfiles.handlers import ASGIStaticFilesHandler

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()  # ← BEFORE any notes_app import

from channels.routing import ProtocolTypeRouter, URLRouter
from channels.auth import AuthMiddlewareStack
from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns  # ← AFTER (it imports GroupChatConsumer)

application = ProtocolTypeRouter({
    "http":      ASGIStaticFilesHandler(django_asgi_app),  # static files — development only
    "websocket": AuthMiddlewareStack(
        URLRouter(websocket_urlpatterns)  # r"^ws/groups/(?P<group_pk>\d+)/chat/$"
    ),
})

GroupChatConsumer — lifecycle:

class GroupChatConsumer(AsyncWebsocketConsumer):
    async def connect(self):
        user     = self.scope['user']
        group_pk = self.scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk']

        if not user.is_authenticated:
            await self.close(); return

        is_member = await database_sync_to_async(self.check_membership)(group_pk, user)
        if not is_member:
            await self.close(); return

        self.room_group_name = f"chat_group_{group_pk}"
        await self.channel_layer.group_add(self.room_group_name, self.channel_name)
        await self.accept()

        # send the 50 most recent messages
        history = await database_sync_to_async(self.load_history)(group_pk)
        for msg in reversed(history):
            await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({'type': 'history', **msg}))

    async def disconnect(self, close_code):
        await self.channel_layer.group_discard(self.room_group_name, self.channel_name)

    async def receive(self, text_data):
        data    = json.loads(text_data)
        content = data.get('content', '').strip()
        if not content:
            return
        user = self.scope['user']
        await database_sync_to_async(self.save_message)(
            int(self.scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk']), user, content
        )
        await self.channel_layer.group_send(
            self.room_group_name,
            {'type': 'chat_message', 'content': content, 'author': user.username}
        )

    async def chat_message(self, event):
        await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({'type': 'chat_message', **event}))

database_sync_to_async + materialization:

# ✅ CORRECT: list() materializes the QuerySet in the worker thread, before returning
def load_history(self, group_pk):
    return list(
        ChatMessage.objects.filter(group_id=group_pk)
        .select_related('author')
        .order_by('-timestamp')[:50]
        .values('content', 'author__username', 'timestamp')
    )

# ❌ WRONG: returns a lazy QuerySet → SynchronousOnlyOperation
def load_history_bad(self, group_pk):
    return ChatMessage.objects.filter(group_id=group_pk)  # lazy!

Redis channel layer:

# settings.py
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels_redis.core.RedisChannelLayer",
        "CONFIG": {
            "hosts": [REDIS_URL],
            "socket_timeout": None,    # ← None = no timeout for idle WS
        },
    }
}

socket_timeout=None is critical: without it, the Redis connection is closed when idle → TimeoutError on the next message.

Polling vs WebSocket:

HTTP Polling (setInterval 1s):
  100 clients × 1 req/s = 100 HTTP requests/sec
  Each request: TCP handshake + HTTP headers + response
  Latency: up to 1000ms

WebSocket:
  100 clients = 100 open connections (persistent)
  Messages: < 50ms
  Load: only on real events
