docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
Before writing any async code in Django, you need to understand one simple thing: why did the idea of asynchrony appear at all?

The answer is not in the syntax — it is in how computers wait.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine a cook in a restaurant.

The synchronous cook: puts water on the stove, stands there watching it until it boils. Only then does he chop the carrots. Then he waits again.

The asynchronous cook: puts water on the stove, and while the water heats up, chops the carrots. Hears the signal and returns to the stove.

There is one cook. There is no parallel kitchen. But the second cook gets much more done in the same time — because he does not wait in vain.

That is the essence of asynchronous programming.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Synchronous execution The program performs operations strictly in order. The next one starts only after the previous one finishes Asynchronous execution The program can pause one operation and run another while the first one is waiting Blocking operation An operation that completely stops the thread of execution until it finishes Non-blocking operation An operation that starts in the background without stopping the thread I/O-bound task A task where most of the time is spent waiting for input/output: network, disk, DB CPU-bound task A task where most of the time is spent on CPU computation Concurrency A program's ability to have several tasks "in progress" at the same time (not necessarily in parallel) Parallelism Physically running several tasks at the same time on different CPU cores Cooperative multitasking A task voluntarily "steps aside" on its own and hands control to the next one Event loop An infinite loop that tracks which task is ready to continue

docs.title: Why asynchrony exists: the blocking problem
Let's look at the speeds
docs.text:
If we introduce a human time scale (L1 cache = 3 seconds):

Operation Real time "Human" equivalent L1 cache hit ~1 ns 3 seconds RAM access ~100 ns 5 minutes SSD read ~100 µs 3.5 days Network request ~150 ms 14 years

When a Django view makes a request to an external API, the OS thread simply stands there waiting for 14 notional years. It does nothing else. It just waits.

If 100 users hit such an endpoint at the same time, the server will freeze 100 threads. That quickly exhausts memory.

Asynchrony solves this problem: instead of freezing the thread, the program does other work while it waits.

docs.title: Sync vs Async: a comparison table
docs.text: Characteristic Synchronous code Asynchronous code Execution Strictly sequential Can switch between tasks Blocking Blocks the thread during I/O Does not block — hands over control Code complexity Simpler A bit more complex Number of threads One thread = one task One thread = many tasks Ideal task CPU-bound I/O-bound Dangerous task Slow parallel I/O CPU-bound (blocks the event loop)

docs.title: How it works: the execution sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Synchronous thread
    participant A as Asynchronous Event Loop
    participant DB as Database / API

    Note over S: Request 1
    S->>DB: Blocking request (requests.get)
    Note over S: The thread is frozen. Waiting.
    DB-->>S: Response (after 2 seconds)
    Note over S: Request 2 (only now)

    Note over A: Request 1
    A->>DB: Non-blocking request (await client.get, httpx.AsyncClient)
    Note over A: Pauses Request 1, moves on to Request 2
    Note over A: Request 2
    A->>DB: await client.get
    DB-->>A: Response to Request 1
    Note over A: Returns to Request 1
    DB-->>A: Response to Request 2

In the synchronous version it takes 4 seconds (2 + 2). In the asynchronous one, ~2 seconds, because both requests run "at the same time".

docs.title: The difference between concurrency and parallelism
docs.text:
This is an important difference that people often confuse.

Parallelism is physically simultaneous execution on different CPU cores:

Core 1: [Task A =========]
Core 2: [Task B =========]

Concurrency is switching between tasks on a single thread:

Thread: [Task A ----][Task B ----][Task A ----][Task B ----]

asyncio is concurrency, not parallelism. One thread, many tasks. While one task waits on the network, another runs.

docs.title: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Task] --> B{Where is the time spent?}
    B -->|Waiting for network / DB / disk| C[I/O-bound]
    B -->|Computation on the CPU| D[CPU-bound]

    C --> E[Async is effective ✅]
    D --> F[Async is harmful ❌]

    E --> G[httpx, aiohttp, async ORM]
    F --> H[Celery, ProcessPoolExecutor]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class A,C,D step;
    class B decision;
    class E,G,H success;
    class F error;

docs.title: ❌ Synchronous code — blocks the thread
docs.text:
import time

def fetch_user():
    time.sleep(2)  # Simulates a DB query
    return {"id": 1, "name": "Alice"}

def fetch_posts():
    time.sleep(2)  # Simulates an API request
    return [{"title": "Post 1"}]

# Takes 4 seconds (2 + 2)
user = fetch_user()
posts = fetch_posts()

docs.title: ✅ Asynchronous code — does not block
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def fetch_user():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Does not block! Hands over control
    return {"id": 1, "name": "Alice"}

async def fetch_posts():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return [{"title": "Post 1"}]

async def main():
    # Run concurrently — ~2 seconds instead of 4
    user, posts = await asyncio.gather(fetch_user(), fetch_posts())

asyncio.run(main())

The key difference: unlike time.sleep(), asyncio.sleep() does not block the thread — it hands control to the event loop while it waits.

docs.title: ❌ "Async is always faster"
docs.text:
# This is NOT faster code — it is just async syntax wrapped around CPU work
async def compute():
    result = sum(range(10_000_000))  # CPU-bound! Blocks the event loop
    return result

The problem: sum(range(10_000_000)) is a CPU-bound operation. It does not "wait" — it actively computes. Wrapping it in async def changes nothing — the event loop is frozen for the entire computation.

Rule: Async only helps when there is real waiting (I/O): network, database, file system.

docs.title: ❌ "Async = parallelism"
docs.text:
# The two functions do NOT run simultaneously on different CPU cores
# This is switching within a single thread
async def task_a():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)

async def task_b():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)

# Concurrency, not parallelism
await asyncio.gather(task_a(), task_b())

Write a synchronous function fetch_three_urls() that calls time.sleep(1) three times and prints a message after each call. Measure the execution time with time.time().

Then rewrite it as an asynchronous version with asyncio.sleep(1) and asyncio.gather(). Compare the times.

docs.title: Task 2

docs.title: Task 3

docs.text:

  • [ ] I can explain the difference between sync and async code
  • [ ] I know the difference between concurrency and parallelism
  • [ ] I understand that async is effective only for I/O-bound tasks

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Asynchronous programming exists because of the huge difference in speed between the CPU and external operations (network, disk, DB). Synchronous code forces the thread to sit idle while waiting — async code switches to another task during that time.

Async is concurrency (switching between tasks), not parallelism (simultaneous execution on different cores). It is a good fit for I/O-bound tasks and harmful for CPU-bound ones.

In the next document, we will look at how Python implements this idea with asyncio.

→ 02_asyncio.md

docs.title: 02 — Python asyncio: how async code runs
Why you need this
docs.text:
You already know that async is needed for I/O-bound tasks. But how exactly does Python run this code?

What happens when you write async def? What is await? Why does calling an async function not start anything?

This document explains the mechanics from the inside.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine a waiter in a restaurant.

The waiter (the event loop) goes around the tables (coroutines). Each table may have an order in the "being cooked in the kitchen" state or the "ready to serve" state.

The waiter does not stand by the stove and wait. He goes around all the tables in a circle: if a dish is not ready, he moves on. When the kitchen signals "ready", he returns to exactly that table.

await is the moment when the waiter hands the order to the kitchen and goes to the next table.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means async def Declares a coroutine function — a function that can pause Coroutine object The object returned when you call an async function (not the result!) await Pauses the coroutine and hands control to the event loop Event loop The central scheduler — an infinite loop that manages tasks Task A coroutine wrapped in an object so the event loop can schedule it asyncio.create_task() Schedules a coroutine to run in the background without waiting for it to finish asyncio.gather() Runs several coroutines in parallel and waits for all of them Cooperative multitasking Each coroutine decides for itself when to hand over control (via await)

docs.title: How it works: step by step
1. async def is not an ordinary function
docs.text:
async def fetch_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return {"data": "result"}

# Calling it does NOT run the function!
coro = fetch_data()
print(type(coro))  # <class 'coroutine'>

# To run it, you need an event loop or await
result = await fetch_data()  # only inside an async context

When you call an async def function, you get a coroutine object. It is like a recipe, not a finished dish. The event loop will execute this recipe when its turn comes.

docs.title: 2. await — a suspension point
docs.text:
async def view_handler():
    # await: the coroutine pauses here
    # the event loop can run other tasks while we wait
    data = await fetch_from_database()
    return data

await does two things: 1. Hands control to the event loop 2. Resumes execution when the operation is complete — from the very same place

docs.title: 3. The event loop — the heart of asyncio
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Event Loop starts] --> B{Are there tasks in the queue?}
    B -->|yes| C[Takes the next Task]
    C --> D[Runs it until the first await]
    D --> E[Task is suspended]
    E --> F[Registers an I/O callback]
    F --> B
    B -->|no| G[Waits for I/O events]
    G --> H[I/O completed]
    H --> I[Task goes back into the queue]
    I --> B

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,C,D,F,G,I step;
    class B decision;
    class H success;
    class E warning;

The event loop never sleeps aimlessly. It either runs a task or waits for a signal from the OS ("I/O completed").

docs.title: Coroutine lifecycle
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["Coroutine created<br>async def call"] --> B["Pending<br>in the queue"]
    B --> C["Running<br>Event loop executes it"]
    C --> D["Suspended<br>hit await"]
    D --> B
    C --> E["Done<br>returned a result"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;

    class E success;

docs.title: ❌ Sequential — gives no advantage
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def fetch_user():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Wait 2 sec
    return {"id": 1}

async def fetch_posts():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Wait another 2 sec
    return [{"title": "Post 1"}]

async def main():
    # await one after another — 4 seconds
    user = await fetch_user()
    posts = await fetch_posts()
    print(user, posts)

asyncio.run(main())
# Total time: ~4 seconds

docs.title: ✅ Concurrent with gather — gives an advantage
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def fetch_user():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return {"id": 1}

async def fetch_posts():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return [{"title": "Post 1"}]

async def main():
    # Run both at the same time — 2 seconds
    user, posts = await asyncio.gather(fetch_user(), fetch_posts())
    print(user, posts)

asyncio.run(main())
# Total time: ~2 seconds

gather starts all the coroutines and waits until all of them finish. The results are returned in the same order as the arguments.

docs.title: create_task vs gather: the difference
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def background_task(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"{name} finished")
    return name

async def main():
    # create_task — schedule in the background, don't wait right away
    task_a = asyncio.create_task(background_task("A", 2))
    task_b = asyncio.create_task(background_task("B", 1))

    print("Tasks scheduled, continuing work...")

    # Now we wait for the results
    result_a = await task_a  # "A"
    result_b = await task_b  # "B"
create_task gather When it starts Immediately, in the background Immediately, all together Returns A Task object A list of results When to wait You can await later Waits for all at once Use case Background logic + main logic Parallel requests

docs.title: How the event loop manages several tasks
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant EL as Event Loop
    participant T1 as Task 1 (fetch_user)
    participant T2 as Task 2 (fetch_posts)
    participant IO as Network / DB

    EL->>T1: Starts Task 1
    T1->>IO: await asyncio.sleep(2)
    Note over T1: Suspended
    EL->>T2: Switches to Task 2
    T2->>IO: await asyncio.sleep(2)
    Note over T2: Suspended
    Note over EL: Waiting for I/O
    IO-->>EL: Task 1 and Task 2 are ready
    EL->>T1: Resumes Task 1
    T1-->>EL: Returns the result
    EL->>T2: Resumes Task 2
    T2-->>EL: Returns the result

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 1: forgot await
docs.text:
async def get_data():
    return "result"

async def main():
    # Without await, this is a coroutine object, not the result!
    data = get_data()
    print(data)  # <coroutine object get_data at 0x...>

# ✅ Correct
async def main():
    data = await get_data()
    print(data)  # "result"

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 2: time.sleep() inside an async function
docs.text:
import time

async def my_view():
    time.sleep(2)  # BLOCKS the event loop for 2 seconds!
    return "ok"

What happens: time.sleep() is a synchronous function. It blocks the whole thread — including the event loop. All other requests hang.

# ✅ Correct
import asyncio

async def my_view():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Hands control to the event loop
    return "ok"

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 3: CPU-bound work in an async function
docs.text:
async def process():
    # This blocks the event loop for the entire computation!
    result = [x**2 for x in range(10_000_000)]
    return result

CPU-bound tasks should be moved to a ProcessPoolExecutor or Celery — not into async functions.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Write three async functions: fetch_weather(), fetch_news(), fetch_stock_price() — each one "waits" 1 second with asyncio.sleep(1).

Run them: - sequentially (with three separate awaits) — measure the time - in parallel (with asyncio.gather) — measure the time

Compare the results.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text: Write a function run_with_tasks() that: 1. Schedules three tasks with asyncio.create_task() 2. Prints "Tasks scheduled" after scheduling (before they finish) 3. Waits for the result of each task

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Explain: what happens if you write time.sleep(5) inside an async function? Why is it bad? How do you fix it?

docs.text:
• [ ] I understand that async def returns a coroutine object, not a result
  • [ ] I know what await does
  • [ ] I can explain how the event loop manages several tasks
  • [ ] I understand the difference between gather() and create_task()
  • [ ] I know why time.sleep() is dangerous in async code

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
async def declares a coroutine function; calling it returns a coroutine object — not the result. await is a suspension point: the coroutine stops and hands control to the event loop, which runs other tasks.

asyncio.gather() lets you run several coroutines at the same time and significantly reduce the execution time of I/O-bound operations. create_task() schedules a task in the background without waiting for it immediately.

The main danger: time.sleep() and CPU-bound code block the event loop — async does not save you from that.

docs.title: 03 — WSGI and ASGI: how Django got async support
Why this matters
docs.text:
You already know how to write async def functions. But if you simply write an async def Django view and deploy it on a regular server, nothing special will happen.

For Django to truly serve thousands of concurrent connections, it needs the right infrastructure. That infrastructure is called ASGI.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine a call center.

WSGI call center: For every incoming call there is one operator who deals only with that customer. While the customer is thinking or waiting for an answer, the operator just sits silently and waits along with them. If 100 more customers call, you need 100 operators.

ASGI call center: One operator can handle several conversations at once. While one customer "puts the call on hold" to check something, the operator answers another one. A single operator efficiently serves dozens of connections.

WSGI is the first call center. ASGI is the second.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means WSGI Web Server Gateway Interface — the standard for synchronous Python applications ASGI Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface — the standard for async Python applications Gunicorn A popular WSGI server (multiple OS threads/processes) Uvicorn A fast ASGI server based on uvloop Daphne An ASGI server from the Django team (supports WebSockets) Hypercorn An ASGI server with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support wsgi.py Django's entry point for WSGI servers asgi.py Django's entry point for ASGI servers

docs.title: WSGI: the classic standard and its limitations
docs.text:
WSGI appeared in 2003 as a single standard for Python web applications. It is simple and reliable — for its time.

How WSGI works: 1. The client sends an HTTP request 2. The server allocates a separate OS thread (or process) for that request 3. Django processes the request synchronously 4. The response is sent to the client 5. The thread is released

The problem: every request = one blocked thread. While Django waits for a response from the database or an API, the thread just sits there. For 100 concurrent requests you get 100 frozen threads. Memory and resources are wasted.

WSGI is a good fit for: - Standard CRUD applications - Fast requests (< 100ms) - Low load

WSGI is a poor fit for: - WebSockets (persistent connections) - Streaming (large files, SSE) - High concurrency (thousands of simultaneous requests)

docs.title: ASGI: the modern standard
docs.text:
ASGI (2018) is the async successor to WSGI. Instead of allocating a thread per connection, an ASGI server uses an event loop.

A single event loop can "juggle" thousands of connections at the same time — because while one is waiting for the database, another one is being processed.

graph TD
    subgraph WSGI ["WSGI (Synchronous)"]
        A1[Request 1] --> B1[Thread 1: frozen]
        A2[Request 2] --> B2[Thread 2: frozen]
        A3[Request 3] --> B3[Thread 3: frozen]
    end

    subgraph ASGI ["ASGI (Asynchronous)"]
        C1[Request 1] --> EL[Event Loop]
        C2[Request 2] --> EL
        C3[Request 3] --> EL
        EL --> D["Cooperative switching<br>One thread — all requests"]
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class A1,A2,A3,C1,C2,C3,EL step;
    class B1,B2,B3 error;
    class D success;

docs.title: WSGI vs ASGI: comparison table
docs.text: Characteristic WSGI ASGI Year introduced 2003 2018 Execution type Synchronous Asynchronous Threads 1 thread = 1 request 1 event loop = N requests WebSockets ❌ Not supported ✅ Supported Streaming Limited support ✅ Full support Async views Emulation (one loop per request) ✅ Native support Servers Gunicorn, uWSGI Uvicorn, Daphne, Hypercorn Django support Standard (since 1.0) Since Django 3.0+

docs.title: Why Django needs ASGI for real async
docs.text:
Technically, Django can run an async def view even under a WSGI server. But this is how it does it:

For every request to an async view, Django creates a temporary event loop inside an OS thread, runs the view, and destroys the loop.

This: - Wastes resources creating/destroying the event loop - Keeps the thread blocked (the WSGI thread is not released) - Gives no concurrency benefit at all

Real asynchrony is when the ASGI server itself manages the event loop and Django runs views natively, without extra threads.

docs.title: ASGI Request Lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Browser / WebSocket
    participant N as Nginx
    participant U as Uvicorn / Daphne
    participant D as Django ASGI App
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    C->>N: HTTP or WebSocket request
    N->>U: Forwards the request via a socket
    U->>D: Passes ASGI scope + events
    D->>DB: await User.objects.aget(id=1)
    Note over D: The event loop suspends the view<br>(the thread is NOT blocked)
    DB-->>D: Data is ready
    D-->>U: HttpResponse
    U-->>N: Response stream
    N-->>C: Final response

docs.title: Uvicorn
docs.text:
pip install uvicorn
uvicorn myproject.asgi:application --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4
  • The fastest option for plain HTTP and WebSocket
  • Built on uvloop (a faster replacement for the standard asyncio event loop)
  • Recommended for production with Gunicorn as the process manager

docs.title: Daphne
docs.text:
pip install daphne
daphne -b 0.0.0.0 -p 8000 myproject.asgi:application
  • The official ASGI server from Django/Channels
  • Ideal for WebSocket applications
  • Since Channels 4 it is not installed automatically: use pip install daphne or pip install "channels[daphne]" (our requirements.txt has daphne>=4.0)

docs.title: Hypercorn
docs.text:
pip install hypercorn
hypercorn myproject.asgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
  • Supports HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
  • A good choice if you need HTTP/2

docs.title: The asgi.py file in Django
docs.text:
When you create a Django project with the django-admin startproject command, an asgi.py file is generated automatically:

# myproject/asgi.py
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')

# Entry point for the ASGI server
application = get_asgi_application()

This file is the equivalent of wsgi.py, but for ASGI servers. Uvicorn, Daphne and Hypercorn look for exactly the application object in this file.

If you use Django Channels for WebSockets, asgi.py is extended:

# myproject/asgi.py (with Channels)
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
from channels.routing import ProtocolTypeRouter, URLRouter

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')

application = ProtocolTypeRouter({
    "http": get_asgi_application(),
    "websocket": URLRouter([...]),
})

docs.title: ❌ Running async Django under Gunicorn without ASGI
docs.text:
# This is WSGI — async views get no benefit
gunicorn myproject.wsgi:application

# ✅ Correct for async — ASGI via Uvicorn
uvicorn myproject.asgi:application --workers 4

docs.title: ❌ Thinking any server will do
docs.text: Django will not raise an error if you run an async view under WSGI. The code will simply run slower and without any concurrency benefit.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text: Find the asgi.py file in your Django project. Read it. Which function does it import from Django? What does get_asgi_application() return?

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Install uvicorn and run your Django project via ASGI:

pip install uvicorn
uvicorn myproject.asgi:application --reload

Compare it with python manage.py runserver. What changed in the logs?

docs.text:
• [ ] I understand what WSGI is and why it was created
  • [ ] I understand how ASGI differs from WSGI
  • [ ] I know what the asgi.py file is for
  • [ ] I can name at least two ASGI servers and their differences
  • [ ] I understand why an async view under WSGI gives no benefit

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
WSGI is a synchronous standard: one thread per request. Under heavy load and with I/O-bound tasks, threads are wasted.

ASGI solves this problem: one event loop serves thousands of connections. While one is waiting for the database, another is being processed. Django has supported ASGI since version 3.0.

To deploy ASGI Django, people use Uvicorn (speed), Daphne (WebSockets), or Hypercorn (HTTP/2). The entry point is the asgi.py file.

docs.title: 04 — Django Async Views: how to write them and when to use them
Why this matters
docs.text:
Now you have the foundation: you know asyncio, you understand the event loop, and you know what ASGI is. Time to move on to Django itself.

What does an async view look like? How does Django run it? When is it actually useful?

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
A regular sync view is a waiter who takes an order, goes to the kitchen, stands there waiting for the dish to be ready, then returns to the customer. Everything stops.

An async view is a waiter who takes an order, passes it to the kitchen and immediately returns to the dining room. When the dish is ready, they bring it out. Meanwhile, they have served three more customers.

But there is a catch: if the cook (the ORM) still works synchronously, the waiter is still forced to wait. async def is only half the job.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Sync view A regular def function — runs in an OS thread Async view An async def function — can suspend itself and not block the event loop Middleware Layers that process the request/response before and after the view Context switch Switching between the async event loop and a sync OS thread SynchronousOnlyOperation A Django error raised when sync code runs in an async context

docs.title: What an async view looks like
Sync view (regular)
docs.text:
from django.http import JsonResponse

def my_sync_view(request):
    # Runs synchronously in an OS thread
    return JsonResponse({"status": "ok", "mode": "sync"})

docs.title: Async view (minimal)
docs.text:
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def my_async_view(request):
    # Runs on the event loop (under ASGI)
    return JsonResponse({"status": "ok", "mode": "async"})

The only difference is async def. Django automatically detects the view type and runs it accordingly.

docs.title: How Django runs an async view
docs.text:
The result depends on which server you use:

graph TD
    A[Request to the URL Router] --> B{Is the view async def?}
    B -->|no| C["Run synchronously<br>in an OS thread"]
    B -->|yes| D{Which server?}

    D -->|WSGI| E["Create a temporary<br>event loop in the thread"]
    D -->|ASGI| F{Is there sync middleware?}

    F -->|yes| G["Context switch: Async ↔ Sync ↔ Async<br>~1ms penalty each time"]
    F -->|no| H["Native execution<br>on the main Event Loop ✅"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class A,C step;
    class B,D,F decision;
    class H success;
    class E error;
    class G warning;

docs.title: Pure Async Lifecycle (maximum performance)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant ASGI as ASGI Server
    participant AM as Async Middleware
    participant AV as Async View

    B->>ASGI: HTTP Request
    ASGI->>AM: Passes the request (Event Loop)
    AM->>AV: await view(request)
    Note over AV: View awaits the DB or an API<br>(Yields control to the event loop)
    AV-->>AM: HttpResponse
    AM-->>ASGI: HttpResponse
    ASGI-->>B: HTTP Response

The whole path goes through the event loop. No context switches. Maximum efficiency.

docs.title: Mixed Sync/Async: the switching penalty
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["ASGI Server<br>Event Loop"] -->|switch| B["Sync Middleware<br>OS Thread"]
    B -->|switch| C["Async View<br>async def"]
    C -->|switch| D["Sync Middleware<br>Response Phase"]
    D -->|switch| E["ASGI Server<br>Response"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class A,E step;
    class C success;
    class B,D error;

Each switch costs about 1 millisecond of penalty. If the middleware is synchronous, Django has to switch back and forth between the event loop and an OS thread on every request.

docs.title: An async view with a real example: an external API
docs.text:
import httpx
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def weather_view(request):
    city = request.GET.get("city", "Kyiv")

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        # await: the view is suspended, the event loop serves others
        response = await client.get(
            f"https://api.example.com/weather?city={city}",
            timeout=5.0
        )
        data = response.json()

    return JsonResponse({
        "city": city,
        "temperature": data["temp"],
        "description": data["desc"]
    })

While client.get() is waiting for a response from the external server, Django can serve other users. That is exactly the advantage of an async view.

docs.title: An async view with several parallel requests
docs.text:
import asyncio
import httpx
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def dashboard_view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        # Start three requests at the same time
        weather_task = client.get("https://api.example.com/weather")
        news_task = client.get("https://api.example.com/news")
        stocks_task = client.get("https://api.example.com/stocks")

        # Wait for all three — time = time of the slowest request
        weather, news, stocks = await asyncio.gather(
            weather_task, news_task, stocks_task
        )

    return JsonResponse({
        "weather": weather.json(),
        "news": news.json(),
        "stocks": stocks.json()
    })

Instead of 3 seconds (1+1+1) we get ~1 second — the time of the slowest of the three.

docs.title: When async views are useful
docs.text:
✅ Several external API requests — run in parallel via gather instead of sequentially

✅ Long-lived connections — WebSockets, long polling, Server-Sent Events

✅ High concurrency — thousands of simultaneous requests with low CPU load

✅ Streaming responses — sending large data in chunks

docs.title: When async views are NOT useful
docs.text: Situation Reason WSGI server The thread is blocked anyway — no benefit Sync middleware in the stack Context switches wipe out any gain Standard CRUD ORM + a fast query — a sync view is simpler and sufficient CPU-bound computation Blocks the event loop — worse than sync Database transactions transaction.atomic() is not natively supported in async

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Don't make a view async just because you can.

An async view adds complexity: you need an ASGI server, async middleware, and async ORM methods. If your view makes one database query and returns a template, a sync view is simpler, clearer and perfectly sufficient.

An async view is justified when there is a real I/O bottleneck: several external API requests, WebSockets, or high concurrency.

docs.title: ❌ Sync ORM in an async view
docs.text:
from django.http import JsonResponse
from myapp.models import User

async def user_view(request):
    # ERROR! A standard ORM call in an async context
    user = User.objects.get(id=1)  # Will raise SynchronousOnlyOperation!
    return JsonResponse({"name": user.username})

docs.title: ✅ Correct — an async ORM method
docs.text:
async def user_view(request):
    user = await User.objects.aget(id=1)  # The asynchronous variant
    return JsonResponse({"name": user.username})

More on the async ORM in the next document.

docs.title: Testing async views
docs.text:
Django provides AsyncRequestFactory for testing:

from django.test import AsyncRequestFactory, TestCase
from myapp.views import my_async_view

class MyAsyncViewTest(TestCase):
    async def test_async_view(self):
        factory = AsyncRequestFactory()
        request = factory.get('/async-url/')

        # await — because the view is asynchronous
        response = await my_async_view(request)

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

Run it with uvicorn and check both in a browser or with curl.

  • [ ] I know what a context switch is and why it costs ~1ms

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An async view in Django is simply async def instead of def. But to get real benefits you need an ASGI server and async middleware. Under WSGI, an async view runs with no concurrency benefit.

Async views are useful for I/O-bound tasks: several external API requests, WebSockets, streaming. For standard CRUD, a sync view is simpler and perfectly sufficient.

The main trap: sync ORM in an async view will raise SynchronousOnlyOperation. More on that in the next document.

docs.title: 05 — Async ORM: why an async view does not make the database asynchronous
Why this matters
docs.text:
You wrote an async def view. Well done. But inside it you used a regular User.objects.get(id=1) — and Django crashed with a SynchronousOnlyOperation error.

Why? Isn't the view async?

This document explains: async def does not magically make the ORM asynchronous. And what to do about it.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine an async view as a modern asynchronous office where everyone communicates via a messenger — nobody waits by the phone.

But the database is an old archive in the basement, where everything is on paper and synchronous. To get a document, you have to physically go there, stand in line and bring the paper back.

If you write messages through the messenger (async) but fetch documents in person (sync ORM), the whole office waits until you come back.

The async ORM is a courier: you send a request, the courier goes to the archive, and meanwhile you keep working.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Lazy QuerySet A QuerySet that does NOT hit the database when it is created Evaluation The moment a QuerySet actually runs the SQL query SynchronousOnlyOperation A Django exception: sync code is running in an async context aget() Async version of get() acount() Async version of count() afirst() Async version of first() adelete() Async version of delete() asave() Async version of save() async for Async iteration over a QuerySet without blocking

docs.title: The problem: why the sync ORM blocks an async view
docs.text:
The standard database adapters (psycopg2, mysqlclient) are purely synchronous. They make a network request to PostgreSQL and block the thread until they get a response.

If you call such an adapter from inside the async event loop, you block the entire event loop. All other requests "hang".

Django protects you from this: if it detects an async context, it raises an exception:

from django.http import JsonResponse
from myapp.models import Article

async def article_view(request):
    # ❌ ERROR! Sync ORM in an async context
    article = Article.objects.get(id=1)
    return JsonResponse({"title": article.title})

django.core.exceptions.SynchronousOnlyOperation:
You cannot call this from an async context - use a thread or sync_to_async.

Django literally says: "You can't do this here. Either use a thread or sync_to_async."

docs.title: Important: filter() is safe, get() is not
docs.text:
The most common confusion among beginners is that filter() does not run SQL.

graph LR

    B -->|.filter .exclude .order_by .values| C["Lazy AST<br>No SQL query"]
    C --> D[Safe in async ✅]

    B -->|.aget .acount .afirst .adelete| E["SQL in a thread pool<br>via sync_to_async"]
    E --> F[Safe in async ✅]

    B -->|.get .count .first .delete<br>for item in qs| G[Synchronous SQL]
    G --> H[SynchronousOnlyOperation ❌]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

docs.title: filter() is not an SQL query yet
docs.text:
async def view(request):
    # This is SAFE — filter() only builds a QuerySet, it does not run SQL
    qs = Article.objects.filter(published=True).order_by("-created_at")

    # This will run SQL — the async version is needed
    count = await qs.acount()

    return JsonResponse({"count": count})

filter(), exclude(), order_by(), values(), annotate() are all lazy operations. They only build a description of the query (an AST). SQL runs only when you ask for the data: get(), first(), list(), for item in qs.

docs.title: Table: sync ORM → async ORM
docs.text: Synchronous method Asynchronous counterpart What it does .get(...) .aget(...) Returns a single object .first() .afirst() The first one or None .last() .alast() The last one or None .count() .acount() Number of records .exists() .aexists() Whether there is at least one .delete() .adelete() Delete .update(...) .aupdate(...) Update obj.save() await obj.asave() Save the object for obj in qs async for obj in qs Iterate over a QuerySet list(qs) await sync_to_async(list)(qs) or [o async for o in qs] Get a list

docs.title: Examples of correct async ORM usage
Get a single object
docs.text:
from myapp.models import User

async def user_detail_view(request, user_id):
    # ✅ aget instead of get
    try:
        user = await User.objects.aget(id=user_id)
    except User.DoesNotExist:
        return JsonResponse({"error": "Not found"}, status=404)

    return JsonResponse({"id": user.id, "name": user.username})

docs.title: Iterating over a QuerySet
docs.text:
async def articles_view(request):
    # ✅ async for instead of for
    articles = []
    async for article in Article.objects.filter(published=True):
        articles.append({"id": article.id, "title": article.title})

    return JsonResponse({"articles": articles})

docs.title: List comprehension with async for
docs.text:
async def articles_view(request):
    # ✅ Async list comprehension
    articles = [
        {"id": a.id, "title": a.title}
        async for a in Article.objects.filter(published=True).order_by("-created_at")[:10]
    ]
    return JsonResponse({"articles": articles})

docs.title: Save an object
docs.text:
async def create_article_view(request):
    article = Article(
        title="New article",
        published=True
    )
    await article.asave()  # ✅

    return JsonResponse({"id": article.id})

docs.title: ORM Execution Model
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant EL as ASGI Event Loop
    participant AV as Async View
    participant ORM as Django ORM
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    EL->>AV: Route Request
    AV->>ORM: await User.objects.aget(id=1)
    Note over AV: The view yields control<br>to the event loop
    ORM->>DB: SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE id=1
    DB-->>ORM: Data row
    ORM-->>AV: User instance
    AV-->>EL: HttpResponse

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
transaction.atomic() is not yet natively supported in async mode:

# ❌ Does not work directly in an async view
async def view(request):
    with transaction.atomic():
        ...

# ✅ Via sync_to_async (details in the next document)
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async

@sync_to_async
def create_with_transaction():
    with transaction.atomic():
        user = User.objects.create(username="new_user")
        Profile.objects.create(user=user)
    return user

async def view(request):
    user = await create_with_transaction()

docs.title: CONN_MAX_AGE
docs.text:
In async mode it is recommended to disable CONN_MAX_AGE (persistent connections) or use dedicated connection poolers:

# settings.py
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
        # ...
        "CONN_MAX_AGE": 0,  # Disable persistent connections
    }
}

docs.title: ❌ Iterating with a regular for
docs.text:
async def view(request):
    # ERROR! A regular for runs synchronous SQL
    for article in Article.objects.all():
        print(article.title)  # SynchronousOnlyOperation!

docs.title: ✅ Correct — async for
docs.text:
async def view(request):
    async for article in Article.objects.all():
        print(article.title)  # ✅

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An async def view does not magically make the ORM asynchronous. Standard ORM methods (get, count, for) block the event loop and lead to SynchronousOnlyOperation.

Django provides async counterparts: aget, acount, afirst, adelete, asave, async for. filter() and similar "builder" methods are lazy and safe in an async context.

Transactions and some other operations require sync_to_async — more on that in the next document.

docs.title: 06 — sync_to_async: the bridge between sync and async code
Why this matters
docs.text:
Not all code can simply be "made async". Some libraries work only synchronously. There are database transactions. There is legacy code.

sync_to_async and async_to_sync are two "bridges" that let you safely run sync code in an async context (and vice versa) without blocking the event loop.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine an international airport.

There is terminal A (the async zone) and terminal B (the sync zone). Passengers can't just run across the runway — there are dedicated transfers.

sync_to_async is a shuttle from the async terminal to the sync one. The async view "puts" the sync code on the shuttle, it travels to the sync terminal, does the work and comes back. Meanwhile, the async terminal serves other passengers.

async_to_sync is a shuttle in the opposite direction: for sync code that needs to "reach" an async function.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means sync_to_async Wraps a sync function so it can be safely called from an async context async_to_sync Wraps an async function so it can be called from a sync context Thread-sensitive mode The default mode: sync code runs in one fixed thread Thread pool A pool of OS threads for running sync code in the background Context switch Switching between the event loop and an OS thread Zigzag anti-pattern Constant sync↔async switching that wipes out any benefit

docs.title: sync_to_async: running sync code from an async view
Basic syntax
docs.text:
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async

# Option 1: decorator
@sync_to_async
def get_user_from_db(user_id):
    from myapp.models import User
    return User.objects.get(id=user_id)  # Sync ORM — OK here

async def my_view(request):
    user = await get_user_from_db(1)  # Safe call
    return JsonResponse({"name": user.username})

# Option 2: inline
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async
from myapp.models import User

async def my_view(request):
    # Wrap the sync function inline
    user = await sync_to_async(User.objects.get)(id=1)
    return JsonResponse({"name": user.username})

docs.title: How it works internally
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant EL as ASGI Event Loop
    participant Adapter as sync_to_async
    participant Thread as Sync Thread (Pool)
    participant DB as Database

    EL->>Adapter: await get_user_from_db(1)
    Note over EL: The event loop suspends the view<br>SERVES OTHER REQUESTS
    Adapter->>Thread: Passes the sync function to a thread
    Thread->>DB: User.objects.get(id=1) — blocking SQL
    DB-->>Thread: Data row
    Thread-->>Adapter: User instance
    Adapter-->>EL: Resumes the view with the result

The event loop is not blocked while the sync code runs. It keeps serving other users while the thread executes the synchronous database query.

docs.title: Thread-sensitive mode: why it exists
docs.text:
By default, sync_to_async runs in thread_sensitive=True mode.

Why this matters: Database libraries (psycopg2, SQLite) require the connection to be opened and used in the same thread. If each call lands in a different thread, errors occur.

Thread-sensitive mode guarantees that all sync code from one request runs in one dedicated thread.

# thread_sensitive=True (default) — one fixed thread
@sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=True)
def db_operation():
    return User.objects.get(id=1)

# thread_sensitive=False — a new thread for every call
@sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=False)
def isolated_operation():
    return do_something_thread_safe()

docs.title: Wrapping ORM transactions
docs.text:
Transactions (transaction.atomic()) are not natively supported in async mode — they need to be run via sync_to_async:

from django.db import transaction
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async
from myapp.models import User, Profile

@sync_to_async
def create_user_with_profile(username, email):
    with transaction.atomic():
        user = User.objects.create_user(username=username, email=email)
        Profile.objects.create(user=user, bio="")
        return user

async def register_view(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        user = await create_user_with_profile(
            username=request.POST["username"],
            email=request.POST["email"]
        )
        return JsonResponse({"id": user.id, "created": True})

All the transactional logic lives inside the sync function. The async view just calls it through the bridge.

docs.title: async_to_sync: async code in a sync context
docs.text:
Sometimes you need the reverse: a regular sync view has to call an async function (for example, an async HTTP client):

from asgiref.sync import async_to_sync
import httpx

async def fetch_data_async(url):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get(url)
        return response.json()

# A regular sync view
def my_sync_view(request):
    # Call the async function from a sync context
    data = async_to_sync(fetch_data_async)("https://api.example.com/data")
    return JsonResponse(data)

async_to_sync creates a temporary event loop, runs the async function in a separate thread, waits for the result and returns it to the sync context.

docs.text:
graph TD

        AV[Async View]
        AC[Async Coroutine]
    end

    subgraph Sync ["Sync Context (OS Threads)"]
        ORM["Django ORM<br>Legacy Code"]
        SM[Sync Middleware]
    end

    AV -->|sync_to_async| ORM
    SM -->|async_to_sync| AC

    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;

docs.title: Zigzag Anti-Pattern: what not to do
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[ASGI Server] -->|Native async| B[Async Middleware]
    B -->|Context switch ⚠️| C[Sync Middleware]
    C -->|Context switch ⚠️| D[Async View]
    D -->|sync_to_async ⚠️| E[Sync ORM]
    E -->|return ⚠️| D
    D -->|Context switch ⚠️| C
    C -->|Context switch ⚠️| B
    B --> A

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class A,B,D step;
    class C,E error;

Each ⚠️ is a ~1ms penalty. Under heavy load, this adds up.

Rule: minimize the number of sync/async boundary crossings. If most of your code is sync, keep it sync. Don't turn the whole stack async for the sake of a few async operations.

docs.title: ❌ Constant switching instead of isolation
docs.text:
async def view(request):
    # Bad: each call is a separate context switch
    user = await sync_to_async(User.objects.get)(id=1)
    profile = await sync_to_async(Profile.objects.get)(user=user)
    articles = await sync_to_async(list)(Article.objects.filter(author=user))
    await sync_to_async(Log.objects.create)(action="view", user=user)

docs.title: ✅ Better: gather all the sync work into one function
docs.text:
@sync_to_async
def get_user_data(user_id):
    user = User.objects.get(id=user_id)
    profile = Profile.objects.get(user=user)
    articles = list(Article.objects.filter(author=user))
    Log.objects.create(action="view", user=user)
    return user, profile, articles

async def view(request):
    user, profile, articles = await get_user_data(1)

One boundary crossing instead of four. The code is cleaner and more efficient.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
sync_to_async is a bridge: it lets you safely run sync code (the ORM, transactions, legacy libraries) from an async context without blocking the event loop. The sync code runs in a dedicated thread.

async_to_sync is the reverse bridge: for calling async functions from a sync context.

The main rule: minimize the number of sync/async boundary crossings. Gather all the sync work into one function and make a single call instead of several.

docs.title: 07 — Async HTTP Clients: making external requests the right way
Why this matters
docs.text:
You already know how to write async views and you know about sync_to_async. Now for the most common real-world use case: external HTTP requests.

Every Django backend sooner or later calls external APIs: payment gateways, weather services, microservices. And this is where the problem starts — if you use requests, you block the event loop.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine a courier delivering letters.

Sync courier (requests): drives to the first address, stands at the door and waits until the owner opens it. Only after that does the courier go to the second address. The third comes only after the second.

Async courier (httpx): drops letters into all the mailboxes at once. Doesn't wait for anyone to open the door. Just drops the letter into the mailbox and rushes on to the next one.

One async courier gets more done than three sync couriers.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means requests Python's standard sync HTTP library httpx A modern HTTP client: supports both sync and async modes aiohttp An async-only HTTP client (fully asynchronous) httpx.AsyncClient The async variant of the httpx client asyncio.gather Running several async operations in parallel Connection pool A cache of open connections for reuse

docs.title: Why requests blocks an async view
docs.text:
requests is a great library for sync code. But inside an async view it is dangerous:

import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def weather_view(request):
    # ❌ WRONG: requests.get blocks the entire event loop!
    response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather")
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

What happens: 1. requests.get() is a synchronous function 2. It blocks the OS thread until it gets a response 3. But that OS thread is our event loop! 4. All other async requests "hang" for the entire wait

If the external API takes 3 seconds to respond, your whole server is frozen for 3 seconds for all users.

docs.title: Table: requests vs httpx vs aiohttp
docs.text:
Characteristic requests httpx aiohttp Mode Sync only Sync and async Async only API similarity — Almost identical to requests Its own API ASGI compatibility ❌ Blocks the event loop ✅ Full ✅ Full HTTP/2 ❌ ✅ Partial Migration effort — Minimal Requires learning Recommendation Legacy WSGI apps Modern ASGI Django High-performance async

Recommendation for ASGI Django: use httpx.AsyncClient. The API is almost identical to requests — a minimal learning curve.

docs.title: A single request: sync vs async
❌ Synchronous request (blocking)
docs.text:
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

def sync_weather_view(request):
    # Sync view + sync client — the right pair for WSGI
    response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather?city=Kyiv")
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

Under WSGI this is fine. Under ASGI in an async view it is dangerous.

docs.title: ✅ Asynchronous request (non-blocking)
docs.text:
import httpx
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def async_weather_view(request):
    city = request.GET.get("city", "Kyiv")

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        # await: the view is suspended, the event loop serves others
        response = await client.get(
            f"https://api.example.com/weather?city={city}",
            timeout=10.0
        )
        data = response.json()

    return JsonResponse({
        "city": city,
        "temperature": data.get("temp"),
        "description": data.get("desc")
    })

async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client is the right way. The client: - automatically reuses connections (connection pooling) - is closed after the async with block - does not keep resources open

docs.title: Several parallel requests via gather
docs.text:
The biggest advantage of async HTTP is parallel requests:

sequenceDiagram
    participant V as Django View
    participant API1 as API 1 (weather)
    participant API2 as API 2 (news)
    participant API3 as API 3 (stocks)

    Note over V, API3: Synchronous version — 3 seconds
    V->>API1: requests.get() (1s)
    API1-->>V: response
    V->>API2: requests.get() (1s)
    API2-->>V: response
    V->>API3: requests.get() (1s)
    API3-->>V: response

    Note over V, API3: Asynchronous version — ~1 second
    V->>API1: await client.get()
    V->>API2: await client.get()
    V->>API3: await client.get()
    Note over V: The event loop is free!
    API1-->>V: response
    API2-->>V: response
    API3-->>V: response

docs.title: Code for parallel requests
docs.text:
import asyncio
import httpx
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def dashboard_view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
        # Define all the requests
        weather_req = client.get("https://api.example.com/weather?city=Kyiv")
        news_req = client.get("https://api.example.com/news?lang=uk")
        stocks_req = client.get("https://api.example.com/stocks?ticker=AAPL")

        # Run all three at the same time
        # Time = time of the slowest of the three (not the sum!)
        weather, news, stocks = await asyncio.gather(
            weather_req,
            news_req,
            stocks_req,
            return_exceptions=True  # Don't fail if one API is unavailable
        )

    return JsonResponse({
        "weather": weather.json() if not isinstance(weather, Exception) else None,
        "news": news.json() if not isinstance(news, Exception) else None,
        "stocks": stocks.json() if not isinstance(stocks, Exception) else None,
    })

return_exceptions=True is very important: if one of the three APIs is unavailable, gather returns the exception as a value instead of stopping everything.

docs.title: ✅ Context manager (recommended)
docs.text:
async def view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get("https://api.example.com/data")
    # client is closed automatically
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

docs.title: ✅ Reusing the client (for production)
docs.text:
If the view is called often, it is better to keep a single client for the whole lifetime of the application:

# services/http_client.py
import httpx

# One client for the whole application
_client = None

async def get_client() -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    global _client
    if _client is None:
        _client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0)
    return _client

# views.py
from services.http_client import get_client

async def my_view(request):
    client = await get_client()
    response = await client.get("https://api.example.com/data")
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

docs.title: ❌ requests in an async view without a wrapper
docs.text:
import requests

async def bad_view(request):
    # Blocks the whole server!
    data = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()
    return JsonResponse(data)

docs.title: ✅ If you can't use httpx, wrap it in sync_to_async
docs.text:
import requests
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async

@sync_to_async
def fetch_data_sync():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()

async def view(request):
    # Now the sync call runs in a separate thread — the event loop is free
    data = await fetch_data_sync()
    return JsonResponse(data)

This is not as efficient as httpx, but it is safe.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
requests is a synchronous library. Inside an async view it blocks the entire event loop. The right alternative is httpx.AsyncClient with await.

The main advantage of async HTTP: asyncio.gather() lets you run several requests in parallel. Three APIs at 1 second each → ~1 second total instead of 3.

For production: use return_exceptions=True in gather so that one unavailable API does not break the whole response.

→ 08_benchmarking.md

docs.title: 08 — Benchmarking: how to compare sync and async Django objectively
Why this matters
docs.text:
"Async is faster" — you've heard that already. But how do you prove it? How do you measure it?

Most beginners compare things the wrong way: they test a single request and are surprised that async is not faster. Or they test against public APIs and get 429 Too Many Requests.

This document is about what to measure and how to measure it correctly.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine two checkouts in a supermarket.

Old checkout (sync): one customer — the cashier serves them, everyone else waits in line.

New checkout (async): the cashier starts scanning the first customer's items, and while the system is "thinking", starts scanning the second customer's items. No idle time.

If one customer comes, both checkouts handle it equally well. The difference shows only when 50 people arrive at once.

Benchmarking a single request is testing with one customer. It proves nothing.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Latency Time from sending a request to receiving the response (milliseconds) Throughput Number of requests the server handles per second (RPS) Concurrency Number of simultaneous connections/requests IO-bound workload A workload where most of the time is spent waiting for I/O Load testing Testing under load (many simultaneous requests) Mock API A local fake server for tests without a real external API

docs.title: ✅ Throughput (RPS) under load
docs.text:
How many requests per second the server handles with N concurrent clients.

This is the main metric for async. Async does not make a single request faster — it lets you serve more requests at the same time.

docs.title: ✅ Latency as concurrency grows
docs.text:
How response time changes as you go from 1 → 10 → 100 → 500 concurrent clients.

A sync server will start degrading under heavy load (a queue of threads). Async holds up much longer.

docs.title: ✅ Maximum concurrency before degradation
docs.text: The number of concurrent clients at which latency starts to grow. This is the server's "threshold".

docs.title: ❌ A single request
docs.text:
Sync view: 45ms
Async view: 47ms

Async may be slightly slower for a single request — because of the event loop overhead. This is normal and not important.

docs.title: ❌ CPU-bound operations
docs.text:
async def bad_benchmark(request):
    # CPU-bound in async — blocks the event loop
    result = sum(range(10_000_000))
    return JsonResponse({"result": result})

Here async loses unconditionally. This is not a scenario for async.

docs.title: ❌ Tests against public APIs
docs.text:
# Don't do this — the public API will block you due to its rate limit
response = await client.get("https://api.openweathermap.org/...")

During load testing you send hundreds of requests per second. Public APIs have rate limits and block such requests. The results will be wrong.

docs.title: The correct methodology
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Define the scenario] --> B{Is the task I/O-bound?}
    B -->|no| C["Use sync Django<br>Or Celery for CPU"]
    B -->|yes| D[Spin up a local mock API/DB]
    D --> E["Configure an ASGI server<br>Uvicorn or Daphne"]
    E --> F[Check that middleware is async]
    F --> G[Run a load testing tool]
    G --> H[Measure RPS at N concurrent users]
    H --> I["Compare sync vs async at<br>10, 50, 100, 500 concurrent"]

docs.title: A local Mock API for tests
docs.text:
Never test against real external APIs. Spin up a local mock:

# mock_api.py — a simple mock server with FastAPI or aiohttp
from fastapi import FastAPI
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/weather")
async def weather():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.3)  # Simulate a 300ms response
    return {"temp": 22, "desc": "Sunny"}

@app.get("/news")
async def news():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)  # Simulate a 500ms response
    return {"items": ["News 1", "News 2"]}

# Start the mock API
uvicorn mock_api:app --port 8002   # 8001 is already taken by the web service

Now test your Django views against http://localhost:8002 — no rate limits, controlled latency.

docs.title: Load testing: an example with locust
docs.text:
# locustfile.py
from locust import HttpUser, task, between

class DjangoUser(HttpUser):
    wait_time = between(0.1, 0.5)

    @task
    def sync_view(self):
        self.client.get("/api/sync-weather/")

    @task
    def async_view(self):
        self.client.get("/api/async-weather/")

pip install locust
locust -f locustfile.py --host=http://localhost:8000
# Open http://localhost:8089 and start the test

Test parameters: - Users: 100–500 - Spawn rate: 10 users/sec - Duration: 60 seconds

docs.title: Sync vs Async: a typical timeline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant OS as OS Threads (Sync)
    participant EL as Event Loop (Async)
    participant API as Mock API (300ms)

    Note over OS, API: Sync Django — 1 thread per request
    OS->>API: User 1 request
    Note over OS: Thread BLOCKED (300ms)
    API-->>OS: User 1 response
    OS->>API: User 2 request
    Note over OS: Thread BLOCKED (300ms)
    API-->>OS: User 2 response

    Note over EL, API: Async Django — 1 event loop
    EL->>API: User 1 request
    Note over EL: NOT blocked
    EL->>API: User 2 request
    Note over EL: NOT blocked
    EL->>API: User 3 request
    API-->>EL: User 1 response
    API-->>EL: User 2 response
    API-->>EL: User 3 response

docs.title: Benchmarking Checklist
docs.text:
Before each test, check:

  • [ ] You are testing an IO-bound workload (not CPU-bound)
  • [ ] You are using a local mock API (not a public one)
  • [ ] For sync — gunicorn with --workers or WSGI
  • [ ] For async — uvicorn or daphne (ASGI)
  • [ ] Middleware in the async stack — all async (verify it!)
  • [ ] You use asyncio.sleep() to simulate latency (not time.sleep())
  • [ ] You test concurrency from 10 to 500+ simultaneous users
  • [ ] You measure RPS (not only the latency of a single request)
  • [ ] You checked the database connection pool — is it exhausted?

docs.title: Why the database connection pool is a critical bottleneck
docs.text:
Async allows thousands of simultaneous requests. But if the database allows at most 20 connections, 980 requests will wait in a queue regardless of async.

# settings.py
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
        # ...
        "OPTIONS": {
            # Django 5.1+ built-in connection pool (requires psycopg 3: psycopg[pool])
            "pool": {
                "min_size": 2,      # Minimum open connections
                "max_size": 20,     # Maximum simultaneous connections
            },
        },
        "CONN_MAX_AGE": 0,          # Must be 0 with a pool (persistent connections are incompatible)
    }
}

Our project uses psycopg2-binary, so the built-in pool is not enabled here: it requires switching to psycopg 3.

Under async load: monitor pg_stat_activity in PostgreSQL — if the connection count is close to the maximum, that is the bottleneck, not your code.

docs.title: ❌ Testing one request and drawing a conclusion
docs.text:
# One request — proves nothing
curl http://localhost:8000/api/weather/
# Sync: 45ms
# Async: 48ms
# "Async is slower!" — a wrong conclusion

docs.title: ✅ Testing under concurrent load
docs.text:
# Apache Bench: 1000 requests, 50 concurrent
ab -n 1000 -c 50 http://localhost:8000/api/weather/

# Sync result: ~15 RPS (threads get exhausted)
# Async result: ~200+ RPS (the event loop copes)

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Spin up a simple mock API (you can use python -m http.server or FastAPI). Write two Django endpoints: - /sync/ — a sync view with requests.get() to the mock API - /async/ — an async view with httpx.AsyncClient()

Run both under uvicorn. Test them with Apache Bench or locust.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text: Write two Django views, one with asyncio.sleep(0.5) and one with time.sleep(0.5). Run a load test and compare RPS. Explain the result.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Check your Django project: are all the middleware in the MIDDLEWARE list async-compatible? How can you check this?

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I understand the difference between latency and throughput
  • [ ] I know that the benefits of async show only under concurrent load
  • [ ] I understand why you must not test against public APIs
  • [ ] I know that time.sleep() in async is a benchmarking mistake
  • [ ] I understand the role of the database connection pool under async load

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Async Django outperforms sync not for a single request, but for hundreds of simultaneous ones. You need to test throughput (RPS) as concurrency grows, not the latency of a single request.

Always use a local mock API instead of a public one. Check that the whole stack (middleware, ORM) is async-compatible. Don't forget about the database connection pool — it can become the real bottleneck sooner than the event loop.

docs.title: 09 — Real-World Use Cases: when async Django is really needed
Why this matters
docs.text:
You have gone the whole way: asyncio, ASGI, async views, async ORM, sync_to_async, httpx, benchmarking.

The last question: when is all this actually worth using?

Async is a tool. Like a hammer: perfect for nails and useless for screws. This document is a map: where the nails are and where the screws are.

docs.title: 🧠 Mental model
docs.text:
Imagine an emergency services dispatcher.

Synchronous dispatcher: takes one call, fully resolves the situation (sends a vehicle, waits for confirmation, closes the case), then takes the next one.

Asynchronous dispatcher: takes 10 calls at once. Tells each caller "got it, a vehicle is on the way" and keeps them updated. Doesn't wait for each vehicle to arrive — just coordinates.

For complex cases that require full attention (CPU-bound), the synchronous dispatcher is better. For coordinating many simultaneous connections, the asynchronous one is.

docs.title: Async Suitability Matrix
docs.text: Task type Example Architecture Reason Concurrent I/O Aggregating data from 5 APIs ASGI + Async View + httpx await frees the event loop between requests Persistent connections Chat, live dashboard, WebSockets Django Channels + ASGI One event loop holds thousands of open connections High-volume webhooks Stripe, GitHub webhooks Async View + ASGI Instantly accepts and acknowledges without blocking Streaming responses CSV/JSON streaming, SSE Async + StreamingHttpResponse Sends data in chunks without blocking the server Standard CRUD Article list, user profile Sync View (WSGI or ASGI) The ORM is fast enough, async adds complexity Image/Video processing Avatar resizing, video conversion Celery Worker CPU-bound: blocks the event loop, better in the background ML inference Text classification, recommendations Celery + GPU Worker Heavy CPU/GPU, not for the event loop PDF/report generation Reports, invoices Celery Worker CPU-bound + I/O, runs for a long time

docs.title: 1. Aggregating from several external APIs
docs.text:
The classic use case: a dashboard that collects data from several sources.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant V as Django Async View
    participant A1 as Billing API (0.8s)
    participant A2 as Inventory API (1.2s)
    participant A3 as Shipping API (0.6s)

    B->>V: GET /dashboard/
    Note over V: Starts all three in parallel
    V->>A1: await client.get()
    V->>A2: await client.get()
    V->>A3: await client.get()
    Note over V: The event loop is free!
    A3-->>V: 0.6s — response
    A1-->>V: 0.8s — response
    A2-->>V: 1.2s — response
    Note over V: Total time: ~1.2s (not 2.6s!)
    V-->>B: Aggregated response
import asyncio
import httpx
from django.http import JsonResponse

async def dashboard_view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
        billing, inventory, shipping = await asyncio.gather(
            client.get("https://billing.internal/summary"),
            client.get("https://inventory.internal/status"),
            client.get("https://shipping.internal/active"),
            return_exceptions=True
        )

    return JsonResponse({
        "billing": billing.json() if not isinstance(billing, Exception) else None,
        "inventory": inventory.json() if not isinstance(inventory, Exception) else None,
        "shipping": shipping.json() if not isinstance(shipping, Exception) else None,
    })

docs.title: 2. WebSockets and chat systems
docs.text:
Django Channels with ASGI lets one event loop hold thousands of open WebSocket connections:

# consumers.py (Django Channels)
from channels.generic.websocket import AsyncWebsocketConsumer
import json

class ChatConsumer(AsyncWebsocketConsumer):
    async def connect(self):
        self.room_name = self.scope["url_route"]["kwargs"]["room_name"]
        await self.channel_layer.group_add(self.room_name, self.channel_name)
        await self.accept()

    async def disconnect(self, close_code):
        await self.channel_layer.group_discard(self.room_name, self.channel_name)

    async def receive(self, text_data):
        data = json.loads(text_data)
        # Broadcast the message to the whole group
        await self.channel_layer.group_send(
            self.room_name,
            {"type": "chat_message", "message": data["message"]}
        )

    async def chat_message(self, event):
        await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({"message": event["message"]}))

docs.title: 3. High-volume webhooks
docs.text:
Endpoints that receive thousands of webhook requests (Stripe, GitHub):

from django.http import JsonResponse
from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async

@csrf_exempt
async def stripe_webhook_view(request):
    if request.method != "POST":
        return JsonResponse({"error": "Method not allowed"}, status=405)

    payload = request.body

    # Quickly acknowledge receipt (Stripe expects < 30s)
    # The real processing happens in a Celery task
    await sync_to_async(enqueue_webhook_processing)(payload)

    return JsonResponse({"status": "received"})

docs.title: 4. Server-Sent Events (Live updates)
docs.text:
import asyncio
from django.http import StreamingHttpResponse

async def live_updates(request):
    async def event_stream():
        count = 0
        while True:
            count += 1
            yield f"data: {{\"update\": {count}}}\n\n"
            await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Update every 2 seconds

    return StreamingHttpResponse(
        event_stream(),
        content_type="text/event-stream"
    )

docs.title: CPU-bound tasks: the event loop freezes
docs.text:
# ❌ DON'T do this — it blocks the whole server
async def generate_report_view(request):
    # PDF generation — CPU-bound!
    pdf_bytes = generate_pdf_report(request.user.id)  # 10 seconds
    return HttpResponse(pdf_bytes, content_type="application/pdf")

While the PDF is being generated, the server responds to nobody.

docs.title: The right architecture: a Celery Worker
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Browser] -->|POST /generate-report/| B["Django View<br>Sync or Async"]
    B -->|Celery task| C[Redis / RabbitMQ]
    B -->|202 Accepted + task_id| A
    C --> D["Celery Worker<br>Generates PDF"]
    D --> E["Saves the file<br>Notifies user"]
    A -->|GET /report/status/task_id| B
    B --> F["{ status: done, url: ... }"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

    class A,B,C,E step;
    class F success;

# tasks.py (Celery)
from celery import shared_task

@shared_task
def generate_pdf_report(user_id):
    # CPU-bound — safe in a Celery worker
    user = User.objects.get(id=user_id)
    pdf = create_pdf(user)  # Takes as long as it needs
    save_to_storage(pdf, user_id)
    notify_user(user_id)

# views.py
from django.http import JsonResponse
from .tasks import generate_pdf_report

def request_report_view(request):
    # Start the task and return a response immediately
    task = generate_pdf_report.delay(request.user.id)
    return JsonResponse({"task_id": str(task.id), "status": "processing"}, status=202)

docs.title: ❌ Async everywhere for no reason
docs.text:
# You have a regular CRUD view — why async?
async def article_list_view(request):
    articles = [a async for a in Article.objects.all()[:20]]
    return JsonResponse({"articles": [...]})

If a view simply reads from its own database and returns JSON, a sync view is simpler, clearer and doesn't require ASGI, the async ORM and the whole stack.

docs.text:
# Async is justified: three external APIs at the same time
async def dashboard_view(request):
    weather, news, stocks = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_weather(), fetch_news(), fetch_stocks()
    )
    return JsonResponse({...})

docs.title: Final summary of the whole lesson
docs.text:
You have gone the full way from the basics to practice:

01 — Sync vs Async: Asynchrony exists because of the huge speed difference between the CPU and external operations. Async is concurrency (switching), not parallelism (simultaneous execution).

02 — asyncio: async def returns a coroutine object. await is a suspension point. The event loop manages all tasks. gather() runs several coroutines concurrently.

03 — ASGI: WSGI — one thread per request. ASGI — an event loop serves thousands. Uvicorn, Daphne, Hypercorn are ASGI servers for Django.

04 — Async Views: async def view under ASGI — native execution. Sync middleware adds context switch penalties. An async view does not automatically mean better performance.

05 — Async ORM: filter() is lazy and safe. get() and for are blocking and will raise SynchronousOnlyOperation. Use aget(), acount(), async for.

06 — sync_to_async: A bridge between the sync and async worlds. Sync code runs in a dedicated thread, the event loop stays free. Minimize the number of boundary crossings.

07 — Async HTTP Clients: requests blocks the event loop. httpx.AsyncClient + gather is the right pair for parallel API requests.

08 — Benchmarking: The benefits of async show only under concurrent load. Test RPS, not the latency of a single request. Use a local mock API.

09 — Use Cases: Async for I/O-bound concurrent tasks. Celery for CPU-bound. A sync view for standard CRUD.

The main rule: async is a tool for specific problems. If there is no problem, you don't need the tool. Start with regular sync Django, and add async only where there is a real bottleneck.
