docs.title: The problem with synchronous servers
docs.text: In a traditional WSGI architecture, every connection requires a separate OS thread. A thread takes ~8 MB of RAM and is blocked for the entire time it waits for I/O. With 10,000 concurrent users, the server spends ~80 GB of RAM on threads alone — even if they spend 99% of their time just waiting.

docs.title: Time scale: why I/O is so slow
docs.text:
Operation Real time "Human" equivalent CPU cache (L1) 1 ns 3 seconds RAM 100 ns 5 minutes SSD read 100 µs 3.5 days TCP round trip 100 ms ~9.5 years External API 500 ms ~48 years

Asyncio solves this with cooperative multitasking: instead of keeping a thread blocked for ~48 "human years", await frees the Event Loop to serve thousands of other connections.

docs.title: Coroutine
docs.text:
A special function defined with async def that: - When called, returns a coroutine object (executes nothing) - When awaited with await, runs until its first internal await - On await asyncio.sleep(), suspends itself, saves its state and hands control to the Event Loop

async def my_coroutine():      # Definition
    ...

obj = my_coroutine()           # Call → coroutine object (FROZEN)
result = await my_coroutine()  # Execute and wait for the result

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
asyncio.Task is a wrapper around a coroutine that schedules its execution on the Event Loop.

task = asyncio.create_task(my_coroutine())  # Schedules NOW, does not wait
result = await task                          # Explicitly wait for completion

Task states: 

create_task() → [PENDING] → [RUNNING] → [DONE / CANCELLED]
                                 ↑            ↓
                           on await     result or exception

docs.title: Event Loop
docs.text:
The central scheduler of asyncio. How it works:

while True:
    1. Run all READY tasks up to their first await
    2. Ask the OS: which sockets/timers are ready? (epoll/kqueue)
    3. Move completed tasks to the READY queue
    4. Repeat

docs.title: 3. Coroutine Lifecycle
docs.text:
Call async def func()
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ coroutine object│  ← STATE: GEN_CREATED
│ code: lines...  │    Nothing is executed!
│ locals: {}      │
└────────┬────────┘
         │ await func() or asyncio.run(func())
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│   RUNNING       │  ← Executes line by line
│                 │
│  ... code ...   │
│  await <awaitable>  ← PAUSE
└────────┬────────┘
         │ await
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│   SUSPENDED     │  ← State saved (locals, position)
│ waiting for I/O │    The Event Loop is free!
└────────┬────────┘
         │ I/O completed
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│   RUNNING       │  ← Resumes from the await point
└────────┬────────┘
         │ return
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│   CLOSED        │  ← GEN_CLOSED, result available
└─────────────────┘

docs.title: Where does the "waiting" actually happen?
docs.text: When Python executes await asyncio.sleep(1): 1. The Event Loop registers a timer with the OS 2. The coroutine moves to SUSPENDED 3. The OS uses epoll/kqueue — a hardware-backed notification mechanism 4. The Python thread sleeps, using ~0% CPU 5. After 1 second the OS wakes Python up, and the Event Loop resumes the coroutine

docs.title: 5. Cooperative vs Preemptive Multitasking
docs.text:
Preemptive (Threading) Cooperative (Asyncio) Who interrupts The OS, forcibly, at any moment The coroutine, voluntarily, via await Race conditions Yes — you need Lock/Semaphore Less often — switches happen only at await, but state can change between awaits (asyncio.Lock) Stack ~8 MB/thread ~2 KB/coroutine Max concurrent ~500–1000 ~100,000+ Blocking call Stops 1 thread Stops the entire Event Loop

The key danger of asyncio: a single blocking call (time.sleep, requests.get) stops EVERYTHING — not just one task.

docs.title: Core functions
docs.text:
# Program entry point
asyncio.run(main())
asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)

# Scheduling tasks
task = asyncio.create_task(coro())
tasks = asyncio.gather(coro1(), coro2(), coro3())
results = await asyncio.gather(*coros, return_exceptions=True)

# Waiting
await asyncio.sleep(seconds)        # Releases the Event Loop
await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=5.0)  # With a timeout

# Checking status
task.done()        # True if finished
task.cancelled()   # True if cancelled
task.result()      # Returns the result or raises the exception
task.cancel()      # Sends CancelledError into the task

# Current Event Loop
loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()

# Delegating blocking code
result = await loop.run_in_executor(executor, sync_func, *args)

docs.title: async with and async for
docs.text:
# async context manager
async with aiofiles.open("file.txt") as f:
    data = await f.read()

# async generator / iterator
async for item in async_generator():
    process(item)

docs.title: Replacement table
docs.text: Synchronous (BLOCKING) Asynchronous (CORRECT) time.sleep(n) await asyncio.sleep(n) requests.get(url) await session.get(url) (aiohttp) open(path).read() await aio_file.read() (aiofiles) psycopg2.connect(...) await asyncpg.connect(...) subprocess.run(cmd) await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(...) CPU-bound loop await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, func)

docs.title: run_in_executor — the bridge between worlds
docs.text:
import asyncio
import concurrent.futures

process_pool = concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor()
thread_pool = concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor()

async def handle_request():
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()

    # CPU-bound → ProcessPoolExecutor (bypasses the GIL)
    result = await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, heavy_computation)

    # Legacy sync I/O → ThreadPoolExecutor
    data = await loop.run_in_executor(thread_pool, legacy_db_query)

    return result, data

docs.title: Three kinds of endpoints in FastAPI
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI
import asyncio, time

app = FastAPI()

# ✅ async def + await: best for async I/O
@app.get("/users")
async def get_users(pool):
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        return await conn.fetch("SELECT * FROM users")

# ❌ async def + blocking: the worst (blocks the entire Event Loop!)
@app.get("/broken")
async def broken_endpoint():
    time.sleep(2)               # Stops the WHOLE server!
    return {"status": "bad"}

# ⚠️ def (not async): FastAPI automatically runs it in a threadpool
@app.get("/legacy")
def legacy_endpoint():
    time.sleep(2)               # OK — a separate thread, the loop is free
    return {"status": "ok but limited"}

docs.title: The FastAPI rule:
docs.text:
• async def + only await operations → Event Loop (optimal)
  • async def + a blocking call → disaster
  • def (sync) → automatic threadpool (safe, but limited)

docs.title: WebSocket scale
docs.text:
Synchronous WSGI (Gunicorn threads):
  10,000 WebSocket connections → 10,000 threads → ~80 GB RAM
  (practically impossible)

Asyncio ASGI (uvicorn):
  10,000 WebSocket connections → 10,000 coroutine objects → ~20 MB RAM
  (easy — only memory for the state)

docs.title: 9. Threading vs Multiprocessing vs Asyncio
docs.text: Threading Multiprocessing Asyncio Model N threads, 1 process N processes 1 thread, 1 process GIL One shared by all Each has its own One (not a limitation) Scheduling Preemptive (OS) Preemptive (OS) Cooperative (await) Memory/unit ~8 MB/thread ~50 MB/process ~2 KB/coroutine Race conditions Yes No Less often (only at await) CPU-bound ❌ GIL ✅ True parallelism ❌ Blocks the loop I/O-bound ✅ OK ✅ OK ✅ Best Max concurrent ~500 ~CPU cores ~100,000+ Ideal for Legacy sync libraries ML, image, math Web, API, WebSocket

docs.title: A solution for combined workloads (FastAPI production)
docs.text:
HTTP request → FastAPI async endpoint
    │
    ├── DB query → asyncpg (async) → await
    ├── HTTP call → aiohttp (async) → await  
    └── CPU work → ProcessPoolExecutor → run_in_executor → await

docs.title: Anti-pattern 1: Blocking in async (the most frequent mistake)
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS
async def endpoint():
    time.sleep(2)          # Stops the whole server!
    requests.get(url)      # Blocks the Event Loop!
    psycopg2.execute(...)  # Stops all connections!

# CORRECT
async def endpoint():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    async with session.get(url) as r: ...
    async with pool.acquire() as conn: await conn.fetch(...)

docs.title: Anti-pattern 2: A forgotten await
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS — RuntimeWarning, nothing is executed
result = fetch_data()        # Returns a coroutine object!

# CORRECT
result = await fetch_data()  # Executes and waits

docs.title: Anti-pattern 3: A Task without a reference (the exception disappears)
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS
asyncio.create_task(risky_op())  # The exception will be swallowed!

# CORRECT
task = asyncio.create_task(risky_op())
try:
    await task
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Task failed: {e}")

docs.title: Anti-pattern 4: CPU-bound in async (freezes the loop)
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS
async def process():
    result = sum(i*i for i in range(10**8))  # Blocks the loop for seconds!

# CORRECT
async def process():
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    result = await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, heavy_sync_func)

docs.title: Anti-pattern 5: Main finishes before the Task
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS
async def main():
    asyncio.create_task(background_work())
    # The Event Loop stops → the Task is destroyed!

# CORRECT
async def main():
    task = asyncio.create_task(background_work())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # Let the Task start
    await task               # Explicitly wait

docs.title: Pattern 1: Connection Pool with a Semaphore
docs.text:
class ConnectionPool:
    def __init__(self, max_size: int):
        self._semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(max_size)

    async def __aenter__(self):
        await self._semaphore.acquire()
        return await self._create_connection()

    async def __aexit__(self, *args):
        self._semaphore.release()

docs.title: Pattern 2: Retry with Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
async def with_retry(coro_factory, max_retries=3, base_delay=1.0):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            return await coro_factory()
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                raise
            delay = base_delay * (2 ** attempt)
            await asyncio.sleep(delay)

docs.title: Pattern 3: Producer-Consumer with asyncio.Queue
docs.text:
async def producer(queue: asyncio.Queue, items):
    for item in items:
        await queue.put(item)
    await queue.put(None)  # sentinel

async def consumer(queue: asyncio.Queue):
    while True:
        item = await queue.get()
        if item is None:
            break
        await process(item)
        queue.task_done()

docs.title: Pattern 4: Rate Limiter
docs.text:
class AsyncRateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, max_calls: int, period: float = 1.0):
        self._semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(max_calls)
        self._period = period

    async def __aenter__(self):
        await self._semaphore.acquire()
        asyncio.create_task(self._release_after_period())
        return self

    async def _release_after_period(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(self._period)
        self._semaphore.release()

    async def __aexit__(self, *args):
        pass

docs.title: Debugging tools
docs.text:
# 1. Debug mode via an environment variable
PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 python app.py

# 2. Verbose asyncio logging
PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 python -W always app.py

# 3. Debug mode in code
asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)

# 4. A custom exception handler
def handle_exception(loop, context):
    logger.error(f"Unhandled exception: {context}")

loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
loop.set_exception_handler(handle_exception)

docs.title: What debug mode detects
docs.text: Problem What debug mode reports A coroutine was never awaited RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited A blocking function > 100ms Executing took X.XX seconds An exception in a Task without await A log message at GC time Slow callbacks Executing callback took X seconds

docs.title: Analyzing a typical stack trace
docs.text:
Task exception was never retrieved
future: <Task finished name='Task-2' coro=<risky_op() at app.py:15>
exception=ValueError('...')>
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 17, in risky_op   ← Where the exception occurred
    raise ValueError(...)
ValueError: ...

Rule: if you see "Task exception was never retrieved", find the place where the Task was created and add a try/except around await task.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
The Notes Chat App Docker Compose stack:

# docker-compose.yml (simplified)
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes: [postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data]

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

  web:
    build: .
    command: ["sh", "./entrypoint.sh"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/notes
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    depends_on: [db, redis]
    ports: ["8001:8001"]

  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
      - staticfiles:/staticfiles:ro
    ports: ["80:80"]
    depends_on: [web]

  celery-worker:
    build: .
    command: ["celery", "-A", "notes_project", "worker", "--loglevel=info"]
    depends_on: [db, redis]

  celery-beat:
    build: .
    command: ["celery", "-A", "notes_project", "beat", "--loglevel=info"]
    depends_on: [db, redis]

  selenium:                  # profiles: ["test"]
    image: selenium/standalone-chrome
    ports: ["4444:4444"]

  selenium-tests:            # profiles: ["test"]
    build: .
    command: ["python", "manage.py", "test", "notes_app.tests.test_selenium", "-v", "2"]
    depends_on: [web, nginx, selenium]

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:
  staticfiles:
  celerybeat_data:

entrypoint.sh — startup sequence:

#!/bin/sh
set -eu

# 1. PostgreSQL and Redis are already healthy: depends_on + healthcheck in docker-compose.yml guarantee it

# 2. Apply migrations
if [ "${RUN_MIGRATIONS:-1}" = "1" ]; then
    python manage.py migrate --noinput
fi

# 3. Collect static files
if [ "${RUN_COLLECTSTATIC:-1}" = "1" ]; then
    python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
fi

# 4. Seed demo data (if SEED_DEMO_DATA=1)
if [ "${SEED_DEMO_DATA:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    python manage.py seed_demo_data ${seed_args}   # --force or --force --reset
fi

# 5. Start the Uvicorn ASGI server (with --reload in dev)
exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8001 --proxy-headers

Nginx configuration for WebSocket:

# nginx/nginx.conf
upstream django {
    server web:8001;
}

server {
    listen 80;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://django;
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }

    # WebSocket upgrade
    location /ws/ {
        proxy_pass http://django;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade    $http_upgrade;   # ← required for WS
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    }

    # Static files — Nginx serves them directly (not Django)
    location /static/ {
        alias /staticfiles/;
    }
}

Environment variables — secrets:

# .env (never commit it to git)
SECRET_KEY=django-prod-secret-key-here
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/notes
REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
DEBUG=False
ALLOWED_HOSTS=notes.example.com,www.notes.example.com

# In Python (the production approach):
import os
SECRET_KEY = os.environ['SECRET_KEY']   # ← Exception if missing (no default!)
# The teaching project currently uses os.environ.get("SECRET_KEY", "django-insecure-...")
# with a dev default — remove that default in production.

Production checklist:

✓ DEBUG=False
✓ SECRET_KEY — from env, not in the code
✓ DATABASE_URL — missing → Exception (no SQLite fallback!)
✓ ALLOWED_HOSTS — specific domains
✓ HTTPS — CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE
✓ Static files — Nginx, not Django
✓ DebugExceptionMiddleware — only if DEBUG
✓ Logrotate / log aggregation
✓ Health check endpoint
✓ CI: tests green before deploying

After installing Docker, sign up at Docker Hub — the main public registry of Docker images.

docker login               # log in to Docker Hub from the terminal
docker logout              # log out

Docker Hub contains official images for: - Languages: python, node, golang, java - Databases: postgres, mysql, redis, mongodb - Web servers: nginx, traefik, caddy - Your own applications: uploaded with the docker push command

docs.title: The problem Docker solves
docs.text:
Before Docker, deploying software meant constantly answering the question:

"It works on my machine — why does it crash on the server?"

The answer was always the same: the environment is different. A different OS, different library versions, different system dependencies, different Python paths.

Docker solves this by packaging not just your code — but the entire runtime environment your code depends on.

docs.title: The right mental model: the shipping container
docs.text:
Before containerized shipping, cargo was loaded onto ships as individual items. Loading and unloading was slow, unreliable, and different in every port.

The invention of the standardized shipping container changed everything: - The same container fits any ship, truck, or crane - The contents don't depend on the vehicle - The vehicle doesn't depend on the contents

Docker is exactly that, but for software:

Physical shipping Docker Shipping container Docker container Goods inside Your application + dependencies Ship / truck Any server with Docker Port infrastructure Docker daemon Container specification standard OCI (Open Container Initiative)

docs.title: What Docker is NOT
docs.text:
Docker is not a virtual machine. This is the most common misconception.

Virtual machine:                  Docker container:

┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│    Your app         │           │    Your app         │
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│    Guest OS         │           │    Libs/Deps        │
│    (full Linux/Win) │           │    (no OS kernel!)  │
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│    Hypervisor       │           │    Docker Engine    │
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│    Host OS          │           │  Host OS (shared)   │
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│    Physical hardware│           │    Physical hardware│
└─────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────┘

Size: ~1–10 GB                    Size: ~10–500 MB
Startup: ~30–60 sec               Startup: ~0.1–2 sec

The key difference: Containers share the host OS kernel. They don't emulate hardware. That makes them much faster and lighter than VMs.

docs.title: Why Docker: three axes of pain
docs.text: Pain Without Docker With Docker Environment drift "It works on my machine" An identical environment everywhere Dependency hell Python 3.8 vs 3.11 conflicts Each app has its own isolated libraries Deployment complexity Ansible scripts, SSH, manual steps docker run on any machine

docs.title: 2.1 Image
docs.text:
Definition: A Docker image is an immutable, layered filesystem snapshot that contains everything needed to run an application: OS libraries, the runtime, dependencies, application code, and the startup command.

Mental model: An image is a recipe (or a class in OOP). It defines what a container will look like, but doesn't run anything by itself.

Role in the system: - Built once, run many times - Stored in registries (Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GitHub Container Registry) - Identified by name + tag: python:3.11-slim, nginx:1.25, myapp:v2.3

Relationship to the others: - Dockerfile → builds → Image - Image → is instantiated into → Container - Images consist of layers — every RUN, COPY, ADD instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer

Image layer architecture:

Layer 4: COPY app/ /app          ← your code (changes often)
Layer 3: RUN pip install -r ...  ← dependencies (change sometimes)
Layer 2: RUN apt-get install ... ← system libraries (rarely change)
Layer 1: FROM python:3.11-slim   ← base image (shared between images)

Layers are cached and shared. If layers 1–3 haven't changed, Docker reuses them — only layer 4 is rebuilt. That's why layer order matters.

docs.title: 2.2 Container
docs.text:
Definition: A container is a running instance of an image. It is an isolated process on the host OS with its own filesystem, network interface, and process space.

Mental model: If an image is a class, then a container is an object — an instance created from that class. You can create many containers from one image.

Role in the system: - Runs the actual workload - Has a writable layer on top of the immutable image layers - Is ephemeral by default — after it is stopped and removed, all written data is lost - Has a lifecycle: created → running → paused → stopped → removed

Container = Image layers (immutable) + Writable layer (ephemeral)

┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│  Writable layer (container data) │ ← lost on rm
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│  Image layer 4: app code         │ ← read-only
│  Image layer 3: pip packages     │ ← read-only
│  Image layer 2: system libs      │ ← read-only
│  Image layer 1: base OS          │ ← read-only (shared)
└──────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2.3 Volume
docs.text:
Definition: A Docker volume is a managed storage mechanism that lives outside the container's writable layer. Data in a volume persists even after the container is removed.

Mental model: A volume is a USB flash drive that you plug into a container. The container can be deleted, but the USB drive — and its data — remains.

Role in the system: - Stores persistent data: databases, uploaded files, logs - Can be shared between several containers - Managed by Docker (stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/ on Linux)

Types:

Type Syntax Use case Named volume mydata:/app/data Production databases, persistent app data Bind mount /host/path:/container/path Development — live code reloading tmpfs mount --tmpfs /app/cache Sensitive data that must not reach the disk

docs.title: 2.4 Network
docs.text:
Definition: A Docker network is a virtual networking layer that lets containers communicate with each other and with the outside world.

Mental model: A network is a private office LAN. Containers on the same network can reach each other by service name (like a hostname). Containers on different networks are isolated.

Role in the system: - Enables communication between services (API → Database) - Isolates environments (production and staging containers don't see each other) - Controls what is reachable from the host machine (published ports)

Built-in network drivers:

Driver Description bridge The default. An isolated virtual network on the host. Containers communicate by service name host The container uses the host's network stack. No isolation — rarely used none No network. Full isolation overlay Multi-host networking. Used in Docker Swarm / Kubernetes

docs.text:
flowchart TD
    User(["Developer / CI Pipeline"])
    CLI["Docker CLI<br>docker build / run / push"]
    Daemon["Docker Daemon<br>dockerd"]
    Registry[("Docker Registry<br>Hub / ECR / GHCR")]
    Images[("Images<br>immutable layers")]
    Containers[("Containers<br>running processes")]
    Volumes[("Volumes<br>persistent storage")]
    Networks[("Networks<br>virtual LANs")]

    User --> CLI
    CLI -->|REST API / Unix socket| Daemon
    Daemon -->|push / pull| Registry
    Daemon --> Images
    Daemon -->|instantiates| Containers
    Containers -->|mounts| Volumes
    Containers -->|connects to| Networks
    Images -->|immutable base for| Containers

docs.title: Diagram explanation
docs.text:
1. Developer → Docker CLI Every Docker command (docker build, docker run, docker ps) is handled by the Docker CLI — the client tool. The CLI itself doesn't do the heavy lifting.

2. Docker CLI → Docker Daemon The CLI talks to the Docker Daemon (dockerd) via a REST API over a Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock). The daemon is the background service that actually manages everything. That's why you sometimes get "permission denied" errors — you need access to this socket.

3. Daemon → Registry When you run docker pull python:3.11 or docker push myapp:v2, the daemon connects to a registry — a remote image store. Docker Hub is the default public registry. Companies use private registries (AWS ECR, GitHub Container Registry).

4. Images → Containers The daemon uses images as immutable base layers. When a container starts, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top of the image layers.

5. Containers → Volumes & Networks Running containers interact with the outside world through: - Volumes — for reading/writing persistent data - Networks — for talking to other containers or publishing ports on the host

docs.title: 4. The Docker Workflow (the real lifecycle)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Code(["Write code<br>+ Dockerfile"])
    Build(["docker build<br>Create the Image"])
    Image[("Image<br>v1.0")]
    Run(["docker run<br>Start the container"])
    Container(["Running<br>container"])
    Debug(["Debug<br>docker logs / exec"])
    Fix(["Fix the code"])
    Push(["docker push<br>To the registry"])
    Registry[("Registry<br>Hub / ECR")]

    Code --> Build --> Image --> Run --> Container
    Container --> Debug --> Fix --> Build
    Image --> Push --> Registry

    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

docs.title: Step by step: a developer's real process
docs.text:
Step 1 — Write code + Dockerfile

You write your application AND a Dockerfile that describes how to package it. The Dockerfile lives in your repository next to the code.

# Example: a Python FastAPI service
FROM python:3.11-slim                   # base image

WORKDIR /app                            # working directory inside the container

COPY requirements.txt .                 # copy only requirements first (layer cache)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt  # install dependencies

COPY . .                               # copy the application code

EXPOSE 8000                            # document which port the app uses
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Step 2 — docker build: create the image

docker build -t myapi:v1.0 .

Docker reads the Dockerfile top to bottom, executes each instruction, and creates a new layer for each one. The result is an image tagged myapi:v1.0.

Step 3 — docker run: start the container

docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name api-server myapi:v1.0

Docker creates a container from the image and starts it. -d runs it in the background. -p 8000:8000 forwards host port 8000 to port 8000 inside the container.

Step 4 — The running container

Your application is now running in an isolated environment. It has its own filesystem, network, and process space, but shares the host kernel.

Step 5 — Debug

docker logs api-server          # view stdout/stderr
docker logs -f api-server       # follow logs in real time
docker exec -it api-server sh   # open a shell inside the running container

Step 6 — Fix the code → Rebuild

You found a bug. Fix the code, then rebuild the image. Docker's layer cache means only the changed layers are rebuilt — usually fast.

# Only the COPY . . layer is rebuilt if the code changed
docker build -t myapi:v1.1 .

Step 7 — Push to the registry

docker tag myapi:v1.1 ghcr.io/myorg/myapi:v1.1
docker push ghcr.io/myorg/myapi:v1.1

The image is now available to any server, CI/CD pipeline, or colleague.

docs.title: docker run
docs.text:
docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND]

Creates and starts a new container from an image.

Flag Meaning -d Background mode (detached) -p HOST:CONTAINER Publish a port --name NAME Give the container a name -e KEY=VALUE Set an environment variable -v VOLUME:PATH Mount a volume --rm Automatically remove the container after it stops -it Interactive + pseudo-TTY (for a shell) 
# Real examples:
docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret --name pg postgres:15
docker run --rm -it python:3.11-slim bash
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 -v mydata:/app/data --name api myapi:v1.0

Common mistake: Forgetting -d and blocking the terminal, or forgetting --rm and piling up stopped containers.

docs.title: docker start / docker stop / docker restart
docs.text:
docker stop api-server          # graceful stop (SIGTERM → SIGKILL after 10s)
docker start api-server         # start a stopped container
docker restart api-server       # stop + start
docker kill api-server          # immediate stop (SIGKILL, no grace period)

Common mistake: Using docker kill in production — always prefer docker stop for a graceful shutdown.

docs.title: docker ps
docs.text:
docker ps               # running containers
docker ps -a            # all containers (including stopped ones)
docker ps -q            # container IDs only (useful for scripts)

# Stop all running containers:
docker stop $(docker ps -q)

# Remove all stopped containers:
docker rm $(docker ps -aq -f status=exited)

docs.title: docker rm
docs.text:
docker rm api-server            # remove a stopped container
docker rm -f api-server         # force remove (even if running)

Common mistake: Confusing docker stop (stops gracefully) with docker rm (removes). You need to stop first and then remove, or use -f.

docs.title: docker build
docs.text:
docker build -t NAME:TAG CONTEXT_PATH

docker build -t myapp:1.0 .                       # from the current directory
docker build -t myapp:1.0 -f Dockerfile.prod .    # custom Dockerfile name
docker build --no-cache -t myapp:1.0 .            # ignore the layer cache (clean build)
docker build --target builder -t myapp:dev .      # build up to a specific stage (multi-stage)

Common mistake: Building from the wrong context (. means "send the current directory to the daemon"). Large directories slow down the build. Use .dockerignore.

docs.title: docker pull / docker push
docs.text:
docker pull python:3.11-slim                      # download from a registry
docker push ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:v1.0              # upload to a registry

docs.title: docker images
docs.text:
docker images                   # list all local images
docker images -q                # image IDs only
docker images myapp             # filter by name

docs.title: docker tag
docs.text:
docker tag SOURCE_IMAGE TARGET_IMAGE
docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:1.0
docker tag myapp:1.0 myapp:latest

Common mistake: Thinking that tag creates a copy. It creates an alias — both names point to the same image layers.

docs.title: docker logs
docs.text:
docker logs api-server          # print all logs
docker logs -f api-server       # follow (like tail -f)
docker logs --tail 50 api-server        # last 50 lines
docker logs --since 10m api-server      # logs from the last 10 minutes

Common mistake: Not using -f when debugging a running service — you need the stream.

docs.title: docker exec
docs.text:
docker exec -it CONTAINER COMMAND

Runs a command inside an already running container without stopping it.

docker exec -it api-server bash         # open a bash shell
docker exec -it api-server sh           # open sh (for alpine images)
docker exec api-server env              # print environment variables
docker exec -it pg psql -U postgres     # connect to PostgreSQL inside the container

Common mistake: Using docker exec to "fix" things by manually editing files inside a running container. That change is lost on restart. Always fix it in the Dockerfile or the application code.

docs.title: docker inspect
docs.text:
docker inspect CONTAINER|IMAGE
docker inspect api-server | python3 -m json.tool   # formatted output
docker inspect -f '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' api-server  # extract a specific field

Returns full JSON metadata: network, mounts, environment variables, state, and so on.

docs.title: docker stats
docs.text:
docker stats                    # resource usage for all containers
docker stats api-server         # a specific container

Shows CPU%, memory usage, network and disk I/O in real time. The htop equivalent for containers.

docs.title: System cleanup
docs.text:
# Remove stopped containers
docker container prune

# Remove dangling images (untagged, from old builds)
docker image prune

# Remove all unused images (not referenced by any container)
docker image prune -a

# Remove unused volumes
docker volume prune

# Remove unused networks
docker network prune

# Nuclear option: remove EVERYTHING unused (containers, images, networks, build cache)
docker system prune -a --volumes

Common mistake: Running docker system prune on a production server without checking what is "unused" — it may delete images referenced by stopped containers that you are about to restart.

Check disk usage first:

docker system df        # shows disk usage by images, containers, volumes

docs.title: Why you need Compose
docs.text:
Real applications are never a single container. A typical web service has:

Your API (Python/FastAPI)
    + PostgreSQL database
    + Redis cache
    + Celery worker
    + Nginx reverse proxy

Managing this with separate docker run commands is painful: - You have to remember the exact flags for each service - You have to create networks and volumes manually - Starting/stopping requires running 5+ commands in the right order - Environment variables and secrets have to be passed manually every time

Docker Compose solves this with a single docker-compose.yml that declaratively defines all services, their configuration, and how they are connected.

flowchart TD
    Nginx["Nginx<br>Port 80/443"]
    WebApp["FastAPI<br>Port 8000"]
    Worker["Celery Worker<br>no port"]
    Database[("PostgreSQL<br>Port 5432")]
    Redis[("Redis<br>Port 6379")]

    Nginx -->|proxy_pass| WebApp
    WebApp -->|SQL queries| Database
    WebApp -->|task queue| Redis
    Worker -->|task processing| Redis
    Worker -->|SQL writes| Database

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class WebApp,Worker step;
    class Database,Redis success;
    class Nginx warning;

docs.title: A real docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
services:
  api:
    build: ./services/api          # build from a local Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"                # publish to the host
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy  # wait until the DB is ready
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    volumes:
      - ./services/api:/app        # bind mount for development (live reload)
    networks:
      - backend

  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data   # named volume for persistence
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U user -d mydb"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - backend

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks:
      - backend

  worker:
    build: ./services/worker
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    networks:
      - backend

volumes:
  pgdata:                          # Docker-managed persistent volume

networks:
  backend:                         # isolated virtual network for all services
    driver: bridge

docs.title: How services talk to each other
docs.text:
Inside a Compose network, every service is reachable by its name as a hostname.

From the 'api' container:
  Connect to PostgreSQL: postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
                                                      ^^
                                                      service name = hostname

  Connect to Redis: redis://redis:6379
                                ^^^^^
                                service name = hostname

Docker's built-in DNS resolver automatically maps names to IP addresses. You don't need to hard-code IP addresses.

docs.title: Essential Compose commands
docs.text:
docker compose up                   # start all services (foreground)
docker compose up -d                # start all services (background)
docker compose up --build           # rebuild images before starting
docker compose down                 # stop and remove containers + networks
docker compose down -v              # also remove volumes (CAREFUL: data loss)
docker compose logs -f api          # follow logs of a specific service
docker compose exec api bash        # shell in a running service
docker compose ps                   # list running services
docker compose restart api          # restart one service
docker compose build api            # rebuild the image of just one service

docs.title: Why containers are ephemeral
docs.text:
Every container has a writable layer on top of the image layers. When the container is removed, this layer is deleted. This is intentional — it makes containers disposable and reproducible.

Container lifecycle and data:

docker run postgres → [Container A] writes data to the writable layer
docker rm [Container A] → ALL DATA DELETED

docker run postgres → [Container B] starts EMPTY

This is a feature, not a bug. But it means you have to opt into persistence explicitly.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Container (ephemeral)"
        App["Application"]
        WritableLayer["Writable layer<br>lost on rm"]
    end

    subgraph "Persistent storage"
        NamedVolume[("Named Volume<br>pgdata")]
        BindMount["Bind Mount<br>./code → /app"]
    end

    App -->|reads/writes| WritableLayer
    App -->|stores DB data| NamedVolume
    App -->|live code| BindMount

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class App step;
    class NamedVolume success;
    class WritableLayer error;
    class BindMount warning;

docs.title: Named Volumes vs Bind Mounts
docs.text:
Named Volumes — Docker manages the storage location:

# Create and use a named volume
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15

# Inspect the volume
docker volume inspect pgdata

# The volume survives container removal:
docker rm -f my-postgres    # container removed
# the pgdata volume still exists with all its data
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15   # the data is back!

Bind Mounts — you specify the exact path on the host:

# Mount the current directory into the container (development)
docker run -v $(pwd):/app -p 8000:8000 myapi:dev

# Mount a specific config file
docker run -v $(pwd)/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf nginx

When to use which:

Scenario Use DB files (PostgreSQL, MySQL) Named volume Development — live code reloading Bind mount Log files you need to access from the host Bind mount Production data that must survive restarts Named volume Secrets / credentials Named volume or Docker secrets CI/CD builds (one-off) Nothing — the ephemeral writable layer

docs.title: Volume commands
docs.text:
docker volume create mydata
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect mydata
docker volume rm mydata
docker volume prune              # remove all unused volumes

docs.title: How Docker networking works
docs.text:
When Docker starts, it creates a virtual network interface on the host (docker0 on Linux). Containers connect to virtual networks that are bridged through this interface.

flowchart TD
    Internet(["Internet"])
    HostPort["Host port :80<br>(published)"]
    HostPort2["Host port :8000<br>(published)"]
    Bridge["bridge network<br>172.17.0.0/16"]
    Nginx["nginx<br>172.17.0.2"]
    API["api<br>172.17.0.3"]
    DB["postgres 172.17.0.4<br>(no published port)"]
    Redis["redis 172.17.0.5<br>(no published port)"]

    Internet --> HostPort --> Nginx
    Internet --> HostPort2 --> API
    Nginx -->|internally: api:8000| API
    API -->|internally: postgres:5432| DB
    API -->|internally: redis:6379| Redis

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class Internet,Bridge,Nginx,API step;
    class DB,Redis success;
    class HostPort,HostPort2 warning;

docs.title: Publishing ports vs internal networking
docs.text:
Published ports (-p HOST:CONTAINER): Make a container port reachable from the host machine (and therefore from the network). Publish only what needs to be reachable from outside.

Internal networking: Containers on the same Docker network can communicate on any port by service name — without publishing that port on the host.

# WRONG: publishing the DB port to the outside (security risk)
docker run -p 5432:5432 postgres     # anyone can connect to your DB!

# RIGHT: the DB stays internal, the API is published
docker run -p 8000:8000 api          # the API is public
docker run postgres                  # the DB is reachable only inside the Docker network

docs.title: Network commands
docs.text:
docker network create mynet                     # create a custom bridge network
docker network ls                               # list networks
docker network inspect mynet                    # full details (IP ranges, connected containers)
docker network connect mynet api-container      # connect a running container to the network
docker network disconnect mynet api-container   # disconnect a container from the network
docker network rm mynet                         # remove the network

docs.title: DNS resolution inside Docker
docs.text:
Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside every container. It automatically resolves service names to container IP addresses.

# From the 'api' container:
ping db          # resolves to the postgres container IP
ping redis       # resolves to the redis container IP
curl http://nginx/health   # resolves to the nginx container

This means your application configuration should use service names, never IP addresses.

docs.title: Mistake 1: Using the latest tag
docs.text:
# BAD
FROM python:latest
FROM node:latest

The latest tag means "whatever is the current latest at build time". Today that's Python 3.12. Next week it might be Python 3.13 with breaking changes. Your builds become non-reproducible.

# GOOD: pin the exact version
FROM python:3.11.9-slim
FROM node:20.15.1-alpine

Rule: Always pin exact versions in FROM instructions. Treat them like the versions in requirements.txt.

docs.title: Mistake 2: Storing data inside containers
docs.text:
# BAD: writing to the container filesystem
docker exec api-server sh -c "echo 'config' > /app/config.json"
# This config is lost when the container restarts

# GOOD: use volumes for any data that must persist
services:
  api:
    volumes:
      - ./config:/app/config     # bind mount the config from the host
      - appdata:/app/data        # named volume for generated data

Any file written directly into the container's writable layer is ephemeral. If the container crashes, is replaced by a new version, or is restarted by an orchestrator — that data is gone. Use volumes.

docs.title: Mistake 3: Not cleaning up resources
docs.text:
# After weeks of development, check disk usage:
docker system df

Common causes of disk bloat: - Stopped containers piling up from every docker run without --rm - Dangling images — intermediate layers from repeated builds (named <none>:<none>) - Old named volumes from deleted projects - Build cache from docker build

# Regular maintenance commands:
docker container prune          # remove stopped containers
docker image prune              # remove dangling images
docker system prune             # remove containers, networks, dangling images
docker system prune -a          # also remove unused images (not just dangling ones)

Always use --rm for one-off containers:

docker run --rm python:3.11 python -c "print('hello')"
# The container is removed automatically after it exits

docs.title: Mistake 4: Misusing docker exec
docs.text:
# BAD: "fixing" a running container via exec
docker exec api-server pip install missing-package
# The package is installed ONLY in the running container
# Next container restart: the package is gone
# Next deployment: the package is missing
# Other team members: the package is missing

# BAD: editing code directly inside the container
docker exec -it api-server vim /app/main.py

docker exec is a diagnostic tool, not a way to change the container (technically it can modify files, but those changes vanish on restart). It's for inspecting what is going on — checking logs, running psql to query the DB, debugging a network issue.

# GOOD uses of docker exec:
docker exec -it postgres psql -U user -d mydb    # connect to the DB to explore
docker exec api-server env                        # check environment variables
docker exec api-server python -c "import sys; print(sys.path)"  # debug imports
docker exec -it api-server curl localhost:8000/health  # check an internal endpoint

Any real change must go into your Dockerfile or application code, followed by docker build and a redeploy.

docs.title: Mistake 5: Wrong order of Dockerfile instructions
docs.text:
# BAD: code changes invalidate the dependency layer
COPY . .                           # changes every time the code changes
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # reinstalls ALL dependencies even if they didn't change!

# GOOD: dependencies are cached if requirements.txt hasn't changed
COPY requirements.txt .            # copy only requirements first
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # cached if requirements.txt hasn't changed
COPY . .                           # copy the code last (changes often)

Docker rebuilds from the first changed layer downward. Put rarely changing instructions first and frequently changing ones last.

docs.title: 1. Image layering: order for cache efficiency
docs.text:
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Layer 1: System dependencies (rarely change)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    gcc \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Layer 2: Python dependencies (change sometimes)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Layer 3: Application code (changes often)
COPY . .

CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Rule: Stable → Semi-stable → Volatile. Dependencies before code.

docs.title: 2. Small images: use Alpine or Slim variants
docs.text:
Base image Size Usage python:3.11 ~1 GB Never in production python:3.11-slim ~130 MB The standard choice for production python:3.11-alpine ~50 MB Smallest, but may lack libraries gcr.io/distroless/python3 ~30 MB Maximum security (no shell) 
# Use slim or alpine where possible:
FROM python:3.11-slim
FROM node:20-alpine
FROM nginx:1.25-alpine

Also: always clean package manager caches in the same layer:

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    build-essential \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*   # MUST be in the same RUN to reduce the layer size

docs.title: 3. Multi-stage builds for production
docs.text:
Build tools, compilers, and test dependencies should not be in your production image.

# Stage 1: Builder (has compilers, dev tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --prefix=/install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Production (minimal, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim AS production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local    # copy only the installed packages
COPY src/ .
CMD ["python", "main.py"]

The production image contains only what is needed to run — not to build. A smaller attack surface, a smaller size.

docs.title: 4. Reproducibility: .dockerignore
docs.text:
# .dockerignore — prevents unnecessary files from being sent to the Docker daemon
.git
.gitignore
__pycache__
*.pyc
*.pyo
.env
.env.*
.venv
venv/
node_modules/
*.log
dist/
build/
.pytest_cache/
.mypy_cache/

Without .dockerignore, COPY . . sends your entire directory (including .git, venv, node_modules) to the Docker daemon. This slows builds down significantly and increases the image size.

docs.title: 5. Dev vs Prod: separate Compose files
docs.text:
docker-compose.yml          ← base configuration (shared services)
docker-compose.dev.yml      ← dev overrides (bind mounts, debug ports)
docker-compose.prod.yml     ← prod overrides (resource limits, restart policies)

# docker-compose.yml (base)
services:
  api:
    image: myapi:${TAG:-latest}
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=${DATABASE_URL}

# docker-compose.dev.yml (dev override)
services:
  api:
    build: .                           # local build for dev
    volumes:
      - .:/app                         # live reload
    environment:
      - DEBUG=true
    command: uvicorn main:app --reload

# docker-compose.prod.yml (prod override)
services:
  api:
    restart: always                    # auto-restart on failure
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 512M

# Development:
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up

# Production:
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d

docs.title: 6. Security basics
docs.text:
Never run as root:

# Create an unprivileged user
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app
USER app                    # all following instructions run as 'app'

Never store secrets in the Dockerfile or the image:

# BAD: the secret is baked into an image layer (visible in history)
ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=supersecret

# GOOD: pass it at runtime
# docker run -e DATABASE_PASSWORD=$SECRET_FROM_VAULT myapi

Use a read-only filesystem where possible:

docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapi    # read-only filesystem except /tmp (in memory)

Scan images for vulnerabilities:

docker scout cves myapi:v1.0    # Docker's built-in scanner
trivy image myapi:v1.0          # Trivy (a popular open-source scanner)

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Build:     docker build -t name:tag .
Run:       docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name app name:tag
Logs:      docker logs -f app
Shell:     docker exec -it app bash
Stop:      docker stop app
Remove:    docker rm app
Images:    docker images
Cleanup:   docker system prune -a

Compose:
  Start:   docker compose up -d --build
  Stop:    docker compose down
  Logs:    docker compose logs -f service
  Shell:   docker compose exec service bash

docs.title: 11. Official Images for the Python Advanced Course
docs.text: All the images listed are official and available on Docker Hub.

docs.title: 11.1 Python
docs.text:
Image: python — the official Python interpreter image.

docker pull python:3.11-slim
Tag Size When to use python:3.11 ~1 GB Never in production python:3.11-slim ~130 MB Standard: production services python:3.11-alpine ~50 MB Minimal size (less compatibility) 
# Start a Python REPL in a container
docker run --rm -it python:3.11-slim python

# Run a script from the current directory
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/app -w /app python:3.11-slim python my_script.py

docs.title: 11.2 PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Image: postgres — the official image of the PostgreSQL relational DBMS.

docker pull postgres:16-alpine
Environment variable Required Default value POSTGRES_PASSWORD Yes — POSTGRES_USER No postgres POSTGRES_DB No = POSTGRES_USER 
# Start PostgreSQL
docker run -d \
  --name my-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=user \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=mydb \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16-alpine

# Connect via psql
docker exec -it my-postgres psql -U user -d mydb

docs.title: 11.3 MongoDB
docs.text:
Image: mongo — the official image of the MongoDB document-oriented NoSQL database.

docker pull mongo:7
Environment variable Description MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME Admin user name MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD Admin password MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE Initial database 
# Start MongoDB
docker run -d \
  --name my-mongo \
  -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=admin \
  -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=secret \
  -p 27017:27017 \
  -v mongodata:/data/db \
  mongo:7

# Connect via mongosh
docker exec -it my-mongo mongosh -u admin -p secret

# Python connection (pymongo)
from pymongo import MongoClient
client = MongoClient("mongodb://admin:secret@localhost:27017/")
db = client["mydb"]

docs.title: 11.4 Redis
docs.text:
Image: redis — the official image of the in-memory data store. Used as a cache, a message broker (Celery), and for pub/sub.

docker pull redis:7-alpine

# Start Redis
docker run -d \
  --name my-redis \
  -p 6379:6379 \
  redis:7-alpine

# Connect via redis-cli
docker exec -it my-redis redis-cli

# Basic redis-cli commands:
# SET key value
# GET key
# DEL key
# KEYS *

# Python connection (redis-py)
import redis
r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
r.set("name", "Docker")
print(r.get("name"))  # Docker

docs.title: 11.5 Neo4j
docs.text:
Image: neo4j — the official image of the Neo4j graph DBMS. It stores data as nodes and relationships.

docker pull neo4j:5
Port Purpose 7474 Neo4j Browser (web interface) 7687 Bolt protocol (for application connections) 
# Start Neo4j
docker run -d \
  --name my-neo4j \
  -p 7474:7474 \
  -p 7687:7687 \
  -e NEO4J_AUTH=neo4j/password \
  -v neo4jdata:/data \
  neo4j:5

# Open in the browser:
# http://localhost:7474
# Login: neo4j / Password: password

# Python connection (neo4j driver)
from neo4j import GraphDatabase
driver = GraphDatabase.driver("bolt://localhost:7687", auth=("neo4j", "password"))

with driver.session() as session:
    session.run("CREATE (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})")
    result = session.run("MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name")
    for record in result:
        print(record["n.name"])

docs.title: 11.6 Ubuntu
docs.text:
Image: ubuntu — the official Ubuntu OS image. Used as a base image or for interactive sessions.

docker pull ubuntu:24.04

# Start an interactive Ubuntu session
docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash

# Install packages and test
docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash -c "
  apt-get update -qq && \
  apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip && \
  python3 --version
"

docs.text:
Image Version Port Purpose python 3.11-slim — Running Python applications postgres 16-alpine 5432 Relational DB mongo 7 27017 Document NoSQL DB redis 7-alpine 6379 Cache / message broker neo4j 5 7474, 7687 Graph DB ubuntu 24.04 — Base OS / learning environment
