docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Before running any command, you need to understand: what is Linux, and why does it matter to a backend developer?

Most of the world's Django applications, API services, databases, and web servers run on Linux. If you write Python/Django code, sooner or later you'll have to run it not only on your laptop but on a real server. That server will almost certainly be Linux.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
A Linux server is like a rented room in a data center where your Django application lives permanently, even when your laptop is turned off.

Your laptop is your personal machine. You turn it on when you need it and turn it off when you're done. But a website has to be available 24/7. That requires a server — a computer that never shuts down and is always connected to the internet.

Most of these servers run Linux. Not because it's perfect, but because it is:

  • free — you can install it without a license;
  • stable — it can run for years without a reboot;
  • flexible — it can be configured for any task;
  • efficient — it needs fewer resources than Windows Server;
  • open — thousands of developers around the world keep improving it.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Operating system (OS) A program that manages the hardware and lets you run other programs Linux An operating system kernel, written by Linus Torvalds in 1991 Distribution The Linux kernel + a set of tools + a package manager. For example: Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS Ubuntu The most popular distribution for servers and for beginners WSL Windows Subsystem for Linux — a Linux terminal inside Windows Server A computer (or cloud VM) that is permanently connected to the network and runs services Deployment The process of moving code from development to a server Terminal A text interface for working with the operating system

docs.title: How Linux is structured
docs.text:
Linux consists of several layers:

+---------------------------------------------------+
|           Your programs (User Space)               |
|   Django, PostgreSQL, Nginx, Python, pip...        |
+---------------------------------------------------+
|              Shell (bash, zsh, sh)                 |
|   The interface between you and the kernel         |
+---------------------------------------------------+
|              Linux Kernel                          |
|   Manages memory, processes, files, network        |
+---------------------------------------------------+
|              Hardware                              |
|   CPU, RAM, disk, network card                     |
+---------------------------------------------------+

The kernel is the heart of the system. It talks directly to the hardware. Your programs never access the hardware directly — they ask the kernel via system calls (syscalls).

The shell is like a translator between you and the kernel. You type commands in the terminal → the shell understands them → the shell asks the kernel to do something.

User Space is where all programs live: Django, PostgreSQL, Nginx, your Python scripts.

docs.title: How Linux differs from Windows
docs.text: Linux Windows Price Free Paid license Management Mostly via the terminal Mostly via a GUI Servers ~70% of the world's servers A smaller share Filesystem Case-sensitive (File.txt ≠ file.txt) Case-insensitive Updates Without a reboot (mostly) Often requires a restart Docker Native Requires WSL or a VM

docs.title: What a distribution is
docs.text:
Linux is just the kernel. But to use it, you also need tools, a file manager, a package manager, and command-line utilities. The kernel + tools bundle = a distribution.

Popular distributions:

Distribution What it's used for Ubuntu Servers, development, the easiest start Debian Stable servers, long-term support CentOS / Rocky Linux Enterprise servers Arch Linux Experienced users, maximum control Alpine Linux Docker images (very small size)

In this lesson we'll use Ubuntu — the most common choice for Django developers and cloud servers.

docs.title: What WSL is
docs.text:
If you're on Windows, you can install WSL — Windows Subsystem for Linux. It is a full Linux environment inside Windows.

# Install WSL (in Windows PowerShell with administrator rights)
wsl --install

# Start Ubuntu
wsl

WSL gives you a real Ubuntu terminal without having to buy a separate server or install a VM. It's the easiest way to start practicing Linux on a Windows machine.

docs.title: The path of code from laptop to user
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Dev["Your laptop<br>(Python/Django)"] --> Git["GitHub / GitLab<br>(code storage)"]
    Git --> Server["Linux server<br>(Ubuntu)"]
    Server --> App["Django app<br>(Gunicorn/Uvicorn)"]
    App --> Users["Site users<br>(browser)"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class Dev,Git,Server,App step;
    class Users success;

Here is what a typical path looks like:

  1. You write code on your laptop.
  2. You push it to a Git repository (GitHub/GitLab).
  3. On the server you run git pull — downloading the new version.
  4. You start Django via Gunicorn or Uvicorn.
  5. Nginx accepts requests from users and passes them to Django.
  6. Users see your site.

docs.title: Linux server architecture for Django
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Internet["Internet"] --> Nginx["Nginx<br>(port 80/443)"]
    Nginx --> Gunicorn["Gunicorn / Uvicorn<br>(port 8000)"]
    Gunicorn --> Django["Django Application"]
    Django --> DB["PostgreSQL<br>(port 5432)"]
    Django --> Cache["Redis<br>(port 6379)"]
    Django --> Static["Static files<br>(/var/www/static)"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class Internet,Nginx,Gunicorn,DB,Cache,Static step;
    class Django success;

Each component is a separate program on the server. They all run in parallel and communicate with each other via the network or the filesystem.

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Thinking that Linux and the terminal are the same thing.

Linux is an operating system. The terminal is just one of the ways to control it.

Mistake 2: Being afraid that you'll "break something".

You can practice freely on your own WSL or a test server. For important operations there are always backups and confirmation prompts.

Mistake 3: Thinking you need to memorize all the commands.

In reality you need to understand the logic and know where to look (man, --help, Google). Over time, the commands you need will stick on their own.

Mistake 4: Running runserver in production.

python manage.py runserver is for local development only. On a server you need Gunicorn/Uvicorn + Nginx.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Open WSL or an Ubuntu terminal and enter: 

uname -a
Read the output and find: which Linux kernel do you have installed?

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Enter: 

cat /etc/os-release
Which Ubuntu are you using?

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Draw by hand or in your notes a diagram: how your Django project gets from your laptop to the user's browser. Use the terms: laptop, Git, server, Nginx, Django, database.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I can explain what Linux is and why it is used on servers
  • [ ] I understand the difference between the Linux kernel and a distribution
  • [ ] I know what Ubuntu and WSL are
  • [ ] I can describe the path of code from the laptop to the user
  • [ ] I understand why runserver must not be used in production

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Linux is the foundation of most modern servers. As a Python/Django developer, you'll regularly connect to Linux servers, start services, read logs, and deploy your applications. The next file is about the terminal and the shell: how to talk to Linux in the first place.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The terminal is your main tool for working with Linux. Everything you'll do on a server — connecting, running programs, viewing files, managing services — happens through the terminal.

There's no need to be afraid of the "black screen". It's just a different way of interacting with a computer: text commands instead of mouse clicks.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
The terminal is the window through which you talk to the operating system. The shell is the language you speak.

An analogy: imagine you're calling customer support. The terminal is the phone (the device). The shell is the language of the conversation (for example, Ukrainian or English).

A terminal (terminal, console) is a program that displays a text interface. On your laptop it might be: - Windows Terminal (for WSL) - iTerm2 (macOS) - GNOME Terminal (Ubuntu)

A shell is an interpreter program that reads your commands and executes them. The most popular shell is Bash (Bourne Again Shell).

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Terminal / Console A program that shows a text interface Shell A command interpreter (bash, zsh, sh, fish) Bash The most common shell on Linux Prompt The invitation to type a command ($ or #) Command The name of the program we run Option / Flag Extra settings for a command (-l, --all) Argument The data we pass to a command (a path, a file name) stdin Standard input (what you type) stdout Standard output (the command's result) stderr Standard error output Exit code The numeric result of running a command (0 = success)

docs.title: What the prompt looks like
docs.text:
When you open a terminal, you see something like this:

student@ubuntu:~$

This means: - student — your username - ubuntu — the server name (hostname) - ~ — the current directory (tilde = home directory) - $ — a regular user - # — the root user (superuser)

If you see # instead of $, you're working as root. That's dangerous for everyday work. Leave root with exit.

docs.title: Command structure
docs.text:
ls -la /home/user

ls        -la       /home/user
^          ^            ^
command   options    argument
  • ls — the command (the list program): show a list of files
  • -la — two options together: -l (detailed view) and -a (show hidden files)
  • /home/user — the argument: which directory to show

Options can be written in different ways: 

ls -l -a         # separately
ls -la           # combined (short form)
ls --all         # long form

docs.title: Basic commands to get started
docs.text:
# Where am I right now?
pwd
pwd — Print Working Directory. Shows the full path to the current directory.

# Who am I?
whoami
Prints the current user's name.

# What's the current date and time?
date


# Clear the screen
clear
Or press Ctrl+L — same effect.

# Print text to the screen
echo "Hello Linux"


# View a command's documentation
man ls
man — manual. Shows the full documentation. Press q to exit.

# Short help for commands
ls --help

# View recently entered commands
history

docs.title: What stdin, stdout, stderr are
docs.text:
Every program in Linux has three standard data streams:

flowchart LR
    Input["stdin<br>What you type"] --> Command["Command<br>(program)"]
    Command --> Output["stdout<br>Normal output"]
    Command --> Errors["stderr<br>Error messages"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class Input,Command step;
    class Output success;
    class Errors error;

Example: 

ls /home          # stdout: a list of files
ls /не-існує      # stderr: the error "No such file or directory"

docs.title: Redirecting output
docs.text:
ls > files.txt        # write stdout to a file
ls >> files.txt       # append stdout to the end of a file
ls 2> errors.txt      # write stderr to a file

docs.title: Pipe
docs.text:
ls -la | grep ".py"

| (pipe) — takes the stdout of one command and passes it as stdin to another.

This command: 1. ls -la — prints a list of files 2. | — passes that list on 3. grep ".py" — filters the lines that contain .py

docs.title: What an exit code is
docs.text:
After it runs, every command returns an exit code — a numeric result:

  • 0 — success
  • 1 or another non-zero number — an error
ls /home
echo $?      # 0 — all good

ls /не_існує
echo $?      # 2 — error

$? is a special variable that holds the exit code of the previous command. This matters for Bash scripts.

docs.title: Useful shortcuts
docs.text:
Shortcut What it does Ctrl+C Stop the current command Ctrl+Z Suspend it and send it to the background Ctrl+D End the session (logout) Ctrl+L Clear the screen Tab Autocomplete a command or path ↑ / ↓ Navigate through the command history Ctrl+R Search the history Ctrl+A Jump to the start of the line Ctrl+E Jump to the end of the line

Tab is the most useful shortcut. Press it twice if you don't know how to continue a command — Linux will show you the options.

docs.title: An example with a Django project
docs.text:
# Start the Django server
python manage.py runserver

While the server is running, you see its output in the terminal (stdout). Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

# Start it and see the output right away
python manage.py runserver 2>&1 | tee server.log

This command: - 2>&1 — redirects stderr to stdout - | tee server.log — saves the output to a file and shows it on screen at the same time

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: command not found

The program isn't installed or isn't in PATH. Check: did you install it? Is your virtualenv activated?

Mistake 2: Permission denied

Not enough permissions. Check the file's permissions or use sudo (but carefully).

Mistake 3: I ran a heavy command and don't know how to stop it.

Press Ctrl+C. If that doesn't help — Ctrl+Z, then kill %1.

Mistake 4: Mixing up > and >>.

> overwrites the file. >> appends to the end. If you use >, the previous contents will be gone.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Open a terminal and run: 

whoami
pwd
date
uname -r
What does each result mean?

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Run: 

echo "Hello, $(whoami)!"
What happened? Why was $(whoami) executed inside the string?

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Run: 

ls /tmp
echo $?
ls /not_existing_dir
echo $?
Compare the exit codes. What does the difference mean?

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Enter: 

history | tail -10
What did this command do? Break down its structure: where is the command, where is the pipe, where is the argument?

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I understand the difference between a terminal and a shell
  • [ ] I can explain what Bash is
  • [ ] I can read the structure of a command: command, options, arguments
  • [ ] I understand stdin, stdout, stderr
  • [ ] I know what exit code 0 and a non-zero code mean
  • [ ] I can stop a running program with Ctrl+C

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: The terminal isn't scary. It's just a text-based way to control Linux. The shell reads your commands and executes them. The structure of a command is always the same: name + options + arguments. The next step is learning to find your way around the filesystem.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
On a server there are no folders with icons and no files you can drag with the mouse. There is only the terminal. To find a config file, go into the project directory, copy or delete a file — you need to know the basic navigation commands.

This is the foundation. Without understanding the filesystem, you can't deploy projects, read logs, or configure services.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
The Linux filesystem is one big tree that starts at the root /. Everything is a node in this tree: directories, files, even devices.

Windows has drives: C:\, D:\. Linux has no drives — there is one root directory /, and everything else is inside it.

docs.title: Filesystem structure
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Root["/"] --> Home["/home — users' home directories"]
    Root --> Etc["/etc — configuration files"]
    Root --> Var["/var — variable data: logs, cache"]
    Root --> Usr["/usr — programs and libraries"]
    Root --> Tmp["/tmp — temporary files"]
    Root --> Opt["/opt — third-party programs"]
    Root --> Srv["/srv — service data"]
    Home --> Student["/home/student — your home"]
    Student --> Projects["projects/"]
    Projects --> Django["my_django_app/"]
    Var --> Log["/var/log — logs"]
    Etc --> Nginx["/etc/nginx — Nginx config"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class Root,Home,Etc,Var,Usr,Tmp,Opt,Srv,Projects,Log,Nginx step;
    class Student,Django success;

docs.title: The most important directories
docs.text: Directory Purpose / The root of the filesystem. Everything starts here /home Users' home directories /home/student Your personal directory /etc Configuration files for the system and services /var/log Logs: Nginx, system logs, your services' logs /tmp Temporary files (deleted after a reboot) /usr/bin System programs (python, git, nginx) /opt Third-party programs you install manually /srv Web service data (Django static, media)

docs.title: Key path symbols
docs.text:
Symbol What it means / The root — when at the start of a path / The separator between parts of a path ~ The current user's home directory . The current directory .. The parent directory (one level up)

Examples: 

/home/student/projects   # absolute path
~/projects               # the same (via ~)
./manage.py              # a file in the current directory
../settings.py           # a file one level up

docs.title: Find out where you are
docs.text:
pwd
Print Working Directory. Shows the full current path.

docs.title: Change directory
docs.text:
cd /home/student/projects   # absolute path
cd projects                  # relative path (from the current one)
cd ..                        # one level up
cd ~                         # to the home directory
cd -                         # to the previous directory

docs.title: List files and directories
docs.text:
ls                   # simple list
ls -l                # detailed list (permissions, size, date)
ls -a                # including hidden files (starting with .)
ls -la               # detailed + hidden
ls /etc              # list a specific directory

Example output of ls -la: 

drwxr-xr-x 3 student student 4096 Jun 10 12:00 projects
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student  234 Jun 10 11:50 manage.py
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student   98 Jun 10 11:45 requirements.txt


# Directory tree
tree
tree -L 2            # only 2 levels deep

docs.title: Creating
docs.text:
mkdir my_project             # create a directory
mkdir -p a/b/c               # create nested directories

touch file.txt               # create an empty file
touch settings.py            # or update the modification date of an existing one

docs.title: Viewing file contents
docs.text:
cat file.txt                 # show the entire contents
less file.txt                # view page by page (q — quit)
head -20 file.txt            # first 20 lines
tail -20 file.txt            # last 20 lines
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log   # follow a file in real time

docs.title: Copying
docs.text:
cp file.txt copy.txt             # copy a file
cp -r my_project/ backup/        # copy a directory recursively

docs.title: Moving and renaming
docs.text:
mv file.txt new_name.txt         # rename
mv file.txt /tmp/                # move
mv old_dir/ new_dir/             # rename a directory

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
⚠️ Linux has no recycle bin. You can't get a deleted file back.

rm file.txt                  # delete a file
rm -r my_project/            # delete a directory recursively
rmdir empty_dir/             # delete an EMPTY directory

docs.title: The danger of rm -rf
docs.text:
rm -rf /            # NEVER DO THIS

-r — recursively (all files and subfolders), -f — without confirmation (force). If you run this at the root of the filesystem, you'll destroy the entire system without any warning.

Safety rules: - Always check the path before rm -rf - Use ls first to see what will be deleted - On production servers, never run rm -rf without a backup

docs.title: Finding files
docs.text:
find . -name "settings.py"              # find a file by name
find /var/log -name "*.log"             # find all .log files
find . -type f -name "*.py"             # files only (not directories)
find . -type d -name "migrations"       # directories only

grep -r "SECRET_KEY" .                  # find text in files
grep -rn "def create_user" .            # with line numbers

docs.title: Useful commands for Python/Django
docs.text:
# Where is python?
which python3

# Where are the packages installed?
pip show django

# View the project structure
tree my_django_project/ -L 2

# Find all migration files
find . -path "*/migrations/*.py" -not -name "__init__.py"

docs.title: Absolute vs relative path
docs.text:
Absolute path — always starts with /
  /home/student/projects/my_app/settings.py

Relative path — relative to the current directory
  (if you are in /home/student/)
  projects/my_app/settings.py
  or ./projects/my_app/settings.py

When to use which: - Absolute — in scripts and configs (reliable, independent of cd) - Relative — in the terminal for quick navigation

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: No such file or directory

Check: is the name spelled correctly? Linux is case-sensitive: manage.py ≠ Manage.py

Mistake 2: Deleted the wrong thing.

Always check with ls before rm. There's no recycle bin.

Mistake 3: Permission denied when entering a directory.

You don't have the x (execute) permission on the directory. Check the permissions with ls -la.

Mistake 4: Mixing up / and ~.

/ is the system root. ~ is your home directory /home/student.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/practice/django_project
cd ~/practice/django_project
touch manage.py requirements.txt .env
mkdir app templates static
ls -la
Explain what you created and where it is located.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
echo "DEBUG=True" > .env
cat .env
echo "SECRET_KEY=test123" >> .env
cat .env
Explain the difference between > and >>.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
cp -r ~/practice/django_project ~/practice/django_project_backup
ls ~/practice/
What happened?

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
find ~/practice -name "*.py"
grep -r "DEBUG" ~/practice
What did these commands find?

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I can explain the structure of /home, /etc, /var/log
  • [ ] I understand the difference between an absolute and a relative path
  • [ ] I can navigate with cd and see a listing with ls -la
  • [ ] I can create, copy, move, and delete files
  • [ ] I understand the danger of rm -rf and check the path before deleting
  • [ ] I can find a file with find and text with grep

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: The Linux filesystem is a tree starting at the root /. Each directory has its own purpose: /etc for configs, /var/log for logs, /home for your files. Basic commands: pwd, cd, ls, mkdir, touch, cp, mv, rm. The next step is permissions and users.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Linux is a multi-user system. Several people, several programs, and several services can all work on one server. To keep them from getting in each other's way and from accessing each other's data, Linux uses a permissions system.

As a Python/Django developer, you'll regularly run into Permission denied errors. To fix them, you need to understand how permissions work.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
Imagine that every file is a folder of documents. Permissions are the locks: who can read, who can edit, who can run.

Every file and directory in Linux has: - an owner (user/owner) — usually whoever created the file - a group (group) — a set of users with shared permissions - permissions (permissions) — what can be done with the file

docs.title: How to read permissions
docs.text:
Run ls -la and you'll see lines like this:

-rwxr-xr--  1  student  www-data  4096  Jun 10 12:00  manage.py
^            ^     ^        ^        ^                    ^
type+perms  links owner   group    size                  name

docs.title: The first character — the file type
docs.text: Character Type - Regular file d Directory l Symbolic link

docs.title: The next 9 characters — the permissions
docs.text:
rwxr-xr--
^^^       — owner permissions (owner)
   ^^^    — group permissions (group)
      ^^^ — permissions for everyone else (others)

docs.title: What r, w, x mean
docs.text: Character Name For a file For a directory r read Can read the contents Can see the list of files w write Can modify and delete Can create/delete files x execute Can run it as a program Can enter it with cd - no permission — —

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
-rwxr-xr--

-    = regular file
rwx  = the owner can: read, write, execute
r-x  = the group can: read, execute (write — NO)
r--  = everyone else can: only read

docs.title: Numeric permissions (octal)
docs.text:
Permissions are often written as numbers:

Character Number r 4 w 2 x 1 - 0

The permissions for each set are the sum of the numbers:

rwx = 4+2+1 = 7
r-x = 4+0+1 = 5
r-- = 4+0+0 = 4
--- = 0+0+0 = 0

Typical combinations:

Number Characters Meaning 755 rwxr-xr-x Owner: everything; Group and Others: read and execute 644 rw-r--r-- Owner: read+write; Everyone: read only 600 rw------- Only the owner can read and write 777 rwxrwxrwx Everyone can do everything (dangerous!)

docs.title: The chmod command — changing permissions
docs.text:
chmod +x script.sh          # add the execute permission for everyone
chmod -x script.sh          # remove the execute permission
chmod 755 script.sh         # set specific permissions
chmod 644 settings.py       # typical for config files
chmod -R 755 /var/www/      # recursively for a directory

Explanation: 

chmod +x script.sh
chmod — change mode. +x — add (+) the execute permission (x). Without it, Linux will refuse to run the file as a script.

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa
A private SSH key must have 600 permissions — only the owner can read it. If the permissions are broader, SSH will refuse to connect.

docs.title: The chown command — changing the owner
docs.text:
chown student file.txt              # change the owner
chown student:www-data file.txt     # change the owner and group
chown -R www-data /var/www/         # recursively

When you need it: If you copied files via scp or sudo, root may become the owner. Then Nginx or Gunicorn won't be able to read the files.

docs.title: What sudo is
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo nano /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

sudo — Superuser Do. Lets you run a command with superuser (root) privileges, even if you're a regular user.

Imagine you're renting an apartment. Regular commands are what you can do in your own room. sudo is asking the landlord (root) to do something in the shared areas.

Why you shouldn't work as root all the time:

  1. A mistake in a command can destroy the system without warning
  2. Programs started as root have access to everything
  3. If a service is hacked, the attacker gets root privileges
  4. The normal working mode is as a regular user

docs.title: The whoami and id commands
docs.text:
whoami          # the current user's name
id              # uid, gid, and all of the user's groups
id student      # the groups of a specific user

docs.title: A practical example — a Django project on a server
docs.text:
# View the project files' permissions
ls -la /var/www/myapp/

# Make the startup script executable
chmod +x /var/www/myapp/start.sh

# Hand the files over to the Nginx user
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/myapp/static/

# Make the config accessible only to the owner
chmod 600 /var/www/myapp/.env

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Permission denied when running a script

Run chmod +x script.sh

Mistake 2: Permission denied when working with Nginx/static

Check that the Nginx process (www-data) has read permission on the directory

Mistake 3: Setting chmod 777 on all files "just to make sure it works"

This is dangerous. Any program on the server will be able to modify your files. Use the minimum necessary permissions.

Mistake 4: The SSH key isn't accepted

Check: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa and chmod 700 ~/.ssh/

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
touch test_file.py
ls -la test_file.py
What permissions does the newly created file have? What does each character mean?

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
chmod +x test_file.py
ls -la test_file.py
chmod 644 test_file.py
ls -la test_file.py
chmod 755 test_file.py
ls -la test_file.py
Follow how the permissions change after each command.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
mkdir secret_config
touch secret_config/.env
echo "SECRET_KEY=abc123" > secret_config/.env
chmod 700 secret_config/
chmod 600 secret_config/.env
ls -la secret_config/
ls -la secret_config/.env
Explain what you did and why these permissions are the right choice for secret files.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I can read the output of ls -la and explain each permission character
  • [ ] I understand the difference between r, w, x for files and directories
  • [ ] I know the numeric form of permissions: 755, 644, 600
  • [ ] I can change permissions with chmod
  • [ ] I can change the owner with chown
  • [ ] I understand what sudo is and why you shouldn't be root all the time

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Permissions protect files from unauthorized access. Every file has an owner, a group, and permissions (r/w/x) for three categories. chmod changes permissions, chown changes the owner, sudo grants temporary root privileges. The next step is processes, ports, and services.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: When you run python manage.py runserver, a process starts — Django listens on port 8000. When you deploy to a server, Nginx and Gunicorn are processes too. To understand why "the site won't open" or "the port is already in use", you need to know how to manage processes and services.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Process A running program in memory. It has its own PID PID Process ID — the unique number of a process Foreground The process occupies the terminal. Ctrl+C stops it Background The process runs in the background. The terminal is free Daemon A background service process without a terminal Port A numeric address (0–65535) for a network connection Service A program managed by systemd (start, stop, autostart) systemd The service management system in Ubuntu/Debian

docs.title: View running processes
docs.text:
ps aux
ps — process status. Shows all processes on the system.

USER   PID  %CPU %MEM   COMMAND
root     1   0.0  0.1   /sbin/init
student 1234  2.1  1.5   python manage.py runserver
www-data 5678  0.1  0.3   nginx: worker process

ps aux | grep python        # find Python processes
ps aux | grep nginx         # find Nginx processes

docs.title: Interactive monitor
docs.text:
top         # updates in real time
htop        # a better version (needs installing: sudo apt install htop)

In top/htop: press q to quit, k to terminate a process by PID.

docs.title: Terminate a process
docs.text:
kill 1234           # send the SIGTERM signal (ask it to exit)
kill -9 1234        # SIGKILL (force kill, no chance to clean up)
killall python      # terminate all processes named python
pkill -f "manage.py runserver"   # find and terminate by pattern

kill -9 is a last resort. The process won't have time to save its data. Try a plain kill first.

docs.title: Foreground and Background
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver          # foreground — blocks the terminal
python manage.py runserver &        # background — & at the end

jobs                                # show background jobs
fg                                  # bring back the last background job
fg %1                               # bring back job #1
bg                                  # resume a suspended job in the background

If you press Ctrl+Z while a foreground process is running, it is suspended and goes to the background (status Stopped).

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
A port is like a room number in a hotel. The IP address is the hotel's address, the port is the room number.

When Django listens on port 8000, it means: anyone who connects to this server on port 8000 gets a response from Django.

docs.title: Well-known ports
docs.text: Port Service 22 SSH 80 HTTP 443 HTTPS 5432 PostgreSQL 6379 Redis 8000 Django runserver (default) 8080 Alternative HTTP

docs.title: Check open ports
docs.text:
ss -tulpn                   # all open ports and processes
ss -tulpn | grep :8000      # a specific port

lsof -i :8000               # which process is using port 8000
lsof -i :5432               # is PostgreSQL running?

Example output of ss -tulpn: 

Netid  State  Local Address:Port   Process
tcp    LISTEN 0.0.0.0:8000         python manage.py runserver
tcp    LISTEN 0.0.0.0:80           nginx
tcp    LISTEN 127.0.0.1:5432       postgres

docs.title: Services and systemd
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Boot["The server boots"] --> Systemd["systemd starts first<br>(PID 1)"]
    Systemd --> Nginx["nginx.service"]
    Systemd --> Postgres["postgresql.service"]
    Systemd --> Myapp["myapp.service<br>(your Django)"]
    Systemd --> Redis["redis.service"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class Boot,Nginx,Postgres,Redis step;
    class Myapp success;
    class Systemd warning;

systemd is the first process started after the system boots (PID 1). It is responsible for starting and managing all services.

docs.title: systemctl commands
docs.text:
# Service status
systemctl status nginx
systemctl status postgresql

# Start / stop / restart
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl reload nginx        # re-read the config without stopping

# Autostart at boot
sudo systemctl enable nginx        # add to autostart
sudo systemctl disable nginx       # remove from autostart

# List all services
systemctl list-units --type=service

docs.title: Viewing service logs
docs.text:
journalctl -u nginx                 # all Nginx logs
journalctl -u nginx -f              # follow the logs in real time
journalctl -u nginx --since today   # today's logs
journalctl -u myapp -n 50          # last 50 lines

docs.title: The full request chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    User["User<br>opens the site"] --> Port80["Port 80/443<br>HTTPS"]
    Port80 --> Nginx["Nginx process<br>(nginx.service)"]
    Nginx --> Port8000["Port 8000<br>PROXY PASS"]
    Port8000 --> Gunicorn["Gunicorn process<br>(myapp.service)"]
    Gunicorn --> Django["Django Application"]
    Django --> DB["PostgreSQL<br>Port 5432"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class User,Nginx,Gunicorn,DB step;
    class Django success;
    class Port80,Port8000 warning;

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Address already in use on startup

The port is already taken by another process. Find it: lsof -i :8000, and terminate the old process.

Mistake 2: You ran python manage.py runserver and closed the terminal — the server stopped.

A foreground process is tied to the terminal. For production, use systemd or Docker.

Mistake 3: Nginx is running, but the site won't open.

Check: systemctl status nginx and journalctl -u nginx -n 20. The config may be invalid.

Mistake 4: Confusing a port with a PID.

A PID is a process identifier (for example 1234). A port is a network address (for example 8000).

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver &
ps aux | grep manage
jobs
kill %1
Start Django in the background, find its process, then stop it.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
ss -tulpn
lsof -i :8000
Which ports are open right now? Which processes are listening on them?

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
What changed after start?

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I can find the PID of a running process with ps aux
  • [ ] I understand the difference between foreground and background
  • [ ] I can stop a process with kill
  • [ ] I know the main ports: SSH (22), HTTP (80), Django (8000), PostgreSQL (5432)
  • [ ] I can check what is listening on a port with ss -tulpn or lsof
  • [ ] I can check the status of a service and restart it with systemctl

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: A process is a running program with a unique PID. A port is a network address on which a process listens for connections. A service is a process managed by systemd (autostart, restart, logs). Understanding these three concepts means understanding how your Django lives on a server.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A server has no App Store and no .exe files. To install Nginx, Python, PostgreSQL, or any other program, you use a package manager. For Python libraries — pip.

Understanding the difference between system packages and Python packages matters so you don't break your environment and don't get confused about where a particular version of Python or Django comes from.

docs.title: Two levels of packages
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    OS["Operating system<br>(Ubuntu)"] --> APT["apt: system programs<br>Nginx, Python, Git, PostgreSQL"]
    Python["Python project"] --> PIP["pip: Python libraries<br>Django, requests, celery"]
    APT --> System["Installed into /usr/bin, /usr/lib<br>— for the whole system"]
    PIP --> Venv["Better installed into a virtualenv<br>— isolated per project"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class OS,APT,Python,PIP step;
    class Venv success;
    class System warning;

apt installs programs for the operating system. pip installs Python libraries for a Python project.

docs.title: Updating the package list
docs.text:
sudo apt update
It doesn't install anything — it only downloads the current list of available packages from the repositories. Always run it before install.

docs.title: Upgrading installed packages
docs.text:
sudo apt upgrade
Upgrades all installed packages to newer versions.

docs.title: Installing packages
docs.text:
sudo apt install nginx
sudo apt install python3
sudo apt install python3-venv
sudo apt install python3-pip
sudo apt install git
sudo apt install postgresql
sudo apt install redis-server
sudo apt install htop curl wget tree

docs.title: Removing packages
docs.text:
sudo apt remove nginx            # remove the program
sudo apt purge nginx             # remove + configuration files
sudo apt autoremove              # remove unneeded dependencies

docs.title: Searching for a package
docs.text:
apt search nginx
apt show nginx                   # detailed information about the package
dpkg -l | grep nginx             # is the package installed?

docs.title: Installing libraries
docs.text:
pip install django
pip install django==4.2.0        # a specific version
pip install "django>=4.0,<5.0"  # a version range
pip install django psycopg2-binary celery redis

docs.title: Working with requirements.txt
docs.text:
pip freeze                       # list all installed packages
pip freeze > requirements.txt    # save to a file

pip install -r requirements.txt  # install from a file

docs.title: Package information
docs.text:
pip show django                  # version, dependencies, location
pip list                         # all installed packages
pip list --outdated              # what can be upgraded

docs.title: Why virtualenv matters
docs.text:
Without a virtualenv, every pip install goes into the system Python. That's a problem:

  • Project A requires Django==3.2, Project B — Django==4.2. A conflict.
  • You upgraded a library for one project — and broke another.
  • The production server has the wrong version installed.

A virtualenv isolates the libraries of each project:

flowchart TD
    System["System Python 3.11"] --> P1["project_A/.venv/<br>Django 3.2, pillow 9.0"]
    System --> P2["project_B/.venv/<br>Django 4.2, pillow 10.0"]
    System --> P3["project_C/.venv/<br>FastAPI, sqlalchemy"]

    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class P1,P2,P3 success;
    class System warning;

docs.title: virtualenv commands
docs.text:
# Create a virtualenv
python3 -m venv .venv

# Activate (Linux/Mac)
source .venv/bin/activate

# Deactivate
deactivate

# After activation — install the dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

After activation you'll see (.venv) before the prompt: 

(.venv) student@ubuntu:~/myproject$

docs.title: Where to keep the virtualenv
docs.text:
• Always in the project directory: .venv/
  • Add it to .gitignore — don't commit it
# .gitignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env

docs.title: A typical sequence on a new server
docs.text:
# 1. Update the system
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# 2. Install system dependencies
sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip git nginx -y

# 3. Clone the project
git clone https://github.com/you/myproject.git
cd myproject

# 4. Create a virtualenv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# 5. Install Python dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Running pip install without an activated virtualenv

The library will be installed into the system Python. Check: which pip should point to .venv/bin/pip.

Mistake 2: pip: command not found

Use pip3 or python3 -m pip, or install it via sudo apt install python3-pip.

Mistake 3: Not adding .venv to .gitignore

A virtualenv contains thousands of files and weighs 100+ MB. It doesn't belong in Git.

Mistake 4: Forgetting sudo apt update before install

Without updating, you may install an old version or get a "package not found" error.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install tree htop -y
tree --version
htop --version
Make sure both programs were installed.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
mkdir ~/test_project && cd ~/test_project
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install django
python -c "import django; print(django.__version__)"
pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt
deactivate
Follow each step. Explain what is happening.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Open two terminals. In one, activate the virtualenv and enter which python. In the other — without the virtualenv. Compare the results.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I understand the difference between apt and pip
  • [ ] I can install a system program with apt install
  • [ ] I can create and activate a virtualenv
  • [ ] I understand why each project needs a virtualenv
  • [ ] I can save and restore dependencies with pip freeze and requirements.txt

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: apt is for system programs (Nginx, PostgreSQL, Git). pip is for Python libraries (Django, requests). A virtualenv isolates each project's libraries. Always activate .venv before working on a project. The next step is SSH and connecting to a server.

docs.title: 07. SSH and Connecting to a Server
Why this matters
docs.text:
The server sits in a data center thousands of kilometers away. To work on it, you need SSH (Secure Shell). It is a protocol that lets you securely connect to a remote server and control it through the terminal, as if you were sitting right next to it.

SSH is the main tool of DevOps engineers and backend developers. Without it you can't deploy, read logs, or configure a service.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
SSH is like a secure tunnel between your laptop and the server. Everything you type is encrypted and sent to the server. The response comes back encrypted.

Connecting over SSH looks like this: you open a terminal on your laptop, type one command — and you get a terminal on the server. As if you "jumped" over there.

docs.title: Basic connection
docs.text:
ssh user@server_ip

Where: - ssh — the program used to connect - user — the username on the server - server_ip — the server's IP address or domain

Examples: 

ssh student@192.168.1.10
ssh deploy@mysite.com
ssh ubuntu@ec2-54-123-45.compute.amazonaws.com

docs.title: First login — the fingerprint
docs.text:
On the first connection, SSH will ask: 

The authenticity of host '192.168.1.10' can't be established.
ECDSA key fingerprint is SHA256:abc123...
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?

Enter yes. The server will be recorded in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. On later connections there will be no check.

If the fingerprint has changed and you get the warning "WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED", it may mean an attack or that the server was recreated. Find out the reason before connecting.

docs.title: Why keys are better than a password
docs.text:
• A password can be brute-forced
  • A key is mathematically hard to crack
  • With a key you don't need to type a password every time
  • You can block a specific key without changing the password

docs.title: How SSH keys work
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Laptop as Your computer
    participant Server as Linux server

    Note over Laptop: You have a key pair:<br/>~/.ssh/id_rsa (private)<br/>~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub (public)
    Note over Server: The public key is stored<br/>in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

    Laptop->>Server: I want to connect (SSH request)
    Server->>Laptop: Sends a random challenge
    Laptop->>Laptop: Signs the challenge with the private key
    Laptop->>Server: Sends the signed challenge
    Server->>Server: Verifies the signature with the public key
    Server-->>Laptop: Access granted

SSH keys work as a pair: the private key stays on your computer, and the public key is placed on the server. The server recognizes you not by a password, but by the fact that you have the right private key.

The golden rule: the private key (id_rsa) — never give it to anyone. The public key (id_rsa.pub) — you can put it anywhere.

docs.title: Generating keys
docs.text:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Prompts: 

Enter file in which to save the key (/home/student/.ssh/id_ed25519): [Enter]
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase): [your passphrase or Enter]

After that, two files will appear: 

~/.ssh/id_ed25519        # private key — NEVER SHOW IT TO ANYONE
~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub    # public key — can be shared


cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub   # view the public key

docs.title: Copying the public key to the server
docs.text:
ssh-copy-id user@server_ip

Or manually: 

# View the public key
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# On the server — add it to authorized_keys
echo "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... your@email" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 700 ~/.ssh/

docs.title: SSH file permissions (important!)
docs.text:
chmod 700 ~/.ssh/
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519          # private key
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub      # public key
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

SSH will refuse to connect if the permissions on the key are too open.

docs.title: scp — a simple copy
docs.text:
# Copy a file to the server
scp file.txt user@server:/home/user/

# Copy a file from the server
scp user@server:/home/user/file.txt ./

# Copy a directory
scp -r ./myproject/ user@server:/home/user/

docs.title: rsync — smart synchronization
docs.text:
rsync -av ./project/ user@server:/home/user/project/

-a — preserve permissions and attributes, -v — verbose (show what is being synced).

rsync copies only the changed files — faster than scp for repeated syncs.

docs.title: SSH Config — so you don't have to type long commands
docs.text:
Instead of: 

ssh -i ~/.ssh/my_key deploy@192.168.1.50 -p 2222

Add to ~/.ssh/config: 

Host myserver
    HostName 192.168.1.50
    User deploy
    Port 2222
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/my_key

Now you can do: 

ssh myserver
scp file.txt myserver:/home/deploy/

docs.title: Safe practices
docs.text:
• Disable password login after setting up keys (PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config)
  • Don't run SSH on port 22 on public servers (use a non-standard port)
  • Use ed25519 instead of rsa — it's more modern and more secure
  • Never put a private key in Git or send it by email
  • Add a passphrase to the key for extra protection

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Permission denied (publickey)

Check: has the public key been copied to the server? Are the permissions on ~/.ssh/ correct?

Mistake 2: Sent the private key instead of the public one

id_rsa is private. id_rsa.pub is public (with .pub). Always send only the .pub file.

Mistake 3: WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED

Remove the line with the server's old key: ssh-keygen -R server_ip

Mistake 4: ssh: connect to host ... port 22: Connection refused

SSH isn't running or uses a different port. Check: sudo systemctl status ssh

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
ls -la ~/.ssh/
If the directory doesn't exist, it is created automatically when you generate a key.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "test_key"
ls -la ~/.ssh/
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
What is inside the public key?

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
If you have access to a server or can use localhost: 

ssh-copy-id student@localhost
ssh student@localhost
Try connecting with the key.

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text: Add an entry to ~/.ssh/config for an imaginary server and explain what each line means.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I can connect to a server with ssh user@ip
  • [ ] I understand the difference between a private and a public key
  • [ ] I can generate an SSH key with ssh-keygen
  • [ ] I know how to copy the public key to a server
  • [ ] I can copy files with scp and rsync
  • [ ] I understand why the private key must never be given to anyone

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: SSH is an encrypted tunnel for working with a remote server. A key pair (private + public) replaces the password and is more secure. The public key goes on the server. The private key stays only with you. The next step is environment variables and secrets.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A Django project contains things that must not be stored in code: database passwords, SECRET_KEY, API keys, tokens. If they end up in Git, the whole world (or attackers) will see them.

Environment variables are a way to pass confidential data to a program without writing it into the code.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
Imagine your Django project is a cake recipe. The code is the recipe (you can share it). The database passwords and SECRET_KEY are the secret ingredient that you don't write in the recipe but pass on separately, by word of mouth.

Environment variables are the "word of mouth" part. They live in the operating system or in a .env file, but not in the code.

docs.title: What an environment variable is
docs.text:
An environment variable is a KEY=value pair that exists in a process's runtime environment.

echo $HOME          # /home/student
echo $USER          # student
echo $PATH          # /usr/bin:/usr/local/bin:...
printenv            # all environment variables

PATH is one of the most important variables. Linux looks for programs in the directories listed in PATH. That's why you can type python instead of /usr/bin/python3.

docs.title: Set a variable in the current session
docs.text:
export DEBUG=True
export DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost/mydb

docs.title: View the value
docs.text:
echo $DEBUG
echo $DATABASE_URL
printenv DEBUG

docs.title: Remove a variable
docs.text:
unset DEBUG

A variable set with export exists only in the current terminal session. Once the terminal is closed, it's gone.

docs.title: The .env file
docs.text:
So you don't have to type the variables by hand every time, they are stored in a .env file:

DEBUG=True
SECRET_KEY=your-very-secret-key-change-me-in-production
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app_user:app_password@localhost:5432/app_db
ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1
EMAIL_HOST=smtp.gmail.com
EMAIL_HOST_USER=yourmail@gmail.com
EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD=your_app_password
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0

.env is just a text file. The format: KEY=value, one per line. No spaces around =.

docs.title: .env and .gitignore
docs.text:
.env is always added to .gitignore:

# .gitignore
.env
.env.local
.env.production
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

Instead of .env, Git stores .env.example — a template without real values:

# .env.example
DEBUG=True
SECRET_KEY=change-me
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/dbname
ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost

docs.title: The python-decouple package
docs.text:
pip install python-decouple dj-database-url

# settings.py
import dj_database_url
from decouple import config

SECRET_KEY = config('SECRET_KEY')
DEBUG = config('DEBUG', default=False, cast=bool)
DATABASE_URL = config('DATABASE_URL')
# decouple only reads the string — DATABASES must be built from it separately:
DATABASES = {'default': dj_database_url.parse(DATABASE_URL)}
ALLOWED_HOSTS = config('ALLOWED_HOSTS', default='localhost').split(',')

docs.title: The django-environ package
docs.text:
pip install django-environ

# settings.py
import environ

env = environ.Env(
    DEBUG=(bool, False)
)
environ.Env.read_env('.env')

SECRET_KEY = env('SECRET_KEY')
DEBUG = env('DEBUG')
DATABASES = {'default': env.db()}

docs.title: Or os.environ directly
docs.text:
import os

SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY', 'fallback-only-for-dev')
DEBUG = os.environ.get('DEBUG', 'False') == 'True'

docs.title: Passing variables through systemd
docs.text:
If Django runs as a systemd service, variables are passed via EnvironmentFile:

# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My Django App
After=network.target

[Service]
User=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/var/www/myapp/.env
ExecStart=/var/www/myapp/.venv/bin/gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

In this case the .env file is read by systemd, not by bash: 

sudo chmod 600 /var/www/myapp/.env
sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/www/myapp/.env

docs.title: Passing variables to Docker
docs.text:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    env_file:
      - .env
    environment:
      - DEBUG=False

or via a separate file: 

docker run --env-file .env django-app

docs.title: Security rules
docs.text:
✓ Keep all secrets in .env
✓ Add .env to .gitignore BEFORE the first commit
✓ Keep .env.example in Git (without real values)
✓ Permissions on .env — 600 (only the owner can read)
✓ In production: different values than in dev

✗ Don't store SECRET_KEY or passwords in settings.py
✗ Don't commit .env to Git
✗ Don't send .env by email or Slack
✗ Don't use the same SECRET_KEY in dev and production

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Committed .env with real passwords

Change all passwords and keys immediately. Remove it from the Git history: git filter-branch or git-filter-repo. Assume they are compromised.

Mistake 2: KeyError: 'SECRET_KEY' when starting Django

The variable isn't set. Check: does the .env file exist? Is it being read correctly?

Mistake 3: The same DEBUG=True value on dev and on production

In production, always DEBUG=False. If DEBUG=True in production, Django shows stack traces to every user.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
export MY_NAME="Linux Student"
echo "Hello, $MY_NAME!"
printenv MY_NAME

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Create a Django project and move SECRET_KEY into .env: 

django-admin startproject config .
pip install python-decouple
In settings.py, replace SECRET_KEY = '...' with reading it from .env.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Make sure .gitignore contains .env. Run git status and check that .env doesn't appear in the list of files to commit.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I understand what an environment variable is and why it's needed
  • [ ] I can set a variable with export and read it with echo $VAR
  • [ ] I know the format of a .env file
  • [ ] I understand why .env must not be committed to Git
  • [ ] I can read variables in Django with python-decouple or os.environ

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Environment variables are a way to keep secrets separate from code. Django reads SECRET_KEY, database passwords, and email settings from .env or from environment variables. .env always goes in .gitignore. The next step is Bash scripts for automation.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Imagine typing 15 commands by hand every time you deploy: git pull, source .venv/bin/activate, pip install -r requirements.txt, python manage.py migrate, python manage.py collectstatic, sudo systemctl restart myapp... It is slow, and sooner or later you will skip something or make a typo.

A Bash script is a file that contains all of these commands in order. You run a single file, and it does everything for you.

docs.title: Simple explanation
docs.text: A Bash script is a list of commands written to a file. Instead of typing them by hand one after another, you run a single file and it does everything for you.

docs.title: Shebang: the first line of a script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

The first line of a script always starts with #! (the shebang). It specifies which program should execute the file.

/usr/bin/env bash means "find bash via env" (a more reliable option than #!/bin/bash, because bash may live in different locations).

docs.title: Your first script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

echo "Starting Django project setup..."

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

echo "Done!"

Save it to a file named setup.sh, make it executable, and run it:

chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

PROJECT_DIR="/var/www/myapp"
VENV_DIR="$PROJECT_DIR/.venv"
APP_USER="www-data"

echo "Project: $PROJECT_DIR"
echo "Virtualenv: $VENV_DIR"

Rules for variables in Bash: - No spaces: NAME="value" ✓, NAME = "value" ✗ - Read them with $: $NAME or ${NAME} - Quotes matter: "$NAME" preserves spaces

docs.title: Conditions (if/else)
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

if [ -f ".env" ]; then
    echo ".env file found"
else
    echo "ERROR: .env file is missing"
    exit 1
fi

Useful checks:

Condition What it checks [ -f file ] the file exists [ -d dir ] the directory exists [ -z "$VAR" ] the variable is empty [ "$A" = "$B" ] the strings are equal [ $N -gt 0 ] the number is greater than 0

docs.title: Exit codes in scripts
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Stop at the first error
set -e

git pull origin main
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python manage.py migrate

echo "Deployment successful!"

set -e is a very useful option: if any command returns a non-zero exit code, the script stops. Without it, the script keeps running even after an error.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Run a command for each argument
for app in users notes tags; do
    echo "Running migrations for $app..."
    python manage.py migrate $app
done

# Iterate over files
for file in *.py; do
    echo "File: $file"
done

docs.title: Command-line arguments
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

ENVIRONMENT=${1:-development}   # $1 is the first argument, development by default

echo "Deploying to environment: $ENVIRONMENT"

if [ "$ENVIRONMENT" = "production" ]; then
    echo "Warning: deploying to production!"
fi

Running it: 

./deploy.sh production
./deploy.sh            # will use development

docs.title: A real deployment script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

echo "=== Deploying the Django project ==="

# Variables
APP_DIR="/var/www/myapp"
VENV="$APP_DIR/.venv"
SERVICE_NAME="myapp"

# Update the code
cd "$APP_DIR"
git pull origin main

# Update dependencies
source "$VENV/bin/activate"
pip install -r requirements.txt --quiet

# Apply migrations
python manage.py migrate --noinput

# Collect static files
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Restart the service
sudo systemctl restart "$SERVICE_NAME"

echo "=== Deployment finished! ==="
echo "Service status:"
systemctl status "$SERVICE_NAME" --no-pager

docs.title: Debugging a script
docs.text:
bash -x script.sh         # run with tracing (shows every command)
set -x                    # turn on tracing inside the script
set +x                    # turn off tracing

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Permission denied when running the script

You forgot chmod +x script.sh

Mistake 2: ./script.sh: line 1: $'\r': command not found

The file was saved in Windows format (CRLF). Fix it with: sed -i 's/\r//' script.sh

Mistake 3: The script keeps going after an error and breaks the server

Add set -e at the start of the script

Mistake 4: Spaces around = in variables

NAME="value" ✓, NAME = "value" ✗ — Bash will treat NAME as a command

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text: Write setup.sh for a Django project that: 1. Checks that .env exists 2. Creates a virtualenv (if it does not exist) 3. Installs dependencies 4. Runs migrations

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text: Write deploy.sh that: 1. Runs git pull 2. Runs pip install -r requirements.txt 3. Runs python manage.py migrate 4. Runs python manage.py collectstatic --noinput 5. Checks the exit code of each step

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
bash -x setup.sh 2>&1 | head -30
Run the script with tracing and analyze the output.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I understand what a shebang is and why it is needed
  • [ ] I can write a script with variables, conditions, and loops
  • [ ] I know that set -e stops the script on an error
  • [ ] I know how to make a script executable with chmod +x
  • [ ] I can write a simple deployment script for Django

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: A Bash script is a set of commands in a file. The shebang specifies the interpreter. set -e stops the script on an error. Real deployment starts with writing a script that automates all the manual steps. The next step is the Makefile, another way to organize commands.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Every Python/Django project has commands you run all the time: pip install -r requirements.txt, python manage.py migrate, python manage.py runserver, pytest, ruff check ....

A Makefile is a "button panel" for your project. Instead of long commands, you get short aliases. Instead of remembering gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application --workers 4 --bind 0.0.0.0:8000, you just type make run.

docs.title: Simple explanation
docs.text:
A Makefile is like a restaurant menu. You do not write out the recipe every time; you just say "I want pizza" and the kitchen knows what to do.

Instead of: 

python -m pytest --cov=. --cov-report=term-missing -v

You write: 

make test

docs.title: Makefile structure
docs.text:
target: dependencies
    recipe
  • target is the command name (what you type after make)
  • dependencies are what must run first (optional)
  • recipe is the commands to execute

Important: the indentation before a recipe is a Tab, not spaces. Make will not accept spaces.

docs.title: A basic Makefile for a Django project
docs.text:
.PHONY: install migrate makemigrations run shell test pytest lint format collectstatic superuser clean setup

install:
    pip install -r requirements.txt

migrate:
    python manage.py migrate

makemigrations:
    python manage.py makemigrations

run:
    python manage.py runserver

shell:
    python manage.py shell

test:
    python manage.py test

pytest:
    pytest --tb=short

lint:
    ruff check .

format:
    ruff format .

collectstatic:
    python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

superuser:
    python manage.py createsuperuser

clean:
    find . -name "*.pyc" -delete
    find . -name "__pycache__" -type d -exec rm -rf {} +

setup: install migrate collectstatic
    @echo "Project is set up!"

docs.title: .PHONY: an important detail
docs.text:
.PHONY: install migrate run test

Make was originally a tool for building files (C/C++). It checks whether a file with the target's name exists. If there is a file called install, Make will say "nothing to be done".

.PHONY tells Make: "these targets are not files; always run them".

docs.title: Dependencies between targets
docs.text:
.PHONY: setup install migrate collectstatic

install:
    pip install -r requirements.txt

migrate: install
    python manage.py migrate

collectstatic:
    python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

setup: install migrate collectstatic
    @echo "=== Project is ready! ==="

make setup

This runs: install → migrate → collectstatic → the message.

@echo: the @ suppresses printing the command itself and shows only the result.

docs.title: Passing variables
docs.text:
PORT ?= 8000
WORKERS ?= 4

run:
    python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:$(PORT)

gunicorn:
    gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application --workers $(WORKERS) --bind 0.0.0.0:$(PORT)

make run                   # PORT=8000 by default
make run PORT=9000         # a different port
make gunicorn WORKERS=8    # more workers

docs.title: Makefile with Docker
docs.text:
.PHONY: build up down logs shell-web migrate collectstatic restart

build:
    docker compose build

up:
    docker compose up -d

down:
    docker compose down

logs:
    docker compose logs -f

shell-web:
    docker compose exec web bash

migrate:
    docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate

collectstatic:
    docker compose exec web python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

restart:
    docker compose restart web

Now deployment comes down to: 

make build
make up
make migrate

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Dev["Developer"] --> MakeRun["make run"]
    Dev --> MakeTest["make test"]
    Dev --> MakeLint["make lint"]
    Dev --> MakeDeploy["make deploy"]

    MakeRun --> CMD1["python manage.py runserver"]
    MakeTest --> CMD2["pytest --tb=short"]
    MakeLint --> CMD3["ruff check ."]
    MakeDeploy --> CMD4["git pull"]
    CMD4 --> CMD5["pip install -r requirements.txt"]
    CMD5 --> CMD6["python manage.py migrate"]
    CMD6 --> CMD7["systemctl restart myapp"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class Dev,CMD1,CMD2,CMD3,CMD4,CMD5,CMD6,CMD7 step;
    class MakeRun,MakeTest,MakeLint,MakeDeploy success;

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Makefile:3: *** missing separator. Stop.

You used spaces instead of a Tab. Check your editor and configure it to use Tabs instead of spaces for Makefiles.

Mistake 2: make: 'install' is up to date.

You forgot .PHONY. There is a file named install.

Mistake 3: The command runs, but nothing is shown

You used @ where it is not needed, or the other way around. @ hides the command, but not its output.

docs.text:
• [ ] I understand the structure of a Makefile: target, dependencies, recipe
  • [ ] I know the indentation is a Tab, not spaces
  • [ ] I understand why .PHONY is needed
  • [ ] I can write a Makefile for a Django project with the main commands
  • [ ] I know how to pass variables to make: make run PORT=9000

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: A Makefile is a "button panel" for your project. Instead of long commands, you get short aliases. Use .PHONY for targets that are not files. Tabs, not spaces. The next step is deploying Django to a real Linux server.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deployment means running the application stack on a server with production settings. Notes Chat App is deployed with Docker Compose using Uvicorn (ASGI) + Nginx + PostgreSQL + Redis + Celery.

This section is part of Part X. Linux, DevOps and Deployment.

docs.text:
# Check before deploying:
docker compose exec web python manage.py check --deploy
Parameter Dev Production DEBUG True False SECRET_KEY in settings.py from env, at least 50 characters DATABASE_URL PG from docker compose (required, SQLite is not supported) PG from env, missing → Exception ALLOWED_HOSTS ['*'] specific domains Static files Django dev server Nginx /static/ → volume SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE False True (HTTPS) CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE False True DebugExceptionMiddleware active only if DEBUG: Logs console file / Sentry

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
You've written a Django project. It runs on your laptop. Now you need real users to be able to see it — over the internet, 24/7. That is what deployment is.

This file is a step-by-step guide: from git clone to a working website.

docs.title: What deployment is
docs.text:
Deployment is the process of moving code from your local development environment to a server where it will be available to users.

flowchart TD
    Local["Local Django project<br>(laptop, DEBUG=True)"] --> Git["Push to Git<br>(GitHub/GitLab)"]
    Git --> Server["Pull on Linux server<br>(Ubuntu)"]
    Server --> Venv["Create a virtualenv<br>Install dependencies"]
    Venv --> Env["Configure .env<br>(DEBUG=False, DB credentials)"]
    Env --> Migrate["python manage.py migrate"]
    Migrate --> Static["python manage.py collectstatic"]
    Static --> AppServer["Start Gunicorn/Uvicorn"]
    AppServer --> Nginx["Nginx accepts requests<br>and proxies them to the app server"]
    Nginx --> Users["Users"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class Local,Git,Server,Venv,Migrate,Static,AppServer,Nginx step;
    class Users success;
    class Env warning;

docs.title: Preparing the server
docs.text:
# Connect to the server
ssh ubuntu@your_server_ip

# Update the system
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install the required packages
sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip git nginx -y

# Install PostgreSQL (if you use it)
sudo apt install postgresql postgresql-contrib -y

docs.title: Setting up PostgreSQL on the server
docs.text:
sudo -u postgres psql

-- Inside psql:
CREATE DATABASE myapp_db;
CREATE USER myapp_user WITH PASSWORD 'strong_password_here';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE myapp_db TO myapp_user;
\q

docs.title: Cloning and configuring the project
docs.text:
# Go to the directory for web projects
cd /var/www/

# Clone the repository
sudo git clone https://github.com/you/myproject.git myapp
sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /var/www/myapp
cd /var/www/myapp

# Create a virtualenv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Install Gunicorn (if it is not in requirements.txt)
pip install gunicorn

docs.title: The .env file on the server
docs.text:
nano /var/www/myapp/.env

DEBUG=False
SECRET_KEY=your-production-secret-key-very-long-and-random
DATABASE_URL=postgres://myapp_user:strong_password_here@localhost:5432/myapp_db
ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-domain.com,www.your-domain.com,your_server_ip
STATIC_ROOT=/var/www/myapp/staticfiles
MEDIA_ROOT=/var/www/myapp/media

chmod 600 /var/www/myapp/.env

DEBUG=False in production is mandatory. Otherwise Django shows stack traces with database data.

docs.title: Migrations and static files
docs.text:
source /var/www/myapp/.venv/bin/activate
cd /var/www/myapp

python manage.py migrate
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
python manage.py createsuperuser   # if you need an admin

collectstatic gathers all static files (CSS, JS, images) into a single STATIC_ROOT directory. Nginx serves them directly from there, without touching Django.

docs.title: Checking that Django starts
docs.text:
# Test — start it and see whether there are errors
python manage.py check --deploy

# Start Gunicorn manually (to check)
gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000

If you open http://your_server_ip:8000 in a browser, the site should open (without CSS, because Nginx is not configured yet).

Stop Gunicorn: Ctrl+C

docs.title: A systemd service for Django
docs.text:
Create the service file:

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service

[Unit]
Description=Django Application - myapp
After=network.target

[Service]
User=www-data
Group=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/var/www/myapp/.env
ExecStart=/var/www/myapp/.venv/bin/gunicorn \
    myapp.wsgi:application \
    --workers 3 \
    --bind unix:/run/myapp.sock \
    --log-file /var/log/myapp/gunicorn.log \
    --access-logfile /var/log/myapp/access.log
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# Create a directory for logs
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/myapp
sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/log/myapp

# Give www-data ownership of the project
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/myapp

# Start it and enable autostart
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start myapp
sudo systemctl enable myapp
sudo systemctl status myapp

--bind unix:/run/myapp.sock — Gunicorn listens on a Unix socket instead of a TCP port. This is faster and safer for local communication with Nginx.

docs.title: Nginx configuration
docs.text:
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name your-domain.com www.your-domain.com;

    location /static/ {
        alias /var/www/myapp/staticfiles/;
    }

    location /media/ {
        alias /var/www/myapp/media/;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://unix:/run/myapp.sock;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
}

# Activate the config
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t              # check the syntax
sudo systemctl restart nginx

docs.text: runserver Gunicorn Single-threaded Several workers (parallel requests) Designed for debugging Optimized for production Does not support Unix sockets Supports them Slow Fast No SSL Nginx adds SSL

Mistake 2: CSS/JS do not load

Mistake 3: 502 Bad Gateway

Mistake 4: Database errors
