docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Deploying Django means: clone the code, configure .env, create a virtualenv, install dependencies, run migrations and collectstatic, start Gunicorn via systemd, and configure Nginx. Next, we will look at Nginx and Gunicorn in more detail.

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
Django on its own is just a Python application. For it to handle thousands of requests in parallel, serve static files quickly, and communicate over HTTPS, you need a combination: Nginx + Gunicorn/Uvicorn.

Understanding this architecture means understanding how your site actually runs on a server.

docs.title: The overall picture
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant Nginx as Nginx
    participant App as Gunicorn/Uvicorn
    participant Django as Django App
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    Browser->>Nginx: HTTPS request (port 443)
    Nginx->>Nginx: SSL termination
    Note over Nginx: /static/ → files on disk
    Nginx->>App: Proxy pass (Unix socket)
    App->>Django: Calls the WSGI/ASGI application
    Django->>DB: SQL query
    DB-->>Django: Data
    Django-->>App: HTTP Response
    App-->>Nginx: Response
    Nginx-->>Browser: HTML/JSON (HTTPS)

docs.title: Nginx
docs.text: Nginx is like a doorman at the entrance to a building. It greets every visitor, checks their requests, hands out simple things (static files) right away, and passes complex tasks further inside (to Django).

docs.title: What Nginx does:
docs.text:
1. Accepts HTTP/HTTPS requests on ports 80 and 443
  2. SSL termination — decrypts HTTPS and passes it on internally as HTTP
  3. Serves static files (/static/, /media/) directly from disk — without Django
  4. Reverse proxy — forwards dynamic requests to Gunicorn/Uvicorn
  5. Load balancing — can distribute requests across several app servers
  6. Rate limiting — basic-level DDoS protection

docs.title: Minimal Nginx configuration
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.com www.example.com;

    # Django static files
    location /static/ {
        alias /var/www/myapp/staticfiles/;
        expires 30d;                          # cache for 30 days
        add_header Cache-Control "public";
    }

    # Media files (uploaded by users)
    location /media/ {
        alias /var/www/myapp/media/;
    }

    # Everything else goes to Django through Gunicorn
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://unix:/run/myapp.sock;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

docs.title: Checking and restarting
docs.text:
sudo nginx -t                      # check the config syntax
sudo systemctl reload nginx        # re-read the config without stopping
sudo systemctl restart nginx       # full restart

docs.title: Gunicorn
docs.text:
Gunicorn is like a team of waiters. Nginx (the doorman) passes on the orders, and Gunicorn runs several "waiters" (workers), each of which can handle its own request at the same time.

Gunicorn (Green Unicorn) is a Python WSGI HTTP Server. It implements the WSGI protocol to run Django.

docs.title: Running Gunicorn
docs.text:
gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application \
    --workers 3 \
    --bind unix:/run/myapp.sock \
    --log-level info \
    --access-logfile /var/log/myapp/access.log \
    --error-logfile /var/log/myapp/error.log

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter What it means myapp.wsgi:application Path to Django's WSGI object --workers 3 Number of parallel processes --bind unix:/run/myapp.sock Listen on a Unix socket --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 Or on a TCP port --timeout 30 Request timeout in seconds

docs.title: How many workers?
docs.text:
The general rule: workers = 2 * CPU_cores + 1

nproc           # number of CPU cores

On a server with 2 CPUs: 5 workers. Too many workers = too little RAM for each one.

docs.title: Uvicorn
docs.text:
Uvicorn is an ASGI server. It is used instead of Gunicorn when a Django project uses async views, WebSocket, or Django Channels.

pip install uvicorn

uvicorn myapp.asgi:application \
    --workers 4 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
    --log-level info

docs.title: Gunicorn + Uvicorn workers
docs.text:
A popular combination: Gunicorn as the process manager + Uvicorn as the ASGI worker:

gunicorn myapp.asgi:application \
    -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker \
    --workers 4 \
    --bind unix:/run/myapp.sock

docs.title: WSGI vs ASGI
docs.text: WSGI ASGI What it is Web Server Gateway Interface Async Server Gateway Interface Synchronous/async Synchronous Supports async Django myapp.wsgi:application myapp.asgi:application Server Gunicorn Uvicorn, Daphne When to use Standard Django without async Django async views, WebSocket, Channels

docs.title: Why Nginx serves static files, not Django
docs.text:
Django can serve static files with DEBUG=True during development. In production this is a disaster:

  • Django loads the file into Python memory and sends it byte by byte
  • Nginx reads the file from disk and sends it at the OS level — 10–100 times faster
  • Every static file request through Django occupies a worker, which is then unavailable for real requests

That is why collectstatic + Nginx for /static/ is mandatory practice.

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: 502 Bad Gateway

Gunicorn is not running or the socket is not accessible. systemctl status myapp

Mistake 2: CSS does not load (404 for /static/)

collectstatic was not run, or the path in the Nginx alias is wrong

Mistake 3: Gunicorn started, but Nginx does not see the socket

Check the socket path. The Nginx worker and Gunicorn must have permissions on the /run/ directory

Mistake 4: ModuleNotFoundError in Gunicorn

The virtualenv is not activated. Use the full path: /var/www/myapp/.venv/bin/gunicorn

docs.text: Draw the diagram by hand: browser → Nginx → Gunicorn → Django → PostgreSQL. Explain what each component does.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3 --log-level debug
Run it and look at the output. How many worker processes started?

docs.text:
• [ ] I can explain the difference between Nginx and Gunicorn
  • [ ] I understand what a reverse proxy is
  • [ ] I know why Nginx serves static files rather than Django
  • [ ] I understand the difference between WSGI and ASGI
  • [ ] I can write a minimal Nginx config for Django

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Nginx is the doorman: it accepts requests, serves static files, and proxies to Gunicorn. Gunicorn is the team of workers: it handles requests in parallel and runs Django. Uvicorn is for async Django. Together they provide production-ready operation of the site.

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
The site is down. What do you do? Without logs you are blind — you don't know where the error happened, at what time, or why. With logs, you have answers.

Being able to read logs and look for a problem systematically is one of the most important skills in working with a server.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text: Logs are an event journal. Every time someone opens a page, an error occurs, or a service stops, it is written to the log. Later you can read this journal and understand what happened.

docs.title: Where to look for logs
docs.text: Logs Where they are System logs journalctl or /var/log/syslog Nginx access log /var/log/nginx/access.log Nginx error log /var/log/nginx/error.log Your Django service journalctl -u myapp or /var/log/myapp/ PostgreSQL /var/log/postgresql/ Django debug The terminal where Gunicorn is running

docs.title: tail — the last lines
docs.text:
tail /var/log/nginx/error.log           # last 10 lines
tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log     # last 50 lines
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log       # follow in real time

-f (follow) is the most useful option. The terminal updates and shows new lines as they appear. Open a second terminal and make requests to the site — you will see them in the logs in real time.

docs.title: journalctl — systemd logs
docs.text:
journalctl -u myapp                     # all logs of the service
journalctl -u myapp -f                  # follow in real time
journalctl -u myapp -n 100             # last 100 lines
journalctl -u myapp --since today       # for today
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -u nginx -p err             # errors only

docs.title: grep — filtering logs
docs.text:
grep "ERROR" /var/log/nginx/error.log
grep "500" /var/log/nginx/access.log
grep -i "traceback" /var/log/myapp/gunicorn.log
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log | grep "POST"

docs.title: Nginx access log
docs.text:
192.168.1.1 - - [10/Jun/2026:12:34:56 +0000] "GET /api/notes/ HTTP/1.1" 200 1234 "-" "Mozilla/5.0..."
Part What it means 192.168.1.1 Client IP 10/Jun/2026:12:34:56 Date and time GET /api/notes/ HTTP method and URL 200 HTTP status code 1234 Response size in bytes

docs.title: HTTP status codes
docs.text: Code What it means 200 OK 301/302 Redirect 400 Bad Request (client error) 403 Forbidden (no permission) 404 Not Found 500 Internal Server Error (Django error) 502 Bad Gateway (Gunicorn unavailable) 503 Service Unavailable

docs.title: Django stack trace
docs.text:
[2026-06-10 12:34:56 +0000] [1234] [ERROR] Exception in application

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/var/www/myapp/.venv/lib/.../django/db/models/sql/compiler.py", line 456
    return super().execute_sql(result_type)
  File "..."
    ...
django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to server: Connection refused

Read from the bottom up: the last error is OperationalError: could not connect to server. Django cannot connect to PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Checklist: "the site won't open"
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Problem["The site won't open"] --> SSH{"Is the server reachable<br>over SSH?"}
    SSH -->|no| FixSSH["Server or network problem<br>— contact your hosting provider"]
    SSH -->|yes| Nginx{Is Nginx running?}
    Nginx -->|no| StartNginx["sudo systemctl start nginx"]
    Nginx -->|yes| Gunicorn{Is Gunicorn running?}
    Gunicorn -->|no| StartGunicorn["sudo systemctl start myapp"]
    Gunicorn -->|yes| Logs["Check the logs: journalctl -u myapp -n 50"]
    Logs --> DB{Database error?}
    DB -->|yes| FixDB["Check DATABASE_URL and the PostgreSQL status"]
    DB -->|no| Static{404 for static files?}
    Static -->|yes| FixStatic["collectstatic + check the Nginx alias"]
    Static -->|no| Config["Check ALLOWED_HOSTS and .env"]

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    class Logs step;
    class SSH,Nginx,Gunicorn,DB,Static decision;
    class StartNginx,StartGunicorn,FixDB,FixStatic,Config success;
    class Problem,FixSSH error;

docs.title: The full checklist in text form
docs.text:
## If the site won't open

- [ ] Is the server reachable over SSH?
- [ ] Is Nginx running? → `systemctl status nginx`
- [ ] Is the Nginx config valid? → `nginx -t`
- [ ] Is the Gunicorn/Django service running? → `systemctl status myapp`
- [ ] Are there errors in the Nginx logs? → `journalctl -u nginx -n 50`
- [ ] Are there errors in the Django logs? → `journalctl -u myapp -n 50`
- [ ] Is PostgreSQL running? → `systemctl status postgresql`
- [ ] Have the migrations been applied? → `python manage.py migrate`
- [ ] Has collectstatic been run?
- [ ] Is .env configured? (`DEBUG=False`, `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `DATABASE_URL`)
- [ ] Are the ports open? → `ss -tulpn | grep -E ':80|:443|:8000'`
- [ ] Is the firewall not blocking? → `sudo ufw status`

docs.title: Logging in Django
docs.text:
# settings.py
LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'disable_existing_loggers': False,
    'handlers': {
        'file': {
            'level': 'ERROR',
            'class': 'logging.FileHandler',
            'filename': '/var/log/myapp/django.log',
        },
    },
    'loggers': {
        'django': {
            'handlers': ['file'],
            'level': 'ERROR',
            'propagate': True,
        },
    },
}

# In your own code
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def create_note(request):
    logger.info(f"User {request.user} creates a note")
    try:
        # ...
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to create note: {e}", exc_info=True)

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Looking for the error "at random" without reading the logs

Always start with the logs. 90% of problems are visible right away.

Mistake 2: Reading logs from the top

The latest events are at the bottom. Read tail -n 50, not the whole file.

Mistake 3: journalctl shows nothing

Check the service name: systemctl list-units --type=service | grep myapp

docs.text:
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log &
curl http://localhost/
Explain what appeared in the logs after the request.

docs.text:

  • [ ] I can use tail -f to follow logs in real time
  • [ ] I can read a stack trace and find the cause of an error
  • [ ] I understand the meaning of HTTP status codes (200, 404, 500, 502)
  • [ ] I know the systematic checklist for diagnosing "the site won't open"

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Logs are the first place to look when there are problems. tail -f for real time, journalctl -u for systemd services, grep for filtering. A systematic checklist helps you find the problem quickly. The next step is Docker.

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
"It works on my laptop" is a classic phrase that destroys a team's productivity. The laptop has Python 3.11, the server has 3.9. The laptop has PostgreSQL 15, CI has 13. The result: bugs that are impossible to reproduce.

Docker solves this problem: the whole project, together with its dependencies, is packaged into a container that works the same way everywhere.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
A Docker image is like a recipe plus a box with everything needed to run the application. A container is an already running instance of that box. You can start 10 containers from one image — and they will all be identical.

Without Docker: 

Developer laptop:      Python 3.11, Django 4.2, PostgreSQL 15
CI server:             Python 3.9,  Django 4.2, PostgreSQL 13
Production server:     Python 3.10, Django 4.1, PostgreSQL 14
Different environments → unexpected bugs.

With Docker: 

Laptop / CI / Production: one and the same image → identical behavior

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Image A template (frozen snapshot) of a file system + metadata Container A running instance of an image (a process with an isolated environment) Dockerfile Instructions for building an image Registry A store of images (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry) Volume Persistent data storage outside the container Port mapping Binding a container port to a host port

docs.title: Container vs Virtual Machine
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph VM ["Virtual Machine"]
        HW1["Hardware"] --> Hypervisor["Hypervisor<br>(VMware/VirtualBox)"]
        Hypervisor --> GuestOS1["Guest OS 1<br>(a whole kernel)"]
        Hypervisor --> GuestOS2["Guest OS 2<br>(a whole kernel)"]
        GuestOS1 --> App1["App"]
        GuestOS2 --> App2["App"]
    end

    subgraph Docker ["Docker"]
        HW2["Hardware"] --> HostOS["Host OS + Linux Kernel"]
        HostOS --> DockerEngine["Docker Engine"]
        DockerEngine --> C1["Container 1<br>(a process)"]
        DockerEngine --> C2["Container 2<br>(a process)"]
        C1 --> App3["App"]
        C2 --> App4["App"]
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class HW1,App1,App2,HW2,HostOS,DockerEngine,App3,App4 step;
    class C1,C2 success;
    class Hypervisor,GuestOS1,GuestOS2 warning;
VM Docker Container Isolation A full OS A process in an isolated namespace Size Gigabytes Megabytes Startup Minutes Seconds Resources Heavy Light

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions for building an image.

# Base image
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy requirements first (Docker cache)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Then copy all the code
COPY . .

# Environment variables
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# The port it will listen on
EXPOSE 8000

# Startup command
CMD ["gunicorn", "myapp.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

docs.title: Why COPY requirements.txt first?
docs.text: Docker caches every layer. If requirements.txt has not changed, Docker does not reinstall the dependencies but takes them from the cache. This speeds up the build when the code changes.

docs.title: Building an image
docs.text:
docker build -t myapp:latest .
docker build -t myapp:v1.2.3 .

-t — the image name and tag. . — the directory containing the Dockerfile.

docs.title: Running a container
docs.text:
docker run myapp:latest
docker run -p 8000:8000 myapp:latest
docker run -p 8000:8000 -d myapp:latest        # -d = detached (background)
docker run -p 8000:8000 --name mycontainer myapp
docker run --env-file .env -p 8000:8000 myapp

-p 8000:8000 — bind the container's port 8000 to the host's port 8000.

docs.title: Managing containers
docs.text:
docker ps                           # running containers
docker ps -a                        # all, including stopped ones
docker stop mycontainer             # stop
docker start mycontainer            # start a stopped one
docker rm mycontainer               # remove
docker rm -f mycontainer            # force remove

docs.title: Logs and running commands
docs.text:
docker logs mycontainer             # container logs
docker logs -f mycontainer          # follow the logs
docker exec -it mycontainer bash    # enter the container
docker exec mycontainer python manage.py migrate

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
docker images                       # list of images
docker rmi myapp:latest             # remove an image
docker pull python:3.12-slim        # download from Docker Hub

docs.title: Volumes — persisting data
docs.text:
A container is isolated. If you stop and remove a container, all the data inside it disappears. Volumes are used to persist data.

# Mount a host directory into the container
docker run -v /var/data/postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

# Or a named volume
docker volume create myapp_data
docker run -v myapp_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

docs.title: .dockerignore
docs.text:
The Docker equivalent of .gitignore — so that unnecessary files are not copied into the image:

# .dockerignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
.git/
*.log
node_modules/

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Code changes do not appear after docker run

You need to rebuild the image: docker build -t myapp . && docker run myapp

Mistake 2: The container stops immediately after starting

The process exited. Check: docker logs mycontainer

Mistake 3: PostgreSQL data disappears after a restart

No volume is attached. Add -v postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

Mistake 4: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

Docker is not running. sudo systemctl start docker

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text: Write a Dockerfile for a Django project: python:3.12-slim, install the dependencies, copy the code.

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
docker build -t django-test .
docker run -p 8000:8000 -e DEBUG=True django-test
Does http://localhost:8000 open?

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
docker exec -it <container_id> bash
ls -la
cat requirements.txt
exit
Explain where you ended up after docker exec -it ... bash.

docs.text:
• [ ] I understand the difference between a Docker image and a container
  • [ ] I can write a basic Dockerfile for Django
  • [ ] I know the commands: build, run, ps, logs, exec, stop, rm
  • [ ] I understand why volumes are needed and that without them data will disappear
  • [ ] I know what .dockerignore is

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Docker packages an application together with its dependencies — the same environment everywhere. A Dockerfile is the build instruction. docker build → image, docker run → container. Volumes are for persisting data between restarts. The next step is Docker Compose for running several containers together.

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
A Django project is not a single container. It usually consists of: - Django app (Gunicorn) - PostgreSQL - Redis (for Celery or caching) - Celery worker - Nginx

Starting each one manually via docker run with long parameters is complicated and inconvenient. Docker Compose lets you describe the whole stack in one file and start everything with a single command.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text: Docker Compose is like an orchestra conductor. You describe which "musicians" (containers) should play, and one command starts them all together in the right order.

docs.title: A minimal docker-compose.yml for Django
docs.text:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    env_file:
      - .env
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: app_db
      POSTGRES_USER: app_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app_password
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app_user -d app_db"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  postgres_data:

docs.title: A production docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
services:
  web:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    command: gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3
    expose:
      - "8000"
    volumes:
      - static_files:/app/staticfiles
      - media_files:/app/media
    env_file:
      - .env
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    restart: always

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    env_file:
      - .env.db
    restart: always
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $POSTGRES_USER -d $POSTGRES_DB"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: always

  worker:
    build: .
    command: celery -A myapp worker --loglevel=info
    env_file:
      - .env
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    restart: always

  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/conf.d:/etc/nginx/conf.d
      - static_files:/var/www/static
      - media_files:/var/www/media
    depends_on:
      - web
    restart: always

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  static_files:
  media_files:

docs.title: services
docs.text:
Each key inside services: is a container name:

services:
  web:      # Django app
  db:       # PostgreSQL
  redis:    # Redis

docs.title: build vs image
docs.text:
# Build from a Dockerfile
build: .

# Or use a ready-made image
image: postgres:16

docs.title: ports vs expose
docs.text:
ports:
  - "8000:8000"      # HOST:CONTAINER — accessible from outside

expose:
  - "8000"           # only between containers in the Compose network

In production: expose for web (only Nginx has access), ports: "80:80" for Nginx.

docs.title: volumes
docs.text:
volumes:
  - .:/app                    # bind mount: host directory → container
  - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data    # named volume

A bind mount (.:/app) is convenient in development: code changes are immediately visible in the container without a rebuild.

docs.title: depends_on
docs.text:
depends_on:
  db:
    condition: service_healthy   # wait until PostgreSQL is ready

Without condition: service_healthy, Django may start before PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.

docs.title: restart
docs.text:
restart: always          # always restart on failure
restart: unless-stopped  # except when explicitly stopped
restart: on-failure      # only on error

docs.title: Basic Docker Compose commands
docs.text:
# Start the whole stack
docker compose up
docker compose up -d           # in the background (detached)
docker compose up --build      # rebuild the images before starting

# Stopping
docker compose down
docker compose down -v         # stop and remove volumes (data!)

# Logs
docker compose logs
docker compose logs -f         # follow in real time
docker compose logs web        # logs of a specific service

# Run a command in a container
docker compose exec web bash
docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate
docker compose exec web python manage.py createsuperuser
docker compose exec web python manage.py shell

# Status
docker compose ps

# Restart one service
docker compose restart web

docs.title: Networking between containers
docs.text:
Docker Compose automatically creates a network, and all services are on it. They communicate by service name:

# settings.py (or .env)
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'HOST': 'db',        # service name from docker-compose.yml
        'PORT': '5432',
        'NAME': 'app_db',
        'USER': 'app_user',
        'PASSWORD': 'app_password',
    }
}

Instead of localhost — db. Instead of localhost:6379 for Redis — redis:6379.

flowchart LR
    Browser["Browser"] --> Nginx["nginx<br>port 80"]
    Nginx --> Web["web (Django+Gunicorn)<br>port 8000"]
    Web --> DB["db (PostgreSQL)<br>port 5432"]
    Web --> Redis["redis<br>port 6379"]
    Worker["worker<br>(Celery)"] --> DB
    Worker --> Redis

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    class Browser,Nginx,DB,Redis,Worker step;
    class Web success;

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: could not connect to server: Connection refused when starting Django

PostgreSQL has not started yet. Add a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy in depends_on.

Mistake 2: Code changes are not reflected

In dev mode you need a bind mount: - .:/app. Or rebuild: docker compose up --build.

Mistake 3: docker compose down -v deleted the database data

-v removes volumes! To stop without losing data, just use docker compose down.

Mistake 4: HOST=localhost for the database in Docker

In the Compose network it is HOST=db (the service name), not localhost.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Write a docker-compose.yml for Django + PostgreSQL. Start it and check: 

docker compose up --build
docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py shell
Inside the shell: from django.contrib.auth.models import User; User.objects.all()

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Check that the services can see each other: 

docker compose exec web ping db

docs.text:
• [ ] I understand the structure of docker-compose.yml: services, volumes, ports
  • [ ] I know the difference between ports and expose
  • [ ] I understand that containers communicate by service name, not via localhost
  • [ ] I can start the stack with docker compose up --build
  • [ ] I know the commands: exec, logs, down, ps

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Docker Compose lets you describe the whole stack in YAML and start it with one command. Containers in one Compose file form a shared network and find each other by service name. For dev — a bind mount of the code. For prod — named volumes for data. The next step is the DevOps workflow.

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text: You wrote some code. You ran git push. Five minutes later the changes are already in production — automatically. No manual SSH, no copying files, no "I just deployed, please check". That is a DevOps workflow.

docs.title: What DevOps is
docs.text:
DevOps is neither a job title nor a set of tools. It is a culture and a set of practices that help teams deliver changes quickly and safely from a developer's laptop to a production server.

DevOps = Development + Operations.

In the past: developers wrote code, and a separate team (operations) deployed and maintained it. Between them stood a "wall" and constant conflicts.

Today: teams are jointly responsible for the whole path of the code — from writing it to monitoring it in production.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text: Concept What it means CI (Continuous Integration) Automatic code checks on every push CD (Continuous Delivery) Automatic preparation for deployment CD (Continuous Deployment) Automatic deployment to production Pipeline A sequence of steps from code to production Staging A test server that imitates production Production The real server for end users Rollback Reverting to the previous working version IaC Infrastructure as Code — servers described as code

docs.title: The path of code from laptop to production
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Dev["Developer<br>writes code"] --> Push["git push<br>to GitHub"]
    Push --> CI["CI:<br>tests + linter"]
    CI -->|"failed"| Notify["Notification<br>to the developer"]
    CI -->|"passed"| Build["Build:<br>docker build"]
    Build --> Registry["Push image<br>to Registry"]
    Registry --> Staging["Deploy<br>to Staging"]
    Staging --> ManualQA{"Manual QA<br>(or auto E2E)"}
    ManualQA -->|"OK"| Production["Deploy<br>to Production"]
    Production --> Monitor["Monitoring<br>logs, metrics"]
    Monitor -->|"problems found"| Rollback["Rollback<br>to the previous version"]
    Monitor --> Dev

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef decision fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef error    fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,stroke-width:3px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;
    class Dev,Push,CI,Build,Registry,Staging step;
    class ManualQA decision;
    class Production success;
    class Notify,Rollback error;
    class Monitor warning;

docs.title: CI — Continuous Integration
docs.text:
CI runs automatically on every push to the repository and performs:

  1. ruff check . — linter
  2. pytest — tests
  3. Possibly: safety check — vulnerability check

If something fails, the pull request cannot be merged. Code with broken tests will not get into main.

docs.title: GitHub Actions — an example CI for Django
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: Django CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      db:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_DB: test_db
          POSTGRES_USER: test_user
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test_pass
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Run linter
        run: ruff check .

      - name: Run tests
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://test_user:test_pass@localhost:5432/test_db
          DEBUG: "True"
          SECRET_KEY: "ci-test-secret-key"
        run: pytest --tb=short

docs.title: CD — Continuous Deployment
docs.text:
After a successful CI run — automatic deployment:

# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (part)
  deploy:
    needs: test            # only if the tests passed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

    steps:
      - name: Deploy to server
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.SERVER_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd /var/www/myapp
            git pull origin main
            source .venv/bin/activate
            pip install -r requirements.txt
            python manage.py migrate --noinput
            python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
            sudo systemctl restart myapp

docs.title: Staging and Production
docs.text:
Staging is a mirror of production. You deploy there first, check that everything works, and only then deploy to production.

[Developer] → [Git] → [CI] → [Staging] → [Manual/Auto QA] → [Production]

On staging: - A real database (a copy or test data) - Real Docker, Nginx, Gunicorn - But access is restricted (not public)

Advantages: - Bugs are found before users see them - You can test migrations - The QA team can check new features

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: If something breaks after a deployment, you need to go back quickly.

docs.title: Option 1: Git rollback
docs.text:
git log --oneline -5           # find the previous commit
git checkout HEAD~1            # or a specific SHA
sudo systemctl restart myapp

docs.title: Option 2: Docker image tags
docs.text:
# The previous image is still in the registry
docker pull myapp:v1.2.3
docker compose up -d           # with the previous version

docs.title: Option 3: Via CI/CD
docs.text: Most CI/CD systems have a "Redeploy previous build" button.

docs.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
docs.text:
If you describe the server configuration in code, you can version it, reproduce it, review changes, and deploy it again after a disaster.

Instead of manually configuring Nginx, PostgreSQL, and the firewall, this is described in files (Terraform, Ansible, Pulumi) and run automatically.

For a beginner: docker-compose.yml and Bash scripts are enough. Terraform and Ansible are the next level.

docs.title: Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Deploying manually without a script

One day you will forget collectstatic or migrate and the site will break.

Mistake 2: Deploying without tests

Without CI, tests do not run automatically and bugs get into production.

Mistake 3: No staging

You see the behavior for the first time in production. There is no way to reproduce the problem.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text: Draw the pipeline for your Django project: from git push to the live site. What are the steps? What is automatic and what is manual?

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text: Add .github/workflows/ci.yml to your project with the steps: install, ruff, pytest. Check that it runs on push.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Write deploy.sh — a script for deploying to the server that runs git pull, migrate, collectstatic, restart.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
• [ ] I can explain what CI/CD is
  • [ ] I understand why Staging is needed
  • [ ] I know what a rollback is and how to do one
  • [ ] I can write a basic GitHub Actions workflow for Django
  • [ ] I understand the path of code from push to production

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: DevOps is a set of practices for delivering code quickly and safely. CI checks the tests on every push. CD automates deployment. Staging is a safe place for testing before production. Rollback is the retreat plan. The next step is the Kubernetes overview.

docs.title: Why you need this
docs.text:
You have mastered Docker and Docker Compose. One server, one docker compose up — and everything works. But what if you have 50 containers, 10 servers, and the system has to restart itself on failure, scale under load, and update without stopping?

That is what Kubernetes exists for.

This file is only an overview. Kubernetes is a large course of its own. Here you will get a mental model: why it exists and when it becomes necessary.

docs.title: A simple explanation
docs.text:
Docker Compose is convenient when you have one server or a small project. Kubernetes is needed when there are many containers and many servers, and the system has to restart, scale, and distribute the load between them on its own.

Docker Compose is a remote control for a single TV. Kubernetes is a management system for a whole cinema with hundreds of screens, each showing a different film, and if one screen breaks, the system itself moves the audience to another one.

docs.title: When Docker Compose is no longer enough
docs.text: Situation Docker Compose Kubernetes 1 server, 5 containers Excellent Overkill 3+ servers Difficult Designed for this Auto-scaling No Yes Self-healing (auto-restart) Partially Yes, automatically Zero-downtime deployment Difficult Built in 100+ microservices Hard to manage This is what it exists for

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term What it means Cluster A set of servers (nodes) managed by Kubernetes Node One server in the cluster (physical or VM) Pod The smallest unit in Kubernetes. Contains 1+ containers Deployment Describes the desired state of Pods (how many replicas, which image) Service A stable address for a set of Pods (load balancing) Namespace Logical isolation inside the cluster ConfigMap Configuration (without secrets) for Pods Secret Encrypted data (passwords, keys) for Pods Ingress The cluster's equivalent of an Nginx reverse proxy

docs.title: Cluster architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Internet["Internet"] --> Ingress["Ingress Controller<br>(similar to Nginx)"]

    subgraph Cluster["Kubernetes Cluster"]
        Ingress --> Service1["Service: django-web"]
        Service1 --> Pod1["Pod: django app #1"]
        Service1 --> Pod2["Pod: django app #2"]
        Service1 --> Pod3["Pod: django app #3"]

        Pod1 --> ServiceDB["Service: postgres"]
        Pod2 --> ServiceDB
        Pod3 --> ServiceDB

        ServiceDB --> PodDB["Pod: PostgreSQL"]

        subgraph Node1["Node 1 (server)"]
            Pod1
            PodDB
        end

        subgraph Node2["Node 2 (server)"]
            Pod2
            Pod3
        end
    end

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;

    class Internet,Service1,ServiceDB step;
    class Pod1,Pod2,Pod3,PodDB success;
    class Ingress warning;

Kubernetes automatically: - Places Pods on free Nodes - Restarts a Pod if it crashes - Balances traffic between Pods - Replaces Pods during an update (one at a time, without downtime)

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: django-web
spec:
  replicas: 3             # 3 copies of Django
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: django-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: django-web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: django
          image: myapp:v1.2.3
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: SECRET_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: myapp-secrets
                  key: secret-key

docs.title: Self-healing — automatic recovery
docs.text:
If a Pod crashes, Kubernetes notices it through health checks and automatically starts a new one:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 30

The Django endpoint /health/ returns 200 OK, which means everything is fine. If it returns an error several times in a row, Kubernetes restarts the container.

docs.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
docs.text:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: django-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: django-web
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

When CPU load is > 70%, Kubernetes automatically increases the number of Pods. When the load drops, it decreases it.

docs.title: Kubernetes vs Docker Compose
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Simple ["Small project<br>(1 server)"]
        DC["Docker Compose"] --> DCF["✓ Simple, quick start<br>✓ Sufficient"]
    end

    subgraph Complex ["Complex project<br>(10+ servers)"]
        K8s["Kubernetes"] --> K8sF["✓ Auto-scaling, Self-healing<br>✓ Zero-downtime updates, Multi-node"]
    end

    Simple -->|"grows"| Complex

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;

    class DC,K8s step;
    class DCF,K8sF success;

docs.title: Managed Kubernetes
docs.text:
If you don't want to maintain a cluster manually, cloud providers offer Kubernetes as a service:

Provider Service Google Cloud GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) AWS EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) Azure AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) DigitalOcean DOKS

You describe Deployments and Services → the cloud manages the Nodes, networking, and master updates.

docs.title: What to learn before Kubernetes
docs.text:
Kubernetes is a complex system. Starting with it without a foundation is a waste of time.

1. ✅ Linux and the terminal
2. ✅ Docker and Dockerfile
3. ✅ Docker Compose
4. ✅ Manual deployment (without Kubernetes)
5. ✅ Basic CI/CD
    ↓
6. → Kubernetes

docs.title: Task 2

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Install Minikube (local Kubernetes for learning): 

# Install minikube
curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube

minikube start
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces

docs.text:

  • [ ] I understand the concepts of self-healing and auto-scaling

docs.title: Short summary
docs.text: Kubernetes is a container orchestrator for complex systems with many servers. It automatically restarts, scales and updates Pods. For small projects, Docker Compose is enough. Kubernetes becomes relevant when you outgrow a single server. The next file is the roadmap and where to go next.

docs.title: You have completed this lesson
docs.text:
If you've reached this file and worked through the whole lesson — congratulations. You are no longer afraid of Linux. You understand how your Python code lives on a real server.

But this is not the end — it is the beginning. DevOps and server-side development are a huge field of knowledge. This roadmap will help you understand where you are now and where to go next.

docs.title: Level 1. Using Linux with confidence
docs.text:
What you can do after this lesson:

  • [ ] Navigate the file system (cd, ls, pwd, find)
  • [ ] Work with files (cp, mv, rm, chmod, chown)
  • [ ] Understand access permissions (rwx, 755, 644, 600)
  • [ ] Manage processes (ps, kill, top, jobs)
  • [ ] Connect over SSH (ssh, ssh-keygen, scp)
  • [ ] Read logs (tail -f, journalctl, grep)

What to practice next: - Work in the terminal every day instead of a GUI - Learn vim or nano for editing files on the server - Get to know tmux or screen for persistent sessions

docs.title: Level 2. Being able to run a backend project
docs.text:
What you can do after this lesson:

  • [ ] Install dependencies via apt and pip
  • [ ] Set up a virtualenv
  • [ ] Configure .env for production
  • [ ] Run migrate and collectstatic
  • [ ] Start Gunicorn/Uvicorn
  • [ ] Configure basic Nginx

What to practice next: - Deploy a real Django project to a VPS (DigitalOcean, Hetzner) - Set up HTTPS with Let's Encrypt + Certbot - Study Django check --deploy — recommendations for production

docs.title: Level 3. Automating your work
docs.text:
What you can do after this lesson:

  • [ ] Write Bash scripts with variables, conditions, and loops
  • [ ] Use set -e and exit codes
  • [ ] Write a Makefile for the project
  • [ ] Read and filter logs
  • [ ] Set up a systemd service

What to practice next: - Write a complete deploy.sh for your project - Learn cron for scheduled tasks - Get to know logrotate for log rotation

docs.title: Level 4. Containerization
docs.text:
What you can do after this lesson:

  • [ ] Write a Dockerfile for Django
  • [ ] Build and run Docker images
  • [ ] Write a docker-compose.yml for the stack
  • [ ] Run Django + PostgreSQL + Redis via Compose
  • [ ] Run migrate and shell via docker compose exec

What to practice next: - Optimize the Dockerfile: multi-stage builds, minimal image size - Study Docker volumes and networks in more detail - Deploy a production stack with Nginx + Gunicorn in Docker Compose

docs.title: Level 5. DevOps basics
docs.text:
What you can do after this lesson:

  • [ ] Understand a CI/CD pipeline
  • [ ] Write a basic GitHub Actions workflow
  • [ ] Know the difference between Staging and Production
  • [ ] Understand rollback strategies
  • [ ] Have a mental model of DevOps culture

What to practice next: - Set up a full CI/CD pipeline for your project - Study GitHub Actions in more detail: secrets, caching, matrix - Get to know automated E2E tests in CI

docs.title: Level 6. Next — cloud and specialization
docs.text: After Levels 1–5 you are ready to move in any direction:

docs.title: Cloud Platforms
docs.text: Platform Why learn it DigitalOcean An easy start with VPS and managed databases AWS The largest platform: EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda GCP GKE (Kubernetes), Cloud Run, BigQuery Hetzner Cheap and reliable VPS for learning

Ansible   → automating server configuration

SSL/TLS and certificates

docs.title: Your first real project
docs.text: The best way to consolidate your knowledge is to deploy a real project:

docs.title: A minimal plan
docs.text:
1. Rent a VPS (DigitalOcean $5/month, Hetzner €4/month)
  2. Install Ubuntu 22.04
  3. Connect over SSH with a key
  4. Deploy your Django project: git + virtualenv + Gunicorn + Nginx
  5. Set up HTTPS with Certbot (free)
  6. Add a systemd service for automatic restarts
  7. Set up GitHub Actions for automatic deployment

After that you have a real production server and hands-on deployment experience. That is worth more than 10 books you have read.

docs.title: A final thought
docs.text:
You have come all the way from "what is Linux" to understanding CI/CD, Docker Compose and Kubernetes. This is the foundation on which all modern backend development is built.

The most important thing now is practice. Open a terminal, rent a VPS, deploy your project. Every command you type by hand becomes part of your experience.

Linux stops being scary once you start using it every day.

docs.title: Deployment Checklist
docs.text: A production checklist separates what is ready from what is merely desired.

docs.title: What the student will learn
docs.text:
• the basic mental model of the topic;
  • how the topic works in Django;
  • where to see it in the final project;
  • how to verify that the understanding is not only theoretical.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Be able to open the repository.
  • Understand that all paths in the documentation are relative to the notes_chat_app root.

docs.title: Required before production
docs.text:

  • Real ALLOWED_HOSTS.
  • SECRET_KEY from the environment.
  • PostgreSQL with a backup strategy.
  • Redis for Channels.
  • collectstatic and static serving.
  • HTTPS and secure cookies.
  • Application server without --reload.
  • Reverse proxy.
  • Logging and monitoring.

docs.text: notes_chat_app is the final project of the course, built on Django 5.2. It combines CRUD, group sharing of objects, a WebSocket chat, a full testing pyramid, and Docker Compose in a single codebase.

docs.text:
HTTP Request
  └─► notes_project/urls.py  (include notes_app.urls)
       └─► notes_app/urls.py  (@login_required, path)
            └─► views.py  (coordination only)
                 ├─► forms.py      (validation, clean_*)
                 ├─► selectors.py  (scoped QuerySet — read)
                 └─► services.py   (create/update/delete)

Rule: views.py contains no ORM queries. selectors.py contains no mutations. services.py knows nothing about HTTP.

docs.text: Model Specifics Note priority 1–4 (PositiveSmallIntegerField, CheckConstraint), group FK SET_NULL, notebook FK SET_NULL, tags M2M TodoList shared_with M2M(User) — shared access through direct sharing ShoppingList shared_with M2M(User) + group FK SET_NULL — two kinds of sharing ChatMessage author FK CASCADE, group FK CASCADE — no SET_NULL; when a group is deleted, its messages are deleted Reminder CASCADE from Note — when a note is deleted, its reminders are deleted UserProfile OneToOneField(User, CASCADE) — display_name(100), bio, avatar_url, timezone

docs.title: Deletion behavior
docs.text:
User deleted       → all of their Note, Notebook, Tag, TodoList, ShoppingList, ChatMessage → CASCADE
Notebook deleted   → Note.notebook → SET_NULL  (notes are not deleted)
Note deleted       → Reminder → CASCADE
Group deleted      → Note.group → SET_NULL, ShoppingList.group → SET_NULL
                   → ChatMessage → CASCADE  (messages are deleted!)
TodoList deleted   → TodoItem → CASCADE
ShoppingList deleted → ShopItem → CASCADE

docs.title: Selectors
docs.text:
notes_app/selectors.py is the read-only ORM layer; it always returns materialized data or a QuerySet before rendering.

Function What it returns get_user_notes(user, *, archived, notebook, tag, search) QuerySet[Note] with select_related('notebook'), prefetch_related('tags') get_note_detail(user, note_id) Note or None (owner + group members) get_pinned_notes(user, limit=5) QuerySet[Note] get_user_notebooks(user) QuerySet[Notebook] get_user_tags(user) QuerySet[Tag] get_user_todo_lists(user) QuerySet[TodoList] (own) get_shared_todo_lists(user) QuerySet[TodoList] (shared_with) get_todo_list_detail(user, pk) TodoList or None get_user_shopping_lists(user) own shopping lists get_shared_shopping_lists(user) shared_with lists get_shopping_list_detail(user, pk) with group access get_user_groups(user) QuerySet[Group] where the user is a member get_group_with_members(group_id, user) group + prefetched members get_pending_reminders() reminders with remind_at <= now

Access rule for shared objects:

# read: the owner OR a group member
Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user.groups.all())

# write: the owner only
Q(user=user)

docs.title: GroupChatConsumer
docs.text:
notes_app/consumers.py contains the single WebSocket consumer.

class GroupChatConsumer(AsyncWebsocketConsumer):
    async def connect(self)          # auth + membership check → accept or close
    async def disconnect(self, code) # group_discard
    async def receive(self, text_data) # JSON parse → save_message → group_send
    async def chat_message(self, event) # broadcast from the channel layer → send to the client

    # sync helpers (called via database_sync_to_async)
    def check_membership(self, group_pk, user)  → bool
    def load_history(self, group_pk)            → list[dict]  # the latest 50
    def save_message(self, group_pk, user, content) → ChatMessage

ASGI import order (asgi.py):

# CORRECT: django.setup() → get_asgi_application() → import consumers
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()   # ← BEFORE any notes_app import
from notes_app.consumers import GroupChatConsumer  # ← only AFTER

database_sync_to_async + materialization:

# ✅ correct: list() materializes the data before it leaves the worker
history = await database_sync_to_async(self.load_history)(group_pk)

def load_history(self, group_pk):
    return list(
        ChatMessage.objects.filter(group_id=group_pk)
        .select_related('author')
        .order_by('-created_at')[:50]
        .values('content', 'author__username', 'created_at')
    )

docs.title: IDOR protection
docs.text:
All object-level queries use a scoped queryset, never a bare .get(pk=pk):

# selectors.py
def get_note_detail(user, note_id):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    return Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups),
        pk=note_id
    ).select_related('notebook', 'group').prefetch_related('tags').first()

If the result is None, the view returns Http404.

docs.text: Object Read Write (edit/delete) Note owner + group members owner only Notebook owner owner Tag owner owner TodoList owner + shared_with owner ShoppingList owner + shared_with + group owner ChatMessage group members (WS) —

docs.title: WebSocket authentication
docs.text: AuthMiddlewareStack reads the session cookie during the WS handshake → scope["user"]. The consumer checks user.is_authenticated and check_membership() in connect(). An unauthenticated user or a non-member → await self.close().

docs.title: Testing pyramid
docs.text:
File Class Count What it tests test_models.py TestCase ~25 constraints, __str__, on_delete test_services.py TestCase ~65 return value + persistence test_forms.py TestCase ~20 valid/invalid data, clean_* test_views.py TestCase ~85 status codes, redirects, IDOR test_consumers.py TransactionTestCase ~10 WS connect, message, reject test_tasks.py TestCase ~18 Celery task, email, repeat, JSON view test_selenium.py StaticLiveServerTestCase / ChannelsLiveServerTestCase ~23 E2E flow + Toast notifications Total 200+

Why TransactionTestCase for consumers:

TestCase wraps each test in a transaction → rollback afterwards.
The async consumer reads the DB from a separate worker thread —
  that thread does not see TestCase's uncommitted transaction.
→ setUp objects "disappear" for the consumer.
→ ALWAYS use TransactionTestCase for WebSocket tests.

Running:

# unit + integration + consumer
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test \
  notes_app.tests.test_models notes_app.tests.test_services \
  notes_app.tests.test_forms notes_app.tests.test_views \
  notes_app.tests.test_consumers -v 2

# Selenium (requires the running stack)
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2

docs.title: The layering principle (Views → thin)
docs.text:
views.py         ← HTTP coordination (thin layer)
  ↓ forms.py     ← input data validation
  ↓ selectors.py ← read queries (returns a QuerySet or a list)
  ↓ services.py  ← write operations (atomic transactions)
  ↓ models.py    ← domain schema

Business logic is not added directly to a view without a documented reason.

AuthMiddlewareStack reads the session cookie from the WS handshake and populates scope["user"].

docs.title: connect()
docs.text:
1. Checks scope["user"].is_authenticated → close() if not.
  2. Reads group_pk from scope["url_route"]["kwargs"].
  3. Checks that the group exists and the user is a member via database_sync_to_async (check_membership) — close() if not a member.
  4. Adds the channel to the room group: channel_layer.group_add(room_group_name, self.channel_name).
  5. accept() — the WebSocket handshake.
  6. Loads the last 50 messages (load_history) and sends them to the client as frames with "type": "history".

docs.title: receive()
docs.text:
1. Parses JSON: {"content": "..."}.
  2. Checks content — if it is empty or longer than 2000 characters, ignores it.
  3. Saves the ChatMessage via database_sync_to_async.
  4. Publishes an event to the channel group: channel_layer.group_send(room_group_name, {...}).
  5. Every consumer in the group receives the event through chat_message() and sends JSON to its client.

docs.title: disconnect()
docs.text: 1. Removes the channel from the room group: channel_layer.group_discard(...).

docs.title: database_sync_to_async
docs.text:
The Django ORM is synchronous. In an async consumer, all ORM operations must run in a worker thread via database_sync_to_async:

from channels.db import database_sync_to_async

@database_sync_to_async
def load_history(self, group_pk):
    qs = (
        ChatMessage.objects
        .filter(group_id=group_pk)
        .select_related('author')
        .order_by('-timestamp')[:50]
    )
    messages = list(qs.values('id', 'author__username', 'content', 'timestamp'))
    messages.reverse()
    return messages

list(queryset.values(...)) is mandatory. A lazy QuerySet returned into the async context will raise SynchronousOnlyOperation.

docs.title: Without REDIS_URL (locally without Docker)
docs.text:
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer",
    }
}

Suitable for a single process only. Messages are not passed between different uvicorn workers.

docs.title: With REDIS_URL (Docker / production)
docs.text:
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels_redis.core.RedisChannelLayer",
        "CONFIG": {
            "hosts": [{
                "address": _REDIS_URL,
                "socket_timeout": None,  # critical — without it, TimeoutError when idle
                "socket_connect_timeout": 5,
                "health_check_interval": 30,
            }],
        },
    }
}

socket_timeout=None — without it, RedisChannelLayer closes the connection after an idle timeout → TimeoutError on the next message.

docs.title: Testing the consumer (TransactionTestCase)
docs.text:
from django.test import TransactionTestCase

class GroupChatConsumerTest(TransactionTestCase):
    def setUp(self):   # SYNC setUp, not asyncSetUp
        ...

TransactionTestCase (not TestCase) is used because TestCase wraps each test in a transaction that the database_sync_to_async worker thread cannot see. TransactionTestCase does not wrap → the data is visible from all threads.

docs.title: XSS protection
docs.text:
The JavaScript client escapes HTML before inserting it into the DOM:

function escapeHtml(text) {
    const div = document.createElement('div');
    div.appendChild(document.createTextNode(text));
    return div.innerHTML;
}

Message content is inserted through escapeHtml(), not directly through innerHTML.

docs.title: Background Tasks and Browser Notifications
docs.text: notes_chat_app implements its reminder system on two levels: a background email worker (Celery) and browser polling with a Bootstrap Toast.

docs.title: The problem and the solution
docs.text:
A Django view cannot send an email exactly at the scheduled time: it runs only in response to an HTTP request. If the browser is not open, the reminder will not fire.

Solution: the Celery Worker, a separate process that is always active and runs tasks independently of the browser.

docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Beat["Celery Beat<br>(every 60 sec)"] -->|task name + args| Broker
    Broker["Redis DB 1<br>(broker / result backend)"] -->|task message| Worker
    Worker["Celery Worker<br>(concurrency=2)"] -->|send_mail| Email["Email<br>(console in dev)"]
    Worker -->|is_sent=True| DB[("PostgreSQL")]
    Worker -->|create next Reminder| DB

    Browser["Browser JS<br>(every 60 sec)"] -->|GET /reminders/check/| Django
    Django["Django view<br>reminders_check()"] -->|SELECT| DB
    Django -->|JSON| Browser
    Browser -->|Bootstrap Toast| User["👤 User"]

# notes_app/tasks.py
@shared_task
def send_reminder_notifications():
    from .models import Reminder
    now = timezone.now()
    pending = (
        Reminder.objects
        .select_related('note__user')
        .filter(remind_at__lte=now, is_sent=False)
    )
    for reminder in pending:
        user = reminder.note.user
        if user.email:
            send_mail(...)
        reminder.is_sent = True
        reminder.save(update_fields=['is_sent'])
        _schedule_next(reminder)

docs.title: 3. Repeating reminders
docs.text:
def _schedule_next(reminder):
    if reminder.repeat_pattern == 'none':
        return
    from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta
    delta_map = {
        'daily':   relativedelta(days=1),
        'weekly':  relativedelta(weeks=1),
        'monthly': relativedelta(months=1),  # preserves the correct month length
    }
    delta = delta_map.get(reminder.repeat_pattern)
    if delta:
        Reminder.objects.create(
            note=reminder.note,
            remind_at=reminder.remind_at + delta,
            message=reminder.message,
            is_sent=False,
            repeat_pattern=reminder.repeat_pattern,
        )

relativedelta (from python-dateutil) correctly handles different month lengths, unlike timedelta(days=30).

docs.title: Selector
docs.text:
# notes_app/selectors.py
def get_due_reminders_for_browser(user):
    now = timezone.now()
    return list(
        Reminder.objects
        .filter(
            note__user=user,
            remind_at__lte=now,
            remind_at__gte=now - timedelta(hours=1),   # display window: 1 hour
        )
        .select_related('note')
        .order_by('remind_at')
        .values('id', 'message', 'remind_at', 'note__title')
    )

docs.text:
# test_tasks.py — key tests
@override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='django.core.mail.backends.locmem.EmailBackend')
def test_marks_due_reminder_as_sent(self):
    r = self._reminder(offset_minutes=-5)
    send_reminder_notifications()
    r.refresh_from_db()
    self.assertTrue(r.is_sent)

def test_ignores_future_reminders(self):
    r = self._reminder(offset_minutes=+10)
    send_reminder_notifications()
    r.refresh_from_db()
    self.assertFalse(r.is_sent)

def test_daily_repeat_creates_next_reminder(self):
    r = self._reminder(offset_minutes=-5, repeat='daily')
    original_at = r.remind_at
    send_reminder_notifications()
    next_r = Reminder.objects.filter(note=self.note, is_sent=False).first()
    diff = (next_r.remind_at - original_at).total_seconds()
    self.assertAlmostEqual(diff, 86400, delta=60)

override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='...locmem...') captures emails in django.core.mail.outbox without an SMTP server.

def test_toast_appears_for_due_reminder(self):
    Reminder.objects.create(
        note=self.note,
        remind_at=timezone.now() - timedelta(minutes=30),
        message='JS toast test',
    )
    self._login_via_cookie()
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/notes/')

    toast = WebDriverWait(self.driver, 10).until(
        EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, '.toast.show'))
    )
    self.assertIn('Selenium Reminder Note', toast.text)

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text: notes_chat_app is a learning Django application that brings all the key topics of the course together in a single codebase: CRUD, authentication, sharing through groups, testing, and a real-time chat.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text: Students often find it hard to see how the separate Django topics fit together into one coherent application. This project demonstrates every layer, from models to WebSocket, in a single codebase.

docs.title: User roles
docs.text: Role Capabilities Anonymous index, register, login Authenticated manages their own notes, todo lists, shopping lists, notebooks, tags Group member sees group notes and group shopping lists, writes in the group chat

docs.title: What is implemented

URL Mechanism /accounts/login/ LoginView (built-in) /accounts/logout/ LogoutView (built-in) /accounts/password_change/ PasswordChangeView (built-in) /register/ a custom view in notes_app/views.py

@login_required or LoginRequiredMixin protects all views except register, login, index.

docs.title: Authorization and IDOR protection
docs.text: All object queries use a scoped QuerySet, never a bare Note.objects.get(pk=pk).

docs.title: Access pattern through selectors
docs.text:
# selectors.py — read: owner or group member
def get_note_for_user(user, pk):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    return Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups),
        pk=pk
    ).first()

# selectors.py — edit/delete: owner only
def get_note_for_edit(user, pk):
    return Note.objects.filter(user=user, pk=pk).first()

If the result is None → Http404 or PermissionDenied.

docs.title: What it protects against
docs.text: Threat Protection IDOR (someone else's note by pk) queryset scoped by user=user Reading other people's group notes the queryset includes group__in=user_groups Editing someone else's object only Q(user=user) for mutating ops Mass assignment of tags tag_ids are filtered: Tag.objects.filter(user=user, pk__in=tag_ids)

docs.title: Group sharing
docs.text: Model Mechanism Note group = FK(Group, SET_NULL) — group members can see the note ShoppingList group = FK(Group, SET_NULL) and shared_with = M2M(User) TodoList shared_with = M2M(User) — direct sharing with users ChatMessage through a Group — only group members can connect to the chat

docs.title: WebSocket authorization
docs.text:
GroupChatConsumer.connect() checks:

  1. scope["user"].is_authenticated — anonymous → close(4003).
  2. Whether scope["user"] is a member of group group_pk → not a member → close(4004).

The check runs through database_sync_to_async before accept().

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Django's CSRF middleware is active by default (CsrfViewMiddleware in MIDDLEWARE).

WebSocket connections are not subject to CSRF (a separate protocol); authorization uses the session cookie.

docs.title: DebugExceptionMiddleware
docs.text:
Production security issue

notes_project/middleware.py implements DebugExceptionMiddleware, which returns the full traceback to the browser without checking DEBUG. In production this exposes implementation details to clients. It is kept for teaching purposes; before deploying to production you must remove it or restrict it with an if settings.DEBUG condition.

docs.title: Passwords and SECRET_KEY
docs.text:
• Passwords are hashed with Django's PBKDF2 by default.
  • SECRET_KEY is read from an environment variable (.env → docker-compose.yml).
  • DEBUG=False and ALLOWED_HOSTS are required before a production deployment.

docker compose up --build

# Subsequent runs
docker compose up

The stack is available at http://localhost (Nginx → port 80 → Django on 8001).

docs.title: Student Tasks
docs.text: Practical tasks for Notes Chat App at three difficulty levels.

docs.title: Level 1 — Minimal
docs.text:
Add a new field to the Note model, create and apply a migration, and show the field in the detail template.

Steps:

  1. Add the field in notes_app/models.py (for example, color = models.CharField(max_length=7, default='#808080', blank=True)).
  2. Create the migration: docker compose run --rm web python manage.py makemigrations.
  3. Apply it: docker compose run --rm web python manage.py migrate.
  4. Show the field in templates/notes_app/note_detail.html.

Criteria:

  • The migration file exists in notes_app/migrations/.
  • manage.py check passes without errors.
  • The template displays the field without errors.
  • Existing tests pass: docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_models -v 2.

docs.title: Level 2 — Core
docs.text:
Add an archive/unarchive flow through a service, a view, a URL, and a test.

Steps:

  1. Note already has an is_archived field; use it.
  2. Add a function in notes_app/services.py (similar to toggle_pin).
  3. Add a selector in notes_app/selectors.py to fetch archived notes.
  4. Add a view in notes_app/views.py.
  5. Add a URL in notes_app/urls.py.
  6. Add a test in notes_app/tests/test_services.py or test_views.py.

Criteria:

  • The business logic lives in services.py (not in the view).
  • The read query lives in selectors.py.
  • Access rules are tested (it is impossible to archive someone else's note).
  • All existing tests pass.

docs.title: Level 3 — Advanced
docs.text: Restore the async HTTP demo or fix the Docker production blockers.

docs.title: Option A: Async HTTP demo
docs.text:
Current state: async_views.py, async_selectors.py, async_services.py are absent from the working tree.

Implement an async view for the note list: - Use async def note_list_async(request). - Wrap the ORM calls with database_sync_to_async. - Register the URL. - Write a test.

docs.title: Option B: Production Docker
docs.text:
1. Move SECRET_KEY into an environment variable.
  2. Add a DEBUG=False mode with a correct ALLOWED_HOSTS.
  3. Remove DebugExceptionMiddleware or restrict it with an if settings.DEBUG condition.
  4. Replace uvicorn --reload with a production command.
  5. Document all the changes.

Criteria (both options):

  • The command is documented.
  • Tests / checks pass, or the blocker is described honestly.
  • Existing features do not break.

docs.title: Test modules
docs.text: File Base class What it tests test_models.py TestCase constraints, __str__, deletion behavior (CASCADE/SET_NULL) test_services.py TestCase create/update/delete operations, security (mass assignment of tags), business rules test_forms.py TestCase validation, scoped querysets in form fields (Tag, Notebook for the current user) test_views.py TestCase HTTP status codes, redirects, IDOR protection, force_login test_consumers.py TransactionTestCase WebSocket connect, receive, disconnect, auth test_tasks.py TestCase the reminder Celery task, email, repeats, the JSON endpoint test_selenium.py StaticLiveServerTestCase / ChannelsLiveServerTestCase E2E browser flows through Chrome

docs.title: Why TransactionTestCase for consumers
docs.text:
TestCase wraps each test in a transaction (SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK). database_sync_to_async runs the ORM in a separate worker thread. That thread does not see TestCase's uncommitted transaction → setUp objects "disappear".

TransactionTestCase does not wrap tests → all threads see the data.

setUp in TransactionTestCase is sync, not async: Django test cases don't call asyncSetUp (that is a unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase API), so data setup goes in a regular setUp, even when the tests themselves are async def.

docs.title: Async Lab — WebSocket and Django Channels
docs.text:
Goal: explore the lifecycle of GroupChatConsumer, understand why database_sync_to_async is needed, and learn to test WebSocket with WebsocketCommunicator.

Related files: notes_app/consumers.py, notes_app/tests/test_consumers.py, notes_project/asgi.py.

docs.title: Part 1 — Consumer lifecycle
docs.text:
Open notes_app/consumers.py and find class GroupChatConsumer(AsyncWebsocketConsumer).

For each of the three methods, describe in a comment what happens:

Method What it does When it is called connect() During the WS handshake (before accept) receive() When the browser has sent text disconnect() When the connection is closed

Task: find the line where the consumer closes the connection for an anonymous user. Which close code does it use? What does that code mean?

docs.title: Part 2 — database_sync_to_async
docs.text:
Problem: the Django ORM is synchronous. In an async context, calling ChatMessage.objects.create(...) directly will raise:

SynchronousOnlyOperation: You cannot call this from an async context

Solution: database_sync_to_async runs the ORM in the Django thread pool:

from channels.db import database_sync_to_async

@database_sync_to_async
def _save_message(self, content):
    return ChatMessage.objects.create(
        group=self.group,
        author=self.user,
        content=content,
    )

Questions:

  1. Why is list(queryset.values(...)) mandatory when returning data from database_sync_to_async?
  2. What happens if you return a lazy QuerySet into the async context and access it later?
  3. Find the place in consumers.py where the latest 50 messages are loaded. Which SQL operation runs?

docs.title: Part 3 — WebsocketCommunicator
docs.text:
WebsocketCommunicator tests a consumer without a real browser or server.

Study the helper from test_consumers.py:

from channels.testing import WebsocketCommunicator
from notes_project.asgi import application

def _make_communicator(group_pk, user):
    communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
        application,
        f"/ws/groups/{group_pk}/chat/"
    )
    communicator.scope['user'] = user
    communicator.scope['url_route'] = {'kwargs': {'group_pk': str(group_pk)}}
    return communicator

Questions:

  1. Why set scope['user'] manually? Why does AuthMiddlewareStack not kick in during the test?
  2. Why do consumer tests inherit from TransactionTestCase rather than TestCase?

docs.title: Part 4 — Write your own test
docs.text:
Task: write a test that verifies that after a disconnect the consumer is correctly removed from the channel group (another participant does not receive messages for the disconnected one):

# notes_app/tests/test_consumers.py — add the method to the existing class
async def test_disconnected_user_does_not_receive_messages(self):
    from channels.testing import WebsocketCommunicator
    from notes_project.asgi import application

    comm_alice = _make_communicator(self.group.pk, self.user1)
    comm_bob   = _make_communicator(self.group.pk, self.user2)

    await comm_alice.connect()
    await comm_bob.connect()

    # Bob disconnects
    await comm_bob.disconnect()

    # Alice sends a message
    await comm_alice.send_json_to({'content': 'Only for Alice'})
    msg = await comm_alice.receive_json_from()
    self.assertEqual(msg['content'], 'Only for Alice')

    # Bob must NOT receive anything (he is not in the group)
    # receive_nothing() returns True if there are no messages
    self.assertTrue(await comm_bob.receive_nothing())

    await comm_alice.disconnect()

Run it (with exec, not run):

docker compose up -d
docker compose exec web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_consumers -v 2

docs.title: Evaluate and choose (analysis and evaluation level)
Q.1. WebSocket vs HTTP Polling: where is the line?
docs.text:
Notes Chat App uses WebSocket for the group chat.

Evaluate: - Which feature in Notes Chat App could be implemented with polling, and would that be acceptable? (Reminders? The note list? Todo updates?) - With 1000 active users, how many HTTP requests/sec does polling at a 2-second interval generate? How many with WebSocket? - Name two scenarios where polling is better than WebSocket. Justify your answer. - Find where the WS connection is established in group_chat.js. What happens on disconnect? Is there reconnect logic?

docs.title: Q.2. InMemoryChannelLayer vs RedisChannelLayer: what to choose and when?
docs.text:
# Option A: In-Memory (no Redis)
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {"BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer"}
}

# Option B: Redis
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels_redis.core.RedisChannelLayer",
        "CONFIG": {"hosts": [REDIS_URL], "socket_timeout": None},
    }
}

Evaluate: - Imagine the production server runs 3 Uvicorn workers. What happens to the chat with Option A? - With Option B, if Redis is unavailable, what happens to the chat? - Find in settings.py which option is active when REDIS_URL is present and when it is not. - Draw a conclusion: "Option A is appropriate when..., Option B is mandatory when..."

docs.title: Q.3. async def view vs def view: where is async justified?
docs.text:
Django 5.2 supports async def views.

# Sync view
def note_list(request):
    notes = selectors.get_user_notes(user=request.user)
    return render(request, 'note_list.html', {'notes': notes})

# Async view
async def note_list(request):
    # list() runs the SQL in the worker thread; a lazy QuerySet in render() → SynchronousOnlyOperation
    notes = await database_sync_to_async(
        lambda: list(selectors.get_user_notes(user=request.user))
    )()
    return render(request, 'note_list.html', {'notes': notes})

Evaluate: - Why does Notes Chat App use sync views instead of async for most views? - In which scenario does an async view give a real benefit for this project? - What makes debugging async views harder compared to sync ones? - Look through views.py: is there at least one async view? If not, why?

docs.title: Forms Lab — Form validation and security
docs.text:
Goal: understand how Django Forms protect against invalid and malicious input, and learn to write custom validation and scoped querysets.

Related files: notes_app/forms.py, notes_app/tests/test_forms.py.

docs.title: Part 1 — Take apart NoteForm
docs.text:
Open notes_app/forms.py and find class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm).

class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def __init__(self, *args, user=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if user:
            self.fields['notebook'].queryset = Notebook.objects.filter(user=user)
            self.fields['tags'].queryset = Tag.objects.filter(user=user)
            self.fields['group'].queryset = user.groups.all()
        else:
            self.fields['notebook'].queryset = Notebook.objects.none()
            self.fields['tags'].queryset = Tag.objects.none()
            self.fields['group'].queryset = Group.objects.none()

Questions:

  1. What happens if you do not filter the queryset by user? What is the security threat?
  2. Why Notebook.objects.none() instead of an empty list?
  3. Why is user passed as a keyword-only argument (*args, user=None)?

Answer to question 1: without filtering, a student can put the notebook_id of someone else's notebook into the HTML request. By default Django accepts any existing pk, so without a scoped queryset this is IDOR through a form.

docs.title: Part 2 — Take apart TagForm.clean_name()
docs.text:
class TagForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def clean_name(self):
        name = self.cleaned_data['name'].strip().lower()
        ...

Task: find the full implementation of clean_name() in forms.py. Determine:

  • what clean_name checks;
  • whether tag uniqueness per user is defined at the model level (unique_together) or only in the form;
  • what happens if you remove clean_name and try to create two identical tags.

docs.title: Part 3 — Write a test for the scoped queryset
docs.text:
Goal: make sure NoteForm does not show another user's notebooks.

# Add to notes_app/tests/test_forms.py
from django.test import TestCase
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from notes_app.forms import NoteForm
from notes_app.models import Notebook

class NoteFormQuerysetScopeTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pw')
        self.bob = User.objects.create_user('bob', password='pw')
        self.alice_nb = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.alice, title="Alice NB")
        self.bob_nb = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.bob, title="Bob NB")

    def test_notebook_queryset_scoped_to_user(self):
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        notebook_qs = form.fields['notebook'].queryset
        self.assertIn(self.alice_nb, notebook_qs)
        self.assertNotIn(self.bob_nb, notebook_qs)

    def test_notebook_queryset_empty_without_user(self):
        form = NoteForm()
        self.assertEqual(form.fields['notebook'].queryset.count(), 0)

Run it:

docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_forms -v 2

docs.title: Part 4 — Add your own validation
docs.text:
Task: add a clean_title() method to NoteForm that:

  1. Strips spaces at the beginning and end.
  2. Rejects titles shorter than 3 characters.
  3. Rejects titles that start with http:// or https://.
def clean_title(self):
    title = self.cleaned_data['title'].strip()
    if len(title) < 3:
        raise forms.ValidationError("The title must be at least 3 characters long.")
    if title.lower().startswith(('http://', 'https://')):
        raise forms.ValidationError("The title cannot be a URL.")
    return title

Write a test that checks all three cases (short title, URL title, valid title).

Criterion: form.is_valid() returns False for invalid titles and True for valid ones.

forms.py contains ShareForm, a form for sharing an object with another user by email/username.
