Q.1. Where is it more correct to check tag uniqueness: in the form or in the model?

# Option A: only in the form's clean_name()
class TagForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def clean_name(self):

        ...

# Option B: unique_together at the model level

When do you need both?

What would get more complicated? - Formulate a criterion: "I choose ModelForm when..., and Form when..."

docs.text:
# Approach A: validation in the form's clean_title()
class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    def clean_title(self):
        title = self.cleaned_data['title'].strip()
        if len(title) < 3:
            raise ValidationError("Title is too short.")
        return title

# Approach B: validation in the service
def create_note(user, title, content, ...):
    if len(title.strip()) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Title is too short.")
    ...

Evaluate: - What happens if an API endpoint or a management command calls create_note directly (without the form)? - Where is title validation implemented in Notes Chat App? Find it in forms.py. - When is validation in the service mandatory? - Does Notes Chat App need validation duplicated in both the form and the service?

docs.title: ORM Lab — Query optimization
docs.text:
Goal: understand the N+1 problem and learn to use select_related, prefetch_related, and annotate on the real Notes Chat App code.

Prerequisites: a running Docker stack, familiarity with selectors.py.

docs.title: Part 1 — Take apart the existing code
docs.text:
Open notes_app/selectors.py and find the get_user_notes function:

def get_user_notes(user, *, archived=False, notebook=None, tag=None, search=None):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    qs = Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups), is_archived=archived
    ).select_related('notebook', 'group').prefetch_related('tags')
    ...

Questions for analysis:

  1. Why select_related('notebook', 'group') here and not prefetch_related?
  2. Why prefetch_related('tags') and not select_related?
  3. What happens if you remove both: how many queries will the template run for a list of 20 notes?

docs.title: Part 2 — Find the N+1
docs.text:
Open get_user_notebooks:

def get_user_notebooks(user):
    return Notebook.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
        note_count=Count('notes', filter=Q(notes__is_archived=False))
    )

Task: try removing annotate(note_count=...) and instead count the notes in Python in a loop. Measure the difference with Django Debug Toolbar or Django logging.

docs.title: Enabling SQL logging
docs.text:
Add this to settings.py (for development only):

LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'handlers': {
        'console': {'class': 'logging.StreamHandler'},
    },
    'loggers': {
        'django.db.backends': {
            'handlers': ['console'],
            'level': 'DEBUG',
        },
    },
}

Or in the Django shell:

docker compose run --rm web python manage.py shell

from django.db import connection, reset_queries
from django.conf import settings
settings.DEBUG = True

from notes_app.selectors import get_user_notebooks
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

reset_queries()
user = User.objects.first()
notebooks = list(get_user_notebooks(user))
for nb in notebooks:
    print(nb.note_count)     # already there — no extra query
print(len(connection.queries))

docs.title: Part 3 — Compare get_todo_list_detail
docs.text:
def get_todo_list_detail(user, pk):
    return TodoList.objects.prefetch_related(
        'items'
    ).get(Q(user=user) | Q(shared_with=user), pk=pk)

Task: add select_related('user') to this queryset. Explain why this can reduce the number of queries when displaying "this list belongs to user X".

docs.title: Part 4 — Independent task
docs.text:
Condition: get_group_with_members in selectors.py uses prefetch_related('user_set'). Write a test that confirms that no more than 3 SQL queries run for a group with 10 members (the group + the user_set prefetch + the .exists() membership check), not 1 + N.

# notes_app/tests/test_selectors.py (new file)
from django.test import TestCase
from django.db import connection, reset_queries
from django.test.utils import override_settings
from django.contrib.auth.models import User, Group
from notes_app.selectors import get_group_with_members

class GroupMembersQueryCountTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.owner = User.objects.create_user('owner', password='pw')
        self.group = Group.objects.create(name='testgroup')
        self.owner.groups.add(self.group)
        for i in range(9):
            u = User.objects.create_user(f'member{i}', password='pw')
            u.groups.add(self.group)

    @override_settings(DEBUG=True)
    def test_query_count(self):
        reset_queries()
        result = get_group_with_members(self.group.pk, self.owner)
        _ = list(result.user_set.all())  # materialize the prefetch
        self.assertLessEqual(len(connection.queries), 3)

Criterion: the test passes without errors and the query count is ≤ 3.

docs.title: Rules derived from the code
docs.text: Situation Solution An FK you always read together with the object select_related('field') M2M or reverse FK (one → many) prefetch_related('field') You need a count without loading the related objects annotate(n=Count('related')) The queryset is not materialized yet call list() or iterate in the template N+1 in a template {% for tag in note.tags.all %} without prefetch → N+1

docs.title: Evaluate and choose (analysis and evaluation level)
docs.text: These tasks do not have a single correct answer; what matters is the quality of the argument.

docs.title: Q.1. annotate vs a Python loop
docs.text:
Here are two implementations of counting notes in a Notebook:

# Implementation A — annotate
Notebook.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
    note_count=Count('notes', filter=Q(notes__is_archived=False))
)

# Implementation B — Python
notebooks = list(Notebook.objects.filter(user=user))
for nb in notebooks:
    nb.note_count = Note.objects.filter(notebook=nb, is_archived=False).count()

Evaluate: - How many SQL queries does each implementation run for 20 Notebooks? - Under what conditions could Implementation B be acceptable? - Where does Notes Chat App use Implementation A? Find it in selectors.py. - Write a justified choice (2–4 sentences) for this specific project.

docs.title: Q.2. select_related vs prefetch_related: where is the line?
docs.text:
# In get_user_notes:
.select_related('notebook', 'group').prefetch_related('tags')

Evaluate: - Why do notebook and group go through select_related, while tags goes through prefetch_related? - What would happen if tags used select_related? - Could notebook use prefetch_related? What would the difference in the number of queries be? - Formulate a rule: "I choose select_related when..., and prefetch_related when..."

Open selectors.py and find the get_shopping_list_detail function.

Evaluate: - Does it use select_related or prefetch_related? If not, are they needed? - How many SQL queries run when displaying 50 items of a shopping list? - Propose an optimization (or argue that the existing code is sufficient). - Write a test that measures the query count and confirms your assessment.

docs.title: Testing Lab — A regression test for a permission bug
docs.text:
Goal: learn to write a test that catches a permission bug before it reaches production. Understand the difference between TestCase and TransactionTestCase.

Related files: notes_app/tests/test_views.py, notes_app/tests/test_services.py, notes_app/tests/test_consumers.py.

docs.title: Part 1 — Read the existing IDOR test
docs.text:
Open notes_app/tests/test_views.py and find the IDOR test (an attempt to access someone else's note).

A typical pattern:

def test_cannot_access_other_users_note(self):
    alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pw')
    bob = User.objects.create_user('bob', password='pw')
    note = Note.objects.create(user=bob, title="Bob's note", content="secret")

    self.client.force_login(alice)
    response = self.client.get(reverse('notes_app:note_detail', kwargs={'pk': note.pk}))
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

Questions:

  1. Why is 404 expected rather than 403?
  2. What happens if the selector returns Note.objects.get(pk=pk) without filtering by user?
  3. How does force_login differ from client.login(username=..., password=...)?

docs.title: Part 2 — Write a regression test
docs.text:
Scenario: you suspect that ownership is not checked when a note is edited. Write a test that confirms the bug and then proves it has been fixed.

# notes_app/tests/test_views.py — add the class
class NoteEditPermissionTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice_edit', password='pw')
        self.bob = User.objects.create_user('bob_edit', password='pw')
        self.bob_note = Note.objects.create(
            user=self.bob, title="Bob's private note", content="top secret"
        )

    def test_alice_cannot_edit_bobs_note(self):
        """Alice must not be able to edit Bob's note."""
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)
        url = reverse('notes_app:note_edit', kwargs={'pk': self.bob_note.pk})
        response = self.client.get(url)
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

    def test_alice_cannot_post_to_bobs_note(self):
        """A POST to someone else's note must also return 404."""
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)
        url = reverse('notes_app:note_edit', kwargs={'pk': self.bob_note.pk})
        response = self.client.post(url, {'title': 'hacked', 'content': 'x', 'priority': 1})
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)
        # the note has not changed
        self.bob_note.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertEqual(self.bob_note.title, "Bob's private note")

Run it:

docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_views -v 2

docs.title: Part 3 — A test for deletion behavior
docs.text:
Task: write a test that checks the behavior when a note is deleted: its Reminders are deleted (CASCADE), but the Notebook remains.

# notes_app/tests/test_models.py — add the method
def test_note_deletion_cascades_to_reminders(self):
    from django.utils import timezone
    note = Note.objects.create(user=self.user, title="Test", content="")
    from notes_app.models import Reminder
    Reminder.objects.create(note=note, remind_at=timezone.now())
    note_pk = note.pk
    note.delete()
    self.assertFalse(Reminder.objects.filter(note_id=note_pk).exists())

docs.text:

Copy any test from test_consumers.py and try changing TransactionTestCase to TestCase. Run:

# services.py (approximate pattern)

note.tags.set(tags)

    alien_tag = Tag.objects.create(user=other_user, name='alien')

docs.title: Evaluate and choose (analysis and evaluation level)
Q.1. TestCase vs TransactionTestCase: which one to choose and when?
docs.text:
Scenario: you are writing a test for a new feature, reminders (Reminder). A reminder is created through a service, and then a Celery task (hypothetically) saves the result to the DB in a separate worker process.

Evaluate: - Why might TestCase fail to work for this scenario? - Find a comment or pattern in test_consumers.py that explains the difference. - If you were testing the create_reminder service without a Celery worker, which class would you choose? Why? - Is there a performance trade-off between TestCase and TransactionTestCase? Where is it noticeable?

docs.title: Q.2. Mock vs a real DB in service tests
docs.text:
Two approaches to testing create_note:

# Approach A: a real DB (TestCase)
class CreateNoteTest(TestCase):
    def test_note_is_saved(self):
        note = services.create_note(user=self.user, title='T', content='')
        self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)

# Approach B: mocked ORM
from unittest.mock import patch
class CreateNoteTest(TestCase):
    @patch('notes_app.services.Note.objects.create')
    def test_note_save_called(self, mock_create):
        mock_create.return_value = MagicMock(pk=1)
        services.create_note(user=self.user, title='T', content='')
        mock_create.assert_called_once()

Evaluate: - What does each approach actually test? What does each miss? - Approach B will pass even if create_note is broken (saves to the wrong table). Why? - Find in test_services.py which approach was chosen. Why is it the right decision for Django? - Formulate a rule: "I mock when..., and I do not mock when..."

docs.title: Q.3. Where does test coverage matter most?
docs.text:
Notes Chat App has 200+ tests in 7 files. Imagine you have 10 hours to write new tests.

Evaluate: - Which two files/modules need tests the most? Justify through the risk of failure and its cost. - In which situations does 100% code coverage not guarantee security? Give a concrete example from the project. - Compare the value of one IDOR test (test_views.py) and one __str__ test (test_models.py). Which is more critical? - Write a list of 5 tests you would add first, and explain the priority of each.

docs.title: ORM Cheatsheet — Django QuerySet API
docs.text: A quick reference for all the main Django ORM operations. The examples are adapted for notes_chat_app (models: Note, Notebook, Tag, TodoItem, User).

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Basic CRUD
  • Filtering — filter / exclude
  • Lookup Types — double underscore
  • Q objects — OR / NOT conditions
  • F objects — fields in expressions
  • Aggregation and annotation
  • select_related and prefetch_related
  • values / values_list
  • order_by / distinct / only / defer
  • Updating and deleting
  • ManyToMany operations
  • Chaining and lazy evaluation
  • get_object_or_404 and get_or_create
  • Transactions
  • Raw SQL (when the ORM is not enough)

docs.title: CREATE
docs.text:
# objects.create() — INSERT + returns the object
note = Note.objects.create(user=alice, title='Test', priority=2)

# Or: __init__ + save()
note = Note(user=alice, title='Test', priority=2)
note.save()   # INSERT INTO notes_app_note ...

# bulk_create — insert several rows in one query
Note.objects.bulk_create([
    Note(user=alice, title='Note 1'),
    Note(user=alice, title='Note 2'),
    Note(user=alice, title='Note 3'),
])
# SQL: INSERT INTO notes_app_note (...) VALUES (...), (...), (...)
# WARNING: does not call .save(), and pre_save/post_save signals do not fire

# get_or_create — find or create
tag, created = Tag.objects.get_or_create(
    user=alice, name='python',
    defaults={'color': '#3776AB'}
)
# created=True  → the tag was created (did not exist)
# created=False → the tag was found (already existed)

docs.title: READ
docs.text:
# all() — all records (lazy!)
notes = Note.objects.all()
# The SQL runs only on iteration/list()/count() etc.

# get() — exactly one object or an exception
note = Note.objects.get(pk=1)
# DoesNotExist  if not found
# MultipleObjectsReturned  if more than one is found

# first() / last() — first/last or None
note = Note.objects.filter(user=alice).first()   # None if not found
note = Note.objects.filter(user=alice).last()

# count() — number of rows (SELECT COUNT(*))
n = Note.objects.filter(user=alice).count()

# exists() — EXISTS query (the fastest way to check)
if Note.objects.filter(user=alice, is_pinned=True).exists():
    ...
# SQL: SELECT 1 FROM notes_app_note WHERE ... LIMIT 1   (very fast!)

# filter() — a selection (QuerySet)
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=alice, is_archived=False)

docs.title: UPDATE
docs.text:
# A single object
note = Note.objects.get(pk=1)
note.title = 'New title'
note.save()                              # UPDATE ... SET title=... (all fields)

note.save(update_fields=['title', 'updated_at'])
# UPDATE ... SET title=..., updated_at=...  (only the listed ones → more efficient)

# Bulk update (QuerySet.update)
Note.objects.filter(user=alice).update(is_archived=True)
# SQL: UPDATE notes_app_note SET is_archived=TRUE WHERE user_id=alice.id
# Returns the number of updated rows (int)
# WARNING: does not call .save(), and signals do not fire

# update_or_create
notebook, created = Notebook.objects.update_or_create(
    user=alice, title='Work',          # lookup fields
    defaults={'color': '#0d6efd', 'is_default': True}   # what to update/set
)

docs.title: DELETE
docs.text:
# A single object
note = Note.objects.get(pk=1)
note.delete()   # DELETE FROM notes_app_note WHERE id=1
# CASCADE automatically deletes the related Reminder objects

# Bulk delete
Note.objects.filter(user=alice, is_archived=True).delete()
# Returns (count, {model: count})
# → (5, {'notes_app.Note': 5, 'notes_app.Reminder': 12})

# Delete everything (CAREFULLY!)
Note.objects.all().delete()   # Deletes ALL notes!

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
# Several conditions = AND
Note.objects.filter(user=alice, is_pinned=True, priority=3)
# SQL: WHERE user_id=... AND is_pinned=TRUE AND priority=3

# Chaining filter() = AND
Note.objects.filter(user=alice).filter(is_pinned=True)
# SQL: WHERE user_id=... AND is_pinned=TRUE   (same result)

# exclude() = NOT
Note.objects.exclude(is_archived=True)
# SQL: WHERE NOT is_archived=TRUE   (= WHERE is_archived=FALSE)

Note.objects.exclude(priority__in=[1, 2])
# SQL: WHERE priority NOT IN (1, 2)

# Combining filter + exclude
Note.objects.filter(user=alice).exclude(is_archived=True)
# SQL: WHERE user_id=... AND NOT is_archived=TRUE

docs.title: Lookup Types
docs.text:
# ── Comparison ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(priority__exact=3)         # = 3    (same as priority=3)
Note.objects.filter(priority__gt=1)            # > 1
Note.objects.filter(priority__gte=2)           # >= 2
Note.objects.filter(priority__lt=3)            # < 3
Note.objects.filter(priority__lte=2)           # <= 2
Note.objects.filter(priority__range=(1, 3))    # BETWEEN 1 AND 3

# ── Strings ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(title__exact='Django')     # = 'Django' (case-sensitive)
Note.objects.filter(title__iexact='django')    # = 'django' (case-insensitive)
Note.objects.filter(title__contains='ang')     # LIKE '%ang%'
Note.objects.filter(title__icontains='ang')    # ILIKE '%ang%'
Note.objects.filter(title__startswith='Dj')   # LIKE 'Dj%'
Note.objects.filter(title__istartswith='dj')  # ILIKE 'dj%'
Note.objects.filter(title__endswith='.md')    # LIKE '%.md'
Note.objects.filter(title__regex=r'^\d+')     # REGEXP (case-sensitive)
Note.objects.filter(title__iregex=r'^\d+')    # REGEXP (case-insensitive)

# ── NULL ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(notebook__isnull=True)     # IS NULL
Note.objects.filter(notebook__isnull=False)    # IS NOT NULL

# ── Lists ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(priority__in=[1, 2])       # IN (1, 2)
Note.objects.filter(id__in=[1, 5, 10, 42])    # IN (1, 5, 10, 42)
# Also: you can pass a QuerySet!
active_user_ids = User.objects.filter(is_active=True).values_list('id', flat=True)
Note.objects.filter(user_id__in=active_user_ids)   # Subquery!

# ── Dates ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(created_at__year=2026)
Note.objects.filter(created_at__month=6)
Note.objects.filter(created_at__day=13)
Note.objects.filter(created_at__hour=10)
Note.objects.filter(created_at__date=date(2026, 6, 13))
Note.objects.filter(created_at__gte=datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc))

# ── FK Traversal (double __ = JOIN) ────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(notebook__title='Work')          # JOIN notebooks WHERE title='Work'
Note.objects.filter(notebook__user=alice)            # 2 levels of JOIN
Note.objects.filter(notebook__title__icontains='w') # JOIN + ILIKE
Note.objects.filter(tags__name='python')             # JOIN through the M:N junction table

# ── Reverse FK ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Find Notebooks that have at least one note:
Notebook.objects.filter(notes__isnull=False).distinct()
# Find Notebooks with HIGH-priority notes:
Notebook.objects.filter(notes__priority=Note.PRIORITY_HIGH)

docs.title: Q objects
docs.text:
from django.db.models import Q

# OR
Note.objects.filter(Q(title__icontains='django') | Q(content__icontains='django'))
# SQL: WHERE (title ILIKE '%django%' OR content ILIKE '%django%')

# AND (explicit)
Note.objects.filter(Q(is_pinned=True) & Q(priority=3))

# NOT
Note.objects.filter(~Q(is_archived=True))
# SQL: WHERE NOT is_archived = TRUE

# Combining Q and kwargs
Note.objects.filter(
    Q(user=alice) | Q(group__in=alice_groups),
    is_archived=False   # ← kwargs are always AND
)
# SQL: WHERE (user_id=... OR group_id IN (...)) AND is_archived=FALSE

# Dynamic filters — build up Q:
query = Q()
if search:
    query &= Q(title__icontains=search) | Q(content__icontains=search)
if tag:
    query &= Q(tags=tag)
notes = Note.objects.filter(query, user=alice)

docs.title: F objects
docs.text:
from django.db.models import F

# Compare a field with a field
Note.objects.filter(updated_at__gt=F('created_at'))
# SQL: WHERE updated_at > created_at

# Atomic update without a race condition:
TodoItem.objects.filter(todo_list=todo_list).update(order_position=F('order_position') + 1)
# SQL: UPDATE ... SET order_position = order_position + 1
# WITHOUT F: you need SELECT → Python → UPDATE (two queries + a race condition!)

# Using it in annotate:
from django.db.models import ExpressionWrapper, DurationField
from django.db.models.functions import Now
Note.objects.annotate(
    age=ExpressionWrapper(Now() - F('created_at'), output_field=DurationField())
)

# F in save():
item.order_position = F('order_position') + 1
item.save(update_fields=['order_position'])
# SQL: UPDATE ... SET order_position = order_position + 1

docs.title: Aggregation and annotation
docs.text:
from django.db.models import Count, Avg, Max, Min, Sum

# ── aggregate() — one value for the whole QuerySet ────────────────────────
Note.objects.aggregate(total=Count('id'))
# → {'total': 42}

Note.objects.filter(user=alice).aggregate(
    total=Count('id'),
    pinned=Count('id', filter=Q(is_pinned=True)),
    avg_priority=Avg('priority'),
    max_priority=Max('priority'),
    min_priority=Min('priority'),
)
# → {'total': 42, 'pinned': 5, 'avg_priority': 1.8, 'max_priority': 3, 'min_priority': 1}

# ── annotate() — a value for EACH row ────────────────────────────────────
Notebook.objects.annotate(note_count=Count('notes'))
# SELECT *, COUNT(note.id) AS note_count FROM notebooks LEFT JOIN notes ...
# notebook.note_count is available on every object!

# Filtered annotate:
Notebook.objects.annotate(
    active_notes=Count('notes', filter=Q(notes__is_archived=False)),
    pinned_notes=Count('notes', filter=Q(notes__is_pinned=True)),
)

# annotate + filter (filtering BY THE ANNOTATION):
Notebook.objects.annotate(
    note_count=Count('notes')
).filter(note_count__gt=5)
# Notebooks with more than 5 notes

# annotate + order_by:
Notebook.objects.annotate(
    note_count=Count('notes')
).order_by('-note_count')
# Sorted by the number of notes

# Tags with a note count (a real example from selectors.py):
Tag.objects.filter(user=user).annotate(
    note_count=Count('notes')
).order_by('name')

docs.title: select_related and prefetch_related
docs.text:
# ── select_related: ForeignKey / OneToOne → JOIN (1 query) ────────────────
# WITHOUT optimization: N+1
notes = Note.objects.all()
for note in notes:
    print(note.notebook.title)   # ← 1 SQL query per iteration!

# With select_related: 1 SQL JOIN
notes = Note.objects.select_related('notebook', 'user').all()
# SQL: SELECT notes.*, notebooks.*, auth_user.*
#      FROM notes
#      LEFT OUTER JOIN notebooks ON (notes.notebook_id = notebooks.id)
#      INNER JOIN auth_user ON (notes.user_id = auth_user.id)

# Depth (nested FK):
notes = Note.objects.select_related('notebook__user')
# Access: note.notebook.user.username — no extra SQL!

# ── prefetch_related: ManyToMany / reverse FK → 2 queries ────────────────
# WITHOUT optimization:
for note in notes:
    for tag in note.tags.all():   # ← 1 SQL query per note!
        print(tag.name)

# With prefetch_related: 2 SQL queries total (regardless of the number of notes)
notes = Note.objects.prefetch_related('tags')
# SQL 1: SELECT * FROM notes_app_note WHERE ...
# SQL 2: SELECT tags.* FROM tags
#         INNER JOIN notes_app_note_tags ON ...
#         WHERE notes_app_note_tags.note_id IN (1, 2, 3, ...)
# Django joins them in memory itself

# Reverse FK:
notes = Note.objects.prefetch_related('reminders')
# Access: note.reminders.all() → from the cache, no SQL

# ── Combining ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
notes = Note.objects.filter(user=user, is_archived=False) \
    .select_related('notebook', 'user') \
    .prefetch_related('tags', 'reminders') \
    .order_by('-is_pinned', '-priority')
# TOTAL: 3 SQL queries for any number of notes!

# ── Prefetch with a filter (Prefetch object) ─────────────────────────────
from django.db.models import Prefetch

notes = Note.objects.prefetch_related(
    Prefetch('reminders', queryset=Reminder.objects.filter(is_sent=False))
    # Load only reminders that have not been sent
)
# note.reminders.all() → only is_sent=False (from the cache)

docs.title: values / values_list
docs.text:
# values() → a list of dicts (faster than full objects)
Note.objects.values('title', 'priority')
# → [{'title': 'Test', 'priority': 1}, {'title': 'Django', 'priority': 2}]
# SQL: SELECT title, priority FROM notes_app_note

# values() with FK traversal:
Note.objects.values('title', 'notebook__title')
# → [{'title': 'Test', 'notebook__title': 'Work'}, ...]
# SQL: SELECT notes.title, notebooks.title FROM ... JOIN ...

# values_list() → a list of tuples (even faster)
Note.objects.values_list('title', 'priority')
# → [('Test', 1), ('Django', 2), ...]

# flat=True → one column = a flat list
note_ids = Note.objects.filter(user=alice).values_list('id', flat=True)
# → [1, 5, 10, 42]  (not [(1,), (5,), ...])

# A useful application:
tag_ids = note.tags.values_list('id', flat=True)
# → [3, 7, 12] — tag IDs for a form

# Checking whether an id is in the list:
if request.user.id in group.user_set.values_list('id', flat=True):
    ...

docs.title: order_by / distinct / only / defer
docs.text:
# ── Sorting ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.order_by('priority')              # ASC (ascending)
Note.objects.order_by('-priority')             # DESC (descending)
Note.objects.order_by('-is_pinned', '-priority', '-updated_at')  # Multiple

Note.objects.order_by('?')                    # Random (SLOW on large tables!)
Note.objects.order_by()                       # Remove ordering

# Sorting by FK:
Note.objects.order_by('notebook__title')      # By notebook title

# ── distinct() ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# A JOIN through tags can produce duplicates → distinct removes them:
Note.objects.filter(tags__name='python').distinct()
# SQL: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM notes JOIN note_tags JOIN tags WHERE ...

# ── Limiting (slicing) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
Note.objects.all()[:10]                       # LIMIT 10
Note.objects.all()[10:20]                     # LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10
Note.objects.all()[0]                         # The first one (LIMIT 1)
Note.objects.all()[-1]                        # ⚠️ NOT SUPPORTED! Use .last()

# ── only() / defer() — load only the fields you need ─────────────────────
# only(): load ONLY the listed fields
Note.objects.only('id', 'title', 'priority')
# SQL: SELECT id, title, priority FROM notes_app_note
# WARNING: accessing another field → an extra SELECT!

# defer(): load ALL fields EXCEPT the listed ones
Note.objects.defer('content')   # content = a large TextField
# SQL: SELECT id, title, priority, is_pinned, ... FROM ... (without content)
# Useful when content = a large text not needed in the list

# iterator() — do not cache the QuerySet (for large selections)
for note in Note.objects.filter(user=alice).iterator():
    process(note)   # Does not load everything into memory at once

docs.title: Updating and deleting
docs.text:
# ── update() — bulk update with one SQL query ─────────────────────────────
Note.objects.filter(user=alice, is_archived=False).update(
    is_archived=True
)
# SQL: UPDATE notes_app_note SET is_archived=TRUE WHERE user_id=... AND is_archived=FALSE
# Returns: int (number of updated rows)

# With F():
TodoItem.objects.filter(todo_list=todo_list).update(order_position=F('order_position') + 1)

# With a condition:
from datetime import timedelta
from django.utils import timezone
Note.objects.filter(
    created_at__lt=timezone.now() - timedelta(days=365)
).update(is_archived=True)
# Archive notes older than a year

# ── delete() — bulk delete ───────────────────────────────────────────────
deleted_count, breakdown = Note.objects.filter(
    user=alice, is_archived=True
).delete()
# deleted_count = 5
# breakdown = {'notes_app.Note': 5, 'notes_app.Reminder': 12}
# Django automatically deletes related objects (CASCADE)

# ── bulk_update() — bulk update of objects ───────────────────────────────
notes = list(Note.objects.filter(user=alice))
for note in notes:
    note.is_archived = True
Note.objects.bulk_update(notes, ['is_archived'])
# One UPDATE instead of N separate .save() calls

docs.title: ManyToMany
docs.text:
note = Note.objects.get(pk=1)
tag_py = Tag.objects.get(name='python', user=alice)
tag_dj = Tag.objects.get(name='django', user=alice)

# Add
note.tags.add(tag_py)                    # INSERT INTO note_tags (note_id, tag_id)
note.tags.add(tag_py, tag_dj)           # Several at once

# Remove a specific one
note.tags.remove(tag_py)                 # DELETE FROM note_tags WHERE note_id=... AND tag_id=...

# Check whether it is present
note.tags.filter(pk=tag_py.pk).exists()

# Clear all
note.tags.clear()                        # DELETE FROM note_tags WHERE note_id=...

# Set exactly (replace):
note.tags.set([tag_py, tag_dj])         # DELETE old + INSERT new
note.tags.set(Tag.objects.filter(user=alice, name__in=['python', 'django']))

# Reverse — notes with a tag:
tag_py.notes.all()                       # related_name='notes' on the ManyToManyField
tag_py.notes.filter(user=alice)

# Number of tags on a note:
note.tags.count()                        # SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ...

# All tags:
note.tags.all()
note.tags.order_by('name')
note.tags.values_list('name', flat=True)  # → ['django', 'python']

docs.title: Chaining
docs.text:
# A QuerySet is LAZY — SQL does not run when it is created
qs = Note.objects.filter(user=alice)    # Nothing yet!
qs = qs.filter(is_archived=False)       # Refinement
qs = qs.select_related('notebook')      # Optimization
qs = qs.order_by('-priority')           # Sorting

# The SQL runs only here:
result = list(qs)                       # ← SELECT here!
count  = qs.count()                     # ← SELECT COUNT(*) here!
first  = qs.first()                     # ← SELECT ... LIMIT 1 here!
exists = qs.exists()                    # ← SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1 here!
for note in qs: ...                     # ← SELECT here!

# A QuerySet can be passed to a template — the SQL runs during rendering
return render(request, 'template.html', {'notes': qs})
# The Django Template Engine iterates over qs → SQL here!

# Store the result in Python (run the SQL now):
notes_list = list(qs)          # Loads everything into memory
notes_tuple = tuple(qs)

# Cloning a QuerySet (does not run SQL):
cloned_qs = qs.all()           # A new QuerySet with the same parameters

docs.title: get_object_or_404 and get_or_create
docs.text:
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, get_list_or_404
from django.http import Http404

# get_object_or_404 — get() or Http404
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
# If not found → Http404 → Django 404 page
# NOT: DoesNotExist → 500 Internal Error

# With several conditions (IDOR protection!):
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)
# → 404 if the note does not exist OR belongs to another user

# get_list_or_404 — QuerySet or Http404
notes = get_list_or_404(Note, user=request.user, is_pinned=True)
# → Http404 if the list is empty

# Raising Http404 manually:
if not Note.objects.filter(pk=pk, user=request.user).exists():
    raise Http404("Нотатку не знайдено")

# get_or_create — find or create (atomic):
tag, created = Tag.objects.get_or_create(
    user=alice,
    name='python',                         # Lookup fields
    defaults={'color': '#3776AB'}          # Values used only on CREATE
)
# If 'python' already exists → created=False, tag = existing
# If not → created=True, tag = new

# update_or_create:
notebook, created = Notebook.objects.update_or_create(
    user=alice,
    title='Work',                          # Lookup fields
    defaults={'color': '#0d6efd'}          # Update these fields (always)
)

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
from django.db import transaction

# Context manager:
with transaction.atomic():
    note = Note.objects.create(user=alice, title='Test')
    tags = Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids, user=alice)
    note.tags.set(tags)
    # On an exception → ROLLBACK of both operations
# COMMIT if everything is OK

# Decorator:
@transaction.atomic
def create_notebook(user, title, is_default=False):
    if is_default:
        Notebook.objects.filter(user=user, is_default=True).update(is_default=False)
    return Notebook.objects.create(user=user, title=title, is_default=is_default)

# select_for_update — row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE):
with transaction.atomic():
    note = Note.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=1)
    # Other transactions wait until this block finishes
    note.is_pinned = not note.is_pinned
    note.save()

docs.title: Raw SQL
docs.text:
# When the ORM is not enough:

# Manager.raw() — raw SQL, returns a RawQuerySet
notes = Note.objects.raw(
    "SELECT * FROM notes_app_note WHERE user_id = %s ORDER BY priority DESC",
    [alice.id]
)

# connection.cursor() — full control
from django.db import connection

with connection.cursor() as cursor:
    cursor.execute(
        "SELECT notebook_id, COUNT(*) FROM notes_app_note WHERE user_id=%s GROUP BY notebook_id",
        [alice.id]
    )
    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    # → [(1, 5), (2, 12), ...]

# WARNING: always use parameterized queries!
# ❌ cursor.execute(f"SELECT * WHERE id = {pk}")  → SQL injection!
# ✅ cursor.execute("SELECT * WHERE id = %s", [pk])  → safe

docs.title: Quick cheatsheet
docs.text:
# READING
Note.objects.all()                              # All (lazy)
Note.objects.filter(user=user)                  # WHERE
Note.objects.exclude(is_archived=True)          # NOT
Note.objects.get(pk=1)                          # One or an exception
Note.objects.first() / .last()                  # First/last or None
Note.objects.count()                            # SELECT COUNT(*)
Note.objects.exists()                           # SELECT 1 LIMIT 1

# OPTIMIZATION
.select_related('notebook', 'user')             # FK → JOIN
.prefetch_related('tags', 'reminders')          # M:N / reverse FK → 2 queries
.only('id', 'title')                            # Load only these fields
.defer('content')                               # All fields except content

# FILTERING
filter(priority__gt=1)                          # > 1
filter(title__icontains='django')               # ILIKE '%django%'
filter(notebook__isnull=True)                   # IS NULL
filter(tags__name='python')                     # M:N JOIN
filter(Q(a=1) | Q(b=2))                        # OR
filter(~Q(archived=True))                       # NOT

# SORTING AND LIMITING
.order_by('-priority', '-updated_at')           # ORDER BY
.distinct()                                     # SELECT DISTINCT
[:10]                                           # LIMIT 10
[10:20]                                         # LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10

# AGGREGATION
.count()                                        # COUNT(*)
.aggregate(avg=Avg('priority'))                 # {'avg': 1.8}
.annotate(n=Count('notes'))                     # Per-row count

# VALUES (without full objects)
.values('title', 'priority')                    # → [{'title': ...}, ...]
.values_list('id', flat=True)                   # → [1, 2, 3, ...]

# WRITING
Note.objects.create(user=user, title='T')       # INSERT + return
Note.objects.filter(...).update(field=val)      # UPDATE (bulk)
Note.objects.filter(...).delete()               # DELETE (bulk)
note.save(update_fields=['title'])              # UPDATE (one record, selected fields)

# MANY-TO-MANY
note.tags.add(tag1, tag2)                       # INSERT
note.tags.remove(tag1)                          # DELETE
note.tags.set([tag1, tag2])                     # DELETE + INSERT
note.tags.clear()                               # DELETE all
note.tags.all()                                 # SELECT

# TRANSACTIONS
with transaction.atomic(): ...                  # ROLLBACK on an exception

docs.title: Consumer tests (WebsocketCommunicator)
docs.text:
from channels.testing import WebsocketCommunicator
from channels.db import database_sync_to_async
from django.test import TransactionTestCase, override_settings  # not TestCase!
from notes_project.asgi import application

# TransactionTestCase: the async consumer reads the DB from a separate thread.
# TestCase wraps the test in a transaction — it is invisible to that thread.
@override_settings(CHANNEL_LAYERS={"default": {"BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer"}})
class ConsumerTest(TransactionTestCase):

    def setUp(self):  # sync setUp, not asyncSetUp
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('testuser', password='pass')
        self.group = Group.objects.create(name='Test')
        self.group.user_set.add(self.user)

    async def test_member_can_connect(self):
        communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application,
            f"/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/",
            headers=[(b"cookie", b"sessionid=...")]
        )
        connected, _ = await communicator.connect()
        self.assertTrue(connected)
        await communicator.disconnect()

from django.test import TestCase, Client

class ViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.client = Client()
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('u', password='p')

    def test_anonymous_redirected(self):
        response = self.client.get('/notes/')
        self.assertRedirects(response, '/accounts/login/?next=/notes/')

    def test_authenticated_can_see_list(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.user)   # bypass form login
        response = self.client.get('/notes/')
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

    def test_post_creates_note(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.user)
        response = self.client.post('/notes/new/', {
            'title': 'Test Note',
            'content': 'Body',
        })
        self.assertRedirects(response, '/notes/')
        self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)

docs.title: Django Network Architecture — Knowledge System
docs.text: This file is the main learning map. Start here. The material is organized from network fundamentals up to Django production architecture.

docs.title: Learning map
docs.text:
LEVEL 1: Network fundamentals
    → What the Internet is
    → IP, DNS, TCP, HTTP, HTTPS
    → Sockets, Ports, Client/Server

LEVEL 2: How a request reaches Python
    → Nginx → WSGI/ASGI → Django
    → The full stack trace of a request

LEVEL 3: Django as a system
    → Project structure
    → MVT architecture
    → Request Lifecycle

LEVEL 4: Django components
    → URL Routing
    → Views (FBV/CBV)
    → Templates (DTL)
    → ORM + Migrations

LEVEL 5: Production architecture
    → Nginx + Gunicorn + Docker
    → PostgreSQL + Redis + Celery
    → Scaling, Security, Deployment

docs.title: Must read before Django
docs.text: File What it gives you network_foundation.md A systematic understanding of the Internet: IP, DNS, TCP, HTTP, HTTPS, REST API network_mermaid.md Visual diagrams: DNS resolving, TCP handshake, TLS, the full Browser→Server lifecycle

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• IP address — a unique identifier of a computer on the network
  • DNS — translates github.com into 140.82.121.4
  • TCP — guaranteed packet delivery (handshake, sequence numbers)
  • Port — indicates which program the traffic goes to (80→Nginx, 5432→PostgreSQL)
  • HTTP — a text protocol: method + path + headers + body
  • HTTPS — HTTP + TLS encryption
  • Stateless — HTTP does not remember anything between requests → Cookies + Sessions
  • Socket — a bidirectional connection endpoint between programs

docs.title: Part 2 — How a request reaches Python
The full path of an HTTP request
docs.text:
Browser
  │
  │ DNS: example.com → 203.0.113.10
  │ TCP + TLS Handshake
  │ HTTP GET /products/
  ▼
Nginx (Reverse Proxy :443)
  │ Static file? → serves it from disk (CSS, JS, PNG)
  │ Dynamic request? → forwarding
  ▼
Gunicorn (Process Manager)
  │ Manages Python workers
  ▼
Uvicorn Worker (ASGI) or uWSGI (WSGI)
  │ HTTP bytes → Python dict (environ)
  ▼
Django Application
  │ Middleware → URL Dispatcher → View → ORM → Template
  ▼
PostgreSQL / Redis
  │ SQL query → data
  ▼
HTTP Response → Gunicorn → Nginx → Browser

docs.title: URL Routing
docs.text:
File What it gives you Django_URL_Routing.md URL Dispatcher, path converters, GET/POST params, Forms, ModelForms, CreateView

Key concepts: - Route lookup goes top to bottom and stops at the first match - include() — splits routes into isolated modules - <int:pk>, <str:username> — capture variables from the URL - Static routes must come before dynamic ones

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
File What it gives you Django_Views.md FBV vs CBV, Generic Views (ListView, DetailView, CreateView), lifecycle

Key concepts: - A view is the central orchestrator: receives a request → queries the DB → returns a response - FBV (Function-Based Views) — simple, explicit, flexible - CBV (Class-Based Views) — OOP, inheritance, less duplication - Generic Views — ListView, DetailView, CreateView automate CRUD

docs.title: Templates (DTL)
docs.text:
File What it gives you Django_Templates.md DTL syntax, context system, security (XSS), template inheritance

Key concepts: - {{ variable }} — outputs variables (with automatic HTML escaping) - {% tag %} — logic: for, if, extends, block, url, csrf_token - {{ var|filter }} — transformation: |date, |truncatewords, |lower - Template inheritance: base.html → child templates via {% extends %}

docs.title: ORM and the database
docs.text:
File What it gives you Django_ORM.md QuerySet API, the N+1 problem, transactions, MVCC, production pitfalls

Key concepts: - A QuerySet is lazy: SQL runs only on iteration - select_related — a JOIN at the SQL level (for ForeignKey) - prefetch_related — a separate query + a Python join (for ManyToMany) - The N+1 problem — 1 query for the list + N queries in a loop → disaster - transaction.atomic() — atomic DB operations - MVCC — PostgreSQL keeps row versions for transaction isolation

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: File What it gives you DJANGO_MIGRATIONS.md Migration mechanics, dependency graph, common problems

docs.title: Services, Selectors & Serializers
docs.text:
File What it gives you DJANGO_SERVICES_SELECTORS.md The business layer: Services (mutations), Selectors (reads), Serializers as a transport boundary DJANGO_SERVICES.md Only services.py: stateless functions, transactions, on_commit, side effects, patterns DJANGO_SELECTORS.md Only selectors.py: CQRS-light, named queries, N+1, ORM optimizations, patterns DJANGO_SERIALIZERS.md Only serializers.py: Input/Output, validate(), fields, a pure Python function, errors DJANGO_TASKS.md Only tasks.py: Celery, broker, retry, on_commit, idempotency, patterns

Key concepts: - services.py — business logic, @transaction.atomic, on_commit for side effects - selectors.py — read-only ORM queries, select_related, prefetch_related, CQRS-light - InputSerializer / OutputSerializer — explicit contracts instead of ModelSerializer - A service knows nothing about HTTP — it is called the same way from a View, Celery or the CLI - N+1 is centralized in the Selector instead of spreading across Views and Tasks

Key concepts: - makemigrations — generates a Python plan of changes (does not change the DB) - migrate — executes SQL (changes the DB) - Dependency graph — migrations run in the correct order automatically - Migration files — committed to Git together with the code

docs.title: Technology stack
docs.text: Component Role Nginx Reverse proxy, SSL, serving static files Gunicorn Process manager for Python workers Uvicorn ASGI worker with an event loop (async) uWSGI WSGI worker (sync, traditional) PostgreSQL The main relational database Redis Cache, sessions, Celery broker Celery Background tasks (email, reports, processing) Docker Environment isolation and reproducibility

docs.title: 🎓 How to use this course — A beginner's guide
New to frontend?
docs.text: If HTML, CSS, and Django are new concepts for you, don't worry. This course is built so that you can figure things out from scratch.

docs.title: The course's mental model
docs.text:
Imagine you are building a house:

Layer Technology Analogy Foundation + walls HTML The structure of the house — where the windows are, where the doors are Paint + finishing CSS The appearance — colors, fonts, spacing IKEA furniture Bootstrap Ready-made components — no need to build a table from scratch Architect Django Templates Generates different houses from a single blueprint Automated foreman Django Ninja API — the house can "talk" to other systems Custom solutions Advanced Templates Complex systems for large projects Property manager Django Admin An interface for managing the whole house

docs.title: Three levels of understanding
docs.text:
Every topic has three levels:

  1. "What it is and how to use it" — you can write code and it works
  2. "How it works inside" — you understand what happens in the browser/Django
  3. "Architectural consequences" — you know why it should be done exactly this way and not another

The goal of this course is to bring you to level 2-3.

docs.title: How the browser processes a web page (the main context)
docs.text:
Before you start, understand this general flow:

You type a URL into the browser
        ↓
DNS translates the domain into an IP address
        ↓
The HTTP request flies to the server
        ↓
Django receives the request → urls.py → view function
        ↓
The view takes data from the database
        ↓
Django Templates generates an HTML string (SSR)
        ↓
The HTTP response flies back to the browser
        ↓
The browser parses the HTML → builds the DOM
        ↓
The browser loads the CSS → builds the CSSOM
        ↓
DOM + CSSOM = Render Tree
        ↓
Layout: the browser calculates sizes and positions
        ↓
Paint: the browser draws the pixels
        ↓
Composite: the GPU combines the layers
        ↓
You see the page! 🎉

docs.title: 🗺️ The student's path — A detailed guide
docs.text: How to use this path: - Go through the steps in order — each step builds on the previous one - For each step: read → write the code by hand → open it in the browser → play with DevTools - Don't move on to the next step until you can explain the previous one "in simple words"

docs.title: A checkpoint question for each level
docs.text:
Before moving on, ask yourself:

HTML level (steps 0-4): Can I explain how the browser turns HTML text into a visual element?

CSS level (steps 5-7): Do I understand why position: absolute behaves differently depending on the parent element?

Bootstrap level (steps 8-10): Can I explain why Bootstrap uses min-width (not max-width) in media queries?

Django Templates level (steps 11-14): Do I understand the difference between {{ }} and {% %}? Can I explain when Python dies and only HTML lives on?

Advanced level (steps 15-22): Do I understand when to use HTMX instead of JavaScript, and why?

docs.title: 📊 Dependency map between concepts
docs.text:
Read from left to right: if a concept is on the left, you need to understand it to understand the concept on the right.

HTML DOM
   ├──→ CSS Rendering Pipeline (CSSOM + DOM = Render Tree)
   │        └──→ Bootstrap Grid (uses Flexbox/CSS)
   │                 └──→ Bootstrap Components (Card, Modal, Navbar)
   └──→ HTML Forms (method, action, enctype)
            └──→ Django Forms (request.POST, is_valid(), save())
                     └──→ crispy-forms (forms + Bootstrap styling)

Django Templates (DTL)
   ├──→ Template Inheritance ({% extends %}, {% block %})
   │        └──→ SaaS Dashboard Architecture (3-level hierarchy)
   ├──→ Context Processors (global template variables)
   ├──→ Custom Template Tags (Python functions in templates)
   └──→ Jinja2 (alternative template engine, macros)

Django Ninja
   ├──→ Pydantic Schemas (data validation)
   ├──→ render() vs TemplateResponse (SSR)
   └──→ HTMX (server-driven UI, HTML fragments)
            └──→ Infinite Scroll, Live Search, Optimistic UI

Django Admin
   ├──→ ModelAdmin (list_display, fieldsets)
   ├──→ N+1 Problem (select_related, list_select_related)
   ├──→ Unfold (modern UI framework for admin)
   └──→ Dashboard Widgets (Chart, Card, Tracker, Cohort)

docs.title: 🆘 Stuck? Use this algorithm
docs.text:
A problem with HTML?
  → F12 → Elements → check the DOM (not the source! the DOM may differ)
  → HTML_BASICS §12 (common mistakes), §16 (DevTools)

A problem with CSS?
  → F12 → Elements → Styles (is the rule crossed out?)
  → F12 → Elements → Computed (which value is ACTUALLY applied?)
  → CSS_BASICS §16 (debugging algorithm), §4 (specificity)

A problem with the Bootstrap Grid?
  → Temporarily add: .row { background: rgba(255,0,0,0.1) }
  → BOOTSTRAP_5 §2 (Grid math), §3 (breakpoints)

A problem with a Django Template?
  → Django Debug Toolbar → Templates → context
  → Check: did you pass the context to render()?
  → DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP §2 (dot-lookup), §9 (anti-patterns)

A problem with a form (CSRF)?
  → F12 → Network → POST request → headers → is there a csrfmiddlewaretoken?
  → DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP §3 (csrf_token)

Way too many SQL queries?
  → Django Debug Toolbar → SQL panel
  → DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP §8, DJANGO_ADMIN_UNFOLD §5

HTMX doesn't work?
  → F12 → Network → is a request sent on interaction?
  → F12 → Console → are there any JavaScript errors?
  → ADVANCED_TEMPLATES §7

Django Admin is slow?
  → Django Debug Toolbar on the Admin list → check the SQL count
  → DJANGO_ADMIN_UNFOLD §5 (N+1), §12 (InfinitePaginator)

docs.title: Django ORM and Databases — Knowledge System
docs.text: This file is the main learning map. Start here. The material is organized from the foundations of relational databases to deep Django ORM patterns.

docs.title: Learning map
docs.text:
LEVEL 1: The relational foundation
    → Why databases exist
    → Tables, rows, columns, types
    → Primary Key, Foreign Key, Constraints
    → Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)

LEVEL 2: Architectural thinking for databases
    → Schema design: translating domains to relations
    → ACID properties and the CAP theorem
    → Relationship systems (1:1, 1:N, M:N, Referential Integrity)

LEVEL 3: SQL as a query language
    → SELECT, WHERE, JOIN (INNER/LEFT/RIGHT/FULL)
    → GROUP BY, Aggregations
    → How the database executes a query (Parsing → Planning → Execution)

LEVEL 4: Django ORM — internal mechanics
    → Models, Managers, QuerySets
    → Lazy Evaluation
    → SQL generation and traversal via __

LEVEL 5: The migration system
    → makemigrations → dependency graph → migrate
    → Schema version control

LEVEL 6: Django model architecture
    → The Field System and the object lifecycle
    → SQLite vs PostgreSQL

LEVEL 7: Debugging and performance
    → N+1 Query Problem
    → select_related vs prefetch_related
    → QuerySet.query introspection

LEVEL 8: Django Forms — the Trust Boundary
    → request.POST → QueryDict → is_valid() → cleaned_data
    → Validation Pipeline: to_python → validate → run_validators → clean_<field> → clean
    → ModelForm + save(commit=False) + M:N transactions
    → Widget architecture + Bootstrap CSS injection
    → CSRF protection + the PRG pattern

LEVEL 9: A real Django project
    → notes_chat_app/ — 9 models (User, Notebook, Note, Tag, Reminder,
                        TodoList, TodoItem, ShoppingList, ShopItem)
    → Services/Selectors architecture
    → QuerySet API: select_related, prefetch_related, F(), atomic()

docs.title: The relational foundation
docs.text:
• Primary Key — a unique row identifier (cannot repeat)
  • Foreign Key — a column that stores the PK of another table (a link between tables)
  • 1NF — all attributes are atomic; 2NF — they depend on the PK; 3NF — no transitive dependencies
  • ACID — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability (PostgreSQL guarantees this)
  • CAP — Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance (you can only have 2 of 3 in a distributed system)

docs.title: Django ORM
docs.text:
• QuerySet — lazy: SQL is executed only on iteration/slice/len/list()
  • select_related — a JOIN at the SQL level (for ForeignKey, OneToOne) → 1 query
  • prefetch_related — a separate query + a Python join (for ManyToMany, reverse FK) → 2 queries
  • The N+1 problem — 1 query for the list + N queries in a loop = disaster
  • F() — operations at the database level (no race condition)
  • transaction.atomic() — atomic blocks: all or nothing

docs.title: Relationship types in Django
docs.text: Relationship Django field SQL mechanism 1:N ForeignKey An FK in the "many" table 1:1 OneToOneField FK + UNIQUE constraint M:N ManyToManyField A junction table, automatically

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Solution N+1 queries 1000+ SQL queries per page select_related, prefetch_related save() instead of F() when incrementing Race condition: data loss F('views_count') + 1 atomic() exception trap TransactionManagementError Catch exceptions OUTSIDE the block DecimalField instead of FloatField for money Rounding errors Always DecimalField for currency No select_related in a ListView N+1 when rendering the template Always select_related for FKs cursor.execute(f"...{user_input}...") SQL injection cursor.execute("...%s", [user_input]) Note.objects.filter(...) directly in a View Violates Services/Selectors All QuerySets → into selectors.py request.POST[key] directly into the ORM Trust boundary violation Via form.cleaned_data after is_valid()

 4. DJANGO_FORMS.md                   ← Forms: Trust Boundary, Validation Pipeline, PRG
 5. POSTGRESQL_ADVANCED.md            ← MVCC, WAL, connecting via Docker, prod stack
 6. INDEXING_DEEP.md                  ← B-Tree, GIN, EXPLAIN ANALYZE
 7. TRANSACTIONS_CONCURRENCY.md       ← Deadlocks, race conditions, select_for_update()
 8. ORM_MERMAID.md (all diagrams)     ← You consolidate the whole architecture
 9. DJANGO_SERVICES_SELECTORS.md      ← The full architecture: View→Service→Selector→ORM, data flow, anti-patterns
10. DJANGO_SELECTORS.md               ← In depth: CQRS-light, N+1 in one place, naming convention
11. DJANGO_SERVICES.md                ← In depth: stateless, atomic, on_commit, Celery as transport
12. notes_chat_app/README.md           ← Step-by-step tutorial: design → PostgreSQL
13. notes_app/models.py    ← Read it as learning material with comments
14. notes_app/selectors.py ← The SELECT layer: N+1 solutions, Prefetch, annotate
15. notes_app/services.py  ← Business logic: atomic(), F(), select_for_update()
16. notes_app/forms.py     ← The Trust Boundary in practice: user-filtered FK/M:N
17. docs/reference/legacy_source/orm_laboratory_reference.md ← Interactive lab: run every cell and look at the SQL
18. notes_chat_app/README.md          ← CBV tutorial: as_view(), dispatch(), Generic Views, Mixins
19. notes_app/views.py ← CBV code: compare each class with the FBV original
20. docs/reference/legacy_source/forms_views_laboratory_reference.md ← Forms & Views lab: Trust Boundary, RequestFactory, Client

After this path you understand not just "how to write a QuerySet", but why the Django ORM works exactly the way it does, how forms protect against XSS/CSRF, how MVCC guarantees isolation, why deadlocks happen, and how to avoid them in production.

docs.title: Lesson: Django Authentication and Security — Navigation
docs.text:
Project: crispy_notes_chat_app — a notes application with a full auth stack and group access

Level: For students who are already familiar with Django basics (models, views, templates, forms)

What we study: - Authentication and authorization in Django - Sessions, cookies, the login/logout flow - Password reset and password change - Object protection (IDOR prevention) - Groups for shared access to notes - Django security settings - OWASP Top 10 and security architecture

docs.title: Step 1 — Theory: What is security?
docs.text:
📄 SECURITY_FOUNDATIONS.md

CIA Triad, Trust Boundary, Attack Surface, Defense-in-Depth, password hashing, CSRF, Least Privilege. Start here if you have never heard of cybersecurity.

docs.title: Step 2 — Authentication in Django
docs.text:
📄 AUTH_BASICS.md

  • Authentication (who are you?) vs Authorization (what are you allowed to do?)
  • Django components: User, authenticate(), login(), logout()
  • Middleware — how Django "knows" who is sending the request
  • @login_required — protecting views
  • Mermaid diagram: middleware lifecycle

docs.title: Testing in Python and Django: a beginner's guide
docs.text: After this file you will understand how to go through the lesson, which files to read first, what exactly you need to be able to do by hand, and how tests relate to a real Django project.

docs.title: 1. Why you need this
docs.text:
Imagine an ordinary situation: you added an is_archived field to the note model. Seems like a small thing. But after that, the following may break:

  • the note list;
  • the creation form;
  • the edit page;
  • the "active notes" filter;
  • access permissions;
  • a template that expected a different set of fields.

Without tests you check this by hand. You open the browser, log in, create a note, edit it, delete it, look at the admin. Once is fine. Ten times a day is already tiring. In a week you will forget to check something.

Tests are needed so that the program performs some of the checks by itself.

An important thought:

Tests do not prove that a program is perfect. They give you enough confidence to change code without being afraid of every line.

This lesson is for a student who already knows a bit of Python/Django and wants to move from "I just run the site and look at it with my eyes" to "I write checks that can be run many times".

docs.title: 2. Mental model
docs.text:
Tests are not "yet another Python syntax". They are a way of thinking.

Imagine a house with an alarm system:

  • the alarm does not build walls;
  • it does not make the doors stronger;
  • it does not catch every possible problem;
  • but when something important is breached, it gives a signal quickly.

It is the same with code. A test does not make your function correct automatically. But it pins down the expected behavior:

I expect that:
if the user is not logged in,
then the note creation page will redirect them to login.

After that, the test can be run after every change. If the behavior breaks, the test fails.

docs.title: 3. What the student should be able to do after the lesson
docs.text:
After going through the whole lesson, you should be able to:

Skill What it means in practice Write a simple unit test Test the function add(), calculate_total(), slugify_title() Run tests python -m unittest, pytest, python manage.py test Read a test failure Understand what was expected and what was received Test a Django model Check __str__, custom methods, ownership Test a Django form Check valid/invalid data, form.errors, cleaned_data Test a Django view Check the status code, redirect, template, context Test permissions Check that User A cannot edit User B's data Create test data With an object in the test, setUp(), setUpTestData(), fixtures Use mock Don't send a real email and don't call an external API Write a Selenium E2E smoke test Login -> create note -> note appears in browser Run coverage See which parts of the code were executed during the tests

docs.title: 4. A 2-minute basic example
docs.text:
Create the file math_utils.py:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

Create the file test_math_utils.py:

from math_utils import add


def test_add_two_numbers():
    result = add(2, 3)

    assert result == 5

Run:

pytest

What happened here:

Part What it does add(2, 3) Calls the code under test result Stores the actual result assert result == 5 Compares reality with the expectation pytest Finds the test and runs it

If you change the function to an incorrect one:

def add(a, b):
    return a - b

the test will fail. And that's good. The test shows: "the behavior is no longer what we expected".

docs.title: 5. How to read this lesson
docs.text:
Don't read it all like a dry book. Every file has to be worked through by hand.

The recommended way:

  1. Read the "Why you need this" section.
  2. Retype the code by hand.
  3. Run the command.
  4. Deliberately break the code.
  5. See how the test fails.
  6. Fix the code.
  7. Answer the self-check questions.

If you only read and don't run anything, the topic will seem abstract.

docs.title: 6. Testing levels
docs.text:
Level What it checks Speed Example Unit test A single function or method Very fast calculate_total(10, 2) == 20 Integration test The interaction of several parts Medium A Form saves a Model to the test database Functional test Behavior from the point of view of a scenario Medium/slow Login -> create note E2E / Selenium A real browser and the whole user journey Slow Firefox opens the site, enters data, clicks Regression test An old bug has not come back Depends on the level A test for an already fixed bug

The mental pyramid:

        E2E / Selenium
      integration tests
    unit tests

Why it is like this:

  • unit tests should be the foundation: there are many of them, they are cheap and fast;
  • integration tests check that the parts work together;
  • E2E tests give high confidence, but they are slow and fragile, so there should be few of them.

docs.title: 7. Three levels of understanding
docs.text:
Level Name What the student should understand 1 What it is and how to use it How to write a simple test and run it 2 How it works inside How the test runner finds tests, creates the test database, executes assertions 3 Architectural consequences Why code with pure functions, services, and explicit dependencies is easier to test

An example of an architectural conclusion:

Bad for testing:

def create_note(request):
    # here HTTP, the form, email, the database, and business logic are all together
    ...

Better:

def create_note_for_user(user, title, content):
    note = Note.objects.create(owner=user, title=title, content=content)
    send_note_created_email(user.email)
    return note

The second option is easier to test: you can test the service separately, the view separately, and the email separately via a mock.

docs.text: File Level What's inside What to do by hand TESTING_FOUNDATIONS.md 1 Philosophy, bug, regression, assertion, the pyramid Write your first simple test case UNITTEST_BASICS.md 2 unittest, TestCase, assert methods, setUp() Run python -m unittest PYTEST_BASICS.md 2 pytest, fixtures, parametrization, pytest-django Run pytest, write a fixture DJANGO_TESTING.md 3 TestCase, test database, Client, templates, permissions Test a model/form/view TEST_DATA_AND_FIXTURES.md 3 Test data, setUp, setUpTestData, factories Remove duplication of test data MOCKING_AND_PATCHING.md 4 mock, patch, email/API/payment Mock the email service TESTING_PRACTICE_PROJECT.md 4 A full notes project, Selenium, Docker, coverage Assemble a full test suite SELENIUM.md 3 WebDriver, By strategies, waits, StaticLiveServerTestCase, session cookie trick Run your first Selenium script CI_CD.md 4 CI/CD, GitHub Actions, django-tests.yml line by line Review a workflow run in GitHub Actions

docs.title: 10. Quick start
docs.text:
If you are short on time, take the minimal route:

  1. TESTING_FOUNDATIONS.md up to the section on AAA.
  2. PYTEST_BASICS.md up to the first fixture.
  3. DJANGO_TESTING.md up to the model/form/view tests.
  4. TESTING_PRACTICE_PROJECT.md sections 1-5.
  5. SELENIUM.md up to the section on the session cookie trick.

The full route:

  1. all files in order;
  2. retype every example by hand;
  3. deliberately break every test once;
  4. SELENIUM.md — work through WebDriver, By strategies, waits, the session cookie trick;
  5. at the end, add tests to your own Django project;
  6. CI_CD.md — automate running the tests with GitHub Actions.

docs.title: 11. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens How to fix it Reading tests as theory It seems everything is clear without running it Run every example Writing only the happy path A beginner wants to prove that the code works Add invalid data, permissions, edge cases Using Selenium for everything A browser test looks "the most real" Selenium only for critical paths Mocking everything in sight You want to isolate the code completely Mock the external boundaries: email, API, payment Chasing 100% coverage The number looks like quality Check the substance of the assertions

docs.title: 12. Practice
docs.text:
1. Create a testing_playground folder.
  2. Write a function calculate_total(price, quantity).
  3. Write a test for the normal case.
  4. Write a test for quantity = 0.
  5. Deliberately break the function and see what a test failure looks like.
  6. Explain in your own words: what exactly this test proved and what it did not prove.

docs.title: 13. Self-check questions
docs.text:
1. Why do tests increase confidence but not prove that a program is perfect?
  2. Why should unit tests be fast?
  3. Why shouldn't you write E2E tests for every small button?
  4. What is a regression test?
  5. Why does code that is easy to test often have a better architecture?

docs.title: Asynchronous Django: from the basics to production
docs.text: A series of learning documents for students of the Python/Django course. Topic: asynchronous programming — from Python asyncio to real Django projects.

docs.title: Who this lesson is for
docs.text:
This lesson is for you if:

  • you already know basic Python (functions, classes, loops);
  • you have started learning Django and understand what a view, the ORM, and request/response are;
  • you have heard the word "async" but don't yet fully understand why it exists and how it works.

After this lesson you will understand not just the syntax, but why async exists and when it is really worth using.

    B --> C["03 — ASGI<br>How does Django get async support?"]

    D --> E["05 — Async ORM<br>Why doesn't the ORM become async automatically?"]

    F --> G["07 — Async HTTP Clients<br>How do you make external requests correctly?"]
    G --> H["08 — Benchmarking<br>How do you objectively compare sync and async?"]
    H --> I["09 — Use Cases<br>When is async really needed?"]

docs.text: No. File Topic What the student will understand 1 01_sync_vs_async.md Synchronous vs asynchronous execution Why async exists and what blocking is 2 02_asyncio.md Python asyncio How a coroutine, await, and the event loop work together 3 03_asgi.md WSGI and ASGI Why Django needs ASGI for real async 4 04_django_async_views.md Django Async Views How to write an async def view and when it is useful 5 05_async_orm.md Async ORM Why an async view does not make the ORM asynchronous automatically 6 06_sync_to_async.md sync_to_async How to safely connect sync and async code in Django 7 07_async_http_clients.md Async HTTP Clients Why requests blocks and how to use httpx 8 08_benchmarking.md Benchmarking How to correctly measure sync vs async performance 9 09_async_use_cases.md Real-world Use Cases When async is really needed and when it is not

docs.title: Recommended reading order
docs.text:
Read in order — from 01 to 09. Each next document builds on the previous one.

If you only want the Django practice, skip the deep asyncio part and read: 01 → 03 → 04 → 05 → 06 → 09

docs.title: What you need to know before you start
docs.text:
• [ ] Basic Python syntax: functions, classes, loops, dictionaries
  • [ ] What a Django view is (at least minimally)
  • [ ] What an HTTP request / response is
  • [ ] What a database and an ORM are (at the level of User.objects.get(id=1))

docs.title: What you will be able to do afterwards
docs.text:
• [ ] Explain the difference between sync and async execution
  • [ ] Write an async def view in Django
  • [ ] Make async ORM queries correctly (aget, async for)
  • [ ] Wrap sync code with sync_to_async
  • [ ] Make several external API requests in parallel with httpx and gather
  • [ ] Understand when async is really needed and when it is overengineering

docs.title: Important warning
docs.text:
Async ≠ "always faster".

Asynchrony is a tool for specific tasks. If you add async def everywhere without understanding it, you are not improving the code — you are adding complexity.

This lesson will explain when this tool is really needed.

  • you have heard the words "Docker", "Nginx", "SSH", "CI/CD" and want to finally figure out what they are.

docs.title: Lesson: Django Testing — Testing Django applications
docs.text: Lesson project: crispy_notes_chat_app/ — a personal notes manager with authentication, groups, and crispy forms. We will learn to test every layer of this application.

docs.title: Why test?
docs.text:
Imagine: you added groups to notes. Everything looks fine. But 3 weeks later, after refactoring selectors.py, notes are no longer filtered by group — and you don't know about it, because checking 34 views by hand takes too long.

Tests are an automatic alarm system. They check "does everything still work" in seconds.

WITHOUT TESTS:
  git push → CI green → deploy → users see other people's notes

WITH TESTS:
  git push → CI: FAIL test_note_visible_only_to_owner → we fix it before deploying

docs.title: 🏔 The testing pyramid
docs.text:
/\
       /E2E\          ← Selenium: a real browser, a full scenario
      /──────\           (slow, fragile, expensive)
     /  Integr.\      ← Django TestClient: requests + responses + DB
    /────────────\       (medium speed, realistic)
   /    Unit      \   ← pytest/unittest: a single function/method/class
  /────────────────\     (instant, isolated, easy to write)

Rule: 70% unit → 20% integration → 10% E2E

.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows

docs.title: 01 · BASICS — What is a test?
docs.text:
A test is a function that: 1. Prepares the state (Arrange) 2. Performs an action (Act) 3. Checks the result (Assert)

# The AAA pattern (Arrange / Act / Assert)
def test_capitalize():
    # Arrange — prepare the input data
    text = "hello world"

    # Act — perform the action we are testing
    result = text.capitalize()

    # Assert — check whether the result is correct
    assert result == "Hello world"

docs.title: 02 · APPROACHES — unittest vs pytest
docs.text:
Criterion unittest.TestCase pytest Style Class + methods Functions or classes Setup setUp() / tearDown() @pytest.fixture Django django.test.TestCase pytest-django Assertion assertEqual(a, b) assert a == b Running manage.py test pytest

In Django you usually use django.test.TestCase (a subclass of unittest.TestCase) — it automatically wraps each test in a transaction and rolls back the changes after each test.

docs.title: 03 · DJANGO TESTCASE — Specifics
docs.text:
from django.test import TestCase
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

class MyTest(TestCase):
    """
    django.test.TestCase:
    - Creates a test DB (separate from the working one!)
    - Each test is wrapped in a transaction → rollback after the test
    - So you can freely create/modify/delete objects
    - Provides self.client — an HTTP client for testing views
    """

    def setUp(self):
        # setUp() is called BEFORE each test
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')

    def tearDown(self):
        # tearDown() is called AFTER each test (usually not needed)
        pass

    def test_user_created(self):
        self.assertEqual(User.objects.count(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.user.username, 'alice')

docs.title: 04 · ARCHITECTURE of crispy_notes_chat_app for testing
docs.text:
Views (HTTP layer)
    ↓ → test_views.py  (Integration: request → response → DB)
Services (business logic)
    ↓ → test_services.py  (Unit: function → result in the DB)
Selectors (queries)
    ↓ → test_selectors.py  (Unit: query → the correct objects)
Forms (validation)
    ↓ → test_forms.py  (Unit: data → valid/invalid + cleaned_data)
Models (data layer)
    ↓ → test_models.py  (Unit: constraints, relationships, __str__)

The key advantage of the services architecture: each layer can be tested in isolation.

docs.title: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
docs.text:
IDOR is when user A can read/modify an object belonging to user B.

# An example IDOR test (views):
def test_cannot_edit_other_users_note(self):
    """Alice must not edit Bob's notes."""
    bob_note = Note.objects.create(user=self.bob, title='Bob secret')

    # Alice tries to edit Bob's note
    self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass')
    response = self.client.get(f'/notes/{bob_note.pk}/edit/')

    # We expect 404 (not 200 and not 403!)
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

docs.title: Form queryset filtering
docs.text:
def test_note_form_filters_notebooks_by_user(self):
    """Alice must not see Bob's notebooks in her form."""
    bob_notebook = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.bob, title="Bob's notebook")

    form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)

    # Bob's notebook must not be in Alice's queryset
    self.assertNotIn(bob_notebook, form.fields['notebook'].queryset)

docs.title: 06 · TESTING VIEWS — Django Test Client
docs.text:
from django.test import TestCase, Client

class NoteViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass123')

    def test_note_list_requires_login(self):
        """An anonymous user is redirected to login."""
        self.client.logout()
        response = self.client.get('/notes/')
        self.assertRedirects(response, '/accounts/login/?next=/notes/')

    def test_note_create_post(self):
        """A POST to /notes/new/ creates a note and redirects."""
        response = self.client.post('/notes/new/', {
            'title': 'Test Note',
            'content': 'Content',
            'priority': 1,
        })
        self.assertRedirects(response, '/notes/')
        self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(Note.objects.first().user, self.user)

docs.title: 07 · MOCKING — When is it needed?
docs.text:
When the code interacts with external systems:

from unittest.mock import patch

class EmailTest(TestCase):
    @patch('django.core.mail.send_mail')
    def test_password_reset_sends_email(self, mock_send_mail):
        response = self.client.post('/accounts/password_reset/', {
            'email': 'alice@example.com'
        })
        # Check that send_mail was called
        mock_send_mail.assert_called_once()
