docs.title: My first Django project — Hello, Django!
docs.text:
A step-by-step guide for absolute beginners. We will create a minimal site that shows the text "Hello, Django!" in the browser and has a fully functional admin panel.

Python and Django compatibility:

Python Django 3.10 – 3.13 5.1.x or 5.2.x 3.14 5.2+ only (5.1 does not support Python 3.14)

Check your version: python --version If you have Python 3.14, requirements.txt is already configured correctly (Django>=5.2).

docs.title: What you will get in the end
docs.text:
http://localhost:8000/        →  Hello, Django!
http://localhost:8000/about/  →  This is my first Django page!
http://localhost:8000/admin/  →  Admin panel (superuser login)

docs.title: Final project structure
docs.text:
simple_django_project/        ← you are here now
├── venv/                     ← virtual environment (do not touch this folder)
├── db.sqlite3                ← SQLite database (appears after migrate)
├── hello_project/            ← Django settings package (settings, urls)
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   └── wsgi.py
├── hello_app/                ← our application (views, urls)
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── views.py              ← this is WHERE we write handler functions
│   └── urls.py               ← this is WHERE we define the app's routes
├── manage.py                 ← CLI orchestrator
└── requirements.txt          ← this file already exists

docs.title: Step-by-step instructions
docs.text:
All commands are run from the simple_django_project/ folder

Check where you are: the pwd command (Linux/Mac) or cd (Windows)

docs.title: Step 1 — Open a terminal in this folder
docs.text:
PyCharm: View → Tool Windows → Terminal — opens a terminal already in the project folder.

A regular terminal (from the root of the PY-Course-Victor-Nikoriak-23_02 repository): 

cd module_5\lesson_Django_Network_Architecture\simple_django_project

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a virtual environment
docs.text:
A virtual environment is an isolated Python environment. Packages you install here do not affect other projects.

python -m venv venv

After this, a venv/ folder will appear.

docs.title: Step 3 — Activate the virtual environment
docs.text:
You need to activate it every time you open a new terminal!

Windows (Command Prompt): 

venv\Scripts\activate

Windows (PowerShell): 

venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Linux / Mac: 

source venv/bin/activate

After activation, (venv) will appear in the terminal prompt: 

(venv) C:\...\simple_django_project>

docs.title: Step 4 — Install Django
docs.text:
upgrade pip 

python -m pip install --upgrade pip
install the dependencies 
pip install -r requirements.txt
or

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Check that Django was installed: 

python -m django --version
It should show: 5.2.x (if Python 3.14) or 5.1.x / 5.2.x (if Python 3.10–3.13)

If Django is already installed and you need to upgrade to 5.2: 

pip install -r requirements.txt --upgrade

docs.title: Step 5 — Create a Django project
docs.text:
django-admin startproject hello_project .

The dot . at the end is required! It means "create in the current folder". Without the dot, Django will create an extra nested directory.

After this command, the following will appear: 

simple_django_project/
├── hello_project/    ← new settings package
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   └── wsgi.py
└── manage.py         ← new file

docs.title: Step 5.1 — Check that the server starts
docs.text: python manage.py runserver

docs.title: Step 6 — Apply migrations (create tables in the DB)
docs.text:
python manage.py migrate

What does this do? Django includes built-in applications (django.contrib.auth, django.contrib.admin, etc.). Each of them has its own tables in the database. migrate creates these tables in the db.sqlite3 file.

WITHOUT this step, the admin panel will crash with the error: OperationalError: no such table: auth_user

After it runs, a db.sqlite3 file will appear, and in the terminal you will see: 

Applying auth.0001_initial... OK
Applying admin.0001_initial... OK
...

docs.title: Step 7 — Create administrator credentials
docs.text:
python manage.py createsuperuser

Django will ask: 

Username: admin
Email address: (you can leave it empty, press Enter)
Password: ****
Password (again): ****
Superuser created successfully.

This username/password is used to log in to the admin panel at http://localhost:8000/admin/

docs.title: Step 8 — Check that the server and admin start
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver

Open the browser: - http://localhost:8000/ → Django start page (the rocket) - http://localhost:8000/admin/ → admin panel, enter the login from Step 7

if there are problems, check whether port 8000 on your machine is taken by other applications.

Stop the server: Ctrl + C

docs.title: Step 9 — Create an application
docs.text:
A Django project consists of one or more applications (apps). Each application is responsible for a certain part of the functionality.

python manage.py startapp hello_app

A hello_app/ folder with automatically generated files will appear.

docs.title: Step 10 — Register the application in settings.py
docs.text:
Open the hello_project/settings.py file.

Find the INSTALLED_APPS list and add 'hello_app' at the end:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    'hello_app',    # ← ADD THIS LINE
]

Why is this important? Django knows about an application only if it is in INSTALLED_APPS. Without this, Django will not look for views, templates and commands in hello_app/.

docs.title: Step 11 — Write your first view functions
docs.text:
Open the hello_app/views.py file.

Instead of its current contents, write:

from django.http import HttpResponse


def index(request):
    """Home page — returns a simple text message."""
    return HttpResponse("Hello, Django!")


def about(request):
    """The 'About us' page."""
    return HttpResponse("This is my first Django page!")

What is a view function? - It accepts request (the HTTP request from the browser) - Performs some logic - Returns an HttpResponse (the response to the browser)

HttpResponse("text") is the simplest response: just text.

docs.title: Step 12 — Create URL routes for the application
docs.text:
Create a new file hello_app/urls.py and write in it:

from django.urls import path
from . import views

# app_name — required if namespace= is specified in the main urls.py
# Lets you refer to routes as: 'hello_app:index', 'hello_app:about'
app_name = "hello_app"

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),
    path('about/', views.about, name='about'),
]

What is happening here? - app_name = "hello_app" — the namespace name of this application - path('', views.index) — a request to / → calls views.index - path('about/', views.about) — a request to /about/ → calls views.about - name='index' — the route name inside the namespace

docs.title: Step 13 — Connect the routes to the main urls.py
docs.text:
Open hello_project/urls.py.

It currently looks like this: 

from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
]

Replace it with: 

from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', include('hello_app.urls', namespace='hello_app')),  # ← ADD THIS LINE
]

What is include()? include('hello_app.urls') tells Django: "for this URL prefix, read the routes from the hello_app/urls.py file".

namespace='hello_app' isolates the route names of this application. It requires app_name = "hello_app" in hello_app/urls.py — otherwise Django fails with ImproperlyConfigured.

docs.title: Step 14 — Run the server and check the result
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver

Open the browser:

URL Result http://localhost:8000/ Hello, Django! http://localhost:8000/about/ This is my first Django page! http://localhost:8000/admin/ Admin panel — enter the login from Step 7

Congratulations! Your first Django site with an admin panel works! 🎉

docs.title: The Django admin panel — a full explanation
What it is
docs.text:
Django Admin is an automatically generated web interface for managing data in the database. It is built into Django and available right after migrate + createsuperuser.

It is not a "separate project" — it is a regular Django application, django.contrib.admin, with its own models, views and templates. It is included in INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py.

http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/               ← home page (list of sections)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/user/     ← list of users
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/user/add/ ← create a new user
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/group/    ← list of groups (roles)

docs.title: Where the data is stored
docs.text:
In plain Django (without configuring PostgreSQL), the data is stored in the db.sqlite3 file.

simple_django_project/
└── db.sqlite3    ← this is the entire database (a single file!)

SQLite is an embedded database that does not need a separate server. The file is created automatically by the python manage.py migrate command.

Tables Django creates in db.sqlite3:

Table What it stores auth_user Users: username, password (hash), email, is_staff, is_superuser auth_group Groups/roles: group name auth_permission Permissions: name + which model it belongs to auth_user_groups Relationship: which user is in which group auth_user_user_permissions Relationship: a user's individual permissions django_session Sessions: who is logged in (cookie → record in the DB) django_admin_log Log of actions in the admin panel (who changed what) django_content_type Registry of content types (for the permission system) django_migrations Which migrations have already been applied

You can view the raw data with any SQLite viewer (for example, DB Browser for SQLite).

docs.title: The Users section — http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/user/
docs.text:
A list of all users in the system. Each user has:

Field What it means Username Login name Email Email address (optional) Password Stored as a hash (PBKDF2+SHA256) — never stored in plain text First/Last name First name and last name Active Whether they can log in (False = blocked) Staff status Whether they have access to /admin/ Superuser status Whether they have ALL permissions (bypasses permission checks) Groups Which groups (roles) are assigned User permissions Individual permissions (on top of group ones)

User types:

Superuser  → is_superuser=True → all permissions, no restrictions
Staff user → is_staff=True     → access to /admin/, but only with the assigned permissions
Regular    → both False         → no access to /admin/

You created a superuser with the python manage.py createsuperuser command — it has all permissions.

docs.title: The Groups section — http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/group/
docs.text:
A group = a named set of permissions (a role).

Instead of assigning permissions to each user separately, you create a group "Editors" with the required permissions and add people to it.

An example of real usage:

Group "News editors"
    ✅ news.add_article    ← can create articles
    ✅ news.change_article ← can edit articles
    ❌ news.delete_article ← can NOT delete
    ❌ news.view_user      ← does NOT see users

Group "Moderators"
    ✅ news.delete_article ← can delete
    ✅ auth.view_user      ← sees the list of users

When you add a user to a group, they automatically get all of its permissions.

Django permission format: <app>.<action>_<model>

news.add_article      ← add articles
news.change_article   ← edit articles
news.delete_article   ← delete articles
news.view_article     ← view articles
auth.add_user         ← add users

Django automatically generates 4 permissions for each model (add, change, delete, view).

docs.title: Action log (django_admin_log)
docs.text:
Every action in the admin panel is logged automatically:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ → Recent actions (right column)

It is stored in the django_admin_log table: - who performed the action (user) - what they did (added / changed / deleted) - which object (content_type + object_id) - when (action_time)

docs.title: How to add your own models to the admin
docs.text:
For your models (for example Article) to appear in the admin panel, you need to register them in hello_app/admin.py:

from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Article  # import the model

# The simple option — a single line
admin.site.register(Article)

After this, the /admin/hello_app/article/ section with automatic CRUD will appear.

docs.title: SQLite vs PostgreSQL
docs.text:
SQLite (default) PostgreSQL Startup Nothing needed, it is a file Separate server Where the file is db.sqlite3 in the project folder On the DB server Suitable for Development, learning, prototypes Production Concurrent writes Locks the file Full concurrency Configuration in settings.py 'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3' 'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql'

In the news_portal/ project, PostgreSQL is already configured via Docker.

docs.title: Summary: all commands in order
docs.text:
# 1. Go to the folder
cd module_5\lesson_Django_Network_Architecture\simple_django_project

# 2. Create and activate venv
python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate

# 3. Install Django
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 4. Create the project
django-admin startproject hello_project .

# 5. Apply migrations (creates db.sqlite3 with tables)
python manage.py migrate

# 6. Create an administrator
python manage.py createsuperuser

# 7. Check the admin panel
python manage.py runserver
# → http://localhost:8000/admin/

# 8. Create the application
python manage.py startapp hello_app
# (then we edit the files manually — steps 10–13)

docs.title: Bonus: create your first model
docs.text: Let's add a simple Note model — to understand how the Django ORM connects a Python class with a database table.

docs.title: What we will get
docs.text:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/hello_app/note/     ← list of notes
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/hello_app/note/add/ ← create a note

docs.title: Step B1 — Describe the model in models.py
docs.text:
Open hello_app/models.py and write:

from django.db import models


class Note(models.Model):
    """
    Model = a Python class that describes a database table.

    The Django ORM automatically:
        - creates the 'hello_app_note' table in db.sqlite3
        - generates the id field (PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT) automatically
        - provides an API: Note.objects.all(), Note.objects.create(...) etc.
    """

    # CharField → VARCHAR in SQL, limited string length
    title = models.CharField(
        max_length=200,          # maximum 200 characters
        verbose_name='Title'     # field name in the admin panel
    )

    # TextField → TEXT in SQL, unlimited text
    content = models.TextField(
        blank=True,              # the field is optional in the form
        verbose_name='Text'
    )

    # DateTimeField with auto_now_add=True → TIMESTAMP
    # automatically records the creation time of the record
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(
        auto_now_add=True,
        verbose_name='Created'
    )

    def __str__(self):
        # This is the string representation of the object.
        # Displayed in the admin panel instead of "Note object (1)"
        return self.title

    class Meta:
        verbose_name = 'Note'
        verbose_name_plural = 'Notes'
        ordering = ['-created_at']  # newest notes first

docs.title: Step B2 — Register the model in the admin panel
docs.text:
Open hello_app/admin.py and write:

from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Note  # import our model


@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    # Which columns to show in the list table
    list_display = ('title', 'created_at')

    # Fields for the search box
    search_fields = ('title', 'content')

docs.title: Step B3 — Generate a migration
docs.text:
python manage.py makemigrations

Django compares models.py with the current DB state and generates a file with the changes:

Migrations for 'hello_app':
  hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model Note

What was created? The hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py file is a Python script that describes the SQL that needs to be executed. It is generated automatically and does not need editing.

docs.title: Step B4 — Apply the migration to the database
docs.text:
python manage.py migrate

Applying hello_app.0001_initial... OK

Now the hello_app_note table has appeared in db.sqlite3:

-- What Django executed for you:
CREATE TABLE "hello_app_note" (
    "id"         INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    "title"      VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    "content"    TEXT NOT NULL,
    "created_at" DATETIME NOT NULL
);

docs.title: Step B5 — Check in the browser
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ — a new section "Notes" has appeared.

  1. Click "Add note"
  2. Enter a title and text
  3. Click Save
  4. The note is saved in db.sqlite3 → the hello_app_note table

docs.title: What happened under the hood
docs.text:
models.py (Python class)
    ↓  python manage.py makemigrations
hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py  (plan of changes)
    ↓  python manage.py migrate
db.sqlite3 → hello_app_note table  (the real DB)
    ↓  admin.site.register(Note)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/hello_app/note/  (web interface)

Rule: after any change to models.py, always do two steps: 

python manage.py makemigrations   # record the plan
python manage.py migrate          # apply it to the DB

docs.title: Django ORM — basic queries against the model
docs.text:
After you create a model, Django gives you a full API for working with data. Try it in the Django shell:

python manage.py shell

from hello_app.models import Note

# Create a note
Note.objects.create(title="First note", content="Hello Django!")

# Get all notes
Note.objects.all()
# → <QuerySet [<Note: First note>]>

# Filter
Note.objects.filter(title="First note")

# Count
Note.objects.count()
# → 1

# Get one
note = Note.objects.get(id=1)
note.title
# → 'First note'

# Delete
note.delete()

# Exit the shell
exit()

The Django shell is a regular Python interpreter, but with Django loaded. Very handy for quickly testing DB queries.

docs.text:
The admin is for staff only. Now let's make a public page where visitors see the list of notes.

Route: http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/ → list of all notes

The full request path: 

Browser GET /notes/
    ↓ urls.py finds the route
    ↓ views.py gets the data from the DB via the ORM
    ↓ templates/hello_app/note_list.html renders the HTML
    ↓ HttpResponse → browser

docs.title: Step C1 — Create a folder for templates
docs.text:
Django looks for templates in the <app>/templates/<app>/ folder. This duplication (hello_app/templates/hello_app/) is needed to avoid name conflicts between different applications.

The structure you need to create:

hello_app/
└── templates/
    └── hello_app/
        └── note_list.html    ← we will create this file below

Command to create the folders:

# Windows PowerShell
mkdir hello_app\templates\hello_app

# Linux / Mac
mkdir -p hello_app/templates/hello_app

docs.title: Step C2 — Create the note_list.html template
docs.text:
Create the file hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html: 

note_list.html


<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="uk">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My notes</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; max-width: 600px; margin: 40px auto; }
        .note { border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 15px; margin: 10px 0; border-radius: 4px; }
        .date { color: #888; font-size: 0.85em; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>

    <h1>Notes</h1>

    {# if notes — check whether there are notes in the list #}
    {# 'notes' is the name of the variable passed by the view (context['notes']) #}
    {% if notes %}

        {# for note in notes — loop over each note in the list #}
        {# Django renders this block for each object #}
        {% for note in notes %}
        <div class="note">
            <!-- {{ note.title }} — outputs the value of the title field of the note object -->
            <h2>{{ note.title }}</h2>

            <!--
                {{ note.content }} — the note text.
                If content is empty, nothing is output.
            -->
            {% if note.content %}
                <p>{{ note.content }}</p>
            {% endif %}

            <!--
                {{ note.created_at|date:"d.m.Y H:i" }}
                |date:"format" — a filter for formatting the date
            -->
            <p class="date">{{ note.created_at|date:"d.m.Y H:i" }}</p>
        </div>
        {% endfor %}

    {% else %}
        <!-- Shown if there are no notes -->
        <p>No notes yet.
           <a href="/admin/hello_app/note/add/">Add one in the admin panel →</a>
        </p>
    {% endif %}

    <hr>
    <a href="/admin/">← Admin panel</a>

</body>
</html>

docs.title: Step C3 — Add a view function to views.py
docs.text:
Open hello_app/views.py and add a new function (do not replace the existing ones):

from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.shortcuts import render   # ← add render to the import
from .models import Note              # ← import the model


def index(request):
    """Home page."""
    return HttpResponse("Hello, Django!")


def about(request):
    """The 'About us' page."""
    return HttpResponse("This is my first Django page!")

def note_list(request):
    """
    Page with the list of notes.

    What happens:
    1. Note.objects.all() — runs SELECT * FROM hello_app_note ORDER BY created_at DESC
       (the DESC order is set in class Meta: ordering = ['-created_at'])
    2. render() — takes the template, fills in the data (context) and returns HTML
    """

    # ORM query: get all notes from the DB
    # The result is a QuerySet: a lazy list of Note objects
    notes = Note.objects.all()

    # context — a dictionary of data we pass to the template
    # Key 'notes' → in the template: {{ notes }}, {% for note in notes %}
    context = {
        'notes': notes,
    }

    # render(request, 'path/to/template', context)
    # Django looks for the template in hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', context)

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),
    path('about/', views.about, name='about'),
    path('notes/', views.note_list, name='note_list'),   # ← ADD THIS LINE
]

    path('notes/', views.note_list, name='note_list'),

docs.title: The full path of the GET /notes/ request, step by step
docs.text:
1. Browser: GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/

2. Django: reads ROOT_URLCONF = 'hello_project.urls'
           hello_project/urls.py → include('hello_app.urls')
           hello_app/urls.py → path('notes/', views.note_list)

3. views.note_list(request) is called:
           Note.objects.all()
           → SQL: SELECT * FROM hello_app_note ORDER BY created_at DESC
           → returns QuerySet [<Note: ...>, ...]

4. render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': queryset})
           Django finds the template: hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html
           Fills in the data: {% for note in notes %} → HTML lines

5. HttpResponse(HTML) → the browser renders the page

This is Django's MVT architecture: - M (Model) — Note in models.py — stores the data - V (View) — note_list in views.py — gets the data, decides what to show - T (Template) — note_list.html — renders the HTML

docs.title: Bonus 3:  Django Debug Toolbar — Runtime Introspection for the Django ORM
What Django Debug Toolbar is
docs.text:
django-debug-toolbar is a middleware-based debugging system for Django that lets you see:

  • SQL queries
  • ORM performance
  • timings
  • middleware execution
  • template rendering
  • cache usage
  • headers
  • signals
  • profiling information

The toolbar is added right into the browser as a floating debug panel.

docs.title: The architectural idea
docs.text:
Django Debug Toolbar is:

Runtime Introspection Layer

That is, a system that:

  • intercepts the request/response lifecycle
  • listens to ORM queries
  • measures performance
  • shows the internal state of the Django runtime

docs.title: Why this is very important
docs.text:
The ORM in Django is "lazy".

For example:

posts = Post.objects.all()

The SQL is NOT executed yet.

The toolbar lets you see:

  • when the SQL was actually executed
  • how many queries there were
  • which joins there were
  • where the N+1 problem occurs

docs.title: ORM → SQL Visibility
docs.text:
Without the toolbar:

posts = Post.objects.all()

looks like "magic".

docs.title: With the toolbar
docs.text:
You see the real SQL:

SELECT * FROM posts;

docs.title: N+1 Problem
docs.text:
For example:

for post in posts:
    print(post.author.name)

The toolbar will show:

101 queries executed

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
The ORM runs:

SELECT * FROM author WHERE id=...

for each post separately.

docs.title: This is already ORM optimization engineering
docs.text:
The toolbar effectively teaches:

  • select_related()
  • prefetch_related()
  • annotate()
  • lazy evaluation
  • query planning

docs.title: Middleware Order Important
docs.text:
The toolbar middleware should be placed:

  • as early as possible
  • but AFTER middleware that changes the response encoding

For example:

GZipMiddleware
↓
DebugToolbarMiddleware

docs.title: 5. INTERNAL_IPS
docs.text:
The toolbar is shown only for internal IPs.

INTERNAL_IPS = [
    "127.0.0.1",
]

docs.title: SQL Panel
docs.text:
Shows:

  • all SQL queries
  • execution time
  • duplicated queries
  • stack traces

docs.title: Templates Panel
docs.text:
Shows:

  • which templates were rendered
  • inheritance chain
  • context variables

docs.title: Cache Panel
docs.text:
Shows:

  • cache hits
  • cache misses

docs.title: Headers Panel
docs.text:
Shows:

  • request headers
  • response headers

docs.title: Signals Panel
docs.text: Shows Django signals.

docs.title: SQL Panel
docs.text: It is the one that makes the ORM "visible".

docs.title: Lazy QuerySets
docs.text:
posts = Post.objects.all()

The SQL is not executed yet.

docs.title: SQL trigger
docs.text:
The SQL is executed only when:

list(posts)

for p in posts

posts[0]

docs.text:
Python code
↓
ORM
↓
REAL SQL
↓
Database Cost

docs.title: Bootstrap Notes — Beautiful notes with Django + Bootstrap 5
docs.text:
A step-by-step guide for students. We will turn a simple Django project (with bare HTML) into a full-fledged Bootstrap 5 application with a Navbar, cards, forms, alerts and an admin panel.

Prerequisites: This project is a continuation of simple_django_project. You should already understand what a View, URL, Model and Template are. If not, first go through module_5/lesson_Django_Network_Architecture/simple_django_project/README.md.

# At the end of the file add:
INTERNAL_IPS = ['127.0.0.1']

# Bootstrap 5 messages integration
from django.contrib.messages import constants as messages
MESSAGE_TAGS = {
    messages.DEBUG:   'secondary',
    messages.INFO:    'info',
    messages.SUCCESS: 'success',
    messages.WARNING: 'warning',
    messages.ERROR:   'danger',
}

What is MESSAGE_TAGS? Django Messages (flash messages after a POST) have their own levels: success, error, etc. A Bootstrap Alert uses alert-success, alert-danger. MESSAGE_TAGS maps between them. More details: BOOTSTRAP_5.md §4 — Bootstrap Alerts.

Django looks for templates in <app>/templates/. We will create base.html outside hello_app/templates/hello_app/ — directly in hello_app/templates/, so that it is available globally.

docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="uk">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>{% block title %}Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %}</title>

    <!--
        Bootstrap 5 CSS — included in <head>.
        Why: the browser reads CSS before rendering the page body.
        If you include it at the end, you get a "flash of unstyled content".
        Theory: CSS_BASICS.md §0 — Rendering Pipeline.
    -->
    <link rel="stylesheet"
          href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css"
          integrity="sha384-QWTKZyjpPEjISv5WaRU9OFeRpok6YctnYmDr5pNlyT2bRjXh0JMhjY6hW+ALEwIH"
          crossorigin="anonymous">

    <!-- Bootstrap Icons — a separate icon library -->
    <link rel="stylesheet"
          href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/font/bootstrap-icons.css">

    <!-- Slot for additional CSS on specific pages -->
    {% block extra_css %}{% endblock %}
</head>
<body class="bg-light d-flex flex-column min-vh-100">
<!--
    Sticky Footer — three Bootstrap classes solve the "floating" footer problem.
    d-flex flex-column — body becomes a vertical flex container.
    min-vh-100 — body always takes at least 100% of the window height.
    flex-grow-1 on <main> below — main takes all the free space between nav and footer.
    Theory: CSS_BASICS.md §9 — Flexbox, Bootstrap §3 — Utility Classes.
-->

    <!--
        NAVBAR — the Bootstrap navigation component.
        navbar-expand-lg: horizontal on large screens, a hamburger on small ones.
        Theory: BOOTSTRAP_5.md §5 — Navbar, Responsive collapse.
    -->
    <nav class="navbar navbar-expand-lg navbar-dark bg-dark shadow-sm">
        <div class="container">

            <!-- Brand — site name / logo -->
            <a class="navbar-brand fw-bold" href="{% url 'hello_app:note_list' %}">
                <i class="bi bi-journal-text me-2"></i>Bootstrap Notes
            </a>

            <!-- Hamburger button for mobile (xs/sm/md) -->
            <button class="navbar-toggler" type="button"
                    data-bs-toggle="collapse"
                    data-bs-target="#navbarNav"
                    aria-controls="navbarNav"
                    aria-expanded="false"
                    aria-label="Open menu">
                <span class="navbar-toggler-icon"></span>
            </button>

            <!-- Navigation links (hidden on mobile) -->
            <div class="collapse navbar-collapse" id="navbarNav">
                <ul class="navbar-nav me-auto">
                    <li class="nav-item">
                        <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'hello_app:note_list' %}">
                            <i class="bi bi-list-ul me-1"></i>All notes
                        </a>
                    </li>
                    <li class="nav-item">
                        <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'hello_app:note_create' %}">
                            <i class="bi bi-plus-circle me-1"></i>New note
                        </a>
                    </li>
                </ul>
                <ul class="navbar-nav">
                    <li class="nav-item">
                        <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'admin:index' %}">
                            <i class="bi bi-gear me-1"></i>Admin
                        </a>
                    </li>
                </ul>
            </div>

        </div>
    </nav>

    <!-- Main content — flex-grow-1 stretches main between the navbar and the footer -->
    <main class="container my-4 flex-grow-1">

        <!--
            Django Messages → Bootstrap Alerts.
            messages — a Context Processor that is automatically available in all templates.
            message.tags → 'success'/'danger'/'warning' (mapping from MESSAGE_TAGS in settings.py).
            Theory: BOOTSTRAP_5.md §4 — Alert, DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §8 — Bootstrap Forms.
        -->
        {% if messages %}
            {% for message in messages %}
            <div class="alert alert-{{ message.tags }} alert-dismissible fade show" role="alert">
                <i class="bi bi-{% if message.tags == 'success' %}check-circle{% elif message.tags == 'danger' %}exclamation-triangle{% else %}info-circle{% endif %} me-2"></i>
                {{ message }}
                <button type="button" class="btn-close" data-bs-dismiss="alert"
                        aria-label="Close"></button>
            </div>
            {% endfor %}
        {% endif %}

        <!--
    Slot for the content of a specific page.
    Each child page inserts its own content here.
    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §4 — Template Inheritance.
         -->
        {% block content %}{% endblock %}

    </main>

    <!-- Footer -->
    <footer class="bg-dark text-center text-white-50 py-3 mt-5">
        <small>Bootstrap Notes © 2026 — a learning project</small>
    </footer>

    <!--
        Bootstrap JS Bundle (includes Popper.js).
        defer — loaded after the HTML.
        Why: Modal, Navbar collapse and Toast need JS.
        Theory: BOOTSTRAP_5.md §8 — Bootstrap JS Architecture.
    -->
    <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"
            integrity="sha384-YvpcrYf0tY3lHB60NNkmXc4s9bIOgUxi8T/jzmAgD0SnMiKKmFClVgaFa11iGj0E"
            crossorigin="anonymous" defer></script>

    <!-- Slot for page-specific JS -->
    {% block extra_js %}{% endblock %}

</body>
</html>

The key idea of base.html: One file contains the Bootstrap CDN, Navbar, Footer and Messages. All other templates only write {% extends 'base.html' %} and fill in {% block content %}. Changing the Navbar or Footer in one place — automatically applies everywhere.

docs.title: Step C3 — Sticky Footer (the footer is always at the bottom)
docs.text:
Problem: if a page has little content (for example, 1–2 notes or an empty list), the footer "hangs" in the middle of the page, with empty background below it.

Cause: by default <body> is exactly as tall as its content. When the content is shorter than the window height, the body ends, the footer comes after it, and the rest of the window is empty background.

Solution — a Sticky Footer with Bootstrap Flexbox:

<!-- BEFORE: -->
<body class="bg-light">
    ...
    <main class="container my-4">

<!-- AFTER: -->
<body class="bg-light d-flex flex-column min-vh-100">
    ...
    <main class="container my-4 flex-grow-1">

What these classes do:

Class Where What it does d-flex <body> Turns body into a flex container flex-column <body> Flex direction: vertical (navbar → main → footer) min-vh-100 <body> Body takes at least 100% of the window height (100vh) flex-grow-1 <main> Main stretches over all the free space between the navbar and footer

Visual diagram:

┌────────────────────── body (min-vh-100) ──────────────────────┐
│  <nav>        — fixed height                                  │
│  <main>       — flex-grow-1: takes all that is left    ↕↕↕   │
│  <footer>     — fixed height, always at the bottom            │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Theory: CSS_BASICS.md §9 — Flexbox: flex-direction, flex-grow, min-height. This is a standard pattern for any site where the footer must be at the bottom of the page.

docs.title: Phase D — The list of notes with Bootstrap Cards
docs.text: Theory: Read BOOTSTRAP_5.md §6 — Card Grid, row-cols-*, h-100. Read CSS_BASICS.md §9–10 — Flexbox and Grid (Bootstrap is built on them).

docs.title: Step D1 — Rewrite hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html
docs.text:
{% extends 'hello_app/base.html' %}
{% load django_bootstrap5 %}

{% block title %}My notes — Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

<!--
    Page Header.
    Here we show the page title, the number of notes
    and the button for creating a new note.
-->
<div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-4">
    <div>
        <h1 class="h2 mb-1">
            <i class="bi bi-journal-text me-2 text-primary"></i>
            My notes
        </h1>

        <!--
            The length filter counts the number of items in the notes list.
            We do not write Django syntax in curly braces here, because HTML comments
            are still processed by the Django template engine.
        -->
        <p class="text-muted mb-0">
            {{ notes|length }} notes
        </p>
    </div>

    <a href="{% url 'hello_app:note_create' %}" class="btn btn-primary">
        <i class="bi bi-plus-lg me-1"></i>
        New note
    </a>
</div>

<!--
    Condition: if the notes list is not empty, show the card grid.
    If the list is empty, the Empty State below will be shown.
-->
{% if notes %}

    <!--
        Bootstrap Grid:
        row-cols-1 — one column on small screens;
        row-cols-md-2 — two columns on medium screens;
        row-cols-lg-3 — three columns on large screens;
        g-4 — gaps between cards.
    -->
    <div class="row row-cols-1 row-cols-md-2 row-cols-lg-3 g-4">

        <!--
            The loop over notes starts below.
            Each note is rendered as a separate Bootstrap Card.
            IMPORTANT: do not write a Django for tag in this comment.
        -->
        {% for note in notes %}
        <div class="col">

            <!--
                Card — the Bootstrap component for a single note.
                h-100 makes cards the same height within a row.
                shadow-sm adds a light shadow.
            -->
            <div class="card h-100 shadow-sm">

                <div class="card-body">

                    <!--
                        The note title is a link to the detail page.
                    -->
                    <h5 class="card-title">
                        <a href="{% url 'hello_app:note_detail' pk=note.pk %}"
                           class="text-decoration-none text-dark">
                            {{ note.title }}
                        </a>
                    </h5>

                    <!--
                        If the note has content, show a short preview.
                        truncatechars cuts long text to the given number of characters.
                    -->
                    {% if note.content %}
                    <p class="card-text text-muted small">
                        {{ note.content|truncatechars:100 }}
                    </p>
                    {% else %}
                    <p class="card-text text-muted small fst-italic">
                        No content.
                    </p>
                    {% endif %}

                </div>

                <!--
                    Card footer: creation date and action buttons.
                    timesince shows how much time has passed since creation.
                -->
                <div class="card-footer bg-transparent d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
                    <small class="text-muted">
                        <i class="bi bi-clock me-1"></i>
                        {{ note.created_at|timesince }} ago
                    </small>

                    <!--
                        A group of small buttons: edit and delete.
                    -->
                    <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm">
                        <a href="{% url 'hello_app:note_edit' pk=note.pk %}"
                           class="btn btn-outline-secondary"
                           title="Edit">
                            <i class="bi bi-pencil"></i>
                        </a>

                        <a href="{% url 'hello_app:note_delete' pk=note.pk %}"
                           class="btn btn-outline-danger"
                           title="Delete">
                            <i class="bi bi-trash"></i>
                        </a>
                    </div>
                </div>

            </div>
        </div>
        {% endfor %}

    </div>

{% else %}

    <!--
        Empty State.
        Shown when there are no notes in the database yet.
    -->
    <div class="text-center py-5">
        <i class="bi bi-journal-x display-1 text-muted d-block mb-3"></i>

        <h4 class="text-muted">
            No notes yet
        </h4>

        <p class="text-muted">
            Create your first note and it will appear here.
        </p>

        <a href="{% url 'hello_app:note_create' %}" class="btn btn-primary mt-2">
            <i class="bi bi-plus-lg me-1"></i>
            Create a note
        </a>
    </div>

{% endif %}

{% endblock %}

docs.text: Theory: Read BOOTSTRAP_5.md §9 — Bootstrap Forms. Read DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §7 — Bootstrap Forms in Django. Read HTML_BASICS.md §5 — HTML Forms, input types.

docs.title: Step E1 — Create hello_app/forms.py
docs.text:
Create a new file hello_app/forms.py:

from django import forms
from .models import Note


class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    """
    ModelForm — automatically generates form fields from the Note model.
    Django takes the field types from the model and generates the matching HTML inputs.
    CharField(max_length=200) → <input type="text" maxlength="200">
    TextField → <textarea>

    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §7 — ModelForm internals.
    """

    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ['title', 'content']  # which fields to include in the form
        widgets = {
            # Add the Bootstrap class='form-control' to each field
            # Without this Django renders bare HTML without Bootstrap styles
            'title': forms.TextInput(attrs={
                'class': 'form-control',
                'placeholder': 'Enter the note title...',
                'autofocus': True,
            }),
            'content': forms.Textarea(attrs={
                'class': 'form-control',
                'rows': 6,
                'placeholder': 'Note text...',
            }),
        }
        labels = {
            'title': 'Title',
            'content': 'Content',
        }

docs.title: Step E2 — Updating views.py
docs.text:
Open hello_app/views.py and add the new view functions:

from django.shortcuts import render, redirect, get_object_or_404
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.contrib import messages   # ← Django Messages

from .models import Note
from .forms import NoteForm           # ← our form


def index(request):
    """Redirect from / to /notes/."""
    return redirect('hello_app:note_list')


def note_list(request):
    """List of all notes."""
    notes = Note.objects.all()
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})


def note_detail(request, pk):
    """
    Note detail.
    get_object_or_404: if a note with this pk does not exist → returns 404 (not 500).
    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §6 — HttpRequest/Response.
    """
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_detail.html', {'note': note})


def note_create(request):
    """
    The PRG (Post/Redirect/Get) pattern:
    GET  → show an empty form
    POST → process, save → redirect to the list (so that F5 does not duplicate)
    Without a redirect: F5 after a POST repeats the save → a duplicate note.
    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §8 — PRG Pattern.
    """
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            note = form.save()
            # Django Message — the flash message is displayed after the redirect
            messages.success(request, f'Note "{note.title}" created successfully!')
            return redirect('hello_app:note_list')
    else:
        form = NoteForm()

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_form.html', {
        'form': form,
        'action': 'Create',
        'title': 'New note',
    })


def note_edit(request, pk):
    """Editing a note — the same PRG, but the form is initialized with instance=note."""
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, instance=note)
        if form.is_valid():
            form.save()
            messages.success(request, f'Note "{note.title}" updated!')
            return redirect('hello_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)
    else:
        form = NoteForm(instance=note)  # instance fills the form with the current data

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_form.html', {
        'form': form,
        'note': note,
        'action': 'Save changes',
        'title': f'Edit: {note.title}',
    })


def note_delete(request, pk):
    """
    Deletion via POST (not GET!).
    GET → confirmation page.
    POST → delete → redirect.
    Never delete via GET — it is dangerous (CSRF, prefetch).
    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §8 — Security, CSRF.
    """
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        title = note.title
        note.delete()
        messages.warning(request, f'Note "{title}" deleted.')
        return redirect('hello_app:note_list')

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_confirm_delete.html', {'note': note})

docs.text:
Open hello_app/urls.py and replace its contents:

from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = 'hello_app'

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),
    path('notes/', views.note_list, name='note_list'),
    path('notes/new/', views.note_create, name='note_create'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/', views.note_detail, name='note_detail'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/edit/', views.note_edit, name='note_edit'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/delete/', views.note_delete, name='note_delete'),
]

What is <int:pk>? A path converter — it captures an integer from the URL and passes it to the view as the pk argument. /notes/42/ → pk=42 → Note.objects.get(pk=42).

docs.title: Step F2 — hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_form.html
docs.text:
{% extends 'hello_app/base.html' %}

{% load django_bootstrap5 %}

{% block title %}{{ title }} — Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

<div class="row justify-content-center">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-8 col-lg-6">

        <div class="card shadow-sm">
            <div class="card-header">
                <h1 class="h4 mb-0">
                    <i class="bi bi-{% if note %}pencil{% else %}plus-circle{% endif %} me-2"></i>
                    {{ title }}
                </h1>
            </div>

            <div class="card-body">
                <!--
                    {% csrf_token %} — REQUIRED in every POST form!
                    Without it Django returns 403 Forbidden.
                    CSRF: Cross-Site Request Forgery protection.
                    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §8 — CSRF.
                -->
                <form method="post" novalidate>
                    {% csrf_token %}

                    <!--
                        Option 1 — manual form rendering (Bootstrap classes explicitly).
                        Each field: label → input → errors.
                        Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §7 — Manual Form.
                    -->
                    {% for field in form %}
                    <div class="mb-3">
                        <label for="{{ field.id_for_label }}" class="form-label fw-semibold">
                            {{ field.label }}
                            {% if field.field.required %}
                                <span class="text-danger" title="Required field">*</span>
                            {% endif %}
                        </label>

                        <!--
                            field is a Django BoundField.
                            When rendered, it uses the widget from forms.py.
                            We already added class='form-control' in NoteForm.
                            Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §7 — Widget attrs.
                        -->
                        {{ field }}

                        {% if field.help_text %}
                            <div class="form-text text-muted">{{ field.help_text }}</div>
                        {% endif %}

                        <!--
                            Validation errors — the Bootstrap is-invalid class.
                            field.errors — a list of error strings.
                        -->
                        {% for error in field.errors %}
                            <div class="invalid-feedback d-block">
                                <i class="bi bi-exclamation-circle me-1"></i>{{ error }}
                            </div>
                        {% endfor %}
                    </div>
                    {% endfor %}

                    <!-- Form buttons -->
                    <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center pt-2">
                        <a href="{% if note %}{% url 'hello_app:note_detail' pk=note.pk %}{% else %}{% url 'hello_app:note_list' %}{% endif %}"
                           class="btn btn-outline-secondary">
                            <i class="bi bi-x-lg me-1"></i>Cancel
                        </a>
                        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">
                            <i class="bi bi-check-lg me-1"></i>{{ action }}
                        </button>
                    </div>
                </form>
            </div>
        </div>

    </div>
</div>

{% endblock %}

Option 2 — automatic rendering with django-bootstrap5:

Instead of the manual {% for field in form %} loop, you can write a single line: 

{% load django_bootstrap5 %}
{% bootstrap_form form %}
The django-bootstrap5 package automatically adds all Bootstrap classes, labels and errors. Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §7 — django-bootstrap5.

{{% extends 'hello_app/base.html' %}

{% block title %}Delete note — Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

<div class="row justify-content-center">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-6">

        <!--
            A Bootstrap Alert with the danger class — a warning.
            Theory: BOOTSTRAP_5.md §4 — Alerts.
        -->
        <div class="card border-danger shadow-sm">
            <div class="card-header bg-danger text-white">
                <h4 class="mb-0">
                    <i class="bi bi-exclamation-triangle me-2"></i>
                    Confirm deletion
                </h4>
            </div>
            <div class="card-body">
                <p class="mb-3">
                    Do you really want to delete the note
                    <strong>"{{ note.title }}"</strong>?
                </p>
                <p class="text-danger small">
                    <i class="bi bi-info-circle me-1"></i>
                    This action cannot be undone.
                </p>

                <!--
                    Deletion via POST — never via GET.
                    A GET can be executed automatically (prefetch, bots).
                    A POST requires a deliberate user action + CSRF protection.
                    Theory: DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §8 — HTTP Methods.
                -->
                <form method="post">
                    {% csrf_token %}
                    <div class="d-flex gap-2">
                        <a href="{% url 'hello_app:note_detail' pk=note.pk %}"
                           class="btn btn-outline-secondary flex-fill">
                            <i class="bi bi-x-lg me-1"></i>Cancel
                        </a>
                        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-danger flex-fill">
                            <i class="bi bi-trash me-1"></i>Delete
                        </button>
                    </div>
                </form>
            </div>
        </div>

    </div>
</div>

{% endblock %}

docs.title: Phase G — Unfold Admin
docs.text:
What is django-unfold? A library that replaces the standard Django Admin with a Tailwind-CSS-styled interface. It requires no changes to the logic — it only changes inheritance and adds an UNFOLD dictionary to settings.py.

Theory: Read DJANGO_ADMIN_UNFOLD.md §2 — ModelAdmin, §7 — UNFOLD config, sidebar navigation.

docs.title: Step G1 — Updating hello_project/settings.py
docs.text:
Add the UNFOLD dictionary after MESSAGE_TAGS:

from django.urls import reverse_lazy
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

UNFOLD = {
    "SITE_TITLE": "Bootstrap Notes",       # title in <title>
    "SITE_HEADER": "Bootstrap Notes",      # large header in the sidebar
    "SITE_SUBHEADER": "Notes management",
    "SHOW_HISTORY": True,
    "SHOW_VIEW_ON_SITE": False,
    "SHOW_BACK_BUTTON": True,
    "SIDEBAR": {
        "show_search": False,
        "show_all_applications": False,
        "navigation": [
            {
                "title": _("Content"),
                "separator": False,
                "collapsible": False,
                "items": [
                    {
                        "title": _("Notes"),
                        "icon": "description",  # Material Symbol icon
                        "link": reverse_lazy("admin:hello_app_note_changelist"),
                    },
                ],
            },
            {
                "title": _("Access"),
                "separator": True,
                "collapsible": False,
                "items": [
                    {
                        "title": _("Users"),
                        "icon": "people",
                        "link": reverse_lazy("admin:auth_user_changelist"),
                    },
                    {
                        "title": _("Groups"),
                        "icon": "group",
                        "link": reverse_lazy("admin:auth_group_changelist"),
                    },
                ],
            },
        ],
    },
}

icon — the name of an icon from Google Material Symbols. Write the name in lowercase with underscores: description, people, add_circle.

docs.title: Step G2 — Updating hello_app/admin.py
docs.text:
from django.contrib import admin
from django.contrib.auth.admin import UserAdmin as BaseUserAdmin
from django.contrib.auth.admin import GroupAdmin as BaseGroupAdmin
from django.contrib.auth.models import User, Group
from django.utils.html import format_html

# unfold.admin.ModelAdmin replaces django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin
from unfold.admin import ModelAdmin
from unfold.forms import AdminPasswordChangeForm, UserChangeForm, UserCreationForm

from .models import Note


# Django registers User and Group without Unfold — unregister them and register again
admin.site.unregister(User)
admin.site.unregister(Group)


@admin.register(User)
class UserAdmin(BaseUserAdmin, ModelAdmin):
    form = UserChangeForm
    add_form = UserCreationForm
    change_password_form = AdminPasswordChangeForm


@admin.register(Group)
class GroupAdmin(BaseGroupAdmin, ModelAdmin):
    pass


@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ['title', 'short_content', 'created_at']
    search_fields = ['^title', 'content']
    list_filter = ['created_at']
    readonly_fields = ['created_at']
    ordering = ['-created_at']
    list_per_page = 20

    @admin.display(description='Content (preview)')
    def short_content(self, obj):
        if not obj.content:
            return '—'
        preview = obj.content[:80] + ('...' if len(obj.content) > 80 else '')
        return format_html('<span style="color:#6b7280">{}</span>', preview)

The key difference from the standard Django Admin:

Before (Django Admin) After (Unfold Admin) class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin) class NoteAdmin(ModelAdmin) No User/Group re-registration unregister + register with Unfold forms Branding: admin.site.site_header = ... Branding: UNFOLD["SITE_HEADER"] in settings.py No sidebar navigation UNFOLD["SIDEBAR"]["navigation"]

docs.title: Phase H — Django Debug Toolbar (SQL panel)
docs.text:
Theory: Read DJANGO_TEMPLATES_BOOTSTRAP.md §9 — DjDT. Read DJANGO_ADMIN_UNFOLD.md §5 — Query Architecture, N+1.

The toolbar is already connected (we added it in Settings and URLs). Go to http://localhost:8000/notes/ — a black DJDT panel will appear on the right.

What to explore:

Panel What to look for SQL How many queries for /notes/? There should be 1–2 Templates Which templates were used (base.html + note_list.html) Headers Request/Response headers Time Template rendering time

If the toolbar does not appear: 1. DEBUG = True in settings.py? 2. Is INTERNAL_IPS = ['127.0.0.1'] present in settings.py? 3. 'debug_toolbar' in INSTALLED_APPS? 4. debug_toolbar_urls() in urls.py? 5. Does the page have a <body> tag? (Needed to inject the panel)

docs.text: Error Cause Solution TemplateDoesNotExist: base.html base.html is not where Django looks for it The file must be in hello_app/templates/base.html (not in hello_app/templates/hello_app/) NoReverseMatch: 'note_create' The URL name is not registered or the namespace is wrong Check hello_app/urls.py and app_name = 'hello_app' 403 Forbidden after a POST {% csrf_token %} is missing in the form Add {% csrf_token %} inside the <form> Bootstrap styles are not applied class='form-control' was not added to the widget Check NoteForm.Meta.widgets in forms.py Debug Toolbar does not appear Not all conditions are met Check the checklist in Phase H IntegrityError on save title cannot be empty Check form validation: form.is_valid() ImproperlyConfigured: namespace app_name is missing in urls.py Add app_name = 'hello_app' Cards of different heights No h-100 on .card Add the h-100 class to <div class="card"> Footer in the middle of the page <body> has the height of its content, not of the window Add d-flex flex-column min-vh-100 to <body> and flex-grow-1 to <main>

docs.title: Notes Project — from model design to PostgreSQL
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through the full cycle: come up with a data structure → draw the schema → write the models → migrations → queries → selectors/services → templates → switch from SQLite to PostgreSQL.

The project is a personal records manager: notes, reminders, notebooks, to-do lists, shopping lists. Different data types were chosen on purpose to show every type of relationship between tables.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Architectural foundation (read before the code) - 01 · DOMAIN → SCHEMA — the design method - 02 · RELATIONSHIP TYPES — where the FK lives - 03 · APPLICATION LAYERS — layered architecture - 04 · NORMALIZATION — one truth for one fact - 05 · MIGRATIONS — Git for the DB schema

🔬 orm_laboratory.ipynb — an interactive lab: run each cell and look at the SQL

Step-by-step implementation 1. Step 0 — From domain to schema (the right start) 2. Step 1 — Designing the domain: what we are building 3. Step 2 — Identifying entities and relationships 4. Step 3 — ER diagrams (table schemas) 5. Step 4 — Writing Django models 6. Step 5 — Migrations: schema → database 7. Step 6 — First run with SQLite 8. Step 7 — Architecture: Services & Selectors 9. Step 8 — Views and templates 10. Step 9 — QuerySet API: basic queries 11. Step 10 — Switching from SQLite to PostgreSQL 12. Project file structure

docs.title: 01 · DOMAIN → SCHEMA
docs.text:
"Design before code." Mistake #1 — starting with class Note(models.Model) and adding fields "on the fly". A month later — a schema refactor = a migration that is hard to roll back in production. 30 minutes of design = weeks of time saved.

The architecture board describes 7 steps from business words to a working database:

# Step What you do Example 1 DOMAIN Describe in words what you are building "A user has notebooks. Notebooks contain notes. Notes have tags and reminders." 2 ENTITIES Find the nouns in the text User, Notebook, Note, Tag, Reminder, TodoList, ShoppingList 3 ATTRIBUTES What do we know about each entity? Note → title, content, priority, is_pinned, updated_at… 4 RELATIONSHIPS How are the entities related? 1:1 User↔Profile · 1:N Notebook→Notes · M:N Note↔Tag 5 NORMALIZATION Remove duplication author_name in Note? — No, only an FK to User 6 on_delete What happens when the parent is deleted? CASCADE / SET_NULL / PROTECT / RESTRICT 7 DJANGO MODEL Only now do we write models.py ← Mistake #1: starting here

⚠️ Anti-pattern. Starting with class Note(models.Model) and adding fields "on the fly". The ER diagram is a contract between you and the database. Break it in code — and you pay with a migration.

docs.title: 02 · RELATIONSHIP TYPES
docs.text: There are three types of relationships between tables. The question "where does the FK live?" is not a technical question, it is an architectural one.

docs.title: 1:1 — OneToOneField
docs.text:
FK + UNIQUE · "user has exactly one profile"

USER                          USER_PROFILE
┌──────────────┬──────────┐   ┌────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ id  bigint PK│          │──►│ id    bigint PK│                  │
│ username     │          │   │ user_id bigint │ UNIQUE FK        │
└──────────────┴──────────┘   │ display varchar│                  │
                              │ timezone       │                  │
                              └────────────────┴──────────────────┘

class UserProfile(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(
        User, on_delete=CASCADE,
        related_name='profile',
    )

Why is this 1:1? A regular FK + UNIQUE on the column. The reverse is an attribute (not a QuerySet): user.profile. Useful for vertical partitioning: 5 basic fields in User, 20 optional ones in Profile — we don't clutter the main table.

docs.title: 1:N — ForeignKey
docs.text:
FK on the "Many" side · "notebook has many notes"

NOTEBOOK                    NOTE              NOTE              NOTE
┌──────────┬──────────┐     ┌───────────────────────┐
│ id       │ bigint PK│──┬─►│ id          bigint PK │
│ title    │ varchar  │  │  │ notebook_id bigint FK │← FK here!
└──────────┴──────────┘  ├─►│ title       varchar   │
                         │  └───────────────────────┘
                         ├─► (another note)
                         └─► (another note)

class Note(models.Model):
    notebook = models.ForeignKey(
        Notebook, on_delete=SET_NULL,
        null=True, related_name='notes',
    )

Where does the FK live? Always on the Many side. Notebook does not store a list of notes — Note stores notebook_id. That is the physics of SQL: one column = one value.

docs.title: M:N — ManyToManyField
docs.text:
Via a junction table · Django creates it automatically

NOTE                  NOTE_TAGS (junction)    TAG
┌──────────┬──────┐   ┌──────────┬──────────┐  ┌──────────┬──────────┐
│ id       │  PK  │──►│ note_id  │ bigint FK│  │ id       │  PK      │
│ title    │      │   │ tag_id   │ bigint FK│─►│ name     │ varchar  │
└──────────┴──────┘   └──────────┴──────────┘  └──────────┴──────────┘
                       UNIQUE(note_id, tag_id)
                       Django: hello_app_note_tags

class Note(models.Model):
    tags = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True)

# Django creates it ITSELF: hello_app_note_tags(note_id, tag_id)
note.tags.add(tag_py, tag_dj)   # INSERT × 2 into the junction
tag_py.notes.all()              # reverse → SELECT JOIN

Junction = a separate table. There is no magic here — it is an ordinary table with two FKs. Want to add added_at or role to the relationship? Pass through= and describe your own junction model.

docs.title: on_delete — what happens when the parent is deleted?
docs.text:
⚠️ Mistake: CASCADE by default for everything → deleting a single user can wipe out hundreds of rows. Always choose the strategy consciously. It is a business decision, not a technical one.

Strategy What it does When to choose it CASCADE Delete the children automatically Reminder → Note: a reminder without a note makes no sense SET_NULL FK → NULL, the children live on Note → Notebook: a note exists without a notebook. The field must be null=True SET_DEFAULT FK → the default value Note → Notebook: move it to the "Default" notebook PROTECT ProtectedError, deletion is forbidden Tag: don't allow deleting a tag while it is in use RESTRICT Forbid, but allow a cascade from a higher level Complex domains with several levels of ownership DO_NOTHING The DB decides by itself (often = orphan) Almost never. Only if you manage consistency manually (triggers)

docs.title: 03 · APPLICATION LAYERS
docs.text: Thin Views · Selectors Read · Services Write Each layer has one responsibility. Breaking this rule is the main cause of the "fat view" anti-pattern.

docs.title: Layered architecture
docs.text:
HTTP REQUEST
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  views.py                               │
│  ✓ parses the request                   │
│  ✓ calls a selector / service           │
│  ✓ render / redirect                    │
│  ✗ no QuerySets                         │
└────────────┬───────────────┬────────────┘
             │ READ →        │ WRITE →
             ▼               ▼
┌────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│  selectors.py      │  │  services.py                 │
│  SELECT only       │  │  CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE    │
│                    │  │                              │
│  get_user_notes()  │  │  create_note()               │
│  get_note_detail() │  │  update_note()               │
│  get_notebooks()   │  │  toggle_todo_item()          │
│  get_reminders()   │  │  mark_reminder_sent()        │
│                    │  │                              │
│  select_related,   │  │  transaction.atomic,         │
│  prefetch_related, │  │  F(), select_for_update      │
│  annotate — here   │  │  — here                      │
└────────┬───────────┘  └───────────┬──────────────────┘
         │ SELECT                   │ INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
         └──────────┬───────────────┘
                    ▼
             ┌─────────────┐
             │  PostgreSQL │
             │  Database   │
             └─────────────┘

Why separate them? The same query is needed in a View, a Celery task, an API endpoint, a test. Without selectors.py you copy the QuerySet into 10 places. Change the logic → 10 places to update. With selectors.py → one function that everyone uses.

docs.title: Responsibility matrix
docs.text:
Layer ✓ Does ✗ Does not models.py Structure · fields · relationships · constraints · indexes Business logic, HTTP selectors.py SELECT QuerySets · annotate · prefetch · filters INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE services.py CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE · transaction · F() · locks HTTP, render, redirect views.py Parse the request · call a selector/service · render QuerySets, business logic forms.py Validate HTTP input · clean_* DB queries (except a queryset for choices) templates/ HTML markup · context from the View Any logic

Check yourself: if you see Note.objects.filter(...) in views.py, that is a signal to move it into selectors.py. If you see an access-permission check condition in a template, that is a violation too.

docs.title: READ flow — tracing GET /notes/?q=python
docs.text:
01 │ Browser      │ GET /notes/?q=python
02 │ urls.py      │ match → views.note_list
03 │ views.py     │ search = request.GET['q']
04 │ views.py     │ selectors.get_user_notes(user, search='python')
05 │ selectors.py │ QuerySet.filter().select_related('notebook').prefetch_related('tags')
06 │ ORM          │ SQLCompiler → 2 SQL (note + tags prefetch)
07 │ PostgreSQL   │ executes the plan, returns rows
08 │ ORM          │ ModelIterable → list[Note] with a populated _result_cache
09 │ views.py     │ render('note_list.html', {notes, tags, notebooks})
10 │ Browser      │ 200 OK · HTML

The View stays thin: 3 lines of code (parse + delegate + render). All the complexity is in selectors.get_user_notes: filters, JOINs, the prefetch cache.

docs.title: WRITE flow — tracing POST /notes/create/
docs.text:
01 │ Browser      │ POST /notes/create/ form=...
02 │ views.py     │ form = NoteForm(POST, user=request.user) · is_valid?
03 │ views.py     │ services.create_note(user, title, tag_ids)
04 │ services.py  │ with transaction.atomic():
05 │ services.py  │ Note.objects.create(...) → BEGIN, INSERT note
06 │ services.py  │ Tag.objects.filter(user=user, id__in=...) · ownership check
07 │ services.py  │ note.tags.set(valid) → INSERT × N into the junction
08 │ PostgreSQL   │ COMMIT · on_commit callbacks
09 │ views.py     │ messages.success(...)  ·  return redirect('note_detail', pk)
10 │ Browser      │ 302 → GET /notes/42/  (PRG pattern: F5 is safe)

PRG (Post / Redirect / Get). A POST does not render — it redirects. F5 repeats the GET — that is safe. Without PRG: F5 = a duplicate record.

Ownership via FK traversal. Tag.objects.filter(user=user, id__in=...) — don't let a user attach someone else's tags to their own note.

docs.title: 04 · NORMALIZATION
docs.text: "One truth for one fact." Normalization is the process of finding and eliminating duplication in a relational schema. Goal: every fact is stored in exactly one place.

docs.title: Before / After — 3NF by example
docs.text:
❌ BEFORE (1NF) — everything in a single employees table:

id name dept_id dept_name location salary 1 Alice 10 Engineering Kyiv 50000 2 Bob 10 Engineering Kyiv 45000 3 Carol 20 Design Lviv 48000 4 Dan 10 Engineering Kyiv 52000 5 Eva 20 Design Lviv 49000

Problem: "Engineering / Kyiv" is repeated 3 times. Moved to Kharkiv? UPDATE 1000 rows. Made a typo in the name? Inconsistency.

--- → 3NF: move it into a separate table ---

✅ AFTER — employees (FK → departments.id):

id name dept_id salary 1 Alice 10 50000 2 Bob 10 45000 3 Carol 20 48000 4 Dan 10 52000 5 Eva 20 49000

✅ departments — one truth:

id name location 10 Engineering Kyiv 20 Design Lviv 
# Django model after normalization:
class Department(models.Model):
    name     = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    location = models.CharField(max_length=80)

class Employee(models.Model):
    name       = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    department = models.ForeignKey(Department, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    salary     = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)

Moving now: UPDATE departments SET location='Kharkiv' WHERE id=10; 1 row instead of 1000. Inconsistency is impossible.

docs.title: The three normal forms — cheat sheet
docs.text:
Form Rule Violation — example 1NF All values are atomic, no arrays in a cell tags = "python,django,orm" in a single column 2NF All non-key attributes depend on the whole PK In a (order_id, product_id) table → product_name depends only on product_id 3NF No transitive dependencies (A→B→C where B is not a key) employee.dept_name depends on dept_id, not on employee.id

Practical rule: if changing one fact requires an UPDATE of > 1 row, the schema is not normalized.

docs.title: 05 · MIGRATIONS
docs.text: "Git for the database schema." Each migration is a commit that describes schema changes. Django tracks which ones have already been applied in django_migrations.

docs.title: Migration Lifecycle — from a model change to ALTER TABLE
Migration Dependency Graph (DAG)

graph TD

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text:
# Generate a migration with a descriptive name
python manage.py makemigrations --name add_word_count_to_note

# View the SQL before running it (always do this before migrate!)
python manage.py sqlmigrate hello_app 0003

docs.title: Migration rules
docs.text: Rule Why ✅ New field: always default= or null=True Without a default — what should be written into existing rows? ✅ Descriptive name --name add_word_count 0003_add_word_count is more readable than 0003_note ✅ Commit migrations to git Otherwise your colleagues won't be able to update their DB ✅ sqlmigrate before migrate You check the SQL that will be executed ❌ Editing an applied migration Production and dev get out of sync — a disaster ❌ Deleting migrations from git Breaks the dependency graph

docs.title: Step 0 — From domain to schema
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: Database design is not "which table should I add". It is modeling the real world. First you think in the language of the business: "a user can have notebooks, each notebook contains notes, notes can have tags". Then you translate this into data structures. Django models are the last step, not the first.

📚 Where mistakes begin: Most DB schema problems happen because the developer starts writing code right away without thinking about relationships. A month later it turns out a new relationship is needed — and adding it without a massive migration is impossible. 30 minutes of design = weeks of time saved.

❌ Common mistake: Starting by writing the model. The right order: domain → entities → attributes → relationships → normalization → Django model.

docs.title: The design process (the right order):
docs.text:
1. DOMAIN — describe in words what we are building
   "A user has notebooks. Notebooks contain notes.
    Notes can be in to-do lists. There are reminders with a date."

2. ENTITIES — find the "nouns" in the domain description
   User, Notebook, Note, To-do list, List item,
   Reminder, Shopping list, Product, Tag

3. ATTRIBUTES — for each entity: what do we know about it?
   Note: title, content, created_at, is_pinned, priority

4. RELATIONSHIPS — how are the entities related to each other?
   Note → Notebook: many notes in one notebook (FK)
   Note ↔ Tag: one note, many tags; one tag, many notes (M:N)

5. NORMALIZATION — check: is there duplication?
   If Note has an author_name field, that duplicates User. Replace it with an FK.

6. CHOOSING on_delete — what happens when the parent record is deleted?
   Deleting a Notebook → delete all its notes (CASCADE)?
   Or move them to a "General notebook" (SET_DEFAULT)?

7. DJANGO MODEL — only after all of the above

docs.title: Step 1 — Designing the domain
docs.text: We are building a personal records manager — like Notion or Evernote, but simplified.

docs.title: What our product should be able to do:
docs.text: Feature Description 📓 Notebooks Collections of notes (like folders). Each note is in one notebook 📝 Notes Text records with a title, content, tags, priority 🏷️ Tags Labels for notes. One note = many tags. One tag = many notes ✅ To-do lists A to-do list. Each list has items with a checkbox 🛒 Shopping lists A list of products with a quantity and whether it was bought ⏰ Reminders Notifications tied to a note or a date 📌 Pinning Notes can be pinned to the top

docs.title: Analyzing relationships by type:
docs.text:
ONE-TO-ONE (1:1) — "one has exactly one":
  User ←→ UserProfile
  (each user has one profile, one profile belongs to one user)

ONE-TO-MANY (1:N) — "one has many":
  User → Notebook          (one user, many notebooks)
  Notebook → Note          (one notebook, many notes)
  User → Note              (a note has an author)
  User → TodoList          (one user, many to-do lists)
  TodoList → TodoItem      (one list, many items)
  User → ShoppingList      (one user, many shopping lists)
  ShoppingList → ShopItem  (one list, many products)
  Note → Reminder          (one note can have several reminders)

MANY-TO-MANY (M:N) — "many related to many":
  Note ↔ Tag  (a note has tags, a tag is in many notes)

docs.title: Where the FK lives — the "Many side" rule:
docs.text:
Notebook → Note (1:N):

  notebooks:                   notes:
  ┌────┬──────────┐            ┌────┬─────────────┬─────────────┐
  │ id │ title    │            │ id │ title        │ notebook_id │  ← FK here
  ├────┼──────────┤            ├────┼─────────────┼─────────────┤
  │  1 │ Work     │◄───────────│  1 │ Django ORM   │      1      │
  │  2 │ Personal │◄───────────│  2 │ Python tips  │      1      │
  │    │          │◄───────────│  3 │ Borscht soup │      2      │
  └────┴──────────┘            └────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘

Notebook does NOT store a list of notes.
Note stores a REFERENCE to its notebook (notebook_id=1).

docs.title: Step 4 — Django models
docs.text:
The detailed model code is in hello_app/models.py. Here are the key principles:

# A brief overview of all the models and their relationships

class UserProfile(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(User, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='profile')
    # OneToOne = FK + UNIQUE. Each User → at most one Profile.


class Tag(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=CASCADE)
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    # Tags are bound to a specific user (privacy!)
    class Meta:
        unique_together = [('user', 'name')]  # Alice and Bob can have the same tag


class Notebook(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='notebooks')
    title = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    is_default = models.BooleanField(default=False)


class Note(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='notes')
    notebook = models.ForeignKey(Notebook, on_delete=SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True)
    tags = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True)
    # Three types of relationships in one model:
    # user: FK (required, CASCADE)
    # notebook: FK (optional, SET_NULL — a note can exist without a notebook)
    # tags: M:N (Django automatically creates the junction table)
    priority = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=1)
    is_pinned = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    is_archived = models.BooleanField(default=False)


class Reminder(models.Model):
    note = models.ForeignKey(Note, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='reminders')
    remind_at = models.DateTimeField()
    is_sent = models.BooleanField(default=False)


class TodoList(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='todo_lists')

class TodoItem(models.Model):
    todo_list = models.ForeignKey(TodoList, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='items')
    text = models.CharField(max_length=500)
    is_done = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    order_position = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)


class ShoppingList(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='shopping_lists')

class ShopItem(models.Model):
    shopping_list = models.ForeignKey(ShoppingList, on_delete=CASCADE, related_name='items')
    quantity = models.DecimalField(max_digits=8, decimal_places=2, default=1)
    # DecimalField for money and quantities! FloatField → 0.1+0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
    estimated_price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2, null=True)

docs.title: Step 5 — Migrations
docs.text:
🧠 Mental model: Migrations are Git for the database schema. Each migration is a "commit" that describes schema changes. Django tracks which migrations have already been applied in the django_migrations table. migrate runs only the new ones.

❌ Common mistake: Editing a migration that has already been applied. If a migration has already been applied in production and you edit it, production and development get out of sync. Changing an applied migration = a disaster. If you need a change → a new migration.

docs.title: Migration workflow — step by step:
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Django as Django
    participant DB as Database

    Dev->>Django: We change models.py
    Dev->>Django: python manage.py makemigrations
    Django->>Django: Compares models.py with the latest migration state
    Django-->>Dev: Generates 0002_extended_models.py
    Dev->>Django: python manage.py migrate
    Django->>DB: ALTER TABLE / CREATE TABLE (DDL)
    DB-->>Django: OK
    Django->>DB: INSERT INTO django_migrations (app, name)
    Django-->>Dev: Applied 0002_extended_models

cd module_5/lesson_Django_ORM_Database/notes_project

# 2. Check that hello_app is in INSTALLED_APPS
# settings.py → INSTALLED_APPS must contain 'hello_app'

# Migrations for 'hello_app':
#   hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py

#       TodoList, TodoItem, ShoppingList, ShopItem

# 4. View the SQL that will be executed (without executing it)

# 5. Run the migration

# 6. Show the state of all migrations
