docs.title: Reading order for this step
docs.text:
1. Environment and first run — venv, Django, startproject, the first run
  2. Project structure — anatomy of Request/Response, manage.py, settings.py
  3. URLs and Views — view functions, URL patterns, reverse()
  4. Templates — your first HTML template, render(), the MVT architecture
  5. Django Admin — the admin panel, your first model, the ORM shell
  6. Checkpoint — checklist, common mistakes, practical exercises

docs.title: Django Admin
docs.text: Django Admin is an automatically generated web interface for managing data. It is a built-in Django app, django.contrib.admin, with its own models, views and templates. It is available right after migrate + createsuperuser.

docs.title: What you see after logging in
docs.text:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/               ← main page (list of sections)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/user/     ← list of users
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/user/add/ ← create a new user
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/group/    ← list of groups (roles)

Django administration                         Logged in as: admin
  AUTHENTICATION AND AUTHORIZATION
    Groups    → add / edit groups
    Users     → all users, password changes, permissions

docs.title: The Users section
docs.text:
A list of all users in the system. Each user has:

Field What it means Username Login name Email Email address (optional) Password A hash (PBKDF2+SHA256) — never stored in plain text First/Last name First name and last name Active Whether the user can log in (False = blocked) Staff status Whether the user has access to /admin/ Superuser status Whether the user has ALL permissions (bypasses permission checks) Groups Which groups (roles) are assigned User permissions Individual permissions (on top of group permissions)

docs.title: The Groups section (groups/roles)
docs.text:
A group = a named set of permissions (a role).

Instead of assigning permissions to each user separately, you create an "Editors" group with the required permissions and add people to it.

Group "News editors"
    ✅ news.add_article    ← can create articles
    ✅ news.change_article ← can edit articles
    ❌ news.delete_article ← CANNOT delete
    ❌ news.view_user      ← CANNOT see users

Group "Moderators"
    ✅ news.delete_article ← can delete
    ✅ auth.view_user      ← sees the list of users

Django permission format: <app>.<action>_<model>

hello_app.add_note      ← add notes
hello_app.change_note   ← edit notes
hello_app.delete_note   ← delete notes
hello_app.view_note     ← view notes
auth.add_user           ← add users

Django automatically generates 4 permissions for every model (add, change, delete, view).

docs.title: Action log (django_admin_log)
docs.text:
Every action in the admin panel is logged automatically:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ → Recent actions (right column)

The django_admin_log table stores: - who performed the action (user) - what they did (added / changed / deleted) - which object (content_type + object_id) - when (action_time)

docs.title: Step B1 — Your first model in models.py
docs.text:
Open hello_app/models.py and write:

from django.db import models


class Note(models.Model):
    """
    A model = a Python class that describes a database table.

    The Django ORM automatically:
        - creates the 'hello_app_note' table in db.sqlite3
        - generates the id field (PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT)
        - provides an API: Note.objects.all(), Note.objects.create(...) etc.
    """

    # CharField → VARCHAR in SQL, a string of limited length
    title = models.CharField(
        max_length=200,
        verbose_name='Заголовок'
    )

    # TextField → TEXT in SQL, unlimited text
    content = models.TextField(
        blank=True,
        verbose_name='Текст'
    )

    # DateTimeField with auto_now_add=True — set on CREATE, never changes
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(
        auto_now_add=True,
        verbose_name='Створено'
    )

    # auto_now=True — updated on every SAVE
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(
        auto_now=True,
        verbose_name='Оновлено'
    )

    def __str__(self):
        # String representation: shown in the admin panel
        # instead of "Note object (1)"
        return self.title

    class Meta:
        verbose_name = 'Нотатка'
        verbose_name_plural = 'Нотатки'
        ordering = ['-created_at']   # newest notes first

docs.title: Field types and their SQL equivalents
docs.text:
# CharField — a short string, max_length is required
title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
# SQL: title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL

# TextField — long text, no length limit
content = models.TextField(blank=True)
# blank=True: not required in Django forms
# SQL: content TEXT NOT NULL   (Django fills in default='' in Python, not in the DB)

# DateTimeField with auto_now_add
created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
# SQL: created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL   (Django sets the time on the first save())

# BooleanField
is_pinned = models.BooleanField(default=False)
# SQL: is_pinned BOOLEAN NOT NULL   (default=False lives in Python, not as an SQL DEFAULT)

# IntegerField with choices
PRIORITY_CHOICES = [(1, 'Низький'), (2, 'Середній'), (3, 'Високий')]
priority = models.SmallIntegerField(choices=PRIORITY_CHOICES, default=1)
# SQL: priority SMALLINT NOT NULL   (default=1 lives in Python)

# ForeignKey — an N→1 relationship
user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='notes')
# SQL: user_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES auth_user(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

docs.title: Step B2 — Register the model in the admin panel
docs.text:
Open hello_app/admin.py and write:

from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Note


@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display    = ('title', 'created_at')          # Columns in the list
    search_fields   = ('title', 'content')             # Fields to search
    list_filter     = ('created_at',)                  # Filters on the right
    ordering        = ('-created_at',)                 # Sorting
    readonly_fields = ('created_at', 'updated_at')     # Not editable

Result: http://localhost:8000/admin/hello_app/note/ — full CRUD for notes.

docs.title: Step B3 — Generate a migration
docs.text:
python manage.py makemigrations

Migrations for 'hello_app':
  hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model Note

hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py is an automatically generated Python script that describes the SQL that needs to be executed. Do not edit it by hand.

docs.title: Step B4 — Apply the migration to the database
docs.text:
python manage.py migrate

Applying hello_app.0001_initial... OK

Now the hello_app_note table has appeared in db.sqlite3:

-- What Django executed for you:
CREATE TABLE "hello_app_note" (
    "id"         integer NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    "title"      varchar(200) NOT NULL,
    "content"    text NOT NULL,
    "created_at" datetime NOT NULL,
    "updated_at" datetime NOT NULL
);

docs.title: The two-step rule
docs.text:
# After ANY change to models.py — always two steps:
python manage.py makemigrations   # Record the plan of changes
python manage.py migrate          # Apply it to the DB

# makemigrations WITHOUT migrate:
# → the Python class exists, the DB table does not → OperationalError on the first query

docs.title: What happens between models.py and the DB
docs.text:
models.py (Python class)
    ↓ python manage.py makemigrations
hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py  (plan of changes)
    ↓ python manage.py migrate
db.sqlite3 → hello_app_note table  (the real DB)
    ↓ @admin.register(Note)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/hello_app/note/  (web interface)

docs.title: Step B5 — Check it in the browser
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ — a new section "Нотатки" (the model's verbose_name_plural) has appeared.

  1. Click "Add note" / "Додати нотатку"
  2. Enter a title and text
  3. Click Save
  4. The note is saved in db.sqlite3 → the hello_app_note table

docs.title: Django ORM — basic queries in the shell
docs.text:
python manage.py shell

from hello_app.models import Note

# CREATE — INSERT INTO
Note.objects.create(title="Перша нотатка", content="Привіт Django!")
Note.objects.create(title="Django ORM", content="Дуже потужний!")

# READ — SELECT
Note.objects.all()                              # → QuerySet [<Note: Перша нотатка>, ...]
Note.objects.count()                            # → 2
Note.objects.filter(title__icontains='django')  # → case-insensitive search
Note.objects.get(id=1)                          # → <Note: Перша нотатка> or DoesNotExist
Note.objects.first()                            # → the first object
Note.objects.order_by('-created_at')            # → newest first

# UPDATE — UPDATE SET
note = Note.objects.get(id=1)
note.title = "Змінена нотатка"
note.save()                      # → UPDATE hello_app_note SET title=... WHERE id=1

# DELETE — DELETE FROM
note.delete()                                   # → delete one record
Note.objects.filter(id__gt=5).delete()         # → delete all with id > 5

# QuerySets are lazy:
qs = Note.objects.all()   # ← SQL is NOT EXECUTED YET
print(qs)                  # ← SQL runs only here!

# Useful lookups:
Note.objects.filter(title__icontains='перша')   # icontains = case-insensitive LIKE
Note.objects.filter(title__startswith='Django')
Note.objects.filter(created_at__year=2026)
Note.objects.filter(id__in=[1, 2, 3])
Note.objects.exclude(title='секрет')            # WHERE NOT (title = 'секрет')

The Django shell is a regular Python interpreter, but with Django loaded. It is handy for quickly testing ORM queries without writing views.

docs.title: Full registration: admin.site.register vs @admin.register
docs.text:
# Option 1: simple
admin.site.register(Note)

# Option 2: with configuration (better)
@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ('title', 'created_at')

Both do the same thing, but @admin.register is more readable and lets you set list_display, search_fields and list_filter at the same time.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: This section is the final check of Step 1. Complete the practical exercises, go through the checklist and review the table of common mistakes before moving on to Step 2.

docs.title: All commands in order
docs.text:
# 1. Create and activate a venv
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate      # Linux/Mac
# or: venv\Scripts\activate  # Windows

# 2. Install Django
pip install -r requirements.txt
# or: pip install django

# 3. Create the project (the dot matters!)
django-admin startproject hello_project .

# 4. Apply the initial migrations
python manage.py migrate

# 5. Create an administrator
python manage.py createsuperuser

# 6. Check the admin panel
python manage.py runserver
# → http://localhost:8000/admin/

# 7. Create an app
python manage.py startapp hello_app

# 8. Register hello_app in settings.py
# (add 'hello_app' to INSTALLED_APPS)

# 9. Write view functions (views.py) and URL routes (urls.py)

# 10. Connect hello_app.urls to hello_project/urls.py (include)

# 11. Describe the model in models.py
# 12. Create a migration
python manage.py makemigrations

# 13. Apply the migration
python manage.py migrate

# 14. Register the model in admin.py (@admin.register)

# 15. Final check
python manage.py runserver
# http://localhost:8000/        → Hello, Django!
# http://localhost:8000/about/  → text
# http://localhost:8000/notes/  → list of notes
# http://localhost:8000/admin/  → admin panel

docs.title: Changes in files
docs.text: File What you did hello_project/settings.py Added 'hello_app' to INSTALLED_APPS hello_app/models.py Wrote the Note model (CharField, TextField, DateTimeField) hello_app/admin.py Registered NoteAdmin via @admin.register hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py Generated automatically by makemigrations hello_app/views.py Wrote the functions index(), about(), note_list() hello_app/urls.py Created the file with app_name and the routes /, /about/, /notes/ hello_project/urls.py Connected the routes via include() hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html Your first HTML template

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Error Cause Solution AttributeError: 'super' object has no attribute 'dicts' Python 3.14 is incompatible with Django 5.1 pip install django --upgrade (installs 5.2+) OperationalError: no such table: auth_user Migrations were not run python manage.py migrate OperationalError: no such table: hello_app_note migrate was not run after makemigrations python manage.py migrate ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django' The venv is not activated or Django is not installed Activate the venv → pip install -r requirements.txt Page not found (404) at / The route is not registered Check urls.py in both files ImproperlyConfigured: Specifying a namespace... namespace= is set in include(), but app_name is missing from hello_app/urls.py Add app_name = "hello_app" to hello_app/urls.py NameError: name 'Note' is not defined views.py does not import the model Add from .models import Note to views.py Django does not see hello_app Not added to INSTALLED_APPS Add 'hello_app' to settings.py django-admin: command not found Django is not installed or the venv is not activated Activate the venv, then pip install django ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'hello_project' You are not running from the project root Go to the folder that contains manage.py DisallowedHost ALLOWED_HOSTS does not contain the host Add the host to ALLOWED_HOSTS in settings.py CSRF verification failed {% csrf_token %} is missing from the form Add {% csrf_token %} inside the <form> The server does not stop — Press Ctrl + C in the terminal

docs.title: Practical exercises
docs.text:
1. Go through steps 1–9 on your own and get Hello, Django! in the browser.

  2. Add a third route /contact/ with a view function contact() that returns a string with your name and email.

  3. Add a route /greet/<str:name>/ that returns "Привіт, {name}!".

  4. Create the Note model, make a migration, open the admin panel and add 3 notes by hand.

  5. In the Django shell: find the note with id=2, change its title, and save it. Check it in the admin panel.

  6. (Bonus) Add the field is_pinned = models.BooleanField(default=False) to the Note model. Create a new migration. Make sure the field has appeared in the admin panel.

docs.title: Self-check checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] http://localhost:8000/ → Hello, Django!
  • [ ] http://localhost:8000/about/ → text
  • [ ] http://localhost:8000/notes/ → HTML list of notes
  • [ ] http://localhost:8000/admin/ → admin panel (superuser login)
  • [ ] I understand the difference between startproject and startapp
  • [ ] I know why makemigrations and migrate are two separate steps
  • [ ] The Note model appears in the admin panel
  • [ ] I can perform CRUD through the Django shell (create, filter, get, save, delete)
  • [ ] I understand how Django finds a view by URL (the URLconf chain)
  • [ ] I know the difference between superuser / staff / regular user
  • [ ] render() takes request, a template path and a context dict
  • [ ] The template lives in hello_app/templates/hello_app/ (the doubled folder is correct)

docs.title: Summary of concepts
docs.text: Concept Where in the code URL route hello_app/urls.py → path('about/', views.about) View function hello_app/views.py → def about(request): return HttpResponse(...) Connecting app URLs hello_project/urls.py → include('hello_app.urls') Namespace app_name = 'hello_app' + namespace='hello_app' Reverse URL reverse('hello_app:about') or {% url 'hello_app:about' %} Path converter path('notes/<int:pk>/', ...) Template hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html Context render(request, 'шаблон.html', {'notes': queryset}) Model → DB makemigrations + migrate ORM CRUD create, filter, get, .save(), .delete() Admin registration @admin.register(Note) in admin.py MVT Model → View → Template

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Step 2 → Bootstrap Notes — Bootstrap 5, ModelForm, full CRUD with the PRG pattern, the first notes_project.

docs.title: Environment and first run
docs.text:
Python and Django compatibility:

Python Django Note 3.10 – 3.13 5.1.x or 5.2.x A stable pair 3.14+ 5.2+ only 5.1 does not support Python 3.14 3.9 4.2.x (LTS) Old, but still supported

Check: python --version

docs.title: Step 1 — Virtual Environment
docs.text:
A virtual environment is an isolated Python environment. The packages you install into it do not affect other projects or the system Python.

# Create a venv in the current folder
python -m venv venv

After this, a venv/ folder appears.

docs.title: Activation
docs.text:
# Linux / macOS
source venv/bin/activate

# Windows PowerShell
venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Windows Command Prompt
venv\Scripts\activate.bat

After activation, (venv) appears in the terminal prompt: 

(venv) ~/projects/hello_django $

Activate it every time you open a new terminal in the project. Forgot to activate it? pip install django will install into the system Python → version conflicts.

# Deactivate (return to the system Python):
deactivate

# Check that the right Python is being used:
which python    # macOS/Linux → should be .../venv/bin/python
where python    # Windows

docs.title: Step 2 — Install Django
docs.text:
# Upgrade pip (recommended)
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

# Install Django (latest stable)
pip install django

# Or a specific version:
pip install django==5.2.2

# Save the dependencies to requirements.txt
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# Install from requirements.txt (for another developer):
pip install -r requirements.txt

Check the installation: 

python -m django --version
# → 5.2.2

docs.title: Step 3 — Create the project
docs.text:
django-admin startproject hello_project .

The dot . at the end is required!

With the dot: hello_project/ and manage.py are in the current folder ✓ Without the dot: Django creates hello_project/hello_project/ → unnecessary nesting ✗

Result: 

./
├── hello_project/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py   ← configuration
│   ├── urls.py       ← main router
│   ├── asgi.py       ← for uvicorn/daphne
│   └── wsgi.py       ← for gunicorn
└── manage.py         ← CLI orchestrator

Check that the server starts: 

python manage.py runserver

docs.title: Step 4 — Apply migrations
docs.text:
python manage.py migrate

Django includes built-in apps (django.contrib.auth, django.contrib.admin etc.). Each of them has tables in the database. migrate creates these tables in db.sqlite3.

Command output: 

Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions
Running migrations:
  Applying contenttypes.0001_initial... OK
  Applying auth.0001_initial... OK
  Applying admin.0001_initial... OK
  Applying sessions.0001_initial... OK

docs.title: Tables Django creates automatically
docs.text:
Table What it stores auth_user Users: username, password (PBKDF2+SHA256 hash), email, is_staff, is_superuser auth_group Groups/roles: name auth_permission Permissions: name + model (add_note, change_note, delete_note, view_note) auth_user_groups M:N: user ↔ group auth_user_user_permissions M:N: user ↔ permission django_session Sessions (the sessionid cookie → a DB record) django_admin_log Log of actions in the admin panel (who changed what and when) django_migrations Which migrations have already been applied (so they are not repeated) django_content_type Registry of all models (for generic FKs)

Without migrate, the admin panel crashes: OperationalError: no such table: auth_user

docs.title: Step 5 — Create a superuser
docs.text:
python manage.py createsuperuser

Django will ask: 

Username (leave blank to use 'niko'): admin
Email address: admin@example.com
Password:
Password (again):
Superuser created successfully.

docs.title: User types in Django
docs.text:
Superuser  → is_superuser=True, is_staff=True
             All permissions automatically.
             Bypasses permission checks.
             Access to /admin/ and all objects.

Staff user → is_staff=True, is_superuser=False
             Can log in to /admin/, but only with assigned permissions.
             Does not see models without explicit permissions.

Regular    → is_staff=False, is_superuser=False
             An ordinary user. No access to /admin/.
             Can use the application's frontend.

Check in the browser: - http://localhost:8000/ → the Django start page (the rocket) - http://localhost:8000/admin/ → the admin panel; enter the login from this step

docs.title: Step 6 — Create an app
docs.text:
A Django project consists of one or more apps. Each app is responsible for a specific part of the functionality.

python manage.py startapp hello_app

This command creates: 

hello_app/
├── __init__.py
├── admin.py        ← Registering models for Django Admin
├── apps.py         ← HelloAppConfig — the app configuration
├── models.py       ← Models (empty)
├── tests.py        ← Tests
├── views.py        ← View functions (empty)
└── migrations/
    └── __init__.py

Register the app in hello_project/settings.py:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    'hello_app',    # ← ADD THIS LINE
]

Why do you need to register it? Django knows about an app only if it is in INSTALLED_APPS. Without this: - Django does not look for templates in hello_app/templates/ - python manage.py makemigrations ignores hello_app/models.py - Django Admin does not know about the models from hello_app/ - management commands from hello_app/management/ are not available

docs.title: All commands in order
docs.text:
# 1. Create and activate a venv
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate      # Linux/Mac
# or: venv\Scripts\activate  # Windows

# 2. Install Django
pip install -r requirements.txt
# or: pip install django

# 3. Create the project (the dot matters!)
django-admin startproject hello_project .

# 4. Apply the initial migrations
python manage.py migrate

# 5. Create an administrator
python manage.py createsuperuser

# 6. Check the admin panel
python manage.py runserver
# → http://localhost:8000/admin/

# 7. Create an app
python manage.py startapp hello_app
# (next, we edit the files by hand — on the following pages)

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text: This page explains why Django looks the way it does. Before writing code, understand the architecture.

docs.title: 01 · How Django handles a request
docs.text: The most important question: what happens when you type http://localhost:8000/about/ into the browser?

docs.title: The full Request/Response cycle
docs.text:
Browser                    runserver (manage.py)              Django
   │                              │                              │
   │  GET /about/  ───────────────►                              │
   │                              │  ProtocolTypeRouter          │
   │                              │  (WSGI or ASGI)              │
   │                              │         │                    │
   │                              │  SecurityMiddleware          │
   │                              │  SessionMiddleware           │
   │                              │  CommonMiddleware            │
   │                              │  CsrfViewMiddleware          │
   │                              │  AuthenticationMiddleware    │
   │                              │  MessageMiddleware           │
   │                              │         │                    │
   │                              │  URLconf → hello_project/urls.py
   │                              │         │                    │
   │                              │  include → hello_app/urls.py │
   │                              │         │                    │
   │                              │  path('about/', about_view)  │
   │                              │         │                    │
   │                              │  about(request)              │
   │                              │         │                    │
   │                              │  HttpResponse("Це моя...")   │
   │                              │         │                    │
   │  ◄───────────── 200 OK  ─────│         │                    │
   │  (body: "Це моя перша...")   │                              │

docs.title: The three participants
docs.text:
URLS.PY            → "Who will respond?"   path('about/', views.about)
VIEWS.PY           → "What to respond?"    return HttpResponse("...")
TEMPLATE/RESPONSE  → "How will it look?"   a string or HTML

A restaurant analogy: - urls.py = the host: "Table 5 — your waiter is Marko" - views.py = the cook: receives the order and prepares the dish - HttpResponse = the plate that goes back to the guest

docs.title: 02 · Project structure
docs.text:
After django-admin startproject hello_project . and startapp hello_app you will have:

./
├── manage.py               ← CLI: run the server, migrations, shell, tests
│
├── hello_project/          ← Project configuration (one for the whole project)
│   ├── __init__.py         ← Empty: makes the folder a Python package
│   ├── settings.py         ← All settings: DB, INSTALLED_APPS, TEMPLATES...
│   ├── urls.py             ← Main URLconf: includes the apps' urls.py
│   ├── wsgi.py             ← Entry point for WSGI servers (Gunicorn, uWSGI)
│   └── asgi.py             ← Entry point for ASGI servers (Uvicorn, Daphne)
│
├── hello_app/              ← An app (one of possibly several)
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── admin.py            ← Registering models in Django Admin
│   ├── apps.py             ← AppConfig configuration
│   ├── models.py           ← Models: Python class → DB table
│   ├── views.py            ← View functions: request → response
│   ├── urls.py             ← App URLs (must be created by hand)
│   ├── forms.py            ← ModelForm and Form classes (must be created)
│   ├── migrations/         ← Automatically generated migration files
│   │   └── __init__.py
│   └── templates/          ← HTML templates (must be created)
│       └── hello_app/
│           └── index.html
│
└── db.sqlite3              ← DB file (appears after migrate)

docs.title: Why are hello_project/ and hello_app/ different things?
docs.text:
hello_project/   = CONFIGURATION
  One for the whole site.
  settings.py, urls.py, wsgi.py.
  Contains no business logic.
  You rarely edit it after the initial setup.

hello_app/       = FUNCTIONALITY
  There can be several (notes_app, users_app, chat_app).
  models.py, views.py, forms.py, templates/.
  All of the application's code lives here.
  Each app = an isolated unit of functionality.

Rule: one app = one responsibility. notes_app → notes. users_app → profiles. Do not mix everything into one big app.

docs.title: 03 · manage.py
docs.text: manage.py is Django's CLI orchestrator. All interaction with the project goes through it.

docs.title: The most important commands
docs.text:
# ── Development server ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py runserver                 # http://localhost:8000/
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8080   # a different port and host (for the network)

# ── Migrations ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py makemigrations            # Generates a migration plan from models.py
python manage.py makemigrations hello_app  # Only for one app
python manage.py migrate                   # Applies all migrations to the DB
python manage.py migrate hello_app 0002    # Roll back to a specific migration
python manage.py showmigrations            # Show the state of all migrations

# ── Administration ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py createsuperuser           # Create a superuser interactively
python manage.py changepassword alice      # Change a user's password

# ── Code generation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py startapp blog_app         # A new app
python manage.py startproject config .     # A new project configuration

# ── Interactive shell ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py shell                     # Python shell with the Django context

# ── SQL ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py sqlmigrate hello_app 0001 # Show the SQL a migration will run
python manage.py dbshell                   # psql / sqlite3 shell

# ── Checks ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py check                     # Check the configuration without running
python manage.py check --deploy            # Check production settings

# ── Tests ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py test                      # All tests
python manage.py test hello_app            # Tests of a specific app
python manage.py test hello_app.tests.test_models -v 2

# ── Static files ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python manage.py collectstatic             # Collect static files into STATIC_ROOT

docs.title: How does manage.py know about your project?
docs.text:
# manage.py — the first line after the shebang:
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'hello_project.settings')
# ↑ Tells Django where to find settings.py
# When running in Docker, this is often overridden with an ENV variable

docs.title: 04 · settings.py — anatomy of the configuration
docs.text:
settings.py is Django's brain. Read every setting; don't just copy it.

# hello_project/settings.py

# ── Security ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SECRET_KEY = 'django-insecure-...'   # Secret for CSRF, sessions, signatures
# In production: read it from os.environ or a .env file!
# os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY') — never store it in git

DEBUG = True
# True:  detailed error pages with a traceback → ONLY in development
# False: Production → a generic error without a traceback

ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
# List of domains that may access the site
# DEBUG=True → ALLOWED_HOSTS is not checked (localhost is always allowed)
# Production: ['example.com', 'www.example.com']


# ── Installed apps ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',         # /admin/ — the admin panel
    'django.contrib.auth',          # User model, login/logout
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',  # ContentType framework (generic relations)
    'django.contrib.sessions',      # Sessions: the django_session table
    'django.contrib.messages',      # Flash messages
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',   # Static files: /static/

    # Third-party (installed via pip):
    # 'crispy_forms',
    # 'crispy_bootstrap5',

    # Your apps — always AT THE END:
    'hello_app',
]
# If an app is listed here → Django looks for models, views, templates, static in it


# ── Middleware — the request processing chain ────────────────────────────────
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    # ↑ HTTPS redirect, HSTS, XSS protection headers

    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    # ↑ Loads the session from the DB → request.session

    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    # ↑ Adds a trailing slash, APPEND_SLASH

    'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',
    # ↑ Checks the CSRF token in POST requests → 403 if missing

    'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware',
    # ↑ Reads the session → sets request.user
    # IMPORTANT: after SessionMiddleware!

    'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware',
    # ↑ Flash messages: messages.success(request, ...)

    'django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware',
    # ↑ X-Frame-Options: DENY → protection against clickjacking
]
# Order is critical! Middleware is called in sequence (request↓, response↑)


# ── URL configuration ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ROOT_URLCONF = 'hello_project.urls'


# ── Templates ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TEMPLATES = [{
    'BACKEND': 'django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates',
    'DIRS': [BASE_DIR / 'templates'],  # Global templates (not inside an app/)
    'APP_DIRS': True,                  # Look for templates/ in every app
    # APP_DIRS: True → django looks in hello_app/templates/hello_app/*.html
    'OPTIONS': {
        'context_processors': [
            'django.template.context_processors.debug',
            'django.template.context_processors.request',
            # ↑ request is available in the template as {{ request }}
            'django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth',
            # ↑ {{ user }} and {{ perms }} are available in all templates
            'django.contrib.messages.context_processors.messages',
            # ↑ {{ messages }} is available in all templates
        ],
    },
}]


# ── Database ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3',
        'NAME': BASE_DIR / 'db.sqlite3',
    }
}
# SQLite: a single file, ideal for development, not for production
# PostgreSQL (production): ENGINE = 'django.db.backends.postgresql'


# ── Static files ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STATIC_URL = '/static/'


# ── Language and time zone ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
LANGUAGE_CODE = 'uk'            # Language of the admin panel and built-in messages
TIME_ZONE = 'Europe/Kyiv'
USE_I18N = True
USE_TZ = True                   # Store datetimes in UTC in the DB
# USE_TZ=True: datetimes in the DB are always UTC → converted on display

DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD = 'django.db.models.BigAutoField'
# BigAutoField → id: bigint (64-bit)

docs.title: SQLite vs PostgreSQL
docs.text:
SQLite (this step) PostgreSQL (Steps 5–9) Running Nothing needed, it is a file A separate server Where the file is db.sqlite3 in the project folder On the DB server Suitable for Development, learning, prototypes Production Concurrent writes Locks the file Full concurrency Configuration 'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3' 'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql'

In notes_chat_app (Step 5 and later) there is no SQLite fallback — only PostgreSQL via Docker is used.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
HttpResponse("text") is the simplest response. But a real Django project uses templates (HTML files): 

# Instead of HttpResponse("text")
return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})
This page will teach you how to build public HTML pages with data from the DB.

docs.title: How data travels to the browser
docs.text:
Browser GET /notes/
    ↓ urls.py finds the route
    ↓ views.py gets data from the DB via the ORM
    ↓ templates/hello_app/note_list.html renders HTML
    ↓ HttpResponse → browser

This is Django's MVT architecture: - M (Model) — Note in models.py — stores the data - V (View) — note_list in views.py — gets the data and decides what to show - T (Template) — note_list.html — renders HTML

docs.title: Step C1 — Create a folder for templates
docs.text:
Django looks for templates in the <app>/templates/<app>/ folder. This doubling (hello_app/templates/hello_app/) is needed to avoid name conflicts between different apps.

The structure you need to create:

hello_app/
└── templates/
    └── hello_app/
        └── note_list.html    ← we will create this file below

Command for creating the folders:

# Windows PowerShell
mkdir hello_app\templates\hello_app

# Linux / Mac
mkdir -p hello_app/templates/hello_app

docs.title: Step C2 — Create the note_list.html template
docs.text:
Create the file hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="uk">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Мої нотатки</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; max-width: 600px; margin: 40px auto; }
        .note { border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 15px; margin: 10px 0; border-radius: 4px; }
        .date { color: #888; font-size: 0.85em; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>

    <h1>Нотатки</h1>

    {# if notes — check whether there are notes in the list #}
    {# 'notes' — the name of the variable the view passes in (context['notes']) #}
    {% if notes %}

        {# for note in notes — loop over every note in the list #}
        {% for note in notes %}
        <div class="note">
            <!-- {{ note.title }} — outputs the value of the note object's title field -->
            <h2>{{ note.title }}</h2>

            {% if note.content %}
                <p>{{ note.content }}</p>
            {% endif %}

            <!--
                {{ note.created_at|date:"d.m.Y H:i" }}
                |date:"format" — a filter for formatting a date
            -->
            <p class="date">{{ note.created_at|date:"d.m.Y H:i" }}</p>
        </div>
        {% endfor %}

    {% else %}
        <!-- Shown if there are no notes -->
        <p>Нотаток поки немає.
           <a href="/admin/hello_app/note/add/">Додати в адмін-панелі →</a>
        </p>
    {% endif %}

    <hr>
    <a href="/admin/">← Адмін-панель</a>

</body>
</html>

docs.title: Step C3 — Add a view function to views.py
docs.text:
Open hello_app/views.py and add a new function (do not replace the existing ones):

from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.shortcuts import render   # ← add render to the import
from .models import Note              # ← import the model


def index(request):
    """Home page."""
    return HttpResponse("Hello, Django!")


def about(request):
    """The 'About us' page."""
    return HttpResponse("Це моя перша сторінка на Django!")


def note_list(request):
    """
    A page with the list of notes.

    What happens:
    1. Note.objects.all() — SELECT * FROM hello_app_note ORDER BY created_at DESC
       (the DESC order is set in class Meta: ordering = ['-created_at'])
    2. render() — takes the template, fills in the data (context) and returns HTML
    """

    # ORM query: get all notes from the DB
    # The result is a QuerySet: a lazy list of Note objects
    notes = Note.objects.all()

    # context — a dict of data we pass to the template
    # The key 'notes' → in the template: {{ notes }}, {% for note in notes %}
    context = {
        'notes': notes,
    }

    # render(request, 'path/to/template', context)
    # Django looks for the template in hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', context)

docs.title: Step C4 — Add a URL route to hello_app/urls.py
docs.text:
from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = "hello_app"

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),
    path('about/', views.about, name='about'),
    path('notes/', views.note_list, name='note_list'),   # ← ADD THIS LINE
]

path('notes/', views.note_list) — a request to /notes/ → calls views.note_list

docs.title: Step C5 — Check it in the browser
docs.text:
python manage.py runserver
URL Result http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/ A styled list of notes http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/hello_app/note/add/ Add a note via the admin

Add a few notes via the admin → refresh /notes/ — they will appear on the page.

docs.title: Final structure after templates
docs.text:
hello_app/
├── models.py          ← Note model
├── views.py           ← index, about, note_list
├── urls.py            ← /, /about/, /notes/
├── admin.py           ← NoteAdmin
├── migrations/
│   └── 0001_initial.py
└── templates/
    └── hello_app/
        └── note_list.html

docs.title: The full path of a GET /notes/ request, step by step
docs.text:
1. Browser: GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/

2. Django: reads ROOT_URLCONF = 'hello_project.urls'
           hello_project/urls.py → include('hello_app.urls')
           hello_app/urls.py → path('notes/', views.note_list)

3. views.note_list(request) is called:
           Note.objects.all()
           → SQL: SELECT * FROM hello_app_note ORDER BY created_at DESC
           → returns a QuerySet [<Note: ...>, ...]

4. render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': queryset})
           Django finds the template: hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html
           Fills in the data: {% for note in notes %} → HTML lines

5. HttpResponse(HTML) → the browser renders the page

docs.title: What's next with templates
docs.text:
At this step, the template is a single file with no hierarchy. In Step 4 (Templates and Forms) you will build:

base.html              ← a shared HTML skeleton (navbar, footer)
layouts/dashboard.html ← a SaaS dashboard layout
pages/note_list.html   ← a specific page inherits from dashboard

Crispy Forms, Bootstrap 5, Context Processors — it is all there.

docs.title: URLs and Views
docs.text: Here you will write your first view functions and URL routes. This is the heart of Django — the code that receives a request and returns a response.

docs.title: Step 7 — Write view functions
docs.text:
Open hello_app/views.py:

from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.shortcuts import render


def index(request):
    """Home page."""
    return HttpResponse("Hello, Django!")


def about(request):
    """About us page."""
    return HttpResponse("Це моя перша сторінка на Django!")

docs.title: Anatomy of a view function
docs.text:
def index(request):
    #       ↑
    #  HttpRequest object — contains:
    #    request.method   → 'GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'
    #    request.GET      → QueryDict: parameters ?q=search&page=2
    #    request.POST     → QueryDict: the POST form body
    #    request.user     → the logged-in User or AnonymousUser
    #    request.session  → dict-like: the user's session
    #    request.META     → HTTP headers: REMOTE_ADDR, HTTP_HOST...
    #    request.FILES    → uploaded files
    #    request.COOKIES  → browser cookies

    return HttpResponse("Hello!")
    #         ↑
    #  HttpResponse — the response to the browser:
    #    status_code=200 (by default)
    #    content_type='text/html; charset=utf-8'
    #    body: 'Hello!'

docs.title: Response types
docs.text:
from django.http import (
    HttpResponse,            # 200 OK with any content
    HttpResponseRedirect,    # 302 Redirect
    Http404,                 # raised as an exception → 404 page
    JsonResponse,            # 200 OK with a JSON body
)
from django.shortcuts import render, redirect, get_object_or_404

# The most common in views.py:
return render(request, 'hello_app/index.html', {'key': value})
# → renders an HTML template with a context → 200

return redirect('hello_app:note_list')
# → 302 Redirect to a URL from reverse()

return redirect('hello_app:note_detail', pk=42)
# → 302 Redirect with an argument

raise Http404("Не знайдено")
# → Django returns a 404 page

note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
# → Note.objects.get(pk=pk), but instead of DoesNotExist → Http404

docs.title: Step 8 — URL routes
docs.text:
Create a new file hello_app/urls.py:

from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = "hello_app"    # ← Namespace

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),        # → /
    path('about/', views.about, name='about'),  # → /about/
]

Why app_name? Without it, the link {% url 'hello_app:index' %} does not work. Django raises: ImproperlyConfigured: Specifying a namespace in include() without providing an app_name

Connect it to the main hello_project/urls.py:

from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', include('hello_app.urls', namespace='hello_app')),
    #     ↑                              ↑
    #   empty prefix →               namespace for {% url %}
    #   hello_app URLs start
    #   right from the root /
]

docs.title: How Django finds the view for a GET /about/ request
docs.text:
GET /about/
    ↓
hello_project/urls.py:
  path('', include('hello_app.urls', ...))
  → prefix '' → PASS

hello_app/urls.py:
  path('about/', views.about, name='about')
  → 'about/' == 'about/' → MATCH!

views.about(request) is called
  → HttpResponse("Це моя перша сторінка...")

docs.title: Anatomy of path()
docs.text:
from django.urls import path, include, re_path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    # path(route, view, kwargs=None, name=None)
    path('about/', views.about, name='about'),
    #      ↑          ↑               ↑
    #   URL string  callable        unique route name
]

docs.title: Path Converters — capturing values from the URL
docs.text:
urlpatterns = [
    # <int:pk> — capture an integer
    path('notes/<int:pk>/', views.note_detail, name='note_detail'),
    # /notes/42/ → the view receives pk=42

    # <str:username> — capture a string (does not include '/')
    path('users/<str:username>/', views.user_profile, name='user_profile'),
    # /users/alice/ → the view receives username='alice'

    # <slug:slug> — only letters, digits, hyphens
    path('articles/<slug:slug>/', views.article, name='article'),
    # /articles/my-first-post/

    # <uuid:pk> — UUID format
    path('orders/<uuid:pk>/', views.order_detail, name='order_detail'),

    # <path:file_path> — includes '/'
    path('files/<path:file_path>/', views.serve_file, name='serve_file'),
    # /files/images/2026/photo.jpg → file_path='images/2026/photo.jpg'
]

docs.title: Two-level URLconf — include()
docs.text:
# hello_project/urls.py (main)
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),

    # include() connects another app's URLconf
    path('', include('hello_app.urls', namespace='hello_app')),
    # '' → all URLs without a prefix go to hello_app.urls
    # namespace='hello_app' → for {% url 'hello_app:index' %}

    # Or with a prefix:
    path('notes/', include('hello_app.urls', namespace='hello_app')),
    # Then /notes/ + '' (in hello_app.urls) = /notes/
]

# hello_app/urls.py (modular)
from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = 'hello_app'   # ← Required when include() has a namespace!
# Without app_name: ImproperlyConfigured: Specifying a namespace in include() without providing an app_name

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),        # ← '' here
    path('about/', views.about, name='about'),
]

docs.title: reverse() — generating URLs programmatically
docs.text:
# In a view:
from django.urls import reverse
from django.shortcuts import redirect

def some_view(request):
    # Instead of hardcoding '/notes/':
    url = reverse('hello_app:note_list')
    return redirect(url)

# Or directly:
return redirect('hello_app:note_list')

# In a template:
# {% url 'hello_app:note_detail' pk=note.pk %}
# → /notes/42/

Why reverse() instead of hardcoding /notes/? If you change a URL in urls.py, reverse() automatically generates the new URL. With a hardcoded /notes/ → you have to search and replace throughout the code.

docs.title: Django Admin
docs.text: In Step 1 you already registered NoteAdmin with a simple @admin.register(Note). Here we will extend it into a full-fledged admin class with custom columns, search, filters and computed fields.

docs.title: What you already have after Step 1
docs.text:
hello_app/admin.py after Step 1:

from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Note


@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display    = ('title', 'created_at')
    search_fields   = ('title', 'content')
    list_filter     = ('created_at',)
    ordering        = ('-created_at',)
    readonly_fields = ('created_at',)

This is already not bad. But let's look at each option separately.

docs.title: Extended NoteAdmin
docs.text:
from django.contrib import admin
from django.utils.html import format_html
from .models import Note


@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    # ─── List ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    list_display    = ['title', 'short_content', 'created_at']
    # Columns in the list table: title, text preview, date
    # The first column is always a link to the detail page

    search_fields   = ['^title', 'content']
    # '^title' → LIKE 'search%' (faster)  vs  'title' → LIKE '%search%'
    # 'content' → full-text search

    list_filter     = ['created_at']
    # Filters on the right: "Any date", "Today", "This week"...

    ordering        = ['-created_at']
    # Sorting: newest first (overrides the ordering from Meta)

    list_per_page   = 20
    # Pagination: 20 records per page

    # ─── Detail ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    readonly_fields = ['created_at']
    # These fields are shown but not editable (auto_now_add → already editable=False)

    # ─── Computed column ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    @admin.display(description='Зміст (preview)')
    def short_content(self, obj):
        """Shows the first 80 characters of content in the list."""
        if not obj.content:
            return '—'
        preview = obj.content[:80] + ('...' if len(obj.content) > 80 else '')
        return format_html('<span style="color:#6b7280">{}</span>', preview)

docs.title: list_display
docs.text:
list_display = ['title', 'short_content', 'created_at']
# ↑ Each item is either a model field, a NoteAdmin method, or a model method

# A model field:
list_display = ['title', 'created_at']

# A NoteAdmin method with @admin.display:
@admin.display(description='Зміст (preview)')
def short_content(self, obj):
    return obj.content[:80]

# A model method:
# In models.py:
def preview(self):
    return self.content[:80]
# In admin.py:
list_display = ['title', 'preview', 'created_at']

docs.title: search_fields — search syntax
docs.text:
search_fields = ['^title', 'content', '=status']
# Prefix | SQL LIKE          | When to use
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
# (none) | LIKE '%query%'    | Full-text (slow on large tables)
# '^'    | LIKE 'query%'     | Search from the start (indexable, faster)
# '='    | = 'query'         | Exact match
# '@'    | Full-text         | PostgreSQL full-text (__search, needs django.contrib.postgres; not SQLite)

docs.title: list_filter — built-in filters
docs.text:
list_filter = ['created_at', 'is_public']
# DateTimeField → automatic filters: "Any date", "Today", "This week"...
# BooleanField → "All", "Yes", "No"

docs.title: format_html — safe HTML in the admin
docs.text:
from django.utils.html import format_html

@admin.display(description='Статус')
def status_badge(self, obj):
    color = 'green' if obj.is_active else 'red'
    label = 'Активна' if obj.is_active else 'Архів'
    # format_html inserts HTML safely:
    # → escaping for all {}  → protection against XSS
    return format_html(
        '<span style="color:{};font-weight:bold">{}</span>',
        color,   # ← escaped
        label,   # ← escaped
    )
    # Don't concatenate strings! f"<span>{obj.title}</span>" → XSS if title contains <script>

docs.title: admin.site.register vs @admin.register
docs.text:
# Option 1: admin.site.register (old style)
admin.site.register(Note, NoteAdmin)

# Option 2: @admin.register (modern, a decorator)
@admin.register(Note)
class NoteAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    ...

# The result is the same. @admin.register is more readable.

class TagAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ['name', 'slug']
    prepopulated_fields = {'slug': ('name',)}
    # prepopulated_fields: automatically fills slug from name (via JS)

docs.title: ModelForm and CRUD
docs.text: On this page you will build a complete CRUD for Note: a create/edit form (ModelForm), protection against duplicates (PRG), flash messages, and Bootstrap templates.

docs.title: Theory: ModelForm
docs.text: ModelForm — Django automatically generates an HTML form from a Python model. One class replaces 50 lines of HTML.

docs.title: Without ModelForm vs With ModelForm
docs.text:
# ❌ WITHOUT ModelForm: you describe every field by hand
class NoteFormManual(forms.Form):
    title   = forms.CharField(max_length=200, label='Title')
    content = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea, required=False, label='Text')
    # + duplication with the model — when models.py changes → you must edit here too

# ✅ WITH ModelForm: a single line fields = [...]
class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model  = Note
        fields = ['title', 'content']
        # Django looks at Note.title (CharField(max_length=200)) itself
        # and generates forms.CharField(max_length=200)
        # Synchronization is automatic when the model changes

docs.title: What ModelForm generates automatically
docs.text:
Note model                        NoteForm generates
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CharField(max_length=200)     →   forms.CharField(max_length=200)
                                  widget=TextInput
                                  → <input type="text" maxlength="200">

TextField(blank=True)         →   forms.CharField(required=False)
                                  widget=Textarea
                                  → <textarea rows="10"></textarea>

SmallIntegerField(choices)    →   forms.TypedChoiceField(choices=...)
                                  widget=Select
                                  → <select><option>...</option></select>

BooleanField(default=False)   →   forms.BooleanField(required=False)
                                  widget=CheckboxInput
                                  → <input type="checkbox">

ForeignKey(Notebook)          →   forms.ModelChoiceField(
                                      queryset=Notebook.objects.all())
                                  widget=Select
                                  → <select> with all notebooks

ManyToManyField(Tag)          →   forms.ModelMultipleChoiceField(
                                      queryset=Tag.objects.all())
                                  widget=SelectMultiple

docs.title: The form cycle: GET → POST → redirect
docs.text:
def note_create(request):

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST)
        # request.POST: QueryDict {'title': ['Note'], 'content': ['']}
        # NoteForm is bound to the data → bound form

        if form.is_valid():
            # is_valid() does the following:
            # 1. Converts strings from request.POST into Python types
            # 2. Runs the validators of every field
            # 3. Runs clean_<field>() if present
            # 4. Runs form.clean() (cross-field validation)
            # If there are errors → is_valid() = False → form.errors is populated

            note = form.save()
            # form.save() = form.instance.save()
            # Executes INSERT INTO hello_app_note (...) VALUES (...)
            # Returns the saved object

            return redirect('hello_app:note_list')
    else:
        form = NoteForm()
        # Unbound form — empty

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_form.html', {'form': form})
    # If is_valid() = False → we return THE SAME form with errors
    # form.errors: {'title': ['This field is required.']}

docs.title: form.save() and form.save(commit=False)
docs.text:
# form.save() — saves and returns the object
note = form.save()   # INSERT INTO + return Note instance

# form.save(commit=False) — does not save, returns an unsaved object
note = form.save(commit=False)
note.user = request.user   # ← add fields that are not in the form
note.save()                # ← now we save

# Why commit=False?
# The NoteForm form does not include the user field (IDOR protection)
# So the view adds user = request.user manually before saving
# In notes_chat_app this is a mandatory pattern — without it you get IDOR

docs.title: A form with instance — editing
docs.text:
def note_edit(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, instance=note)
        # Bound form + existing object
        # form.save() → UPDATE instead of INSERT
    else:
        form = NoteForm(instance=note)
        # Form is filled with the current note data

    # Without instance: form.save() is always an INSERT (a duplicate!)
    # With instance: form.save() → UPDATE hello_app_note SET ... WHERE id=note.id

docs.title: Theory: the PRG pattern
docs.text: POST/Redirect/Get is the standard way to handle forms. It protects against duplicates when the user presses F5.

docs.title: The problem without PRG
docs.text:
User → POST /notes/new/ (create the note "Shopping")
  ↓ View saves the note, returns 200 with a confirmation
  ↓ Browser shows the page
  ↓ User presses F5 (refresh)
  ↓ Browser REPEATS the POST request ← PROBLEM!
  ↓ A second "Shopping" note is created!

Result: 2 identical notes. F5 again → 3 notes.

docs.title: The solution — PRG
docs.text:
User → POST /notes/new/
  ↓ View saves the note
  ↓ View returns 302 REDIRECT → /notes/
  ↓ Browser GET /notes/ (follows the redirect automatically)
  ↓ Browser shows the list of notes
  ↓ F5 → repeats GET /notes/ (safe!)

Result: only one note. F5 = reloading the list.

# ✅ Correct — PRG:
def note_create(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            note = form.save()
            return redirect('hello_app:note_list')   # ← 302, not 200!
    else:
        form = NoteForm()
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_form.html', {'form': form})

# ❌ Wrong — no redirect:
def note_create_bad(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            note = form.save()
            return render(request, 'success.html', {'note': note})
            # ↑ The browser stays on the POST URL
            # F5 → browser: "Resend the POST request?" → duplicate!

docs.title: Theory: Django Messages
docs.text: Flash messages are one-time messages that disappear after being viewed once. Perfect for "Note saved" after a redirect.

docs.title: How Messages work
docs.text:
1. POST /notes/new/
   messages.success(request, "Note saved!")
   → the message is stored in the SESSION (not in the response)
   ↓
2. redirect → GET /notes/
   template: {% for message in messages %}{{ message }}{% endfor %}
   → the message is displayed
   → the SESSION is cleared (used once!)
   ↓
3. F5 → GET /notes/ again
   messages = empty → the message is gone

docs.title: Message levels and Bootstrap classes
docs.text:
from django.contrib import messages

messages.debug(request, 'Debug message')
messages.info(request, 'Informational message')
messages.success(request, 'Note saved successfully!')
messages.warning(request, 'Note deleted.')
messages.error(request, 'Error while saving.')

Configure it in hello_project/settings.py:

from django.contrib.messages import constants as messages

MESSAGE_TAGS = {
    messages.DEBUG:   'secondary',   # → alert-secondary
    messages.INFO:    'info',        # → alert-info
    messages.SUCCESS: 'success',     # → alert-success
    messages.WARNING: 'warning',     # → alert-warning
    messages.ERROR:   'danger',      # → alert-danger (Bootstrap uses danger!)
}

docs.title: Messages in the template (base.html)
docs.text:
{% if messages %}
    {% for message in messages %}
    <div class="alert alert-{{ message.tags }} alert-dismissible fade show mb-3" role="alert">
        {{ message }}
        <button type="button" class="btn-close" data-bs-dismiss="alert"></button>
    </div>
    {% endfor %}
{% endif %}

docs.title: Theory: Template Inheritance
docs.text: A single base.html contains the Bootstrap CDN, Navbar, and Footer. All other pages only fill in blocks.

docs.title: How Django processes templates with
docs.text:
1. render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', context)

2. Django finds the template:
   APP_DIRS=True → hello_app/templates/hello_app/note_list.html

3. It encounters {% extends 'base.html' %}
   → loads base.html
   → finds all {% block name %}...{% endblock %}

4. For every block:
   → if the child template overrides it → uses the child's content
   → if not → uses the base content

5. {{ variable }} → replaced with the context value

docs.title: base.html blocks
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="uk">
<head>
    <title>{% block title %}Bootstrap Notes{% endblock %}</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="...bootstrap.min.css">
    {% block extra_css %}{% endblock %}
    <!--
        extra_css: an empty block — a child can add page-specific CSS
    -->
</head>
<body>
    <nav>...</nav>
    <main>
        {% block content %}{% endblock %}
        <!--
            content: the MAIN block — every page fills in its own
        -->
    </main>
    <footer>...</footer>
    <script src="...bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script>
    {% block extra_js %}{% endblock %}
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Child template
docs.text:
{% extends 'base.html' %}

{% block title %}My notes{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

docs.title: Step 3 — NoteForm (ModelForm)
docs.text:
Create hello_app/forms.py:

from django import forms
from .models import Note


class NoteForm(forms.ModelForm):
    """
    ModelForm for Note.
    Django automatically generates fields from the model:
      title (CharField(max_length=200)) → TextInput
      content (TextField(blank=True))   → Textarea
    """

    class Meta:
        model  = Note
        fields = ['title', 'content']
        # NOT included: created_at (auto_now_add) — Django sets it automatically

        widgets = {
            'title': forms.TextInput(attrs={
                'class':       'form-control',
                'placeholder': 'Enter a title...',
                'autofocus':   True,
            }),
            'content': forms.Textarea(attrs={
                'class': 'form-control',
                'rows':  6,
                'placeholder': 'Note text...',
            }),
        }
        labels = {
            'title':   'Title',
            'content': 'Content',
        }
        help_texts = {
            'title':   'A short, descriptive title (up to 200 characters)',
            'content': 'The main content of the note. This field is optional.',
        }

    def clean_title(self):
        """
        Custom validator for the title field.
        clean_<field_name>() is called after the standard validators.
        """
        title = self.cleaned_data.get('title', '').strip()
        if len(title) < 3:
            raise forms.ValidationError('The title must be at least 3 characters long.')
        return title   # ← IMPORTANT: return the cleaned value!

docs.title: Step 4 — CRUD views
docs.text:
hello_app/views.py:

from django.shortcuts import render, redirect, get_object_or_404
from django.contrib import messages

from .models import Note
from .forms import NoteForm


def index(request):
    """Home → redirect to the list."""
    return redirect('hello_app:note_list')


def note_list(request):
    """List of all notes."""
    notes = Note.objects.all()              # SELECT * FROM hello_app_note
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})


def note_detail(request, pk):
    """Detail of a single note."""
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)   # get() or 404
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_detail.html', {'note': note})


def note_create(request):
    """
    GET  → empty form
    POST → validation → saving → redirect (PRG)
    """
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            note = form.save()
            messages.success(request, f'Note "{note.title}" created successfully!')
            return redirect('hello_app:note_list')
    else:
        form = NoteForm()

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_form.html', {
        'form':   form,
        'action': 'Create',
        'title':  'New note',
    })


def note_edit(request, pk):
    """
    GET  → form filled with the current data (instance=note)
    POST → update (UPDATE, not INSERT)
    """
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, instance=note)
        if form.is_valid():
            form.save()
            messages.success(request, f'Note "{note.title}" updated!')
            return redirect('hello_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)
    else:
        form = NoteForm(instance=note)   # Fill with the current data

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_form.html', {
        'form':   form,
        'note':   note,
        'action': 'Save changes',
        'title':  f'Edit: {note.title}',
    })


def note_delete(request, pk):
    """
    GET  → confirmation page
    POST → deletion → redirect (DELETE only via POST!)

    Why only POST?
    If DELETE worked via GET: <a href="/notes/1/delete/"> or <img src=...>
    would delete the note when the page loads.
    POST requires a form with csrf_token → protected.
    """
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        title = note.title   # Save it before deleting
        note.delete()
        messages.warning(request, f'Note "{title}" deleted.')
        return redirect('hello_app:note_list')

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_confirm_delete.html', {'note': note})

docs.title: get_object_or_404 — protection against DoesNotExist
docs.text:
# ❌ Without get_object_or_404:
note = Note.objects.get(pk=pk)
# If not found → DoesNotExist exception → 500 Internal Server Error

# ✅ With get_object_or_404:
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
# If not found → Http404 → 404 Not Found page (correct!)

# Filtering by several fields (IDOR protection):
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)
# → 404 if the note does not exist OR belongs to another user

docs.title: Step 5 — URL routes
docs.text:
hello_app/urls.py:

from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = 'hello_app'

urlpatterns = [
    path('',                        views.index,       name='index'),
    path('notes/',                  views.note_list,   name='note_list'),
    path('notes/new/',              views.note_create, name='note_create'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/',         views.note_detail, name='note_detail'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/edit/',    views.note_edit,   name='note_edit'),
    path('notes/<int:pk>/delete/',  views.note_delete, name='note_delete'),
]

Important: notes/new/ comes before notes/<int:pk>/

'notes/new/' → does not match <int:pk> because 'new' is not an int → OK
'notes/42/'  → <int:pk> → pk=42 → OK

The <int:pk> converter accepts only digits ([0-9]+), so 'new' does not
match it even if the order is reversed — there is no ValueError.
But with a broader pattern the order is critical:
'notes/<slug:slug>/' placed higher → 'new' → slug='new' → the wrong view!
Django checks urlpatterns FROM TOP TO BOTTOM → the first match wins.
More specific patterns go higher!

docs.text:
CREATE:  GET  /notes/new/        → note_create view → empty form
         POST /notes/new/        → form.save() → redirect → flash message
         GET  /notes/            → list with the new note + flash message

READ:    GET  /notes/            → note_list view → QuerySet → template
         GET  /notes/42/         → note_detail view → get_object_or_404 → template

UPDATE:  GET  /notes/42/edit/    → note_edit view → form with instance=note
         POST /notes/42/edit/    → NoteForm(POST, instance=note).save() → UPDATE → redirect

DELETE:  GET  /notes/42/delete/  → note_delete view → confirmation
         POST /notes/42/delete/  → note.delete() → redirect → flash message

docs.title: Models and migrations
docs.text: In bootstrap_notes the Note model is already defined in models.py — you inherit it from Step 1. This page explains its anatomy, how Django turns a class into a database table, and how to run the project from scratch.

docs.title: What the project already has
docs.text:
bootstrap_notes is a continuation of hello_project. hello_app/models.py contains:

from django.db import models


class Note(models.Model):
    title      = models.CharField(max_length=200, verbose_name='Title')
    content    = models.TextField(blank=True, verbose_name='Text')
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True, verbose_name='Created')

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

    class Meta:
        verbose_name        = 'Note'
        verbose_name_plural = 'Notes'
        ordering            = ['-created_at']

And a simple view:

def note_list(request):
    notes = Note.objects.all()
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})

The /notes/ page displays notes in plain HTML without Bootstrap. Our goal is to replace this template and add a full CRUD.

docs.title: Anatomy of a model: from a Python class to an SQL table
docs.text:
Note (Python class)                hello_app_note (SQL table)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
id (auto BigAutoField)          →  id bigint NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY
title (CharField(max_length=200)) →  title varchar(200) NOT NULL
content (TextField(blank=True)) →  content text NOT NULL  (no SQL DEFAULT)
created_at (DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)) → created_at timestamp NOT NULL

# models.Model — the base class for all Django models
class Note(models.Model):
    #           ↑ we inherit from models.Model → we get:
    #           - id (PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT) automatically
    #           - Note.objects (Manager) → ORM API
    #           - .save(), .delete() methods

    title = models.CharField(
        max_length=200,          # VARCHAR(200) in SQL
        verbose_name='Title'     # field name in the admin panel
    )

    content = models.TextField(
        blank=True,              # Can be empty in forms
        verbose_name='Text'      # null=False by default!
                                 # → TEXT NOT NULL (the empty string '' comes from the form/Python, not the DB)
    )

    created_at = models.DateTimeField(
        auto_now_add=True,       # Set automatically on CREATE
        verbose_name='Created'   # auto_now_add=True → editable=False!
                                 # Will not appear in forms
    )

docs.title: blank=True vs null=True
docs.text:
# blank=True — form validation: the field is optional
content = models.TextField(blank=True)
# → the form accepts an empty string

# null=True — database: can store NULL
content = models.TextField(null=True, blank=True)
# → the DB stores NULL instead of ''

# For CharField/TextField — do not use null=True
# Django convention: an empty string '' instead of NULL in string fields
# Why: NULL and '' are different values, two states of "empty"

# null=True is useful for numeric fields:
age = models.IntegerField(null=True, blank=True)
# → "not specified" (NULL) vs "0" — different values

docs.title: auto_now_add vs auto_now
docs.text:
# auto_now_add=True: CREATION time
created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
# Set once on INSERT → never changes
# editable=False → will not appear in forms

# auto_now=True: time of the LAST UPDATE
updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)
# Updated on EVERY save()
# editable=False → will not appear in forms

# Both:
class Note(models.Model):
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)  # creation time
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)      # update time

docs.title: str and Meta
docs.text:
def __str__(self):
    return self.title
    # String representation of the object:
    # Without __str__: "Note object (1)"  ← inconvenient
    # With __str__:    "Shopping list"    ← clear
    #
    # Used in: the admin panel, the Django shell,
    # ModelChoiceField (select) in forms

class Meta:
    verbose_name        = 'Note'
    verbose_name_plural = 'Notes'
    # These strings are displayed in the admin panel
    # Without them: "Note" / "Notes" (Django's English defaults)

    ordering = ['-created_at']
    # Default ordering: '-' means DESC (newest first)
    # Equivalent: Note.objects.order_by('-created_at')
    # Every QuerySet without .order_by() will use this ordering

docs.title: The migration cycle
docs.text:
models.py (Python class)
    ↓
python manage.py makemigrations
    ↓
hello_app/migrations/0001_initial.py  (a plan of changes in Python)
    ↓
python manage.py migrate
    ↓
DB: hello_app_note (a real table)

# Show the SQL the migration will execute:
python manage.py sqlmigrate hello_app 0001

-- Output (SQLite):
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE "hello_app_note" (
    "id"         integer NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    "title"      varchar(200) NOT NULL,
    "content"    text NOT NULL,
    "created_at" datetime NOT NULL
);
COMMIT;

docs.title: The two-step rule
docs.text:
# After ANY change to models.py — always two steps:
python manage.py makemigrations   # Record the plan
python manage.py migrate          # Apply it to the DB

# makemigrations WITHOUT migrate:
# The Python class is updated, the table in the DB is old
# → OperationalError: column does not exist

docs.title: Step 3. CRUD and architecture
docs.text:
Training project: notes_project — a standalone application that starts with SQLite and moves to PostgreSQL. This is the third step of the evolution. You go through the full cycle: from domain design to a finished application with the Services & Selectors architecture.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have completed:

  • Step 1. Hello Django — a basic Django project, the first HttpResponse
  • Step 2. Bootstrap Notes — ModelForm, PRG, Bootstrap CRUD

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• The 7-step methodology of database design: Domain → Entities → Attributes → Relationships → Normalization → on_delete → Django Model
  • ER diagrams — all relationship types: 1:1, 1:N, M:N
  • Services & Selectors — an architectural separation of responsibility layers
  • selectors.py — only SELECT queries, with optimization
  • services.py — CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE with transaction.atomic()

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. Domain design — the 7-step methodology, where the truth lives, requirements analysis
  2. ER diagrams — relationship types, the on_delete matrix, the full schema of 11 tables
  3. Django models — the full code of all models, the ORM QuerySet API
  4. Migrations — Migration Lifecycle, the dependency DAG, the first run with SQLite
  5. Services and Selectors — layer architecture, READ/WRITE flow, full code
  6. QuerySet in depth — normalization, N+1, select_related, prefetch_related, F(), transactions
