docs.text:
Location: notes_app/views.py

from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, User
from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from django.http import Http404
from . import selectors, services


@login_required
def group_list(request):
    """The list of groups the current user belongs to."""
    groups = selectors.get_user_groups(request.user)
    return render(request, 'notes_app/group_list.html', {'groups': groups})


@login_required
def group_create(request):
    """
    Creating a new group. The creator automatically becomes the first member.

    Validation — via the GroupCreateForm form, not by hand via request.POST.get().
    Advantages of forms over raw POST:
      • clean_name() checks name uniqueness automatically
      • All errors are available via form.errors → we render them in the template
      • Consistent with the other views — one approach across the whole project
      • DRY: validation logic in one place (forms.py), not in every view
    """
    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = GroupCreateForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            group = services.create_group(
                name=form.cleaned_data['name'],
                creator=request.user,
            )
            messages.success(request, f'✅ Групу «{group.name}» створено! Ви перший учасник.')
            return redirect('notes_app:group_detail', pk=group.pk)
    else:
        form = GroupCreateForm()
    return render(request, 'notes_app/group_form.html', {
        'form': form, 'title': 'Нова група', 'action': 'Створити',
    })


@login_required
def group_detail(request, pk):
    """
    Group view: members + actions (add/remove/leave).

    One view — three actions through a single POST:
      action='add'    → add a member by username
      action='remove' → remove a specific member (by user_pk)
      action='leave'  → the current user leaves the group
    """
    group = selectors.get_group_with_members(pk, request.user)
    if group is None:
        raise Http404('Групу не знайдено або у вас немає доступу.')

    error = None

    if request.method == 'POST':
        action = request.POST.get('action')

        if action == 'add':
            username = request.POST.get('username', '').strip()
            ok, msg = services.add_user_to_group(group, username)
            if ok:
                messages.success(request, f'«{username}» додано до групи.')
                return redirect('notes_app:group_detail', pk=pk)
            else:
                error = msg

        elif action == 'remove':
            remove_pk = request.POST.get('user_pk')
            try:
                target = User.objects.get(pk=remove_pk)
                if target == request.user:
                    messages.error(request, 'Щоб покинути групу — використай кнопку "Покинути".')
                else:
                    services.remove_user_from_group(group, target)
                    messages.success(request, f'«{target.username}» видалено з групи.')
            except User.DoesNotExist:
                pass
            return redirect('notes_app:group_detail', pk=pk)

        elif action == 'leave':
            group_name = group.name
            services.remove_user_from_group(group, request.user)
            messages.info(request, f'Ви покинули групу «{group_name}».')
            return redirect('notes_app:group_list')

    return render(request, 'notes_app/group_detail.html', {
        'group':   group,
        'members': group.user_set.all(),
        'error':   error,
    })


@login_required
def group_delete(request, pk):
    """
    Deleting a group.
    Only a group member may delete it; a non-member → 403 (we know the group exists).
    """
    group = get_object_or_404(Group, pk=pk)
    if not group.user_set.filter(pk=request.user.pk).exists():
        raise PermissionDenied   # 403: we know it exists, but we have no access
    if request.method == 'POST':
        name = group.name
        services.delete_group(group)
        messages.warning(
            request,
            f'Групу «{name}» видалено. Спільні нотатки і списки стали особистими.'
        )
        return redirect('notes_app:group_list')
    return render(request, 'notes_app/group_confirm_delete.html', {'group': group})

Key pattern — one view, three actions:

POST /groups/5/   {action: 'add',    username: 'bob'}     → add Bob
POST /groups/5/   {action: 'remove', user_pk: 99}         → remove user.pk=99
POST /groups/5/   {action: 'leave'}                       → the current user leaves

Why one view rather than three URLs?
  - All group management logic is in one place
  - A shared membership check in the view
  - Easier to test (one TestCase test class)
  - Fewer URL patterns

}

docs.title: Step 2 — Registration (Registration View)
docs.text:
django.contrib.auth.urls does not include registration — you have to write it yourself:

# notes_app/views.py
from django.contrib.auth.forms import UserCreationForm
from django.contrib.auth import login
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.contrib import messages


def register(request):
    """
    Registering a new user.
    After successful registration — auto-login and redirect to note_list.
    """
    if request.user.is_authenticated:
        # Already logged in → don't show the registration form
        return redirect('notes_app:note_list')

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = UserCreationForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            user = form.save()
            # auto-login: don't make the user log in right after registering
            login(request, user)
            messages.success(request, f'Вітаємо, {user.username}! Акаунт створено.')
            return redirect('notes_app:note_list')
    else:
        form = UserCreationForm()

    return render(request, 'registration/register.html', {'form': form})

docs.title: Object Permissions — Protecting Against IDOR
docs.text: The most common vulnerability in web applications (OWASP A01): Broken Access Control — a user gains access to someone else's data.

docs.title: What IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is
docs.text:
Alice is registered. She sees the URL of her note: /notes/42/edit/
She thinks: "What happens if I change 42 to 43?"
Alice navigates to: /notes/43/edit/
If the view does not check the owner → Alice edits BOB's note!

This is an IDOR attack — Insecure Direct Object Reference.
OWASP A01 (Broken Access Control) — the most frequent cause of data leaks.

docs.title: The AuthN vs AuthZ difference (with an SQL example)
docs.text:
# ─── PROBLEM: @login_required is only AuthN, not AuthZ! ─────────────────────
@login_required
def note_edit(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)   # ← IDOR vulnerability!
    # Alice is logged in → @login_required lets her through ✓
    # But note(pk=43) belongs to Bob → Alice edits someone else's data! ✗

# Generated SQL:
# SELECT * FROM note WHERE pk = 43
# → returns Bob's note! No user_id check at all!


# ─── SOLUTION: add user= to get_object_or_404 ───────────────────────────────
@login_required
def note_edit(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)   # ← AuthZ ✓
    # pk=43 + user=Alice
    # SQL: SELECT * FROM note WHERE pk=43 AND user_id=42
    # Bob has note(pk=43, user_id=99) → user_id=42 does not match → 404

The golden rule: 

@login_required               = "are you logged in?"        (AuthN)
get_object_or_404(            = "is this object yours?"     (AuthZ)
    Note, pk=pk,
    user=request.user
)

Why 404 and not 403? 

403 Forbidden → we say: "This resource exists, but you have no access"
                The attacker knows id=43 exists → may try other attacks

404 Not Found  → we say: "No such resource exists"
                The attacker doesn't know whether it exists → less information for an attack

Principle: do not reveal that other people's objects exist.

docs.title: Pattern for shared objects (owner OR group member)
docs.text:
# Notes can belong to a group → the check is more complex:
from django.db.models import Q

@login_required
def note_detail(request, pk):
    user_groups = request.user.groups.all()
    note = get_object_or_404(
        Note.objects.filter(
            Q(user=request.user) | Q(group__in=user_groups)
        ),
        pk=pk
    )
    # Alice sees the note if:
    #   note.user == Alice (personal note)
    #   OR note.group in Alice.groups.all() (group note)
    #
    # SQL:
    # SELECT * FROM note
    # WHERE pk = 43
    #   AND (user_id = 42 OR group_id IN (1, 3))
    # → If neither → 404
    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_detail.html', {'note': note})

docs.title: Full note_edit implementation with all checks
docs.text:
# notes_app/views.py — full note_edit implementation:

from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, redirect, render
from django.contrib import messages
from django.db.models import Q
from .models import Note
from .forms import NoteForm
from . import services, selectors


@login_required
def note_edit(request, pk):
    """
    Editing a note — two levels of checks:
    1. @login_required          → AuthN: logged in?
    2. Q(user) | Q(group)       → read access: own note or group note?
    3. note.user == request.user → AuthZ write: only the owner can edit

    Why a Q-filter and not get_object_or_404(..., user=request.user)?
      get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user) would block
      group members from viewing the note via the URL /notes/<pk>/edit/.
      The real logic: a group member can READ the note (sees it),
      but only the owner can EDIT it.
    """
    user_groups = request.user.groups.all()
    note = get_object_or_404(
        Note.objects.filter(Q(user=request.user) | Q(group__in=user_groups)),
        pk=pk,
    )
    # ↑ SQL: SELECT * FROM note WHERE pk=<pk> AND (user_id=<uid> OR group_id IN (...))
    # → 404 if neither the owner nor a group member

    if note.user != request.user:
        # A group member can VIEW the note but cannot edit someone else's
        messages.error(request, 'Ти не можеш редагувати нотатку іншого користувача.')
        return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=pk)

    if request.method == 'POST':
        form = NoteForm(request.POST, instance=note, user=request.user)
        if form.is_valid():
            # tags — an M2M field; NoteForm.cleaned_data['tags'] → QuerySet of Tag objects
            # the service needs tag_ids separately (we don't pass the dict directly!)
            tags = form.cleaned_data.get('tags')
            tag_ids = [t.id for t in tags] if tags else []
            services.update_note(
                note,
                title=form.cleaned_data['title'],
                content=form.cleaned_data.get('content', ''),
                priority=form.cleaned_data.get('priority', note.priority),
                notebook=form.cleaned_data.get('notebook'),
                is_pinned=form.cleaned_data.get('is_pinned', note.is_pinned),
                group=form.cleaned_data.get('group'),
                tag_ids=tag_ids,
            )
            # update_note(note, *, title, content, ...) — keyword-only args
            # You can't call it as update_note(note, form.cleaned_data) → TypeError
            messages.success(request, f'✅ Нотатку "{note.title}" оновлено!')
            return redirect('notes_app:note_detail', pk=note.pk)
    else:
        form = NoteForm(instance=note, user=request.user)

    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_form.html', {
        'form': form,
        'title': f'Редагувати: {note.title}',
        'note': note,
        'action': 'Зберегти зміни',
    })


@login_required
def note_delete(request, pk):
    # Similarly: Q-filter for access + owner check before deleting
    user_groups = request.user.groups.all()
    note = get_object_or_404(
        Note.objects.filter(Q(user=request.user) | Q(group__in=user_groups)),
        pk=pk,
    )
    if note.user != request.user:
        messages.error(request, 'Ти не можеш видалити нотатку іншого користувача.')
        return redirect('notes_app:note_list')
    if request.method == 'POST':
        title = note.title
        services.delete_note(note)
        messages.warning(request, f'🗑️ Нотатку "{title}" видалено.')
        return redirect('notes_app:note_list')
    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_confirm_delete.html', {'note': note})

Before vs After:

# ✗ BEFORE (IDOR vulnerability):
note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk)
# SQL: SELECT * FROM note WHERE pk=43
# Returns Bob's note if pk=43 — no owner check at all!

# ✓ AFTER for owned objects (Notebook, TodoList, etc.):
notebook = get_object_or_404(Notebook, pk=pk, user=request.user)
# SQL: SELECT * FROM notebook WHERE pk=43 AND user_id=42
# pk=43 + user_id=42 → not found → 404

# ✓ AFTER for shared objects (Note — can belong to a group):
user_groups = request.user.groups.all()
note = get_object_or_404(
    Note.objects.filter(Q(user=request.user) | Q(group__in=user_groups)),
    pk=pk,
)
# SQL: SELECT * FROM note WHERE pk=43 AND (user_id=42 OR group_id IN (1,3))
# Owner OR group member — both get read access
# For writes: we additionally check note.user == request.user

docs.title: Password Security — Resetting and Changing a Password
docs.text: Django provides a complete password management system "out of the box" through django.contrib.auth. You don't need to write a single view for login, logout, password reset or change.

docs.title: Why you shouldn't write your own password views
docs.text:
Password management is a security-critical task. Common mistakes when writing your own views:

  • Passing the password in the URL (a GET parameter) → the password ends up in server logs and browser history
  • One-time tokens without expiration → an old token can be reused
  • Storing the password in plain text instead of a hash → a database breach = all passwords compromised
  • No rate limiting → brute force attacks

Django contrib.auth does it right: PBKDF2 + salt, one-time HMAC tokens (72 h), protection against user enumeration (it does not reveal whether an email exists in the database).

docs.title: What include('django.contrib.auth.urls') wires up
docs.text:
# notes_project/urls.py (or hello_project/urls.py in crispy_notes_project):
path("accounts/", include("django.contrib.auth.urls")),

This automatically registers 8 URLs:

URL View Name (for {% url %}) Template (you must create it) /accounts/login/ LoginView login registration/login.html /accounts/logout/ LogoutView logout (redirect, no template) /accounts/password_change/ PasswordChangeView password_change registration/password_change_form.html /accounts/password_change/done/ PasswordChangeDoneView password_change_done registration/password_change_done.html /accounts/password_reset/ PasswordResetView password_reset registration/password_reset_form.html /accounts/password_reset/done/ PasswordResetDoneView password_reset_done registration/password_reset_done.html /accounts/reset/<uidb64>/<token>/ PasswordResetConfirmView password_reset_confirm registration/password_reset_confirm.html /accounts/reset/done/ PasswordResetCompleteView password_reset_complete registration/password_reset_complete.html

Takeaway: 8 URLs + 8 views are already written by Django — you only write the HTML templates!

docs.title: Password Reset Flow — 5 steps
docs.text:
Step 1: /accounts/password_reset/
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Alice forgot her password → enters her email in the form
→ password_reset_form.html

Step 2: Django handles the POST
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Django looks for a User with that email (says nothing if not found —
safe behavior: we don't reveal whether such an email exists)
Generates a unique token (PasswordResetTokenGenerator): an HMAC keyed with SECRET_KEY over
user.pk + password hash + last_login + email + timestamp
(after a password change or a login the old token becomes invalid)
Sends an email with the link:
  /accounts/reset/<uidb64>/<token>/

[DEV: EMAIL_BACKEND = console → the email is printed to the terminal / docker logs]
[PROD: EMAIL_BACKEND = smtp → a real email via SMTP]

Step 3: /accounts/password_reset/done/
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Django shows: "Check your inbox" (regardless of whether the email was found)
→ password_reset_done.html

Step 4: /accounts/reset/<uidb64>/<token>/
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Alice follows the link from the email
Django: uidb64 → user_pk, token → verifies the signature
Is it valid? (72 h, single-use — invalidated after use)
If OK → a form for the new password + password validators
→ password_reset_confirm.html

Step 5: Success → /accounts/reset/done/
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Password saved (hashed with PBKDF2 and a salt) → all of this user's sessions are reset
→ password_reset_complete.html

docs.title: How PBKDF2 stores passwords
docs.text:
# What is stored in the database (auth_user.password):
'pbkdf2_sha256$1000000$salt$hash'
#  ↑algorithm   ↑iterations  ↑salt ↑hash

# Plain text is never stored!
# Even Django doesn't know the original password — it only checks the hash.

# Verification:
# authenticate(request, username='alice', password='mysecret')
# → pbkdf2_sha256(1000000 iterations, 'mysecret' + stored_salt)
# → compares with stored_hash
# → returns a User or None

# Why 1 000 000 iterations (the default in Django 5.2)?
# If an attacker steals the database → brute force:
#   SHA-256 without stretching: 10 billion attempts/sec
#   PBKDF2 with 1000000 iter:  ~10 000 attempts/sec (1 000 000 times slower!)

docs.title: Password Validators — 4 built-in protections
docs.text:
# settings.py — 4 built-in validators:
AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS = [
    # Is the password similar to the username / email / first_name?
    {"NAME": "django.contrib.auth.password_validation.UserAttributeSimilarityValidator"},
    # At least 8 characters (configurable: "OPTIONS": {"min_length": 10})
    {"NAME": "django.contrib.auth.password_validation.MinimumLengthValidator"},
    # Is it in the list of the 20 000 most common passwords? ("password", "123456", "qwerty"...)
    {"NAME": "django.contrib.auth.password_validation.CommonPasswordValidator"},
    # Does it consist only of digits?
    {"NAME": "django.contrib.auth.password_validation.NumericPasswordValidator"},
]

# Validators run:
# 1. On registration (UserCreationForm)
# 2. On password change (PasswordChangeForm, PasswordResetConfirmView)
# 3. On set_password() → validate_password()
#    NOT on User.objects.create_user() unless you call validate_password()!

docs.title: Security Settings — What and Why
docs.text: Django has plenty of security settings. Most of them are "off" by default so as not to break localhost development. In production you need to turn them on.

docs.title: Table: each setting and what it protects against
docs.text: Setting Value What it protects against SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True JS cannot read sessionid XSS → Session Hijacking SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = "Lax" Cookie only from the same site CSRF via cross-site forms CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = False JS can read csrftoken (False = for fetch/axios in the WebSocket chat) X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY" Forbids <iframe> embedding Clickjacking attacks SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True Don't "guess" the MIME type XSS via forged files DEBUG = False Hides stack traces Leaking SECRET_KEY and code ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['mysite.com'] Only this domain HTTP Host header attacks CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = [...] Allowed HTTPS origins CSRF via ngrok/proxy

docs.title: What leaks with DEBUG = True in production
docs.text:
A server error with DEBUG=True shows:
  ✗ The full stack trace (file paths, function names, lines of code)
  ✗ The values of ALL local variables at the moment of the error
  ✗ SECRET_KEY leaks! (an attacker can forge session cookies and CSRF tokens)
  ✗ All SQL queries are kept in memory → memory leak under load
  ✗ INSTALLED_APPS, DATABASES, MIDDLEWARE — the whole config is visible in the browser

DEBUG = False + ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['mysite.com'] are mandatory in production.

docs.title: ALLOWED_HOSTS and SECRET_KEY
docs.text:
# settings.py

# ALLOWED_HOSTS — only these hosts can send requests:
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['localhost', '127.0.0.1']   # dev
# PROD:
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['mysite.com', 'www.mysite.com']

# Without ALLOWED_HOSTS with DEBUG=False → Django rejects all requests!
# SuspiciousOperation: Invalid HTTP_HOST header

# SECRET_KEY — the foundation of session, CSRF and signing security:
SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY', 'fallback-dev-key')
# NEVER commit the real SECRET_KEY to the repository!
# If SECRET_KEY leaks → an attacker can forge sessionid cookies
# → log in as any user without a password

docs.title: Production HTTPS settings (uncomment on the server)
docs.text:
# settings.py — commented out in dev (so that localhost works over HTTP):

# SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
# ↑ The cookie is sent ONLY over HTTPS
# Without it: a man-in-the-middle can intercept sessionid over HTTP

# CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
# ↑ Same for the CSRF cookie

# SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
# ↑ Any HTTP request → 301 Moved Permanently → HTTPS

# SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000  # 1 year
# ↑ The browser remembers: HTTPS ONLY for 1 year
# (HTTP Strict Transport Security header)
# WARNING: once enabled, it's hard to roll back! The browser caches it and ignores HTTP.

docs.title: Attacks these settings protect against — concrete scenarios
XSS → Session Hijacking (SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY)
docs.text:
Attack:
1. The attacker finds an XSS vulnerability (for example, injects <script> into a comment)
2. JavaScript in Alice's browser runs: document.cookie
3. It returns: "sessionid=abc123; csrftoken=xyz..."
4. Sends the cookie to evil.com → the attacker logs in as Alice

Protection SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True:
document.cookie → "csrftoken=xyz..."  (sessionid is MISSING — HttpOnly is not readable by JS)
The attacker cannot steal sessionid even with XSS.

docs.title: CSRF Attack (SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE + {% csrf_token %})
docs.text:
Attack (without protection):
1. Alice is logged in to mysite.com → the browser stores the sessionid cookie
2. Alice opens evil.com — it has a hidden form:
   <form action="https://mysite.com/notes/delete/1/" method="post">
   <input type="hidden" name="confirm" value="yes">
   JavaScript: form.submit()
3. The browser sends the request to mysite.com → automatically adds Alice's cookie!
4. The server sees a valid sessionid → performs the action as Alice

Protection SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = "Lax":
  The cookie is not sent with cross-site POST requests
  evil.com → form.submit() → the cookie is NOT added → 403

Protection {% csrf_token %}:
  POST without csrfmiddlewaretoken → 403 Forbidden
  evil.com doesn't know Alice's current token → the attack is impossible

docs.title: Clickjacking (X_FRAME_OPTIONS)
docs.text:
Attack:
1. evil.com embeds mysite.com via an <iframe>
2. Places a transparent div over the "Delete account" button
3. Alice thinks she is clicking on evil.com, but she is actually clicking the hidden mysite.com
4. The action is performed on mysite.com under Alice's session

Protection X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY":
The browser refuses to embed mysite.com in an <iframe>
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'  (the modern CSP alternative, works over both HTTP and HTTPS)

docs.title: Checking security headers in the browser
docs.text:
F12 → Network → any request → Response Headers:

X-Frame-Options: DENY                ← X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY"
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff      ← SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True

(Over HTTPS, with the _SECURE settings:)
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000  ← SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000

docs.title: Run Django's security deployment checklist
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py check --deploy

It shows warnings about security settings. In dev some warnings are expected (for example, HTTPS-specific ones). In production they should all be green.

Example output: 

SystemCheckError: System check identified some issues:

WARNINGS:
?: (security.W004) You have not set a value for the SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS setting.
?: (security.W008) Your SECRET_KEY has less than 50 characters.
?: (security.W012) SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is not set to True.

docs.title: Step 6. Django Testing from A to Z
docs.text:
This step covers two projects: crispy_notes_project (standalone, SQLite, no Docker) and notes_chat_app (Docker + PostgreSQL + Redis + WebSocket).

You will see how each level of tests protects a different layer of the system.

Result: 129+ tests — 123 pass + 6 Selenium (skipped without geckodriver/Remote Chrome)

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have completed:

  • Step 1. Hello Django — the first HttpResponse, URL routing
  • Step 2. Bootstrap Notes — ModelForm, PRG, Bootstrap CRUD
  • Step 3. CRUD and architecture — Services & Selectors, PostgreSQL
  • Step 4. Templates and Forms — Crispy Forms, Dashboard, Context Processor
  • Step 5. Auth and Security — Login/Logout, IDOR, Group Sharing

docs.title: Learning project vs Notes Chat App
docs.text: crispy_notes_project (Steps 1–6) notes_chat_app (Steps 7–11) Running tests python manage.py test hello_app.tests docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests Database SQLite PostgreSQL (Docker) What is tested models, services, forms, views, selenium The same + consumers (WebSocket) Selenium geckodriver / local Firefox Remote Chrome in Docker (selenium:4444) CI/CD GitHub Actions → ubuntu-latest → Chrome headless GitHub Actions → PostgreSQL + Redis + selenium services Number of tests 129 (123 pass + 6 selenium skip) 129+ (+ consumer tests) Unique Standalone, no Docker GroupChatConsumer, WebsocketCommunicator, TransactionTestCase

docs.text:
• Why tests — the fire alarm analogy, a real scenario with selectors.py
  • The testing pyramid — unit / integration / E2E: different cost, different speed
  • Django TestCase — the test database, ROLLBACK after each test, setUp, BaseServiceTest
  • The AAA pattern — Arrange / Act / Assert: the structure of every test
  • test_models.py — constraints, validators via full_clean(), the SET_NULL test
  • test_services.py — persistence test, security (Mass Assignment), a transactional invariant
  • test_forms.py — bound/unbound forms, queryset security, cleaned_data
  • test_views.py — Django Test Client, force_login, ownership 404, IDOR prevention
  • test_consumers.py — WebsocketCommunicator, TransactionTestCase, database_sync_to_async (notes_chat_app)
  • test_selenium.py — StaticLiveServerTestCase, Remote Chrome in Docker, the session cookie trick

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• [ ] tests/__init__.py exists (an empty file — without it Django won't find the tests)
  • [ ] Every test method starts with test_
  • [ ] A child class setUp() that overrides the parent one calls super().setUp()

docs.title: Unit tests (models, services, forms)
docs.text:
• [ ] Validators are checked via full_clean(), not .objects.create()
  • [ ] After delete() of a related object → refresh_from_db() before checking
  • [ ] SET_NULL behavior is documented by a test
  • [ ] Security test: someone else's tag/notebook is not attached

docs.title: Integration tests (views)
docs.text:
• [ ] Integration tests use force_login(), not login()
  • [ ] Every protected URL is checked for a redirect for anonymous users
  • [ ] Bob gets 404 for Alice's notes (not 403)
  • [ ] IDOR prevention: Alice cannot POST into Bob's notebook

docs.title: Consumer tests (notes_chat_app)
docs.text:
• [ ] TransactionTestCase is used, not TestCase
  • [ ] communicator.scope['user'] is set before connect()
  • [ ] await communicator.disconnect() in every test
  • [ ] database_sync_to_async for all database access from async code

docs.title: Selenium E2E
docs.text:
• [ ] @unittest.skipUnless(SELENIUM_AVAILABLE, ...) on the class
  • [ ] _DockerLiveServerMixin for the Docker environment (notes_chat_app)
  • [ ] Selenium: exec, not run, to launch in Docker
  • [ ] manage.py test returns OK (even with skipped=6)

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
• [ ] .github/workflows/ci.yml in the repository root
  • [ ] Job 1: unit + integration + consumer without selenium
  • [ ] Job 2: selenium with needs: test (runs after Job 1)
  • [ ] PostgreSQL and Redis as GitHub Actions services
  • [ ] health-cmd for PostgreSQL and Redis
  • [ ] The coverage report is saved as an artifact

Write a test that checks: if a user deletes a TodoList, all related TodoItem records are deleted along with it (CASCADE).

def test_todo_items_deleted_when_todo_list_deleted(self):

    TodoItem.objects.create(todo_list=todo_list, text='Milk')
    TodoItem.objects.create(todo_list=todo_list, text='Bread')

docs.text:
Write a test that confirms: Bob (logged in) cannot edit Alice's note (Bob gets 404).

# Hint:
def test_non_owner_cannot_edit_note(self):
    alice_note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Private')
    self.client.force_login(self.bob)

    response = self.client.get(
        reverse('notes_app:note_edit', args=[alice_note.pk])

    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, ___)  # what goes here?

docs.title: Exercise 3 — Consumer test (level: advanced)
docs.text:
Write a test that confirms: if a group with pk=999 doesn't exist, the consumer rejects the connection.

# Hint: use WebsocketCommunicator with a nonexistent pk
async def test_nonexistent_group_rejects_connection(self):
    communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
        application,
        '/ws/groups/999/chat/',
    )
    communicator.scope['user'] = self.alice

    connected, code = await communicator.connect()
    self.assertFalse(connected)
    await communicator.disconnect()

docs.title: GitHub Actions CI
docs.text: Goal: every git push automatically runs the same tests you have just learned to write. Without your involvement. On a clean server. With the result in GitHub within 2–3 minutes.

docs.title: Where the workflow lives
docs.text:
notes_chat_app/                   ← repository root
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── ci.yml                ← GitHub only sees files in .github/workflows/

GitHub Actions reads workflows ONLY from the .github/workflows/ directory in the repository root.

docs.title: What happens on git push
docs.text:
You:     git push origin main
         │
         ▼
GitHub:  Detect event → push to main
         │
         ▼
Azure:   Provision Ubuntu 24.04 VM (new, clean)
         │
         ├── Job 1: Unit + Integration + Consumer (~1-2 min)
         │     checkout → python 3.12 → pip install
         │     → PostgreSQL service → Redis service
         │     → manage.py test models/services/forms/views/consumers
         │     Result: ✅ or ❌
         │
         └── Job 2: Selenium E2E (~1-2 min) — only if Job 1 ✅
               checkout → pip install → migrations
               → PostgreSQL + Redis + Selenium Chrome service

docs.title: Job 1: Unit + Integration + Consumer Tests
docs.text:
jobs:
  test:
    name: Unit + Integration + Consumer tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

runs-on: ubuntu-latest — a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VM on Azure. After completion the VM is destroyed. There is no state between runs.

    services:
      # PostgreSQL in GitHub Actions (a separate container)
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_DB:       test_notes_db
          POSTGRES_USER:     test_user
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test_pass
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U test_user -d test_notes_db"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-retries 5

      # Redis for the channel layer
      redis:
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports: ['6379:6379']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 5s

services — additional Docker containers that run alongside the runner VM. health-cmd + health-interval + health-retries — GitHub Actions waits until the service becomes healthy before starting the steps.

    env:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://test_user:test_pass@localhost:5432/test_notes_db
      REDIS_URL:    redis://localhost:6379/0
      SECRET_KEY:   ci-secret-key-not-for-production
      DEBUG:        "False"
      ALLOWED_HOSTS: localhost,127.0.0.1

Environment variables for Django. DATABASE_URL points to the PostgreSQL service container (localhost:5432).

Step 1 — Checkout

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

Clones the whole repository onto the VM. Without this step the runner has not a single file of your code.

Step 2 — Setup Python

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
          cache: pip

Installs Python 3.12. cache: pip caches ~/.cache/pip between runs (similar to actions/cache, but built into setup-python).

Step 3 — Install dependencies

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4 — Run Unit + Integration tests

      - name: Run Unit + Integration tests
        run: |
          python manage.py test \
            notes_app.tests.test_models \
            notes_app.tests.test_services \
            notes_app.tests.test_forms \
            notes_app.tests.test_views \
            notes_app.tests.test_consumers \
            -v 2

Runs 123+ tests. The modules are listed explicitly, without test_selenium — Selenium is in a separate job.

-v 2 — verbose: each test is printed on its own line. This is useful in CI: you immediately see the name of the test that failed.

If any test returns FAILED → the step returns exit code 1 → GitHub Actions considers the step failed → the job stops → Job 2 (selenium) does not run.

docs.title: test_consumers.py — WebSocket tests
docs.text:
Specific to notes_chat_app

This section describes testing GroupChatConsumer — a WebSocket consumer that exists only in notes_chat_app. crispy_notes_project (standalone) does not have this section.

docs.title: TransactionTestCase: why not TestCase?
docs.text:
from django.test import TransactionTestCase  # not TestCase!

The reason:

TestCase:
  Wraps each test in a transaction with a ROLLBACK after the test.
  The async consumer reads the database from a separate worker thread via database_sync_to_async.
  That thread does NOT SEE the uncommitted TestCase transaction
  → setUp objects "disappear" for the consumer
  → The test fails with DoesNotExist or empty querysets.

TransactionTestCase:
  Does NOT wrap tests in a transaction.
  The data is VISIBLE to all threads (the database_sync_to_async worker thread sees it too).
  The cost: after each test, all tables are TRUNCATEd (slower).
  For consumer tests this is the right choice.

asyncSetUp() and Django

asyncSetUp() is a method of unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase. Django's TestCase and TransactionTestCase never call it, in any version (they only run async def test_* methods through async_to_sync). Use a synchronous setUp() — it runs in a regular thread, which is correct for TransactionTestCase.

docs.title: WebsocketCommunicator from channels.testing
docs.text:
WebsocketCommunicator simulates a WebSocket connection without a real browser:

WebsocketCommunicator
    ↓
ASGI application (asgi.py)
    ↓
ProtocolTypeRouter → WebSocket scope
    ↓
AuthMiddlewareStack (but in tests we set scope['user'] manually)
    ↓
URLRouter → /ws/groups/<pk>/chat/
    ↓
GroupChatConsumer.connect()
              .receive()
              .disconnect()

The key feature: communicator.scope['user'] = self.alice — we bypass AuthMiddlewareStack and set the user directly. This is reliable and avoids having to emulate a cookie or session in the test.

docs.title: database_sync_to_async in tests
docs.text:
In consumer tests you need database_sync_to_async from channels.db for any database access from async code:

from channels.db import database_sync_to_async

# Writing to the database:
await database_sync_to_async(ChatMessage.objects.create)(
    group=self.group, author=self.alice, content='Hello world'
)

# Reading from the database:
count = await database_sync_to_async(ChatMessage.objects.count)()
self.assertEqual(count, 1)

# Checking a queryset via exists():
exists = await database_sync_to_async(
    lambda: ChatMessage.objects.filter(content='Hello').exists()
)()

docs.title: Full test_consumers.py code
docs.text:
# notes_app/tests/test_consumers.py
from channels.testing import WebsocketCommunicator
from channels.db import database_sync_to_async
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, User
from django.test import TransactionTestCase  # not TestCase!

from notes_app.models import ChatMessage
from notes_project.asgi import application   # ← ASGI app for WebSocket tests


class GroupChatConsumerTest(TransactionTestCase):
    """
    Testing GroupChatConsumer via WebsocketCommunicator.

    Why TransactionTestCase:
      TestCase wraps each test in a transaction.
      The async consumer reads the database from a separate worker thread via database_sync_to_async.
      That thread doesn't see the uncommitted TestCase transaction → setUp objects "disappear".
      TransactionTestCase doesn't wrap in a transaction → the data is visible to all threads.
    """

    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')
        self.group = Group.objects.create(name='TestGroup')
        self.group.user_set.add(self.alice)
        # bob is not a group member (for the non-member test)

    async def test_authenticated_member_can_connect(self):
        """A logged-in group member can connect to the chat."""
        communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application,
            f'/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/',
        )
        communicator.scope['user'] = self.alice   # AuthMiddlewareStack bypass

        connected, subprotocol = await communicator.connect()
        self.assertTrue(connected)

        await communicator.disconnect()

    async def test_non_member_cannot_connect(self):
        """Bob is not a group member → the consumer closes the WS (code 4404)."""
        communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application,
            f'/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/',
        )
        communicator.scope['user'] = self.bob   # not a member

        connected, code = await communicator.connect()
        self.assertFalse(connected)

        await communicator.disconnect()

    async def test_anonymous_cannot_connect(self):
        """AnonymousUser → the consumer closes (code 4403)."""
        from django.contrib.auth.models import AnonymousUser
        communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application,
            f'/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/',
        )
        communicator.scope['user'] = AnonymousUser()

        connected, code = await communicator.connect()
        self.assertFalse(connected)

        await communicator.disconnect()

    async def test_connected_member_receives_history(self):
        """After connect, the consumer sends the message history."""
        # Arrange: add a message to the database
        await database_sync_to_async(ChatMessage.objects.create)(
            group=self.group,
            author=self.alice,
            content='Hello world'
        )

        communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application,
            f'/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/',
        )
        communicator.scope['user'] = self.alice

        await communicator.connect()

        # Act: receive the first message
        response = await communicator.receive_json_from()

        # Assert: it is history
        self.assertEqual(response['type'], 'history')
        self.assertEqual(response['content'], 'Hello world')
        self.assertEqual(response['author'], 'alice')

        await communicator.disconnect()

    async def test_send_message_saves_to_db_and_broadcasts(self):
        """The message is saved to the database and sent back."""
        self.group.user_set.add(self.bob)   # bob is in the group too

        comm_alice = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application, f'/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/'
        )
        comm_bob = WebsocketCommunicator(
            application, f'/ws/groups/{self.group.pk}/chat/'
        )
        comm_alice.scope['user'] = self.alice
        comm_bob.scope['user']   = self.bob

        await comm_alice.connect()
        await comm_bob.connect()

        # Alice sends a message
        await comm_alice.send_json_to({'content': 'Hello Bob!'})

        # Bob receives the broadcast
        bob_msg = await comm_bob.receive_json_from()
        self.assertEqual(bob_msg['type'], 'message')
        self.assertEqual(bob_msg['content'], 'Hello Bob!')
        self.assertEqual(bob_msg['author'], 'alice')

        # Check that it was saved to the database
        count = await database_sync_to_async(ChatMessage.objects.count)()
        self.assertEqual(count, 1)

        await comm_alice.disconnect()
        await comm_bob.disconnect()

docs.text:
• [ ] TransactionTestCase is used, not TestCase
  • [ ] setUp() is synchronous (not asyncSetUp)
  • [ ] communicator.scope['user'] is set before connect()
  • [ ] await communicator.disconnect() in every test (even if connected=False)
  • [ ] Database access from async code goes through database_sync_to_async

docs.title: Two form modes: bound vs unbound
docs.text:
A Django form is not just HTML. It is validation, normalization and a security barrier.

# UNBOUND form — without data (for displaying an empty form)
form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
# form.is_bound → False
# Useful for testing queryset fields (security)

# BOUND form — with data (for processing a POST request)
form = NoteForm(data={'title': 'Test', 'priority': 1}, user=self.alice)
# form.is_bound → True
# You can call form.is_valid(), form.cleaned_data, form.errors

docs.title: How to test a form without HTTP
docs.text:
# A form can be tested directly, without client.post():

form = TagForm(data={'name': 'Python', 'color': '#ff0000'}, user=self.alice)

# Checking validity:
form.is_valid()              # True or False — this is what we check
form.cleaned_data['name']   # 'python' — the normalized value
form.errors                  # {'name': ['...']} — errors per field

# Checking a valid form:
form = NoteForm(data={'title': 'Test', 'priority': 1}, user=self.alice)
self.assertTrue(form.is_valid(), msg=form.errors)
# ↑ msg=form.errors — if it fails, we'll see WHY it is invalid

# Checking an invalid form:
form = NoteForm(data={'title': '', 'priority': 1}, user=self.alice)
self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())
self.assertIn('title', form.errors)
# ↑ We check that the error is in a SPECIFIC field (not a general one)

docs.title: Structure of test_forms.py
docs.text:
# notes_app/tests/test_forms.py
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, User
from django.test import TestCase

from notes_app.forms import GroupCreateForm, NoteForm, TagForm
from notes_app.models import Notebook, Tag


class BaseFormTest(TestCase):
    """Base class: alice and bob for security tests."""

    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')


class TagFormTest(BaseFormTest):
    """Tests for TagForm normalization and basic validation."""

    def test_name_normalized_to_lowercase(self):
        """The tag name is stored in lowercase."""
        form = TagForm(data={'name': 'PYTHON', 'color': '#3776AB'}, user=self.alice)
        self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())
        self.assertEqual(form.cleaned_data['name'], 'python')

    def test_name_strips_whitespace(self):
        """'  work  ' → 'work' (leading/trailing spaces are removed)."""
        form = TagForm(data={'name': '  work  ', 'color': '#ff0000'}, user=self.alice)
        self.assertTrue(form.is_valid())
        self.assertEqual(form.cleaned_data['name'], 'work')

    def test_empty_name_is_invalid(self):
        form = TagForm(data={'name': '', 'color': '#000000'}, user=self.alice)
        self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())
        self.assertIn('name', form.errors)

    def test_name_too_long_is_invalid(self):
        form = TagForm(data={'name': 'x' * 51, 'color': '#000000'}, user=self.alice)
        self.assertFalse(form.is_valid())

docs.title: NoteFormSecurityTest — the full security block
docs.text:
class NoteFormSecurityTest(BaseFormTest):
    """
    The most important block of form tests — we check that the queryset
    filters only the current user's objects (protection against IDOR).
    """

    def setUp(self):
        super().setUp()
        # Both users have their own notebooks
        self.alice_notebook = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.alice, title="Alice's")
        self.bob_notebook   = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.bob,   title="Bob's")
        # Alice has a tag
        self.alice_tag = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='my-tag')
        self.bob_tag   = Tag.objects.create(user=self.bob,   name='bob-secret')

    def test_notebook_queryset_contains_user_notebooks(self):
        """Alice sees HER notebook in the dropdown."""
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertIn(self.alice_notebook, form.fields['notebook'].queryset)

    def test_notebook_queryset_excludes_other_user_notebooks(self):
        """
        Alice does NOT see Bob's notebooks — IDOR is impossible.

        WITHOUT protection in the form:
            NoteForm().fields['notebook'].queryset = Notebook.objects.all()
            → Alice sees Bob's Private Notebook in the dropdown!
            → Alice picks Bob's notebook → Alice's note is written into Bob's
            → Bob sees someone else's notes in his notebook → DATA LEAK

        With protection (our NoteForm.__init__):
            queryset = Notebook.objects.filter(user=self.user)
            → Alice sees only her own notebooks → IDOR is impossible
        """
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertNotIn(self.bob_notebook, form.fields['notebook'].queryset)

    def test_tag_queryset_contains_user_tags(self):
        """Alice sees her tags in the dropdown."""
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertIn(self.alice_tag, form.fields['tags'].queryset)

    def test_tag_queryset_excludes_other_user_tags(self):
        """Alice does NOT see Bob's tags."""
        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertNotIn(self.bob_tag, form.fields['tags'].queryset)

    def test_group_queryset_excludes_groups_user_not_in(self):
        """Alice doesn't see groups she is not a member of."""
        group = Group.objects.create(name="Bob's Team")
        self.bob.groups.add(group)        # only Bob is in the group

        form = NoteForm(user=self.alice)
        self.assertNotIn(group, form.fields['group'].queryset)

    def test_form_without_user_has_empty_querysets(self):
        """
        If the form is created without user= (a developer mistake):
            form = NoteForm(data=request.POST)  ← forgot user=request.user

        DANGEROUS: queryset = Notebook.objects.all() → all notebooks are visible
        SAFE (our code): queryset = Notebook.objects.none() → an empty list

        Better to show the user an empty dropdown than to leak all the data.
        """
        form = NoteForm()  # user not passed
        self.assertFalse(form.fields['notebook'].queryset.exists())
        self.assertFalse(form.fields['tags'].queryset.exists())

docs.title: What lives in a model (and what can break)
docs.text:
Question: Why test models? They are just fields and relations.

Answer: A model contains business rules. If they are violated, the application silently misbehaves.

Note model
  ├── priority: validators=[MinValueValidator(1), MaxValueValidator(4)]
  │     If someone removes the validators → the form will accept priority=99
  │     → Priority display will break (KeyError in PRIORITY_CHOICES)
  │
  ├── group: ForeignKey(Group, on_delete=SET_NULL)
  │     If changed to CASCADE → deleting a group will delete all notes!
  │     → Users lose data, and you find out in production
  │
  ├── notebook: ForeignKey(Notebook, on_delete=SET_NULL)
  │     If CASCADE → deleting a notebook deletes its notes
  │
  ├── is_pinned: BooleanField(default=False)
  │     If the default becomes True → all new notes become pinned
  │     → Sorting breaks
  │
  ├── __str__: "📌 {title}" or "{title}"
  │     If the format changes → Django Admin and logs display it incorrectly
  │
  └── Tag: UniqueConstraint(fields=['user', 'name'])
        If removed → two 'python' tags for one user → bugs in forms

docs.title: Structure of the tests/ package
docs.text:
notes_app/
├── models.py
├── views.py
├── forms.py
├── services.py
├── selectors.py
├── consumers.py
└── tests/                          ← a package (a directory with __init__.py)
    ├── __init__.py                  ← REQUIRED! Empty.
    │                                  Without it Django won't find the tests → "Found 0 test(s)"
    ├── test_models.py               ← Unit: constraints, __str__, SET_NULL
    ├── test_services.py             ← Unit: business logic, security
    ├── test_forms.py                ← Unit: validation, queryset filtering
    ├── test_views.py                ← Integration: HTTP, ownership, redirects
    ├── test_consumers.py            ← Consumer: WebSocket lifecycle
    └── test_selenium.py             ← E2E: browser

Why a tests/ package and not a single tests.py?

# Option 1: a single tests.py file
notes_app/tests.py   ← everything in one place → grows to 3000+ lines, hard to navigate

# Option 2: a tests/ package (our option)
notes_app/tests/
    test_models.py    ← models only
    test_services.py  ← services only
    test_forms.py     ← forms only
    test_views.py     ← integration
    test_consumers.py ← WebSocket
    test_selenium.py  ← E2E

Advantages: - Run them separately: manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_services - Each file = one layer of the system → easy to find a test - CI can run different files in parallel

docs.title: How to test validators with full_clean()
docs.text:
# IMPORTANT: validators do not run on .save() or .objects.create()!
# They run only through full_clean() or a ModelForm.

# WRONG (validators won't be checked):
note = Note.objects.create(user=user, title='Test', priority=5)
# ← Django will simply save priority=5! (validators are ignored)
# ← A CheckConstraint in the database might fire → IntegrityError
# ← But validators (MinValueValidator, MaxValueValidator) won't!

# RIGHT — via full_clean():
note = Note(user=user, title='Test', priority=5)  # ← we DON'T save right away
note.full_clean()   # ← validators run here → ValidationError

# full_clean() performs:
# 1. clean_fields()    — field validators (MinValueValidator, MaxValueValidator...)
# 2. clean()           — custom model validation
# 3. validate_unique() — unique / unique_together
# 4. validate_constraints() — Meta.constraints (UniqueConstraint, CheckConstraint)

# In a test:
def test_priority_above_4_raises_validation_error(self):
    note = Note(user=self.user, title='Test', priority=5)
    with self.assertRaises(ValidationError) as ctx:
        note.full_clean()
    self.assertIn('priority', ctx.exception.message_dict)
    #              ↑ we check that the error is exactly in the priority field

docs.title: The SET_NULL test — protection against CASCADE
docs.text:
def test_note_group_becomes_null_when_group_deleted(self):
    """
    We check that Note.group = ForeignKey(Group, on_delete=SET_NULL)
    works correctly: deleting the group → the note becomes personal.

    If someone changes it to CASCADE → this test will FAIL and show:
    DoesNotExist: Note matching query does not exist.
    → we find out BEFORE deploying that the change broke users' data.
    """
    group = Group.objects.create(name='Family')
    note  = Note.objects.create(user=self.user, title='Family note', group=group)

    group.delete()               # delete the group

    note.refresh_from_db()       # ← REQUIRED! read the fresh state from the database
    self.assertIsNone(note.group)# the note survived, group = NULL

Why refresh_from_db()? After group.delete() the note object in memory still holds the old reference. refresh_from_db() re-reads it from the database.

What Selenium tests (and what unit tests can't)
docs.text:
Django Test Client (integration):         Selenium (E2E):
  ✓ HTTP statuses                          ✓ JavaScript behavior
  ✓ HTML content (assertContains)          ✓ CSS visibility of elements
  ✓ Redirect                               ✓ Form submit via a button
  ✓ Template context                       ✓ WebSocket connection in the browser
  ✗ JavaScript events                      ✓ Bootstrap dropdown
  ✗ CSS display:none                       ✓ Real navigation between pages
  ✗ form.submit() via a button             ✓ Ajax requests
  ✗ WebSocket in the browser               ✗ Very slow (~10s/test)

docs.title: Why there are few Selenium tests
docs.text:
Unit test: 0.01s  ×  100 = 1 second
Selenium:  10s    ×  100 = 16 minutes

+ Selenium is brittle: changing a CSS class breaks a test even if the logic is correct
+ It needs geckodriver or chromedriver, a specific browser version
+ It is unstable in CI without implicitly_wait

Rule: E2E tests only for CRITICAL user flows.
      Everything else — unit/integration.

docs.title: Selenium in Docker — the architecture
docs.text:
[test runner — web container]
  │
  │ HTTP  →  StaticLiveServerTestCase  →  Django live server :PORT
  │
  │ WebDriver protocol  →  http://selenium:4444/wd/hub
  │                            │
  │                     [selenium container]
  │                       standalone-chrome
  │                            │
  │                     Chrome → GET http://web:PORT/
  │
  │ ← DOM / assertions

The key problem without the Docker adaptation: localhost in the Chrome container ≠ localhost in the test runner. Solution: bind to 0.0.0.0, Chrome connects via http://web:PORT.

docs.title: _DockerLiveServerMixin — adapting for Docker
docs.text:
class _DockerLiveServerMixin:
    """
    Adapts StaticLiveServerTestCase to work with Selenium in Docker.

    Problem: LiveServerTestCase binds to 127.0.0.1 by default.
    In Docker: the selenium container cannot reach 127.0.0.1 of the web container.

    Solution:
      1. host = '0.0.0.0' → bind to all interfaces
      2. live_server_url: replace '0.0.0.0' with 'web' (Docker DNS)
         http://0.0.0.0:PORT → http://web:PORT

    WEB_HOST env var: docker-compose.yml → web.environment.WEB_HOST = "web"
    Without Docker (locally): WEB_HOST is not set → the url stays localhost
    """
    host = '0.0.0.0'

    @property
    def live_server_url(self):
        url = super().live_server_url   # http://0.0.0.0:PORT
        web_host = os.environ.get('WEB_HOST')
        if web_host:
            return url.replace('0.0.0.0', web_host)   # http://web:PORT
        return url

docs.title: _make_driver() — a WebDriver for Docker and local runs
docs.text:
def _make_driver():
    """
    Returns a Chrome WebDriver depending on the environment:
      - SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL is set → Remote WebDriver (Docker selenium container)
      - Not set → local Chrome (headless)
    """
    remote_url = os.environ.get('SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL')
    # = 'http://selenium:4444/wd/hub' (from docker-compose.yml)

    options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
    options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage')
    # --disable-dev-shm-usage: Chrome in Docker uses /tmp instead of /dev/shm
    # (by default /dev/shm in Docker = 64MB → Chrome crashes)

    if remote_url:
        return webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=remote_url,
            options=options,
        )
    else:
        options.add_argument('--headless')   # locally: no GUI window
        return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

docs.title: The Session Cookie Trick — logging in without the form
docs.text:
def _login_via_cookie(self, user):
    """
    Logging in without filling in the login form in the browser.
    Much faster and more reliable than filling in the form.

    Method:
    1. The Test Client (server side) creates a session in the test database
    2. We copy the sessionid cookie into Selenium Chrome
    3. Chrome sends this cookie → Django considers Chrome logged in

    Why:
    - The login form may have CSRF, JS validation, a reCAPTCHA
    - The session cookie trick is always reliable
    - Faster: 1 HTTP request instead of the form
    """
    self.client.force_login(user)                     # ← server: session in the database
    session_cookie = self.client.cookies['sessionid'] # ← extract the cookie value

    # Chrome must be on our domain before add_cookie
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/')        # ← any URL of the site

    self.driver.add_cookie({
        'name':  'sessionid',
        'value': session_cookie.value,
        'path':  '/',
    })
    # Now Chrome is logged in as user ✓

@unittest.skipUnless(SELENIUM_AVAILABLE, "selenium not installed")
class SeleniumLoginFlowTest(_DockerLiveServerMixin, StaticLiveServerTestCase):
    """E2E test: login form → dashboard."""

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.driver = _make_driver()
        cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)   # wait up to 5 sec for an element

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        cls.driver.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            username='alice', password='testpass123'
        )

        session_cookie = self.client.cookies['sessionid']
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/')
        self.driver.add_cookie({
            'name':  'sessionid',
            'value': session_cookie.value,
            'path':  '/',
        })

    def test_login_form_and_redirect(self):
        """Filling in the login form → redirect to /notes/."""

docs.title: Why services are easy to test
docs.text:
Services are the best layer for unit tests. No HTTP, no templates, just logic.

VIEWS (HTTP layer):                    SERVICES (business logic):
  Receives the request                   create_note(user=alice, title='Test')
  Parses the form                        Takes Python objects
  Checks CSRF                            Returns a result
  Calls a service                        Saves to the database
  Renders a template                     No dependencies on HTTP!
  Depends on: HTTP, sessions,
  forms, templates, middleware         We test it directly:
  → Hard to test in isolation            result = services.create_note(...)
                                         self.assertEqual(result.title, 'Test')

# KIND 1: checking the RETURNED OBJECT (return value)
def test_create_note_returns_note_object(self):
    note = services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
    self.assertIsInstance(note, Note)
    self.assertEqual(note.title, 'Test')
    self.assertEqual(note.user, self.alice)

# KIND 2: checking the DATABASE STATE (persistence test)

    services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
    self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)
    # ↑ We check what was SAVED, not only what was returned

# WHY BOTH?

# Together — full coverage

def test_toggle_pin_note_persisted_in_db(self):
    """
    IMPORTANT: we check that the change is saved to the database, not only in memory.

    Buggy code could do:
        def toggle_pin_note(note):
            note.is_pinned = True   ← changed it in Python memory
            return note             ← but didn't save it! (no note.save())

    The test EXPLICITLY reads from the database again:
    """
    note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Test', is_pinned=False)
    services.toggle_pin_note(note)

    # Load a NEW object from the database — ignore the one cached in memory
    note_from_db = Note.objects.get(pk=note.pk)
    self.assertTrue(note_from_db.is_pinned)
    #                ↑ really True in the database, not only in the object's memory

docs.title: Security test: Mass Assignment via tag_ids
docs.text:
def test_create_note_ignores_other_users_tags(self):
    """
    Attack: the attacker sends a POST with a tag_id that belongs to Bob.
    POST /notes/new/ → tag_ids=[bob_secret_tag_id]

    WITHOUT PROTECTION (vulnerable):
        note.tags.set(Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids))
        → Bob's tag gets attached to Alice's note
        → Alice sees Bob's secret tag in her note → DATA LEAK

    WITH PROTECTION (our code in services.py):
        note.tags.set(Tag.objects.filter(id__in=tag_ids, user=user))
        → filter(user=user) blocks other users' tags
    """
    bob_tag = Tag.objects.create(user=self.bob, name='bob-secret')

    note = services.create_note(
        user=self.alice, title='Note', tag_ids=[bob_tag.id]
    )

    self.assertEqual(note.tags.count(), 0)   # ← the other user's tag was not attached

docs.title: Testing transactional logic
docs.text:
def test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default(self):
    """
    Business rule: a user has ONLY ONE default notebook.

    The code in services.py:
        with transaction.atomic():
            if is_default:
                Notebook.objects.filter(user=user, is_default=True)
                                .update(is_default=False)   ← RESET the old one
            return Notebook.objects.create(..., is_default=is_default)  ← CREATE the new one

    If you remove the .update() line → two notebooks with is_default=True
    → the note form picks the "first" one → unpredictable behavior

    This test will catch it IMMEDIATELY.
    """
    old = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Old', is_default=True)

    new = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='New', is_default=True)

    old.refresh_from_db()       # ← read the fresh state of the old notebook
    self.assertFalse(old.is_default)  # the old one was reset ✓
    self.assertTrue(new.is_default)   # the new one was set ✓

docs.title: Testing isolation between users
docs.text:
def test_create_notebook_default_does_not_affect_other_users(self):
    """
    A critical test for a multi-user system.

    BUGGY CODE (doesn't filter by user):
        Notebook.objects.filter(is_default=True).update(is_default=False)
        ↑ Resets the default FOR ALL USERS! Bob loses his default.

    CORRECT CODE:
        Notebook.objects.filter(user=user, is_default=True).update(...)
        ↑ Resets only for the specific user. Bob is safe.
    """
    alice_nb = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Alice', is_default=True)
    bob_nb   = services.create_notebook(user=self.bob,   title='Bob',   is_default=True)

    # Alice creates another default:
    services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Alice2', is_default=True)

    bob_nb.refresh_from_db()
    self.assertTrue(bob_nb.is_default)   # Bob's default was not touched ✓

def test_add_user_to_group_duplicate_returns_false(self):
    """
    add_user_to_group() returns (bool, message).
    On a duplicate → (False, 'bob вже є членом').

    Why check twice? The function could return (True, '') but not add the user,
    or add the user but return (False, ''). We check both aspects.
    """
    group = services.create_group(name='Team', creator=self.alice)
    services.add_user_to_group(group, self.bob.username)   # first time ✓

    ok, message = services.add_user_to_group(group, self.bob.username)  # second time

    self.assertFalse(ok)                       # ← the function returned False
    self.assertIn('вже є членом', message)     # ← the message contains the text
    self.assertEqual(group.user_set.count(), 2) # ← the database didn't change (alice + bob, not 3)

# notes_app/tests/test_services.py
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, User
from django.test import TestCase

from notes_app import services
from notes_app.models import Note, Notebook, Tag, TodoList


class BaseServiceTest(TestCase):
    """
    Base class for all service tests.
    All subclasses automatically get self.alice and self.bob.
    """
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')


class NoteServiceTest(BaseServiceTest):

    def test_create_note_sets_correct_user(self):
        note = services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
        self.assertEqual(note.user, self.alice)

    def test_create_note_returns_note_object(self):
        note = services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
        self.assertIsInstance(note, Note)

    def test_create_note_saves_to_database(self):
        services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
        self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)

    def test_create_note_assigns_tags(self):
        tag1 = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='work')
        tag2 = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='python')

        note = services.create_note(
            user=self.alice, title='Tagged', tag_ids=[tag1.id, tag2.id]
        )

        note_tags = list(note.tags.all())
        self.assertIn(tag1, note_tags)
        self.assertIn(tag2, note_tags)

    def test_create_note_ignores_other_users_tags(self):
        """
        Attack: the attacker sends POST /notes/new/ with a tag_id that belongs to Bob.
        Protection: filter(id__in=tag_ids, user=user) blocks other users' tags.
        """
        bob_tag = Tag.objects.create(user=self.bob, name='bob-secret')

        note = services.create_note(
            user=self.alice, title='Note', tag_ids=[bob_tag.id]
        )

        self.assertEqual(note.tags.count(), 0)

    def test_toggle_pin_note_persisted_in_db(self):
        """We check that the change is saved to the database, not only in memory."""
        note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Test', is_pinned=False)
        services.toggle_pin_note(note)

        note_from_db = Note.objects.get(pk=note.pk)
        self.assertTrue(note_from_db.is_pinned)


class NotebookServiceTest(BaseServiceTest):

    def setUp(self):
        super().setUp()   # ← REQUIRED! Call the parent class setUp

    def test_create_notebook_returns_notebook(self):
        nb = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Work')
        self.assertIsInstance(nb, Notebook)

    def test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default(self):
        """Business rule: a user has ONLY ONE default notebook."""
        old = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Old', is_default=True)
        new = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='New', is_default=True)

        old.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertFalse(old.is_default)
        self.assertTrue(new.is_default)

    def test_create_notebook_default_does_not_affect_other_users(self):
        """The invariant is reset for only ONE user."""
        alice_nb = services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Alice', is_default=True)
        bob_nb   = services.create_notebook(user=self.bob,   title='Bob',   is_default=True)

        services.create_notebook(user=self.alice, title='Alice2', is_default=True)

        bob_nb.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertTrue(bob_nb.is_default)


class GroupServiceTest(BaseServiceTest):

    def test_create_group_adds_creator_as_member(self):
        """The creator automatically becomes the first member."""
        group = services.create_group(name='Team', creator=self.alice)
        self.assertIn(self.alice, group.user_set.all())

    def test_add_user_to_group_returns_true_on_success(self):
        group = services.create_group(name='Team', creator=self.alice)
        ok, msg = services.add_user_to_group(group, self.bob.username)
        self.assertTrue(ok)
        self.assertEqual(msg, '')

    def test_add_user_to_group_returns_false_for_unknown_username(self):
        group = services.create_group(name='Team', creator=self.alice)
        ok, msg = services.add_user_to_group(group, 'ghost_user_xyz')
        self.assertFalse(ok)
        self.assertIn('не знайдено', msg)

    def test_add_user_to_group_returns_false_for_duplicate(self):
        """Adding an existing member → False, not an exception."""
        group = services.create_group(name='Team', creator=self.alice)
        services.add_user_to_group(group, self.bob.username)      # first time ✓
        ok, msg = services.add_user_to_group(group, self.bob.username)  # second time

        self.assertFalse(ok)
        self.assertIn('вже є членом', msg)

    def test_delete_group_sets_note_group_to_null(self):
        """Deleting a group → Note.group = NULL (SET_NULL)."""
        group = services.create_group(name='Fam', creator=self.alice)
        note  = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Family note', group=group)

        services.delete_group(group)

        note.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertIsNone(note.group)

docs.title: test_views.py — Integration tests with the Test Client
Django Test Client
docs.text:
Question: What does an integration test check that a unit test CANNOT?

self.client is django.test.Client, a built-in HTTP client for tests.

# Automatically available in every TestCase as self.client
from django.test import TestCase

class MyTest(TestCase):
    def test_something(self):
        self.client  # ← ready to use

It doesn't open a real browser. It simulates an HTTP request inside the Django process: bypassing the network, but going through the entire Django middleware stack.

self.client.get('/notes/')
    ↓
SecurityMiddleware         → checks HTTPS headers
SessionMiddleware          → loads the session from the test database
AuthenticationMiddleware   → sets request.user
CsrfViewMiddleware         → CSRF check (disabled for test client POST)
note_list view             → @login_required → selectors → QuerySet
HTML Response              ← the template is rendered with real data
    ↓
response.status_code       → 200 / 302 / 404
response.content           → HTML bytes
response.context           → the template context (for assertContains)

docs.title: What an integration test catches that a unit test WON'T
docs.text: What it checks Unit (services) Integration (views) @login_required protects the view ✗ ✓ URL routing (/notes/ → note_list) ✗ ✓ redirect after POST (302 → /notes/pk/) ✗ ✓ form errors in the template context ✗ ✓ Bob gets 404 when trying to access ✗ ✓ The page HTML contains the note title ✗ ✓ The create_note() business logic is correct ✓ ✓

docs.title: force_login vs login
docs.text:
# force_login — fast, no password check (the standard in tests)
self.client.force_login(self.alice)
# → doesn't run the auth pipeline, doesn't check the password
# → simply sets the session cookie → request.user = alice
# → ideal for tests where we don't care about the login process itself

# login — the full auth pipeline (only if you are testing the login process itself)
success = self.client.login(username='alice', password='pass123')
# → authenticate() + login() + session
# → Use only in test_selenium or test_login_flow

docs.title: Key response attributes
docs.text:
response = self.client.get(reverse('notes_app:note_list'))

response.status_code      # → 200, 302, 404, 403, 500
response.context          # → the template context {'notes': queryset, 'form': form}
response.content          # → the response HTML as bytes
response['Location']      # → the redirect URL (if 302)
response.context['form'].errors  # → {'title': ['This field is required.']}

docs.text:
# HTTP status codes
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)    # OK
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)    # redirect
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)    # not found
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 403)    # forbidden

# Checking a redirect
self.assertRedirects(response, reverse('notes_app:note_list'),
                     fetch_redirect_response=False)
# fetch_redirect_response=False — we don't make a second GET request

# Text in the HTML
self.assertContains(response, 'Alice Note')    # the string is in the HTML
self.assertNotContains(response, 'Bob Secret') # the string is NOT in the HTML

# Checking that the URL contains login
self.assertIn('/accounts/login/', response['Location'])

# Form errors
self.assertIn('title', response.context['form'].errors)

# Presence in the database

self.assertEqual(Note.objects.count(), 1)

class NoteListViewTest(BaseViewTest):

        """An anonymous user → redirect to /accounts/login/?next=/notes/"""
        response = self.client.get(reverse('notes_app:note_list'))

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)
        self.assertIn('/accounts/login/', response['Location'])

    def test_authenticated_gets_200(self):

        response = self.client.get(reverse('notes_app:note_list'))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

    def test_note_list_shows_only_user_notes(self):

        Note.objects.create(user=self.bob, title="Bob's Secret Note")
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)

        response = self.client.get(reverse('notes_app:note_list'))

        self.assertNotContains(response, "Bob's Secret Note")

class NoteDetailViewTest(BaseViewTest):

    def test_owner_gets_200(self):
        note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Alice Note')
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)
        response = self.client.get(
            reverse('notes_app:note_detail', args=[note.pk])
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

    def test_non_owner_gets_404(self):
        """
        Bob tries to open Alice's note.
        selectors.get_note_detail(request.user, pk):
          → Note.objects.filter(Q(user=bob) | Q(group__in=bob_groups)).get(id=note_id)
          → SELECT WHERE pk=alice_note.pk AND (user_id=bob.id OR group_id IN (...))
          → Note.DoesNotExist → the view raises Http404 → 404

        Why 404 and not 403?
          403: "the resource exists, but access is forbidden" → the attacker knows the id exists
          404: "no such resource"                             → less information for an attack
        """
        alice_note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Alice Private')
        self.client.force_login(self.bob)

        response = self.client.get(
            reverse('notes_app:note_detail', args=[alice_note.pk])
        )

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

    def test_group_member_can_view_shared_note(self):
        """A group member sees a group note."""
        group = Group.objects.create(name='Team')
        group.user_set.add(self.alice, self.bob)
        note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Team Note', group=group)

        self.client.force_login(self.bob)
        response = self.client.get(
            reverse('notes_app:note_detail', args=[note.pk])
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

class NoteCreateViewTest(BaseViewTest):

    def setUp(self):
        super().setUp()
        self.url = reverse('notes_app:note_create')

    def test_valid_post_creates_note_and_redirects(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)

        response = self.client.post(self.url, data={
            'title': 'New Note',
            'content': 'Content',
            'priority': 2,
        })

        # Check the redirect after a successful POST (the PRG pattern)
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

        # Check that the record exists in the database
        self.assertTrue(Note.objects.filter(title='New Note', user=self.alice).exists())

    def test_invalid_post_returns_form_with_errors(self):
        """An empty title → the form is invalid → 200 (not a redirect)."""
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)

        response = self.client.post(self.url, data={
            'title': '',    # empty → invalid
            'priority': 1,
        })

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertFalse(Note.objects.exists())   # the note was not created

class NoteCreateIDORTest(BaseViewTest):

    def test_note_create_with_bobs_notebook_fails(self):
        """
        Alice tries POST /notes/new/ with notebook=bob_notebook.id

        WITHOUT protection in the form: Alice could write a note into Bob's notebook
        WITH protection (NoteForm queryset): the form is invalid → 200, the note is not created
        """
        bob_nb = Notebook.objects.create(user=self.bob, title="Bob's Private")
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)

        response = self.client.post(
            reverse('notes_app:note_create'),
            data={
                'title': 'IDOR Attack',
                'notebook': bob_nb.pk,   # ← someone else's notebook
                'priority': 1,
            }
        )

        # The form is invalid → 200 (not a redirect)
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        # The note was not created → IDOR blocked ✓
        self.assertFalse(Note.objects.filter(title='IDOR Attack').exists())

docs.title: What each category of tests checks
docs.text:
AuthenticationViewTest    ← @login_required on every view
NoteListViewTest          ← multi-tenant: alice sees only her own notes
NoteDetailViewTest        ← ownership + group-based access
NoteCreateViewTest        ← form valid/invalid, IDOR prevention, note.user = request.user
NoteEditViewTest          ← ownership: someone else's → 404; your own → 302
NoteDeleteViewTest        ← ownership + cascade: the note is deleted from the database
NotebookViewTest          ← ownership: get_object_or_404(user=request.user)
