docs.title: Why tests matter and how they work
01 · WHY TESTS
docs.text:
The key question: How do you know nothing broke after your changes?

The answer without tests: run it by hand, click around the site, and hope. The answer with tests: run one command and see everything in 30 seconds.

docs.title: Analogy: a fire alarm
docs.text:
A house without an alarm: you discover the fire when it is already burning. A house with an alarm: you learn about the spark BEFORE everything goes up in flames.

Tests = your code's alarm system. They check "is everything still correct" on every change.

WITHOUT TESTS                           WITH TESTS
──────────────────────────────────────  ──────────────────────────────────────
You write a new feature                 You write a new feature
You click through 10+ pages by hand     You run: manage.py test
"Looks ok"                              FAIL: test_note_visible_only_to_owner
git push → deploy                       You see EXACTLY what broke
A week later: "Bug in production!"      You fix it BEFORE the deploy
You become a detective hunting the cause git push → deploy → all green

docs.title: A real scenario: you change selectors.py
docs.text:
# OLD version (correct):
def get_user_notes(user, *, archived=False):
    user_groups = user.groups.all()
    return Note.objects.filter(
        Q(user=user) | Q(group__in=user_groups),   # ← own + group notes
        is_archived=archived,
    )

# NEW version after "refactoring" (bug!):
def get_user_notes(user, *, archived=False):
    return Note.objects.filter(
        user=user,    # ← forgot the Q filter for groups!
        is_archived=archived,
    )

Without tests: All group notes disappear for every user. Customers discover it a week after the production deploy.

With tests: test_selectors.py immediately reports: 

FAIL: test_group_notes_visible_to_members
AssertionError: <Note: Team meeting> not found in queryset for bob
You fix it in 2 minutes, before committing.

docs.title: What else tests give you
docs.text: Benefit Explanation Documentation test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default explains the invariant better than a comment Fearless refactoring You change the implementation → the tests confirm the behavior is the same Finding edge cases While writing a test you think: "what if it's None? what if it's empty?" Protection against regressions Bug fixed + test written = the bug never comes back Security checks test_notebook_queryset_excludes_other_user_notebooks: IDOR is impossible CI signal GitHub Actions: FAIL before merge → you don't deploy broken code

docs.title: 02 · THE TESTING PYRAMID
docs.text:
Not all tests are equal. Different levels have different cost and speed.

              ╱╲
             ╱E2E╲          Selenium, Playwright
            ╱──────╲        Real browser, full scenario
           ╱ Integr. ╲      Slow (seconds/test), brittle
          ╱────────────╲    Django Test Client: request → DB → response
         ╱  Consumers   ╲   Medium (100ms/test)
        ╱────────────────╲  WebsocketCommunicator (notes_chat_app only)
       ╱       Unit        ╲ TestCase: function → result
      ╱──────────────────────╲ Fast (1-10ms/test), reliable

    60% Unit | 25% Integration | 10% Consumers | 5% E2E

docs.title: What we test at each level
docs.text:
Unit tests (models, services, forms): 

# Test the function in isolation from HTTP
def test_create_notebook_default_unsets_previous_default(self):
    old = services.create_notebook(user=alice, title='Old', is_default=True)
    new = services.create_notebook(user=alice, title='New', is_default=True)
    old.refresh_from_db()
    self.assertFalse(old.is_default)  # 1 is_default per user is an invariant

Integration tests (views through the Test Client): 

# Test through HTTP: view + DB + response
def test_note_list_shows_only_user_notes(self):
    self.client.force_login(alice)
    response = self.client.get(reverse('notes_app:note_list'))
    self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
    self.assertNotContains(response, "Bob's Secret Note")

Consumer tests (WebSocket, notes_chat_app only): 

# WebsocketCommunicator → consumer → channel layer
async def test_non_member_cannot_connect(self):
    communicator = WebsocketCommunicator(application, f'/ws/groups/{pk}/chat/')
    communicator.scope['user'] = self.bob  # not a member of the group
    connected, code = await communicator.connect()
    self.assertFalse(connected)

E2E tests (Selenium): 

# Test through a real browser: clicks, forms, navigation
def test_user_can_login_and_see_dashboard(self):
    self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/accounts/login/')
    self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'username').send_keys('alice')
    self.driver.find_element(By.NAME, 'password').send_keys('testpass123')
    self.driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, '[type=submit]').click()
    self.assertIn('/notes/', self.driver.current_url)

docs.title: 03 · DJANGO TESTCASE
docs.text: django.test.TestCase is unittest.TestCase + Django magic.

docs.title: What distinguishes Django TestCase from plain unittest
docs.text:
import unittest
from django.test import TestCase

# unittest.TestCase: basic, no DB
class PureUnitTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_math(self):
        self.assertEqual(2 + 2, 4)   # OK, no DB

# django.test.TestCase: with the full Django stack
class DjangoTest(TestCase):
    def test_with_db(self):
        user = User.objects.create_user('alice')  # ← requires the test DB
        self.assertEqual(user.username, 'alice')
        # After the test → ROLLBACK → alice is gone automatically

docs.title: What Django TestCase gives you automatically
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Before ALL tests of the class (setUpClass):                        │
│    → Creates the test DB: CREATE DATABASE test_notes_db             │
│    → Applies all migrations (CREATE TABLE ...)                      │
│    → Loads fixtures if there are any                                │
│                                                                     │
│  Before EACH test:                                                  │
│    → BEGIN TRANSACTION                                              │
│    → Calls setUp()                                                  │
│                                                                     │
│    ┌─── THE TEST RUNS ─────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│    │  User.objects.create(...)  ← INSERT INTO auth_user        │   │
│    │  Note.objects.create(...)  ← INSERT INTO notes_app_note   │   │
│    │  services.create_note(...) ← business logic + INSERT      │   │
│    │  self.assertEqual(...)     ← check                        │   │
│    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                     │
│  After EACH test:                                                   │
│    → ROLLBACK   ← every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE disappears!            │
│    → Calls tearDown()                                               │
│                                                                     │
│  After ALL tests (tearDownClass):                                   │
│    → DROP DATABASE test_notes_db                                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Why rollback is a good thing
docs.text:
class MyTest(TestCase):
    def test_first(self):
        User.objects.create_user('alice')    # ← alice EXISTS
        self.assertEqual(User.objects.count(), 1)
        # After the test → ROLLBACK → alice is gone

    def test_second(self):
        # alice does NOT exist: every test starts from a clean state
        self.assertEqual(User.objects.count(), 0)  # ← 0, not 1!

Without rollback tests would affect each other: - test 1 creates alice → test 2 sees alice → results are unpredictable - The order in which tests run would affect the result

With rollback every test is isolated → the result does not depend on the order.

docs.title: setUp: preparation before each test
docs.text:
class NoteServiceTest(TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        """Runs BEFORE each test. The DB is clean."""
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')
        # These users will exist in every test of this class
        # After each test → ROLLBACK → they disappear → the next setUp creates them again

    def test_something(self):
        # self.alice and self.bob already exist here
        note = services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
        ...

docs.title: BaseServiceTest: DRY for a shared setUp
docs.text:
class BaseServiceTest(TestCase):
    """
    Base class with a shared setUp.
    All subclasses automatically get self.alice and self.bob.
    """
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob   = User.objects.create_user('bob',   password='pass123')


class NoteServiceTest(BaseServiceTest):
    # setUp() is NOT needed: it is inherited from BaseServiceTest
    # self.alice and self.bob are available in every test

    def test_create_note_sets_correct_user(self):
        note = services.create_note(user=self.alice, title='Test')
        self.assertEqual(note.user, self.alice)

docs.title: 04 · THE TEST DATABASE
docs.text: The most important rule: Tests never touch your working DB.

docs.title: How Django creates the test DB
docs.text:
# crispy_notes_project (SQLite):
$ python manage.py test hello_app.tests

Creating test database for alias 'default' ...
#  ↑ Django creates test_<db_name> or an in-memory DB (SQLite)
#    All the data lives there, not in your db.sqlite3!

Found 129 test(s).
...

Destroying test database for alias 'default' ...
#  ↑ The test DB is deleted when the run finishes

# notes_chat_app (PostgreSQL in Docker):
$ docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests

Creating test database for alias 'default' ...
# ↑ Django: CREATE DATABASE test_notes_db
#   A separate empty DB, distinct from notes_db!

docs.title: Three kinds of isolation at once
docs.text:
1. ISOLATION FROM THE REAL DB:
   db.sqlite3 or notes_db (your working one) ≠ the test DB (separate, temporary)
   Tests cannot break your real data.

2. ISOLATION BETWEEN TESTS:
   Each test has its own transaction → rollback.
   Test A does not see Test B's data.
   The execution order does not affect the result.

3. ISOLATION FROM EXTERNAL SYSTEMS:
   Email: EMAIL_BACKEND = console (nothing is actually sent)
   Redis: InMemoryChannelLayer (tests without a real Redis)
   API: needs a mock (unittest.mock.patch)

docs.title: --keepdb: speeding things up with many migrations (notes_chat_app)
docs.text:
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests --keepdb
# First run: CREATE + migrate (slow)
# Subsequent runs: only new migrations (fast)
# Useful when there are many migrations

docs.title: 05 · THE AAA PATTERN
docs.text:
Every test has three clear parts. This is the standard in every language.

def test_create_note_assigns_tags(self):

    # ── ARRANGE: prepare the state ──────────────────────────────────────
    # What does the test need? Create the minimal required state.
    tag1 = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='work')
    tag2 = Tag.objects.create(user=self.alice, name='python')

    # ── ACT: perform what we are testing ────────────────────────────────
    # One call, one action. What exactly are we testing? Only this.
    note = services.create_note(
        user=self.alice, title='Tagged', tag_ids=[tag1.id, tag2.id]
    )

    # ── ASSERT: check the result ────────────────────────────────────────
    # What must be true after Act? Check it precisely.
    note_tags = list(note.tags.all())
    self.assertIn(tag1, note_tags)
    self.assertIn(tag2, note_tags)

docs.title: Rules of a good test
docs.text: Rule Explanation One test, one behavior test_create_note_sets_user ≠ test_create_note_saves_to_db Name = specification test_add_user_to_group_duplicate_returns_false: the name explains everything Independence A test does not depend on the order or on other tests Speed Unit test < 50ms. If it is slow, check whether you are making unnecessary queries Determinism The same test under the same conditions = the same result

docs.title: Common mistakes in test names
docs.text:
# ✗ BAD: unclear what exactly is being tested
def test_note(self): ...
def test_service(self): ...
def test_1(self): ...

# ✓ GOOD: name = what we check → which result we expect
def test_create_note_sets_correct_user(self): ...
def test_note_group_becomes_null_when_group_deleted(self): ...
def test_non_owner_gets_404_on_note_edit(self): ...
def test_notebook_queryset_excludes_other_user_notebooks(self): ...

This step covers two independent projects: 7A (hello_app, a sync vs async comparison) and 7B (notes_chat_app, a WebSocket group chat). The first is a standalone application on SQLite under Uvicorn. The second is a production-like stack with Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis, Daphne and Django Channels.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have completed:

docs.title: 7A. Async Views and the ORM
docs.text: This section is a detailed comparison of the sync and async layers: async_selectors.py, async_services.py, async_views.py side by side with their sync counterparts.

docs.title: async_selectors.py: lazy vs evaluation
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/async_selectors.py

Compare it with the original: hello_app/selectors.py

docs.title: The key idea: lazy vs evaluation
docs.text:
# selectors.py (sync): the original
def get_user_notes(user, ...):
    qs = Note.objects.filter(Q(user=user) | ...)
    qs = qs.select_related('notebook', 'group')
    qs = qs.prefetch_related('tags')
    return qs.order_by('-is_pinned', ...)
    # ↑ SQL has NOT run YET: returns a lazy QuerySet
    # SQL runs in views.py when: for note in notes: ...

# async_selectors.py: the async version
def async_get_user_notes(user, ...):
    qs = Note.objects.filter(Q(user=user) | ...)
    qs = qs.select_related('notebook', 'group')
    qs = qs.prefetch_related('tags')
    return qs.order_by('-is_pinned', ...)
    # ↑ THE SAME LOGIC: also a lazy QuerySet
    # SQL runs in async_views.py when: async for note in notes_qs: ...

docs.title: Table: when SQL runs
docs.text: Django ORM method Type Does SQL run? .filter(...) Lazy ❌ No .select_related(...) Lazy ❌ No .prefetch_related(...) Lazy ❌ No .annotate(...) Lazy ❌ No .order_by(...) Lazy ❌ No .get() Eval ✅ Yes (sync, blocks) .aget() Eval ✅ Yes (async, does not block) .count() Eval ✅ Yes (sync) .acount() Eval ✅ Yes (async) for obj in qs Eval ✅ Yes (sync, blocks) async for obj in qs Eval ✅ Yes (async, does not block)

docs.title: async def only where there is real SQL
docs.text:
# async_get_user_notes: a regular def (lazy QuerySet, no SQL runs)
def async_get_user_notes(user, ...):
    return Note.objects.filter(...).select_related(...).order_by(...)

# async_get_note_detail: async def (real SQL through .aget())
async def async_get_note_detail(user, note_id):
    return await Note.objects.filter(...).select_related(...).aget(id=note_id)
    #      ↑ await: SQL runs asynchronously, the event loop is free while we wait

Rule: if a function returns a lazy QuerySet without running SQL, it can be a regular def, even if it is called from an async view. async def is only needed when there is real I/O inside (.aget(), .acount(), and so on).

docs.title: async_services.py: two approaches
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/async_services.py

Compare it with the original: hello_app/services.py

docs.title: The sync original
docs.text:
# services.py (sync): the original
def create_note(*, user, title, ...):
    with transaction.atomic():         # ← transaction
        note = Note.objects.create(...)
        note.tags.set(valid_tags)
    return note

docs.title: Async through sync_to_async
docs.text:
# async_services.py: async through sync_to_async
# You can't simply make it async def because of transaction.atomic()
async_create_note = sync_to_async(create_note, thread_sensitive=True)
# ↑ Wraps the sync create_note so it can be called safely from an async view
# sync_to_async runs create_note in a dedicated OS thread
# the event loop is free while the thread runs the transaction

docs.title: Comparing the three approaches
docs.text: Operation Approach Why async_create_note sync_to_async(create_note) transaction.atomic() is not supported natively in async async_delete_note await note.adelete() A simple DELETE, a native async ORM method async_toggle_pin_note await qs.aupdate(is_pinned=~F(...)) Atomic UPDATE, native async, without loading the object

docs.title: sync_to_async: what it looks like at runtime
docs.text:
Async View (event loop thread)
    │
    │  await async_create_note(...)       ← the view suspends
    │
    ├─→ sync_to_async: hands off to a worker thread
    │
    │  the event loop serves OTHER requests ←
    │
    │  Worker Thread: runs create_note() + transaction.atomic()
    │
    │  Worker Thread: returns note ──────┐
    │                                     │
    │  the event loop resumes the view ───┘
    │
    └─→ note = <Note object>  ← the view continues

docs.title: async_views.py: syntactic differences
docs.text:
Open the file: hello_app/async_views.py

Compare it with the original: hello_app/views.py

docs.title: Key syntactic differences
docs.text:
# views.py (sync): the original
@login_required
def note_list(request):
    notes = selectors.get_user_notes(request.user)        # lazy QuerySet
    # On the next line the template evaluates the QuerySet in a for loop (sync)
    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})

# async_views.py: the async version
async def async_note_list(request):
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:         # explicit auth check
        return redirect('login')

    notes_qs = async_selectors.async_get_user_notes(request.user)  # lazy (sync def)

    notes = [note async for note in notes_qs]     # async for → SQL runs here
    #        ↑ the await happens inside async for
    #          the event loop is free while the DB responds

    return render(request, 'hello_app/note_list.html', {'notes': notes})
    #     ↑ render() is sync, but safe inside async def (Django 5.x)

docs.title: Where the awaits are and why
docs.text: Line await Why note = await async_selectors.async_get_note_detail(...) ✅ Inside is aget(): real SQL notes = [note async for note in notes_qs] ✅ (implicit) Iterating over a QuerySet = SQL note = await async_services.async_create_note(...) ✅ sync_to_async: runs in a thread await async_services.async_delete_note(note) ✅ adelete(): real SQL await async_services.async_toggle_pin_note(note) ✅ aupdate(): real SQL form = NoteForm(request.POST, user=request.user) ❌ The form is lazy, no heavy I/O form.is_valid() ❌ CPU validation, no I/O return render(...) ❌ Django 5.x renders a sync template safely return redirect(...) ❌ Just an HttpResponse with 302, no I/O

docs.title: note_list vs async_note_list
docs.text: Sync line Async line Why it changed @login_required if not request.user.is_authenticated: @login_required does not support async views def note_list(request): async def async_note_list(request): async def notes = selectors.get_user_notes(...) notes_qs = async_selectors.async_get_user_notes(...) the lazy qs stays lazy (the template evaluates the qs) notes = [note async for note in notes_qs] explicit async iteration return render(...) return render(...) identical

docs.title: Django 4.1+ async ORM methods
docs.text:
Django 4.1 added native async ORM methods:

Sync method Async counterpart What it does qs.get(pk=x) await qs.aget(pk=x) One object or DoesNotExist Model.objects.create(...) await Model.objects.acreate(...) Creates a record qs.update(...) await qs.aupdate(...) Bulk update qs.delete() await qs.adelete() Bulk delete obj.save() await obj.asave() Saves an object obj.delete() await obj.adelete() Deletes an object for obj in qs: async for obj in qs: Iterates over a QuerySet qs.exists() await qs.aexists() Whether there is at least one qs.count() await qs.acount() Number of rows qs.filter(...).first() await qs.filter(...).afirst() The first result or None

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 1: Sync ORM in an async view
docs.text:
async def bad_note_detail(request, pk):
    note = Note.objects.get(pk=pk)  # ← SynchronousOnlyOperation!
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

The error: .get() is sync SQL. In an async context Django raises an exception.

# ✅ Correct
async def good_note_detail(request, pk):
    note = await Note.objects.aget(pk=pk)  # async counterpart of .get()
    return render(request, 'note_detail.html', {'note': note})

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 2: requests.get() in an async view
docs.text:
import requests

async def bad_view(request):
    # requests.get() is sync! It blocks the whole event loop while waiting for the response
    data = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()
    return JsonResponse(data)

The error: The whole server "freezes" for every other user for the duration of the HTTP request.

# ✅ Correct: httpx.AsyncClient
import httpx

async def good_view(request):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        # await: the view suspends, the event loop serves others
        response = await client.get("https://api.example.com/data")
    return JsonResponse(response.json())

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 3: time.sleep() in an async view
docs.text:
import time

async def bad_delay_view(request):
    time.sleep(2)  # Blocks the whole event loop for 2 seconds!
    return HttpResponse("done")

# ✅ Correct: asyncio.sleep()
import asyncio

async def good_delay_view(request):
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Hands control back to the event loop
    return HttpResponse("done")

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 4: Rewriting the whole project in async "because it's trendy"
docs.text:
# ❌ Async is not needed here: extra overhead
async def simple_crud_view(request):
    note = await Note.objects.aget(pk=1)
    return render(request, 'note.html', {'note': note})

# ✅ Simpler and sufficient for ordinary CRUD
def simple_crud_view(request):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=1)
    return render(request, 'note.html', {'note': note})

docs.title: Key differences in async tests
docs.text:
Open side by side: - hello_app/tests/test_views.py: sync tests (NoteListViewTest) - hello_app/tests/test_async_views.py: async tests (AsyncNoteListViewTest)

# test_views.py: a sync test
class NoteListViewTest(TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        # Sync ORM is always OK in setUp
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')

    def test_redirects_to_login(self):
        # Sync HTTP request
        response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    def test_auth_user_gets_200(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)   # sync login
        response = self.client.get(reverse('hello_app:note_list'))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

# test_async_views.py: an async test
class AsyncNoteListViewTest(TestCase):  # TestCase (not AsyncTestCase)

    def setUp(self):
        # setUp is sync, ORM without await is OK
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice_async', password='pass123')

    async def test_redirects_to_login(self):
        client = AsyncClient()                  # AsyncClient instead of self.client
        response = await client.get(            # await client.get()
            reverse('hello_app:async_note_list')
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)

    async def test_auth_user_gets_200(self):
        client = AsyncClient()
        await client.force_login(self.alice)    # await force_login
        response = await client.get(
            reverse('hello_app:async_note_list')
        )
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

docs.title: Comparison table: sync vs async tests
docs.text:
Concept Sync test Async test Base class TestCase TestCase (the same!) setUp def setUp(self) def setUp(self) (sync!) test_ methods def test_*(self) async def test_*(self) HTTP client self.client AsyncClient() GET request self.client.get(url) await client.get(url) Login self.client.force_login(user) await client.force_login(user) ORM in a test Note.objects.create(...) await sync_to_async(Note.objects.create)(...)

Why TestCase and not AsyncTestCase? AsyncTestCase is a subclass of SimpleTestCase and does not support transactions. TestCase wraps each test in a transaction (rollback after the test). Django 4.1+ supports async def test_* in a regular TestCase. That is why we use TestCase with async def test_* methods.

docs.title: Testing in Postman
docs.text:
What is a CSRF token? CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) protection guards against forged cross-site requests. Django checks a special token in every POST request. A browser gets the token automatically through a cookie. With Postman you have to do it by hand.

Step 1: Get the CSRF token with a GET request in Postman

Django sets the csrftoken cookie on the first GET request to any page.

GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/

In the response Postman shows a Cookies tab: - Find the cookie named csrftoken - Copy its value (a long string of letters and digits)

Or through the browser (if it is already open): - F12 → Application → Cookies → http://127.0.0.1:8000 - Copy the csrftoken value

Django automatically includes the cookie manager in Postman (Settings → Cookies). After the first GET request, the csrftoken cookie appears in Postman's Cookie Jar.

Step 2: Log in through Postman

POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/accounts/login/
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Body (x-www-form-urlencoded):
  username      alice
  password      pass123
  csrfmiddlewaretoken   <csrftoken value from step 1>

After a successful login: - Postman saves the sessionid cookie automatically (through the Cookie Jar) - Response status: 302 Redirect (to the home page)

Step 3: GET the list of async notes

GET http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/

Postman automatically sends the sessionid and csrftoken cookies (from the Cookie Jar). You will see an HTML page with the list of notes.

Step 4: POST to create a note through the async view

POST http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/create/
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Headers:
  X-CSRFToken    <csrftoken value>
Body (x-www-form-urlencoded):
  title         Test note via Postman
  content       Note content
  priority      1

docs.title: Benchmark: what you can and cannot measure
What you should NOT expect
docs.text:
# ❌ A single request proves nothing
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/        # Sync: 45ms
curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/  # Async: 48ms
# "Async is slower!" is a WRONG conclusion

Async has overhead from the event loop. For a single request, sync can be faster.

docs.title: What actually shows the difference
docs.text:
The difference becomes visible under concurrent load (50+ simultaneous requests):

# 1000 requests, 50 concurrent (requires apache-httpd or apache2-utils)
ab -n 1000 -c 50 http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/         # sync
ab -n 1000 -c 50 http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/   # async

Note: SQLite is not an ideal DB for an async performance benchmark. SQLite has a global write lock. For a real async benchmark use PostgreSQL with a connection pool.

docs.title: Why Docker for this project
docs.text:
Without Docker, Python adds every package from .venv to sys.path. If one workspace contains several Django projects with the same package names (notes_project, notes_app), Python may load the wrong project. Docker solves this once and for all: the container has only /app in sys.path, with no third-party packages from elsewhere.

Without Docker:                     With Docker:
sys.path = [                        sys.path = [
  lesson_Django_authentication/..., ← /app ← only notes_chat_app
  lesson_Django_Async/...,          ]
  ...                               WORKDIR /app → ENV PYTHONPATH=/app
]

docs.title: Official documentation
docs.text:
Topic Link Django async views https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/async/ Django async ORM https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/models/querysets/#async-queries sync_to_async https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/async/#asgiref-sync Django async testing https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/testing/tools/#asynchronous-tests Uvicorn https://uvicorn.dev/ httpx https://www.python-httpx.org/ asgiref https://github.com/django/asgiref asyncio (Python docs) https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html

Async Django is a tool, not a coding style.

Sync Django suits most projects: CRUD, admin, a blog, an API. Async Django is justified when there is a real I/O bottleneck: parallel external API requests, WebSockets, streaming, high concurrency.

This learning project shows the same result with two different architectures. Choose according to the task.

docs.title: 7A. Sync vs Async Django: an overview
What this project is about
docs.text:
This is an already finished Django app for notes (Notes, Notebooks, Tags, TodoList, ShoppingList). We are not rewriting it from scratch: we add async capabilities alongside the sync code.

Two async demonstrations in one project:

# Part 1: Async views (the same result, a different architecture)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/          ← Sync view (classic Django)
http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/    ← Async view (the same result, async ORM)

# Part 2: Real-time chat (here async is the only correct approach)
http://127.0.0.1:8001/groups/<pk>/chat/   ← Group WebSocket chat

Async views and the async ORM show how to write async code. The group chat shows why async is needed: here sync simply does not fit.

Learning status of the async_*.py modules

async_selectors.py, async_services.py, async_views.py and test_async_views.py are created only within this learning step to demonstrate Django async views.

In the final version of Notes Chat App these modules are absent: all async logic is implemented directly in consumers.py (Django Channels) without separate async_*.py files.

docs.title: How a sync request works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant Django as Django (WSGI)
    participant View as views.note_list()
    participant Selector as selectors.get_user_notes()
    participant DB as SQLite

    Browser->>Django: GET /notes/
    Django->>View: Calls note_list(request)
    View->>Selector: get_user_notes(user, ...)
    Selector->>DB: SELECT * FROM notes WHERE user=... JOIN ...
    Note over Django: The thread is BLOCKED, waiting for the DB
    DB-->>Selector: Data rows
    Selector-->>View: QuerySet
    View-->>Django: render(template, context)
    Django-->>Browser: HTML 200 OK

sequenceDiagram

    participant ASGI as Uvicorn (ASGI)
    participant EL as Event Loop
    participant View as async_note_list()
    participant Selector as async_selectors
    participant DB as SQLite

    EL->>View: Starts async_note_list(request)

    View->>DB: async for note in queryset (real SQL)

docs.title: When async is justified and when it is not
docs.text: Async is not "better". Async is "for a different kind of task".

docs.title: ❌ Async is not needed (sync is enough)
docs.text: Feature Why sync is enough Note CRUD Simple DB queries, one request = one response TodoList, ShoppingList No bottleneck, short requests Forms, authentication CPU operations without waiting on I/O Admin panel Rare complex queries, concurrency is not needed

docs.title: ✅ Async is justified
docs.text:
Feature Why async is needed Group chat (this project!) WebSocket = thousands of open connections at once Parallel API requests asyncio.gather() → several requests at once Streaming responses Server-Sent Events, large files High-concurrency API 10,000+ req/s without blocking threads

Rewriting the whole project in async without a real bottleneck is overengineering + more complex code + the same results.

We convert only Notes so that a student can compare the architectures. The group chat is a separate use case where async is the only correct choice.

Open the browser: http://127.0.0.1:8000/

Sign up or log in. See the sync note list: http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/

docs.title: Running async Django with Uvicorn (ASGI)
docs.text: Uvicorn is an ASGI server. Unlike the built-in runserver, it uses the asyncio event loop and serves async views natively.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the dependencies (including wsproto)
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt

Why it matters: requirements.txt contains wsproto, a WebSocket protocol library for uvicorn. Without it uvicorn logs "No supported WebSocket library detected" and returns HTTP 404 for all WS requests. Async views work, but the chat will not.

docs.title: Step 2: Start the ASGI server
docs.text:
uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application --reload --port 8001

Breaking down the command:

Part What it means uvicorn ASGI server (the async counterpart of gunicorn) notes_project.asgi Python module: notes_project/asgi.py :application The object in the module (application = ProtocolTypeRouter(...)) --reload Auto-restart when files change (dev only!) --port 8001 Port 8001 (8000 is taken by runserver)

docs.title: An expected warning (NOT an error)
docs.text:
WARNING:  ASGI 'lifespan' protocol appears unsupported.

Uvicorn tries the lifespan protocol (startup/shutdown hooks) → Django does not implement it → uvicorn logs a WARNING and keeps running. This is normal. The chat and async views work fully. Ignore this message.

Open the browser: http://127.0.0.1:8001/

Now you can compare: - http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes/: sync view (WSGI) - http://127.0.0.1:8001/async/notes/: async view (ASGI) - http://127.0.0.1:8001/groups/: group chat (WebSocket)

Important: Both servers connect to ONE db.sqlite3. The data is the same. The execution architecture is different.

docs.title: URL comparison table
docs.text: Sync URL Async URL What we compare GET /notes/ GET /async/notes/ Note list, lazy ORM vs async for GET /notes/<pk>/ GET /async/notes/<pk>/ Note details, .get() vs .aget() GET/POST /notes/new/ GET/POST /async/notes/create/ Form + create_note vs sync_to_async GET/POST /notes/<pk>/delete/ GET/POST /async/notes/<pk>/delete/ .delete() vs .adelete() (no separate URL) POST /async/notes/<pk>/pin/ .update(F(...)) vs .aupdate(F(...))

docs.title: WSGI vs ASGI
docs.text: WSGI ASGI Standard PEP 3333 (2010) ASGI specification (asgi.readthedocs.io, not a PEP) Protocols HTTP only HTTP + WebSocket + others Model Synchronous (one request = one thread) Asynchronous (coroutines) Servers Gunicorn, uWSGI Uvicorn, Daphne, Hypercorn Django Standard runserver Requires an ASGI application + channels WebSocket ❌ Not supported ✅ Natively

docs.title: Architecture of the notes_chat_app ASGI stack
docs.text:
Browser (HTTP)          Browser (WebSocket)
      │                        │
      ▼                        ▼
   nginx :80  (reverse proxy — forwards requests)
      │                        │
      ▼                        ▼
   Uvicorn ASGI :8001  (one process — both protocols)
      │
      ▼
   ProtocolTypeRouter  (notes_project/asgi.py)
      │
      ├── protocol == "http"
      │       ▼
      │   Django HTTP app (views.py, urls.py, templates)
      │
      └── protocol == "websocket"
              ▼
          AuthMiddlewareStack
              ▼
          WebSocket URLRouter  (notes_project/routing.py)
              ▼
          GroupChatConsumer  (notes_app/consumers.py)
              │
              ├──► PostgreSQL (via database_sync_to_async)
              └──► InMemoryChannelLayer / RedisChannelLayer (pub/sub)
Component Role Equivalent in HTTP Django ProtocolTypeRouter Distinguishes HTTP and WS by protocol type ROOT_URLCONF AuthMiddlewareStack Reads the session cookie → scope['user'] @login_required decorator WebSocket URLRouter Routes a WS URL to a Consumer urls.py GroupChatConsumer Handles the WS connection for its whole lifetime view (but lives longer) InMemoryChannelLayer Pub/sub broadcast between consumers (no direct equivalent)

docs.title: asgi.py — the entry point
docs.text:
# notes_project/asgi.py
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
from django.contrib.staticfiles.handlers import ASGIStaticFilesHandler

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')

# CRITICAL: get_asgi_application() BEFORE any import from notes_app
# The Django app registry (AppConfig.ready()) must be initialized
# BEFORE importing models or consumers.
# If you change the order → AppRegistryNotReady exception.
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()

# Only after get_asgi_application() is it safe to import from notes_app
from channels.routing import ProtocolTypeRouter, URLRouter
from channels.auth import AuthMiddlewareStack
from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns

application = ProtocolTypeRouter({
    # HTTP → regular Django (views.py, templates);
    # ASGIStaticFilesHandler serves /static/ straight from Django (handy in development;
    # in the Docker stack nginx serves /static/)
    "http": ASGIStaticFilesHandler(django_asgi_app),

    # WebSocket → Auth middleware → URL router → Consumer
    "websocket": AuthMiddlewareStack(
        URLRouter(websocket_urlpatterns)
    ),
})

docs.title: The critical import order
docs.text:
# ❌ WRONG — AppRegistryNotReady:
from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns   # ← BEFORE get_asgi_application()
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()

# ✅ CORRECT:
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()                  # ← FIRST
from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns   # ← THEN

Why this matters so much:

The Django app registry is initialized when get_asgi_application() is called.
Until that moment:
  - models are not loaded
  - AppConfig.ready() has not run
  - any import from notes_app.consumers → AppRegistryNotReady

A typical mistake:
  from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns
  # routing.py: from notes_app import consumers
  # consumers.py: from notes_app.models import ChatMessage
  # → AppRegistryNotReady!

docs.title: AuthMiddlewareStack — scope["user"] from the session
docs.text:
WebSocket handshake request:
  GET /ws/groups/7/chat/
  Cookie: sessionid=abc123xyz

AuthMiddlewareStack:
  1. Reads the sessionid cookie from the handshake headers
  2. Finds the session in the Django session backend (DB)
  3. Loads the User from the session
  4. Puts it into scope['user']

Consumer:
  self.user = self.scope['user']
  # → User object (or AnonymousUser if not logged in)

docs.title: What scope is
docs.text:
In ASGI, scope is a dictionary with the connection's metadata. It is the equivalent of request in HTTP views, but for WebSocket:

# scope for a WebSocket connection:
{
    'type': 'websocket',
    'path': '/ws/groups/7/chat/',
    'url_route': {
        'kwargs': {'group_pk': '7'}   # ← from the URL pattern
    },
    'user': <User: viktor>,           # ← loaded by AuthMiddlewareStack
    'headers': [...],                 # ← handshake request headers
    'session': <Session>,             # ← Django session
}

docs.title: How the Consumer uses scope
docs.text:
async def connect(self):
    self.user = self.scope['user']
    # ↑ User is already loaded by AuthMiddlewareStack

    self.group_pk = int(self.scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk'])
    # ↑ group_pk from the URL /ws/groups/<group_pk>/chat/

docs.title: re_path vs path for WebSocket
docs.text:
# path() — simpler:
from django.urls import path
websocket_urlpatterns = [
    path('ws/groups/<int:group_pk>/chat/', consumers.GroupChatConsumer.as_asgi()),
]

# re_path() — regex, more control:
from django.urls import re_path
websocket_urlpatterns = [
    re_path(r'^ws/groups/(?P<group_pk>\d+)/chat/$', consumers.GroupChatConsumer.as_asgi()),
]

# Both options work.
# re_path is the traditional choice for WebSocket (more examples in the documentation)

docs.title: Consumer.as_asgi()
docs.text:
consumers.GroupChatConsumer.as_asgi()
# Equivalent of View.as_view() in HTTP — turns the Consumer class into an ASGI callable
# Each WebSocket connection → a separate Consumer instance

docs.title: nginx: WebSocket proxy
docs.text:
When running behind nginx, WebSocket needs special headers.

# nginx.conf — WebSocket location
location /ws/ {
    proxy_pass http://web:8001;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;          # ← HTTP/1.1 is required for the WS Upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;         # ← 5 minutes for idle WS connections
}

Why proxy_http_version 1.1: The WebSocket Upgrade only works over HTTP/1.1. By default, nginx uses HTTP/1.0 for upstream requests. Without this line the WS Upgrade will not happen → the browser gets HTTP 400.

Why proxy_read_timeout 300s: By default, nginx closes the upstream connection after 60 sec without a response. A WebSocket can stay open for hours without traffic → increase the timeout to 5+ minutes.

docs.title: Common mistakes in the ASGI stack
docs.text: Error Cause Fix AppRegistryNotReady Import from notes_app BEFORE get_asgi_application() Move the imports after the call WS 400 through nginx Missing Upgrade headers proxy_http_version 1.1 + Upgrade headers Consumer not found routing.py is not wired into asgi.py Include websocket_urlpatterns scope['user'] is AnonymousUser AuthMiddlewareStack is missing or the session has expired Check is_authenticated in connect()

docs.text: Next chapter: 7B. Channel Layers and Daphne — Daphne in INSTALLED_APPS, InMemoryChannelLayer vs RedisChannelLayer, socket_timeout=None.

docs.title: Daphne: why it comes first in INSTALLED_APPS
docs.text:
Daphne is an ASGI server from the Django Channels team. It intercepts the python manage.py runserver command and replaces the built-in WSGI server with an ASGI server.

# notes_project/settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'daphne',        # ← FIRST in the list! Must come before 'django.contrib.*'
    'channels',      # Django Channels
    'django.contrib.admin',
    # ... the rest of the apps
    'notes_app',
]

docs.title: What breaks if daphne is not first
docs.text:
# Without 'daphne' first:
$ python manage.py runserver
# → Django starts the built-in WSGI server
# → WebSocket does not work (WSGI does not support WS)
# → No error at all — WS connections simply aren't established

# With 'daphne' first:
$ python manage.py runserver
# → Daphne overrides runserver → starts the ASGI server
# → WebSocket works

If daphne is not placed first, Django may load a different runserver implementation before Daphne gets a chance to override it. The order in INSTALLED_APPS determines the order in which management commands are registered.

docs.title: In production daphne is not required
docs.text:
# In Docker (production) we use uvicorn directly:
exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8001

# → daphne first in INSTALLED_APPS is only needed for the local runserver
# → In production uvicorn is started directly, bypassing manage.py

docs.title: ASGI_APPLICATION instead of WSGI_APPLICATION
docs.text:
# settings.py — Channels requires ASGI_APPLICATION
ASGI_APPLICATION = 'notes_project.asgi.application'

# (WSGI_APPLICATION can stay for compatibility, but Channels uses ASGI_APPLICATION)

docs.title: InMemoryChannelLayer (dev / tests)
docs.text:
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer",
    }
}
Property InMemoryChannelLayer Dependencies None (built into channels) Scaling A single process only Persistence Lost on restart Suitable for Local development, unit tests

InMemory limitation: with several Uvicorn workers, each one has its own InMemoryChannelLayer. Consumers in different workers do not see each other's messages.

docs.title: RedisChannelLayer (production)
docs.text:
CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels_redis.core.RedisChannelLayer",
        "CONFIG": {
            "hosts": [{
                "address": "redis://redis:6379/0",
                "socket_timeout": None,
                "socket_connect_timeout": 5,
                "health_check_interval": 30,
            }],
        },
    }
}
Property RedisChannelLayer Dependencies A Redis server, the channels_redis package Scaling Unlimited (Redis shared between workers) Persistence Messages persist in Redis until delivered Suitable for Production, Docker Compose

docs.title: CHANNEL_LAYERS configuration in settings.py
docs.text:
notes_chat_app automatically picks the channel layer depending on REDIS_URL:

# notes_project/settings.py

# Channel Layer — chosen depending on the environment
_REDIS_URL = os.environ.get('REDIS_URL')

if _REDIS_URL:
    # Docker / Production: RedisChannelLayer
    CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
        "default": {
            "BACKEND": "channels_redis.core.RedisChannelLayer",
            "CONFIG": {
                "hosts": [{
                    "address": _REDIS_URL,
                    # socket_timeout=None — CRITICAL for idle WS connections
                    # Without it channels_redis sets socket_timeout=5
                    # and brpop_timeout=5 conflict → TimeoutError after idling
                    "socket_timeout": None,
                    "socket_connect_timeout": 5,
                    # Checks Redis every 30 sec — prevents a silent disconnect
                    "health_check_interval": 30,
                }],
            },
        }
    }
else:
    # Local dev (no Redis): InMemoryChannelLayer
    CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
        "default": {
            "BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer",
        }
    }

docs.title: Redis DB 0 for Channels
docs.text:
In the setting "address": "redis://redis:6379/0", the 0 is the Redis database index.

Redis DB split (the default convention in notes_chat_app):
  redis://redis:6379/0  ← Django Channels (channel layer)
  redis://redis:6379/1  ← Celery (broker, if configured)

Why separate DBs?
  - Isolation: flushing the Celery queue will not touch WS messages
  - Debugging: redis-cli -n 0 KEYS '*' shows only the channels data
  - By default Redis has 16 DBs (0–15)

docs.title: socket_timeout=None: fixing TimeoutError on an idle WebSocket
The problem
docs.text:
channels_redis default: socket_timeout=5 (5 seconds)
channels_redis uses Redis BRPOP with timeout=5

On an idle WebSocket (nobody writes for > 5 sec):
  BRPOP timeout → channels_redis raises TimeoutError
  → The Consumer gets an exception → the WS connection is closed
  → The user sees: "Connection lost"

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
"CONFIG": {
    "hosts": [{
        "address": _REDIS_URL,
        "socket_timeout": None,          # ← None = no timeout, BRPOP waits indefinitely
        "socket_connect_timeout": 5,     # ← timeout only for establishing the connection (5 sec)
        "health_check_interval": 30,     # ← ping Redis every 30 sec (keeps the connection alive)
    }],
}

Why this is safe: - socket_timeout=None — aioredis has no socket timeout for read operations - BRPOP can wait indefinitely without an error - health_check_interval=30 — a ping every 30 sec so the connection to Redis doesn't silently "die" - nginx proxy_read_timeout=300s — nginx will not close the WS earlier than 5 minutes

docs.title: Detailed explanation
docs.text:
With socket_timeout=5 (the default):
  channels_redis opens an aioredis connection
  channels_redis calls BRPOP (block and pop) on Redis
  BRPOP waits for a new message...

  If there are no messages for 5 seconds:
    aioredis: socket timeout expired → raises TimeoutError
    channels_redis: does not handle it → the exception propagates up
    Consumer: gets an unhandled exception → disconnect
    Browser: WS close code 1006 (abnormal closure)
    JS client: "Connection lost" → will try to reconnect

With socket_timeout=None:
  BRPOP waits indefinitely
  health_check_interval=30: a ping every 30 sec → keeps the Redis connection alive
  No spurious disconnects → the WS connection is stable

The Redis timeout fix in notes_chat_app

This fix is applied in notes_project/settings.py; see the comment next to CHANNEL_LAYERS. socket_timeout=None in the RedisChannelLayer CONFIG fixes TimeoutError on idle WebSocket connections.

docs.title: Full settings check
docs.text:
# Check in the Django shell:
docker compose exec web python manage.py shell

>>> from channels.layers import get_channel_layer
>>> layer = get_channel_layer()
>>> print(type(layer).__name__)
# Expected: RedisChannelLayer (if REDIS_URL is set)
# or:       InMemoryChannelLayer (if REDIS_URL is missing)

>>> import asyncio
>>> asyncio.run(layer.send('test-channel', {'type': 'test'}))
# If there is an exception — Redis is unavailable or the configuration is wrong

docs.title: Full configuration: routing.py and asgi.py
docs.text:
Why: Channels is not just settings. You also need a WebSocket URL router and an ASGI application.

# notes_project/routing.py — WebSocket URL patterns
from django.urls import re_path
from notes_app import consumers

websocket_urlpatterns = [
    # group_pk → scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk'] in the consumer
    re_path(r'^ws/groups/(?P<group_pk>\d+)/chat/$', consumers.GroupChatConsumer.as_asgi()),
]

# notes_project/asgi.py (without the long comments)
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
from django.contrib.staticfiles.handlers import ASGIStaticFilesHandler

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')

# CRITICAL: django.setup() via get_asgi_application() BEFORE app-level imports!
# If you import consumers BEFORE this call → AppRegistryNotReady
django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application()

from channels.routing import ProtocolTypeRouter, URLRouter
from channels.auth import AuthMiddlewareStack
from notes_project.routing import websocket_urlpatterns

application = ProtocolTypeRouter({
    # HTTP → the standard Django ASGI handler (+ /static/ via ASGIStaticFilesHandler)
    "http": ASGIStaticFilesHandler(django_asgi_app),

    # WebSocket → AuthMiddlewareStack → URLRouter → Consumer
    "websocket": AuthMiddlewareStack(
        URLRouter(websocket_urlpatterns)
    ),
})

What each middleware does:

Middleware Role AllowedHostsOriginValidator Rejects WS connections whose Origin is not in ALLOWED_HOSTS (not used in the project; see below) AuthMiddlewareStack Reads the session cookie → populates scope["user"] URLRouter Routes the URL /ws/groups/7/chat/ to GroupChatConsumer

The real asgi.py has no AllowedHostsOriginValidator. For production it is worth adding as protection against Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking: "websocket": AllowedHostsOriginValidator(AuthMiddlewareStack(URLRouter(websocket_urlpatterns))) (imported from channels.security.websocket).

docs.title: Debugging: why the WebSocket does not connect
Step 1 — Browser DevTools → Network → WS
docs.text:
F12 → Network tab → "WS" filter
Open the chat page.

What to look for:
1. Did a WebSocket request appear in the list?
   ─ It did NOT appear → JS does not call new WebSocket(...)
                        → check whether group_chat.js is included
   ─ It appeared → click on it → Status → Messages

2. Status 101 Switching Protocols → WS established ✓
3. Status 403 → the consumer called close() before accept() (not logged in
                or not a group member); with AllowedHostsOriginValidator, also a foreign Origin
4. Status 404 → URL not found → check routing.py
5. Status 500 → error in the Consumer or asgi.py → check the logs

The Messages tab in DevTools: 

▲ sent   → {"content": "Hi"}   (JavaScript → server)
▼ receive → {"type": "message", "message_id": 42, "author": "alice", "content": "Hi", "timestamp": "..."}  (server → browser)

docs.title: Step 2 — Django/Uvicorn logs
docs.text:
# View the logs in real time:
docker compose logs -f web

# Typical messages for a successful WS:
# INFO    WebSocket CONNECT /ws/groups/7/chat/ [127.0.0.1:54321]
# INFO    WebSocket DISCONNECT /ws/groups/7/chat/ [127.0.0.1:54321]

# AuthMiddlewareStack error:
# ERROR   Exception inside application: ...
# → check the import order in asgi.py (django.setup() first!)

docs.title: Step 3 — Check the channel layer
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py shell

from channels.layers import get_channel_layer
import asyncio

layer = get_channel_layer()
print(type(layer).__name__)
# → RedisChannelLayer (if REDIS_URL is set)
# → InMemoryChannelLayer (if REDIS_URL is missing)

# Send/receive test:
async def test_layer():
    await layer.send('test-ch', {'type': 'hello'})
    msg = await layer.receive('test-ch')
    print(msg)  # → {'type': 'hello'}

asyncio.run(test_layer())
# If TimeoutError or ConnectionRefusedError → Redis is unavailable

docs.title: nginx: WebSocket headers — required settings
docs.text:
If Django Channels runs behind nginx (Docker production), nginx must pass the WebSocket Upgrade headers. Without them, the WS handshake will fail even if Django is configured correctly.

# nginx/nginx.conf

http {
    # ── WebSocket Upgrade mapping ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # $http_upgrade = the "Upgrade" header from the browser ("websocket" or "")
    # If Upgrade: websocket → $connection_upgrade = "upgrade"
    # If plain HTTP → $connection_upgrade = "close"
    map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
        default upgrade;
        ""      close;
    }

    upstream django {
        server web:8001;   # "web" — the DNS name of the Django container
    }

    server {
        listen 80;

        location / {
            proxy_pass http://django;

            proxy_set_header Host              $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

            # ── WEBSOCKET UPGRADE (critical!) ─────────────────────────────
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            # ↑ WS requires HTTP/1.1 (keep-alive).
            #   Without it nginx downgrades → HTTP/1.0 → Upgrade is ignored
            #   → WS handshake fails → browser 400 or 101 followed by an immediate close

            proxy_set_header Upgrade    $http_upgrade;
            proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
            # ↑ Pass Upgrade: websocket and Connection: upgrade on to Uvicorn
            #   Uvicorn sees these headers → switches protocol → ASGI WS scope

            proxy_read_timeout 300s;   # WS can live for 5 minutes without activity
            proxy_connect_timeout 75s;
            proxy_send_timeout 300s;
        }
    }
}

What breaks without proxy_http_version 1.1: 

Browser: WebSocket Error: Connection closed before receiving a handshake response
nginx log: 400 Bad Request (WS Upgrade rejected)

docs.title: Common errors table
docs.text: Symptom Cause Solution WS connection 404 routing.py is not wired in or the URL pattern is wrong Check websocket_urlpatterns and the URL in the JS WS connection 403 The consumer rejected the handshake (not logged in or not a group member); or AllowedHostsOriginValidator rejects the Origin, if it was added Log in / check the membership; for the validator, add the hostname to ALLOWED_HOSTS AppRegistryNotReady in asgi.py consumers imported before get_asgi_application() Move the imports after django_asgi_app = get_asgi_application() WebSocket does not work (HTTP OK) daphne is not first in INSTALLED_APPS Move 'daphne' to the first position TimeoutError after idling socket_timeout=5 in RedisChannelLayer Set socket_timeout=None Chat does not sync between tabs InMemoryChannelLayer instead of Redis Check REDIS_URL, switch to RedisChannelLayer nginx: Connection closed before handshake Missing proxy_http_version 1.1 or Upgrade headers Add all 4 WebSocket proxy directives ASGI_APPLICATION not found Wrong path in settings.py ASGI_APPLICATION = 'notes_project.asgi.application' WebSocket 101 but the chat is silent The channel group is split across processes InMemoryChannelLayer in multi-worker mode: each worker has its own memory

docs.title: 7B. Consumer
docs.text: A Consumer is the equivalent of a view, but: - It lives for the whole duration of the connection (not a single request) - It runs as an async coroutine - It handles events: connect, receive, disconnect, channel layer events

docs.title: Consumer lifecycle
docs.text:
The browser opens the chat tab:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. connect()                                     │
  │    ├── checks authentication (is_authenticated)  │
  │    ├── checks membership                         │
  │    ├── group_add() → subscribes to the channel   │
  │    ├── accept() → confirms the WS connection     │
  │    └── send() history × N messages               │
  │                                                   │
  │ 2. receive() ← the browser sent a message        │
  │    ├── validates content                          │
  │    ├── save_message() → PostgreSQL               │
  │    └── group_send() → broadcast to everyone      │
  │                 │                                 │
  │ 3. chat_message() ← the channel layer delivered  │
  │    └── send() → sends to the browser             │
  │                                                   │
  │    (2 and 3 repeat N times)                      │
  │                                                   │
  │ 4. disconnect()                                   │
  │    └── group_discard() → unsubscribes            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The difference between receive() and chat_message()
docs.text:
receive()      — the browser of THIS connection sent a message
chat_message() — the channel layer delivered a broadcast from any participant

When Olya sends "Hi":
  Olya's consumer:   receive() → group_send("chat_group_7", {...})
  Olya's consumer:   chat_message() ← channel layer → send() → Olya's browser
  Masha's consumer:  chat_message() ← channel layer → send() → Masha's browser
  Viktor's consumer: chat_message() ← channel layer → send() → Viktor's browser

docs.title: GroupChatConsumer: the full code
docs.text:
# notes_app/consumers.py
import json

from channels.db import database_sync_to_async
from channels.generic.websocket import AsyncWebsocketConsumer
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group

from .models import ChatMessage


class GroupChatConsumer(AsyncWebsocketConsumer):
    """
    WebSocket consumer for the group chat.

    URL: /ws/groups/<group_pk>/chat/

    Client → Server:
        {"content": "Message text"}

    Server → Client (history):
        {"type": "history", "message_id": 1, "author": "...", "content": "...", "timestamp": "..."}

    Server → Client (live):
        {"type": "message", "message_id": 2, "author": "...", "content": "...", "timestamp": "..."}
    """

    async def connect(self):
        self.user = self.scope['user']

        # 1. Authentication: not logged in → close() before accept() → handshake rejected
        if not self.user.is_authenticated:
            await self.close()
            return

        # 2. group_pk from the URL kwargs (the \d+ regex in routing.py guarantees digits)
        self.group_pk = int(self.scope['url_route']['kwargs']['group_pk'])

        # 3. Membership check (ORM in a worker thread)
        is_member = await self.check_membership(self.group_pk, self.user)
        if not is_member:
            await self.close()
            return

        # 4. Channel group name
        self.room_group_name = f"chat_group_{self.group_pk}"

        # 5. Subscribe to the channel group
        await self.channel_layer.group_add(
            self.room_group_name,
            self.channel_name,
        )

        # 6. Accept the connection
        await self.accept()

        # 7. Send the history (the last 50 messages)
        history = await self.load_history(self.group_pk)
        for msg in history:
            await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({
                'type': 'history',
                'message_id': msg['id'],
                'author': msg['author__username'],
                'content': msg['content'],
                'timestamp': msg['timestamp'].isoformat(),
            }))

    async def disconnect(self, close_code):
        # hasattr check: in case connect() finished before group_add
        if hasattr(self, 'room_group_name'):
            await self.channel_layer.group_discard(
                self.room_group_name,
                self.channel_name,
            )

    async def receive(self, text_data):
        try:
            data = json.loads(text_data)
            content = data.get('content', '').strip()
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, AttributeError):
            return

        # Basic validation: an empty or too long message is silently ignored
        if not content or len(content) > 2000:
            return

        msg = await self.save_message(self.group_pk, self.user, content)

        await self.channel_layer.group_send(
            self.room_group_name,
            {
                'type': 'chat_message',
                'message_id': msg.id,
                'author': self.user.username,
                'content': content,
                'timestamp': msg.timestamp.isoformat(),
            }
        )

    async def chat_message(self, event):
        await self.send(text_data=json.dumps({
            'type': 'message',
            'message_id': event['message_id'],
            'author': event['author'],
            'content': event['content'],
            'timestamp': event['timestamp'],
        }))

    # ─── ORM helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

    @database_sync_to_async
    def check_membership(self, group_pk, user):
        try:
            group = Group.objects.get(pk=group_pk)
            return group.user_set.filter(pk=user.pk).exists()
        except Group.DoesNotExist:
            return False

    @database_sync_to_async
    def load_history(self, group_pk):
        qs = (
            ChatMessage.objects
            .filter(group_id=group_pk)
            .select_related('author')
            .order_by('-timestamp')[:50]
        )
        messages = list(qs.values('id', 'author__username', 'content', 'timestamp'))
        messages.reverse()
        return messages

    @database_sync_to_async
    def save_message(self, group_pk, user, content):
        return ChatMessage.objects.create(
            group_id=group_pk,
            author=user,
            content=content,
        )

Compared with an "ideal" consumer, the decisions here are deliberately simple:

  • a refusal (not is_authenticated, not a group member) is a plain await self.close() without a custom code. Because accept() has not been called yet, the server rejects the handshake (HTTP 403), and the browser sees onclose with code 1006;
  • an empty or too long (> 2000 characters) message is just ignored; no error is sent to the client. The client-side limit is maxlength="2000" on the <input>;
  • every frame carries message_id (the ChatMessage record id), which the JS client stores in data-message-id.

The full docstrings with explanations are in the file notes_app/consumers.py itself.

docs.title: database_sync_to_async: why the ORM needs a wrapper
docs.text: The Django ORM is synchronous. Running sync code directly in an async context blocks the event loop and raises SynchronousOnlyOperation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
# ❌ WRONG — SynchronousOnlyOperation:
async def connect(self):
    group = Group.objects.get(pk=self.group_pk)
    # ↑ sync ORM in an async context → blocks the event loop → exception

# ✅ CORRECT — @database_sync_to_async:
@database_sync_to_async
def check_membership(self, group_pk, user):
    # A regular sync def
    # @database_sync_to_async runs it in the Django thread pool
    # The event loop is free while the thread executes the SQL
    try:
        group = Group.objects.get(pk=group_pk)
        return group.user_set.filter(pk=user.pk).exists()
    except Group.DoesNotExist:
        return False

async def connect(self):
    is_member = await self.check_membership(self.group_pk, self.user)
    # await = "run it in the thread pool and wait for the result without blocking the event loop"

docs.title: How it works under the hood
docs.text:
Event loop (one thread):
  coroutine connect() is running...

  → encounters: await self.check_membership(...)
  → @database_sync_to_async: submit to the thread pool executor
  → Event loop: keeps serving OTHER connections

Thread pool (a separate thread):
  → executes the sync Django ORM query (SELECT ... FROM ...)
  → returns the result

Event loop:
  → receives the result from the thread pool
  → resumes the coroutine connect() from the next line

docs.title: Critical: return a list, not a QuerySet
docs.text:
# ❌ WRONG — the QuerySet is lazy and gets iterated in the async context:
@database_sync_to_async
def load_history(self, group_pk):
    return ChatMessage.objects.filter(group_id=group_pk).values(...)
    # The QuerySet has not executed the SQL! The SQL runs on iteration.
    # Iteration happens in the async context → SynchronousOnlyOperation

# ✅ CORRECT — list() forces the SQL in the worker thread:
@database_sync_to_async
def load_history(self, group_pk):
    qs = (
        ChatMessage.objects
        .filter(group_id=group_pk)
        .select_related('author')
        .order_by('-timestamp')[:50]
    )
    messages = list(qs.values('id', 'author__username', 'content', 'timestamp'))
    # list() executes the SQL HERE, in the worker thread
    messages.reverse()  # chronological order
    return messages      # a Python list — safe to return

docs.title: database_sync_to_async as an inline wrapper
docs.text:
# Option 1: decorator (most common)
@database_sync_to_async
def save_message(self, group_pk, user, content):
    return ChatMessage.objects.create(group_id=group_pk, author=user, content=content)

# Option 2: inline wrapper (for one-off operations)
async def receive(self, text_data):
    msg = await database_sync_to_async(ChatMessage.objects.create)(
        group_id=self.group_pk,
        author=self.user,
        content=content,
    )
Wrapper When to use In this project database_sync_to_async Django ORM (optimized for Django DB connections) check_membership, load_history, save_message sync_to_async Any sync code without the DB (in async_services.py for create_note)

docs.title: How the channel layer delivers a message to all participants
docs.text:
The channel layer is the message bus for Django Channels.
Each Consumer subscribes to a "group" (a named channel).
group_send() → delivers to ALL subscribers of the group.

Channel layer state for the chat of group 7:
  Group "chat_group_7":
    ├── Viktor's consumer (channel_name: "specific.abc123")
    ├── Olya's consumer   (channel_name: "specific.def456")
    └── Masha's consumer  (channel_name: "specific.ghi789")

docs.title: The group_send flow
docs.text:
Viktor sends "Hi":

1. Viktor's consumer: receive("Hi")
2. Viktor's consumer: group_send("chat_group_7", {
       'type': 'chat_message',
       'message_id': 42,
       'author': 'Viktor',
       'content': 'Hi',
       'timestamp': '2025-01-01T12:00:00',
   })

3. The channel layer finds the group "chat_group_7"
   → Viktor's consumer: chat_message(event) → send() → Viktor's browser
   → Olya's consumer:   chat_message(event) → send() → Olya's browser
   → Masha's consumer:  chat_message(event) → send() → Masha's browser

Result: "Hi" appears simultaneously in all three browsers.

docs.title: type → method mapping
docs.text:
# 'type' in group_send → the method name in the Consumer
# Dot → underscore:

group_send(room, {'type': 'chat_message', ...})     → Consumer.chat_message(event)
group_send(room, {'type': 'chat.message', ...})     → Consumer.chat_message(event)
group_send(room, {'type': 'user.joined', ...})      → Consumer.user_joined(event)
group_send(room, {'type': 'typing.indicator', ...}) → Consumer.typing_indicator(event)

An important detail: type: 'chat_message' in group_send() → Django Channels automatically looks for the chat_message() method on the Consumer. A dot in the type → an underscore.

docs.title: InMemoryChannelLayer: pub/sub in memory
docs.text:
Channel layer state when 3 users have opened the chat of group 7:

  Viktor's channel_name: "specific.abc123"
  Olya's channel_name:   "specific.def456"
  Masha's channel_name:  "specific.ghi789"

  group "chat_group_7" → subscribers: ["specific.abc123", "specific.def456", "specific.ghi789"]

Olya sends "Hi":
  Olya's consumer: group_send("chat_group_7", {type: "chat_message", content: "Hi"})
                    │
                    ├── the channel layer finds all subscribers of chat_group_7
                    │
                    ├── delivers the event to Viktor's consumer → chat_message() → send("Hi")
                    ├── delivers the event to Olya's consumer   → chat_message() → send("Hi")
                    └── delivers the event to Masha's consumer  → chat_message() → send("Hi")

Result: "Hi" appears simultaneously in all three browsers.

InMemoryChannelLayer is in-process, for a single server. For production with several servers, channels-redis is used (a channel layer over Redis). In this project settings.py picks RedisChannelLayer when REDIS_URL is set (that is how the Docker stack runs), and InMemoryChannelLayer only locally without Redis. The pub/sub logic is the same for both.

docs.title: What to check in connect()
docs.text:
The full list of checks for a secure Consumer (as they are implemented in notes_app/consumers.py):

Check Code Reaction in the project Authentication if not self.user.is_authenticated close() before accept() Group membership check_membership(group_pk, user) close() before accept() Valid group_pk the (?P<group_pk>\d+) regex in routing.py a non-numeric URL matches no route Group exists except Group.DoesNotExist in check_membership close() before accept() JSON validity except (json.JSONDecodeError, AttributeError) in receive() (ignore) Empty content if not content (ignore) Content length len(content) > 2000 (ignore)

close() without an argument passes no custom code: the handshake is rejected, and the browser gets onclose with code 1006. Custom codes (for example, 4001 for not authenticated, 4003 for no access) can be added as an improvement: await self.close(code=4003). Then the client can tell a refused access from a network drop.

docs.title: disconnect() cleanup
docs.text:
async def disconnect(self, close_code):
    # The hasattr check is MANDATORY:
    # If connect() finished before group_add (for example, authentication was refused),
    # room_group_name may not exist → AttributeError
    if hasattr(self, 'room_group_name'):
        await self.channel_layer.group_discard(
            self.room_group_name,
            self.channel_name,
        )

docs.title: The full flow: from pressing Enter to the message appearing for everyone
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Viktor_JS as Viktor's browser (JS)
    participant Viktor_WS as Viktor's consumer
    participant ChannelLayer as Channel layer
    participant Olya_WS as Olya's consumer
    participant Olya_JS as Olya's browser (JS)
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    Viktor_JS->>Viktor_WS: ws.send({content: "Hi!"})
    Viktor_WS->>DB: save_message() via database_sync_to_async
    DB-->>Viktor_WS: ChatMessage(id=42, timestamp=...)
    Viktor_WS->>ChannelLayer: group_send("chat_group_7", {type:"chat_message", ...})
    par channel layer broadcast
        ChannelLayer->>Viktor_WS: chat_message(event)
        ChannelLayer->>Olya_WS: chat_message(event)
    end
    Viktor_WS->>Viktor_JS: ws.onmessage({type:"message", author:"Viktor", ...})
    Olya_WS->>Olya_JS: ws.onmessage({type:"message", author:"Viktor", ...})
    Note over Viktor_JS,Olya_JS: "Hi!" appears simultaneously in both browsers

This whole path happens without a single HTTP request. Only WebSocket frames.
