docs.title: Nginx
docs.text: Nginx as a reverse proxy: the browser does not connect to Uvicorn directly. Nginx accepts the connection, terminates SSL, serves static files, and proxies everything else.

docs.title: Nginx architecture in this stack
docs.text:
Browser → nginx:80 → routing:

  GET /static/css/main.css
    → alias /staticfiles/css/main.css   ← from the volume, without Django
    → 200 with Cache-Control: max-age=604800

  GET /notes/
    → proxy_pass http://web:8001/notes/  ← HTTP to Uvicorn
    → Django view → HTML → nginx → browser

  WebSocket UPGRADE /ws/groups/7/chat/
    → proxy_http_version 1.1
    → proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade    ← REQUIRED!
    → proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade
    → proxy_pass http://web:8001/ws/groups/7/chat/
    → Uvicorn ASGI → GroupChatConsumer → persistent

docs.title: nginx.conf — complete, with comments
docs.text:
worker_processes auto;   # auto = number of CPU cores
# 2 cores → 2 worker processes

events {
    worker_connections 1024;   # simultaneous connections per worker process
    # 2 cores × 1024 = 2048 simultaneous connections
}

http {
    include /etc/nginx/mime.types;   # .css → text/css, .js → application/javascript

    # ── WebSocket Upgrade handling ────────────────────────────────────────────
    # $http_upgrade = the "Upgrade" header from the browser ("websocket" or "")
    # If the browser sends Upgrade: websocket → $connection_upgrade = "upgrade"
    # If it is a regular HTTP request (Upgrade = "") → $connection_upgrade = "close"
    map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
        default upgrade;
        ""      close;
    }

    # ── Upstream: Django/Uvicorn ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    upstream django {
        server web:8001;   # "web" — DNS name of the service in the Docker network app-net
        # You can add several: server web2:8001; → load balancing
    }

    server {
        listen 80;
        # In production: listen 443 ssl; + ssl_certificate

        client_max_body_size 10M;   # maximum upload size (forms with files)

        # ── Static files (nginx serves them directly) ────────────────────────
        location /static/ {
            alias /staticfiles/;   # volume from collectstatic (web → nginx)
            expires 7d;            # the browser caches for 7 days
            add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
            # "immutable": the browser does not check freshness (files have a hash in their names)
        }

        # ── Everything else → Uvicorn ────────────────────────────────────────
        location / {
            proxy_pass http://django;

            # The client's real IP (without these headers Django sees the nginx IP):
            proxy_set_header Host              $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

            # ── WEBSOCKET UPGRADE (critical!) ─────────────────────────────
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            # ↑ WebSocket requires HTTP/1.1 (connection keep-alive)
            # Without this nginx downgrades to HTTP/1.0 → Upgrade headers are ignored
            # → WS handshake fails → the browser gets 400, or 101 followed immediately by close

            proxy_set_header Upgrade    $http_upgrade;
            proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
            # ↑ We pass Upgrade: websocket and Connection: upgrade on to Uvicorn
            # Uvicorn sees these headers → switches protocol → ASGI WS scope

            proxy_read_timeout 300s;    # a WS connection may live 5 minutes without activity
            proxy_connect_timeout 75s;  # limit for establishing a connection to the upstream
            proxy_send_timeout 300s;    # limit for sending the response to the client
        }
    }
}

docs.title: How staticfiles gets to nginx
docs.text:
1. Dockerfile COPY . .
   → the whole project in /app/

2. entrypoint.sh:
   python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
   → Django collects all static files into STATIC_ROOT (/app/staticfiles/)
   → CSS from crispy_forms, JS, admin, icons — all in one place

3. docker-compose.yml:
   web:   volumes: - staticfiles:/app/staticfiles   ← web WRITES here
   nginx: volumes: - staticfiles:/staticfiles:ro    ← nginx READS here (read-only!)

4. nginx.conf:
   location /static/ { alias /staticfiles/; }      ← nginx → volume → file

→ GET /static/admin/css/base.css
  → nginx → /staticfiles/admin/css/base.css
  → 200 without Python!

docs.title: STATIC_ROOT in settings.py
docs.text:
# settings.py
STATIC_URL = '/static/'

# collectstatic copies all static files here:
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles'   # /app/staticfiles

# Where Django looks for static files (besides <app>/static/):
STATICFILES_DIRS = []  # Django finds <app>/static/ automatically

docs.title: Without nginx vs with nginx
docs.text:
Without nginx:
  Browser → Django/Uvicorn → reads CSS/JS from disk → returns it
  A Python process is involved for every static file

With nginx:
  Browser → nginx → reads CSS/JS from disk directly → returns it
  Django/Uvicorn is not involved at all

Nginx serves static files 5–10x faster and frees Python workers
to handle real requests.

docs.title: WebSocket proxy — why HTTP/1.1 is needed
docs.text:
HTTP/1.0: every request = a new connection
HTTP/1.1: keepalive — the connection stays open

WebSocket Upgrade handshake:
  GET /ws/groups/7/chat/ HTTP/1.1  ← 1.1 is REQUIRED
  Upgrade: websocket
  Connection: Upgrade

If nginx proxies as HTTP/1.0:
  the Upgrade header is ignored
  → the handshake fails
  → the WS connection is not established
  → the browser gets 400 or 404

proxy_http_version 1.1 in location / is a mandatory directive for WebSocket support.

docs.title: Nginx in production (with SSL)
docs.text:
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name your-domain.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/ssl/cert.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/ssl/key.pem;

    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    ssl_ciphers HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5;

    location /static/ {
        alias /staticfiles/;
        expires 7d;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://django;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    }
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name your-domain.com;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;  # HTTP → HTTPS redirect
}

docs.title: Ngrok
docs.text: Why ngrok: localhost:80 is not reachable from the internet. ngrok creates a public HTTPS URL that tunnels to your nginx.

docs.title: How ngrok works
docs.text:
Browser on the Internet → ngrok servers → tunnel → Docker nginx → Django

Without ngrok:
  Django is available only on localhost — nobody else can reach it

With ngrok:
  ngrok provides a public URL: https://fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app
  All traffic from the Internet → ngrok servers → your nginx:80

docs.title: ngrok in Docker Compose
docs.text:
ngrok:
  image: ngrok/ngrok:latest
  command: http --url=${NGROK_DOMAIN} nginx:80
  # ↑ "http" = HTTP tunnel (ngrok adds HTTPS on the client side)
  # --url: a fixed domain (requires ngrok Pro or a static domain)
  # nginx:80 = where to forward traffic (Docker internal DNS)
  environment:
    NGROK_AUTHTOKEN: ${NGROK_AUTHTOKEN}
  ports:
    - "4040:4040"   # ngrok web UI: inspect HTTP traffic
  depends_on:
    nginx: {condition: service_healthy}   # wait for nginx
  networks: [app-net]

The .env file:

NGROK_AUTHTOKEN=2abc123_your_real_token_here
NGROK_DOMAIN=fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app

You can get an NGROK_AUTHTOKEN and reserve a free static domain at dashboard.ngrok.com.

docs.title: Problem: CSRF + ngrok
docs.text:
Symptom: you open https://my-domain.ngrok-free.app/accounts/login/, enter your credentials → 403 Forbidden: CSRF verification failed.

Cause:

POST /accounts/login/ HTTP/1.1
Host: fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app
Origin: https://fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app
X-CSRFToken: abc123...

Django checks the Origin header:
  Is "https://fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app" in CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS?
  CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = []   ← empty → 403

Solution in settings.py:

# settings.py
import os

_ngrok_domain = os.environ.get('NGROK_DOMAIN', '')

CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = (
    [f'https://{_ngrok_domain}']
    if _ngrok_domain else []
)
# CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = ['https://fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app']

# The domain must also be allowed in ALLOWED_HOSTS:
_allowed = os.environ.get('ALLOWED_HOSTS', 'localhost,127.0.0.1')
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [h.strip() for h in _allowed.split(',')]
# + add the ngrok domain:
if _ngrok_domain:
    ALLOWED_HOSTS.append(_ngrok_domain)

In docker-compose.yml:

web:
  environment:
    NGROK_DOMAIN: ${NGROK_DOMAIN}   # pass it from .env into the container

docs.title: How the value is passed along
docs.text:
.env:
  NGROK_DOMAIN=fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app

docker-compose.yml:
  web.environment.NGROK_DOMAIN: ${NGROK_DOMAIN}
  → passes it into the container

settings.py:
  _ngrok_domain = os.environ.get('NGROK_DOMAIN', '')
  CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = ['https://fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app']
  ALLOWED_HOSTS += ['fawn-natural-mayfly.ngrok-free.app']

Django:
  POST /login/ → Origin check → trusted → 200 OK

docs.title: Problem: ERR_NGROK_8012 — no such host nginx
docs.text:
Symptom: ngrok starts, but shows ERR_NGROK_8012: failed to connect to upstream: no such host nginx.

Cause: the ngrok container cannot find nginx by its DNS name. Usually this is because there is no shared network.

Solution: an explicit named network on ALL services:

# Solution: an explicit named network on ALL services
networks:
  app-net:
    driver: bridge

services:
  nginx:
    networks: [app-net]
  ngrok:
    networks: [app-net]   # ← both in app-net → DNS resolution of "nginx" ✓

Without an explicit named network, Docker may create separate automatic networks for different services, and they will not see each other by DNS name.

docs.title: Another problem: ERR_NGROK_334 — session limit
docs.text:
Symptom: ERR_NGROK_334: session limit exceeded.

Cause: ngrok is already running locally AND in Docker — one domain allows only one active connection.

# ❌ Error: ngrok is running both locally and in Docker
ngrok http --url=my-domain.ngrok-free.app 80 &   # locally
docker compose up                                  # ngrok in Docker
# → ERR_NGROK_334: session limit exceeded

# ✅ One way at a time:
# Option A: only through Docker (recommended)
docker compose up -d

# Option B: only locally
ngrok http --url=my-domain.ngrok-free.app 80

docs.title: ngrok dashboard
docs.text:
http://localhost:4040   ← ngrok web UI

It lets you:

  • View all HTTP requests going through the tunnel in real time
  • See request and response headers
  • See the request body (JSON, forms)
  • Replay requests (send the same POST again)
  • Check the CSRF token in the cookie and the POST body

Useful for debugging CSRF: open Inspector → POST /accounts/login/

→ Cookies: csrftoken=<value>
→ Body: csrfmiddlewaretoken=<value>
→ Do they match?

docs.title: NGROK_DOMAIN and NGROK_AUTHTOKEN env vars
docs.text:
Variable Where to get it Why NGROK_AUTHTOKEN dashboard.ngrok.com/authtokens Authenticates the ngrok agent NGROK_DOMAIN dashboard.ngrok.com/domains A fixed public URL (1 free static domain per account)

Without NGROK_DOMAIN, ngrok generates a random URL on every start. With NGROK_DOMAIN the URL is always the same — useful for CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS in settings.py.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: Key difference from SQLite: PostgreSQL is a separate service on the network. Django connects through DATABASE_URL (we parse the connection string in settings.py).

docs.title: How Django connects to PostgreSQL
docs.text:
# notes_project/settings.py
import os
import re

_DATABASE_URL = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')
if not _DATABASE_URL:
    raise Exception("DATABASE_URL не встановлено. Запускай через docker compose.")

# Parse the URL manually
_m = re.match(r'postgres://([^:]+):([^@]+)@([^:]+):(\d+)/(.+)', _DATABASE_URL)
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'NAME':     _m.group(5),
        'USER':     _m.group(1),
        'PASSWORD': _m.group(2),
        'HOST':     _m.group(3),   # ← Docker DNS: "db" → container IP
        'PORT':     _m.group(4),
        'CONN_MAX_AGE': 0,
    }
}

Without DATABASE_URL — an Exception, not SQLite

settings.py has no SQLite fallback. If DATABASE_URL is not set, the application raises an Exception immediately on startup. Always run it through docker compose.

DATABASE_URL in docker-compose.yml looks like this:

web:
  environment:
    DATABASE_URL: postgres://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}
    #                                                               ↑
    #                                          "db" — the service's DNS name in the Docker network app-net

docs.title: Internal DNS in the Docker network
docs.text:
docker-compose.yml:
  services:
    db:    ← service name = DNS name
    redis:
    web:
    nginx:

In the app-net network:
  "db"     → IP of the db container    (postgres)
  "redis"  → IP of the redis container
  "web"    → IP of the web container   (uvicorn)
  "nginx"  → IP of the nginx container

DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/notes_db
                                    ↑
                              Docker DNS resolution

docs.title: Why not SQLite in production
docs.text:
SQLite PostgreSQL Concurrent writes One writer, file locking MVCC — thousands of writers WebSocket + ORM Conflicts with concurrent WS No conflicts Transactions Limited Full ACID + SERIALIZABLE Indexing Basic GIN, GiST, partial indexes Scale ~100K rows comfortably Billions of rows Docker A file inside the container (gets lost!) Separate service + volume

The critical SQLite problem in Docker:

Without a named volume:
  docker compose down → container is removed → db.sqlite3 is removed
  docker compose up   → new DB → all data is lost!

With PostgreSQL + named volume:
  docker compose down → container is removed → the postgres_data volume remains
  docker compose up   → PostgreSQL attaches to the volume → data is preserved

docs.title: Migrations in Docker
docs.text:
Migrations run automatically on every docker compose up through entrypoint.sh:

python manage.py migrate --noinput

Other useful commands:

# Manually (if you need to apply them without restarting):
docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate

# Check the migration state:
docker compose exec web python manage.py showmigrations

# Create a new migration (after changing models.py):
docker compose exec web python manage.py makemigrations

# Connect to PostgreSQL directly:
docker compose exec db psql -U notes_user -d notes_db

# View the tables:
\dt
\d notes_app_note    # schema of a specific table
\q                   # quit

docs.title: CONN_MAX_AGE — persistent connections
docs.text:
# settings.py
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        ...,
        'CONN_MAX_AGE': 0,  # async-compatible: 0 = new connections every time
    }
}

Why CONN_MAX_AGE = 0 for ASGI:

CONN_MAX_AGE > 0 enables persistent connections through thread-local storage. In synchronous WSGI Django, each request is handled in its own thread, so a persistent connection is safe. In asynchronous Uvicorn, one thread serves several coroutines at the same time. If a persistent connection is shared between coroutines → a race condition at the DB connection level.

CONN_MAX_AGE = 60  (bad for ASGI):
  coroutine A → got a connection from the pool
  coroutine B → tries to use the same connection
  → Unpredictable errors or race conditions

CONN_MAX_AGE = 0  (correct for ASGI):
  coroutine A → opens a new connection → query → closes it
  coroutine B → opens a new connection → query → closes it
  → Isolated connections, no conflicts

The Django documentation recommends CONN_MAX_AGE = 0 when using an ASGI server.

docs.title: Data across restarts
docs.text:
docker compose down        # stops the containers, the volume is kept
docker compose up          # postgres_data → data is preserved

docker compose down -v     # -v: removes volumes → the DB is wiped

# docker-compose.yml
volumes:
  postgres_data:    # named volume

services:
  db:
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

docker compose down -v

The -v flag removes all named volumes, including postgres_data. All data in the DB will be destroyed. Use it only when you want a full reset.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text: What to check before you open access to real users.

docs.title: Why you need a checklist
docs.text:
Dev and production are different environments. Django has convenient defaults for dev (DEBUG=True, SQLite, InMemory channels), but they are completely unsafe for production. A checklist helps you not miss a single critical change.

Dev:   DEBUG=True   → stack trace with SECRET_KEY is visible → attacker forges cookies
Prod:  DEBUG=False  → empty 500 error, SECRET_KEY hidden

Dev:   SQLite       → file is destroyed on docker compose down
Prod:  PostgreSQL   → named volume, data persists between restarts

Dev:   InMemory     → WebSocket only within one process
Prod:  Redis        → broadcast between several workers

Dev:   runserver    → WSGI, single-threaded, no static files
Prod:  Uvicorn + nginx → ASGI, several workers, static without Python

docs.title: Security (mandatory)
docs.text:
• [ ] SECRET_KEY — unique, 50+ characters, generated with get_random_secret_key()
  • [ ] DEBUG = False — NEVER True in production
  • [ ] ALLOWED_HOSTS — specific domains, not ['*']
  • [ ] CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS — contains the prod domain and the ngrok domain
  • [ ] SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True — cookie over HTTPS only
  • [ ] CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
  • [ ] SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True — HTTP → HTTPS redirect
  • [ ] SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000 — HSTS for 1 year
  • [ ] .env is in .gitignore — check git status before pushing
  • [ ] Passwords are in .env, not in the code or the Dockerfile

docs.title: HTTPS settings in settings.py
docs.text:
# settings.py — uncomment when you have an SSL certificate:
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True    # cookie over HTTPS only
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True      # HTTP → HTTPS redirect
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000  # the browser remembers HTTPS for 1 year
SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True
SECURE_HSTS_PRELOAD = True

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• [ ] Remove --reload from entrypoint.sh (uvicorn)
  • [ ] Add --workers 4 to uvicorn (4 = 2 × CPU cores)
  • [ ] CONN_MAX_AGE = 0 for ASGI (async-compatible)
  • [ ] nginx expires 7d for static files (caching)
  • [ ] PostgreSQL max_connections matches the number of uvicorn workers
  • [ ] Redis maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (don't let Redis fill up RAM)

docs.title: Production entrypoint.sh
docs.text:
# entrypoint.sh in production — remove --reload, add --workers:
exec python -m uvicorn notes_project.asgi:application \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 8001 \
    --workers 4

docs.title: Django deployment check
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py check --deploy

It shows warnings about security settings. In production they should all be green.

# With DEBUG=True (expected in dev):
WARNINGS:
?: (security.W004) You have not set a value for the SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS setting.
?: (security.W008) Your SECRET_KEY has less than 50 characters.
?: (security.W012) SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is not set to True.
?: (security.W016) You have 'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware' in your
   MIDDLEWARE, but you have not set CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE to True.

# With DEBUG=False and correct settings:
System check identified no issues (0 silenced).

docs.title: Generating a SECRET_KEY
docs.text:
# Option 1: Python (via Docker)
docker compose run --rm web python -c \
    "from django.core.management.utils import get_random_secret_key; print(get_random_secret_key())"

# Option 2: Python (locally)
python3 -c "from django.core.management.utils import get_random_secret_key; print(get_random_secret_key())"

# Option 3: OpenSSL
openssl rand -base64 50

# Option 4: Python secrets
python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(50))"

NEVER use

SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-...   ← generated by Django by default
SECRET_KEY=dev-secret-key-...    ← obviously a test key
Both of these values are public and do not protect cookies or HMAC signatures.

docs.title: 1. Check the tests
docs.text:
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests --failfast
# All tests must be green before deploying

docs.title: 2. Check migrations
docs.text:
docker compose exec web python manage.py showmigrations
# All migrations should have [X]
# If there is [ ] → migrate did not run or there is a new unapplied migration

docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate --check
# Returns exit code 1 if there are unapplied migrations

docs.title: 3. Check static files
docs.text:
docker compose exec nginx curl -I http://localhost/static/admin/css/base.css
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK → nginx serves static files correctly
# HTTP/1.1 404    → collectstatic did not run or the volume is not mounted

docker compose exec web python manage.py collectstatic --dry-run --noinput
# Shows what would be collected without actually copying

docs.title: 4. Check the list of environment variables
docs.text:
docker compose exec web env | sort | grep -vE 'PATH|HOME|USER|SHELL'
# Make sure these exist: SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, ALLOWED_HOSTS
# Make sure DEBUG=False
# Make sure SECRET_KEY != 'dev-secret-key-...'

docs.title: Monitoring and logging
docs.text:
• [ ] LOGGING in settings.py → files or stdout for Docker
  • [ ] nginx access log → analysis (Grafana Loki or ELK)
  • [ ] Health check endpoints respond
  • [ ] Uptime monitor (UptimeRobot, Better Stack)
# settings.py — basic logging configuration:
LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'disable_existing_loggers': False,
    'formatters': {
        'verbose': {
            'format': '{levelname} {asctime} {module} {message}',
            'style': '{',
        },
    },
    'handlers': {
        'console': {
            'class': 'logging.StreamHandler',
            'formatter': 'verbose',   # stdout → docker logs → centralized logging
        },
    },
    'root': {
        'handlers': ['console'],
        'level': 'INFO',
    },
    'loggers': {
        'django.request': {
            'handlers': ['console'],
            'level': 'WARNING',       # only 4xx and 5xx, not every GET
            'propagate': False,
        },
    },
}

# View logs per service:
docker compose logs --since 1h web      # logs for the last hour
docker compose logs --since 1h nginx    # nginx access log
docker compose logs --since 1h --follow web  # live streaming

docs.title: Backing up PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Before any deploy that changes the schema — make a backup:

# Back up the DB to a file:
docker compose exec db pg_dump \
    -U notes_user \
    -d notes_db \
    -F c \
    -f /tmp/backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).dump

# Copy the backup from the container to the host:
docker cp $(docker compose ps -q db):/tmp/backup_*.dump ./backups/

# Restore from the backup:
docker compose exec db pg_restore \
    -U notes_user \
    -d notes_db \
    -F c \
    /tmp/backup.dump

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: If a deploy broke the application — the rollback plan:

docs.title: 1. Roll back the code (previous Docker image)
docs.text:
# Stop the current version:
docker compose down

# Build the previous image (if there is a tag):
git checkout v1.2.3
docker compose up --build

# Or use the cached image:
docker compose up    # no --build, uses the previous build

docs.title: 2. Roll back migrations
docs.text:
# View the list of migrations:
docker compose exec web python manage.py showmigrations notes_app

# Roll back to a specific migration:
docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate notes_app 0005
# ↑ rolls back 0006, 0007, ... to the state after 0005
# WARNING: deletes data from new columns!

Migrations with data

Rolling back a migration that removed a column → impossible (the data is already deleted). Rolling back a migration that added a column → safe (the empty column is simply removed). Always make a backup before a deploy with migrations.

docs.title: Common mistakes on the first deploy

docs.title: Redis and the Channel Layer
docs.text: The InMemoryChannelLayer problem: it keeps messages in the RAM of a single process. If you run 2 uvicorn workers, they cannot see each other → a broadcast will not get through. The Redis channel layer solves this with shared pub/sub.

docs.title: How RedisChannelLayer implements broadcast
docs.text:
Worker 1 (Viktor's Consumer)         Worker 2 (Olia's Consumer)
┌────────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────────┐
│  group_send(            │           │                        │
│    "chat_group_7", ... │──────────►│  Redis pub/sub         │
│  )                      │           │  channel: chat_group_7 │
└────────────────────────┘           │         │              │
                                     │         ▼              │
                                     │  chat_message()        │
                                     │  send() → Olia's browser│
                                     └────────────────────────┘

Redis as a shared message broker:
  Publish: Viktor's Consumer → Redis LPUSH chat_group_7_msgs ...
  Subscribe: Olia's Consumer ← Redis BRPOP chat_group_7_msgs

When Viktor sends a message, his Consumer calls group_send(), which publishes an event to Redis. All Consumers subscribed to the group's channel receive the event and send the message to their browsers. Olia sees Viktor's message in real time even if their Consumers are running in different uvicorn processes.

docs.title: Configuring the channel layer
docs.text:
# settings.py
_REDIS_URL = os.environ.get('REDIS_URL')

if _REDIS_URL:
    CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
        "default": {
            "BACKEND": "channels_redis.core.RedisChannelLayer",
            "CONFIG": {
                "hosts": [{
                    "address": _REDIS_URL,
                    # socket_timeout=None: no limit on reads
                    # (important for long-lived WS connections!)
                    "socket_timeout": None,
                    "socket_connect_timeout": 5,
                    # health_check_interval: Redis is pinged every 30 sec
                    # to detect and recover broken connections
                    "health_check_interval": 30,
                }],
            },
        }
    }
else:
    # Local dev without Docker — InMemory (a single process at a time)
    CHANNEL_LAYERS = {
        "default": {"BACKEND": "channels.layers.InMemoryChannelLayer"}
    }

REDIS_URL in docker-compose.yml:

web:
  environment:
    REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    #                   ↑      ↑  ↑
    #           DNS name    port  DB index
  • redis — the service's DNS name in the app-net Docker network
  • 6379 — the standard Redis port
  • /0 — database index (Redis supports 16 databases, 0–15)

docs.title: Redis DB 0 vs DB 1 — why they differ
docs.text:
This project uses only Redis DB 0. Projects with Celery often allocate separate databases:

Redis DB 0 → Channels (WebSocket pub/sub)
  REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
  → CHANNEL_LAYERS config → channels_redis

Redis DB 1 → Celery (task queue) — if Celery were used
  CELERY_BROKER_URL=redis://redis:6379/1
  → celery.app.conf.broker_url

The separation prevents key conflicts between different systems that write to the same Redis.

docs.title: socket_timeout=None — fixing TimeoutError
docs.text:
Symptom: the nginx log shows 101 (WS upgrade), then a minute later:

"Exception in ASGI application → TimeoutError reading from redis:6379"

Cause:

GroupChatConsumer.receive()
  → channel_layer.group_send()   ← publishes to Redis
  → channel_layer subscribes to the response

Redis responds using brpop_timeout=5 seconds
But if socket_timeout=5 (or less) in the Redis client:
  client-side timeout < server brpop timeout
  → redis.exceptions.TimeoutError
  → ASGI application ERROR
  → the WebSocket connection drops

Solution:

"socket_timeout": None,   # reads without a time limit

brpop_timeout on the server (5 sec) is a natural limit: after that time, if there are no new messages, the server returns None and the loop repeats. socket_timeout=None means the TCP socket is not closed by the client after a certain waiting time.

docs.title: daphne first in INSTALLED_APPS
docs.text:
# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'daphne',    # ← FIRST! Overrides runserver → ASGI instead of WSGI
    'channels',
    'django.contrib.admin',
    # ...
    'notes_app',
]

ASGI_APPLICATION = 'notes_project.asgi.application'

What happens if daphne is NOT first:

python manage.py runserver
# → Django uses the built-in WSGI server
# → WebSocket URL /ws/... → 404
# → GroupChatConsumer is unreachable
# → The group chat does not work

python manage.py runserver
# + daphne first:
# → daphne overrides the runserver command
# → ASGI server with an asyncio event loop
# → WebSocket + HTTP at the same time ✓

daphne intercepts the manage.py runserver command and starts an ASGI development server instead of the standard WSGI one. This is required for local development with WebSocket. In Docker production, uvicorn is used directly through entrypoint.sh — daphne takes no part in startup there, but it must stay first in INSTALLED_APPS for compatibility.

docs.title: Checking Redis in Docker
docs.text:
# Connect to Redis directly:
docker compose exec redis redis-cli

# Useful commands in redis-cli:
KEYS *            # all keys (careful on large DBs!)
TYPE <key>        # key type (string, list, set, zset, hash)
TTL <key>         # key TTL (-1 = no limit, -2 = does not exist)
MONITOR           # live stream of all commands sent to Redis (Ctrl+C to stop)

# Check active channel layer keys:
KEYS asgi.*
# asgi.* — the channels_redis prefix

docs.title: Seed Data
docs.text: seed_demo_data is a Django management command that fills the database with demo data for development. It lets you see the application right away with realistic notes, groups and chat.

docs.title: Why seed data
docs.text:
Problem: on the first docker compose up the database is empty. You see an empty application — no notes, no groups, the chat is silent. It is hard to show students what a real application looks like and hard to check the group features.

Solution: the seed command creates realistic demo data: - 3 users with passwords — you can log in right away - Groups with members — you can test group notes and chat in different tabs - Different kinds of notes (personal, group, pinned, with reminders) — all the functionality is visible - Messages in group chats — the chat doesn't look empty

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Login Password Role demo_alice demo1234 Member of "Команда розробки" and "Сімейний чат" demo_bob demo1234 Member of "Команда розробки" demo_carol demo1234 Member of "Команда розробки" and "Сімейний чат"

Each user has their own UserProfile.

docs.title: Groups and members
docs.text:
Group Members demo_команда_розробки ("Команда розробки", "Dev team") alice, bob, carol demo_сімейний_чат ("Сімейний чат", "Family chat") alice, carol

In the DB the group name carries the demo_ prefix (that prefix is what --reset uses). Alice and Carol are members of both groups → they see the group notes and chat of both groups; Bob only those of "Команда розробки".

docs.title: Each user's notes
docs.text:
Each of the three users gets the same set of 10 notes of their own:

Type Count Total (different priorities 1–3) 10 Pinned (is_pinned=True) 3 With reminders (Reminder) 4 Group (group="Команда розробки") 3

  • Tags: робота, особисте, навчання, важливо, ідеї, перечитати — each with a unique color
  • TodoList: 3 lists ("Задачі спринту", "Домашні справи", "Навчальний план"), the first two TodoItems in each are done
  • ShoppingList: 3 lists, one of them ("Спільні покупки для офісу") belongs to the "Команда розробки" group

docs.title: SEED_DEMO_DATA=1 at startup
docs.text:
When SEED_DEMO_DATA=1 is set in .env, seeding runs automatically on every docker compose up via entrypoint.sh:

# entrypoint.sh
if [ "${SEED_DEMO_DATA:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    seed_args="--force"
    if [ "${SEED_DEMO_RESET:-0}" = "1" ]; then
        seed_args="--force --reset"
    fi
    log "Seeding demo data with args: ${seed_args}"
    python manage.py seed_demo_data ${seed_args}
fi

# docker-compose.yml
web:
  environment:
    SEED_DEMO_DATA: ${SEED_DEMO_DATA:-1}
    # ↑ If .env does not contain SEED_DEMO_DATA — default 1 (seeding enabled)
    SEED_DEMO_RESET: ${SEED_DEMO_RESET:-0}

# .env:
SEED_DEMO_DATA=1   # enables auto-seeding on every docker compose up

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# First run (SEED_DEMO_DATA=1 in .env → automatic on docker compose up):
docker compose up

# Manually — first time (empty DB):
docker compose exec web python manage.py seed_demo_data

# Manually — reset and refill (DB already exists):
docker compose exec web python manage.py seed_demo_data --reset
# --reset: deletes all demo_* users and related data → seeds again

# Without the stack (separate container — only if the DB already has data from a previous up):
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py seed_demo_data

--force in entrypoint.sh

entrypoint.sh runs seed_demo_data --force (or --force --reset when SEED_DEMO_RESET=1). --force lets the seed run even when DEBUG=False; it does not delete existing data. The command is idempotent (update_or_create), so running it again creates no duplicates. --reset first deletes the demo data, then seeds again.

docs.title: Check that the seed worked
docs.text:
# Quick check through the shell:
docker compose exec web python manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from notes_app.models import Note, ChatMessage
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group

print('Users:', User.objects.count())
print('Notes:', Note.objects.count())
print('Groups:', Group.objects.count())
print('ChatMessages:', ChatMessage.objects.count())
"

# Expected output:
# Users: 3
# Notes: 30
# Groups: 2
# ChatMessages: 30 (or more)
# (on a clean DB; the command also prints its own summary after seeding)

# Or directly in PostgreSQL:
docker compose exec db psql -U notes_user -d notes_db -c "
SELECT username FROM auth_user WHERE username LIKE 'demo_%';
"
#  demo_alice
#  demo_bob
#  demo_carol

docs.title: Debugging: when the seed doesn't work
CommandError: Demo data disabled
docs.text:
CommandError: Demo data seeding is disabled when DEBUG=False. Use --force to override.

Cause: seed_demo_data checks DEBUG = True. In production it is disabled by default so it doesn't overwrite real data.

Solution: entrypoint.sh already passes --force, so this error only happens when you run it manually without the flag.

# Correct for a manual run with DEBUG=False:
docker compose exec web python manage.py seed_demo_data --force

docs.title: IntegrityError: duplicate key
docs.text:
The current command is idempotent: it uses update_or_create, so running it again without --reset does not cause this error. It can only happen in your own seed commands that use create(), or when the data was changed by hand:

django.db.utils.IntegrityError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint
"auth_user_username_key"
DETAIL: Key (username)=(demo_alice) already exists.

Solution: 

docker compose exec web python manage.py seed_demo_data --reset
# --reset deletes existing demo_ users before creating new ones

docs.title: DB is not initialized
docs.text:
django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to server

Cause: you tried to run the seed before docker compose up or after docker compose down -v.

Solution: 

docker compose up -d
# Wait until the web container becomes healthy
docker compose ps    # web: healthy?
docker compose exec web python manage.py seed_demo_data

docs.title: Selenium in Docker
docs.text: Difference from the previous steps: here Selenium runs in a separate container (not locally). The Django test server and Chrome are in different containers — a special configuration is needed.

docs.title: Problem: localhost ≠ localhost between containers
docs.text:
WITHOUT Docker Selenium (previous steps):
  Runner VM: Django test server (localhost:PORT) + Chrome (localhost:PORT) ✓
  Chrome sees Django at localhost → OK

With Docker Selenium:
  web container: Django test server (localhost:PORT)
  selenium container: Chrome
    Chrome: http://localhost:PORT → NOT FOUND!
    localhost in the selenium container = the IP of the selenium container itself
    NOT the IP of the web container!

docs.title: The Selenium service in docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
selenium:
  image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
  ports:
    - "4444:4444"    # WebDriver API (used by test_selenium.py)
    - "7900:7900"    # VNC (you can watch the browser live: http://localhost:7900)
  shm_size: '2g'     # Chrome needs shared memory
  networks: [app-net]

selenium/standalone-chrome is the official Selenium image with Chrome built in. It runs selenium-server on port 4444, which webdriver.Remote connects to.

shm_size: '2g' — Chrome uses shared memory (/dev/shm) for rendering. Without it, Chrome crashes when opening complex pages.

Environment variables in the web service for Selenium:

web:
  environment:
    WEB_HOST:            web              # DNS name of the web container
    SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL: http://selenium:4444/wd/hub

docs.title: Solution: _DockerLiveServerMixin
docs.text:
# notes_app/tests/test_selenium.py

class _DockerLiveServerMixin:
    """
    Lets Selenium in a Docker container see the Django test server.

    Problem: LiveServerTestCase usually binds to 127.0.0.1 (localhost only).
    Solution: bind to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) → reachable from the selenium container.

    Also replaces 0.0.0.0 with "web" in live_server_url:
    http://0.0.0.0:PORT → http://web:PORT
    "web" is the DNS name of the web container in the Docker network app-net.
    """
    host = '0.0.0.0'   # StaticLiveServerTestCase.host

    @property
    def live_server_url(self):
        url = super().live_server_url           # http://0.0.0.0:PORT
        web_host = os.environ.get('WEB_HOST')  # = "web" (from the docker-compose.yml env)
        if web_host:
            return url.replace('0.0.0.0', web_host)  # http://web:PORT
        return url


def _make_driver():
    """Returns a Chrome WebDriver: Remote (Docker) or local."""
    remote_url = os.environ.get('SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL')
    # = http://selenium:4444/wd/hub (from docker-compose.yml env web.environment)

    if remote_url:
        # Docker: Chrome runs in the selenium container
        options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
        options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
        options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage')
        # headless is not needed: selenium/standalone-chrome is already headless
        return webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=remote_url,
            options=options,
        )
    else:
        # Locally (without Docker): Chrome on the same machine
        options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
        options.add_argument('--headless')
        options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
        return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)


@unittest.skipUnless(SELENIUM_AVAILABLE, "selenium not installed")
class SeleniumLoginFlowTest(_DockerLiveServerMixin, StaticLiveServerTestCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.driver = _make_driver()
        cls.driver.implicitly_wait(5)  # wait up to 5 sec for an element

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        cls.driver.quit()
        super().tearDownClass()

    def _login_via_cookie(self):
        """Fast login via the session cookie (without the form)."""
        # 1. The Test Client creates a session in the DB
        self.client.force_login(self.user)
        session_cookie = self.client.cookies['sessionid']

        # 2. The browser must be on the domain before add_cookie
        self.driver.get(f'{self.live_server_url}/')

        # 3. Copy the session cookie into Selenium
        self.driver.add_cookie({
            'name': 'sessionid',
            'value': session_cookie.value,
            'path': '/',
        })
        # Now the driver is logged in = the same user as self.client

docs.title: Running with docker compose exec (not run!)
docs.text:
# ❌ WRONG — docker compose run:
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium
# run creates a NEW container
# The new container does not have the DNS alias "web" in the network
# Selenium tries GET http://web:8001/... → Cannot resolve host

# ✅ CORRECT — docker compose exec:
docker compose up -d   # bring the stack up first
docker compose exec web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2
# exec runs INSIDE the already running web container
# the web container is already registered in the Docker network with the alias "web"
# Selenium: GET http://web:8001/ → DNS resolution → IP of the web container

docs.title: Why exec and not run
docs.text:
docker compose run creates a new container from the same image. This container: - Has no registered DNS alias "web" in the app-net network (that alias is bound to the original running container) - Runs its own entrypoint.sh (migrate, collectstatic all over again) - Is isolated from selenium, nginx and the other services of the stack

docker compose exec runs the command inside the already running web container. This container: - Is already registered with the alias "web" in the Docker network - Selenium in the selenium container resolves http://web:PORT → the IP of this container - No repeated migrations or seeding

docs.title: VNC — watch the Selenium browser live
docs.text:
# http://localhost:7900  (password: secret)
# ↑ Opens a VNC viewer where you can see Chrome in real time

Useful for debugging Selenium tests: - You see exactly what the driver finds - You see the state of forms when errors occur - You see JavaScript alerts and popups - You understand why find_element cannot find an element

docs.title: Running all tests
docs.text:
# ─── Through Docker (recommended) ──────────────────────────────────────────

# All unit + integration + consumer tests (run is fine here):
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test \
  notes_app.tests.test_models \
  notes_app.tests.test_services \
  notes_app.tests.test_forms \
  notes_app.tests.test_views \
  notes_app.tests.test_consumers \
  -v 2

# Selenium E2E tests (EXEC, not RUN!):
docker compose up -d                    # bring the stack up first
docker compose exec web python manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_selenium -v 2

# A specific class:
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test \
  notes_app.tests.test_views.NoteListViewTest -v 2

# Stop at the first failure:
docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test notes_app.tests --failfast

# Coverage:
docker compose run --rm web sh -c "
  coverage run manage.py test notes_app.tests.test_models notes_app.tests.test_services \
    notes_app.tests.test_forms notes_app.tests.test_views notes_app.tests.test_consumers
  coverage report --show-missing
"
